PYQ-POL-C04AB45535F2.lead: Option 2: under the Fifth Schedule, transfer of tribal land in Scheduled Areas to private parties (e.g. for mining) can be held void.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Third Schedule
The Third Schedule contains forms of oaths and affirmations, not tribal land protection.
Fifth Schedule
The Fifth Schedule lets the Governor make regulations to prohibit or restrict transfer of land by or among tribals in Scheduled Areas (para 5(2)).
Ninth Schedule
The Ninth Schedule protects listed laws from challenge (Article 31B); it does not void land transfers.
Twelfth Schedule
The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 functional items of municipalities (74th Amendment), not tribal land.

points: In Samatha v. State of AP (1997) the Supreme Court held leases of tribal land in Scheduled Areas to private mining firms void.
This case arose from Visakhapatnam district of Andhra Pradesh.

PYQ-POL-229E9B90C393.lead: Option 3: the Ministry of Home Affairs grants citizenship, including naturalisation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
False: Parliamentary Affairs manages government business in Parliament, not citizenship.
2. Ministry of External Affairs
False: External Affairs handles passports and missions abroad, not grants of citizenship.
3. Ministry of Home Affairs
True: MHA (Foreigners Division) administers the Citizenship Act, 1955 — registration, naturalisation under Section 6, OCI and deprivation.
4. Ministry of Law and Justice
False: the Law Ministry gives legal advice and drafts laws, but does not grant citizenship.

points: Under Section 6, the 'Central Government' grants the naturalisation certificate; in practice this is done by MHA.

PYQ-POL-D14CF0BB7BA4.lead: Official key: option 4. Study answer: option 1 — certiorari brings up the records of a lower court for examination by a superior court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: to bring up the records from lower court for examination by the superior court
This is the literal meaning ('to be certified'): the higher court calls the record and quashes the order if there is excess of jurisdiction or error of law.
✓ study
to restrain the State in case of misuse of powers
Too general; restraining an authority is closer to prohibition or mandamus.
No
an administrative proceeding
Certiorari is a judicial remedy issued by the Supreme Court or a High Court, not an administrative proceeding.
No
based on reasonableness of State action
This is the official key, but certiorari does not re-judge reasonableness on merits; it checks jurisdiction and legal error.
Official key

points: Certiorari is curative (after the order) as well as preventive; prohibition is only preventive (before the order).
It is issued against judicial, quasi-judicial and (after 1991) administrative bodies affecting rights, but not against legislatures or private persons.
PYQ-POL-D14CF0BB7BA4.also: Disputed key: the official key is option 4; Laxmikanth describes certiorari as a higher court calling up a lower court's records, so option 1 is the better answer.

PYQ-POL-D94EAE4CD57E.lead: Option 2: the Government of India Act, 1919 introduced bicameralism for the first time.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Indian Council Act of 1909
It enlarged the single Imperial Legislative Council; it remained unicameral.
Government of India Act of 1919
It replaced the Indian Legislative Council with a Council of State (Upper House) and Legislative Assembly (Lower House).
Government of India Act of 1935
It extended bicameralism to six of eleven provinces, but the Centre already had two houses since 1919.
Indian Independence Act of 1947
It made the Constituent Assembly the legislature; it did not first introduce bicameralism.

points: The 1919 Act also brought direct elections for most members of both Houses.
Do not confuse: 1919 = bicameral Centre; 1935 = bicameral in six provinces.
PYQ-POL-D94EAE4CD57E.also: The 1919 Act is also called the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms.

PYQ-POL-118C09C6C90F.lead: Option 2: rights are moral claims which are recognised and protected by law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Rights are legal claims only
Too narrow — rights also have a moral base
Moral claims recognised and protected by law
Combines the moral base with legal protection — the fullest description
Privileges given by the government
Rights limit the government; they are not favours it can withdraw
Rules imposed on people
That describes duties or laws, not rights

points: Fundamental Rights are enforced through Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC).

PYQ-POL-127FAA08C067.lead: A.K. Gopalan (1950) is not a property case — it was about preventive detention and Article 21.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A.K. Gopalan v. State of Madras
1950 case on preventive detention; the Court read 'procedure established by law' narrowly as any procedure in a valid law.
Golaknath case
1967: held Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; arose from Punjab land-ceiling laws affecting the right to property.
Kesavananda Bharati case
1973: arose from Kerala land reform laws affecting property; it gave the basic structure doctrine.
Minerva Mills case
1980: arose from the takeover of a textile mill (property) under the Sick Textile Undertakings Act; struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment.

points: Three options are linked to land or property disputes; only Gopalan is about personal liberty.
Gopalan's narrow view of Article 21 was reversed in Maneka Gandhi (1978) (LX p148).

PYQ-POL-D0BF4054E3EA.lead: Option 3. Andaman-Cellular Jail, Chandigarh-Le Corbusier, DNH&DD-merged 26 January 2020.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Andaman and Nicobar
3. Archipelago, marine life, Cellular Jail
Port Blair (Sri Vijaya Puram since 2024).
B. Chandigarh
1. Le Corbusier's planning
Modernist city, capital of Punjab and Haryana.
C. DNH and Daman and Diu
2. Merger of two UTs on 26 Jan 2020
The two UTs were merged by the Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu (Merger of Union Territories) Act, 2019, effective 26 January 2020.

points: Option 1 fails: it pairs A-1 (should be 3), B-2 (should be 1), C-3 (should be 2).
Option 2 fails: it pairs A-2 (should be 3), C-3 (should be 2).
Option 4 fails: it pairs A-1 (should be 3), B-3 (should be 1).

PYQ-POL-E0E6B427AC4A.lead: Option 1: 'to safeguard public property and to abjure violence' is a Fundamental Duty, Article 51A(i).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Fundamental duty
These are the exact words of Article 51A(i) (LX p189).
2. Social ethic
Not a constitutional category; the Constitution places this in Part IVA.
3. Fundamental right
Rights in Part III are claims of the citizen against the State; this is an obligation of the citizen.
4. Directive principle
DPSPs in Part IV guide the State, not individual citizens.

points: It was among the ten duties added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
Laxmikanth: duties warn against anti-social acts like destroying public property (LX p190).
PYQ-POL-E0E6B427AC4A.also: Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) were based on the Swaran Singh Committee.

PYQ-POL-5F83A63BCFF6.lead: Option 3 (A-2, B-3, C-4, D-2) is correct: A. Article 39A → 42nd Amendment; B. New Article 45 → 86th Amendment; C. Article 43B → 97th Amendment; D. Article 48A → 42nd Amendment.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Article 39A
2 – 42nd Amendment
Article 39A (equal justice and free legal aid) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, so A matches 2.
B. New Article 45
3 – 86th Amendment
The new Article 45 (early childhood care and education below six) was substituted by the 86th Amendment, 2002, so B matches 3.
C. Article 43B
4 – 97th Amendment
Article 43B (co-operative societies) was inserted by the 97th Amendment, 2011, so C matches 4.
D. Article 48A
2 – 42nd Amendment
Article 48A (environment, forests and wildlife) was also inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, so D matches 2.

points: 1 (44th) and 5 (95th) are distractors: the 44th added 38(2), and the 95th only extended SC/ST seat reservation.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-1, B-2, C-2, D-3 (correct: A-2, B-3, C-4, D-2).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A-1, B-2, D-5 (correct: A-2, B-3, D-2).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-3, B-2, D-3 (correct: A-2, B-3, D-2).
PYQ-POL-5F83A63BCFF6.also: The 86th Amendment also added Article 21A and duty 51A(k).

PYQ-POL-A25C8BB32D7A.lead: Option 2: democratic countries are likely to have a constitution, because a democracy needs basic rules that limit rulers and protect rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: communist
One-party rule; such states may have a written text, but the party stands above it, so it does not truly limit power.
democratic
Rule by the people through elected representatives; it depends on agreed rules about elections, powers and rights, so it needs a constitution.
oligarchic
Rule by a small powerful group, which governs by its own will rather than settled rules.
totalitarian
Total control by one ruler or party; any constitution there is only for show.

points: NCERT: all democratic countries are likely to have a constitution.
A constitution that really limits power is called constitutionalism.

PYQ-POL-WEB-D916C5.lead: Option 1: the Preamble reflects the mind of the makers of the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Preamble
The Preamble: Berubari (1960) called it 'a key to open the mind of the makers'.
The Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights are detailed justiciable rights in Part III, not the summary of the makers' intention.
The Directive Principles of State Policy
Directive Principles are policy guidelines in Part IV, not the summary of intent.
The Fundamental Duties
Fundamental Duties (Part IVA) were added only in 1976, so they cannot show the original makers' mind.

points: LX p76: the Preamble embodies the basic philosophy and fundamental values of the Constitution.
It is based on Nehru's Objectives Resolution (1946).

PYQ-POL-APK-0D7261.lead: Option 4 (Article 21): the Supreme Court has read pollution-free air and water and a life with human dignity into the right to life.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 23
Article 23 bans traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour; the right to clean air and water is read into Article 21, not here.
Article 22
Article 22 gives safeguards on arrest and detention; the right to live with dignity and a clean environment comes from Article 21.
Article 20
Protection in respect of conviction for offences.
Article 21
Protection of life and personal liberty, widely read to include dignity and a clean environment.

points: Subhash Kumar v. State of Bihar (1991): pollution-free water and air are part of Article 21 (LX p136).
Francis Coralie Mullin (1981): life means more than animal existence; it includes living with human dignity.

PYQ-POL-APK-A3D863.lead: Option 4: A is false, but R is true — the term is not defined in the Constitution.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
False
False. The Constitution does not define 'judicial review'; the power comes from Articles 13, 32, 226 etc.
R
True
True. Indira Gandhi (1975) affirmed judicial review as a basic feature.

points: Does R explain A? Does not arise, because A is false.
Option 1 (Both A and R are true, and R explains A) fails: A is false, so "both true" is wrong.
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: A is false, so "both true" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: it reverses the truth values: R is the true one, A the false one.
PYQ-POL-APK-A3D863.also: Minerva Mills (1980) and L. Chandra Kumar (1997) also called it basic structure.

PYQ-POL-WEB-554C25.lead: Option 4 is not a feature: the Constitution does not make the judiciary supreme.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Provides a set of basic rules
True: the Constitution lays down the basic rules for how the State is organised.
✗ (is a feature)
Specifies the power of the Government
True: it defines and limits the powers of the legislature, executive and judiciary.
✗ (is a feature)
Supreme law of the land
True: every law must conform to it; laws violating it are void.
✗ (is a feature)
Specifies the supremacy of the judiciary
False: India has supremacy of the Constitution, not of the judiciary; courts are also bound by it.

points: Indian system is a synthesis of British parliamentary sovereignty and American judicial supremacy — neither is absolute.
Courts can strike down laws (judicial review), but Parliament can amend the Constitution within the basic structure.
So all three organs are under the Constitution.

PYQ-POL-WEB-DA2D02.lead: Option 2: the 73rd Amendment, 1992 created an elaborate system of Panchayati Raj institutions as units of rural self-government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Municipal self-government
Urban local bodies (municipalities) got constitutional status from the 74th Amendment, 1992, which added Part IXA and the Twelfth Schedule.
Panchayats as units of self-government
The 73rd Amendment added Part IX (Articles 243 to 243O) and the Eleventh Schedule with 29 subjects for panchayats.
Commission for Linguistic Minorities
The Constitution provides a Special Officer for Linguistic Minorities under Article 350B, inserted by the 7th Amendment, 1956, not a commission under the 73rd.
Creation of Jharkhand
Jharkhand was created in 2000 by the Bihar Reorganisation Act, an ordinary law under Article 3.

points: The 73rd Amendment came into force on 24 April 1993, celebrated as National Panchayati Raj Day.
Memory hook: 73 = village (rural), 74 = town (urban).

PYQ-POL-APK-18D905.lead: Nallapati Venkatramaiah was the first Speaker of the Andhra State Assembly (1953), so the answer is option 1.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Nallapati Venkatramaiah
Correct; Nallapati Venkatramaiah was the first Speaker of the Andhra State Assembly formed in 1953.
B.V. Subba Reddy
Not the first Speaker of the Andhra State Assembly
K.V. Vema Reddy
Not the first Speaker of the Andhra State Assembly
Divi Kondaiah Chowdary
Not the first Speaker of the Andhra State Assembly

points: Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953 with Kurnool as capital; T. Prakasam was its first Chief Minister.
PYQ-POL-APK-18D905.also: Ayyadevara Kaleswara Rao was the first Speaker of Andhra Pradesh (1956).

PYQ-POL-WEB-901592.lead: Option 3 (2 only): only the right to work is not a Fundamental Right; it is a Directive Principle under Article 41.

head: Right
Fundamental Right?
Why
rows: 1. Right to education
It is a Fundamental Right
Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) makes free and compulsory education for 6 to 14 year olds a Fundamental Right.
2. Right to work
Not a Fundamental Right
Article 41, a Directive Principle, asks the State to secure the right to work within its economic capacity; it is not enforceable in court.
3. Right to form associations
It is a Fundamental Right
Article 19(1)(c) gives citizens the right to form associations, unions and cooperative societies.
4. Right to practise any profession
It is a Fundamental Right
Article 19(1)(g) gives citizens the right to practise any profession or carry on any occupation, trade or business.

points: Option 1 (1 and 2) and option 4 (1 and 3) wrongly treat education or association as not Fundamental Rights.
Option 2 (2 and 4) wrongly treats the right to practise a profession as not a Fundamental Right.
The question asks which are NOT Fundamental Rights, so the true answer is the one that is a DPSP.

PYQ-POL-WEB-54D167.lead: Option 3: Article 51A(c) asks citizens to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: autonomy
Self-rule for a part or body, such as an autonomous council; not in the text of the duty.
authority
Power to give orders; not in the text of the duty.
sovereignty
India's supreme power to decide its internal and external matters, free from foreign control.
privacy
A person's right to be left alone; not in the text of the duty.

points: The duty protects the nation as a whole, so 'sovereignty, unity and integrity' go together.
PYQ-POL-WEB-54D167.also: The 42nd Amendment (1976) also added 'integrity' to the Preamble.

PYQ-POL-351D12726967.lead: Option 2: Granville Austin wrote 'The Indian Constitution: Cornerstone of a Nation' (1966).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Introduction to the Study of the Law of the Constitution
A.V. Dicey (1885) — source of the rule of law idea
The Indian Constitution — Cornerstone of a Nation
Granville Austin wrote this 1966 book, the classic study of how the Indian Constitution was framed, so it is the answer.
Some Characteristics of the Indian Constitution
This book (1953) is by Sir Ivor Jennings, who called the Indian Constitution a 'lawyers' paradise'; it is not Austin's.
Modern Constitutions
This book (1951) is by K.C. Wheare, who called India 'quasi-federal'; it is not Austin's.

points: His later book is 'Working a Democratic Constitution' (1999).
He called FRs and DPSPs together the 'conscience of the Constitution'.

PYQ-POL-B2F1F17082C9.lead: Option 3, Granville Austin, is correct: he wrote that the Directive Principles are 'aimed at furthering the goals of the social revolution'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Ambedkar
Ambedkar described the Directive Principles as a 'novel feature' of the Constitution, not in these words.
2. P. Nikore
P. Nikore is not linked to any well-known description of the Directive Principles; this is a distractor.
3. Austin
Granville Austin, the American scholar of the Indian Constitution, used exactly this phrase about the Directive Principles.
4. B.N. Rau
B. N. Rau, the Constitutional Adviser, said the Directive Principles are moral precepts for the authorities of the State; he did not use this phrase.

points: Austin also called the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together the 'conscience of the Constitution'.
The Supreme Court in Minerva Mills (1980) said FRs and DPSPs together form the core of the commitment to social revolution.

PYQ-POL-3570D718DFD1.lead: Option 4 (official key): freedom of speech and expression is the hallmark of democracy, because it lets people question and criticise rulers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Equality before law
Part of the rule of law; can exist in non-democracies too
Freedom of worship
A religious freedom, not the defining mark of democracy
Rule of law
Law above rulers; also found in non-democracies
Freedom of speech and expression
Core of democracy: open debate and criticism of government

points: Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression in India.

PYQ-POL-3BEC7C3FCF3F.lead: Option 3: the Executive implements laws and policies.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Judiciary
Courts — interpret laws and settle disputes
Legislature
The legislature (Parliament/State Assembly) makes laws; it does not implement them, so it is not the answer.
Executive
President/Governor, ministers and officials — carry out laws
NITI Aayog
Government policy think tank — not a branch of government

points: Three organs: legislature makes, executive implements, judiciary interprets.

PYQ-POL-659357BD4F25.lead: Option 4 (official key): a constitutional government is, by definition, a limited government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Government by legislature
Legislature holds main power — can still be unlimited
Popular government
Chosen by people — elected rulers can still abuse power
Multi-party government
Several parties compete — not the definition
Limited government
Rulers' power fixed and limited by the constitution; rights protected

points: LX: constitutionalism means limited government or limitation on government.

PYQ-POL-6CDBE365A0CD.lead: Option 1: parens patriae means the State acts as the legal guardian of people who cannot protect themselves.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Legal protection of citizens unable to protect themselves
Parens patriae is Latin for 'parent of the nation'; the State steps in as guardian of minors, persons of unsound mind and other helpless people.
Inconsistency between parts of legal instruments
This describes repugnancy or conflict between legal provisions, which courts resolve by rules of interpretation; it has nothing to do with guardianship.
Parliament cannot legislate on State matters
This describes the federal division of legislative powers (Seventh Schedule), not the guardian role of the State.
Court's duty to interpret legislation
This is the general function of judicial interpretation, not a doctrine about protecting the helpless.

points: The doctrine treats the State as a parent: when a person cannot look after his own rights, the State does it for him.
Memory hook: 'patria' = fatherland, 'parens' = parent, so 'the State as parent'.
PYQ-POL-6CDBE365A0CD.also: Supreme Court applied it in Charan Lal Sahu v. Union of India (1990), upholding the Bhopal Gas Leak Act under which the Union represented the victims.

PYQ-POL-805E3CF1DF20.lead: Option 2: despotism, unlimited and arbitrary rule, is the opposite of constitutionalism, which means limited government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Federalism
Division of power between Centre and states by the constitution; it limits power, so it is consistent with constitutionalism.
Despotism
Rule by one person whose will is law, with no legal limits; this is exactly what constitutionalism forbids.
Pluralism
Many groups share influence in society and politics; it supports limited government rather than opposing it.
Socialism
An economic idea of social ownership and equality; it is about economic policy, not about whether power is limited.

points: Constitutionalism = government limited by law; its antithesis is a government with no limits.
Memory hook: constitution 'limits'; despot 'unlimited'.

PYQ-POL-90CAF40678BB.lead: Option 2: audi alteram partem means 'hear the other side', that is, the right to be heard.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Rule against bias
This is the other natural-justice rule, nemo judex in causa sua: no one should be a judge in his own case.
Right to be heard
Audi alteram partem requires that a person be given notice and a fair chance to reply before a decision is taken against him.
Rule of reasonableness
This is the test that State action must not be arbitrary (Article 14); it is not this Latin maxim.
Right to free speech
This is a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(a), unrelated to the hearing rule.

points: Natural justice has two pillars: hear the other side (audi alteram partem) and no bias (nemo judex in causa sua).
Example: a student cannot be expelled without being told the charge and allowed to explain.
PYQ-POL-90CAF40678BB.also: Maneka Gandhi case (1978) read fair procedure and natural justice into Article 21.

PYQ-POL-9F7C6048D10E.lead: Option 1: democracy's special virtue is that it draws the intelligence and character of ordinary people into public life.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Intelligence and character of ordinary men and women
Democracy makes common citizens participate by voting, debating and holding office, so it develops their abilities and sense of responsibility.
Methods for strengthening executive leadership
A strong executive can exist in any system, including dictatorship, so this is not democracy's distinctive virtue.
A superior individual with dynamism and vision
Reliance on one great leader is the idea behind monarchy or dictatorship, not rule by the people.
A band of dedicated party workers
Party cadres matter in many systems, including one-party states; democracy's virtue is wider participation by all citizens.

points: The key word is 'ordinary': democracy rests on the belief that common people can govern themselves.
Thinkers like J.S. Mill praised democracy because participation educates and improves citizens.

PYQ-POL-A0049CBC7CEA.lead: Option 4: liberty in the political sense is the opportunity for each person to develop himself fully.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Protection against tyranny of rulers
This is one older, negative part of liberty, but it does not cover the full meaning of developing one's personality.
Absence of restraint
Pure absence of restraint is negative liberty; without any restraint the strong would oppress the weak.
Opportunity to do whatever one likes
This is licence, not liberty, because it allows a person to harm others' freedom.
Opportunity to develop oneself fully
This is the positive concept of liberty given by Laski and T.H. Green: conditions in which a person can realise his best self.

points: Laski: liberty is the eager maintenance of that atmosphere in which men have the opportunity to be their best selves.
Indian Preamble promises liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship for the same purpose.

PYQ-POL-B06E9B0825CA.lead: Option 1: a State has four elements: population, definite territory, government and sovereignty (independence from external control).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Permanent community, definite territory, independent, organised government
It includes all four elements: people, territory, government and sovereignty, so it is the complete definition.
Politically organised people under one government
It mentions people and government but leaves out territory and sovereignty, so a colony or province would also fit.
Territory, common language, culture, separate government
Common language and culture describe a nation, not a State; a State can have many languages, like India.
Central authority, independent judiciary, own constitution
An independent judiciary and written constitution are not essential elements; the UK has no codified constitution yet is a State.

points: Memory hook: P-T-G-S (Population, Territory, Government, Sovereignty).
Sovereignty is the element that separates a State from a province or colony.

PYQ-POL-B09D1B6C89A2.lead: Option 4: constitutional government means government whose powers are limited by the constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Representative and federal government
Representation and federalism are forms of organisation; a representative or federal government can still be unlimited.
Head of state is a nominal head
This describes the parliamentary form (like India's President), not the idea of limited government.
Head of state has real powers
This describes the presidential form (like the US), again a form of government, not a limit on power.
Government limited by the constitution
This is the meaning of constitutionalism: rulers act only within legal limits and rights are protected.

points: Options 2 and 3 are about who holds executive power; the question is about whether power is limited.
Constitutional government and constitutionalism are the same idea.

PYQ-POL-D3BAEB7426E8.lead: Option 4: constitutionalism recognises the need to limit the powers of government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Is inherent in every Constitution
False: a dictatorship can have a written constitution but no real limits, so having a constitution does not guarantee constitutionalism.
Connotes unlimited Government
False: unlimited government is the opposite of constitutionalism.
Means despotism
False: despotism, arbitrary rule by one person, is the antithesis of constitutionalism.
Recognises need for limitation of powers
True: constitutionalism means government is limited by law, with rights and checks such as separation of powers and judicial review.

points: Distinguish 'constitution' (a document) from 'constitutionalism' (the principle of limited government).
Memory hook: constitutionalism = limited government.

PYQ-POL-D642EA085CBA.lead: Option 3: 'Introduction to the Constitution of India' was written by Durga Das Basu.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: M.V. Pylee
A noted constitutional scholar who wrote 'Constitutional Government in India' and 'India's Constitution', but not the book with this title.
H.J. Tawke
Not a known author of a standard Indian constitutional text; a distractor.
D.D. Basu
Durga Das Basu, jurist, wrote 'Introduction to the Constitution of India' and the multi-volume 'Commentary on the Constitution of India'.
B.B. Tayal
Author of general Indian history and polity textbooks, not of this classic.

points: D.D. Basu's 'Introduction' is one of the most widely used reference books on the Indian Constitution.

PYQ-POL-DE0E2C074048.lead: Option 3: the chief purpose of a constitution is to define and limit the powers of government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Determines objectives for making laws
A constitution may guide law-making, but setting objectives for laws is not its chief purpose.
Creates political offices and government
It does create offices, but even a despot can create offices; the core aim is to restrain how they use power.
Defines and limits powers of government
This is the central purpose: it tells each organ what it can do and what it cannot, protecting citizens from abuse of power.
Secures social justice, equality and security
These are goals stated in some constitutions (e.g. India's Directive Principles), not the defining purpose of every constitution.

points: A constitution answers 'who has power, how much, and where it stops'.
The word 'best' asks for the core purpose, not every function.

PYQ-POL-E18B3A693082.lead: Option 1: despotism, absolute and unchecked rule, is the antithesis of constitutionalism.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Despotism
Unlimited, arbitrary rule by one person; constitutionalism exists to prevent exactly this.
Decentralisation of power
Spreading power to lower levels divides and checks power, so it supports constitutionalism.
Limited power
Limited power is the definition of constitutionalism itself, not its opposite.
Restraint of power
Checks and restraints on power are the tools of constitutionalism, not its opposite.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 all describe ways of limiting power, so they agree with constitutionalism.
Same idea as the other 'antithesis' question in this chapter.

PYQ-POL-EAA7A667FC02.lead: Option 4: reasonable laws ensure liberty; law and liberty are not enemies.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: More laws, less liberty
False as a rule: whether liberty shrinks depends on whether laws are reasonable, not on their number.
Laws are not needed for liberty
False: without law the strong dominate the weak, so liberty needs law to protect it.
Liberty only in absence of law
False: absence of law gives licence and anarchy, not liberty.
Reasonable laws ensure liberty
True: laws that restrain only harmful acts protect everyone's freedom equally.

points: John Locke: where there is no law, there is no freedom.
India follows this idea: Article 19 freedoms can be limited only by 'reasonable restrictions' under Article 19(2)–(6).

PYQ-POL-EB90B504ED58.lead: Option 4: separation of powers is the best safeguard of liberty, because no one organ can become all-powerful.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Committed and independent judiciary
Very helpful for protecting rights, but it is one organ; it works because power is already separated.
Centralisation of powers
Concentrating power in one hand threatens liberty; it is the opposite of a safeguard.
An elected government
Election makes a government legitimate, but an elected majority can still abuse unchecked power.
Separation of powers
Montesquieu argued that liberty is lost when legislative, executive and judicial powers are united in the same hands.

points: Montesquieu, 'The Spirit of the Laws' (1748), is the source of this doctrine.
An independent judiciary is itself a product of separation of powers.

PYQ-POL-F78D4EA5F73C.lead: Option 3: audi alteram partem means the right to be heard.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Right to modify a statement
No such principle is meant by this maxim; a distractor.
Right to consult a lawyer
This is a right of an arrested person under Article 22(1), not the hearing rule.
Right to be heard
The maxim means 'hear the other side': nobody should be decided against without notice and a fair chance to reply.
Produced before magistrate within 24 hours
This is a safeguard against arbitrary arrest under Article 22(2), not this natural-justice rule.

points: Options 2 and 4 are both Article 22 rights of arrested persons; do not confuse them with natural justice.
The other natural-justice rule is the rule against bias (nemo judex in causa sua).

PYQ-POL-WEB-5033D2.lead: Option 4: 'to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India' is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(c).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Preamble
The Preamble speaks of securing 'unity and integrity of the Nation' and fraternity, but does not contain this duty wording.
Directive Principles
DPSPs (Part IV, Articles 36–51) are directions to the State for welfare; they contain no such duty of citizens.
Fundamental Rights
FRs (Part III) are rights of individuals; sovereignty and integrity appear only as grounds for restricting freedoms (Article 19(2)).
Fundamental Duties
Article 51A(c) in Part IVA asks every citizen to uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India.

points: Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation; there are now 11 (86th Amendment, 2002, added the 11th).
Memory hook: 51A(a) respect Constitution, (b) ideals of freedom struggle, (c) sovereignty, unity and integrity.

PYQ-POL-0BC58F4CB541.lead: Only statement 2 is true, so option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Restricts individual liberty in the interest of State authority
False
Restricting liberty for the sake of State power is the mark of authoritarian rule, the opposite of constitutional government.
2. Restricts State authority in the interest of individual liberty
True
Constitutional government places effective limits on the State, through rights, separation of powers and judicial review, so that individuals stay free.

points: Options 1 and 3 wrongly accept statement 1.
Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 2.
Memory hook: constitutional government limits the State, not the citizen.

PYQ-POL-44F99D0A23D6.lead: Option 2: Argentina is a federal republic; Britain, Italy and France are unitary.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Britain
Unitary: a supreme Parliament can change devolved powers by ordinary law.
Argentina
Federal: its constitution divides powers between the national government and the provinces (LX p199).
Italy
Unitary, though it has strong regions (LX p199).
France
Unitary: power is centred in the national government (LX p199).

points: Same fact as the bank question on federations: Laxmikanth lists Argentina with the US, Canada, Australia, Brazil and Switzerland as federal.

PYQ-POL-8586B30A8AAA.lead: Option 4: a diverse society needs a constitution to provide basic rules that give coordination and assurance to all groups.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Enforce religious uniformity
Wrong: forcing one religion on all would destroy diversity, not manage it.
Let rulers dominate others
Wrong: a constitution is meant to limit rulers and prevent domination.
Erase all differences
Wrong: a constitution protects differences, for example through minority rights in Articles 29–30.
Provide fundamental rules for coordination and assurance
Correct: coordination means everyone knows the common rules; assurance means each group trusts that it will not be oppressed.

points: This is NCERT's explanation: the first function of a constitution is to provide basic rules that allow minimal coordination and trust among members of society.

PYQ-POL-A8B87FA08CBD.lead: Official key: option 4 (Parliamentary Supremacy). Study answer: option 2 (Distribution of Powers), the essential feature of every federal constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Supremacy of Judiciary
An independent judiciary is a federal feature, but 'supremacy of judiciary' is not essential; India balances judicial review with parliamentary power.
Distribution of Powers
Powers are divided between Centre and states by the constitution itself; in India through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Seventh Schedule (LX p201).
✓ (study)
Election Commission
A body that conducts elections (Article 324); unitary states also have such bodies, so it is not a federal feature.
Parliamentary Supremacy
This belongs to the British unitary system; in a federation the constitution, not Parliament, is supreme.
✗ (official key)

points: No federation can exist without two levels of government with their own constitutionally divided powers.
Laxmikanth lists dual polity, division of powers, supremacy of the Constitution, rigid Constitution, independent judiciary and bicameralism as federal features (LX p201).
Union List 98, State List 59, Concurrent List 52 subjects (LX p201).
PYQ-POL-A8B87FA08CBD.also: Disputed key: the official key (option 4, Parliamentary Supremacy) contradicts the standard federal features; parliamentary supremacy is a feature of unitary Britain. Study answer: option 2.

PYQ-POL-0415BF6A62B7.lead: Option 3: the Government of India Act, 1935 introduced federal features, provincial autonomy and three legislative lists.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. GoI Act 1858
Ended Company rule; created the Secretary of State and Council of India; a unitary set-up.
2. GoI Act 1919
Introduced provincial dyarchy and devolution of subjects, but no federation or provincial autonomy.
3. GoI Act 1935
Provided an All-India Federation, replaced dyarchy with provincial autonomy and created Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists.
4. Indian Councils Act 1909
Enlarged councils and introduced Muslim separate electorates.

points: Provincial autonomy meant provinces acted as autonomous units with ministers responsible to the legislature (1937-39).
The 1919 Act's central/provincial subject division was only by Devolution Rules, still a unitary structure.

PYQ-POL-24C9BCD0AD53.lead: Option 1: the Regulating Act, 1773 was the first Act to change the Company's constitution at home and its set-up in India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Regulating Act of 1773
First British Act to control and regulate the Company; changed the Court of Directors at home and created the Governor-General of Bengal and Supreme Court in India.
2. Pitt's India Act of 1784
Came later; set up the Board of Control (double government).
3. Charter Act of 1813
Ended the Company's trade monopoly in India (except in tea and trade with China); it came much later than 1773.
4. Government of India Act of 1858
Abolished the Company and transferred the government of India to the British Crown; it is the last, not the first.

points: The key word is 'first': 1773 began parliamentary control.
It also made Bombay and Madras subordinate to Bengal.

PYQ-POL-27CCA0D9C874.lead: Option 2: before 1950 India was governed by the Government of India Act, 1935 (as adapted).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Indian Constitution
Came into force only on 26 January 1950.
2. Government of India Act 1935
Continued as the working constitution till 1950, as adapted under the 1947 Act.
3. Indian Independence Act 1947
Ended British rule and created the dominions, but it was not the governing framework; it said the 1935 Act would govern.
4. All of the above
Wrong, because options 1 and 3 are wrong.

points: Concept: the 1947 Act gave independence; the 1935 Act gave the machinery of government.
Article 395 repealed both Acts in 1950.

PYQ-POL-4BADF252D10C.lead: Option 2: the Federal Court was constituted by the Government of India Act, 1935 and began in 1937.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Act of 1861
Indian Councils Act; associated Indians with law-making. No Federal Court.
2. Government of India Act, 1935
Provided for a Federal Court, set up in 1937, to decide Centre–province disputes.
3. Indian Councils Act, 1909
Morley–Minto reforms; separate electorates. No court.
4. Government of India Act, 1919
Dyarchy and bicameralism. No federal court, as there was no federation.

points: A federal court is needed only when powers are divided between Centre and units, which 1935 did.
Appeals still went to the Privy Council; the Supreme Court replaced the Federal Court on 28 January 1950.

PYQ-POL-5A2FBCF95E93.lead: Option 1: the Indian Independence Act ended British rule but gave no constitution; that task was left to the Constituent Assembly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Act without Constitution
True: it created India and Pakistan but empowered their Constituent Assemblies to frame constitutions.
2. Act with Constitution
False: no constitution was attached to the Act; framing it was left to the Constituent Assemblies.
3. Intended to retain British authority
False: it ended British rule, paramountcy and the Monarch's veto.
4. Formed a new policy for India
Vague; it transferred power rather than framing a policy.

points: Until the Constitution came, the adapted 1935 Act governed.
The Assemblies could even repeal the Independence Act itself.

PYQ-POL-5C880C101932.lead: Option 3 (A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4) is correct: put the events in time order - Simon 1927, Third RTC 1932, Cripps 1942, Cabinet Mission 1946.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Simon Commission
The Simon Commission was appointed in November 1927, two years before the date fixed by the 1919 Act, to review how that Act was working; so A matches 1927.
B. Cabinet Mission
1946; proposed the Constituent Assembly.
C. Third Round Table Conference
Third RTC in 1932 (Nov-Dec); Congress stayed away; led towards the 1935 Act.
D. Cripps Mission
Cripps Mission 1942 offered dominion status after World War II; Congress rejected it.

points: Option 1 fails: A-4 (1942) is wrong, A matches 3; D-3 (1927) is wrong, D matches 4.
Option 2 fails: A-1 (1946) is wrong, A matches 3; B-2 (1932) is wrong, B matches 1; C-3 (1927) is wrong, C matches 2.
Option 4 fails: B-2 (1932) is wrong, B matches 1; C-4 (1942) is wrong, C matches 2; D-1 (1946) is wrong, D matches 4.

PYQ-POL-66196D92202E.lead: ICS exam started in India in 1922 at Allahabad; 1919 Act did not provide it.

head: Stmt
Claim (short)
True/False — why
rows: A
1919 Act provided simultaneous ICS exam
False — came by later rules, not the Act
B ✓
First held at Allahabad, 1922
True — later shifted to Delhi

PYQ-POL-66196D92202E.also: The 1919 Act provided for a Public Service Commission, set up in 1926 on Lee Commission advice.

PYQ-POL-69615026E205.lead: Option 1: before the Constitution of 1950, India was governed by the Government of India Act, 1935.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Government of India Act 1935
Real Act; the working framework till 26 January 1950, as adapted in 1947.
2. Government of India Act 1918
No such Act; 1918 was the year of the Montagu–Chelmsford Report, which led to the 1919 Act.
3. Government of India Act 1945
No such Act exists; it is a distractor. The 1935 Act governed India until 1950.
4. Government of India Act 1948
No such Act exists; it is a distractor. After 1947 India was governed by the adapted 1935 Act.

points: The real Government of India Acts in this period are 1858, 1919 and 1935.
The 1935 Act had 321 sections and 10 schedules, the largest pre-independence Act.

PYQ-POL-697113E4B777.lead: A, B and D are features; C is not. So option 4 (A, B and D only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Federation and provincial autonomy
True
The 1935 Act provided an All-India Federation and replaced dyarchy with provincial autonomy.
B. Dyarchy at the Centre
True
Federal subjects were split into reserved and transferred, though this provision never came into operation.
C. Dyarchy in provinces
False
Provincial dyarchy came in 1919; the 1935 Act abolished it.
D. Distribution of legislative powers
True
Powers were divided into Federal, Provincial and Concurrent Lists.

points: Options 2 and 3 wrongly include C; option 1 drops true D.
Hook: 1935 moved dyarchy up from the provinces to the Centre.
PYQ-POL-697113E4B777.also: The All-India Federation never came into being as princely states did not join.

PYQ-POL-754D885A6A48.lead: Option 2: 'Union List' is not a 1935 Act list; it is the name in today's Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Federal List
The 1935 list of the Centre's subjects (59 items).
Not the answer (was in the Act)
2. Union List
List I of the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution of India.
✓ (not a 1935 list)
3. Provincial List
The 1935 list of provinces' subjects (54 items).
Not the answer (was in the Act)
4. Concurrent List
The 1935 list for both Centre and provinces (36 items).
Not the answer (was in the Act)

points: The 1935 Act called the Centre 'Federal', so its list was the Federal List; the Constitution calls it the 'Union'.
Today Article 246 has Union, State and Concurrent Lists.

PYQ-POL-970DAE9B4BE7.lead: Option 2 (1928): the Nehru Report, drafted by a committee under Motilal Nehru, was the first attempt by Indians to write a constitution for India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: No draft constitution was produced in 1926; the Simon Commission and Birkenhead's challenge came only in 1927.
The All Parties Conference committee under Motilal Nehru submitted its report (the Nehru Report) in August 1928.
1930 is the year of the Simon Commission report and the First Round Table Conference, not the Nehru Report.
1932 is the year of the Communal Award and the Poona Pact, not a draft constitution.

points: Lord Birkenhead challenged Indians to frame an agreed constitution, and the all-British Simon Commission (1927) angered Indian parties; the Nehru Report was the answer.
It demanded Dominion Status, a list of fundamental rights and joint electorates with reserved seats for minorities.
Memory hook: Simon came in 1927, Nehru replied in 1928.

PYQ-POL-A4A9ECBB89B5.lead: Option 3: the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of our Constitution are modelled on the three lists of the Government of India Act, 1935.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Morley-Minto Reforms, 1909
The Indian Councils Act, 1909 enlarged legislative councils and brought separate electorates for Muslims; it did not divide powers.
Montagu-Chelmsford Act, 1919
The 1919 Act only separated central and provincial subjects through Devolution Rules inside a unitary set-up, with dyarchy in provinces.
Government of India Act, 1935
It divided powers into a Federal List (59 items), Provincial List (54) and Concurrent List (36), the direct model for the Seventh Schedule.
Indian Independence Act, 1947
The 1947 Act ended British rule and created two Dominions; it did not lay down a scheme of division of powers.

points: Seventh Schedule today: Union, State and Concurrent Lists, a direct copy of the 1935 scheme.
Under 1935, residuary powers lay with the Governor-General; today they lie with Parliament under Article 248.
PYQ-POL-A4A9ECBB89B5.also: The 1935 Act also gave the Governor's office, Federal Court, PSCs and emergency provisions.

PYQ-POL-A9DF03A1C244.lead: Option 3 (A, D, B, C): Cripps Mission 1942, Mountbatten Plan 3 June 1947, Indian Independence Act July 1947, Constitution passed 26 November 1949.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: D, A, B, C
Wrong: it puts the Mountbatten Plan (1947) before the Cripps Mission (1942).
A, B, D, C
Wrong: the Independence Act (July 1947) was passed to carry out the Mountbatten Plan (June 1947), so D must come before B.
A, D, B, C
Correct: Cripps (March 1942) → Mountbatten Plan (3 June 1947) → Independence Act (18 July 1947) → Constitution adopted (26 November 1949).
D, A, C, B
Wrong: it starts with 1947 and places the 1949 Constitution before the 1947 Act.

points: Logic link: the Mountbatten Plan proposed partition, and the Independence Act gave legal effect to that plan, so plan comes before Act.
The Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949 and came into force on 26 January 1950.

PYQ-POL-APK-00C0EF.lead: Option 4: Crown sovereignty, a 20-year renewal, end of trade monopoly except tea and China trade, and a grant for education all belong to the Charter Act of 1813.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Charter Act of 1833
It ended the Company's commercial activities altogether and made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India.
Charter Act of 1793
It extended the Company's trade monopoly for another 20 years; it did not end the monopoly or assert Crown sovereignty.
Charter Act of 1853
It separated the legislative and executive work of the Governor-General's council and introduced open competition for civil services, with no fixed time period.
Charter Act of 1813
It asserted the British Crown's sovereignty over Company territories, opened Indian trade to all British merchants except tea and China trade, and set aside ₹1 lakh for literature and science.

points: Statement 4 (the one-lakh grant for revival of literature and promotion of science) is the strongest clue for 1813.
Order of trade: 1793 extended monopoly → 1813 ended it except tea and China → 1833 ended all trade.
PYQ-POL-APK-00C0EF.also: The 1813 Act also allowed Christian missionaries to come to India.

PYQ-POL-APK-0809CC.lead: Option 4 (1909): the Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) formally introduced elected members in the legislative councils.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1906 is the year the Muslim League was founded; no constitutional Act was passed.
1907 is the Surat split of the Congress, not an Act of Parliament on Indian government.
No Government of India or Councils Act was passed in 1908.
The Indian Councils Act, 1909 raised the Central council from 16 to 60 members and brought election, including separate electorates for Muslims.

points: The 1892 Act only allowed indirect 'nomination on recommendation'; the word election was not used. The 1909 Act openly used election.
Lord Minto came to be called the 'Father of Communal Electorate'.
The question loosely calls it a 'Government of India Act'; its proper name is the Indian Councils Act, 1909.

PYQ-POL-APK-5C810F.lead: Option 3: the Regulating Act made the Court of Directors report to the British Government on revenue, civil and military affairs of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Board of Control of six commissioners incl. two Cabinet ministers
False for 1773: the Board of Control was created by Pitt's India Act, 1784.
Officers to disclose property within two months of joining
False for 1773: property disclosure by Company servants was a later provision (Pitt's India Act, 1784); the 1773 Act only banned private trade and taking presents.
Company to submit communications on civil, military affairs and revenues
True: this was how the 1773 Act strengthened British Government control over the Company.
Supreme Court 1774 with powers clearly defined
False: the Court was set up in 1774, but its jurisdiction was vague, which caused conflicts that the Amending Act of 1781 had to correct.

points: The Regulating Act, 1773 was the first step of the British Government to control and regulate the Company's affairs.
It made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General of Bengal (first: Warren Hastings).

PYQ-POL-APK-6931BA.lead: Option 2: the Government of India Act, 1935 provided for a Reserve Bank of India to control currency and credit.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Government of India Act, 1919
It brought dyarchy and bicameralism, and provided for a PSC, but no central bank.
Government of India Act, 1935
LX lists 'establishment of a Reserve Bank of India to control the currency and credit of the country' among its features.
Indian Councils Act, 1909
It enlarged councils and introduced separate electorates; nothing on banking.
Indian Independence Act, 1947
It transferred power to two Dominions; the RBI already existed by then.

points: The RBI was set up in 1935 (the RBI Act was passed in 1934) and was nationalised in 1949.
Hook: '1935 Act = RBI, Federal Court, Federal PSC, Federal Railway Authority, Auditor-General'.
PYQ-POL-APK-6931BA.also: The 1935 Act also provided Federal PSC, Provincial PSCs and a Federal Court.

PYQ-POL-APK-8A6C34.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so the answer is option 3 (Only 1).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Act of the UK Parliament
True
The Government of India Act, 1919 (Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms) was passed by the British Parliament.
2. Dilution of Central and Provincial subjects
False
The Act did not dilute subjects; it classified and demarcated them into central and provincial lists through the Devolution Rules.
3. Covered 10 years from 1909 to 1919
False
The Act came into force in 1921; it only provided for a statutory commission to review it ten years later.
4. Lower House 145 members, 5-year term
False
The Legislative Assembly had about 145 members but a 3-year term; the 5-year term was for the Council of State.

points: Options 1 and 4 fail because statement 4 is false (wrong term of the Lower House).
Option 2 fails because statement 3 is false; the 10-year figure refers to the review commission, not the Act's life.
PYQ-POL-APK-8A6C34.also: The 1919 Act brought dyarchy in provinces and bicameral central legislature.

PYQ-POL-APK-B5065E.lead: Option 2: the Charter Act of 1853 let the Company keep Indian territories 'in trust' for the Crown without fixing any period.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Regulating Act
The 1773 Act began British control over the Company; it did not renew a Charter in 1853.
Charter Act
The 1853 Charter Act renewed Company rule without a fixed term, signalling that Parliament could end it at any time (done in 1858).
Indian Contract Act
An 1872 law on contracts between private parties; not about Company rule.
Negotiable Instruments Act
An 1881 law on cheques, bills and promissory notes; not constitutional.

points: Earlier Charters (1793, 1813, 1833) each gave 20 years; 1853 gave no period, a sign the Company's end was near.
1853 was the last Charter Act.
PYQ-POL-APK-B5065E.also: 1853 Act also separated legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General's Council and opened civil services to open competition.

PYQ-POL-APK-B6D042.lead: Option 4 (1833): the Charter Act of 1833 directed the Government of India to take steps to abolish slavery.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Regulating Act dealt with control over the Company and set up the Calcutta Supreme Court; no slavery clause.
It dealt with open competition for civil services and a separate legislative council.
It ended the trade monopoly (except tea and China) and gave funds for education.
Besides centralisation, it asked the government to improve the condition of slaves and abolish slavery; slavery was abolished by the Indian Slavery Act, 1843.

points: 1833 was the high point of centralisation: the Governor-General of India got exclusive legislative powers for all British India.
Hook: '33 = all-India Governor-General + end of Company trade + anti-slavery'.
PYQ-POL-APK-B6D042.also: 1833 Act made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India (first: Lord William Bentinck).

PYQ-POL-APK-EA7D81.lead: Option 4: the Government of India Act, 1858 transferred the government, territories and revenues of India from the Company to the Crown.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Charter Act, 1853
It renewed Company rule without a time limit; the Company still ruled.
Pitt's India Act, 1784
It created the Board of Control, giving 'double government'; the Company continued.
Regulating Act, 1773
It began British regulation of the Company; it did not transfer power.
Government of India Act, 1858
Passed after the 1857 Revolt, it abolished the Company's rule and vested power in the Crown.

points: It created the Secretary of State for India with a 15-member Council of India.
It abolished the Board of Control and Court of Directors, ending double government.
PYQ-POL-APK-EA7D81.also: The Governor-General became the Viceroy of India; Lord Canning was the first.

PYQ-POL-APK-FECB65.lead: Option 3: the Government of India Act, 1858 ended Company rule and vested all powers in the British Crown.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Charter Act 1833
It ended the Company's trade but the Company stayed as the administrative body.
Charter Act 1853
It continued Company rule 'in trust' without a time limit.
Government of India Act of 1858
The 'Act for the Good Government of India' abolished the East India Company's rule after 1857.
India Councils Act of 1861
It came after Crown rule began; it associated Indians with law-making.

points: India was now governed by and in the name of Her Majesty; the Viceroy was the Crown's direct representative.
The Secretary of State for India, a British Cabinet member, got complete control over Indian administration.

PYQ-POL-C4241BD6AEFE.lead: Option 4: dyarchy (double rule) was the division of provincial subjects into 'transferred' and 'reserved' under the 1919 Act.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Division of central legislature into two houses
That is bicameralism (also brought by the 1919 Act), not dyarchy.
Central and State governments
That is federalism, a division between levels of government, not dyarchy.
Rulers in London and Delhi
Not dyarchy; the closest idea is the 'double government' of the Board of Control and Court of Directors (1784), both in London.
Division of provincial subjects into two categories
Transferred subjects (education, health) went to ministers responsible to the legislature; reserved subjects (police, finance) stayed with the Governor and his council.

points: The word comes from the Greek 'di-arche', meaning double rule.
It was largely unsuccessful and the Simon Commission recommended its abolition.
PYQ-POL-C4241BD6AEFE.also: The 1935 Act ended provincial dyarchy and proposed dyarchy at the Centre instead.

PYQ-POL-E73009C7B342.lead: Option 3 (A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3) is correct: budget discussion came in 1892, communal electorates in 1909, provincial dyarchy in 1919 and proposed central dyarchy in 1935.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Discuss budget, ask questions
4. Indian Councils Act, 1892
1892 Act let councils discuss the budget and ask questions on administration.
B. Excess weight to religious groups
1. Indian Councils Act, 1909
The Indian Councils Act, 1909 (Morley-Minto Reforms) introduced separate electorates for Muslims and gave them weightage beyond their population, so this development belongs to 1909.
C. Dyarchy in provinces
2. GoI Act, 1919
1919 Act split provincial subjects into reserved (Governor) and transferred (ministers).
D. Dyarchy at the Centre
3. GoI Act, 1935
Dyarchy at the Centre (reserved and transferred federal subjects) was provided by the Government of India Act, 1935, but it never came into force because the federation was not formed.

points: Option 1 fails: A-1 (Indian Councils Act, 1909) is wrong, A matches 4; B-3 (GoI Act, 1935) is wrong, B matches 1; C-4 (Indian Councils Act, 1892) is wrong, C matches 2; D-2 (GoI Act, 1919) is wrong, D matches 3.

Option 2 fails: A-2 (GoI Act, 1919) is wrong, A matches 4; B-3 (GoI Act, 1935) is wrong, B matches 1; C-1 (Indian Councils Act, 1909) is wrong, C matches 2; D-4 (Indian Councils Act, 1892) is wrong, D matches 3.

Option 4 fails: A-3 (GoI Act, 1935) is wrong, A matches 4; B-4 (Indian Councils Act, 1892) is wrong, B matches 1; C-1 (Indian Councils Act, 1909) is wrong, C matches 2; D-2 (GoI Act, 1919) is wrong, D matches 3.

PYQ-POL-F5B52F74593B.lead: Option 2 (official key): the Government of India Act, 1858 is taken as defining the 'Government of India' when the Crown took over direct rule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Indian Councils Act, 1861
It expanded the Viceroy's council and began associating Indians; it came after the 1858 Act.
The Government of India Act, 1858
It put India under the Crown, governed 'by and in the name of Her Majesty', with the Secretary of State and Viceroy forming the Government of India.
The Government of India Act, 1919
It reformed an already existing Government of India.
The Indian Independence Act, 1947

PYQ-POL-4F42BF8DA5D9.lead: Official key: option 4 (B, C and D only). Study note: method A (accommodation) is also well documented, which would make option 3.

head: Method
True/False
Why

True (excluded by official key)

Accepted by official key

True
The framers studied about 60 constitutions and selected features, modifying them to suit Indian conditions.

True
Austin's other key method: decisions were reached by broad agreement rather than narrow majority voting.

Correct?

A minor committee that checked whether members were validly elected or nominated. Its chairman was Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar.
Union Powers Committee
A major committee that worked out the powers of the Centre. It was chaired by Jawaharlal Nehru.
Order of Business Committee
A minor committee that arranged the Assembly's business. It was chaired by Dr K. M. Munshi.
Fundamental Rights Sub-Committee
A sub-committee of Sardar Patel's Advisory Committee. It was chaired by J. B. Kripalani.

points: Alladi was also one of the seven Drafting Committee members.
Trap: Munshi and Alladi were both Drafting Committee members, but each chaired a different minor committee.

PYQ-POL-E13FC19EBEB4.lead: A and C are true, B is false, so option 4 (A and C only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Constituted under the Cabinet Mission Plan
True

B. Seats in proportion to geographical area
False
Seats were allotted in proportion to population, roughly one seat for every million people. Area played no part.

points: Option 1 leaves out the true statement C.
Options 2 and 3 include the false statement B.
PYQ-POL-E13FC19EBEB4.also: Each community's members in the provincial assembly elected that community's representatives by single transferable vote.

PYQ-POL-E3863F530924.lead: Option 3: Samvidhan Divas is 26 November, the day the Constitution was adopted in 1949.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 18th November
This date has no link with the Constitution. It is only a distractor close to 26 November.
26th January
Republic Day, when the major part of the Constitution came into force in 1950.
26th November
Samvidhan Divas, observed since 2015, marks the adoption of the Constitution on 26 November 1949.
15th August
Independence Day, marking freedom from British rule in 1947.

points: Before 2015, 26 November was observed as National Law Day.
Hook: November = adopted; January = in force.

PYQ-POL-EB1048CC641B.lead: Option 2: Section 8(1) of the Indian Independence Act, 1947 gave the Constituent Assembly the power to frame the Dominion's constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Section 6(2)
Section 6 dealt with the law-making powers of the new Dominion legislatures, not with recognising the Assembly.
Section 8(1)
Said that the Dominion Legislature's power to make a constitution would first be exercised by the Constituent Assembly. This made the Assembly sovereign and also a legislature.
Section 10(3)
Section 10 dealt with the services of the Secretary of State (civil servants), not the Assembly.
Section 4(1)
Section 4 dealt with the partition of the province of Punjab, not the Assembly.

points: Because of this, the Assembly also worked as India's first Parliament, chaired by G. V. Mavalankar for ordinary laws.
Section 8(2) kept the Government of India Act, 1935 running until the new Constitution was made.

PYQ-POL-WEB-12D759.lead: Option 1: the Constitution was adopted and enacted on 26 November 1949.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 26th November 1949
The Preamble says the people 'adopt, enact and give to ourselves this Constitution' on this date. The members signed it the same day.
26th January 1949
Nothing of this kind happened on this date; the Assembly was still in its second reading.
26th November 1950
Wrong year; by then the Constitution had already been in force for ten months.
26th January 1950
Date of commencement (Republic Day), when the Constitution came into force, not when it was enacted.

points: Enact or adopt = passed by the Assembly (26 Nov 1949); commence = came into force (26 Jan 1950).
Provisions on citizenship, elections and the provisional Parliament came into force on 26 November 1949 itself.

PYQ-POL-WEB-2E1B31.lead: Option 1: among the options, the earliest demand is the Swaraj Party's in 1934.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Swaraj Party in 1934
In 1934 the Swaraj Party demanded a Constituent Assembly, the same year M. N. Roy first put forward the idea. It is the earliest of the four options.
Congress Party in 1936
The INC first officially demanded a Constituent Assembly in 1935, so 1936 is neither the first nor the earliest.
Muslim League in 1942
In 1942 the League rejected the Cripps Proposals and wanted two separate Assemblies; this is much later.
All Parties Conference in 1946
By 1946 the Cabinet Mission had already planned the Assembly, so this cannot be the first idea.

points: Order: M. N. Roy idea (1934) → INC official demand (1935) → Nehru's declaration (1938) → August Offer accepts it (1940).

PYQ-POL-WEB-3F5670.lead: Option 4: the first Draft Constitution was published in February 1948.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: June 1948
By June 1948 the draft was already out and people were sending comments during the eight-month discussion period.
May 1948
The same: the draft had been published three months earlier and public discussion was going on.
January 1948
Too early; the Assembly only had its short sixth session on 27 January 1948 and the draft was not yet published.
February 1948
The Drafting Committee published its first draft, and people got eight months to discuss it and propose changes.

points: A second draft followed in October 1948 after public comments.
Ambedkar introduced the final draft on 4 November 1948 (first reading).

PYQ-POL-WEB-433F59.lead: Option 4: Ambedkar called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' of the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: identity card of the constitution
N. A. Palkhivala called the Preamble the 'identity card of the Constitution', not the DPSPs.
The most precious part of the constitution
This phrase is used for the Preamble by some members, not by Ambedkar for the DPSPs.
soul of the state
Not Ambedkar's phrase for the DPSPs; Granville Austin called the FRs and DPSPs together the 'conscience of the Constitution'.
a novel feature of the constitution
Ambedkar's words for the DPSPs, which were taken from the Irish Constitution (Ireland had copied them from Spain).

points: Ambedkar called Article 32, not the DPSPs, the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution (LX p0144).

PYQ-POL-WEB-45ADDD.lead: Option 4: Ambedkar called the Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) the heart and soul of the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Right to freedom of religion
Articles 25–28 protect freedom of conscience and religion. Ambedkar did not describe them this way.
Right to property
Was a Fundamental Right originally, but was removed by the 44th Amendment (1978); it was never called heart and soul.
Right to equality
Articles 14–18 give equality before law and end untouchability, but Ambedkar did not use this phrase for them.
Right to Constitutional Remedies
Article 32 lets a person go directly to the Supreme Court to enforce Fundamental Rights. Ambedkar said that without it the other rights would be meaningless.

points: Concept: a right without a remedy is empty; Article 32 is the remedy, so it protects all the other rights.
PYQ-POL-WEB-45ADDD.also: The Supreme Court treats Article 32 as part of the basic structure.

PYQ-POL-WEB-52223D.lead: Option 3: members were elected indirectly by the legislative assemblies of the provinces.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: nominated by the British Parliament
The British Parliament nominated no member. Members for the provinces were elected.
nominated by the Governor General
The Governor General did not nominate members either. Only princely-state members were to be nominated, and that by the rulers.
elected by the Legislative Assemblies of the provinces
Members of each community in each provincial assembly elected their own representatives by single transferable vote.
elected by the INC and Muslim League
Parties contested and won seats (Congress 208, League 73), but the parties themselves did not elect members.

points: So the Assembly was partly elected and partly nominated, and indirectly elected, not by adult franchise.

PYQ-POL-WEB-6330D4.lead: Option 4: the first meeting was held in New Delhi on 9 December 1946.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Calcutta
Calcutta was the former British capital (till 1911), but the Assembly never met there.
Bombay
Bombay hosted Congress sessions and the Experts Committee meeting, not the Assembly's first meeting.
Peshawar
Peshawar was in the North-West Frontier Province and went to Pakistan; the Assembly did not meet there.
Delhi
The Assembly met in the Constitution Hall, New Delhi, now the Central Hall of Parliament.

points: The Muslim League boycotted the meeting, so only 207 members attended.
PYQ-POL-WEB-6330D4.also: Sachchidananda Sinha presided as temporary Chairman.

PYQ-POL-WEB-989010.lead: Option 1: Communist member Somnath Lahiri called the Assembly British-made.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Somnath Lahiri
The Communist Party member said the Assembly was 'working the British plan as the British should like it to be worked out'.
B. R. Ambedkar
As Drafting Committee chairman he defended the Assembly's work; he did not make this charge.
Shyama Prasad Mukherjee
A Hindu Mahasabha member of the Assembly; this criticism is not his.
B. N. Rau
An official adviser, not a member, so he took no part in such debate.

points: The underlying criticism is 'not a sovereign body': critics said the Assembly was created by British proposals (LX p0032).

PYQ-POL-WEB-9C967B.lead: Option 1: Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution on 13 December 1946.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Jawaharlal Nehru
He moved the resolution that laid down the philosophy of the Constitution; it was adopted unanimously on 22 January 1947.
Rajendra Prasad
He was the President of the Assembly and presided; he did not move the resolution.
B. R. Ambedkar
He later chaired the Drafting Committee (from August 1947); he did not move this resolution.
Alladi Krishnaswami Aiyar
A Drafting Committee member and Credentials Committee chairman, not the mover.

points: Its modified version forms the Preamble of the present Constitution.

PYQ-POL-WEB-A5B6F3.lead: Option 3: the Cabinet Mission rejected the demand for a separate Pakistan.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Provincial grouping
Part of the Plan: provinces were to form groups (A, B, C) under a weak Union.
Interim Cabinet of Indians
Part of the Plan: an interim government of Indian leaders was proposed and formed in 1946.
Acceptance of Pakistan
Not in the Plan: it rejected the idea of two Constituent Assemblies and a separate Pakistan, so this is the incorrect statement.
Constitution framing right
Part of the Plan: it set up a Constituent Assembly for Indians to frame their own constitution.

points: It offered grouping as a compromise to satisfy the Muslim League without partition.
Note: this is a 'NOT correct' question, so the ✓ marks the false feature.

PYQ-POL-WEB-AA2141.lead: Option 1: Jawaharlal Nehru moved the National Flag resolution on 22 July 1947.

What it is / means
Correct?

He moved the resolution describing the tricolour with the navy-blue wheel, and it was adopted the same day.
B. R. Ambedkar
He chaired the Drafting Committee; he did not move the flag resolution.
Rajendra Prasad
He chaired the Ad-hoc Committee on the National Flag, but as presiding officer he did not move the resolution.
Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
He chaired the Advisory Committee and Provincial Constitution Committee, not the flag motion.

PYQ-POL-WEB-BA5467.lead: Option 4: Sir B. N. Rau was the Constitutional Adviser to the Constituent Assembly and its Drafting Committee.

What it is / means
Correct?

He was Chairman of the Drafting Committee, so he led it rather than advising it.
Sachidananda Sinha
He was the oldest member and temporary Chairman at the first meeting.
B. N. Rau
An official appointed as Constitutional (Legal) Adviser; he prepared the initial draft the Committee worked on.

points: S. N. Mukherjee was the Chief Draftsman.

PYQ-POL-WEB-BDA322.lead: Option 2: the Bombay Presidency. Ambedkar lost his first seat at Partition and was re-elected from Bombay in 1947.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: West Bengal
West Bengal was created only at Partition (1947); Ambedkar's 1946 seat was in undivided Bengal (Jessore-Khulna), which went to East Pakistan.
the Bombay Presidency
After losing his Bengal seat, he was elected from Bombay in July 1947 to the vacancy left by M. R. Jayakar's resignation.
the then Madhya Bharat
Madhya Bharat was a union of princely states formed in 1948; Ambedkar never represented it.
Punjab
Punjab was partitioned too, and Ambedkar had no connection with its seats.

PYQ-POL-WEB-E283C4.lead: Option 4: H. V. Kamath compared the bulky Constitution to the elephant, the Assembly's symbol.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: B.R. Ambedkar
He defended the length and detail of the Constitution; he did not mock it as elephantine.
Dr. Rajendra Prasad
As President of the Assembly he did not make this remark.
K.M. Munshi
He was a Drafting Committee member and defended the draft.
H.V. Kamath
He said the Assembly had fittingly chosen the elephant as its seal, as the Constitution was the bulkiest in the world.

points: The elephant was the seal (symbol) of the Constituent Assembly.

PYQ-POL-WEB-E283C4.also: Ivor Jennings called it 'too long and too rigid'.

PYQ-POL-WEB-E3BD0D.lead: Option 1: the Assembly adopted Jana Gana Mana as the National Anthem on 24 January 1950.

What it is / means
Correct?

No anthem decision was made on this date; the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.

Around the time the Committee published the Draft Constitution (February 1948), not its creation.

Independence Day; the Committee was formed two weeks later.

A late session date when the draft was being debated, not the date of setting up the Committee.

PYQ-POL-006127B7C80A.lead: Both statements are correct, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. India chose a parliamentary over a presidential system
True
The Constituent Assembly adopted the British (Westminster) parliamentary model for both the Centre and the States.
B. Responsibility was preferred to stability
True

Dr Ambedkar explained that a parliamentary executive is checked daily through questions and no-confidence motions, while a presidential one is stable but checked only periodically; the Assembly preferred daily responsibility.

points: Options 1 and 2 accept only one true statement; option 4 rejects both.
Hook: Presidential = stability (fixed term); Parliamentary = responsibility (can be removed any day).

PYQ-POL-045FBFD305E3.lead: Option 2: after the Right to Education Act, the Centre enacted the Right to Food law, the National Food Security Act, 2013.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

No central Right to Health Act has been enacted; health remains mainly a State List subject.
Right to Food Act
The National Food Security Act, 2013 gave a legal right to subsidised foodgrains, popularly called the Right to Food Act.
Right of Shelter Act
No such central Act exists; housing is handled through schemes like PM Awas Yojana, not a legal right.
Both (1) and (2)
Wrong because option 1 (Right to Health) was never enacted.

Correct?

The 22 languages recognised by the Constitution.

PYQ-POL-0AFA238C3891.lead: India is a federation with strong unitary features — 'quasi-federal'.

PYQ-POL-1391296B0367.lead: Option 3: judicial review was borrowed from the USA, not from the British parliamentary system.

Correct?

Power of courts to strike down unconstitutional laws; it comes from the US Constitution, because Britain follows parliamentary sovereignty.

The PM as real head of the executive is a British feature.
