Passed a 75% local-quota law in 2019; it was challenged but this question refers to Haryana's verdict.
Haryana
Haryana State Employment of Local Candidates Act, 2020 was held to violate Articles 14 and 19(1)(g) on 17 November 2023.

points: Domicile-based reservation in private jobs discriminates against citizens of other States and restricts employers' freedom of trade (Article 19(1)(g)).
The State has appealed to the Supreme Court.

PYQ-POL-1F4C7EE89E76.lead: Article 32 — the Supreme Court enforces Fundamental Rights and strikes down laws that violate them.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 131
Original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court in disputes between the Centre and States.
Article 132
Appellate jurisdiction in constitutional cases from High Courts.
Article 32
Right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights; with Article 13 it is the basis of judicial review of laws.
Article 134
Appellate jurisdiction in criminal cases.

points: Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void; this power is used by the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) (LX p132).
Judicial review is part of the basic structure.

PYQ-POL-21088E280E14.lead: Article 21A recognises the right to education as a Fundamental Right.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 300A
Right to property — a legal right in Part XII, not a Fundamental Right.
Article 20
Protection in respect of conviction for offences.
Article 33
Lets Parliament restrict Fundamental Rights of armed forces, police and similar forces.
Article 21A
Free and compulsory education for children aged 6-14; inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

points: The same 86th Amendment changed Article 45 (early childhood care up to 6) and added Fundamental Duty 51A(k) for parents (LX p150).
In force with the RTE Act from 1 April 2010.

PYQ-POL-256EB350F352.lead: Article 23 prohibits forced labour (along with traffic in human beings and begar).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Exploitation of women
Not the wording of any Article; trafficking of women is covered only as part of 'traffic in human beings'.
Forced labour
Article 23 bans traffic in human beings, begar (unpaid compulsory work) and other forms of forced labour; violation is punishable by law.
Child labour
That is Article 24 (children below 14 in factories, mines, hazardous work).
Untouchability
Untouchability is abolished by Article 17, a separate Fundamental Right; Article 23 is about trafficking and forced labour.

points: Article 23 protects against both the State and private persons (LX p153).
Exception: the State may impose compulsory service for public purposes such as military or social service, without discrimination.

PYQ-POL-268DD5A90576.lead: Article 24 directly deals with exploitation of children (child labour).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 19
Article 19 guarantees six freedoms to citizens (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession); it does not deal with children's exploitation.
Article 24
Prohibits employing children below 14 in factories, mines or hazardous activities.
Article 17
Article 17 abolishes untouchability; it targets caste-based social exclusion, not the exploitation of children.
Article 22
Article 22 gives safeguards against arbitrary arrest and detention; it has nothing specific to do with children.

points: Article 24 is part of the Right against Exploitation (Articles 23-24) (LX p154).
Related protections: Article 21A (education) and DPSP Article 39(e)-(f).

PYQ-POL-28DC968B082A.lead: Doctrine of eclipse: a pre-Constitution law that conflicts with a Fundamental Right becomes dormant, not dead.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Eminent domain
The State's power to take private property for a public purpose.
Pleasure
Civil servants hold office during the pleasure of the President or Governor (Article 310).
Eclipse
The law is 'overshadowed' by the Fundamental Right; it still exists for non-citizens and past acts, and revives if the right is amended to remove the conflict.
Substantive power
Not a recognised constitutional doctrine on this point.

points: Based on Article 13(1) (pre-Constitution laws) and laid down in Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955) (LX p920-921).
Deep Chand (1959) held it does not apply to post-Constitution laws under Article 13(2).

PYQ-POL-2A742BD6819F.lead: Articles 23-24 form the Right against Exploitation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Articles 31-32
Article 31 (property) was deleted in 1978; Article 32 is the Right to Constitutional Remedies.
Articles 29-30
Cultural and Educational Rights (protection of minorities' culture; minority educational institutions).
Articles 25-28
Articles 25-28 form the Right to Freedom of Religion (conscience, denominational affairs, religious taxes and instruction), not the Right against Exploitation.
Articles 23-24
Article 23 bans trafficking, begar and forced labour; Article 24 bans child labour below 14 in hazardous work.

PYQ-POL-2AA0C1551DE1.lead: Mandamus ('we command') orders a public official or body to perform a duty it has failed to perform.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Mandamus
Command to a public official, public body, corporation, inferior court, tribunal or government to do its legal duty.
Quo Warranto
'By what authority' — tests a person's claim to a public office.
Prohibition
'To forbid' — stops a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction.
Certiorari
'To be certified' — quashes an order already passed by a lower court.

points: Mandamus cannot be issued against a private person, for a discretionary duty, for a contract, or against the President or Governors (LX p160).

PYQ-POL-2B6BDA7FBF79.lead: Article 358 suspends the Article 19 freedoms during a National Emergency.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 352
Proclamation of National Emergency (war, external aggression, armed rebellion).
Article 356
President's Rule in a State on failure of constitutional machinery.
Article 358
When a National Emergency is declared on grounds of war or external aggression, Article 19 rights are automatically suspended.
Article 360
Article 360 deals with Financial Emergency; it does not suspend Fundamental Rights, so it does not fit this stem.

points: Article 359 lets the President suspend the right to move courts for enforcement of other rights, except Articles 20 and 21 (LX p262-263).
Since the 44th Amendment, Article 358 does not apply to an emergency on armed rebellion.

PYQ-POL-2C0BF69DA36D.lead: Habeas Corpus can be issued against private persons as well as public authorities.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Quo Warranto
Only against a person holding a substantive public office.
Certiorari
Only against courts, tribunals and (later) administrative authorities.
Habeas Corpus
Any person who detains another — public or private — can be ordered to produce the body before the court.
Mandamus
Only against public officials and bodies; it cannot lie against a private individual.

points: Habeas Corpus means 'to have the body of' (LX p160).
It is not issued where detention is lawful or ordered by a competent court.

PYQ-POL-2C572E95B197.lead: Official key: option 3 (A and B only). Study answer: option 4 (C only) — eminent domain means the State's power to take private property for public purpose.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Police power to detain persons
False
Detention is the State's police power (Article 22 limits it); it is a different sovereign power.
B. Power to impose taxes
False
Taxation is a separate sovereign power (Article 265).
C. Capacity to take private property for public purpose
True
This is exactly what eminent domain means; compensation was the issue in Article 31(2).
D. Capacity to share public burden
False
Spreading public burden is the justification for taxes, not the definition of eminent domain.

points: Option 1 wrongly adds B and D; option 2 picks only D; option 3 (official) picks A and B, both separate powers.
The stem's '4th Amendment Act, 1966' is wrong: the 4th Amendment was 1955 (LX p180).
PYQ-POL-2C572E95B197.also: Disputed key: official key is option 3 (A and B only), but A and B describe police power and taxing power; eminent domain is only C, so the study answer is option 4.

PYQ-POL-2D2DDCF4307F.lead: The 103rd Amendment Act, 2019 added Article 15(6) for EWS reservation (up to 10%) in educational institutions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 103rd Amendment
2019: inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) — up to 10% reservation for Economically Weaker Sections in education and public jobs.
101st Amendment
2016: introduced the Goods and Services Tax.
102nd Amendment
2018: gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B).
104th Amendment
2019 (2020): extended SC/ST reservation in legislatures and ended Anglo-Indian nomination.

points: The Supreme Court upheld the EWS quota 3:2 in Janhit Abhiyan (2022).
EWS reservation does not cover SCs, STs and OBCs who already have reservation (LX p135).

PYQ-POL-2E2FB39E06F8.lead: Article 32 — right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 35
Gives Parliament (not States) power to make laws to give effect to certain Fundamental Rights.
Article 32
Right to Constitutional Remedies; itself a Fundamental Right.
Article 30
Right of minorities to establish and administer educational institutions.
Article 36
Defines 'State' for Part IV (Directive Principles).

points: Ambedkar called Article 32 'the heart and soul' of the Constitution (LX p158).
It is part of the basic structure.

PYQ-POL-30F740E540EA.lead: Part III has six groups of Fundamental Rights today.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong: Part III has six groups today and had seven originally; four groups was never the count.
Equality (14-18), Freedom (19-22), Against exploitation (23-24), Religion (25-28), Cultural and educational (29-30), Constitutional remedies (32).
Original number, before the 44th Amendment removed property in 1978.
Wrong: there are six groups (Equality, Freedom, Against Exploitation, Religion, Cultural and Educational, Constitutional Remedies), not five.

points: Property is now a legal right under Article 300A (LX p127).

PYQ-POL-318C960CC3B3.lead: Both A and B are correct — option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Article 17 abolishes untouchability
True
Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form; enforcing any disability from it is a punishable offence.
B. Action against a private individual
True
Article 17 operates against private persons too; the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 punishes anyone who practises untouchability.

points: Options 1 and 2 drop one true statement; option 4 denies both.
Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 are rights available even against private individuals (LX p140).

PYQ-POL-31D5606301DC.lead: The Vishaka case (1997) dealt with sexual harassment of women at the workplace.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Domestic violence
Covered by the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 — not Vishaka.
Sexual harassment at work place
The Supreme Court laid down binding guidelines using Articles 14, 15, 19(1)(g) and 21 until a law was made.
Unlawful detention
Remedied by habeas corpus; not the issue here.
Dalit atrocity
Dealt with by the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989.

points: The case arose after the gang rape of Bhanwari Devi, a social worker in Rajasthan.
The guidelines were replaced by the POSH Act, 2013 (LX p894).

PYQ-POL-3320276E33CA.lead: Official key: option 2 (A, B and C). Study answer: option 3 (A and B only), because 'equality before law' belongs to Article 14.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex, place of birth
True
This is Article 15(1), word for word: the State shall not discriminate against citizens on these grounds, so the statement is correct.
B. Special provision for women and children
True
This is Article 15(3), word for word: it allows special provisions for women and children, so the statement is correct.
C. Equality before law
False
Equality before law is Article 14; Article 15 is about non-discrimination.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes C and drops B; option 4 drops A.
The official option 2 accepts C, perhaps reading Article 15 as part of the general idea of equality.
PYQ-POL-3320276E33CA.also: Disputed key: official key is option 2 (A, B and C); 'equality before law' is Article 14, so the study answer is option 3 (A and B only).

PYQ-POL-339DEFF854A2.lead: Privacy flows from Article 21 and the freedoms guaranteed in Part III.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 14 + 42nd Amendment
Article 14 is equality; the 42nd Amendment did not create any privacy right.
Article 17 + DPSP
Article 17 is untouchability; Directive Principles are not enforceable rights.
Article 21 + Part III freedoms
Puttaswamy (2017) held privacy is intrinsic to life and liberty in Article 21 and to the freedoms in Part III.
Article 24 + 44th Amendment
Article 24 is child labour; the 44th Amendment is unrelated to privacy.

points: K.S. Puttaswamy (2017): a nine-judge Bench held privacy a Fundamental Right unanimously (LX p151).

PYQ-POL-341A2CC3A630.lead: Fundamental Rights are not absolute because the State can impose reasonable restrictions on them.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Suspended during emergency
A separate feature (Articles 358-359); it is temporary, and Articles 20-21 are never suspended.
Have reasonable restrictions
Rights are 'qualified'; e.g. Article 19(2)-(6) list grounds of restriction, and courts decide whether they are reasonable.
Available only to citizens
False fact: Articles 14, 20, 21, 25 etc. are available to all persons.
Are justiciable
Justiciability means they can be enforced in court; it is a strength, not a limit.

points: Fundamental Rights strike a balance between individual liberty and social control (LX p129).

PYQ-POL-3AFD09013EB0.lead: Official key: option 3 (Parliament). Study answer: option 1 — under Section 2(c) of the NCM Act, 1992, a minority is a community notified by the Central Government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: the Central Government
✓ (study answer)
Section 2(c) of the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992 defines minority as a community notified by the Central Government.
the State Government
A State does not notify minorities for the National Commission's purposes.
the Parliament
✗ (official key)
Parliament made the Act, but the notification itself is an executive act of the Central Government.
the National Commission for Minorities
The Commission only monitors and advises; it does not notify.

points: Six notified communities: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis (1993) and Jains (2014).
Difference between making a law (Parliament) and issuing a notification under it (Government) is the key concept.
PYQ-POL-3AFD09013EB0.also: Disputed key: official key is option 3 (Parliament); under s2(c) of the NCM Act 1992, a minority is a community notified by the Central Government, so the study answer is option 1.

PYQ-POL-3C0D2B4B1600.lead: Article 16(4A) allows reservation in promotions for SCs and STs.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Reservations to physically handicapped
Disability reservation comes from the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016, not Article 16(4A).
Reservations to women
Article 15(3) allows special provisions for women; 16(4A) is not about women.
Reservations to SC/STs
General SC/ST reservation in appointments already rests on Article 16(4); 16(4A) is narrower.
Reservations in matter of promotions
Inserted by the 77th Amendment, 1995, after Indra Sawhney (1992) barred quota in promotions.

points: The 85th Amendment, 2001 added 'consequential seniority' to 16(4A) (LX p138).
Article 16(4B) (81st Amendment, 2000) allows carry-forward of unfilled reserved vacancies.

PYQ-POL-3DE440BC671F.lead: The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act was passed in 1986.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: It banned children below 14 in listed hazardous jobs and regulated other work.
Wrong year (National Child Labour Policy came in 1987, not the Act).
Wrong year: the Act came in 1986; 1988 is when the National Child Labour Project scheme started, not the Act.
Wrong year: the Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act was passed in 1986; 1989 has no link to this Act.

points: The 2016 amendment renamed it the Child and Adolescent Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act and banned children below 14 in all occupations (family-enterprise exception).
It gives effect to Article 24 (LX p154).

PYQ-POL-404930FCD664.lead: B, C and D are true, A is false — option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Only for violation of Fundamental Rights
False
High Courts issue mandamus under Article 226 'for any other purpose' too, i.e. to enforce ordinary legal duties.
B. Against government, inferior courts, other judicial bodies
True
Mandamus can be issued against any public body, corporation, inferior court, tribunal or government.
C. Direct an official not to enforce an unconstitutional law
True
An officer has a legal duty not to enforce an invalid law, so mandamus can command him to refrain.
D. Enforce a statutory duty an officer refuses to do
True
This is the core use: 'we command' a public official to perform the duty he failed or refused to perform.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 all include the false statement A.
Mandamus cannot be issued against a private person, the President or Governors (LX p160).

PYQ-POL-42E54BB4BEC6.lead: 2017 — Puttaswamy (24 August 2017) declared privacy a Fundamental Right.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Year of Shreya Singhal (Section 66A) and the reference of the privacy issue to a larger Bench.
Nine-judge Bench in K.S. Puttaswamy held privacy part of Article 21 and Part III.
Year of the separate Aadhaar judgment (Puttaswamy-II) and Navtej Johar.
Wrong: the nine-judge Bench in K.S. Puttaswamy declared privacy a Fundamental Right in 2017, not 2019.

points: It overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) on this point (LX p151).

PYQ-POL-44A6613A5F04.lead: Article 21 protects life and personal liberty.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 21
No person shall be deprived of life or personal liberty except according to procedure established by law.
Article 23
Prohibits trafficking, begar and forced labour.
Article 24
Prohibits child labour in hazardous work.
Article 20
Protection in respect of conviction for offences.

points: Maneka Gandhi (1978): the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable (LX p148).
Article 21 is available to citizens and foreigners.

PYQ-POL-4586D0A72232.lead: Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12-35).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: I
The Union and its territory (Articles 1-4).
II
Part II (Articles 5-11) deals with Citizenship, not Fundamental Rights, so it is not the answer.
IV
Part IV (Articles 36-51) contains the Directive Principles of State Policy, which are non-justiciable, not Fundamental Rights.
III
Fundamental Rights; called the Magna Carta of India.

points: Inspired by the US Bill of Rights (LX p127).
Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA (Article 51A).

PYQ-POL-46C2E6E50FCC.lead: Option 2 (A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1) is correct: A. A.K. Gopalan → Preventive detention; B. Maneka Gandhi → Personal liberty; C. S.R. Bommai → President's Rule; D. Indra Sawhney → Reservations.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. A.K. Gopalan (1950)
3 – Preventive detention
Upheld the Preventive Detention Act; read Article 21 narrowly.
B. Maneka Gandhi (1978)
2 – Personal liberty
Maneka Gandhi (1978), a passport case, widened 'personal liberty' in Article 21 and held that the procedure depriving it must be just, fair and reasonable, so B matches 2.
C. S.R. Bommai (1994)
4 – President's Rule
Limited misuse of Article 356; floor test.
D. Indra Sawhney (1992)
1 – Reservations
Upheld 27% OBC quota, 50% ceiling, creamy layer.

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-4, B-1, C-2, D-3 (correct: A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives B-1, C-2, D-4 (correct: B-2, C-4, D-1).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-4, B-3, C-1, D-2 (correct: A-3, B-2, C-4, D-1).
PYQ-POL-46C2E6E50FCC.also: Indra Sawhney fixed the 50% ceiling and the creamy-layer rule for OBCs.

PYQ-POL-46DE3AA93AC8.lead: Article 13(1) makes pre-Constitution laws void to the extent of inconsistency with Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 13(1)
Applies to laws in force before 26 January 1950; basis of the doctrine of eclipse.
Article 13(3)
Defines 'law' widely (ordinances, orders, bye-laws, custom etc.).
Article 13(2)
Bars the State from making new laws that abridge Fundamental Rights (post-Constitution laws).
Article 13(4)
Says Article 13 does not apply to amendments under Article 368 (24th Amendment, 1971).

points: 13(1) = old laws, 13(2) = new laws: memorise this pair (LX p920-921).

PYQ-POL-48DCE5CA42EA.lead: B and C are true, A and D are false — option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Absolute in nature
False
They are qualified; the State can impose reasonable restrictions.
B. Justiciable
True
A person can move the courts (Articles 32, 226) to enforce them.
C. Promote political democracy
True
Laxmikanth: they are meant for promoting the ideal of political democracy and prevent authoritarian rule.
D. Taken from the Irish Constitution
False
They were inspired by the US Bill of Rights; the Directive Principles came from Ireland.

points: Options 1 and 4 include the false A; option 2 leaves out the true C (LX p127-129).
Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy.

PYQ-POL-496F281D061D.lead: A writ under Article 32 cannot be used, because property is no longer a Fundamental Right.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Writ under Article 226
Available: High Courts can enforce ordinary legal rights 'for any other purpose'.
Civil suit before a court
Available: since the 44th Amendment (1978) property is an ordinary legal right under Article 300A, so a civil suit can be filed.
Writ under Article 32
Not available: Article 32 enforces only Fundamental Rights.
Case before Lok Adalat
Available: a property dispute can be settled by compromise before a Lok Adalat, so this remedy is not barred.

points: The 44th Amendment, 1978 removed Article 31 and inserted Article 300A (LX p164).
Same question as the Article 226 version earlier.

PYQ-POL-4ADE4E1D118F.lead: The Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 came into force on 1 July 1961.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Date of Presidential assent, not commencement.
1 June 1961
Wrong: the Act came into force on 1 July 1961; 1 June 1961 is not its commencement date.
20 June 1961
Wrong: 20 June 1961 is not the commencement date; the Act was brought into force on 1 July 1961.
1 July 1961
Date of commencement notified by the Central Government.

points: It makes giving, taking or demanding dowry an offence.
Later IPC additions: Section 498A (cruelty, 1983) and 304B (dowry death, 1986).

PYQ-POL-4BB919732E3C.lead: Article 32 empowers the Supreme Court to issue writs.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 228
High Court can withdraw a case involving a substantial question of constitutional law from a lower court.
Article 36
Article 36 only defines 'State' for Part IV (Directive Principles); it gives no power to issue writs.
Article 32
Supreme Court issues writs for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
Article 226
Gives the writ power to High Courts, not the Supreme Court.

points: High Courts' writ power is wider in purpose (also 'any other purpose'), but narrower in territory (LX p160).

PYQ-POL-4CF5E9089C42.lead: This is called protection against double jeopardy — Article 20(2).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: No double Impunity
Not a legal term; impunity means escaping punishment.
No double Jurisprudence
Not a legal term; jurisprudence means the science of law.
No double Jeopardy
'Jeopardy' means risk of punishment; no one may be prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence.
No double Solvation
'Solvation' is not a legal term at all; the protection in Article 20(2) is called double jeopardy.

points: It applies only to proceedings before a court or judicial tribunal, not departmental proceedings (LX p147).
Article 20(1) bars ex-post-facto criminal laws; 20(3) bars self-incrimination.

PYQ-POL-4D8A1F42157D.lead: Option 1: Article 19 freedoms are given only to citizens; the other three Articles protect every person.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Rights under Article 19
Article 19 guarantees six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession) and its text says 'all citizens', so foreigners cannot claim it.
2. Rights under Article 25
Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and religion to 'all persons', so even a foreigner living in India can claim it.
3. Rights under Article 21
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty of 'any person', citizen or foreigner.
4. Rights under Article 14
Article 14 gives equality before law and equal protection of laws to 'any person' within India.

points: Rule of thumb: when the Article says 'citizen', it is citizen-only; when it says 'person', foreigners also get it.
Citizen-only Fundamental Rights: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30.
Memory hook: '15-16-19-29-30' belong to citizens; the rest belong to everyone (except enemy aliens for Article 22).

PYQ-POL-4E2815A3CF9D.lead: Official key: option 1. Correct matching (study answer): option 2 – A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Article 14
III – Equality before the law
Article 14 guarantees equality before the law and equal protection of the laws to every person in India, so A matches III.
B. Article 16
II – Equality of opportunity in public employment
Includes reservation clauses 16(4), 16(4A), 16(6).
C. Article 17
I – Abolition of untouchability
Its practice is an offence (Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955).
D. Article 18
IV – Abolition of titles
Military and academic distinctions are exempt.

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-I, C-III (correct: A-III, C-I).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-I, B-III, C-IV, D-II (correct: A-III, B-II, C-I, D-IV).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-I, C-IV, D-III (correct: A-III, C-I, D-IV).
PYQ-POL-4E2815A3CF9D.also: Disputed key: the official key is option 1 (A-I, B-II, C-III, D-IV), which wrongly pairs Article 14 with untouchability and Article 17 with equality before law; option 2 is correct.

PYQ-POL-4F44363EBDEF.lead: Option 2: the Section 377 reference concerned LGBT rights, because the section criminalised consensual same-sex relations.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The case of Tamil Nadu Chief Minister Jayalalithaa
This was a disproportionate-assets corruption case against a Chief Minister; it had nothing to do with Section 377.
2. Lesbian, gay, bisexual and transgender issues
Section 377 IPC punished 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature', which was used against consensual same-sex adults, so the issue was LGBT rights.
3. Transfer of certain Bhadrachalam-area mandals
Transfer of Bhadrachalam-area mandals was a matter of State reorganisation (Andhra Pradesh–Telangana), not of a criminal law.
4. White-collar crimes
White-collar crimes are financial frauds by professionals; Section 377 was not about them.

points: Suresh Kumar Koushal (2013) had upheld Section 377; curative petitions were then referred to a five-judge Bench in 2016.
Navtej Singh Johar (2018) read down Section 377 to decriminalise consensual adult same-sex conduct, relying on Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21.
The judgment built on the privacy ruling in Puttaswamy (2017).

PYQ-POL-5031979CD36B.lead: Option 2 (A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I) is correct: A. Freedom of speech and expression → Article 19(1)(a); B. Immunity from double prosecution → Article 20; C. Abolition of titles → Article 18; D. Right to legal aid → Article 21.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Freedom of speech and expression
II – Article 19(1)(a)
Freedom of speech and expression is in Article 19(1)(a), one of the six freedoms given only to citizens, so A matches II.
B. Immunity from double prosecution
IV – Article 20
20(2): no one punished twice for the same offence.
C. Abolition of titles
III – Article 18
State cannot confer titles except military or academic.
D. Right to legal aid
I – Article 21
Courts read free legal aid into Article 21 (Hussainara Khatoon, M.H. Hoskot).

points: V (Article 22 – arrest and detention) is the extra item and fits none.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-V, B-I, C-IV, D-II (correct: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-V, B-III, C-II, D-IV (correct: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-I, B-III, C-II, D-V (correct: A-II, B-IV, C-III, D-I).
PYQ-POL-5031979CD36B.also: Article 39A (42nd Amendment) directs the State to provide free legal aid.

PYQ-POL-50E26166E9DB.lead: Option 4: freedom of speech is in Article 19(1)(a), which is given only to citizens.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Right to Equality
The Right to Equality group (Articles 14–18) is not wholly citizen-only, because Article 14 protects 'any person'.
2. Right against Exploitation
The Right against Exploitation (Articles 23–24) protects every person, so foreigners are also protected from forced labour.
3. Right to Freedom of Religion
Freedom of religion (Articles 25–28) is given to 'all persons', citizens and foreigners alike.
4. Right to Freedom of Speech
Freedom of speech and expression is Article 19(1)(a), and Article 19 is available only to citizens.

points: Watch the trap: Articles 15 and 16 inside the equality group are citizen-only, but the group as a whole is not, because Article 14 is for all.
Citizen-only rights: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30.

PYQ-POL-52C20F13D4FF.lead: Option 3: Article 16(4A) allows reservation for SCs and STs in promotions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Reservations to STs
Reservation for STs alone is incomplete; Article 16(4A) covers both SCs and STs.
2. Reservations for SC/ST in appointments
Reservation in initial appointments is the general clause Article 16(4) (backward classes), not 16(4A).
3. Reservations for SC/ST in promotions
Article 16(4A), added by the 77th Amendment Act, 1995, lets the State reserve posts in promotion for SCs and STs who are not adequately represented.
4. All of the above
'All of the above' fails because appointments (16(4)) and an ST-only quota are not what 16(4A) says.

points: Background: Indra Sawhney (1992) said there can be no reservation in promotions; Parliament answered with the 77th Amendment, 1995 inserting 16(4A).
The 85th Amendment, 2001 added 'consequential seniority' to 16(4A).
M. Nagaraj (2006) upheld these amendments subject to data on backwardness, inadequate representation and efficiency (Article 335).

PYQ-POL-53D2661F2CCE.lead: Option 2 is the incorrect statement: Article 20(1) forbids retrospective criminal laws, so Parliament cannot make one.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. No double prosecution and punishment
True
Article 20(2) says no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once (double jeopardy).
2. Parliament can make retrospective criminal law
False
Article 20(1) bars ex post facto criminal laws: no one can be convicted for an act that was not an offence when done, nor given a heavier penalty than the law then allowed.
3. No compulsion to be a witness against oneself
True
Article 20(3) protects an accused from self-incrimination.
4. Article 22 safeguards not available to preventive detainees
True
Article 22(3) says the safeguards of clauses (1) and (2) (being told grounds, a lawyer, production before a magistrate in 24 hours) do not apply to preventive detention.

points: The question asks for the statement that is NOT correct, so the false statement 2 is the answer.
Concept: only criminal laws are barred from retrospective effect; civil and tax laws can be made retrospective.
Options 1, 3 and 4 fail because each of them states a correct protection.

PYQ-POL-557A42B74133.lead: Option 4 (B and C only): foreigners get equality before law (Article 14) and life and personal liberty (Article 21).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Cultural and Educational Rights
False
Articles 29 and 30 protect 'sections of citizens' and minorities, so they are citizen-only.
B. Equality before law
True
Article 14 protects 'any person' within India, so a foreigner can claim it.
C. Protection of life and personal liberty
True
Article 21 protects 'any person', so it covers foreigners too.
D. Article 15 non-discrimination
False
Article 15 says the State shall not discriminate against 'any citizen', so it is citizen-only.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes A; option 2 wrongly includes D; option 3 wrongly includes D and leaves out B.
Foreigners (except enemy aliens) also get Articles 20, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25–28.
Memory hook: 'citizen' in the text = citizen-only; 'person' = everyone.

PYQ-POL-578614405D30.lead: Code a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i matches first chairpersons.

head: Commission
Likely first chairperson
Year
rows: a. NCST
Kunwar Singh
b. NCM
Justice Mohammed Sardar Ali Khan
1993 (statutory)
c. NCSC
Suraj Bhan
d. NCBC
Justice R.N. Prasad

points: NCSC and NCST became separate bodies after the 89th Amendment, 2003.
NCBC got constitutional status under Article 338B by the 102nd Amendment, 2018.

PYQ-POL-591B828C49BC.lead: Option 4: Article 32 jurisdiction is original, because a person can go straight to the Supreme Court without first going to a lower court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Appellate
Appellate jurisdiction means hearing appeals against lower court judgments (Articles 132–136); Article 32 is not an appeal.
2. Advisory
Advisory jurisdiction is the President's reference to the Supreme Court under Article 143.
3. Ordinary
'Ordinary' is not a type of Supreme Court jurisdiction in the Constitution.
4. Original
Original jurisdiction means the case begins in that court; under Article 32 the petition starts directly in the Supreme Court.

points: Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right, so the Supreme Court cannot refuse relief merely because another remedy exists.
It differs from Article 131 (original jurisdiction in Centre–State disputes), which is not about Fundamental Rights.
Article 32 jurisdiction is original but not exclusive: High Courts have concurrent power under Article 226.

PYQ-POL-5CD185446D85.lead: Official key: option 3 (Article 23). Study answer: option 2 (Article 34), because Article 34 is about martial law, not economic safeguards for Scheduled Castes.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 46
State shall promote the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections and protect them from exploitation; it is an economic safeguard.
2. Article 34
Allows Parliament to restrict Fundamental Rights while martial law is in force in an area; it has no link with SC economic safeguards.
3. Article 23
Bans begar, trafficking and forced labour; since bonded labour fell mostly on SCs, it is listed as an economic safeguard.
4. Article 24
Bans child labour in factories, mines and hazardous work; it is also grouped with economic safeguards.

points: The question asks for the Article NOT related, so the odd one out is Article 34.
Economic safeguards for SCs are usually listed as Articles 23, 24 and 46.
The official key (Article 23) picks a genuine safeguard, which is why the study answer differs.
PYQ-POL-5CD185446D85.also: Disputed key: official key is option 3 (Article 23), but Article 23 is an economic safeguard; Article 34 (martial law) is the one not related, so option 2 is the study answer.

PYQ-POL-5D10D5888283.lead: Option 4: Article 12 does not mention courts, so whether the judiciary is 'State' is unclear.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Municipal Corporations
Municipal corporations are 'local authorities', which Article 12 names expressly, so there is no doubt.
2. Educational institutions
Educational institutions are 'State' only if they are instruments of the government (tests from Ajay Hasia); this is case by case, but the standard textbook point of ambiguity is courts.
3. Panchayats
Panchayats are 'local authorities' and are clearly 'State' under Article 12.
4. Courts
The judiciary is not named in Article 12; courts acting judicially are not treated as 'State', but their administrative acts may be, so the status is ambiguous.

points: Article 12 names the Government and Parliament of India, State governments and legislatures, and all local and other authorities.
Naresh Shridhar Mirajkar (1966): a judicial order cannot be challenged as violating Fundamental Rights.
Memory hook: 'Article 12 lists executive and legislature, but stays silent on courts'.

PYQ-POL-602F300F9B4D.lead: Official key: option 1 (all posts). But Section 33 of the 1995 Act reserved not less than 3% of vacancies only in posts identified as suitable for persons with disabilities.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. All posts and services under GoI
Official key; but the Act did not reserve in all posts, only in identified ones.
2. Posts identified as suitable
Section 33 reserved 3% (1% each for blindness/low vision, hearing impairment, locomotor disability/cerebral palsy) in posts identified for each disability.
3. Lower and entry-level jobs only
False: the Act placed no such limit by grade; identified posts can be in any group.
4. Desk jobs only
False: the Act did not confine reservation to desk work; suitability was decided disability-wise.

points: The Government identifies posts suitable for each disability; the quota is computed on total vacancies in the cadre (Union of India v. National Federation of the Blind, 2013).
The RPwD Act, 2016 replaced the 1995 Act and raised the quota to 4%.
PYQ-POL-602F300F9B4D.also: Disputed key: the 1995 Act limited the 3% reservation to posts identified as suitable (Section 33), so option 2 fits the text better than 'all posts'.

PYQ-POL-625DA8B76F85.lead: Official key: option 2 (Article 18). Study answer: option 3, Article 23, which bans begar and forced labour and so covers bonded labour.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence; it is not about labour.
Abolishes titles, except military or academic distinctions; nothing about labour.
Prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other forms of forced labour; bonded labour is a form of forced labour.
Prohibits employing children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work; it is about child labour, not bonded labour.

points: Strictly, the Constitution does not 'define' bonded labour; the definition is in the Bonded Labour System (Abolition) Act, 1976, made to enforce Article 23.
Articles 23 and 24 together form the Right against Exploitation.
PYQ-POL-625DA8B76F85.also: Disputed key: official key is option 2 (Article 18, titles), which has no connection with labour; Article 23 is the study answer.

PYQ-POL-6315A0E8AFC1.lead: Option 2: quo warranto ('by what authority') questions a person's legal right to hold a public office.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Call for records of proceedings of a lower court
Calling for the records of a lower court's proceedings is certiorari.
2. Question the authority of a person to hold a public office
Quo warranto asks the holder of a public office to show by what legal authority he holds it, and removes him if he has none.
3. Direct a public authority to perform its duty
Directing a public authority to perform its duty is mandamus.
4. Remove a case from a lower court to higher court
Moving a case from a lower to a higher court is also done through certiorari (transfer), not quo warranto.

points: It lies only for a substantive public office created by a statute or the Constitution, not a ministerial or private office.
Unlike other writs, any interested person can seek it, not only the aggrieved person.

PYQ-POL-637427A1131A.lead: Option 1: certiorari ('to be certified') orders a lower court or tribunal to send its records to a higher court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Bring the records of the proceedings to the higher court
Certiorari commands the lower court to certify and send the case records, so the higher court can quash an order passed without jurisdiction or with an error of law.
2. Remove a case from one court to another court

Certiorari can also transfer a pending case to the higher court, but the option says 'one court to another' in general and misses the core idea of sending records up to be quashed, so option 1 is the better answer.
3. Questioning the legality of detention of a person
Questioning the legality of a detention is habeas corpus.
4. Direction to do a public duty
Directing performance of a public duty is mandamus.

points: Certiorari is curative (after the order is passed); prohibition is preventive (while the case is pending).
Since 1991 the Supreme Court allows certiorari also against administrative authorities affecting rights, but not against legislative bodies or private persons.

PYQ-POL-65736CB2BA39.lead: B and C are true and A and D are false, so the answer is option 3 (B and C only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Habeas corpus only against public authorities
False
Habeas corpus can be issued against both public authorities and private individuals who detain a person illegally.
B. Mandamus not against private individual/body
True
Mandamus enforces public duties, so it does not lie against a private individual or private body (nor the President or Governors).
C. Prohibition only against judicial/quasi-judicial bodies
True
Prohibition stops a lower court or tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction; it is not available against administrative, legislative or private bodies.
D. Certiorari against legislative bodies and private individuals
False
Certiorari is not available against legislative bodies or private individuals; it lies against judicial, quasi-judicial and (since 1991) administrative authorities.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes A; option 2 includes both false statements A and D; option 4 wrongly includes D.
Memory hook: habeas corpus is the only writ that reaches private persons.

PYQ-POL-65EED9CE550B.lead: Option 4: habeas corpus ('to have the body') orders the detainer to produce the detained person before the court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Quo-Warranto
Quo warranto tests a person's right to a public office, not a detention.
2. Mandamus
Mandamus orders a public official to perform a public duty.
3. Certiorari
Certiorari calls for records of a lower court to quash its order.
4. Habeas Corpus
Habeas corpus requires the detained person to be brought before the court, which then checks the cause and frees him if the detention is illegal.

points: It can be issued against both public authorities and private persons.
It is refused where the detention is lawful, by a court order, for contempt, or outside the court's jurisdiction.

PYQ-POL-6675D5C10A80.lead: Both statements are false, so the answer is option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Constitution defines 'basic structure'
False
The phrase 'basic structure' is not in the Constitution; the Supreme Court created the doctrine in Kesavananda Bharati (1973) and lists its parts case by case.
2. Constitution provides for 'judicial review'
False

The term 'judicial review' is not used in the text; the power is implied from Articles 13, 32, 226 and others, so the statement's claim that the Constitution 'provides for' it by that name is treated as false in this question.

points: Option 1 and option 3 fail because statement 1 is false; option 2 fails because statement 2 (as worded) is also treated as false.
Judicial review itself is part of the basic structure (Minerva Mills 1980, L. Chandra Kumar 1997).

PYQ-POL-66B995530AFB.lead: Option 2: since 1978 property is a legal (constitutional) right under Article 300A, available to every person.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Legal right available to citizens of India only
Wrong: Article 300A says 'no person' shall be deprived of property save by authority of law, so it is not limited to citizens.
2. Legal right available to any person
Correct: it is a legal/constitutional right in Part XII and protects any person, including companies and foreigners.
3. Fundamental right to citizens only
Wrong: the 44th Amendment, 1978 removed property from the Fundamental Rights (Articles 19(1)(f) and 31).
4. Neither a legal right nor a fundamental right
Wrong: it is still a right, enforceable in courts as a constitutional/legal right.

points: The 44th Amendment omitted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 and inserted Article 300A.
For its violation one goes to the High Court under Article 226, not the Supreme Court under Article 32.
Property can be taken only by a law, not by mere executive order.

PYQ-POL-66C7102B892D.lead: Option 3: Article 20 protects against ex post facto laws, double jeopardy and self-incrimination.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 21
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; it is not the specific clause on conviction.
2. Article 22
Article 22 protects against arbitrary arrest and detention, including preventive detention.
3. Article 20
Article 20 gives three protections: 20(1) no retrospective criminal law, 20(2) no double punishment, 20(3) no self-incrimination.
4. Article 23
Article 23 prohibits trafficking and forced labour.

points: Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency (44th Amendment, 1978).
Memory hook: '20 = Three shields of the accused'.

PYQ-POL-672CA7F1D7E2.lead: Option 3: Tamil Nadu's 69% reservation law was put in the Ninth Schedule so it could not be challenged for violating Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Seventh Schedule
The Seventh Schedule contains the Union, State and Concurrent Lists; it gives no immunity.
2. Eighth Schedule
The Eighth Schedule lists the 22 official languages.
3. Ninth Schedule
The Ninth Schedule (Article 31B), added by the 1st Amendment, 1951, protects listed laws from challenge on Fundamental Rights grounds.
4. Fifth Schedule
The Fifth Schedule deals with administration of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes.

points: The 76th Amendment Act, 1994 placed the Tamil Nadu reservation Act in the Ninth Schedule, because 69% exceeds the 50% ceiling of Indra Sawhney.
I.R. Coelho (2007): laws added after 24 April 1973 can still be reviewed for violating the basic structure.

PYQ-POL-6A5483A2C9C6.lead: Option 2: Article 18(1) bars the State from conferring titles except military or academic distinctions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. academic and constitutional titles
There is no exception for 'constitutional titles' in Article 18.
2. military or academic distinctions
Article 18(1): 'No title, not being a military or academic distinction, shall be conferred by the State.'
3. academic and royal titles
Royal titles are exactly what Article 18 abolishes; only the academic part is right.
4. military and royal titles
Both military and royal: royal titles are abolished, so the pair is wrong.

points: Article 18 also bars citizens from accepting foreign titles without the President's consent.
Balaji Raghavan (1995): Bharat Ratna and Padma awards are not titles, but must not be used as prefixes or suffixes.

PYQ-POL-6C7609D2C14F.lead: Option 2: Article 24 forbids employing children below 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous work.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Child marriage
Child marriage is barred by an ordinary law (Prohibition of Child Marriage Act, 2006), not Article 24.
2. Employment of children below 14 in factories and mines
Article 24 prohibits employment of children below 14 years in any factory, mine or hazardous employment.
3. Untouchability
Untouchability is abolished by Article 17.
4. Bonded labour
Bonded labour falls under Article 23 (forced labour).

points: Articles 23 and 24 form the Right against Exploitation.
It does not ban all child work, only work in factories, mines and hazardous jobs; the Child Labour Act, 1986 (amended 2016) enforces it.

PYQ-POL-6F5D85D4F73A.lead: Option 2: 'not punished twice for the same offence' is the doctrine of double jeopardy, Article 20(2).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Doctrine of Repugnancy
Repugnancy deals with a conflict between Union and State laws on a Concurrent List subject (Article 254).
2. Doctrine of Double jeopardy
Double jeopardy means a person cannot be prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence (Article 20(2)).
3. Doctrine of Eclipse
Eclipse means a pre-Constitution law that violates Fundamental Rights becomes dormant, not dead (Article 13(1)).
4. Doctrine of Retribution
Retribution is a theory of punishment (punishment as payback), not a constitutional doctrine.

points: Protection applies only after prosecution and punishment by a court; departmental or administrative action does not count (Maqbool Hussain, 1953).

PYQ-POL-76E6F1F61DC1.lead: Option 1: Subramanian Swamy (2016) upheld criminal defamation (IPC Sections 499 and 500).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Criminal defamation
Criminal defamation was challenged as violating free speech; the Court upheld it, since 'defamation' is an express ground in Article 19(2).
2. Sedition
Sedition (Section 124A) was dealt with in Kedar Nath Singh (1962) and put on hold in 2022, not in this case.
3. Blasphemy
Blasphemy is not a separate offence in the IPC; Section 295A punishes deliberate insult to religion.
4. Obscenity
Obscenity (Section 292) was not the issue in this case.

points: The Court treated reputation as part of the right to life under Article 21, which had to be balanced with Article 19(1)(a).
These IPC sections now correspond to the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 (Section 356).

PYQ-POL-77C9941B15EC.lead: Part III order: Equality (D), Freedom (C), Religion (B), Cultural and Educational (E), Constitutional Remedies (A) — option 2.

head: Order
Right
Articles
rows: D. Right to Equality
Articles 14–18 come first in Part III.
C. Right to Freedom
Articles 19–22 follow the equality group.
B. Right to Freedom of Religion
Articles 25–28 (after the Right against Exploitation, 23–24, which is not listed here).
E. Cultural and Educational Rights
Articles 29–30 protect minorities' culture and institutions.
A. Right to Constitutional Remedies
Article 32 comes last, to enforce all the others.

points: Option 1 puts Cultural rights (E) before Religion (B); option 4 puts E and B before Freedom (C); option 3 is almost the reverse order.
Memory hook: 'E-F-E-R-C-C' — Equality, Freedom, Exploitation, Religion, Cultural, Constitutional remedies.

PYQ-POL-7A33BDAF645D.lead: Option 2: mandamus ('we command') orders a public authority to perform a public duty it has failed to do.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Courts
Mandamus can go to lower courts too, but the standard answer for whom it is issued against is any public authority.
2. Public authority
Correct: it is issued to a public official, body, corporation, lower court, tribunal or government to do its public duty.
3. A private individual
It does not lie against a private individual, because a private person owes no public duty.
4. Private institutions
It does not lie against private bodies, except where they perform a public duty.

points: Mandamus cannot be issued against the President or State Governors, or to enforce a discretionary duty or a private contract.

PYQ-POL-7AADD9E03E00.lead: Option 3: privacy is part of life and personal liberty under Article 21 (Puttaswamy, 2017).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 15
Article 15 bars discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
2. Article 19
Article 19 guarantees six freedoms; privacy links to it but was located mainly in Article 21.
3. Article 21
Article 21: the nine-judge bench in K.S. Puttaswamy (24 August 2017) held privacy an intrinsic part of life and liberty.
4. Article 29
Article 29 protects the language, script and culture of sections of citizens.

points: It overruled M.P. Sharma (1954) and Kharak Singh (1962) on this point.
Privacy is not absolute; limits must pass legality, legitimate aim and proportionality.

PYQ-POL-7C5FA5C4A067.lead: Option 3: A.K. Gopalan (1950) read 'procedure established by law' in Article 21 narrowly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Indira Gandhi Case
Indira Gandhi v. Raj Narain (1975) struck down the 39th Amendment clause on the PM's election; it is about free and fair elections and basic structure.
2. Raj Narayan Case
The Raj Narain case is the same election dispute, not about Article 21's procedure.
3. Gopalan Case
Gopalan held that any procedure laid down by a valid law is enough to deprive liberty; it rejected American 'due process'.
4. Golaknath Case
Golaknath (1967) held Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; it is about amending power.

points: Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruled this view: the procedure must be fair, just and reasonable, close to 'due process'.

PYQ-POL-7CAB9C8D5D22.lead: Option 3: the Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act was passed in 2009.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 2005 is the year of the RTI Act and NREGA, not RTE.
2007 is not linked with RTE; the Bill was passed only in 2009.
The RTE Act was enacted in 2009 (assent in August 2009).
2010 is when it came into force (1 April 2010), not when it was passed — a common trap.

points: It gives effect to Article 21A (free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14).
Article 21A was added by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.

PYQ-POL-7CB608E7C4E9.lead: Option 1: quo warranto literally means 'by what authority (or warrant)'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. What is your authority
Correct: the court asks the office holder to show what authority he has to hold the public office.
2. Illegal authority
'Illegal authority' is what the writ may find, not what the words mean.
3. De Jure authority
De jure means 'by law'; it is not the meaning of quo warranto.
4. De facto authority
De facto means 'in fact'; it is not the meaning either.

points: It prevents illegal usurpation of a public office.
De jure vs de facto example: the President is the de jure head; the Prime Minister is the de facto executive.

PYQ-POL-7CC62124D2A3.lead: Option 3: free and compulsory education for children (6 to 14 years) is a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Reservation for SC's and ST's in promotions
Reservation in promotions (Article 16(4A)) is an enabling power to the State, not a guaranteed right of an individual.
2. Banning child labour
Article 24 bans child labour only in factories, mines and hazardous jobs; it is not a general ban on child labour.
3. Free and compulsory education to children up to the age of 14 years
Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment, 2002, makes education for 6–14 year-olds a Fundamental Right.
4. Hoisting national flag at one's residence
Hoisting the flag was held part of Article 19(1)(a) in Naveen Jindal (2004), but it is not written in the list of Fundamental Rights.

points: The question asks what is written into the list; Article 21A is the express text.
The RTE Act, 2009 implements Article 21A.

PYQ-POL-803B19401388.lead: Option 2: Gujarat was the first State to implement the 10% EWS quota, from 14 January 2019.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Tripura
Tripura did not implement the EWS quota first; Gujarat had already notified it on 14 January 2019.
2. Gujarat
Gujarat applied the EWS quota from 14 January 2019, the day the 103rd Amendment came into force.
3. Madhya Pradesh
Madhya Pradesh adopted the EWS quota only later in 2019, after Gujarat.
4. Odisha
Odisha also adopted EWS reservation later, so it was not the first State.

points: The quota comes from the 103rd Amendment Act, 2019 (Articles 15(6) and 16(6)).
It is over and above existing SC/ST/OBC reservations.

PYQ-POL-8230CB1C5972.lead: Option 3: the 103rd Amendment allows up to 10% reservation for economically weaker sections.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 5% is not the EWS limit; Articles 15(6) and 16(6) allow up to 10%.
15% is the SC reservation share in central jobs, not EWS.
Articles 15(6) and 16(6) allow up to 10% EWS reservation in education and public jobs.
20% is not linked with EWS; the ceiling in the Amendment is 10%.

points: Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (7 November 2022) upheld it by a 3:2 majority.
The Court held economic criteria alone can be a basis for reservation, and excluding SC/ST/OBC from EWS is valid.

PYQ-POL-82ACA523DBB8.lead: Option 3: freedom of religion is in Articles 25 to 28.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 19 to 22
Articles 19–22 form the Right to Freedom.
2. Article 29 to 30
Articles 29–30 are Cultural and Educational Rights.
3. Article 25 to 28
Articles 25–28: 25 conscience and religion, 26 managing religious affairs, 27 no tax for a religion, 28 religious instruction.
4. Article 14 to 18
Articles 14–18 form the Right to Equality.

points: Memory hook: '25 to 28 = four religion Articles'.

PYQ-POL-865AF9CCE260.lead: Option 2: Article 32 lets a person move the Supreme Court directly to enforce Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 31
Article 31 (right to property) was repealed by the 44th Amendment, 1978.
2. Article 32
Article 32 is the Right to Constitutional Remedies; the Supreme Court can issue the five writs.
3. Article 30
Article 30 gives minorities the right to set up and run educational institutions.
4. Article 33
Article 33 lets Parliament restrict Fundamental Rights of armed forces and police.

points: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
It is part of the basic structure and cannot be removed even by amendment.

PYQ-POL-875B90704E4F.lead: Option 2: mandamus is Latin for 'we command' — an order to perform a public duty.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. body
'Body' is the meaning of corpus in habeas corpus.
2. an order
'An order' or 'we command' is the meaning of mandamus.
3. the State
'The State' is not a meaning of any writ name.
4. natural justice
Natural justice is a legal principle (hear both sides, no bias), not a writ meaning.

points: Mandamus is issued to a public authority that has failed to do its legal duty.
Memory hook: 'Man-damus = command'.

PYQ-POL-8AC08B562241.lead: Option 2: after RTE, the Centre brought the National Food Security (Right to Food) Bill, which became the 2013 Act.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Right to Health Act
No central Right to Health Act was introduced then.
2. Right to Food Act
The National Food Security Bill was introduced in Lok Sabha in December 2011 and became the National Food Security Act, 2013.
3. Right of Shelter Act
No central Right to Shelter Act exists, so this option cannot be the law introduced after RTE.
4. Both (1) and (2)
'Both' fails because there was no Right to Health Act.

points: The Food Security Act gives subsidised grain to about two-thirds of the population.
It follows the rights-based approach seen in RTI (2005), NREGA (2005) and RTE (2009).

PYQ-POL-8AC23F763FF4.lead: Option 4: Article 12 defines 'the State' for Part III.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 1
Article 1 says India is a Union of States.
2. Article 2
Article 2 lets Parliament admit or establish new States.
3. Article 10
Article 10 provides for continuity of citizenship.
4. Article 12
Article 12 defines 'State' to include Union and State governments and legislatures and all local or other authorities.

points: Courts treat instrumentalities of government as 'other authorities' (Ajay Hasia, 1981).

PYQ-POL-8B4A831221B2.lead: Option 2: the Right to Property is no longer a Fundamental Right since the 44th Amendment, 1978.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Right to Equality
Right to Equality (Articles 14–18) is still a Fundamental Right.
2. Right to Property
Right to Property was removed from Part III and is now a legal right under Article 300A.
3. Right to Freedom
Right to Freedom (Articles 19–22) is a Fundamental Right.
4. Right against Exploitation
Right against Exploitation (Articles 23–24) is a Fundamental Right.

points: The 44th Amendment omitted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31.
There are now six groups of Fundamental Rights, not seven.

PYQ-POL-8C7C3EB46579.lead: Option 1: Article 14 forbids class legislation but allows reasonable classification.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Class legislation
Class legislation is improper discrimination that gives special privileges to a chosen class arbitrarily; Article 14 forbids it.
2. Reasonable classification
Reasonable classification (based on intelligible differentia with a rational link to the law's object) is allowed.
3. Protective legislation
Protective legislation for weaker sections is permitted, e.g., under Article 15(3) and 15(4).
4. Differential legislation
Differential treatment is allowed if it is based on reasonable classification.

points: Equals must be treated equally; unequals may be treated differently.
Classification must not be arbitrary, artificial or evasive.

PYQ-POL-8DB488C52D02.lead: Option 4: the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 came into force on 1 July 1961.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 20 May 1961 is the date of assent (passing) — a common trap.
2. 1st June 1961
1 June 1961 is not the commencement date fixed for this Act.
3. 20th June 1961
20 June 1961 is not the commencement date either; the Act was notified to start on 1 July.
Correct: the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961 came into force on 1 July 1961, after receiving assent on 20 May 1961.

points: It applies to the whole of India.
Section 498A IPC (cruelty) and 304B IPC (dowry death) were added in 1983 and 1986.

PYQ-POL-9106AE56F56D.lead: Option 4: the definition is inclusive, courts keep widening it, and policy decides control and funding — so 'State' is hard to fix.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Of definition of State
The definition is inclusive ('includes') and 'other authorities' is not defined.
2. Of a series of court decisions
Courts have widened it case by case (Rajasthan SEB 1967, Ajay Hasia 1981, Pradeep Kumar Biswas 2002).
3. Of political considerations
Whether a body is 'State' often depends on government control and funding, a policy-type judgement.
4. All of the above
All three reasons together cause the ambiguity.

points: Memory hook: 'Article 12 = words + cases + policy'.

PYQ-POL-92E39634C4DF.lead: Option 2: double jeopardy is in Article 20(2), part of the Right to Freedom (Articles 19–22).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Right to Equality
Right to Equality (Articles 14–18) deals with equal treatment.
2. Right to Freedom
Right to Freedom includes Article 20, which bars double jeopardy.
3. Right against Exploitation
Right against Exploitation (23–24) is about forced and child labour.
4. Right to Constitutional Remedies
Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) is about enforcement.

points: Article 20(2): no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

PYQ-POL-946A6A8050FA.lead: Option 4: Article 19(1) now guarantees six freedoms to citizens.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 13 is a wrong number; Article 19(1) has sub-clauses (a) to (g), and with (f) deleted only six remain.
44 is the number of the Amendment (1978) that removed the freedom of property, not a count of freedoms.
30 is the Article on minority educational institutions, not the number of freedoms.
Six: speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession/trade.

points: Originally seven; property (19(1)(f)) was omitted by the 44th Amendment, 1978.
Each freedom is subject to reasonable restrictions under clauses (2) to (6).

PYQ-POL-95E6B449F9B7.lead: Option 3 is not correct: habeas corpus lies against private persons too.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It cannot be issued where the detention is outside the jurisdiction of court.
True: it cannot be issued where the detention is outside the court's jurisdiction.
2. It is a bulwark of individual liberty against arbitrary detention.
True: it is a bulwark of personal liberty against arbitrary detention.
3. It can be issued only against public authorities.
False: it can be issued against both public authorities and private individuals.
4. It cannot be issued where the detention is lawful.
True: it cannot be issued where the detention is lawful.

points: It is also refused where detention is by a court order or for contempt of court/legislature.

PYQ-POL-95F0CB851860.lead: Option 2: begar means involuntary work without payment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. voluntary work without payment
Voluntary unpaid work is not begar, since there is no force.
2. an involuntary work without payment
Begar means forced labour without payment.
3. an involuntary work with payment
Paid involuntary work is forced labour, not begar.
4. a statutory compulsion
Statutory compulsion (like compulsory military service) is allowed under Article 23(2).

points: Article 23(1) bans begar, trafficking and forced labour.
Paying below minimum wage can be forced labour (PUDR, 1982).

PYQ-POL-969C87171A34.lead: Option 4: Article 32 is the Right to Constitutional Remedies.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 29
Article 29 protects language, script and culture.
2. Article 30
Article 30 gives minorities the right to run educational institutions.
3. Article 31
Article 31 (property) was repealed in 1978.
4. Article 32
Article 32 lets a person approach the Supreme Court for writs.

points: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

PYQ-POL-96A3ADFBE4E6.lead: Option 4: Article 16(3) lets Parliament prescribe residence for certain public jobs.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 24
Article 24 bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous work; it has no link with residence for jobs.
2. Article 21
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; it is not the Article that bars residence-based discrimination in public jobs.
3. Article 27
Article 27 says no one can be compelled to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion; it has nothing to do with public employment.
4. Article 16
Article 16(3) is the exception to 16(2), which bars job discrimination on residence.

points: Only Parliament, not State legislatures, can make this law (Article 35).
Parliament used it in the Public Employment (Requirement as to Residence) Act, 1957.

PYQ-POL-97244FD83A3D.lead: Option 3: the Central Government notifies minorities under the National Commission for Minorities Act, 1992.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Supreme Court
The Supreme Court interprets 'minority' but does not define it by notification.
2. High Court
High Courts interpret the law in cases but have no power to notify a community as a minority; that is an executive act of the Central Government.
3. Central Government
The Central Government notifies minorities under Section 2(c) of the NCM Act.
4. State Government
State Governments cannot notify national minorities.

points: Six are notified: Muslims, Christians, Sikhs, Buddhists, Parsis and Jains (Jains added in 2014).

PYQ-POL-97612B70243E.lead: Official key: option 2 (both wrong). Study answer: option 1 (both right). Statement B is clearly true; the dispute is only over statement A.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. There is no fundamental right to marry
Disputed

The study answer treats A as true because the Constitution has no express right to marry; but LX p135 lists 'right to marry a person of one's choice' among rights read into Article 21 (Shafin Jahan, 2018), which makes A false.
B. Right to travel abroad is a Fundamental Right
True
Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) and Maneka Gandhi (1978) held that the right to go abroad is part of personal liberty under Article 21.

points: Because B is surely true, options 2 and 3 (which call B wrong) cannot be right on any reading; the official key 2 is therefore weak.
If A is read as true (no express right in the text), the answer is option 1; if A is read as false (Article 21 protects choice of partner), the answer is option 4.
Concept: many rights not written in Part III (privacy, travel abroad, choice of partner) have been read into Article 21 by the Supreme Court.
PYQ-POL-97612B70243E.also: Disputed key: official key is option 2, but statement B is true, so option 2 cannot be correct; the study answer is option 1. Note: LX p135 lists the right to marry a person of one's choice under Article 21, which would point to option 4.

PYQ-POL-981259F90754.lead: Option 1: Article 13(2) bars the State from making laws that abridge Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 13(2)
Article 13(2): any law that takes away or abridges Fundamental Rights is void to the extent of conflict.
2. Article 13(7)
Article 13 has only four clauses, so there is no Article 13(7); this option is a distractor.
3. Article 13(5)
Article 13 has only four clauses, so there is no Article 13(5); this option is a distractor.
4. Article 13(4)
Article 13(4), added by the 24th Amendment (1971), excludes constitutional amendments from Article 13.

points: Article 13(1) covers pre-Constitution laws (doctrine of eclipse).

PYQ-POL-988E531C62A2.lead: Option 2 (Article 20): Article 20(2) says no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Art. 21
Protection of life and personal liberty; no deprivation except by procedure established by law.
Art. 20
Protection in respect of conviction for offences: 20(1) no ex post facto law, 20(2) no double jeopardy, 20(3) no self-incrimination.
Art. 22
Protection against arrest and detention, including preventive detention safeguards.
Art. 19
Six freedoms of citizens such as speech, assembly, movement and profession.

points: Double jeopardy means being tried and punished twice for the same offence; Article 20(2) blocks the second punishment.
The protection applies only to proceedings before a court or judicial tribunal, not to departmental or administrative action for the same act.
Memory hook: Article 20 = three shields for an accused — no retrospective crime, no double punishment, no forced confession.
PYQ-POL-988E531C62A2.also: Article 20 cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency (44th Amendment, 1978).

PYQ-POL-98966D9E30B3.lead: Official key: option 1 (abridges). Article 13(2) says the State shall not make any law which 'takes away or abridges' Part III rights, so options 1 and 3 each quote one half of the same phrase.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Abridges the provisions of Part III
'Abridge' means to cut down or reduce a right; it is one of the two verbs in Article 13(2).
✓ (official)
Alters the provisions of Part IV
Part IV contains the Directive Principles, which are non-justiciable; Article 13 protects only Part III, so this is wrong.
Takes away the provisions of Part III
'Take away' means to remove a right completely; it is the first verb in Article 13(2), so this is equally the text.
✓ (study)
None of the above
Wrong, because the Article's own words match options 1 and 3.

points: Article 13(2) bars any post-Constitution law that takes away or abridges a Fundamental Right; such a law is void to the extent of the conflict.
Article 13 is the textual basis of judicial review over laws that violate Part III (LX p118).
Since both 1 and 3 are partly right, follow the official key in the exam but remember the full phrase 'takes away or abridges'.
PYQ-POL-98966D9E30B3.also: Disputed key: the official key is option 1 (abridges), while the study answer is option 3 (takes away); Article 13(2) uses both words. Article 13(4), added by the 24th Amendment (1971), excludes constitutional amendments from 'law'.

PYQ-POL-9949445CFC8B.lead: Option 3 (Article 21A): it says the State shall provide free and compulsory education to all children aged 6 to 14 years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 19
Six freedoms of citizens such as speech, assembly and profession; it does not deal with schooling.
Article 21
Right to life and personal liberty; courts earlier read education into it, but it is not the specific article.
Article 21A
Right to education for children aged 6–14, inserted by the 86th Amendment Act, 2002.
Article 25
Freedom of conscience and religion; it has nothing to do with education.

points: Before 2002, the Supreme Court read education into Article 21 in Mohini Jain (1992) and Unni Krishnan (1993); the 86th Amendment then made it a separate right.
The RTE Act, 2009 gives effect to Article 21A; both came into force on 1 April 2010 (LX p136).
PYQ-POL-9949445CFC8B.also: The same 86th Amendment changed Article 45 (DPSP) to early childhood care below 6 and added Fundamental Duty 51A(k) for parents.

PYQ-POL-9B2341745553.lead: Official key: option 3 (State). Laxmikanth says all Fundamental Rights are available against the State and some also against private individuals, so the fuller study answer is option 2.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Private individuals
Wrong alone: most rights, like Articles 14 and 19, bind only the State and cannot be claimed against private persons.
Both State and private individuals
All rights bind the State, and Articles 15(2), 17, 23 and 24 also bind private persons, so rights can be claimed against both.
✓ (study)
State
Every Fundamental Right binds the 'State' defined in Article 12; this is the main and classic answer.
✓ (official)
Private companies
Wrong alone: a private company is not 'State' under Article 12, except for the few rights that bind private persons.

points: Article 12 defines 'State' to include the Union and State governments and legislatures, local authorities and other authorities.
Rights that also work against private persons: 15(2) access to shops and public places, 17 untouchability, 23 forced labour, 24 child labour (LX p115).
Exam tip: if 'State' alone is asked, it is the classic answer; if 'both' is offered, the textbook-accurate answer is both.
PYQ-POL-9B2341745553.also: Disputed key: the official key is option 3 (State), while the study answer is option 2 (both State and private individuals) as per LX p115.

PYQ-POL-9BABB167A5F8.lead: Option 3 (Property): the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 removed the right to property from Part III.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Work
Right to work is a Directive Principle (Article 41); it was never a Fundamental Right.
Education
It became a Fundamental Right in 2002 (Article 21A); it was added, not removed.
Property
It was a Fundamental Right under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 until the 44th Amendment deleted them; it is now a legal right under Article 300A.
Information
It is read into Article 19(1)(a) and given by the RTI Act, 2005; it has not ceased to be a right.

points: 'Ceased to be' means it once was a Fundamental Right and no longer is — only property fits.
Article 300A in Part XII says no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law (LX p150).

PYQ-POL-9C662F5674C8.lead: Option 2 (Article 21): the Supreme Court held that choosing a life partner is part of personal liberty and dignity under Article 21.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 19
Six freedoms like speech and movement; marriage choice was not placed under it.
Article 21
Right to life and personal liberty, which the Court reads to include personal autonomy, privacy and choice of partner.
Article 25
Freedom of conscience and religion; conversion may be involved, but the right to choose a spouse rests on Article 21.
Article 29
Protects the language, script and culture of minorities; unrelated to marriage.

points: Shafin Jahan v. Asokan K.M. (Hadiya case, 2018) held that the right to marry a person of one's choice is integral to Article 21.
Shakti Vahini v. Union of India (2018) protected couples from khap panchayat interference on the same basis.
PYQ-POL-9C662F5674C8.also: Supriyo Chakraborty (2023) said there is no unqualified fundamental right to marry as an institution, but choice of partner stays protected.

PYQ-POL-9D42C1CB0887.lead: Option 3 (Article 226): High Courts issue writs under Article 226, for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 35
Gives Parliament (not States) power to make laws to give effect to certain Fundamental Rights; not a writ article.
Article 12
Defines 'State' for Part III; it does not give writ power.
Article 226
Power of High Courts to issue writs for Fundamental Rights and any other legal right.
Article 228
Lets a High Court withdraw a case from a lower court if it involves a substantial question of constitutional interpretation.

points: Article 226 is wider than Article 32 because it covers ordinary legal rights too, not only Fundamental Rights (LX p145).
Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right; Article 226 is not, so the Supreme Court cannot refuse a genuine Article 32 petition as easily.

PYQ-POL-9DF21ADDBAFB.lead: Option 1 (Article 32): it lets a person move the Supreme Court directly for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 32
Right to constitutional remedies: original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court to issue writs for Fundamental Rights.
Article 136
Special leave to appeal — appellate jurisdiction against any court's order, not original.
Article 131
Original jurisdiction, but only for federal disputes between the Centre and States.
Article 226
Writ jurisdiction of High Courts, not the Supreme Court.

points: 'Original' means the case starts in that court; under Article 32 the citizen need not first go to a High Court (LX p115).
Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.

PYQ-POL-A1BEDB62082E.lead: Option 1 (Right to Property): the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 omitted Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 from Part III.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Right to Property
Was a Fundamental Right under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31; removed in 1978 and made a legal right under Article 300A.
Right to Freedom
Articles 19–22; still a Fundamental Right, only clause 19(1)(f) was removed.
Right to Education
Added as Article 21A by the 86th Amendment, 2002 — added, not removed.
Right to Equality
Articles 14–18; still a Fundamental Right.

points: The deletion took effect on 20 June 1979; property is now protected only by Article 300A in Part XII (LX p150).
So a property violation goes to a High Court under Article 226, not directly to the Supreme Court under Article 32.
PYQ-POL-A1BEDB62082E.also: The 44th Amendment also said Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended during an Emergency.
