PYQ-POL-A22F2BB410B6.lead: Official key: option 4 (Future law). But by definition an ex post facto law is a retrospective law that punishes acts already done, so the study answer is option 2.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Earlier law
A law that existed before; 'ex post facto' is not about the age of the law.
Retrospective law
A law that reaches back to acts done before it was made, or raises penalties for them — this is the meaning (LX p133).
✓ (study)
Present law
The law in force today; it carries no backward effect by itself.
Future law
A prospective law applies only to future acts — the opposite of ex post facto.
✓ (official)

points: 'Ex post facto' is Latin for 'from a thing done afterward': a later law applied to an earlier act.
Article 20(1) bars this only for criminal laws; civil and tax laws can be retrospective.
It bars conviction or sentence under such a law, not the trial itself.
PYQ-POL-A22F2BB410B6.also: Disputed key: the official key shows option 4 (future law), but LX p133 defines an ex post facto law as one that imposes penalties retrospectively (option 2).

PYQ-POL-A3C464F8CBC6.lead: Option 2 (Article 21): K.A. Najeeb v. Union of India (2021) granted bail because long undertrial custody violated the right to speedy trial under Article 21.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 16
Equality of opportunity in public employment; unrelated to bail or custody.
Article 21
Life and personal liberty, which includes the right to a speedy trial.
Article 14
Equality before law; not the basis of the ruling.
Article 19
Six freedoms like speech and movement; not the basis of the ruling.

points: The accused had spent over five years in jail under UAPA without trial; a three-judge Bench upheld his bail.
The Court said the bail bar in Section 43-D(5) UAPA cannot override Article 21 when trial is not likely to finish soon.
PYQ-POL-A3C464F8CBC6.also: Speedy trial was first read into Article 21 in Hussainara Khatoon (1979).

PYQ-POL-A4CD0991F7E0.lead: Option 1: the power to impose limits on Fundamental Rights lies with the legislature, not the Supreme Court; the question asks for the incorrect statement.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Power to impose limits is given to the Supreme Court
False: only the legislature imposes restrictions by law; the courts only judge whether they are reasonable (LX p115).
✓ (the incorrect one)
2. Judiciary decides reasonableness of restrictions
True: courts test whether a restriction made by law is reasonable.
3. 44th Amendment omitted Art 19(1) and 31
True in substance: it omitted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 (the right to property).
4. Property taken by executive fiat… (text cut off)
Taken as true: property cannot be taken by executive order alone without the authority of law (Article 300A).

points: 'Except' questions ask you to find the false statement; here statement 1 confuses who restricts rights with who reviews the restriction.
Remember: Parliament/State legislature makes the restriction; the court checks it — that is the balance between liberty and social control.

PYQ-POL-A7629A72C272.lead: Official key: option 3 (is prospective law). But every ex post facto law by definition works retrospectively, so the study answer is option 1.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: is retrospective
It applies to acts done before the law was made or increases their penalty — the very meaning of ex post facto (LX p133).
✓ (study)
represents future law
A future law governs only coming acts; that is the opposite.
is prospective law
Prospective means forward-looking only; an ex post facto law looks backward.
✓ (official)
is a proposed Bill
A Bill is not yet law; ex post facto refers to a law already made.

points: Article 20(1): no conviction except for violating a law in force when the act was done, and no penalty greater than the one then prescribed.
The bar applies only to criminal laws; civil and tax laws may be made retrospective.
PYQ-POL-A7629A72C272.also: Disputed key: the official key shows option 3, but an ex post facto law by definition works retrospectively (option 1).

PYQ-POL-A792422D688A.lead: Option 4 (Article 21): in K. Umadevi v. Government of Tamil Nadu (2025) the Court treated maternity benefit as part of reproductive rights and dignity under the right to life.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Right to education under Article 21A
Free education for children 6–14; unrelated to maternity leave.
Right against exploitation under Article 23
Bans trafficking and forced labour; not the basis here.
Right to equality under Article 14
Equality before law; it was not the main basis of the ruling.
Right to life under Article 21
Includes dignity, health and reproductive choice, which the Court linked to maternity benefit.

points: Her two earlier children were born before she joined service, from a first marriage, so the 'two-child' rule could not deny benefit for the third.
Reproductive choice was earlier read into Article 21 in Suchita Srivastava (2009).

PYQ-POL-A9151258E624.lead: Each writ's Latin name gives its meaning.

head: No.
Writ
Literal meaning
rows: a
Quo Warranto
By what authority
b
Mandamus
We command
c
Habeas Corpus
To have the body of
d
Certiorari
To be certified / informed

points: So the correct code is option 2 (a-ii, b-iii, c-iv, d-i).
Option 1 repeats 'iv' for two items, so it cannot be right.
PYQ-POL-A9151258E624.also: Prohibition means 'to forbid'; it is issued before a lower court decides.

PYQ-POL-A984908A3FA4.lead: Option 1 (Article 33): it empowers Parliament to restrict or abrogate Fundamental Rights of the armed forces and similar forces.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 33
Parliament may restrict rights of armed forces, para-military, police, intelligence agencies and analogous forces to ensure discipline (LX p147).
Article 19
Six freedoms; its clauses (2)–(6) allow general reasonable restrictions, not force-specific ones.
Article 21
Life and personal liberty; it contains no armed-forces clause.
Article 25
Freedom of religion; not about armed forces.

points: Only Parliament, not State legislatures, can make such laws, and such a law cannot be challenged in court for violating Fundamental Rights.
Article 34 restricts rights while martial law is in force in an area.

PYQ-POL-AABBDB75971B.lead: Option 4 (Article 15(3)): it allows the State to make special provisions for women and children.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: General ban on discrimination by the State on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
Special provisions for socially and educationally backward classes, SCs and STs (1st Amendment, 1951).
Reservation for backward classes, SCs and STs in educational institutions, including private ones (93rd Amendment, 2005).
Special provisions for women and children — part of the original Constitution.

points: Clause 3 is an exception to the 'no sex discrimination' rule, allowing protective laws like women-only reservations (LX p120).
15(6), added by the 103rd Amendment (2019), enables EWS provisions.

PYQ-POL-AC92B26EA0EF.lead: Option 2 (Right to Equality): Articles 14 to 18 form the Right to Equality.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Right to Freedom
Right to Freedom is Articles 19-22 (six freedoms, protection in conviction, life and liberty, arrest safeguards), not Articles 14-18.
Right to Equality
Articles 14–18: equality before law, no discrimination, equal job opportunity, abolition of untouchability and titles.
Right against Exploitation
Articles 23–24: forced labour and child labour.
Cultural and Educational Rights
Cultural and Educational Rights are Articles 29-30 (protection of minorities' culture and their educational institutions), not Articles 14-18.

points: 14 equality before law; 15 no discrimination; 16 equal opportunity in public jobs; 17 untouchability abolished; 18 titles abolished (LX p114).
Memory hook: the six groups start at Articles 14, 19, 23, 25, 29 and 32.

PYQ-POL-AC9E5D3B17F3.lead: Option 1 (Article 24): it prohibits employing children below 14 in factories, mines or other hazardous work.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 24
Prohibition of employment of children below 14 in factories, mines and hazardous jobs (LX p140).
Article 21
Life and personal liberty; general, not child labour.
Article 43
DPSP on living wage and decent conditions of work; not binding.
Article 23
Bans trafficking and forced labour (begar) for all persons, not specifically children.

points: Articles 23 and 24 together form the Right against Exploitation.
The Child Labour (Prohibition and Regulation) Act, 1986, amended in 2016, gives it legal force.

PYQ-POL-AD208C7C6B4D.lead: Option 4 (Article 19): freedom of the press is part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article - 14
Equality before law; not about expression.
Article - 21
Life and personal liberty; not the source of press freedom.
Article - 32
Remedy to move the Supreme Court; it enforces rights but does not create press freedom.
Article 19
19(1)(a) freedom of speech and expression, which includes freedom of the press (LX p130).

points: The Constitution does not mention the press separately; courts read it into 19(1)(a) in Romesh Thappar (1950) and Indian Express (1985).
It is subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2).

PYQ-POL-APK-04B6F0.lead: Option 4 (Article 14): the State shall not deny to any person equality before the law or equal protection of the laws.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 11
Gives Parliament power to regulate citizenship by law; Part II.
Article 12
Article 12 defines 'State' for the purposes of Part III; it does not itself guarantee equality before law.
Article 13
Laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void; basis of judicial review.
Article 14
Equality before law and equal protection of laws for any person.

points: It applies to 'any person' — citizens, foreigners and legal persons like companies (LX p120).
'Equality before law' comes from Britain; 'equal protection of laws' from the USA.

PYQ-POL-APK-158179.lead: Option 3 (Mandamus): 'we command' — it orders a public authority to perform its legal duty it has failed to do.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Certiorari
'To be certified' — a higher court quashes an order already passed by a lower court or tribunal.
Prohibition
'To forbid' — stops a lower court from exceeding its jurisdiction in a pending case.
Mandamus
'We command' — directs a public official, body or court to do its legal duty.
Habeas corpus
'To have the body of' — orders production of a detained person to test legality of detention.

points: Mandamus can be issued to public officials, bodies, lower courts and governments, but not to a private person, the President or a Governor (LX p144).
Memory hook: Mandamus = 'Must do'; Prohibition = 'Must not proceed'.

PYQ-POL-APK-24F7A6.lead: Option 2 (Article 330): it reserves seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha (House of the People).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 329
Bars courts from interfering in electoral matters.
Article 330
Reservation of seats for SCs and STs in the Lok Sabha.
Article 331
Nomination of Anglo-Indians to the Lok Sabha (ended in 2020).
Article 332
Reservation for SCs and STs in State Legislative Assemblies.

points: Article 334 sets the time limit; the 104th Amendment, 2019 extended SC/ST reservation to 2030 and ended Anglo-Indian nomination (LX p741).
Memory hook: 330 = Centre (Lok Sabha), 332 = States.

PYQ-POL-APK-29B979.lead: Option 2 ((a) iv     (b) i      (c) ii       (d) iii) is correct: a. Public Interest Litigation → Any person with sufficient interest can sue for others; b. Writ jurisdiction → Writs for enforcing FRs and correcting injustice; c. Proportionality → Government action must be balanced; d. Separation of powers → Independence of judiciary through separation of three organs.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: a. Public Interest Litigation
iv – Any person with sufficient interest can sue for others
Relaxes locus standi (S.P. Gupta, 1981).
b. Writ jurisdiction
i – Writs for enforcing FRs and correcting injustice
Writ jurisdiction lets the Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) issue writs to enforce Fundamental Rights and correct injustice, so b matches i.
c. Proportionality
ii – Government action must be balanced
A restriction must be no more than needed for its purpose.
d. Separation of powers
iii – Independence of judiciary through separation of three organs
Separation of powers keeps the legislature, executive and judiciary each in its own field, which protects the independence of the judiciary, so d matches iii.

points: Note: the List-II wording given for (c) and (d) is loose (ii speaks of 'one branch' power), but option 2 is the only code giving a–iv, which is certain.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-i, B-ii, C-iii, D-iv (correct: A-iv, B-i, C-ii, D-iii).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-iii, C-iv, D-ii (correct: A-iv, C-ii, D-iii).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-ii, C-iii, D-iv (correct: A-iv, C-ii, D-iii).

PYQ-POL-APK-331625.lead: Option 1: Habeas Corpus literally means 'to have the body of'; the court orders the detained person to be produced before it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: To produce the body
Habeas Corpus — tests whether a detention is lawful.
To command the government
This is the meaning of Mandamus ('we command'), a writ ordering a public official to perform a duty, not of Habeas Corpus.
To prohibit an act
Prohibition — stops a lower court from going beyond its jurisdiction.
To protect property rights
Not a writ meaning; property is a legal right under Article 300A.

points: The court examines the cause and legality of detention and frees the person if it is illegal (LX p144).
Unlike mandamus, it can be issued against both public authorities and private persons.

PYQ-POL-APK-3841AD.lead: Option 1 is NOT properly matched: the Supreme Court has not declared access to the internet itself a Fundamental Right under Article 21.

head: Pair
Correctly matched?
Why
rows: 1. Internet access – FR under Article 21
No ✓ (answer)

Anuradha Bhasin (2020) protected speech and trade through the internet under 19(1)(a) and 19(1)(g), but did not declare internet access a separate FR. Kerala HC (Faheema Shirin, 2019) only linked it to education and privacy.
2. Right to privacy – Article 21
Yes
K.S. Puttaswamy (2017), a nine-judge bench, held that privacy is a Fundamental Right under Article 21, so pair 2 is properly matched.
3. Freedom of the press – Article 19(1)(a)
Yes
Implied in speech and expression (Romesh Thappar, 1950).
4. Right to shelter – Article 21
Yes
Recognised in cases such as Chameli Singh (1996).

PYQ-POL-APK-3841AD.also: Kerala High Court (Faheema Shirin, 2019) linked internet access to education and privacy.

PYQ-POL-APK-390EFE.lead: Option 4 (Article 17): it abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 14
Article 14 guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws; it does not specifically abolish untouchability.
Article 15
No discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.
Article 16
Equality of opportunity in public employment.
Article 17
Abolition of untouchability; enforcing any disability from it is an offence.

points: The law punishing it is the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 (originally the Untouchability (Offences) Act) (LX p126).
Article 17 also applies against private persons.

PYQ-POL-APK-505595.lead: Option 2 ((a) ii     (b) iv   (c) i        (d) iii) is correct: a. Maneka Gandhi → Article 21: right to go abroad; b. Shayara Bano → Article 14: triple talaq; c. Indian Young Lawyers Assn → Article 15: Sabarimala entry; d. Indira Sawhney → Article 16: creamy layer.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: a. Maneka Gandhi
ii – Article 21: right to go abroad
Maneka Gandhi (1978) held that the right to go abroad is part of personal liberty under Article 21, so a matches ii.
b. Shayara Bano (2017)
iv – Article 14: triple talaq
Shayara Bano (2017) struck down instant triple talaq as arbitrary and violative of Article 14, so b matches iv.
c. Indian Young Lawyers Assn (2018)
i – Article 15: Sabarimala entry
Indian Young Lawyers Association (2018), the Sabarimala case, allowed women of all ages to enter the temple, relying on equality and non-discrimination including Article 15, so c matches i.
d. Indira Sawhney (1992)
iii – Article 16: creamy layer
Indira Sawhney (1992), on OBC reservation under Article 16(4), upheld it but excluded the creamy layer, so d matches iii.

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-i, B-ii, C-iii, D-iv (correct: A-ii, B-iv, C-i, D-iii).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-iii, B-i, C-iv, D-ii (correct: A-ii, B-iv, C-i, D-iii).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives B-i, C-iii, D-iv (correct: B-iv, C-i, D-iii).
PYQ-POL-APK-505595.also: Indira Sawhney also capped reservations at 50%.

PYQ-POL-APK-57B7BC.lead: Option 1 (Article 1): 'India, that is Bharat, shall be a Union of States.'

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 1
Name and territory of India — a Union of States.
Article 2
Admission or establishment of new States (from outside India).
Article 3
Formation of new States and alteration of areas, boundaries or names of existing States.
Article 4
Laws under Articles 2 and 3 are not constitutional amendments under Article 368.

points: 'Union' shows that the Indian federation is not the result of an agreement among States, and no State can secede (LX p75).
Articles 1–4 form Part I (The Union and its Territory).

PYQ-POL-APK-620E20.lead: Option 1 (Legal Right): since the 44th Amendment (1978), property is a constitutional/legal right under Article 300A, not a Fundamental Right.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Legal Right
A right given by law (here Article 300A in Part XII); protected against executive action but not against legislation.
Fundamental Right
Was so under Articles 19(1)(f) and 31 until 1978; no longer.
Human Right
A broad moral/universal category; the Constitution does not classify property so.
Natural Right
Inborn rights recognised by philosophy, not a legal category in the Indian Constitution.

points: Article 300A: no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law (LX p150).
Its violation is challenged under Article 226 (High Court), not Article 32.

PYQ-POL-APK-623092.lead: Option 2 (Vice-President): under Article 56 the President resigns by a letter addressed to the Vice-President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Chief Justice of India
Administers the oath of office to the President; does not receive the resignation.
The Vice-President of India
Receives the President's resignation and must at once inform the Lok Sabha Speaker (LX p267).
The Prime Minister
Head of government; advises the President but does not receive the resignation.
Chief Election Commissioner
Conducts elections; no role in resignation.

points: The Vice-President also acts as President if the office falls vacant, until a new President is elected within six months.
Memory hook: President and Vice-President resign to each other.
PYQ-POL-APK-623092.also: The Vice-President resigns by writing to the President (Article 67).

PYQ-POL-APK-74D532.lead: Option 1 (Article 22): Article 22(3) says the safeguards of 22(1) and 22(2) do not apply to enemy aliens or persons held under preventive detention.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Protection against arrest and detention; 22(1) grounds and lawyer, 22(2) magistrate within 24 hours (LX p138).
Article 20 protects an accused at conviction (no ex post facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination); it says nothing about enemy aliens and arrest.
Article 23 bans trafficking, begar and forced labour; it has no clauses on arrest safeguards.
Article 24 bans employing children below 14 in factories and mines; it is unrelated to arrest or enemy aliens.

points: An enemy alien is a citizen of a country at war with India, so he gets fewer rights (LX p96).
22(1): right to know grounds of arrest and consult a lawyer; 22(2): production before a magistrate within 24 hours.

PYQ-POL-APK-7FF78B.lead: Option 3 (Both I and II): Fundamental Rights are natural rights made legal and enforceable, and they protect individuals and minorities from arbitrary State action.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Both natural and legal
True: they reflect inherent human rights and are also written in law and enforceable in courts.
True
II. Protect individuals and minorities from arbitrary state action
True: they work as limits on the tyranny of the executive and arbitrary laws of the legislature (LX p52).
True

points: Option 1 wrongly drops statement II; option 2 wrongly drops statement I; option 4 wrongly rejects both.
LX p115: all rights are available against the arbitrary action of the State and are justiciable.

PYQ-POL-APK-855FFA.lead: Option 3 (Article 22(2)): an arrested person must be produced before the nearest magistrate within 24 hours, excluding journey time.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 25(1)
Article 25(1) gives all persons freedom of conscience and religion; it has nothing to do with arrest or the 24-hour rule.
Article 28(1)
Article 28(1) bars religious instruction in institutions wholly maintained by State funds, so it does not fit an arrest question.
Article 22(2)
Production before a magistrate within 24 hours of arrest.
Article 20(2)
Article 20(2) bars punishing a person twice for the same offence (double jeopardy); it is about conviction, not producing an arrested person.

points: Journey time from the place of arrest to the court is excluded from the 24 hours (LX p138).
This safeguard does not apply to enemy aliens or preventive detention (Article 22(3)).

PYQ-POL-APK-91C582.lead: Option 1 (Article 21A): free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 21A
Right to education, inserted by the 86th Amendment, 2002.
Article 44
Article 44 is a Directive Principle asking the State to secure a Uniform Civil Code; it is non-justiciable and not about education.
Article 39A
Article 39A is a Directive Principle on equal justice and free legal aid, so it deals with legal help, not schooling.
Article 12
Article 12 only defines 'State' for Part III; it creates no right at all.

points: It is a Fundamental Right; Article 45 (DPSP) now covers early childhood care below 6 (LX p136).
The RTE Act, 2009 implements it from 1 April 2010.

PYQ-POL-APK-994C20.lead: Option 1 (103rd Amendment): it added Articles 15(6) and 16(6) enabling up to 10% EWS reservation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Constitution (103rd Amendment) Act
2019: up to 10% reservation for economically weaker sections in education and public jobs.
The Constitution (102nd Amendment) Act
The 102nd Amendment (2018) gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes (Article 338B); it did not create the EWS quota.
The Constitution (101st Amendment) Act
The 101st Amendment (2016) introduced the Goods and Services Tax; it is a tax reform, not reservation.
The Constitution (100th Amendment) Act
The 100th Amendment (2015) gave effect to the India–Bangladesh land boundary agreement; it deals with territory, not reservation.

points: The EWS quota is over and above existing SC/ST/OBC reservation and excludes those groups (LX p120).
Upheld in Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India (2022) by 3:2.

PYQ-POL-APK-9FE5D9.lead: Option 3 (Article 25): it guarantees freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 17
Article 17 abolishes untouchability and makes its practice an offence; it does not deal with conscience or religion.
Article 21
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; though broad, freedom of conscience is specifically given by Article 25.
Article 25
Freedom of conscience and religion for all persons.
Article 29
Article 29 protects the language, script and culture of any section of citizens, mainly minorities; it is a cultural right, not freedom of conscience.

points: It is available to all persons, citizens and foreigners (LX p140).
It is subject to public order, morality, health and other Part III provisions.

PYQ-POL-APK-A00F27.lead: Option 4 (Aged persons): Article 15 does not mention the aged for special provisions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Women
Women are expressly covered by Article 15(3), so the State can make special provisions for them.
Children
Children are expressly covered by Article 15(3) along with women, so they are not the answer.
Socially and Educational Backward Classes
Socially and educationally backward classes are covered by Articles 15(4) and 15(5), so special provisions for them are allowed.
Aged Persons
Not covered by Article 15; old age appears in Article 41 (DPSP).

points: The question asks for the group NOT covered, so the group missing from Article 15 is the answer (LX p120).
Article 41 directs the State to give public assistance in old age, sickness and disablement.

PYQ-POL-APK-A7C407.lead: Option 2 is not correctly matched: Financial Emergency is Article 360; Article 311 protects civil servants from dismissal without inquiry.

head: Pair
Correctly matched?
Why
rows: 1. Article 352 – National Emergency
Yes
War, external aggression or armed rebellion.
2. Article 311 – Financial Emergency
No ✓ (answer)
311 = dismissal/removal of civil servants; Financial Emergency = 360 (never declared).
3. Article 21A – Right to Education
Yes
Article 21A (Right to Education for ages 6 to 14) was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002, so pair 3 is correctly matched.
4. Article 315 – Public Service Commissions
Yes
Article 315 provides for a Public Service Commission for the Union (UPSC) and for each State, so pair 4 is correctly matched.

PYQ-POL-APK-A7C407.also: Financial Emergency (Article 360) has never been declared in India.

PYQ-POL-APK-ADE795.lead: Option 4 (14 years): Article 24 bars children below 14 from factories, mines and hazardous work.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 18 years
18 years is the age of majority and voting (Article 326); Article 24 uses 14, not 18.
12 years
12 years is not used anywhere in Article 24; it is a distractor below the real limit of 14.
15 years
15 years is not the constitutional limit; Article 24 clearly says 'below the age of fourteen years'.
14 years
The Article 24 limit, matching the RTE age range 6–14.

points: Article 24 is part of the Right against Exploitation (LX p140).
The 2016 amendment to the Child Labour Act bars adolescents (14–18) from hazardous work.

PYQ-POL-APK-AE9D27.lead: Option 1 (Seven): Annie Besant's Commonwealth of India Bill (1925) listed seven basic rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Seven
Correct: Annie Besant's Commonwealth of India Bill, 1925 demanded seven basic rights for Indians.
Eight
Eight is wrong because the 1925 Bill listed seven rights, not eight.
Nine
Nine is wrong because the 1925 Bill listed seven rights; larger lists came later with the Nehru Report.
Ten
Ten is wrong because the 1925 Bill listed seven rights; the Nehru Report (1928) gave a longer list of 19.

points: The rights included liberty, freedom of conscience, free expression, assembly, equality of sexes, free elementary education and free use of public places.
It was the first organised Indian demand for a declaration of rights; the Nehru Report (1928) followed with a longer list.

PYQ-POL-APK-B0ADE4.lead: Option 1: a whistleblower is a person, usually an insider, who discloses wrongdoing in an organisation to the public or a higher authority.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Discloses wrongdoing to public or higher authority
This is the exact meaning: an insider who exposes corruption or misuse of power, now protected by the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014.
Police officer who arrests corrupt servants
A police officer arresting corrupt officials is doing law enforcement; a whistleblower is an insider who reports wrongdoing, not one who arrests.
Media person spreading scheme awareness
A media person spreading awareness of schemes is doing publicity or journalism; no exposure of wrongdoing inside an organisation is involved.
Social servant raising awareness of injustice
A social worker raising awareness about injustice is an activist; a whistleblower specifically discloses wrongdoing from within an organisation.

points: India passed the Whistle Blowers Protection Act, 2014 to protect such persons from victimisation (LX p709).
The key idea is insider disclosure of corruption or misuse of power.
PYQ-POL-APK-B0ADE4.also: Satyendra Dubey's killing (2003) triggered India's whistleblower protection debate.

PYQ-POL-APK-B1AFA9.lead: Option 2 (Abolition of Untouchability): Article 17 abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice in any form.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Continuance of the Rights of Citizenship
Continuance of citizenship rights is Article 10 in Part II (Citizenship), not Article 17.
Abolition of Untouchability
Article 17 abolishes untouchability, forbids its practice in any form and makes enforcing any disability from it an offence.
Right to Education
Right to Education is Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment in 2002, not Article 17.
Promotion of International Peace
Promotion of international peace is Article 51, a Directive Principle in Part IV, not Article 17.

points: Enforcing any disability from untouchability is an offence punishable by law (LX p126).
The Untouchability (Offences) Act 1955 was renamed the Protection of Civil Rights Act in 1976.

PYQ-POL-APK-C8310F.lead: Option 3 (Article 23): it prohibits traffic in human beings, begar and other forced labour.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 27
Article 27 says no person shall be compelled to pay taxes for promoting a particular religion; it is a religious-freedom right, not about forced labour.
Article 33
Article 33 lets Parliament restrict Fundamental Rights of armed forces and police; it does not ban trafficking.
Article 23
Ban on trafficking, begar and forced labour.
Article 37
Article 37 says Directive Principles are not enforceable by courts but are fundamental in governance; it is in Part IV, not about labour.

points: 'Begar' means compulsory work without payment (LX p139).
The State may still impose compulsory service for public purposes, like military service.
PYQ-POL-APK-C8310F.also: Article 24 (child labour) and Article 23 form the Right against Exploitation.

PYQ-POL-APK-D6C67F.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2): the RTE Act 2009 gives free and compulsory education to ages 6–14 and was enacted to implement Article 21A.

True/False
Why

True: this is the age range in Article 21A and the Act.
True
2. Enacted under Article 21A

True

points: Options 1 and 2 each drop a true statement; option 4 rejects both.
Article 21A (86th Amendment, 2002) and the RTE Act both came into force on 1 April 2010.

PYQ-POL-APK-DC7623.lead: Option 1 (Article 25(1)): all persons are equally entitled to freedom of conscience and to profess, practise and propagate religion.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 25(1)
Article 25(1) gives all persons, citizens and foreigners, freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion.
Article 22(2)
Article 22(2) requires an arrested person to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours; it is about arrest, not religion.
Article 20(2)
Article 20(2) bars double jeopardy (punishing twice for one offence); it is about criminal trials, not religion.
Article 29(2)
Article 29(2) bars denial of admission to State-aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language; it is an education right, not freedom of conscience.

points: It is subject to public order, morality and health (LX p140).
'Propagate' means to spread one's religion, not to convert by force.

PYQ-POL-APK-E1CBE4.lead: Option 1 (Article 25(2)(b)): it lets the State throw open Hindu religious institutions of a public character to all classes and sections of Hindus.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 25(2)(b)
Social welfare and reform, and opening Hindu public temples to all Hindus.
Article 26(a)
Article 26(a) gives religious denominations the right to establish and maintain institutions; it is a denomination's right, not State power to open temples.
Article 25(2)(a)
Article 25(2)(a) lets the State regulate economic, financial, political or secular activities linked to religion; it is not about opening temples.
Article 26(b)
Article 26(b) lets a denomination manage its own affairs in matters of religion; it protects internal autonomy, not temple entry.

points: Here 'Hindus' includes Sikhs, Jains and Buddhists (Explanation II to Article 25) (LX p141).
This clause supports temple-entry laws against caste exclusion.

PYQ-POL-APK-EDC936.lead: Option 1 (Article 332(1)): it reserves seats for SCs and STs in State Legislative Assemblies.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 332(1)
Article 332(1) reserves seats for SCs and STs in every State Legislative Assembly in proportion to their population.
Article 342(1)
Article 342(1) lets the President specify which tribes are Scheduled Tribes in a State; it lists groups, it does not reserve seats.
Article 330(1)
Article 330(1) reserves SC/ST seats in the Lok Sabha, not in State Assemblies, so it fits the Centre, not the States.
Article 340(1)
Article 340(1) lets the President appoint a commission to study backward classes (like the Mandal Commission); it does not reserve seats.

points: Article 334 sets the time limit; now extended up to 2030 by the 104th Amendment (LX p741).
Memory hook: 330 = Lok Sabha, 332 = State Assemblies.

PYQ-POL-APK-FBBDC3.lead: Option 1 (Article 14): it guarantees equality before law and equal protection of laws.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 14
Equality before law and equal protection of laws.
Article 19
Article 19 guarantees six freedoms of citizens like speech and movement; it is the Right to Freedom, not equality.
Article 21
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; it is part of the Right to Freedom group, not equality.
Article 25
Article 25 guarantees freedom of conscience and religion; it belongs to the Right to Freedom of Religion.

points: The full Right to Equality group is Articles 14–18 (LX p114).
Article 14 applies to all persons, not only citizens.

PYQ-POL-APK-FDE3CA.lead: Option 1 (Article 19): Article 19(1)(a) guarantees freedom of speech and expression.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Six freedoms, starting with 19(1)(a) speech and expression.
Article 20 protects an accused in respect of conviction for offences; it does not grant freedom of expression.
Article 18 abolishes titles other than military and academic distinctions; it is part of equality, not expression.
Article 17 abolishes untouchability; it is part of the Right to Equality, not expression.

points: Reasonable restrictions on this freedom are listed in Article 19(2) (LX p130).
Article 19 freedoms are available only to citizens.
PYQ-POL-APK-FDE3CA.also: Press freedom is read into Article 19(1)(a); it is not separately mentioned.

PYQ-POL-B00D76EDB089.lead: Option 3 (The Judiciary): the Supreme Court and High Courts protect Fundamental Rights through writs and judicial review.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Executive
The Executive carries out laws, and its actions are what Fundamental Rights restrain, so it cannot be their guardian.
The President
The President is the constitutional head who acts on the advice of ministers, so he has no power to enforce rights against the State.
The Judiciary
Supreme Court (Article 32) and High Courts (Article 226) enforce rights and strike down laws.
The Parliament
Parliament makes laws, including restrictions on rights, and is itself limited by Part III, so it cannot be the guardian.

points: Under Article 13, courts declare void any law that violates Part III (LX p118).
The guardian must be independent of those whose power the rights restrain.

PYQ-POL-B1C69ED52DE1.lead: Option 1 (Fundamental Rights): the doctrine of eclipse comes from Article 13(1) on pre-Constitution laws that clash with Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Fundamental Rights
Article 13(1): such a law becomes dormant, not dead, and revives if the conflict is removed.
Directive Principles
Directive Principles are non-justiciable guidelines (Part IV); since they cannot make a law void, the eclipse doctrine does not arise.
Fundamental Duties
Fundamental Duties (Article 51A) are obligations of citizens; a law cannot be 'eclipsed' by a duty.
Preamble
The Preamble states the Constitution's ideals and is not enforceable; the eclipse doctrine is not tied to it.

points: Bhikaji Narain Dhakras (1955): the law revived when Article 19(6) was amended (LX p907).
Like the moon in an eclipse: hidden, not destroyed.
PYQ-POL-B1C69ED52DE1.also: Doctrine of severability also comes from Article 13.

PYQ-POL-B1D4C68DFF76.lead: Option 2 (Article 22): Article 22(1) says an arrested person must be told the grounds of arrest.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 21
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty in general; the specific right to know grounds of arrest is in Article 22(1).
Article 22
Article 22 gives safeguards on arrest; clause (1) says the arrested person must be told the grounds of arrest and may consult a lawyer.
Article 20
Article 20 protects an accused at the stage of conviction, not at arrest, so it does not fit.
Article 23
Article 23 bans trafficking and forced labour; it has nothing to do with arrest.

points: Article 22(1) also gives the right to consult a lawyer of one's choice (LX p138).
Article 22(2) requires production before a magistrate within 24 hours.

PYQ-POL-B58E9A3B7705.lead: Paying below minimum wage is forced labour, violating Article 23.

head: No.
Act
Violation?
rows: Banning a book
Can be a valid Art. 19(2) restriction
Not paying minimum wages
Yes — forced labour, Art. 23
Banning secessionist activity
No — sovereignty is a valid ground
No loudspeakers in procession
No — public order, noise control

points: In PUDR v. Union of India (1982, Asiad workers case), the Supreme Court held that paying less than minimum wage is 'forced labour'.
PYQ-POL-B58E9A3B7705.also: Ambiguous question: The source has no key. Option 1 (book ban, Art 19(1)(a)) is the intended answer. Option 2 is also defensible, because paying below minimum wage is forced labour under Art 23 (PUDR 1982, in Laxmikanth).

PYQ-POL-B7C9E1461B6E.lead: Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — the 44th Amendment took property out of Part III and put it in Article 300A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
True. Article 300A in Part XII says no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law; it is a legal (constitutional) right, not a Fundamental Right.
R
True
True. The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 repealed Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 from Part III.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. The same Amendment that removed property from Part III placed it in Article 300A; removal from Fundamental Rights is why it is now only a legal right.
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A, so "does not explain" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (Both A and R are false) fails: both statements are true.

PYQ-POL-B95EAE8AC03F.lead: Option 4: Selvi v. State of Karnataka (2010) held that forced narcoanalysis violates the right against self-incrimination in Article 20(3).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 22
Protection against arrest and detention: grounds of arrest, lawyer, production before a magistrate within 24 hours, preventive detention rules.
No
Article 20(1)
No ex post facto criminal law: a person cannot be punished under a law made after the act, or given a heavier punishment than the law then allowed.
No
Article 20(2)
No double jeopardy: no one can be prosecuted and punished twice for the same offence.
No
Article 20(3)
No person accused of an offence can be compelled to be a witness against himself; a forced narco test extracts statements from the mind against his will.

points: Narcoanalysis makes a person speak under a drug, so the answers are 'compelled testimony'; that is exactly what Article 20(3) forbids.
The Court also said involuntary narco, polygraph and brain-mapping tests intrude on mental privacy and personal liberty under Article 21.
Memory hook: 20(1) old law, 20(2) twice, 20(3) self.

PYQ-POL-B9E8CDE3766F.lead: Option 3: the right against discrimination (Article 15) is given only to citizens; the other three are available to every person, including foreigners.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Right to Life
Article 21 protects life and personal liberty of 'any person', so foreigners also have it.
No
Right to Freedom of Religion
Articles 25-28 are given to 'all persons', so a foreigner can also practise his religion.
No
Right against Discrimination
Article 15 says the State shall not discriminate against 'any citizen' on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth, so it is citizens only.
Right to Equality before Law
Article 14 says the State shall not deny to 'any person' equality before law, so it covers foreigners too.
No

points: Trick: look at the word in the Article. 'Any citizen' means citizens only; 'any person' means everyone.
Citizen-only Fundamental Rights: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30.

PYQ-POL-BB9341FDBD6D.lead: Option 3: certiorari is both preventive and curative; it can stop a case or quash an order already passed by a lower court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: To command a person to perform a function
This is mandamus ('we command'), which orders a public authority to do its legal duty.
No
To examine the legality of a person's claim to a public office
This is quo warranto ('by what authority'), which tests whether a person lawfully holds a public office.
No
To prevent and cure
Certiorari can transfer a pending case (prevent) and also quash an order already made (cure) by a lower court or tribunal.
To prevent a lower court or tribunal from usurping jurisdiction
This describes prohibition, which is only preventive and is issued while the case is still pending.
No

points: Difference to remember: prohibition acts before the order (only prevents); certiorari acts before or after the order (prevents and cures).
Both are issued only against judicial or quasi-judicial bodies, and, after 1991, certiorari can also go to administrative authorities affecting rights.

PYQ-POL-BBAEB4741809.lead: Option 4: the right to education (Article 21A) came into force on 1 April 2010, the same day the RTE Act took effect.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: No event relating to Article 21A happened this year; it is a distractor.

No
Article 21A and the RTE Act were both brought into force on 1 April 2010.

points: Read the verb carefully: 'inserted/amended' = 2002, 'Act enacted' = 2009, 'came into force' = 2010.
Article 21A: free and compulsory education for all children aged 6 to 14 years.

PYQ-POL-BC7E9A9359E7.lead: Option 3: quo warranto ('by what authority') asks a person to show the legal right by which he holds a public office.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Habeas Corpus
'To have the body': the court orders a detaining authority to produce the detained person and show why he is held.
No
Writ of Certiorari
'To be certified': a higher court calls up a lower court's case or quashes its order.
No
Writ of Quo Warranto
The court asks the holder of a substantive public office to show by what authority he holds it, and can oust a usurper.
Writ of officiality
There is no such writ in Article 32 or 226; it is an invented name.
No

points: Article 32 names five writs: habeas corpus, mandamus, prohibition, certiorari and quo warranto.
Quo warranto can be sought by any interested person, not only the aggrieved person; it does not lie for a ministerial or private office.

PYQ-POL-BCFF3014F49A.lead: Option 4: the Punjab and Haryana High Court struck down Haryana's law reserving 75% of private jobs for local residents.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

No
Andhra Pradesh
AP passed a 75% local quota law in 2019, but the question's court ruling was not about it.
No
Haryana

points: The Act reserved 75% of private jobs paying under Rs 30,000 a month for local residents.

PYQ-POL-BFE055E88094.lead: Official key: option 2 (Cannot be amended). Study answer: option 3 — Article 32 can be amended under Article 368 by special majority, but its core cannot be destroyed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Amended only with simple majority
Simple majority is used only for provisions outside Article 368 (like creating States); Article 32 is in Part III, so this is wrong.
No
Cannot be amended
Every part of the Constitution, including Part III, can be amended under Article 368; only the basic structure cannot be destroyed (Kesavananda, 1973). This is the official key.
Official key
Amended with two-thirds majority
Article 368(2) special majority: two-thirds of members present and voting plus a majority of total membership in each House.
✓ study
Amended with ratification by the States
State ratification is needed only for federal provisions listed in the proviso to Article 368(2); Article 32 is not in that list.
No

points: The right to move the Supreme Court is part of the basic structure, so an amendment cannot abolish it — this is why the official key says 'cannot be amended'.
But 'cannot be destroyed' is not the same as 'cannot be amended'; Parliament can still amend Article 32 by special majority.
PYQ-POL-BFE055E88094.also: Disputed key: the official key is option 2; by Article 368 and the basic-structure doctrine, option 3 is the better answer.

PYQ-POL-C1B73002EFC9.lead: Option 4: in April 2025 the Supreme Court held that equal digital access is part of the right to life under Article 21.
