PYQ-POL-APK-95CF94.lead: Option 3: Ambedkar said DPSPs resemble the Instrument of Instructions under the Government of India Act, 1935.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Morley-Minto Reforms; separate electorates for Muslims.
Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms; dyarchy in provinces.
Instruments of Instructions issued to the Governor-General and Governors.
Indian Independence Act, not a Government of India Act.

points: Ambedkar: DPSPs are 'merely another name for the instrument of instructions', but addressed to the legislature and executive.

PYQ-POL-APK-A6A384.lead: Option 2: Article 48A directs protection and improvement of the environment and safeguarding of forests and wildlife.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 48
Organise agriculture and animal husbandry; cow protection.
2. Article 48A
Article 48A, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), directs the State to protect the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife, so it is the answer.
3. Article 50
Article 50 directs separation of the judiciary from the executive; it is not about the environment.
4. Article 51
Article 51 directs promotion of international peace and security; it is not about the environment.

points: Article 48A was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976; the matching duty of citizens is Article 51A(g).

PYQ-POL-APK-C181B3.lead: Article 45 is correct: after the 86th Amendment (2002) it asks the State to provide early childhood care and education for all children until they complete six years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 44
Article 44 asks the State to secure a uniform civil code for all citizens; it says nothing about young children.
2. Article 45
Article 45 now directs early childhood care and education for children below six years; this is exactly the stem.
3. Article 46
Article 46 asks the State to promote the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and other weaker sections; it is not about age-based child care.
4. Article 47
Article 47 asks the State to raise nutrition and living standards, improve public health and prohibit intoxicants; it is not about education.

points: Before 2002, Article 45 promised free and compulsory education for children up to 14 years.
The 86th Amendment made education for 6 to 14 years a Fundamental Right (Article 21A) and rewrote Article 45 for children below 6.
Memory hook: 21A = school age (6 to 14); 45 = before school (below 6).
PYQ-POL-APK-C181B3.also: The same amendment added Fundamental Duty 51A(k): parents or guardians must give children aged 6 to 14 opportunities for education.

PYQ-POL-APK-DA6328.lead: Option 1, M. Y. Pylee, is the official answer: the 'new Magna Carta' description of the Directive Principles is commonly credited to him.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. M. Y. Pylee
M. Y. Pylee, a constitutional scholar, is credited in exam sources with calling the Directive Principles a new Magna Carta of social and economic justice.
2. M. K. Gandhi
M. K. Gandhi died in 1948, before the Constitution was adopted, and did not use this phrase; some DPSPs (village panchayats, prohibition) only reflect his ideas.
3. B. R. Ambedkar
B. R. Ambedkar called the Directive Principles a 'novel feature' and compared them to the Instrument of Instructions; he is not credited with 'new Magna Carta'.
4. D. D. Basu
D. D. Basu is a well-known commentator on the Constitution, but this phrase is not attributed to him.

points: Magna Carta was the charter of rights issued by King John of England in 1215; calling the DPSPs a 'new Magna Carta' means they are a charter of social and economic goals.
Do not mix this up with Part III: Laxmikanth calls the Fundamental Rights the 'Magna Carta of India'.
PYQ-POL-APK-DA6328.also: Disputed key: some sources credit Ambedkar with this phrase; the official key (M. Y. Pylee) is kept. Granville Austin called the Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles together the 'conscience of the Constitution'.

PYQ-POL-C8303B19D7C5.lead: Statements A, B and D are true and C is false, because the 97th Amendment added Part IX-B, not Part X-B. So the answer is option 1 (A, B and D only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
The 97th Amendment Act, 2011 gave co-operative societies constitutional status and protection.
B
True
It made the right to form co-operative societies a Fundamental Right by adding the word 'co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c).
C
False
The new part it added is Part IX-B (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT), placed after Part IX-A on municipalities; Part X deals with Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
D
True
It added Article 43B, a new Directive Principle asking the State to promote voluntary formation and democratic control of co-operative societies.

points: Option 2 (A, B and C only) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement C which is false; it leaves out true statement D.
Option 3 (A and B only) is wrong: it leaves out true statement D.
Option 4 (All of the above) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement C which is false.
Memory hook: IX = Panchayats, IX-A = Municipalities, IX-B = Co-operatives (all local, grassroots bodies).
PYQ-POL-C8303B19D7C5.also: In 2021 (Union of India v. Rajendra Shah) the Supreme Court struck down the parts of Part IX-B dealing with state co-operative societies for want of state ratification.

PYQ-POL-D12584354DEA.lead: Article 43 is correct: it asks the State to secure a living wage, a decent standard of life, full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities for workers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Article 39 lists economic policy goals such as livelihood, fair distribution of resources, equal pay and protection of children; it does not mention leisure.
2. Article 40
Article 40 asks the State to organise village panchayats as units of self-government.
3. Article 42
Article 42 asks for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief, but not leisure or cultural opportunities.
4. Article 43
Article 43 contains the exact words of the stem: living wage, decent standard of life, leisure and social and cultural opportunities.

points: Article 43 is a socialistic directive; its second part, promotion of cottage industries in rural areas, is Gandhian.
Memory hook: 42 = conditions AT work; 43 = life AFTER work (wage, leisure, culture).

PYQ-POL-D18AB709A124.lead: All five items are Directive Principles in Part IV of the Constitution. So the answer is option 4 (a, b, c, d and e).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: a
True
Free legal aid to the poor is in Article 39A, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
b
True
Maternity relief is in Article 42, along with just and humane conditions of work.
c
True
A living wage for workers is in Article 43.
d
True
Safeguarding forests and wildlife is in Article 48A, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
e
True

Option 2 (a and c only) is wrong: it leaves out true statements b and d and e.
Option 3 (a, b and c only) is wrong: it leaves out true statements d and e.
Articles 39A and 48A were added in 1976; Articles 42, 43 and 49 were in the original Constitution.

PYQ-POL-E54C490E2C38.lead: Option 1 is correct: Article 51 directs the State to promote international peace and security.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Promote international peace and security
Article 51 asks the State to promote international peace and security, keep just and honourable relations between nations, respect international law and settle disputes by arbitration.
2. Right to constitutional remedies
The right to constitutional remedies is a Fundamental Right under Article 32, in Part III, not a Directive Principle.
3. Freedom of speech
Freedom of speech and expression is a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(a), in Part III.
4. Protection against arbitrary arrest
Protection against arbitrary arrest and detention is a Fundamental Right under Article 22, in Part III.

points: Article 51 is the last article of Part IV and the only Directive Principle on foreign relations.
Options 2 to 4 are all Fundamental Rights, so they cannot be the aim of a Directive Principle.
PYQ-POL-E54C490E2C38.also: Do not confuse Article 51 (DPSP) with Article 51A (Fundamental Duties, Part IV-A).

PYQ-POL-E66D49535FE6.lead: Article 39A is correct: it asks the State to promote equal justice and provide free legal aid to the poor.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 39A, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), promotes equal justice and free legal aid.
Article 32A was added by the 42nd Amendment but omitted by the 43rd Amendment (1977); it barred the Supreme Court from examining state laws in writ cases, not legal aid.
Article 43A asks the State to secure participation of workers in the management of industries.
Article 48A asks the State to protect the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.

points: The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 set up NALSA and state legal services bodies to give effect to Article 39A.
Note: 39A, 43A and 48A all came by the 42nd Amendment, so knowing the subject of each is the key.

PYQ-POL-E6C738A9F78C.lead: Option 2 (IV, I, II, III) is correct: 48A in 1976, 38(2) in 1978, new Article 45 in 2002, and 43B in 2011.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. I, II, IV, III
Wrong: it puts I (1978) first, but IV (Article 48A, 1976) is the earliest change.
2. IV, I, II, III
Correct: IV (42nd Amendment, 1976), I (44th Amendment, 1978), II (86th Amendment, 2002), III (97th Amendment, 2011).
3. IV, II, I, III
Wrong: it puts II (2002) before I (1978); the 44th Amendment came long before the 86th.
4. I, IV, II, III
Wrong: it puts I (1978) before IV (1976); the 42nd Amendment came first.

points: I: the 44th Amendment (1978) added clause (2) to Article 38, asking the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.
II: the 86th Amendment (2002) changed Article 45 to early childhood care below six years.
III: the 97th Amendment (2011) added Article 43B on co-operative societies; IV: the 42nd Amendment (1976) added Article 48A on environment.

Article 45 is about early childhood care and education for children below six years.
4. Article 39
Article 39 lists economic policy principles such as livelihood, fair distribution of resources and equal pay.

points: Article 51 also asks for just and honourable relations between nations and settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
It is classed as a liberal-intellectual directive.
PYQ-POL-F44F554B7212.also: Article 51 is the only DPSP on foreign relations.

PYQ-POL-F79DE325CF31.lead: Option 3 is correct: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) express distributive justice, meaning wealth and resources should be shared for the common good.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Articles 39(e) and 39(f)
39(e) protects the health of workers and children from abuse, and 39(f) gives children opportunities for healthy development; these protect people, not distribute wealth.
2. Articles 39(a) and 39(b)
39(a) is the right to adequate means of livelihood; only 39(b) of this pair is about distribution.
3. Articles 39(b) and 39(c)
39(b) asks that material resources be distributed for the common good, and 39(c) asks that wealth and means of production not be concentrated; together they are distributive justice.
4. Articles 39(c) and 39(d)
39(d) is equal pay for equal work for men and women; only 39(c) of this pair is about distribution.

points: Distributive justice means removing economic inequality by fairly sharing material resources among people.
Article 31C protects laws that give effect to 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19; that is why these two clauses are special.

PYQ-POL-FAEFC8C1DED4.lead: Option 2 is correct: organising village panchayats (Article 40) reflects Gandhi's idea of village self-rule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Uniform civil code
The uniform civil code (Article 44) is a liberal-intellectual principle, based on liberal ideas of equal law for all.
2. Organisation of village panchayats
Village panchayats as units of self-government (Article 40) are a Gandhian principle.
3. Free and compulsory education
Early childhood care and education (Article 45; earlier free and compulsory education) is a liberal-intellectual principle.
4. Equal pay for equal work
Equal pay for equal work for men and women (Article 39(d)) is a socialistic principle.

points: Laxmikanth groups DPSPs into socialistic, Gandhian and liberal-intellectual principles.
Gandhian principles come from Gandhi's programme of reconstruction: village panchayats, cottage industries, weaker sections, prohibition, cattle protection.
PYQ-POL-FAEFC8C1DED4.also: Other Gandhian DPSPs: cottage industries (43), co-operatives (43B), weaker sections (46), prohibition (47), cattle slaughter ban (48).

PYQ-POL-WEB-0CA278.lead: Article 43 is correct: its second part asks the State to promote cottage industries on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 42
Article 42 asks for just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
2. Article 44
Article 44 asks the State to secure a uniform civil code for citizens.
3. Article 49
Article 49 asks the State to protect monuments and places of national importance.
4. Article 43
Article 43 contains both the living wage for workers and the promotion of rural cottage industries.

points: The cottage industries part of Article 43 is a Gandhian principle; the living wage part is socialistic.
PYQ-POL-WEB-0CA278.also: Promotion of co-operative societies is separately in Article 43B (97th Amendment, 2011).

PYQ-POL-WEB-121BCE.lead: Option 2 is correct: equal justice and free legal aid (Article 39A) was inserted by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The State shall minimise inequalities in income
Minimising inequalities in income (Article 38(2)) was added by the 44th Amendment, 1978, not the 42nd.
2. Equal justice and free legal aid
Equal justice and free legal aid (Article 39A) was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
3. Promotion of co-operative societies
Promotion of co-operative societies (Article 43B) was added by the 97th Amendment, 2011.
4. Provision for early childhood care
Early childhood care below six years (new Article 45) came by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

points: The 42nd Amendment added four DPSPs: 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A.
Memory hook: 42nd = Children, Legal aid, Workers, Environment.

PYQ-POL-WEB-124BD0.lead: Option 1 is correct: Article 51A(f) is the Fundamental Duty to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 51 (A)
Article 51A lists the Fundamental Duties; clause (f) is to value and preserve the rich heritage of our composite culture.
2. Article 43 (A)
Article 43A is a Directive Principle on participation of workers in the management of industries.
3. Article 48 (A)
Article 48A is a Directive Principle on protecting the environment, forests and wildlife.
4. Article 124 (A)
Article 124A was added by the 99th Amendment (2014) for the National Judicial Appointments Commission, struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015.

points: Fundamental Duties were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, as Part IV-A, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.
Do not confuse with Article 49 (DPSP: protect monuments); 51A(f) is a duty of citizens about culture.

PYQ-POL-WEB-243CB9.lead: Option 3 is correct: a Uniform Civil Code means one common set of civil laws on marriage, divorce, inheritance and adoption for all citizens.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Replace criminal laws
Wrong: criminal laws are already uniform across India for all religions; UCC concerns civil (personal) matters only.
2. Abolish parliamentary democracy
Wrong: the UCC has nothing to do with the form of government; parliamentary democracy is part of the basic structure.
3. Establish uniform laws on civil matters like marriage, divorce, inheritance
Correct: Article 44 asks the State to secure uniform laws on civil matters such as marriage, divorce and inheritance for all citizens.
4. Regulate foreign trade
Wrong: foreign trade is a Union List subject regulated by trade laws, not by a civil code.

points: Article 44 (DPSP) says the State shall endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for citizens throughout India.
Today these matters are governed by religion-based personal laws (Hindu, Muslim, Christian, Parsi).
PYQ-POL-WEB-243CB9.also: Goa already has a common civil code; Uttarakhand passed a UCC law in 2024.

PYQ-POL-WEB-291ECB.lead: Option 2 is correct: Article 50 (separation of judiciary from executive) is a Directive Principle in Part IV.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Fundamental Duties
Fundamental Duties are in Article 51A, Part IV-A; Article 50 is not among them.
2. Directive Principles of State Policy
Directive Principles are Articles 36 to 51 in Part IV, so Article 50 falls here.
3. Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights are Articles 12 to 35 in Part III; Article 50 is outside that range.
4. Preamble
The Preamble is the introduction to the Constitution and has no article number.

points: Article 50 asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
It is classed as a liberal-intellectual directive; the CrPC, 1973 gave it effect by separating judicial and executive magistrates.

PYQ-POL-WEB-298C72.lead: Option 4 (3 5 1 2) is correct: A. Directive Principles → Ireland; B. Fundamental Rights → USA; C. Concurrent List → Australia; D. Union with strong Centre → Canada.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Directive Principles
3 – Ireland
The Directive Principles were borrowed from the Irish Constitution (which itself took the idea from Spain), so A matches Ireland.
B. Fundamental Rights
5 – USA
The Fundamental Rights were borrowed from the US Constitution, whose Bill of Rights is the model, so B matches USA.
C. Concurrent List
1 – Australia
Also freedom of trade and joint sitting.
D. Union with strong Centre
2 – Canada
Federation with a strong Centre; residuary powers with the Centre.

points: United Kingdom (4) is the extra item – it gave parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-5, B-4 (correct: A-3, B-5).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives C-2, D-1 (correct: C-1, D-2).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-5, B-4, C-2, D-1 (correct: A-3, B-5, C-1, D-2).

PYQ-POL-WEB-3878B8.lead: Option 2 is the NOT correct statement: Directive Principles cannot override all the Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. They are not enforceable in a court of law.
True: Article 37 says the Directive Principles shall not be enforceable by any court.
2. They can override all the fundamental rights.
False, so it is the answer: only laws giving effect to Article 39(b) and (c) are protected from Articles 14 and 19 by Article 31C; DPSPs cannot override all FRs.
3. They can be related to social and economic justice.
True: Article 38 asks the State to secure a social order based on social, economic and political justice.
4. They can be related to giving free legal aid.
True: Article 39A asks the State to provide free legal aid to the poor.

points: In Minerva Mills (1980) the Supreme Court struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of 31C to all DPSPs and held that balance between FRs and DPSPs is part of the basic structure.
So DPSPs are generally subordinate to FRs, except for 39(b) and (c) laws over Articles 14 and 19.

PYQ-POL-WEB-467736.lead: Option 2 is correct: participation of workers in the management of industries (Article 43A) was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Equal pay for equal work for both men and women
Equal pay for equal work for men and women is Article 39(d), part of the original Constitution.
2. Participation of workers in the management of industries
Participation of workers in the management of industries is Article 43A, added by the 42nd Amendment.
3. Right to work, education and public assistance
The right to work, to education and to public assistance is Article 41, part of the original Constitution.
4. Securing living wage and human conditions of work to workers
Living wage and humane conditions of work are in Articles 42 and 43, both original.

points: The 42nd Amendment added 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A; any option outside this list is an original directive.
PYQ-POL-WEB-467736.also: Memory hook: 'A' suffix articles 39A, 43A, 48A all came in 1976.

PYQ-POL-WEB-47A644.lead: Option 2, Four, is correct: the 42nd Amendment added four Directive Principles: 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Three
Wrong: three is too few; the four are children (39(f)), legal aid (39A), workers (43A) and environment (48A).
2. Four
Correct: Laxmikanth says the 42nd Amendment added four new Directive Principles.
3. Five
Wrong: five is too many; the fifth commonly confused one, 38(2), came by the 44th Amendment (1978).
4. Two
Wrong: two is too few; all four listed above came together in 1976.

points: 39(f): opportunities for healthy development of children; 39A: equal justice and free legal aid; 43A: workers in management; 48A: environment, forests and wildlife.
PYQ-POL-WEB-47A644.also: Later: the 44th Amendment added 38(2), the 86th changed Article 45 and the 97th added 43B.

PYQ-POL-WEB-4E48F3.lead: Option 3 is correct: a UCC would replace religion-based personal laws, such as the Hindu Marriage Act and Muslim Personal Law, with one common code.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Criminal laws
Wrong: criminal laws are already common to all citizens irrespective of religion.
2. Property laws
Wrong: general property laws such as the Transfer of Property Act are not religion-based; only inheritance under personal law is.
3. Religious personal laws (e.g., Hindu Marriage Act, Muslim Personal Law)
Correct: personal laws on marriage, divorce, adoption, inheritance and succession differ by religion, and the UCC seeks to replace them.
4. Environmental laws
Wrong: environmental laws apply equally to everyone and are not personal laws.

points: Article 44 (DPSP) asks the State to endeavour to secure a uniform civil code throughout India.
PYQ-POL-WEB-4E48F3.also: Goa has a common civil code; Uttarakhand enacted a UCC in 2024.

PYQ-POL-WEB-53F763.lead: Article 38 is correct: it asks the State to promote the welfare of the people by securing a social order based on social, economic and political justice.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 37
Article 37 says the Directive Principles are not enforceable by courts but are fundamental in governance.
2. Article 38
Article 38 directs the State to secure a social order permeated by justice for the welfare of the people.
3. Article 39
Article 39 lists specific economic policy principles such as livelihood, distribution of resources and equal pay.
4. Article 36
Article 36 defines 'State' for Part IV, with the same meaning as in Article 12.

points: Article 38(2), added by the 44th Amendment (1978), asks the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.
Article 38 is the base of the welfare state idea in Part IV.

PYQ-POL-WEB-5866F7.lead: Option 2 is correct: Article 46 asks the State to promote the educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and other weaker sections.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. religious minorities.
Wrong: religious minorities' rights to culture and educational institutions are in Articles 29 and 30 (Fundamental Rights), not Article 46.
2. Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and other weaker sections.
Correct: Article 46 names SCs, STs and other weaker sections and asks the State to protect them from social injustice and exploitation.
3. displaced persons from large irrigation projects.
Wrong: displaced persons from irrigation projects are not mentioned anywhere in Article 46.
4. the economically deprived.
Wrong: Article 46 is not limited to the economically deprived; it names SCs and STs and covers their educational interests too.

points: Laxmikanth classes Article 46 as a Gandhian directive, reflecting Gandhi's concern for the upliftment of the oppressed.

PYQ-POL-WEB-5C2D89.lead: Both statements are false: Directive Principles are guidelines to the State, not limitations on its legislative or executive powers. So the answer is option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: False
A law is not invalid because it ignores or goes against a DPSP (Article 37), so DPSPs do not limit legislative power; Fundamental Rights do that under Article 13.
False
Courts cannot enforce DPSPs against the executive either; they are positive instructions on what to do, not bars on what the executive may do.

points: Option 1 (1 only) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement 1 which is false.
Option 2 (2 only) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement 2 which is false.
Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) is wrong: it wrongly includes statements 1 and 2 which are false.
Fundamental Rights are negative (limit the State); Directive Principles are positive (direct the State to act).
PYQ-POL-WEB-5C2D89.also: This UPSC question is often debated; the study answer (Neither 1 nor 2) is kept, because a DPSP never makes a law or an executive act invalid.

PYQ-POL-WEB-6719B9.lead: Option 1 is correct: the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added four new Directive Principles: 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 42nd Amendment Act, 1976
The 42nd Amendment (1976), called the 'mini-Constitution', added 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A.
2. 41st Amendment Act, 1976
The 41st Amendment (1976) raised the retirement age of members of State Public Service Commissions from 60 to 62; it did not touch DPSPs.
3. 40th Amendment Act, 1976
The 40th Amendment (1976) dealt with maritime zones and added laws to the Ninth Schedule; it added no DPSP.
4. 39th Amendment Act, 1975
The 39th Amendment (1975) put the election of the PM and Speaker beyond court challenge; it added no DPSP.

points: In the stem, 'Article 39' refers to clause (f) of Article 39 on healthy development of children.
PYQ-POL-WEB-6719B9.also: The 42nd Amendment also added Fundamental Duties (Part IV-A).

PYQ-POL-WEB-802072.lead: Option 2 is correct: the Goa Civil Code is a uniform civil code applying to all communities in Goa regardless of religion.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It applies only to the Hindu community in Goa.
Wrong: it applies to all residents of Goa, not only Hindus.
2. It is a uniform civil code that applies to all communities regardless of religion.
Correct: Goa follows one common civil code for marriage, divorce and succession for all religions.
3. It is based on British common law.
Wrong: it comes from the Portuguese Civil Code of 1867, not British common law.
4. It allows separate personal laws for different religions.
Wrong: allowing separate religion-based laws is the opposite of a uniform code.

points: Goa kept the Portuguese-era code after it joined India in 1961.
This is why Goa is often given as the model for Article 44.
PYQ-POL-WEB-802072.also: Uttarakhand became the first state after independence to enact a UCC (2024).

PYQ-POL-WEB-85A386.lead: Option 2 is the NOT correct statement: Directive Principles are non-justiciable, meaning courts cannot enforce them (Article 37).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. They provide guidelines for the governance of the country.
True: they are guidelines (like an Instrument of Instructions) for the State in governance and law-making.
2. They are justiciable in nature.
False, so it is the answer: Article 37 says DPSPs shall not be enforceable by any court.
3. They are morally binding on the government.
True: they carry moral and political force; the government is answerable to the people for them.
4. They ensure social and economic development.
True: they aim at social and economic democracy and a welfare state.

points: 'Justiciable' means a person can go to court to get it enforced; Fundamental Rights are justiciable, DPSPs are not.
Article 37 still says DPSPs are fundamental in the governance of the country.

PYQ-POL-WEB-8842BD.lead: Only statement 2 is a Directive Principle; statement 1 is a Fundamental Right. So the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: False
Prohibition of traffic in human beings and forced labour is a Fundamental Right under Article 23 (Right against Exploitation), not a DPSP.
True
Prohibition of intoxicating drinks and harmful drugs except for medicinal purposes is a DPSP under Article 47.

points: Option 1 (1 only) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement 1 which is false; it leaves out true statement 2.
Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement 1 which is false.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) is wrong: it leaves out true statement 2.
Article 47 is a Gandhian directive; Article 23 is enforceable in court because it is in Part III.

PYQ-POL-WEB-884537.lead: Option 4 is correct: Dr. B. R. Ambedkar described the Directive Principles as a 'novel feature' of the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Jawaharlal Nehru
Jawaharlal Nehru moved the Objectives Resolution, but did not give this description of DPSPs.
2. Rajendra Prasad
Rajendra Prasad was President of the Constituent Assembly; he is not linked with this phrase.
3. S. N. Mukherjee
S. N. Mukherjee was the Chief Draftsman of the Constitution in the Assembly; this phrase is not his.
4. B. R. Ambedkar
Ambedkar called DPSPs a 'novel feature' and said the Irish Constitution was the only other one with such principles.

points: Ambedkar also compared DPSPs to the 'Instrument of Instructions' under the Government of India Act, 1935.

PYQ-POL-WEB-8C6ADF.lead: Option 2 is correct: the Directive Principles spell out the programme of a welfare state for India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Preamble
The Preamble states the ideals of justice, liberty and equality, but the detailed welfare programme is in the DPSPs.
2. Directive Principles of State Policy
DPSPs direct the State on livelihood, wages, health, education and social justice; Laxmikanth says they embody the concept of a welfare state, not a police state.
3. Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights mainly limit the State to protect individual freedoms; they do not set out welfare goals.
4. Seventh Schedule
The Seventh Schedule only divides subjects between the Union and the States.

points: A police state only keeps law and order; a welfare state actively works for people's social and economic well-being.

PYQ-POL-WEB-8E05F5.lead: Option 3 is correct: protection of personal law is not a Directive Principle; in fact Article 44 seeks a uniform civil code.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Equal justice and free legal aid
Equal justice and free legal aid is a DPSP under Article 39A.
2. Protection of monuments and places and objects of national importance
Protection of monuments and places of national importance is a DPSP under Article 49.
3. Protection of personal law
No DPSP protects personal laws; Article 44 aims at a uniform civil code that would replace them.
4. Separation of Judiciary from Executive
Separation of judiciary from executive is a DPSP under Article 50.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 are liberal-intellectual or socialistic directives listed in Part IV.

PYQ-POL-WEB-9DE3ED.lead: Option 4 is correct: Directive Principles aim to establish social and economic democracy.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. political democracy
Political democracy (equal right to vote, speak and contest) is secured mainly by Fundamental Rights, not DPSPs.
2. social democracy
Social democracy (equality and dignity in society) is only half the goal; DPSPs also aim at economic justice.
3. Gandhian democracy
Gandhian ideas form only one group of DPSPs, so Gandhian democracy is not the overall purpose.
4. social and economic democracy
Social equality plus fair sharing of wealth, through living wage, work and welfare, is the aim of the DPSPs.

points: Laxmikanth: Fundamental Rights aim at political democracy; Directive Principles aim at social and economic democracy.
DPSPs ask for a welfare State, not just a police State.
PYQ-POL-WEB-9DE3ED.also: Ambedkar said DPSPs embody the ideal of economic democracy.

PYQ-POL-WEB-AA1740.lead: Option 2 is correct: Article 39(c), a Directive Principle, asks the State to prevent concentration of wealth and means of production.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. the Right to Equality
The Right to Equality (Articles 14 to 18) is about equal treatment by law; it does not mention concentration of wealth.
2. the Directive Principles of State Policy
Article 39(c) directs that the economic system should not result in concentration of wealth to the common detriment.
3. the Right to Freedom
The Right to Freedom (Articles 19 to 22) protects personal freedoms, not economic distribution.
4. the Concept of Welfare
Welfare is a general idea, not a specific provision; the specific provision is Article 39(c).

points: Articles 39(b) and 39(c) together express distributive justice and are protected by Article 31C.

PYQ-POL-WEB-AFA490.lead: Option 2 is the wrong statement: Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights to implement Directive Principles, as long as the basic structure is not damaged.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Directive Principles have been held to supplement Fundamental Rights in achieving a Welfare State.
True: courts have held that DPSPs supplement Fundamental Rights in achieving a welfare state.
2. Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights for implementing the Directive Principles.
False, so it is the answer: the 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C to implement DPSPs, and Kesavananda (1973) allowed such amendments within the basic structure.
3. It shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
True: Article 37 says it shall be the duty of the State to apply these principles in making laws.
4. Directive Principles do not confer any enforceable Rights and their alleged breach does not invalidate laws.
True: Article 37 makes DPSPs non-enforceable, so a law is not void merely for breaching them.

points: Limit: amendments must not damage the basic structure (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).

PYQ-POL-WEB-B14161.lead: Option 4 is correct: the Karachi Resolution (1931) of the Congress first set out social and economic rights that later grew into the Directive Principles.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Gandhi Irwin Pact
The Gandhi-Irwin Pact (March 1931) ended the Civil Disobedience Movement; it did not frame socio-economic principles.
2. Poona Pact
The Poona Pact (1932) between Gandhi and Ambedkar was about reserved seats for the Depressed Classes.
3. Second Round Table Conference
The Second Round Table Conference (1931) discussed constitutional reform but produced no such principles.
4. Karachi Resolution
The Karachi session (1931), presided over by Sardar Patel, adopted the resolution on Fundamental Rights and Economic Policy, an early source of the DPSPs.

points: The DPSP idea itself was borrowed from the Irish Constitution (1937), which copied it from the Spanish Constitution.

PYQ-POL-WEB-B96C76.lead: Option 1, Article 51, is correct: it deals with promotion of international peace and security.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 51 asks the State to promote international peace and security and respect international law.
Article 48A asks the State to protect the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.
Article 43A asks the State to secure workers' participation in the management of industries.
Article 41 is the right to work, to education and to public assistance in unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement.

points: Article 51 is the last article of Part IV and is a liberal-intellectual directive.

PYQ-POL-WEB-BB2EBC.lead: Option 3 is correct: the Uniform Civil Code is a Directive Principle under Article 44.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Fundamental Rights
Wrong: no Fundamental Right in Part III guarantees a UCC, so courts cannot order it.
2. Fundamental Duties
Wrong: the Fundamental Duties in Article 51A do not mention a UCC.
3. Directive Principles of State Policy
Correct: Article 44 (Part IV) says the State shall endeavour to secure a uniform civil code for citizens.
4. Preamble objectives
Wrong: the Preamble mentions justice, liberty, equality and fraternity, but not a uniform civil code.

points: Article 44 is classed as a liberal-intellectual directive.

PYQ-POL-WEB-C02F88.lead: Article 50 is correct: it directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 143
Article 143 lets the President seek the Supreme Court's advisory opinion.
2. Article 50
Article 50 is the Directive Principle on separation of judiciary from executive.
3. Article 144
Article 144 requires all civil and judicial authorities to act in aid of the Supreme Court.
4. Article 74
Article 74 provides a Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President.

points: The CrPC, 1973 gave effect to Article 50 by separating judicial magistrates from executive magistrates.

PYQ-POL-WEB-CE62B7.lead: Option 1 is correct: the Directive Principles are in Part IV, Articles 36 to 51.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Part IV
Part IV contains the Directive Principles of State Policy (Articles 36 to 51).
2. Part V
Part V deals with the Union: President, Parliament, Supreme Court and so on.
3. Part VI
Part VI deals with the States: Governor, State Legislature, High Courts and so on.
4. Part III
Part III contains the Fundamental Rights (Articles 12 to 35).

points: The idea was borrowed from the Irish Constitution.
PYQ-POL-WEB-CE62B7.also: Part IV-A (Article 51A) holds the Fundamental Duties.

PYQ-POL-WEB-E1F12B.lead: Option 3 is correct: a UCC means one common set of personal laws for all citizens, whatever their religion.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. To establish a common criminal law for all citizens.
Wrong: criminal law is already common to all (IPC, now the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita).
2. To unify direct and indirect tax laws.
Wrong: unifying indirect taxes was done by GST (101st Amendment, 2016), which has nothing to do with UCC.
3. To provide a common set of personal laws for all citizens, irrespective of religion.
Correct: Article 44 asks the State to secure common laws on marriage, divorce, inheritance, adoption and succession.
4. To standardize administrative procedures across all states.
Wrong: standardising administrative procedures is not a civil code matter.

points: Personal laws today differ by religion; a UCC would make them common.
PYQ-POL-WEB-E1F12B.also: Goa has long had a common civil code; Uttarakhand enacted a UCC in 2024.

PYQ-POL-WEB-E3A363.lead: Article 48A is correct: it directs the State to protect and improve the environment and safeguard forests and wildlife.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 48-A
Article 48A was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) for environment, forests and wildlife.
2. Article 47-A
Article 47-A does not exist in the Constitution; Article 47 is on nutrition, public health and prohibition.
3. Article 47-B
Article 47-B also does not exist; it is a made-up distractor.
4. Article 49-C
Article 49-C does not exist; Article 49 is on protection of monuments.

points: The matching Fundamental Duty is Article 51A(g): protect and improve the natural environment.

PYQ-POL-WEB-E570DE.lead: Option 4 is the INCORRECT statement: Directive Principles are societarian and socialistic, not personal and individualistic.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. They are positive, as they require the State to do certain things.
True: DPSPs are positive, requiring the State to do certain things.
2. These have moral and political sanctions.
True: DPSPs have only moral and political sanctions, not legal sanctions.
3. They aim at establishing social and economic democracy in the country.
True: DPSPs aim at establishing social and economic democracy.
4. They promote welfare of individuals. Hence, they are personal and individualistic.
False, so it is the answer: DPSPs promote the welfare of the community; it is Fundamental Rights that are personal and individualistic.

points: Laxmikanth's comparison table: FRs promote individual welfare; DPSPs promote community welfare.

PYQ-POL-0FBAAD1E5E3A.lead: Official key: option 3 (I, II and IV are incorrect). Only statement III is true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Kesavananda invalidated the first provision of 31C
False
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) struck down the second provision (no court may question the declaration) because judicial review is a basic feature; the first provision was upheld.
II. Minerva also invalidated an extension of the second provision
False
The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended the first provision to cover all Directive Principles, and Minerva Mills (1980) struck down that extension, not any second-provision extension.
III. Minerva stressed harmony and balance of FRs and DPSPs
True
Minerva Mills called the two 'two wheels of a chariot' and said the balance between them is part of the basic structure.
IV. Present view merely repeats Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
False
Champakam held that Directive Principles must run subsidiary to Fundamental Rights; today the courts follow the Minerva idea of balance and harmonious construction.

points: The question asks for incorrect statements, so the answer is I, II and IV = option 3.
Option 1 (III and IV) and option 2 (II, III and IV) wrongly treat III as incorrect; option 4 (only III) names the one correct statement, which is the opposite of what is asked.
Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Amendment, 1971.

PYQ-POL-2419A7E67741.lead: Option 4 (Neither): the Constitution gives no enforcement process for the duties, and they are not correlative to legal duties.

head: Statement
True/False
Why

False
The Constitution itself provides no mechanism for enforcing the duties; there is no legal sanction for their violation, though Parliament is free to make laws (LX p190).

False
They are moral and civic duties, not legal duties that arise against a matching legal right; they are non-justiciable.

PYQ-POL-69869C41F6FC.lead: Option 3: respecting the National Flag is a Fundamental Duty under Article 51A(a).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A statutory obligation
A duty created by an ordinary law of Parliament; the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971 punishes insults, but the duty to respect comes from the Constitution itself.
2. A fundamental right
A right of the citizen under Part III that he can enforce in court; respecting the Flag is something the citizen owes, not something he claims.
3. A fundamental duty
Article 51A(a): abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem (LX p189).
4. A common law obligation
A duty from judge-made English-style law; the Flag duty is written in the Constitution, not in common law.

points: Laxmikanth gives this as an example of a civic duty (LX p189).

PYQ-POL-WEB-9CF1DD.lead: Items 3 and 4 are Directive Principles, not Fundamental Duties, while items 1 and 2 are duties. So the answer is option 3 (3 and 4).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1 Freedom-struggle ideals
True
Cherishing and following the noble ideals of the freedom struggle is a duty under Article 51A(b).
2 Composite culture
True
Valuing and preserving the rich heritage of our composite culture is a duty under Article 51A(f).
3 Interests of SCs/STs
False
Promoting educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections is a Directive Principle in Article 46, a duty of the State.
4 Protect monuments
False
Protecting monuments of historic interest and national importance is a Directive Principle in Article 49, again a duty of the State.

points: Option 1 (1 and 2) is wrong: it wrongly includes 1 and 2; it leaves out 3 and 4.
Option 2 (2 and 3) is wrong: it wrongly includes 2; it leaves out 4.
Option 4 (4 only) is wrong: it leaves out 3.
The question asks which are NOT related to duties, so we choose 3 and 4 (LX p174-175).
Hook: if the sentence tells the State to do something, it is a DPSP; if it tells the citizen, it is a Fundamental Duty.

PYQ-POL-WEB-A3FF12.lead: The answer is option 4: writing names on the walls of Humayun's Tomb damages a public monument, so the duty is Article 51A(i), safeguarding public property.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. To uphold and protect the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India
Article 51A(c) is about upholding sovereignty, unity and integrity of India; scribbling on walls does not threaten the nation's unity.
2. To defend the country and render national service
Article 51A(d) is about defending the country and national service when called upon.
3. To protect and improve the natural environment
Article 51A(g) is about the natural environment (forests, rivers, wildlife); a monument is a built structure, not nature.
4. To safeguard public property
Correct: Article 51A(i) asks citizens to safeguard public property; a protected monument belongs to the public.

points: Article 51A(f) (preserve composite heritage) is also related, but it is not among the options, so 51A(i) is the best fit (LX p175).

PYQ-POL-WEB-A966A8.lead: The answer is 'justiciable': Part III rights can be enforced in courts, while duties cannot, so the duties were kept in a separate Part IVA.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. non-justiciable
Non-justiciable means not enforceable in a court; this describes Fundamental Duties and DPSPs, not Part III.
2. justiciable
Correct: Fundamental Rights in Part III are justiciable, meaning a person can go to court (Article 32 or 226) if they are violated.
3. not enforceable
'Not enforceable' means the same as non-justiciable, which is the opposite of Part III.
4. absolute
Absolute means without any limit; Fundamental Rights are not absolute because they are subject to reasonable restrictions (e.g. Article 19(2)).

points: Laxmikanth: like the Directive Principles, the Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable; the Constitution provides no direct enforcement by courts (LX p176).
Putting unenforceable duties inside an enforceable Part would mix two different natures, so a new Part IVA was created.

PYQ-POL-WEB-BC6A25.lead: The answer is the Swaran Singh Committee (1976), which recommended adding Fundamental Duties to the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Swaran Singh Committee
Correct: the Swaran Singh Committee, set up by the Congress government in 1976, recommended a chapter on duties; the 42nd Amendment added ten (it had suggested eight).
2. Sarkaria Commission
The Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) studied Centre-State relations, not duties.
3. Rajamannar Committee
The Rajamannar Committee (1969) was set up by Tamil Nadu to study Centre-State relations and State autonomy.
4. Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
The Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended three-tier Panchayati Raj.

points: Laxmikanth: the Committee suggested eight duties; the government added ten, and some suggestions (like paying taxes, penalties for non-compliance) were not accepted (LX p174).

PYQ-POL-WEB-BE5FD8.lead: The answer is Article 51A(k): a parent who keeps his 8-year-old child away from school fails the duty to provide education opportunities to a child of 6 to 14 years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 51A (h)
Article 51A(h) is about scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry; it is not about sending a child to school.
2. Article 51A (i)
Article 51A(i) is about safeguarding public property and abjuring violence.
3. Article 51A (j)
Article 51A(j) is about striving for excellence in all spheres of activity.
4. Article 51A (k)
Correct: Article 51A(k), added by the 86th Amendment, 2002, asks parents or guardians to provide education opportunities to children aged 6 to 14, and an 8-year-old falls in this band.

points: The same child also has a Fundamental Right to free and compulsory education under Article 21A (LX p175).

PYQ-POL-WEB-C4586B.lead: Official key: 'statutory' (option 3). But the word that really fits is 'non-statutory' (option 2), because the duties come from the Constitution, not from any Act.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. regulatory
Regulatory means rules framed and enforced by a regulator such as SEBI or TRAI; no authority enforces Fundamental Duties.
2. non-statutory
Non-statutory means not created by an Act of the legislature; the duties come from Article 51A of the Constitution itself, so this fits the blank. (Study answer.)
Best fit
3. statutory
Statutory means created by an ordinary law passed by Parliament or a State Legislature (e.g. NHRC under the 1993 Act); no statute created the duties, so this is weak. (Official key.)
✓ (official)
4. common
Common means ordinary or general; it is not a legal term and gives no meaning here.

points: Fundamental Duties are in Article 51A (Part IVA), added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976, so their source is the Constitution (LX p174).
They are non-justiciable: the Constitution gives no direct penalty for not following them (LX p176).
Parliament can give a duty legal force by a law, e.g. the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971; that law is statutory, but the duty itself stays constitutional.
Courts still consider duties while deciding cases, e.g. Mohan Kumar Singhania (1991).
PYQ-POL-WEB-C4586B.also: Disputed key: the official key 'statutory' does not fit, because no statute created the Fundamental Duties; 'non-statutory' (option 2) is the better answer.

PYQ-POL-WEB-DD38C9.lead: The answer is the Justice Verma Committee (1999), which found that legal provisions already exist to implement some Fundamental Duties.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Rajamannar Commission
The Rajamannar Committee (1969) studied Centre-State relations for Tamil Nadu; it did not study duties.
2. Justice Verma Committee
Correct: the Verma Committee on Fundamental Duties of Citizens (1999) listed existing laws that enforce some duties.
3. Sarkaria Commission
The Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) studied Centre-State relations.
4. Vasantrao Naik Committee
The Vasantrao Naik Committee (1960-61) studied democratic decentralisation (Panchayati Raj) in Maharashtra.

points: Laws it named include the Prevention of Insults to National Honour Act, 1971, the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955, the Wildlife (Protection) Act, 1972 and the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980 (LX p177).

PYQ-POL-WEB-E324C2.lead: The answer is Article 51A, the only Article of Part IVA, which contains the Fundamental Duties.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 45A does not exist; Article 45 is the DPSP on early childhood care and education for children below 6.
Article 32A was inserted by the 42nd Amendment (1976) but repealed by the 43rd Amendment (1977); it was never about duties.
Correct: Article 51A lists the eleven Fundamental Duties.
Article 62B does not exist; Article 62 deals with the time of election to fill a vacancy in the office of President.

points: The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 inserted Part IVA with Article 51A and ten duties, on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation (LX p174).

PYQ-POL-WEB-E6B175.lead: The answer is option 1: 'to respect elders' is a good social value but it is not one of the eleven duties in Article 51A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. To respect elders
Not in Article 51A, so this is the answer: no clause speaks of respecting elders, although it is a moral value.
2. To promote harmony
This is a duty: Article 51A(e) asks citizens to promote harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood.
3. To safeguard public property
This is a duty: Article 51A(i) asks citizens to safeguard public property and abjure violence.
4. To defend the country
This is a duty: Article 51A(d) asks citizens to defend the country and render national service when called upon.

points: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Article 51A: ten added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 and the 11th by the 86th Amendment, 2002 (LX p174-175).
PYQ-POL-WEB-E6B175.also: The 11th duty (education of children 6–14) was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

PYQ-POL-WEB-EB0F4F.lead: The answer is the Soviet Union (USSR): the idea of Fundamental Duties was borrowed from the Constitution of the former USSR.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. UK
From the UK India took parliamentary government, rule of law, single citizenship and bicameralism, but not duties.
2. Germany
From Germany (Weimar Constitution) India took suspension of Fundamental Rights during an emergency.
3. US
From the US India took Fundamental Rights, judicial review and the post of Vice-President, but not duties.
4. Soviet Union (USSR)
Correct: the USSR Constitution placed duties of citizens beside their rights, and India borrowed this idea (along with the ideal of justice in the Preamble).

points: They were added on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (LX p174, sources list p49).
PYQ-POL-WEB-EB0F4F.also: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Article 51A.

PYQ-POL-0CA1BFD3FC9A.lead: Option 3 is correct: Article 368 in Part XX deals with the power of Parliament to amend the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 352
Article 352 lets the President proclaim a National Emergency on war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
Article 249
Article 249 lets Parliament legislate on a State List subject in the national interest after a Rajya Sabha resolution by two-thirds.
Article 368
Article 368 in Part XX gives Parliament the power to amend the Constitution and lays down the procedure.
Article 356
Article 356 provides President's Rule when constitutional machinery fails in a State.

points: The 24th Amendment, 1971 added 'power of Parliament' to the heading.

PYQ-POL-0D819F32BAD0.lead: Option 1 is correct: the 103rd Amendment, 2019 inserted Articles 15(6) and 16(6) for EWS reservation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Articles 15(6) and 16(6)
Article 15(6) allows up to 10% EWS reservation in education and Article 16(6) in public jobs, in addition to existing quotas.
Articles 18A and 19A
There are no Articles 18A or 19A in the Constitution; Article 18 abolishes titles and 19 gives six freedoms.
Articles 21C and 22A
There are no Articles 21C or 22A; only Article 21A (right to education, 86th Amendment) exists.
Articles 14A and 16A
There are no Articles 14A or 16A; the EWS quota was added as new clauses, not new Articles.

points: Upheld in Janhit Abhiyan (2022), 3:2.

PYQ-POL-125CD4BF8602.lead: Option 2 (82nd Amendment) is the official answer: it allowed relaxation in qualifying marks for SC/ST in promotions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The 80th Amendment, 2000 provided an alternative scheme of devolution of Union taxes to States.
The 82nd Amendment, 2000 added a proviso to Article 335 allowing relaxed qualifying marks and standards for SC/ST in reservation in promotions.
The 85th Amendment, 2001 gave consequential seniority to SC/ST employees already promoted through reservation.
The 93rd Amendment, 2005 added Article 15(5) for SC/ST/OBC reservation in private educational institutions.

points: Reservation in promotion itself, Article 16(4A), came via the 77th Amendment, 1995 (not an option).

PYQ-POL-12DAC3082807.lead: Option 2: the 88th Amendment, 2003 made provision for taxes on services by inserting Article 268A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Reservation in government jobs
Reservation in jobs and promotions was handled by other amendments, such as the 77th (1995), 81st, 82nd and 85th, not the 88th.
2. Taxes on services
Correct: the 88th Amendment, 2003 said taxes on services are levied by the Centre and collected and appropriated by the Centre and the States (Article 268A).
3. Anti-defection law
The anti-defection law came through the 52nd Amendment, 1985 (Tenth Schedule) and was tightened by the 91st Amendment, 2003.
4. GST
GST was introduced by the 101st Amendment, 2016, which in fact omitted Article 268A because service tax merged into GST.

points: Service tax was a Union subject added to the Union List as entry 92C by the 88th Amendment.
Memory hook: 88 = service tax; 101 = GST that swallowed it.

PYQ-POL-18DC04E778A0.lead: Option 4: the Electricity Act was enacted in 2003; the 2022 Bill sought to amend that Act.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 2005 is not the year of the Electricity Act; 2005 is remembered for laws like the RTI Act and the NREGA.
2007 is not connected with the Electricity Act; no central electricity law was passed that year.
2001 is the year of the Energy Conservation Act, not the Electricity Act.
Correct: the Electricity Act, 2003 is the main central law on generation, transmission, distribution and trading of power.

points: It replaced the Indian Electricity Act, 1910, the Electricity (Supply) Act, 1948 and the Electricity Regulatory Commissions Act, 1998.
The Electricity (Amendment) Bill, 2022 proposed letting several distribution licensees use the same network, and was referred to a Standing Committee.

PYQ-POL-1ACC1528BF53.lead: Option 2: the 82nd Amendment, 2000 enabled provisions in favour of SCs/STs in promotion matters by relaxing qualifying marks (proviso to Article 335).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 80th Constitutional Amendment
The 80th Amendment, 2000 dealt with Union–State sharing of central taxes (Tenth Finance Commission's alternative scheme), not SC/ST promotions.
2. 82nd Constitutional Amendment
Correct: the 82nd Amendment, 2000 added a proviso to Article 335 letting the State relax qualifying marks and lower evaluation standards for SCs/STs in promotion.
3. 89th Constitutional Amendment
The 89th Amendment, 2003 split the old joint commission and created a separate National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A).
4. 93rd Constitutional Amendment
The 93rd Amendment, 2005 added Article 15(5) for reservation of OBCs, SCs and STs in educational institutions, including private ones; it is about education, not jobs.

points: Reservation in promotion itself was first enabled by the 77th Amendment, 1995 (Article 16(4A)); since the 77th is not among the options, the 82nd is the best answer.
The 85th Amendment, 2001 later added 'consequential seniority' to Article 16(4A).

PYQ-POL-1D280B53E699.lead: Bhojpuri is still only proposed; Bodo, Santhali, Dogri were added in 2003.

PYQ-POL-20304DAFFDCC.lead: Option 2: the 97th Amendment, 2011 gave constitutional status and protection to co-operative societies.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 94th Amendment
The 94th Amendment, 2006 freed Bihar from the duty of having a tribal welfare minister and extended it to Jharkhand and Chhattisgarh (Article 164(1)).
2. 97th Amendment
Correct: the 97th Amendment, 2011 added Part IXB (Articles 243ZH–243ZT), made forming co-operatives a right under Article 19(1)(c) and added Article 43B.
3. 99th Amendment
The 99th Amendment, 2014 created the National Judicial Appointments Commission, later struck down in 2015.
4. 101st Amendment
The 101st Amendment, 2016 introduced GST.

points: Article 43B is a Directive Principle asking the State to promote voluntary formation and democratic control of co-operatives.
PYQ-POL-20304DAFFDCC.also: In Union of India v. Rajendra N. Shah (2021) the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB as far as it applies to State co-operative societies (for want of State ratification), but kept it for multi-State co-operatives.

PYQ-POL-203B5E7D5F65.lead: Option 4: the 102nd Amendment, 2018 gave constitutional status to the National Commission for Backward Classes by inserting Article 338B.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 101st Amendment Act, 2016
The 101st Amendment, 2016 introduced GST; it has nothing to do with backward classes.
2. 89th Amendment Act, 2004
The 89th Amendment (Act of 2003, in force 2004) bifurcated the joint commission into a National Commission for SCs (Article 338) and for STs (Article 338A).
3. 95th Amendment Act, 2010
The 95th Amendment, 2010 extended SC/ST seat reservation and Anglo-Indian nomination in Lok Sabha and Assemblies up to 2020 (Article 334).
4. 102nd Amendment Act, 2018
Correct: the 102nd Amendment, 2018 inserted Article 338B (NCBC) and Article 342A (President notifies the SEBC list).

points: Earlier the NCBC was only a statutory body set up under the NCBC Act, 1993.
PYQ-POL-203B5E7D5F65.also: After the Maratha quota ruling (2021), the 105th Amendment, 2021 restored the power of States to prepare their own SEBC lists.

PYQ-POL-2189588DC937.lead: Option 3: the First Amendment, 1951 added the Ninth Schedule along with Article 31B.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Fourth Amendment Act, 1955
The 4th Amendment, 1955 only added more laws to the Ninth Schedule and made compensation for acquisition non-justiciable; the Schedule already existed.
2. Twenty-ninth Amendment Act, 1972
The 29th Amendment, 1972 only added two Kerala land-reform Acts to the Ninth Schedule.
3. First Amendment Act, 1951
Correct: the First Amendment, 1951 created the Ninth Schedule so that land-reform laws placed in it could not be challenged for violating Fundamental Rights.
4. Seventeenth Amendment Act, 1964
The 17th Amendment, 1964 widened the meaning of 'estate' in Article 31A and added 44 more Acts to the Ninth Schedule.

points: Article 31B says laws in the Ninth Schedule are not void even if they violate Fundamental Rights.
The 4th, 17th and 29th Amendments are close distractors because each one added more laws to the existing Schedule.
PYQ-POL-2189588DC937.also: I.R. Coelho (2007): laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 (the Kesavananda date) can be tested against the basic structure.

PYQ-POL-264F933B9968.lead: Option 3: the 24th Amendment, 1971 declared that Parliament can abridge or take away any Fundamental Right under Article 368.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Twenty-third Amendment
The 23rd Amendment, 1969 extended reservation of seats for SCs/STs and Anglo-Indian nomination for ten more years; it did not touch amending power.
2. Twentieth Amendment
The 20th Amendment, 1966 validated certain appointments of district judges in Uttar Pradesh that the Court had held invalid.
3. Twenty-fourth Amendment
Correct: the 24th Amendment amended Articles 13 and 368 so that a constitutional amendment is not 'law' under Article 13, and made Presidential assent to amendment Bills obligatory.
4. Twenty-eighth Amendment
The 28th Amendment, 1972 ended the special privileges of former ICS officers.

points: It was Parliament's answer to Golak Nath (1967), which had said Fundamental Rights cannot be amended.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld the 24th Amendment but added the basic structure limit.

PYQ-POL-27EA66D85FE4.lead: All four items need ratification by half the State Legislatures, so the answer is option 2 (A, B, C and D).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Article 55 deals with the manner of election of the President, which is a federal provision listed in the proviso to Article 368(2).
B
True
Chapter IV of Part V is the Union Judiciary (Supreme Court); changes to it affect the States and so need ratification.
C
True
Chapter I of Part XI covers legislative relations between the Union and the States, a core federal matter needing ratification.
D
True
Any of the three Lists in the Seventh Schedule divides subjects between Centre and States, so changing a List needs State ratification.

points: Option 1 (B, C and D only) wrongly leaves out A, though Article 55 is in the federal list.
Option 3 (A, B and C only) wrongly leaves out D, the Seventh Schedule Lists.
Option 4 (C and D only) leaves out both A and B.
Such provisions need a special majority of Parliament plus ratification by half the States by simple majority.
PYQ-POL-27EA66D85FE4.also: Other items in this list: Articles 54, 73, 162, 241, 279A, Chapter V of Part VI, representation of States in Parliament, and Article 368 itself.

PYQ-POL-2810307529B0.lead: Option 3: changing a subject in the Union List (Seventh Schedule) needs special majority plus ratification by at least half the States.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Amendment of emergency provisions
Emergency provisions (Part XVIII) are amended by special majority of Parliament alone; State ratification is not needed.
2. Change in Fundamental Rights
Fundamental Rights (Part III) are amended by special majority of Parliament alone, subject to the basic structure.
3. Change in Union List subjects
Correct: any List of the Seventh Schedule is in the proviso to Article 368(2), so it needs half the States' consent because it changes the Centre–State division of power.
4. Rewriting the Preamble text
The Preamble can be amended (as in the 42nd Amendment) by special majority alone, without State ratification.

points: Rule of thumb: if a change shifts power between the Centre and the States, the States must ratify it.
Ratification is by a simple majority in each State Legislature, and there is no time limit for it.

PYQ-POL-28371B66CE5F.lead: Option 3: the 44th Amendment, 1978 removed the right to property from the list of Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The 41st Amendment, 1976 raised the retirement age of members of State Public Service Commissions from 60 to 62.
The 43rd Amendment, 1977 undid some 42nd Amendment changes, like restoring the jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts over the validity of laws.
Correct: the 44th Amendment deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31 and made property a legal right under Article 300A in Part XII.
The 42nd Amendment, 1976 is the 'mini-Constitution'; it did not remove the property right.

points: After 1978, a person deprived of property cannot go directly to the Supreme Court under Article 32 for that alone; the remedy is a High Court writ under Article 226.

PYQ-POL-29FF46036ECA.lead: Option 2: the 91st Amendment was enacted in 2003.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1978 is the year of the 44th Amendment, which undid Emergency-era changes and removed the property right.
Correct: the 91st Amendment, 2003 limited the size of Councils of Ministers and tightened the anti-defection law.
1989 is when the 61st Amendment (Act of 1988) lowering the voting age from 21 to 18 came into force.
2000 is the year of the 80th to 84th Amendments, such as the 82nd on relaxed marks for SC/ST promotions.

points: It capped the Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha or State Assembly (Articles 75(1A), 164(1A)).
It deleted the 'split' exception (one-third of a party) from the Tenth Schedule; only a merger by two-thirds now saves members.

PYQ-POL-2C010BC10AA6.lead: Option 3: the 86th Amendment, 2002 inserted Article 21A, making free and compulsory education for children aged 6–14 a Fundamental Right.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 89th Constitutional Amendment
The 89th Amendment, 2003 created a separate National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A).
2. 88th Constitutional Amendment
The 88th Amendment, 2003 made provision for taxes on services (Article 268A).
3. 86th Constitutional Amendment
Correct: the 86th Amendment added Article 21A, changed Article 45 to early childhood care up to age 6, and added Fundamental Duty 51A(k) for parents.
4. 90th Constitutional Amendment
The 90th Amendment, 2003 kept the representation of STs and non-STs in the Bodoland Territorial Areas District in the Assam Assembly (Article 332(6)).

points: Memory hook: 86 = education right; 21A sits right after the right to life because education was seen as part of a life with dignity.
PYQ-POL-2C010BC10AA6.also: The RTE Act was passed in 2009 and came into force on 1 April 2010.

PYQ-POL-2E0606DF4458.lead: Option 3: the 24th Amendment, 1971 was a direct response to Golak Nath (1967).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Maneka Gandhi Case
Maneka Gandhi (1978) widened Article 21 to require a fair, just and reasonable procedure; it came seven years after the 24th Amendment.
2. Minerva Mills Case
Minerva Mills (1980) struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment; it too came later.
3. Golak Nath Case
Correct: Golak Nath held that Parliament cannot take away or abridge Fundamental Rights because an amendment is 'law' under Article 13, and the 24th Amendment reversed this.
4. Kesavananda Bharati Case
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) came after the 24th Amendment and in fact upheld it, while laying down the basic structure limit.

points: The 24th Amendment added Article 13(4) and Article 368(3), saying Article 13 does not apply to amendments made under Article 368.

PYQ-POL-2E3B1177FDA1.lead: Option 2: the First Amendment, 1951 was mainly meant to protect zamindari abolition and land-reform laws by creating the Ninth Schedule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Fundamental Duties
Fundamental Duties came much later, through the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (Part IVA, Article 51A).
2. Zamindari abolition laws (Ninth Schedule)
Correct: it added Articles 31A and 31B and the Ninth Schedule so that land-reform laws could not be struck down for violating the property right.
3. Emergency provisions
Emergency provisions were changed mainly by the 38th, 42nd and 44th Amendments, not the First.
4. Panchayati Raj
Panchayati Raj got constitutional status through the 73rd Amendment, 1992 (Part IX).

points: It also added Article 15(4) for backward classes and new grounds (public order, friendly relations, incitement to offence) in Article 19(2).

PYQ-POL-2FF4D0426C86.lead: Option 1: the Constitution was amended for the first time in 1951.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct: the First Amendment Act, 1951 was passed by the Provisional Parliament, only about a year after the Constitution began.
1954 has no first amendment; the 3rd Amendment (essential commodities) came that year.
1961 is the year of the 10th Amendment, which made Dadra and Nagar Haveli a Union Territory.
1960 is the year of the 8th and 9th Amendments, not the first.

points: The First Amendment protected land reforms (Ninth Schedule) and added reasonable restrictions on free speech (Article 19(2)).
It was passed under Prime Minister Nehru before the first general elections of 1951–52.

PYQ-POL-318790F2B484.lead: B, C and D describe the 106th Amendment while A describes the 105th, so the answer is option 3 (B, C and D only).

PYQ-POL-4263D5D551CE.lead: Option 2: the 101st Amendment, 2016 introduced the Goods and Services Tax.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Right to Education

PYQ-POL-75FB8437870C.lead: Option 2: the First Amendment, 1951 was mainly aimed at protecting zamindari abolition and land-reform laws.

PYQ-POL-763A1F0E5115.lead: Option 4: Parliament's amending power is limited by the Constitution itself, mainly through Article 368 and the basic structure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Supreme Court
The Supreme Court enforces the limit by judicial review, but it is not the source of the limit; it only interprets the Constitution.
2. Civil Society
Civil society (citizens, NGOs, media) can protest but has no legal power over amendments.
3. States
States must ratify only certain federal amendments under the proviso to Article 368(2); they do not limit the power in general.
4. Constitution
Correct: the Constitution lays down the procedure in Article 368 and its basic structure cannot be destroyed.

points: Kesavananda Bharati (1973): Parliament can amend any part but not the basic structure.
Minerva Mills (1980): limited amending power is itself part of the basic structure.

Meaning
Fits?

PYQ-POL-APK-EA5642.lead: Option 3: Article 261 is the 'full faith and credit' clause, so public acts and records of the Union and every State are accepted everywhere in India.

PYQ-POL-E031E1E1A3A7.lead: Official key: option 1 (A, B and C). But Parliament cannot cede Indian territory to a foreign country under Articles 2–3, so the better answer is option 2 (A, B and D).

Why

True

True

False

True
