It declares the Polavaram Irrigation Project a national project.
3. Section 95
It keeps existing admission quotas in government and private higher education institutions for ten years.
4. Section 99
It does not deal with higher education; it is a distractor from later parts of the Act.

points: Thus students of AP and Telangana kept their common-admission rights for ten years after 2014.
Related: the Thirteenth Schedule lists educational institutions promised to AP (IIT, IIM, AIIMS etc.).

PYQ-POL-WEB-B7D844.lead: Option 1: Section 29 of the AP Reorganisation Act amends the Constitution (Scheduled Tribes) Order, 1950 as directed in the Act's Sixth Schedule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Sixth Schedule (of the Act)
It contains the amendments to the ST Order, 1950, splitting the ST lists for AP and Telangana.
2. Fifth Schedule (of the Act)
It contains the amendments to the Scheduled Castes Order, 1950 under Section 28, not the ST Order.
3. Seventh Schedule (of the Act)
It deals with other matters (funds), not the ST Order.
4. Tenth Schedule (of the Act)
It lists State institutions to be continued, not the ST list.

points: Trap: do not confuse these with the Constitution's Fifth and Sixth Schedules, which deal with Scheduled and Tribal Areas.
Memory hook: Section 28 → SC → Fifth; Section 29 → ST → Sixth.

PYQ-POL-WEB-BF6AAD.lead: Option 3: Part VIII (Sections 76–83) of the AP Reorganisation Act deals with 'Provisions as to services'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Part IV
It provides for the High Court of Andhra Pradesh and the common High Court period.
2. Part VI
It deals with apportionment of assets and liabilities between the two States.
3. Part VIII
It covers All-India Services and the allocation of State government employees between AP and Telangana.
4. Part X
It deals with other matters later in the Act, not services.

points: Services include IAS, IPS and IFS cadres (Sections 76–77) and division of State employees (Sections 77–80).

PYQ-POL-WEB-C52BD8.lead: Statement 2 is true and statement 1 is false, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Members nominated by Provincial Assemblies and States
False. Provincial members were to be elected by the Provincial Assemblies on proportional representation; only Princely States' members were to be nominated by their rulers.
False
2. Province may stay out and sign separate agreement
True. Cripps (March 1942) allowed any Province not accepting the new Constitution to have a separate agreement with Britain.
True

points: Option 1 picks the false statement; option 3 includes it; option 4 rejects the true statement 2.
Gandhi called the offer a 'post-dated cheque'; the opt-out clause was seen as opening the door to partition.

PYQ-POL-WEB-D42A10.lead: Option 2. Section 84 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 sets up the Apex Council for Godavari and Krishna waters and their Management Boards.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Section 20 - ST Order amendment
Wrong pairing: Section 20 is not the ST Order provision
Section 84 - Apex Council
Apex Council of the Union Water Resources Minister and both CMs supervises the Godavari and Krishna Boards
Section 16 - Powers of Judges
Wrong pairing: the section does not deal with powers of judges
Section 25 - road transport permits
Wrong pairing: transport permits are dealt with elsewhere

points: Sections 84-91 form the water-resources part of the Act: Apex Council (84), River Boards (85), Polavaram (90).

PYQ-POL-WEB-D4F306.lead: Option 2: under Article 239(2), a Governor who is also administrator of an adjoining UT acts independently of his State Council of Ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. On aid and advice of his Council of Ministers
False. State ministers have no say in a UT, which is run by the Union through the President.
2. Independently of his Council of Ministers
True. Article 239(2) says so in express words.
3. Forms a choice of ministers
False. No such arrangement exists; the Governor acts as the President's administrator.
4. Governor cannot be administrator
False. Article 239(2) expressly allows the President to appoint a Governor as administrator of an adjoining UT.

points: Example: the Governor of Punjab is also the Administrator of Chandigarh.
This is one of the Governor's 'constitutional discretions' listed by Laxmikanth.

PYQ-POL-WEB-ED2D09.lead: Key: option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2). Statement 2 is clearly false; statement 1 is arguable (see note).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Gandhi in 1948 argued for linguistic provinces
Treated as false by the key: in 1948 the national leadership, including the JVP Committee, advised postponing linguistic reorganisation for the sake of unity after Partition.
False (arguable)
2. Constituent Assembly recommended it
False. The Dhar Commission set up by the Assembly President (June 1948) recommended reorganisation on administrative convenience, not language.
False

points: Option 2 and option 3 accept statement 2, which is clearly wrong.
Andhra State (1 October 1953) was the first linguistic State, after Potti Sriramulu's 56-day fast; the JVP Committee (April 1949) formally rejected language as the basis.
PYQ-POL-WEB-ED2D09.also: Disputed key: if Gandhi's 1948 support is accepted, statement 1 is true and option 1 is the better answer.

PYQ-POL-275F0A31C351.lead: Option 3: Part II, Articles 5–11, deals with Citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Fundamental Rights
False: Fundamental Rights are in Part III, Articles 12–35.
2. Union and its Territory
False: The Union and its Territory is Part I, Articles 1–4.
3. Citizenship
True: Part II (Articles 5–11) identifies who became citizens in 1950 and gives Parliament power to regulate citizenship.
4. Fundamental Duties
False: Fundamental Duties are in Part IVA, Article 51A (42nd Amendment, 1976).

points: Sequence hook: Part I territory → Part II citizenship → Part III rights.

PYQ-POL-44E710B5DC5D.lead: Articles 5 to 8 decide who became a citizen at the commencement.
points: Option 1 is the best fit; the full citizenship Part runs Articles 5–11.
Option 2 leaves out Article 5, the main provision.
Articles 3 and 4 deal with new States, not citizenship.

PYQ-POL-56F9A54A835B.lead: Option 1: Article 10 deals with continuance of the rights of citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Articles 10
True: Article 10 says every citizen continues to be one, subject to any law made by Parliament.
2. Articles 18
False: Article 18 abolishes titles and has nothing to do with continuance of citizenship.
3. Articles 14
False: Article 14 gives equality before law and equal protection of laws.
4. Articles 15
False: Article 15 prohibits discrimination on religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

points: Articles 10 and 11 are the last two Articles of Part II (Citizenship).

PYQ-POL-5A8AE8A68A86.lead: Option 2: Article 11 empowers Parliament to regulate the right of citizenship by law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 10
False: Article 10 only continues existing citizenship, subject to Parliament's law.
2. Article 11
True: Article 11 gives Parliament power to make any provision on acquisition, termination and all other matters of citizenship.
3. Article 12
False: Article 12 defines 'the State' for Part III.
4. Article 13
False: Article 13 makes laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights void.

points: Parliament used Article 11 to enact the Citizenship Act, 1955.

PYQ-POL-704E44D47A56.lead: Option 1: Article 6 deals with persons who migrated to India from Pakistan.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Pakistan
True: Article 6 gave citizenship to migrants from territory now in Pakistan, if ancestry and residence/registration conditions were met.
2. Bangladesh
False: Bangladesh did not exist in 1950; it was East Pakistan, so it was covered under 'Pakistan'.
3. Sri Lanka
False: Sri Lanka is not mentioned in Part II.
4. Nepal
False: Nepal is not mentioned in Part II.

points: Article 7 covers the reverse case: people who migrated from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947.

PYQ-POL-82DB13A71659.lead: Option 4: a migrant from Pakistan who came on or after 19 July 1948 became a citizen only if registered by an officer of the Dominion of India (Article 6).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: His birth was in India before 1947
Article 6 required that the person, a parent or a grandparent was born in undivided India; this applied to every migrant, early or late.
✗ — common to all migrants, not the special test for late arrivals
He was a resident of Pakistan in 1948
Being a resident of Pakistan was simply his starting point as a migrant; it gave no right to Indian citizenship.
He took an oath of allegiance
Article 6 did not ask for any oath; the test was registration after an application.
He was registered by an officer of the Dominion of India
For migrants arriving on or after 19 July 1948, Article 6(b)(ii) required registration by an officer appointed by the Government of the Dominion of India.

points: Article 6 drew a line at 19 July 1948: those who came before it became citizens if they had been ordinarily resident in India since migrating; those who came after it had to be registered.
Registration was allowed only if the person had lived in India for six months before applying.
Memory hook: 'Before 19 July — just stay; after 19 July — register'.

PYQ-POL-8B878D2E5477.lead: Option 3: Article 5 defines who became a citizen of India at the commencement of the Constitution (26 January 1950).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 6
Article 6 gives citizenship to certain persons who migrated to India from Pakistan.
Article 10
Article 10 says that a person who is a citizen under Part II continues to be a citizen, subject to laws made by Parliament.
Article 5
Article 5 gives citizenship at commencement to a person domiciled in India who was born in India, had a parent born in India, or had lived in India for five years before 1950.
Article 11
Article 11 gives Parliament power to make laws on acquisition and termination of citizenship.

points: Part II (Articles 5–11) only identified who were citizens on 26 January 1950; later citizenship is governed by the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Article 5's three tests are joined to domicile: born in India, OR either parent born in India, OR ordinarily resident for five years.

PYQ-POL-8BF9CAA5DB01.lead: Option 4: Article 11 empowers Parliament to make any law on acquisition and termination of citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 7
Article 7 deals with persons who migrated from India to Pakistan after 1 March 1947; they are generally not citizens.
Article 10
Article 10 provides for continuance of citizenship already held under Part II.
Article 12
Article 12 defines 'the State' for Part III (Fundamental Rights); it is not about citizenship.
Article 11
Article 11 lets Parliament regulate citizenship by law, including how it is acquired and lost.

points: Using Article 11, Parliament enacted the Citizenship Act, 1955.
Because the law is made under Article 11, it can be changed by a simple majority, not by the Article 368 procedure.

PYQ-POL-8F58C6DB9EF8.lead: Option 1: Article 9 says a person who voluntarily acquires the citizenship of a foreign State is not a citizen of India under Articles 5, 6 or 8.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 9
Article 9 bars a person from being an Indian citizen if he has voluntarily taken another country's citizenship; India does not allow dual nationality.
Article 11
Article 11 gives Parliament power to regulate citizenship by law.
Article 12
Article 12 defines 'the State' for the purpose of Fundamental Rights.
Article 10
Article 10 says existing citizens continue as citizens, subject to Parliament's laws.

points: Article 9 is the constitutional basis of India's rule against dual citizenship; LX notes that even OCI is not true dual citizenship for this reason.
After 1950, the same idea works through 'termination' under the Citizenship Act, 1955.

PYQ-POL-950B3E4711EC.lead: Option 4: ethnic identity is not a mode of acquiring Indian citizenship; birth, registration and naturalisation are legal modes.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Naturalization
A foreigner who has lived in India for the required period applies and gets a certificate of naturalisation from the Central Government.
✗ — valid mode
Birth
A person born in India gets citizenship, subject to conditions on the parents' citizenship for births after 1987 and 2004.
✗ — valid mode
Registration
Certain persons, such as persons of Indian origin or a person married to an Indian citizen, apply and are registered as citizens.
✗ — valid mode
Ethnic Identity
Belonging to a race, tribe or community; the Citizenship Act gives no citizenship on this basis.
✓ — not a mode

points: The Citizenship Act, 1955 prescribes five modes: birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory.
Indian citizenship rests on law (birth, parentage, residence, application), not on race or ethnicity.

PYQ-POL-971940216D36.lead: Option 4 (A, C and D only): e-governance, energy management and urban mobility are Smart Solutions; 'Innovation Index Centres' is not in the list.

True/False
Why

True
it is a listed Smart Solution, covering online public services, grievance redress and citizen engagement.
B. Innovation Index Centres
False
no such item appears among the Smart Solutions in the Smart Cities Mission guidelines.
C. Energy management
True
smart meters, renewable energy and energy-efficient buildings are listed Smart Solutions.
D. Urban mobility
True
smart parking, intelligent traffic management and integrated multi-modal transport are listed Smart Solutions.

Other Smart Solution areas are waste management and water management; the Mission was launched in June 2015.

PYQ-POL-A9F1C4FBD5C9.lead: An Indian passport was never a condition under Article 5.
points: Article 5 needs domicile in India plus one of three: birth in India, a parent born in India, or five years' residence.
Domicile is compulsory; birth and parent's birth are alternative conditions in the list.

PYQ-POL-APK-007407.lead: Option 4: Article 51A (clause g) makes it a Fundamental Duty to protect and improve the natural environment and to have compassion for living creatures.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 31-D
Article 31D allowed laws against anti-national activities; it was added in 1976 and repealed by the 43rd Amendment, 1977.
Article 31-C
Article 31C protects laws that give effect to certain Directive Principles from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
Article 34-A
There is no Article 34A in the Constitution; Article 34 deals with martial law.
Article 51-A
Article 51A in Part IVA lists the Fundamental Duties; clause (g) is the environment duty.

points: The duty on citizens is 51A(g); the matching duty on the State is the Directive Principle in Article 48A.
Both were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

PYQ-POL-APK-1CDE44.lead: Option 1. Art 10-continuance; Art 8-Indians abroad; Art 9-foreign citizenship; Art 5-commencement.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Article 10
2. Continuance of rights
Article 10 says every person who is a citizen under Part II continues to be one, subject to any law made by Parliament.
B. Article 8
4. Persons of Indian origin abroad
Article 8 gives citizenship to persons of Indian origin living abroad who register with an Indian diplomatic or consular office.
C. Article 9
1. Voluntary foreign citizenship disqualifies
Article 9 says anyone who voluntarily acquires a foreign State's citizenship is not an Indian citizen.
D. Article 5
3. Citizenship at commencement
Article 5 gave citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution to persons domiciled in India who met birth or residence conditions.

points: Option 2 fails: it pairs A-3 (should be 2), B-2 (should be 4), D-4 (should be 3).

PYQ-POL-APK-1D4C27.lead: Option 3: the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 added Fundamental Duties as Part IVA (Article 51A).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 34th Amendment
The 34th Amendment (1974) placed more land reform laws in the Ninth Schedule.
41st Amendment
The 41st Amendment (1976) raised the retirement age of State Public Service Commission members from 60 to 62.
42nd Amendment
The 42nd Amendment (1976), on the Swaran Singh Committee's advice, added ten Fundamental Duties in Article 51A.
45th Amendment
The 45th Amendment (1980) extended SC/ST reservation in legislatures; it did not touch the duties.

points: The 86th Amendment, 2002 added the eleventh duty (parents to provide education to children aged 6–14).
The 44th Amendment, 1978 undid many 42nd Amendment changes but kept the Fundamental Duties.

PYQ-POL-APK-281481.lead: Option 1 (1 and 2): adequate livelihood and equal pay for equal work are socialistic (economic-social) principles under Article 39.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Adequate means of livelihood
True
Article 39(a) is a socialistic principle: it aims at economic justice for all citizens.
2. Equal pay for equal work
True
Article 39(d) is a socialistic principle that removes economic inequality between men and women.
3. Promote cottage industries
False
Article 43's cottage industry clause is a Gandhian principle, based on Gandhi's idea of village self-reliance.
4. Protect environment, forests, wildlife
False
Article 48A is placed under liberal-intellectual principles in LX's classification.

points: Option 2 (1 and 4) wrongly includes the liberal-intellectual principle 4.
Option 3 (2 and 3) wrongly includes the Gandhian principle 3 and drops 1.
Option 4 (1 and 3) wrongly includes the Gandhian principle 3 and drops 2.

PYQ-POL-APK-2B54AA.lead: Option 1 (Only I): the Swaran Singh Committee suggested eight duties; abjuring casteism was not one of them.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Suggested eight duties
True
LX says the Committee suggested eight Fundamental Duties, but the 42nd Amendment added ten.
II. Abjure casteism recommended
False

'Abjure casteism' was not among the Committee's items, and no such duty is in Article 51A; the related duty is to renounce practices derogatory to women and promote harmony beyond religious, linguistic and regional divisions (51A(e)).

points: Option 2 and option 3 are wrong because they accept statement II.
Option 4 is wrong because statement I is true.
The Committee's idea of penalties for not following duties was not accepted by the government.

PYQ-POL-APK-2F45BB.lead: Option 4: owning land or other property never gives Indian citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: By birth
A person born in India gets citizenship under Section 3, subject to conditions on parents' citizenship.
✗ — valid mode
By registration
Persons such as persons of Indian origin or spouses of Indian citizens may apply and be registered under Section 5.
✗ — valid mode
By naturalization
A foreigner with long residence in India may get a certificate of naturalisation under Section 6.
✗ — valid mode
By having ownership of land or other properties
Property ownership is an economic fact, not a legal basis of citizenship; the Act does not recognise it.
✓ — not a mode

points: The five modes are birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory (Citizenship Act, 1955).

PYQ-POL-APK-48E61B.lead: Option 1 — Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 offers a faster route to citizenship to Hindus, Sikhs, Buddhists, Jains, Parsis and Christians from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
R
True
It covers members of these communities who entered India on or before 31 December 2014 to escape religious persecution.

points: Does R explain A? Yes — A says these communities get citizenship, and R says why they were chosen: they fled religious persecution. R gives the reason for A.
Option 2 fails: R actually does explain A.
Option 3 fails: R is in fact true.
Option 4 fails: A is in fact true.
Muslims are not included; the cut-off date is 31 December 2014.

PYQ-POL-APK-6A9E2E.lead: Option 2: Articles 5 to 11 in Part II deal with citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Articles 1–4
Part I: name of the Union, its territory, and creation or change of States.
Articles 5–11
Part II: citizenship at commencement and Parliament's power to regulate it.
Articles 12–18
Part III: definition of State, laws against FRs, and the Right to Equality.
Articles 19–25
Part III: right to freedom, life and liberty, against exploitation, and freedom of religion.

points: Memory hook: Part I = land (1–4), Part II = people (5–11), Part III = rights (12–35).

PYQ-POL-APK-6C69AC.lead: Option 2: democracy helps development because it brings citizen participation and makes the government accountable.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: It promotes authoritarian rule
Authoritarian rule means power in one person or group without accountability, which is the opposite of democracy.
It encourages citizen participation and accountability
People choose and question their rulers through elections, free speech and institutions, so governments must respond to public needs.
It suppresses individual freedom
Democracy protects freedoms such as speech and association; suppressing them is a mark of dictatorship.
It ignores transparency
Democracy needs openness, for example through RTI and a free press; ignoring transparency weakens it.

points: Accountable governments that listen to people tend to spend on schools, health and welfare, which supports development.
Options 1, 3 and 4 all describe features of non-democratic rule.

PYQ-POL-APK-6EF40D.lead: Option 1: Part II (Articles 5–11) deals with citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Part II
Correct; Part II (Articles 5–11) deals with citizenship.
Part III
Wrong; Part III (Articles 12–35) deals with Fundamental Rights, not citizenship.
Part V
Articles 52–151 on the Union government (President, Parliament, Supreme Court, CAG).
Part VII
It dealt with Part B States and was repealed by the 7th Amendment, 1956.

points: Part II only settles who were citizens in 1950; the Citizenship Act, 1955 covers the rest.

PYQ-POL-APK-72CBEE.lead: Option 2: a Citizen's Charter tells people what service standards and timelines to expect and how to get grievances redressed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Promote industrial investment
Investment promotion is the job of industrial policy and investment agencies, not of a service charter.
Provide time-bound service delivery and grievance redress
A Citizen's Charter is a public promise by an office on quality, time limits and complaint remedies.
Increase defence expenditure transparency
Defence spending is examined through budgets, the CAG and Parliament, not a Citizen's Charter.
Reduce population growth
Population control is a health and family welfare policy goal, unrelated to service charters.

points: India began Citizen's Charters in 1997, following the UK's 1991 scheme.
The idea is to make offices accountable to the citizen as a 'customer' of public service.

PYQ-POL-APK-88481B.lead: Option 2: the Citizenship Act, 1955 was amended in 2003, 2015 and 2019, but not in 2008.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The 2003 amendment brought in the 'illegal migrant' concept, the National Register of Citizens provision and Overseas Citizenship of India.
✗ — amended
No amendment to the Citizenship Act was made in 2008.
The 2015 amendment merged the PIO card scheme into the 'Overseas Citizen of India Cardholder' scheme.
✗ — amended
The Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA) eased naturalisation for certain minorities from Afghanistan, Bangladesh and Pakistan.
✗ — amended

points: Other amendment years include 1957, 1960, 1985, 1986, 1992 and 2005.
The 1985 amendment followed the Assam Accord (Section 6A).

PYQ-POL-APK-89AAF0.lead: Option 2: technology in e-governance is meant to improve service delivery and citizen engagement.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: To replace human interaction entirely
E-governance supports officials and citizens; it does not remove human contact, especially for people without digital access.
To enhance citizen engagement and improve service delivery
Online services, faster processing and transparent tracking make government easier to reach and more responsive.
To reduce government expenditure
Saving cost can be a side benefit, but it is not the main purpose.
To increase government control
The aim is service and transparency for citizens, not more control over them.

points: Examples: online certificates, digital payments and grievance portals such as CPGRAMS.
Remember SMART governance: Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent.

PYQ-POL-APK-8B650A.lead: Option 4: depositing money in an Indian bank is not a way of getting citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: birth

Birth in India is a legal mode under Section 3 of the Citizenship Act, 1955, subject to conditions on the parents' citizenship. Because the stem asks what CANNOT give citizenship, this valid mode is not the answer.
✗ — valid mode
neutralization (naturalisation)

This is a misprint for naturalisation: a foreigner with the required years of residence gets a certificate from the Central Government under Section 6. It is a valid mode, so it does not fit 'cannot'.
✗ — valid mode
convention of a territory (incorporation)

This is a misprint for incorporation of territory: when a foreign territory becomes part of India, the Government notifies its people as citizens, as was done for Goa and Puducherry (Section 7). It is a valid mode, so it is not the answer.
✗ — valid mode
depositing money in an Indian Bank

A bank deposit is only a financial investment, and the Citizenship Act has no 'citizenship by investment' route. Since no law gives citizenship for money, this is the one way citizenship CANNOT be obtained.
✓ — not a mode

points: The five modes are birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory.

PYQ-POL-APK-9B9FAE.lead: Option 2: a simple majority is enough, because citizenship law under Article 11 is ordinary law, outside Article 368.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Effective majority
A majority of the effective strength of the House (total minus vacancies); used for removing the Vice-President, Speaker or Deputy Speaker.
Simple majority
A majority of members present and voting, as for ordinary bills.
Absolute majority
A majority of the total membership of the House; it is used only as part of the special majority.
Special majority
Under Article 368: a majority of the total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting.

points: Article 11 lets Parliament make laws on acquiring and losing citizenship.
LX lists 'Citizenship — acquisition and termination' among provisions changed by simple majority, which are not deemed amendments under Article 368.
PYQ-POL-APK-9B9FAE.also: Other simple-majority changes: new States (Articles 2–4), Fifth and Sixth Schedules, quorum in Parliament.

PYQ-POL-APK-A8689A.lead: Option 1 — Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
India does not allow dual citizenship. An Indian who acquires another country's citizenship loses Indian citizenship.
R
True
The Constitution and the Citizenship Act, 1955 provide only one citizenship, Indian citizenship.

points: Does R explain A? Yes — because the law recognises only one citizenship, a person cannot hold Indian and foreign citizenship together. R is the legal basis of A.
Option 2 fails: R actually does explain A.
Option 3 fails: R is in fact true.
Option 4 fails: A is in fact true.
OCI is not dual citizenship and gives no voting right.
PYQ-POL-APK-A8689A.also: Overseas Citizenship came via the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2003 (PIOs of 16 countries), was extended in 2005 to all countries except Pakistan and Bangladesh, and became 'OCI Cardholder' in 2015. It is not dual citizenship and gives no voting right.

PYQ-POL-APK-AF5BFE.lead: Option 1: Article 51A(g) makes protecting the environment a Fundamental Duty of every citizen.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Duty to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, lakes, rivers and wildlife, and to have compassion for living creatures.
Article 51
A Directive Principle asking the State to promote international peace and security.
Article 48A
A Directive Principle placing the duty of environment protection on the State, not on citizens.
Article 61
Procedure for impeachment of the President.

points: The question says 'duty of every citizen', so the answer must be in Part IVA (Article 51A), not Part IV.
Both 51A and 48A were added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

PYQ-POL-APK-B531D5.lead: Option 1: the Right to Information Act, 2005 requires a reply to information requests within a fixed time.

What it is / means
Correct?

National e-governance plan
A 2006 plan to deliver services online; it sets no legal time limit for giving information.

Right to Education Act
The 2009 Act gives free and compulsory education to children aged 6–14.

points: Key word 'information' points to RTI; key word 'timely' points to the 30-day limit.
PYQ-POL-APK-B531D5.also: RTI Act came fully into force on 12 October 2005.

PYQ-POL-APK-E7968C.lead: Option 2: Article 84 sets the minimum age for Rajya Sabha membership at 30 years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Minimum age for Lok Sabha and State Legislative Assembly members.
Minimum age for Rajya Sabha and State Legislative Council members (Article 84(b)).
Minimum age for the President and the Vice-President.
No constitutional office in this context uses 40 as the minimum age.

points: Memory hook: the 'upper' houses (Rajya Sabha, Council) need the 'older' age, 30.

PYQ-POL-APK-FC0A3B.lead: Option 2: the Citizenship Act, 1955 gives five modes of acquiring citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Four
Too few; it leaves out one of the five statutory modes.
Five
Birth, descent, registration, naturalisation and incorporation of territory.
Six
Wrong; the Act gives only five modes, so there is no sixth mode.
Eight
Wrong; the Act gives five modes, not eight.

points: Loss of citizenship has three ways: renunciation, termination and deprivation (LX p0102).

PYQ-POL-D5A5E43E1BCA.lead: Option 2: adoption is not a mode of acquiring citizenship under the Citizenship Act, 1955.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: By registration
Persons such as persons of Indian origin or spouses of Indians apply and get registered (Section 5).
✗ — valid mode
By adoption
Being legally taken as a child by Indian parents; the Act does not list it as a mode.
✓ — not a mode
By birth
Being born in India, with conditions on the parents' citizenship (Section 3).
✗ — valid mode
By descent
Being born outside India to a parent who is an Indian citizen (Section 4).
✗ — valid mode

points: An adopted minor child of Indian citizens can become a citizen only through registration (Section 5(1)(d)), so the mode is registration, not adoption.

PYQ-POL-E4541AA4B129.lead: Option 2: Articles 5 to 11 (Part II) relate to citizenship.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Articles 15 to 21
Fundamental Rights in Part III: non-discrimination, equal opportunity, freedoms and life and liberty.
Articles 5 to 11
Correct; Part II, Articles 5 to 11, deals with citizenship.
Articles 2 to 4
Part I: admission and creation of new States and changes in their boundaries.
Articles 25 to 31
Part III: religion, cultural and educational rights, and Article 31 (property, repealed in 1978).

points: Remember: Part II starts at 5 and ends at 11, just before Article 12 begins Part III.

PYQ-POL-F52BE1C5C794.lead: Option 2: Parliament has the power to regulate citizenship under Article 11.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The union cabinet
The Cabinet runs the government and carries out laws, but it cannot make citizenship law.
The Parliament
Article 11 gives Parliament the power to make any law on acquisition and termination of citizenship.
The Supreme Court
The Court interprets laws and can test their validity, but does not make citizenship rules.
Law commission
An advisory body that recommends legal reforms; it has no law-making power.

points: Parliament used this power to pass the Citizenship Act, 1955.
PYQ-POL-F52BE1C5C794.also: Citizenship is Entry 17 of the Union List.

PYQ-POL-FAEDB1C55EFE.lead: Option 1: Article 5 deals with citizenship at the commencement of the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 5
Citizenship at commencement for persons domiciled in India.
Article 10
Continuance of citizenship already held, subject to Parliament's laws.
Article 11
Parliament's power to regulate citizenship by law.
Article 7
Persons who migrated to Pakistan after 1 March 1947.

points: Under Article 5, a person domiciled in India needed birth in India, a parent born in India, or five years' ordinary residence.

PYQ-POL-WEB-10C92F.lead: Option 2 (I, II and IV only): Articles 29–30, 19 and 16 are available only to citizens, so they are denied to aliens.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Articles 29 and 30
True
Cultural and educational rights of minorities are given only to citizens.
II. Article 19
True
The six freedoms of Article 19 are available only to citizens.
III. Articles 23 and 24
False
Protection against forced labour and child labour applies to all persons, including foreigners.
IV. Article 16
True
Equality of opportunity in public employment is only for citizens.

points: Option 1 is wrong because it includes III and leaves out I and IV.
Option 3 is wrong because it includes III and leaves out I and II.
Option 4 is wrong because III is not denied to aliens.
PYQ-POL-WEB-10C92F.also: Article 15 (non-discrimination) is also for citizens only.

PYQ-POL-WEB-1FBC78.lead: Option 1: Article 19 is available only to citizens.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 19
The six freedoms (speech, assembly, association, movement, residence, profession) are for citizens only.
Article 20
Protection in respect of conviction applies to all persons, citizens and foreigners.
Article 21
Protection of life and personal liberty applies to every person.
Article 22
Safeguards against arbitrary arrest and detention apply to all persons (except enemy aliens).

points: Words in the text help: Article 19 says 'all citizens', while 20–22 say 'no person'.

PYQ-POL-WEB-25A1D0.lead: Option 3 (II, III and IV): protecting weaker sections is a Directive Principle (Article 46), not a Fundamental Duty.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Protect weaker sections from social injustice
False
This is a duty of the State under Article 46 (a DPSP), not a duty of citizens.
II. Develop scientific temper and spirit of inquiry
True
This is Fundamental Duty 51A(h), a duty of citizens, so it is correctly included.
III. Preserve rich heritage of composite culture
True
This is Fundamental Duty 51A(f), a duty of citizens, so it is correctly included.
IV. Safeguard public property and abjure violence
True
This is Fundamental Duty 51A(i), a duty of citizens, so it is correctly included.

points: Option 1 is wrong because it leaves out IV.
Option 2 is wrong because it includes I and leaves out II and IV.
Option 4 is wrong because I is not a Fundamental Duty.

PYQ-POL-WEB-3BD101.lead: Option 4 (1 only): only statement 1 is correct; the USA has dual citizenship and a naturalised Indian citizen can be deprived of citizenship.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Articles 371A to 371I for listed States
True
Special provisions were added for Nagaland (A), Assam (B), Manipur (C), Andhra Pradesh (D, E), Sikkim (F), Mizoram (G), Arunachal Pradesh (H) and Goa (I).
2. India and USA: dual polity, single citizenship
False
Both have a dual polity, but the USA has dual citizenship (national and State), while India has single citizenship.
3. Naturalised citizen can never be deprived
False
Under the Citizenship Act, the Central Government can deprive a citizen by naturalisation or registration for fraud, disloyalty or similar grounds.

points: Option 1 is wrong because it includes 2 and 3.
Option 2 is wrong because it includes 3.
Option 3 is wrong because it includes 3 and leaves out 1.
PYQ-POL-WEB-3BD101.also: Article 371J (Hyderabad-Karnataka region) was added later, in 2012.

PYQ-POL-WEB-463F9E.lead: Option 3: rights are claims of citizens against the State, which the State must respect and protect.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Claims of the State against the citizens
This reverses the idea: the State makes laws and has powers, but rights belong to individuals.
Privileges incorporated in a Constitution
Rights are not favours given at will; writing them in a Constitution only guarantees them.
Claims of the citizens against the State
Rights limit what the State can do to a person; Fundamental Rights can be enforced in court against the State.
Privileges of a few against the many
Rights belong to everyone equally, not to a small group.

points: In India, Part III rights are mostly enforceable against 'the State' as defined in Article 12.

PYQ-POL-WEB-508FE4.lead: Option 2: there is no duty of compulsory national service for 5 years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Cherish noble ideals of the freedom struggle
This is Fundamental Duty 51A(b), so it is a duty and not the answer.
✗ — is a duty
Mandatory national service of 5 years
51A(d) only asks citizens to defend the country and render national service when called upon; no fixed or compulsory period exists.
✓ — not a duty
Develop scientific temper, humanism, inquiry and reform
This is Fundamental Duty 51A(h), so it is a duty and not the answer.
✗ — is a duty
Safeguard public property and abjure violence
This is Fundamental Duty 51A(i), so it is a duty and not the answer.
✗ — is a duty

points: Fundamental Duties are not directly enforceable by courts, so a fixed compulsory service would not fit their nature.
PYQ-POL-WEB-508FE4.also: There are 11 Fundamental Duties; the 11th was added by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

PYQ-POL-WEB-5403C1.lead: Option 2: Indian citizens now have six Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Seven
The original number; the right to property was one of them.
Six
Equality, Freedom, against Exploitation, Freedom of Religion, Cultural and Educational, and Constitutional Remedies.
Four
Too few; no stage of the Constitution had four.
Nine
No such number of Fundamental Rights exists.

points: The 44th Amendment, 1978 removed the right to property from Part III.
PYQ-POL-WEB-5403C1.also: Property is now a legal right under Article 300A.

PYQ-POL-WEB-65CAB0.lead: Option 1: Article 51A(a) asks citizens to abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: constitution
51A(a): abide by the Constitution and respect its ideals and institutions, the National Flag and the National Anthem.
secularism
A value in the Preamble; it is not the word used in 51A(a).
socialism
A value in the Preamble (added in 1976); not the word in 51A(a).
democracy
A value in the Preamble; not the word in 51A(a).

points: The phrase 'its ideals and institutions' only makes sense after 'Constitution'.

PYQ-POL-WEB-713319.lead: Option 1: freedom of trade and profession (Article 19(1)(g)) is only for Indian citizens, so a British citizen cannot claim it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Freedom of trade and profession
Correct; Article 19(1)(g) is available only to citizens, so a British citizen cannot claim it.
Equality before the Law
Article 14 applies to every person, including foreigners.
Protection of life and personal liberty
Wrong; Article 21 applies to every person, including foreigners, so a British citizen can claim it.
Freedom of religion
Wrong; Article 25 applies to all persons, including foreigners, so a British citizen can claim it.

points: Citizens-only rights: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29 and 30.

PYQ-POL-WEB-72D776.lead: Option 4: the Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended Fundamental Duties.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Raja Chelliah Committee
This committee (1991) recommended reforms in India's tax system, such as lower rates and a wider base. It had nothing to do with citizens' duties, so it does not fit.
Santhanam Committee
This committee (1962–64) studied corruption in government and led to the creation of the Central Vigilance Commission. Its subject was vigilance, not Fundamental Duties.
Kelkar Committee
The Kelkar task forces (2002–03) worked on direct tax, indirect tax and fiscal (FRBM) reform. They were economic bodies, not constitutional-duty bodies, so they do not fit.
Swaran Singh Committee

The Congress Party set up this committee in 1976 during the Emergency to suggest constitutional changes, and it recommended a chapter on Fundamental Duties. Its advice led to Part IVA (Article 51A) through the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

points: The 42nd Amendment, 1976 added them as Part IVA, Article 51A.
PYQ-POL-WEB-72D776.also: The committee suggested 8 duties; the 42nd Amendment added 10.

PYQ-POL-WEB-8D20EB.lead: Option 2: in the US, 'dual citizenship' means being a citizen of the country and of the State where one lives or was born.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Two states with two countries
This mixes up States and countries; US dual citizenship works inside one country, not across two. So it does not describe the US system.
A country along with its constituent State
In the US federation a person is a citizen of the USA and also of the State where he lives or was born, such as Texas. This is exactly what 'dual citizenship' means in the US case.
Two states along with two countries
This wrongly adds two countries; the US idea has one country and one State. So it is a confused version of the concept.
Two countries simultaneously
Holding citizenship of two nations at once is 'dual nationality', a different idea. It is not what the stem means by the US federal model.

points: India has single citizenship: there is no separate State citizenship, even though India is federal.

PYQ-POL-WEB-9399C6.lead: Option 1: Article 15 bars discrimination against citizens on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 15
Article 15 forbids the State to discriminate against any citizen on grounds only of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth. These are the exact words of the stem, so it is the answer.
Article 59
Article 59 lays down conditions of the President's office, for example that he cannot be a member of Parliament or hold an office of profit. It is about the President, not discrimination.
Article 25
Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion. It protects religious freedom but does not list the five grounds of discrimination.
Article 40
Article 40 is a Directive Principle asking the State to organise village panchayats. It is about local self-government, so it does not fit.

points: Article 15 is a citizens-only right; Article 14 (equality before law) is for all persons.

PYQ-POL-WEB-99CCFB.lead: Option 4: the statement is not true, because the State can make laws regulating matters linked with religion; the right is not absolute.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Freedom of conscience; profess, practise, propagate
This is a true description of Article 25(1). Since the stem asks for the statement that is NOT true, this option is not the answer.
✗ — true statement
Establish institutions for religious and charitable purposes
This is true: Article 26(a) gives every religious denomination the right to establish and maintain such institutions. A true statement cannot be the answer here.
✗ — true statement
Subject to public order, morality and health
This is true: Articles 25 and 26 both begin with these limits, so the right is not unlimited. Being true, it is not the answer.
✗ — true statement
The State cannot make any law which abrogates this right

This is false, because Article 25(2) lets the State regulate economic, political or secular activities linked with religion and make social reform laws (such as opening Hindu temples to all classes). So this is the untrue statement the stem asks for.
✓ — not true

points: The question asks for the statement that is NOT true.
PYQ-POL-WEB-99CCFB.also: Article 25 is available to all persons, not only citizens.

PYQ-POL-WEB-A4107D.lead: Option 2: the right to acquire, hold and dispose of property is no longer a Fundamental Right.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Reside and settle in any part of India
This is still a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(e). Since citizens do have it, it does not fit the stem.
Acquire, hold and dispose of property
This was Article 19(1)(f), but the 44th Amendment, 1978 deleted it (and Article 31) from Part III. Citizens no longer have it as a Fundamental Right, so it is the answer.
Practise any profession
This is a Fundamental Right under Article 19(1)(g), along with trade, occupation and business. Citizens have it, so it does not fit.
Form co-operative societies
The 97th Amendment, 2011 added 'co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c), making it a Fundamental Right. Citizens have it, so it is not the answer.

points: Property is now only a legal right under Article 300A.

PYQ-POL-WEB-B9481C.lead: Option 4: scientific temper, humanism and inquiry is Fundamental Duty 51A(h).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: There is no Article 52A; Article 52 simply says there shall be a President of India. So it cannot contain any duty.
There is no Article 50A; Article 50 is a Directive Principle on separating the judiciary from the executive. It holds no duty of citizens.
There is no Article 49A; Article 49 is a Directive Principle on protecting monuments of national importance. It is not a Fundamental Duty.
Article 51A in Part IVA lists all Fundamental Duties, and clause (h) is the duty to develop scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform. So it is the answer.

points: All Fundamental Duties are in the single Article 51A.

PYQ-POL-WEB-BE0200.lead: Option 3: citizenship is in Part II, Articles 5 to 11.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Articles 10–17
This range takes the last two citizenship articles (10–11) and runs into Fundamental Rights (12–17). Since citizenship starts at Article 5, it is wrong.
Articles 8–15
This range misses Articles 5–7 and adds Fundamental Rights articles 12–15. So it does not match Part II.
Articles 5–11
This is the whole of Part II, from citizenship at commencement (Art 5) to Parliament's power (Art 11). It is the answer.
Articles 12–18
These articles open Part III: definition of State, laws inconsistent with FRs, and the Right to Equality. None of them deals with citizenship.

points: Part III (Fundamental Rights) begins at Article 12.

PYQ-POL-WEB-C7E308.lead: Option 3: all four statements correctly describe Article 21.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Available to citizens and aliens
True
Article 21 begins 'No person shall be deprived…', and 'person' includes foreigners. So it is not a citizens-only right.
2. Against arbitrary executive and legislative action
True
Since Maneka Gandhi (1978), the Court protects life and liberty from arbitrary laws as well as arbitrary executive orders. So both organs are bound.
3. Right to live with human dignity
True
The Supreme Court has read 'life' as life with human dignity, not mere animal existence. Rights such as livelihood and shelter grew from this reading.
4. Can be taken by procedure established by law
True
Life or liberty may be taken only by a procedure laid down in law. After Maneka Gandhi, that procedure must also be just, fair and reasonable.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 are wrong because each leaves out at least one true statement.
PYQ-POL-WEB-C7E308.also: Article 21 cannot be suspended even during a national emergency (44th Amendment).

PYQ-POL-WEB-C93876.lead: Option 1: the President is the first citizen of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President
Article 52 creates the office of President, who is head of the Indian State and the symbol of the nation. Because he stands first in the Order of Precedence, he is called the first citizen.
Lok Sabha Speaker
The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha and keeps order in the House. He heads one House, not the State, so he is not the first citizen.
Prime Minister
The Prime Minister is head of the government (real executive) but not head of the State. He comes third in the Order of Precedence, after the President and Vice-President.
Chief Justice
The Chief Justice of India heads the Supreme Court, the top of the judiciary. He is not head of the State, so he is not the first citizen.

points: Article 52: there shall be a President of India.

PYQ-POL-WEB-CB1FCB.lead: Option 3: Parliament passed the Citizenship Act in 1955.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: In 1950 the Constitution came into force, with Part II deciding who were citizens on 26 January 1950. The separate law under Article 11 came later, so 1950 is wrong.
In 1945 India was still under British rule and had no Parliament of its own. So no Indian citizenship law could be passed then.
Using its power under Article 11, Parliament passed the Citizenship Act in 1955. It still governs acquisition and loss of citizenship.
1948 is linked to the 19 July 1948 cut-off date in Article 6 for migrants from Pakistan. No citizenship Act was passed by Parliament in that year.

points: The Act has been amended many times, most recently by the Citizenship (Amendment) Act, 2019 (CAA).

PYQ-POL-WEB-D3110F.lead: Option 3: Article 11 gives Parliament plenary power to make citizenship laws.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 8
Article 8 gives citizenship to persons of Indian origin living abroad who register with an Indian diplomatic officer. It grants citizenship to a group but gives no law-making power.
Article 5
Article 5 decides who became a citizen at commencement on the basis of domicile. It is a one-time rule, not a power to legislate.
Article 11

Article 11 says nothing in Part II shall limit Parliament's power to make any law on acquisition, termination and all other matters of citizenship. That full ('plenary') power is exactly what the stem describes.
Article 6
Article 6 gives citizenship to certain migrants from Pakistan. Like Article 5, it is a one-time rule and gives Parliament no power.

points: 'Plenary' means full; Article 11 lets Parliament make any law on citizenship.

PYQ-POL-WEB-D5CD8D.lead: Option 2: the Constitution was adopted on 26 November 1949.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 26 January 1950
This is the date on which the Constitution came into full force, now Republic Day. The Preamble's words 'do hereby adopt' refer to an earlier date, so this is wrong.
26 November 1949
The Constituent Assembly adopted, enacted and gave itself the Constitution on this day, and the Preamble records it. So 'X' is 26 November 1949.
26 January 1949
No constitutional event happened on this date; it mixes the day of 1950 with the year of adoption. It is a trap option.
None of the above
This would be right only if no option gave the adoption date. Since option 2 does, this is wrong.

points: 26 November is now observed as Constitution Day (since 2015).
PYQ-POL-WEB-D5CD8D.also: Some provisions, like citizenship and elections, came into force on 26 November 1949 itself.

PYQ-POL-WEB-D76D27.lead: Option 1. 16(2) public jobs; 29(2) admission; 30(1) minority institutions; 31(1) property.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: 2. No discrimination in public appointment
Article 16(2) bars discrimination in public employment on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex, descent, place of birth or residence.
4. No denial of admission in State-aided institutions
Article 29(2) bars denial of admission to State-maintained or State-aided institutions on grounds of religion, race, caste or language.
3. Minorities' right to run institutions
Article 30(1) gives religious and linguistic minorities the right to establish and administer educational institutions.
1. No deprivation of property save by law
Article 31(1) protected property from deprivation save by law; the 44th Amendment (1978) repealed it and the rule is now Article 300A.

points: Option 2 fails: it pairs A-3 (should be 2), B-1 (should be 4), C-2 (should be 3), D-4 (should be 1).
Option 3 fails: it pairs B-1 (should be 4), D-4 (should be 1).
Option 4 fails: it pairs A-3 (should be 2), C-2 (should be 3).

PYQ-POL-WEB-E49E33.lead: Option 1: the Preamble secures 'liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship' – all five words.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Thought, expression, belief, faith and worship
This is the exact Preamble wording: liberty of thought, expression, belief, faith and worship.
2. Thought, expression, belief and faith
This drops 'worship', so it is incomplete and not the Preamble's text.
3. Expression, belief, faith and worship
This drops 'thought', the first of the five liberties, so it is wrong.
4. Thought, expression, faith and worship
This drops 'belief', so it does not match the Preamble.

points: The Preamble's four ideals are Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty (of thought, expression, belief, faith, worship), Equality (of status and opportunity) and Fraternity.
These liberties are made real through Fundamental Rights, mainly Article 19 (expression) and Articles 25–28 (faith and worship).
Memory hook: 'T-E-B-F-W' – Think, Express, Believe, have Faith, Worship.
PYQ-POL-WEB-E49E33.also: The Preamble promises Justice (social, economic, political), Liberty, Equality and Fraternity.

PYQ-POL-WEB-F63A32.lead: Option 1: Article 22(1) gives an arrested person the right to consult and be defended by a lawyer of his choice.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 22
Article 22 gives protection against arbitrary arrest: the right to be told the grounds, to consult and be defended by a lawyer, and to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.
2. Article 23
Article 23 bans traffic in human beings, begar and forced labour; it does not deal with arrest or legal defence.
3. Article 25
Article 25 gives freedom of conscience and the right to profess, practise and propagate religion; it has nothing to do with arrest.
4. Article 24
Article 24 bans employment of children below 14 years in factories, mines and hazardous work; it is not about arrested persons.

points: The stem's key words 'arrested' and 'right to be defended' point straight to Article 22(1).
These safeguards apply to ordinary (punitive) arrest; Article 22(3) excludes enemy aliens and persons under preventive detention.
If the right is denied, the person can approach the High Court (Article 226) or Supreme Court (Article 32), e.g. by habeas corpus.

PYQ-POL-WEB-D80506.lead: Option 1: no Constitution can guarantee that only good people enter politics; that depends on voters, parties and political culture.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. To ensure participation of good people in politics
This is not a function: a Constitution lays down rules and limits, but who enters politics is decided by elections and parties, not by the text.

3. To define the power of the different organs of government
This is a function: the Constitution creates the legislature, executive and judiciary and defines and limits their powers.
4. To create conditions for a just society
This is a function: the Preamble and Directive Principles (Part IV) aim at social, economic and political justice.

points: Basic functions of a Constitution: set basic rules, decide who has power, limit that power, and state the aspirations of society.

Correct (not a power): the Constitution has no provision letting the Rajya Sabha empower State Legislatures to make laws on Union List subjects.
