points: Ombudsman = officer who handles citizens' complaints against government (from Sweden, 1809).
Petitions Committee: 15 members (LS), 10 (RS).

PYQ-POL-E162AC024CBA.lead: Option 3: 20 members from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong: joint committees like this follow a 2:1 ratio, not equal shares; 15 + 15 is not the composition.
Wrong: 15 + 10 = 25 is not the strength; Lok Sabha has 20 members, not 15.
Correct: the committee has 30 members — 20 from Lok Sabha and 10 from Rajya Sabha — elected by PR-STV.
Wrong: 10 + 10 = 20 is too small and ignores the larger Lok Sabha share.

points: It considers the reports of the National Commissions for SCs and STs.

PYQ-POL-E797393796E7.lead: Option 2: the PAC reviews the CAG's audit reports.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Assist in election of Speaker
Wrong: the Speaker is elected by Lok Sabha members from among themselves (Article 93); no committee assists in that election.
2. Review audit reports of CAG
Correct: the PAC's main function is to examine the CAG's audit reports (appropriation accounts, finance accounts, public undertakings) that the President lays before Parliament.
3. Evaluate government schemes
Wrong: evaluating schemes is mainly done by ministries, NITI Aayog and DRSCs; the PAC only looks at spending after audit.
4. Recommend the Union Budget
Wrong: the Union Budget is prepared by the Finance Ministry and presented under Article 112; the PAC does not recommend it.

points: The Estimates Committee looks at budget estimates; the PAC does a post-mortem of money already spent.
The CAG is the PAC's 'friend, philosopher and guide'.
PYQ-POL-E797393796E7.also: No official key available; this is the study answer.

PYQ-POL-WEB-031114.lead: Option 2: the Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) is a Parliamentary Committee, because its members are elected by Parliament from among MPs of both Houses.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Cabinet Committee
A committee of senior ministers (e.g. Cabinet Committee on Security) set up by the executive. COPU contains no ministers at all, so it is not one.
Parliamentary Committee
A committee of MPs appointed or elected by the House to scrutinise the government. COPU has 22 MPs (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha) elected every year by Parliament.
Committee of a Political Party
An internal body of a party (e.g. a party's central committee). COPU is a body of Parliament with members from all parties chosen by proportional representation.
None of these
Cannot be correct because option 2 accurately describes COPU.

points: COPU was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee; membership rose from 15 to 22 in 1974.
It is one of the three financial committees of Parliament (PAC, Estimates, COPU) and examines reports and accounts of public sector undertakings.
A minister cannot be elected to COPU, which also shows it is a check on the executive, not part of it.

PYQ-POL-WEB-3CB6CB.lead: Option 3: the Public Accounts Committee (PAC) is the watchdog, because it examines spending after it has happened, using the CAG's audit reports, to find waste and irregularities.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Estimate Committee
Examines budget estimates before money is spent and suggests economies; called the 'continuous economy committee'. It is not a post-spending watchdog.
Committee on Public Undertakings
Examines reports and accounts of public sector undertakings only, not departmental expenditure in general.
Public Accounts Committee
Examines the appropriation and finance accounts and CAG audit reports, checking that money was spent as Parliament granted, with economy and propriety.
Committee on Public Assurances
Checks whether ministers have fulfilled promises and undertakings given on the floor of the House; it does not audit spending.

points: PAC was set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act 1919; it has 22 members (15 Lok Sabha, 7 Rajya Sabha) elected for one year.
Since 1967 its chairman is by convention from the Opposition, which suits a watchdog role.
Memory hook: Estimates = before spending (economy); PAC = after spending (audit, watchdog).

PYQ-POL-WEB-3E5839.lead: Option 2: the Estimates Committee works for financial control reform, because it examines the budget estimates and suggests economies and efficiency in public expenditure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Administration reforms
General changes to administrative structure. The committee may suggest efficiency in administration, but only as a means of controlling expenditure, so this is not its core purpose.
Financial Control reforms

Parliament's control over how public money is planned and spent. The committee reports what economies, improvements in organisation and efficiency can be made consistent with the policy behind the estimates.
New Legislation reforms
Framing new laws. Bills go to select/joint committees and the Houses, not to the Estimates Committee.
Estimates for different program reforms
Sounds similar but is a distractor; the committee does not reform programmes, it examines estimates to secure economy.

points: Origin: Standing Financial Committee 1921; first Estimates Committee after independence in 1950 on John Mathai's recommendation.
All 30 members are from Lok Sabha only, elected every year; a minister cannot be a member.
It is called the 'continuous economy committee' because it keeps suggesting economies in public expenditure.

PYQ-POL-WEB-58D2CC.lead: Option 2: the Committee on Subordinate Legislation checks whether the executive is properly using the power to make rules, regulations, sub-rules and bye-laws delegated by Parliament or the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Committee on Government Assurances
Checks whether ministers have kept the assurances and promises they gave in the House.
Committee on Subordinate Legislation
Examines delegated (subordinate) legislation, i.e. rules framed by the executive under an Act, and reports whether the power is exercised within the limits of the delegation.
Rules Committee
Considers the rules of procedure and conduct of business of the House itself, not rules made by the executive.
Business Advisory Committee
Regulates the programme and timetable of the House, allotting time for bills and discussions.

points: Parliament makes laws in outline and lets the executive fill details through rules; this is delegated legislation.
Because the executive is not elected for law-making, Parliament needs a committee to keep watch that it does not go beyond the parent Act.
LX lists this committee among the 'scrutiny and control' standing committees.

PYQ-POL-WEB-7348A8.lead: Option 3 (2 only): the Estimates Committee is the only one of the three that has no Rajya Sabha members; all its 30 members are from Lok Sabha.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Public Accounts Committee
False (has RS members)
PAC has 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha, so it does include Upper House members.
2. Estimates Committee
True (no RS members)
All 30 members are from Lok Sabha; the Rajya Sabha has no representation in this committee.
3. Committee on Public Undertakings
False (has RS members)
COPU has 22 members: 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha since 1974.

points: Option 1 (1 and 2) and option 2 (1 and 3) are wrong because PAC has 7 Rajya Sabha members.
Option 4 (3 only) is wrong because COPU also has 7 Rajya Sabha members.
Reason: the Estimates Committee deals with budget estimates, and money matters are the special domain of the Lok Sabha.

PYQ-POL-WEB-AC8415.lead: Option 1: the PAC consists of 15 members from Lok Sabha and 7 from Rajya Sabha, i.e. 22 members.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 15 Lok Sabha + 7 Rajya Sabha
True. This is the present composition of PAC.
20 Lok Sabha + 10 Rajya Sabha
False. That would total 30; 30 is the size of the Estimates Committee, which has only Lok Sabha members.
Term of five years
False. Members are elected every year; the term is one year.
Finance Minister is Chairperson
False. A minister cannot even be a member; the chairman is appointed by the Speaker from among members and, since 1967, from the Opposition.

points: PAC was first set up in 1921 under the Government of India Act 1919.
Members are elected by Parliament by proportional representation (single transferable vote) so all parties are represented.

PYQ-POL-WEB-D4AA61.lead: Option 3: a member of the PAC holds office for one year, because members are elected afresh every year.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Not more than 15 LS and 10 RS members
False. The number is 15 from Lok Sabha and 7 (not 10) from Rajya Sabha.
Finance Minister is ex officio member
False. A minister cannot be elected as a member of the PAC, since it scrutinises the executive's spending.
Term of one year
True. The term of office of PAC members is one year.
RS members' term extended after retiring from RS
False. Membership depends on being an MP; a member who ceases to be a member of the House ceases to be a member of the committee.

points: Composition: 22 members (15 LS + 7 RS) elected by proportional representation by single transferable vote.
Chairman: appointed by the Speaker; by convention from the Opposition since 1967.

PYQ-POL-WEB-FA6857.lead: Option 1 (A only): only statement A is correct; a minister cannot be a member of the PAC.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. A minister cannot be a member of PAC
True
LX: 'A minister cannot be elected as a member of the committee', because PAC checks the executive's spending.
B. Estimates Committee members are nominated by the Speaker
False
Members are elected by the Lok Sabha every year by proportional representation by single transferable vote; only the chairman is appointed by the Speaker.
C. A minister can be a member of Estimates Committee if nominated
False
A minister cannot be elected to the Estimates Committee either; there is no Speaker nomination route for members.
D. COPU member's tenure is 2 years
False
COPU members are elected every year; the term is one year, like PAC and Estimates.

points: Option 2 (A, B, C) and option 3 (A, B, C, D) wrongly include B and C.
Option 4 (B, C, D) leaves out the only true statement A and includes three false ones.
Memory hook: all three financial committees — elected, one-year term, no ministers.

PYQ-POL-2094068C11E1.lead: Option 2 is the incorrect statement (the answer): in India the President is only the nominal head; the real executive is the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Collective responsibility to House of the People even if some ministers are from Council of States
Correct statement: Article 75(3) makes all ministers, including Rajya Sabha members, responsible to the Lok Sabha.
President is the real head of the executive
Incorrect statement: the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Article 74(1)); he is the nominal (de jure) head.
Ministers individually responsible to President; liable to dismissal even with confidence of Legislature
Correct statement: ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President (Article 75(2)), who can remove one on the PM's advice even when the ministry has the House's confidence.
Tenure of council of ministers depends on… (text cut off)
Presumably 'the confidence of the legislature', which is a correct statement of parliamentary government.

points: Stem is incomplete in the source; read it as 'All of the following are correct EXCEPT'.
De jure (nominal) head = President; de facto (real) head = Prime Minister.

PYQ-POL-3E32CC85DD9E.lead: Option 4 (both b and c): India adopted the parliamentary system because of British influence (familiarity) and because it ensures accountability of the executive to the legislature.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Long tradition of parliamentary politics in India
Overstated: India had only a few decades of limited, British-introduced responsible government, not a long native tradition.
The British influence
Reason: the system had operated in India under British rule, so the framers were familiar with it.
Ensures accountability of executive to legislature
Reason: Ambedkar preferred more responsibility to more stability.
Both b and c
Combines the two valid reasons, so it is the best answer.

points: Other LX reasons: need to avoid legislative-executive conflict; plural nature of Indian society.
PYQ-POL-3E32CC85DD9E.also: Dr Ambedkar: the parliamentary system gives more responsibility; the presidential system gives more stability.

PYQ-POL-715D0E387AFE.lead: Option 3: the main advantage of parliamentary government over presidential is the accountability of the executive to the legislature.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: More stable executive
A merit of the presidential system (fixed term), not of parliamentary.
Better representation of minority interests
Wide representation is a merit, but it is not the main contrast drawn with the presidential system.
Accountability of executive to legislature
The defining advantage: 'responsible government' — questions, debates and no-confidence motions keep ministers answerable.
Better separation of powers
Separation of powers is a presidential feature; the parliamentary system has fusion of powers.

points: Ambedkar: the American system gives more stability, the British more responsibility; India chose responsibility.

PYQ-POL-83273E38C06A.lead: Option 2: the Prime Minister and Council of Ministers run the government; the President is only the nominal head.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President and Council of Ministers
Wrong: the President acts on ministerial advice (Article 74(1)), so he does not run the government.
Prime Minister and Council of Ministers
Correct: they form the real executive, collectively responsible to Lok Sabha.
The Prime Minister
Incomplete: the PM leads, but the government is the whole Council of Ministers acting collectively.
The President
Wrong: the President is only the nominal (de jure) head; the real executive is the Prime Minister and the Council of Ministers.

points: Parliamentary system = cabinet government, led by the PM ('primus inter pares').

PYQ-POL-APK-F43FC5.lead: Option 3: collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers to the Lok Sabha is the feature that marks a parliamentary system.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Separation of Powers
Presidential feature; India has fusion of executive and legislature.
Rule of Law
A principle of all democracies (borrowed from Britain); does not identify the form of government.
Collective responsibility of Council of Ministers
Core parliamentary feature (Article 75(3)): the ministry survives only with the Lok Sabha's confidence.
Judicial Review
Power of courts to strike down laws; borrowed from the US and found in presidential systems too.

points: LX calls collective responsibility the bedrock principle of parliamentary government.

PYQ-POL-BF1FB6E23E9F.lead: Option 3 (i, ii and iii): a presidential system's President is head of State and head of Government and is directly elected; he is not accountable to the legislature.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: i. President is head of State
True
Single executive: the President is the ceremonial head of State.
ii. President is head of Government
True
He also runs the government; there is no separate PM.
iii. Directly elected by people
True
In the classical model (e.g. US, through an electoral college based on popular vote) the President has his own mandate, separate from the legislature.
iv. Accountable to legislature
False
Non-responsibility is a presidential feature: he cannot be removed by a no-confidence vote, only by impeachment.

points: Option 1 (i, ii, iv) and option 4 (ii, iv) wrongly include iv.
Option 2 (i, iii) leaves out ii.

PYQ-POL-CECA30BC23C2.lead: Option 3: in parliamentary government the executive is responsible to the legislature.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Fixed tenure of executive
A fixed tenure of the executive is a feature of presidential government; in a parliamentary system the ministry lasts only while it has the House's confidence.
Executive responsible to judiciary
No system makes the executive politically responsible to courts.
Executive responsible to legislature
Correct: the core parliamentary principle (collective responsibility).
Separation of powers
Presidential feature; parliamentary system has fusion of powers.

points: In India: Article 75(3) for the Union and Article 164(2) for States.

PYQ-POL-D11E528C634A.lead: Option 3: the President's influence is persuasive — he cannot command the ministry but can advise, warn and ask it to reconsider.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Advisory
Wrong way round: it is the Council of Ministers that advises the President (Article 74), not the reverse.
Ceremonial
Too narrow: he has some real influence through being informed and returning advice for reconsideration.
Persuasive
Correct: he can persuade but is bound by advice after reconsideration (Article 74(1), 44th Amendment).
Formal
Describes his legal position as nominal head, but not his actual influence on the ministry.

points: Bagehot: the constitutional head has the right to be consulted, to encourage and to warn.

PYQ-POL-EBAE281D9664.lead: All four — majority rule, responsible, accountable and representative government — are parliamentary features.

head: Code
Feature
In parliamentary system?
rows: A
Majoritarian rule
Yes — majority party forms government
B
Responsible government
Yes — ministry answers to Lok Sabha
C
Executive accountable to legislature
Yes — Article 75(3)
D
Representative democracy
Yes — elected representatives govern

PYQ-POL-F43D793F163A.lead: Official key: option 2 (President). Study answer: option 1 (Prime Minister) — Jennings called the Prime Minister 'the key-stone of the constitution'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Prime Minister
Real head of the executive. Jennings: 'He is the key-stone of the constitution. All roads in the constitution lead to the Prime Minister.'
President
Nominal head of State who acts on ministerial advice; LX gives no 'keystone' description for him. This is the official key, which conflicts with the book.
Speaker
Presiding officer of the Lok Sabha; not described as the keystone.
Governor
Nominal head of a State; irrelevant to the Union constitution.

points: Morley called the PM the 'key stone of the cabinet arch'; Lowell called the Cabinet 'the keystone of the political arch'.
Memory hook: Jennings — constitution; Morley — cabinet arch; Lowell — cabinet = political arch.
PYQ-POL-F43D793F163A.also: Disputed key: the official key gives option 2 (President), but Laxmikanth quotes Jennings calling the Prime Minister 'the key-stone of the constitution'; the President is only the nominal head.

PYQ-POL-WEB-3B706C.lead: Option 4: India has judicial review; Britain follows parliamentary sovereignty, so its courts cannot strike down Acts of Parliament.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Both real and nominal executive
Common to both: Britain has the monarch (nominal) and PM (real).
Collective responsibility
Common to both: ministries in both are responsible to the lower House.
Bicameral legislature
Common to both: Britain has Commons and Lords.
Judicial review
The difference: Indian courts can strike down unconstitutional laws (Articles 13, 32, 226); the British Parliament is sovereign.

points: LX: Parliament in India is not supreme due to a written Constitution, federal system, judicial review and Fundamental Rights.

PYQ-POL-1385F43E6F0F.lead: Option 2: under Article 53(2), the President is the Supreme Commander of the Defence Forces of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Defence Minister
Wrong: the Defence Minister runs the defence ministry and answers to Parliament, but is not the Supreme Commander.
2. President
Correct: Article 53(2) vests the supreme command of the defence forces in the President, its exercise regulated by law.
3. Vice President
Wrong: the Vice-President has no military role; he is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha.
4. Prime Minister
Wrong: the Prime Minister leads the Cabinet that takes real defence decisions, but the constitutional title belongs to the President.

points: Concept: the President is the formal (nominal) commander; real control lies with the Cabinet.
Memory hook: Article 53 = executive power and supreme command, both vested in the President.

PYQ-POL-15A64CC84A96.lead: Option 1: President Pranab Mukherjee assented to the 100th Amendment in 2015.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Pranab Mukherjee
Correct: Pranab Mukherjee (President 2012–2017) assented to the 100th Amendment Act, 2015, which gave effect to the India–Bangladesh Land Boundary Agreement (exchange of enclaves).
2. Ram Nath Kovind
Wrong: Ram Nath Kovind became President only in July 2017, after the 100th Amendment.
3. APJ Abdul Kalam
Wrong: APJ Abdul Kalam was President from 2002 to 2007, long before 2015.
4. Pratibha Devisingh Patil
Wrong: Pratibha Patil was President from 2007 to 2012, before the amendment was passed.

points: Pranab Mukherjee also assented to the 101st Amendment (2016), which introduced GST.
Under Article 368(2), the President must give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill.

PYQ-POL-21076740E68A.lead: Statements I and III are correct, so the answer is option 3 (I and III only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. An ordinance can amend any Central Act
True
Under Article 123(2) an ordinance has the same force as an Act of Parliament, so it can amend or repeal a Central Act.
II. An ordinance can abridge a Fundamental Right
False
An ordinance is a 'law' under Article 13, so like any law it is void if it takes away or abridges a Fundamental Right.
III. An ordinance can come into effect from a back date
True
Like an Act of Parliament, an ordinance can be made retrospective, i.e. effective from an earlier date.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 are wrong because each includes the false statement II.
Also: an ordinance cannot amend the Constitution, as amendment is possible only under Article 368.

PYQ-POL-2343EE5047CF.lead: Option 2: Article 61 lays down the procedure for the impeachment of the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 143
Wrong: Article 143 is the President's power to consult the Supreme Court for its advisory opinion.
2. Article 61
Correct: Article 61 sets the ground (violation of the Constitution), the notice, and the two-thirds majority of total membership in each House.
3. Article 56
Wrong: Article 56 deals with the President's term of office; it only mentions removal 'by impeachment in the manner provided in Article 61'.
4. Article 75
Wrong: Article 75 deals with the appointment of the Prime Minister and other ministers.

points: Process: charge signed by one-fourth members, 14 days' notice, passed by two-thirds of total membership, then investigated and passed similarly by the other House.
No President has been impeached so far.

PYQ-POL-248FC33B4EAD.lead: Option 3: Article 72 gives the President power to grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions and commutations.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 74
Wrong: Article 74 provides the Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President.
2. Article 78
Wrong: Article 78 lays down the duties of the Prime Minister to keep the President informed.
3. Article 72
Correct: Article 72 is the President's pardoning power, covering court-martial sentences, offences against Union laws and death sentences.
4. Article 76
Wrong: Article 76 provides for the Attorney General for India.

points: The Governor's similar power is under Article 161; it does not cover death-sentence pardons or court-martial cases.
Memory hook: 72 for the President, 161 for the Governor.

PYQ-POL-24D14776A79A.lead: Option 2: a pocket veto is the President keeping a bill pending without any time limit, neither assenting nor rejecting it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Speaker of Lok Sabha not allowing presentation of a bill
Wrong: the Speaker refusing to allow a bill is not a veto; a veto is the head of state's power over a passed bill.
2. President keeping a bill pending with him, without any time limit and without approving any
Correct: since Article 111 gives no time limit, the President can simply sit on a bill indefinitely; this is the pocket veto.
3. Prime Minister removing ministers from his Cabinet without any reason
Wrong: the PM removing ministers is about Cabinet formation, not about bills or vetoes.
4. Rajya Sabha vetoing the provisions of a bill approved by Lok Sabha
Wrong: the Rajya Sabha can delay or reject a bill, but that is a legislative disagreement resolved by a joint sitting, not a veto.

points: Giani Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.
The US President must act within 10 days, so India's pocket veto is wider.

PYQ-POL-359ED7ABE8C8.lead: Option 2: Article 61 deals with the impeachment of the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 51
Wrong: Article 51 is a Directive Principle on promotion of international peace and security.
2. Article 61
Correct: Article 61 lays down the procedure for impeaching the President for violation of the Constitution.
3. Article 54
Wrong: Article 54 deals with the election (electoral college) of the President.
4. Article 63
Wrong: Article 63 says there shall be a Vice-President of India.

points: Impeachment needs 14 days' notice and a two-thirds majority of the total membership of each House.
Memory hook: Article 61 = impeachment; Article 62 = time of election to fill vacancy.

PYQ-POL-36CB2B3D4015.lead: All three statements are false, so the answer is option 4 (None).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Acts become invalid if the election is declared void
False
Article 71(2) says acts done by the President before the Supreme Court's decision remain valid.
2. Election can be postponed because some Assemblies are dissolved
False
Article 71(4): the election cannot be challenged on the ground of vacancies in the electoral college, so it goes ahead even if some Assemblies are dissolved.
3. The Constitution prescribes time limits for assent
False
Article 111 gives no time limit to the President; this is why the pocket veto is possible.

points: Option 1 (only one) is wrong because no statement is correct.
Options 2 and 3 are wrong for the same reason.
Concept: the Constitution keeps the presidential office stable and continuous.

PYQ-POL-44AC888926DD.lead: Option 2: the President is elected by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote (Article 55(3)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Prime Minister
Wrong: the Prime Minister is appointed by the President (Article 75), not elected by proportional representation.
2. President
Correct: Article 55(3) says the President's election is by proportional representation through the single transferable vote, by secret ballot.
3. Governor
Wrong: the Governor is appointed by the President (Article 155), not elected.
4. Lok Sabha Speaker
Wrong: the Lok Sabha Speaker is elected by the Lok Sabha by a simple majority of members present and voting.

points: The same method is used for the Vice-President, Rajya Sabha members and MLCs elected by MLAs.
Concept: the system makes the winner secure an absolute majority of the value of votes.

PYQ-POL-5A588F838EAD.lead: Both statements are false, so the answer is option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Executive power of the Union is vested in the Prime Minister
False
Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, not the Prime Minister.
2. PM is ex-officio Chairman of the Civil Services Board
False
The Civil Services Board, which advises on transfers and postings of senior officers, is chaired by the Cabinet Secretary, not the PM.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 are wrong because each treats at least one false statement as true.
The PM heads the Council of Ministers, which exercises the President's power in practice (Article 74).

PYQ-POL-5BD0A0B99C51.lead: Option 2: the President is the constitutional (nominal) head of the Union executive.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Prime Minister
Wrong: the Prime Minister is the real (de facto) head of the executive, not the constitutional head.
2. President
Correct: Article 53 vests executive power in the President, who is the formal head of the state and executive.
3. Supreme Court CJ
Wrong: the Chief Justice of India heads the judiciary, not the executive.
4. Speaker Rajya Sabha
Wrong: the Rajya Sabha has a Chairman (the Vice-President), not a Speaker, and neither heads the executive.

points: Concept: in a parliamentary system the President reigns but does not rule; the PM-led Council of Ministers rules.
Article 74: the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

PYQ-POL-5BF92C0B445E.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3 (1 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The President can summon Parliament at such place as he thinks fit
True
Article 85(1) says the President shall summon each House 'to meet at such time and place as he thinks fit'.
2. The Constitution provides for three sessions a year
False
The Constitution does not mention three sessions; the Budget, Monsoon and Winter sessions exist only by convention.
3. No minimum number of sitting days in a year
True
The Constitution only says the gap between two sessions must not exceed six months; it fixes no minimum days of sitting.

points: Options 1 and 4 are wrong because each misses a true statement, and option 4 also includes the false statement 2.
Option 2 is wrong because statement 2 is false.
Concept: Article 85 means Parliament must meet at least twice a year.

PYQ-POL-69889BEA9FE3.lead: Option 1: conducting elections is not the President's role; it is done by the Election Commission.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Conducting elections
Correct: Article 324 vests the superintendence, direction and control of elections in the Election Commission, so the President does not conduct elections.
2. Passing bills into law
Wrong: a bill becomes law only after the President's assent (Article 111), so he is a part of the law-making process.
3. Summoning and proroguing Parliament
Wrong: summoning and proroguing Parliament is a power of the President under Article 85.
4. Appointing the Prime Minister
Wrong: the President appoints the Prime Minister under Article 75.

points: The President does appoint the Chief Election Commissioner, but the Commission itself conducts elections.
Concept: the President is part of Parliament (Article 79), which is why assent and summoning are his roles.

PYQ-POL-78E26663DA0F.lead: Option 2: Article 53(1) vests the executive power of the Union in the President of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Wrong: the Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha; he is part of the legislature, not the executive.
2. President of India
Correct: Article 53(1) vests the executive power in the President, to be exercised directly or through officers subordinate to him.
3. Prime Minister of India
Wrong: the Prime Minister exercises real power through the Council of Ministers, but the power is constitutionally vested in the President.
4. Chief Justice of India
Wrong: the Chief Justice heads the judiciary, not the executive.

points: Article 74: the Council of Ministers headed by the PM aids and advises the President.
Memory hook: Article 53 = Union executive; Article 154 = State executive (Governor).

PYQ-POL-7EC9CD82CEF6.lead: The official key is option 1 (Radhakrishnan), but the study answer is option 4: Giani Zail Singh used a pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Dr. Sarvepalli Radhakrishnan
Wrong on facts: Dr. S. Radhakrishnan (President 1962–1967) had no connection with the Post Office Bill; this is the official key, which is disputed.
2. Sri. V. V. Giri
Wrong: V.V. Giri (President 1969–1974) was not involved with this bill.
3. Dr. Zakir Hussain
Wrong: Dr. Zakir Husain (President 1967–1969) was not involved with this bill.
4. Giani Zail Singh
Study answer: Giani Zail Singh (President 1982–1987) neither assented to nor returned the bill, which is the pocket veto.

points: The bill was criticised for restricting freedom of the press.
In 1989, President R. Venkataraman sent it back for reconsideration, and the National Front government then dropped it.
Concept: the pocket veto is possible because Article 111 fixes no time limit for assent.
PYQ-POL-7EC9CD82CEF6.also: Disputed key: the official key is option 1 (Radhakrishnan), but Laxmikanth records that Giani Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill in 1986.

PYQ-POL-8A32758F031F.lead: Option 4: under Article 53, the executive power of the Union is vested in the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Council of Ministers headed by PM
Wrong: the Council of Ministers headed by the PM aids and advises the President (Article 74), but the power is not vested in it.
2. Prime Minister
Wrong: the PM is the real head, but the Constitution vests the power in the President.
3. Chief Justice of SC
Wrong: the Chief Justice heads the judiciary, not the executive.
4. President
Correct: Article 53(1) vests the executive power of the Union in the President.

points: The President exercises it directly or through officers subordinate to him.
Concept: vested in the President in law, exercised by the Council of Ministers in practice.

PYQ-POL-8C79ADBFECB1.lead: Option 2: under Article 56(1)(a), the President resigns by writing addressed to the Vice-President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Chief Justice of India
Wrong: the Chief Justice administers the President's oath (Article 60), but does not receive the resignation.
2. Vice President of India
Correct: Article 56(1)(a) says the President may resign by writing under his hand addressed to the Vice-President.
3. Chief Election Commissioner of India
Wrong: the Chief Election Commissioner conducts the presidential election but has no role in resignation.
4. Prime Minister of India
Wrong: the Prime Minister does not receive the President's resignation.

points: The Vice-President must at once inform the Speaker of the Lok Sabha (Article 56(2)).
The Vice-President, in turn, resigns to the President (Article 67(a)).

PYQ-POL-8DB8651DE3B7.lead: Option 4 is the incorrect statement: the Prime Minister does not chair the UPSC.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The executive power of the Union is vested in the President
This statement is correct: Article 53(1) vests the executive power of the Union in the President.
2. The executive power of the Union extends to all matters with respect to which Parliament has power to make laws
This statement is correct: Article 73 extends the Union's executive power to all matters on which Parliament can make laws.
3. The executive power of the Union is exercised by the President directly or through officers subordinate to him
This statement is correct: Article 53(1) says the President exercises it directly or through officers subordinate to him.
4. The Union Public Service Commission is chaired by the Prime Minister
This statement is NOT correct, so it is the answer: the UPSC has its own Chairman, appointed by the President (Article 316); the PM has no role in it.

points: The UPSC is an independent constitutional body (Articles 315–323) that recruits for all-India and central services.
In a 'NOT correct' question, the keyed option is the false statement.

PYQ-POL-9260D9B0400A.lead: Statements A and C are correct, so the answer is option 2 (A and C only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Impeachment on the ground of violation of the Constitution
True
Article 61(1) gives 'violation of the Constitution' as the only ground for impeaching the President.
B. The meaning of violation is explained in Article 61(2)
False
The Constitution does not define 'violation of the Constitution' anywhere; Article 61(2) only lays down the notice and two-thirds majority rules.
C. Impeachment is a quasi-judicial procedure
True
LX calls it quasi-judicial: one House frames the charge and the other investigates it, and the President can appear or be represented.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 are wrong because each includes the false statement B.
Option 3 also leaves out the true statement A.

PYQ-POL-99D22ACCC407.lead: Option 3: the President submits his resignation to the Vice-President (Article 56(1)(a)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Chief Justice of the Supreme Court
Wrong: the Chief Justice administers the oath, but does not receive the resignation.
2. The Prime Minister
Wrong: the Prime Minister does not receive the President's resignation.
3. The Vice-President
Correct: Article 56(1)(a) says the resignation is in writing addressed to the Vice-President.
4. The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Wrong: the Speaker is only informed of the resignation by the Vice-President (Article 56(2)); it is not addressed to him.

points: Memory hook: President and Vice-President resign to each other.
Until a new President is elected (within six months), the Vice-President acts as President.

PYQ-POL-9DE9662F9C8D.lead: Option 4: the President of India is formally addressed as 'His Excellency'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. His Lord ship
Wrong: 'His Lordship' is a form of address traditionally used for judges.
2. His honour
Wrong: 'His Honour' is used for some judges and officials in other countries, not for the Indian President.
3. His Highness
Wrong: 'His Highness' is used for royalty, such as former princely rulers.
4. His Excellency
Correct: 'His Excellency' is the formal diplomatic form of address for a head of state, including the President of India.

points: Since 2012 the government has encouraged 'Rashtrapati ji' or 'Hon'ble President' in Indian usage, but 'His Excellency' remains the formal diplomatic form.
Concept: forms of address follow the office: Excellency for heads of state and Governors.

PYQ-POL-AF3B916244A4.lead: Only statement III is valid as per the key, so the answer is option 1 (Only III).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Suspensive veto for Money Bills but not Finance Bills
False
The President has no suspensive veto over Money Bills; since they are introduced on his recommendation, he cannot return them for reconsideration.
II. Absolute veto over government Bills at all times
False
The absolute veto is used only in rare cases, such as private members' bills or a government bill when the Cabinet resigns before assent; it is not available 'at all times'.
III. India: indefinite pocket veto; USA: qualified veto
True
The Indian President has no time limit for assent, so his pocket veto is indefinite, while the US President's veto can be overridden by a two-thirds majority (qualified veto).
IV. The veto seeks checks and balances
False
As per the key, this is treated as false: LX gives the object of the veto as preventing hasty, ill-considered or unconstitutional legislation, not a balance of powers.

points: Options 2 and 4 are wrong because they include statement II (and option 2 also I).
Option 3 is wrong because it includes statement IV, which the key treats as not valid.
Concept: the veto power exists to make Parliament think again before a bill becomes law.

PYQ-POL-APK-083448.lead: Option 3: Article 55(3) says the President is elected by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and voting is by secret ballot.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Open voting by the electoral college
False. The Constitution requires a secret ballot, so no voter has to reveal his choice.
Directly by the people
False. The election is indirect: only the electoral college of elected MPs and MLAs votes (Article 54).
Proportional representation by single transferable vote, secret ballot
True. This is the exact wording of Article 55(3).
Majority of members present and voting, in the capital
False. A candidate must reach a fixed quota (an absolute majority of valid votes), and voting is held in Parliament House and in each state capital, not only in Delhi.

points: Single transferable vote means each voter ranks candidates (1, 2, 3...); if no one reaches the quota, the lowest candidate is eliminated and his votes go to the next preferences.
Quota = (total valid votes / (1 + 1)) + 1, i.e. more than half the valid votes.
Memory hook: President's election = Indirect + STV + Secret.

PYQ-POL-APK-15AA94.lead: Option 3: Article 53(3)(b) says nothing in Article 53 prevents Parliament from conferring functions by law on authorities other than the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament cannot confer any function on others
False. This is the opposite of Article 53(3)(b), which expressly allows Parliament to do so.
Confer functions with Supreme Court concurrence
False. Article 53(3)(b) needs only a law of Parliament; no Supreme Court concurrence is mentioned.
Nothing in Article 53 prevents Parliament conferring functions by law on other authorities
True. This is the text of Article 53(3)(b).
Parliament may restrict the President's constitutional functions
False. An ordinary law cannot cut down functions the Constitution itself gives the President; that needs a constitutional amendment.

points: Article 53(1) vests the executive power of the Union in the President.
Article 53(3)(a) says existing functions given by law to a state government are not transferred to the President.
So Article 53 does not make the President the only executive channel: Parliament may give statutory powers to other bodies, such as ministers or commissions.

PYQ-POL-APK-1A0B38.lead: Option 1: Article 58(1)(c) says a presidential candidate must be qualified for election as a member of the Lok Sabha.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Lok Sabha
True. Article 58 links the President's qualification to the Lok Sabha.
Rajya Sabha
False. Qualification for the Rajya Sabha is the test for the Vice-President (Article 66), not the President.
State Legislative Assembly
False. The state Assembly is not the House named in Article 58; the test for the President is the Lok Sabha.
State Legislative Council
False. The Council is not mentioned in the President's qualifications at all.

points: Article 58 qualifications: citizen of India, completed 35 years, qualified for Lok Sabha, and holds no office of profit.
Memory hook: President = Lok Sabha; Vice-President = Rajya Sabha (he chairs the Rajya Sabha).

PYQ-POL-APK-1ABA99.lead: Option 3: Article 123 lets the President issue an ordinance at any time except when both Houses are in session, if he is satisfied that immediate action is needed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Speaker or Chairman satisfied that discussion is not possible
False. The Speaker and Chairman have no role; the power belongs to the President alone, on ministerial advice.
Parliament not likely to pass a pending Bill before prorogation
False. This is not a condition in Article 123; an ordinance needs Parliament not to be in session.
Except when both Houses are in session, President satisfied immediate action is necessary
True. This is the text of Article 123(1).
Immediate action needed and no ordinance in the previous six months
False. There is no six-month gap rule; the 'six' rules relate to the lapse of the ordinance and the gap between sessions.

points: An ordinance can be issued when Parliament is in recess or when only one House is sitting.
It must be laid before both Houses and lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved earlier.
The President's satisfaction is not immune: the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the 38th Amendment's bar on judicial review.

PYQ-POL-APK-1E9243.lead: Option 4: Article 53(1) says the executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Union Government
False. 'Union Government' is a general term; Article 53 names the President as the holder of executive power.
The Council of Ministers
False. The Council of Ministers advises the President (Article 74) and exercises power in practice, but power is not vested in it.
The Prime Minister
False. The PM heads the Council of Ministers; he is the real executive, but the Constitution vests power in the President.
The President of India
True. Article 53(1) vests the power in the President, to be exercised by him directly or through subordinate officers.

points: Distinguish 'vested in' (legal owner = President) from 'exercised by' (real executive = Council of Ministers headed by the PM).
This is why the President is called the nominal (de jure) executive and the PM the real (de facto) executive.

PYQ-POL-APK-26125A.lead: Option 1: Article 58(1)(b) requires a candidate to have completed 35 years, so a person below 35 cannot be elected President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Not eligible
True. The age rule of 35 years is absolute.
Eligible if he has completed 30 years
False. 30 years is the minimum age for the Rajya Sabha, not for the President.
Eligible if he has not crossed 70 years
False. There is no upper age limit for the President, and no relaxation of the lower limit.
Eligible if the Chief Election Commissioner declares so
False. The Election Commission conducts the election but cannot relax a qualification fixed by the Constitution.

points: Minimum ages: Lok Sabha 25, Rajya Sabha 30, President / Vice-President / Governor 35.
Only a constitutional amendment could change the 35-year rule.

PYQ-POL-APK-2DE56E.lead: Option 3: Members of state Legislative Councils are NOT in the electoral college for the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Elected MLAs of the states
Included. Article 54 names the elected members of state Legislative Assemblies.
Elected MLAs of the Union Territories
Included. The 70th Amendment (1992) added the elected members of the Assemblies of Delhi and Puducherry.
Elected members of state Legislative Councils
Not included. MLCs, elected or nominated, have no vote in the presidential election, so this is the answer.
Elected members of both Houses of Parliament
Included. Article 54 names the elected members of the Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha.

points: Rule: only ELECTED members of Parliament and of the Assemblies vote; nominated members and Council members do not.
Note: nominated MPs, who cannot vote in the election, can take part in impeachment.

PYQ-POL-APK-32E3DD.lead: Option 4: The President is the constitutional (nominal) head of the Indian State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Union Minister of Home Affairs
False. He is one member of the Council of Ministers, in charge of one ministry.
Chief Justice of India
False. The CJI heads the judiciary, not the State.
Prime Minister
False. The PM is the head of government and the real executive, not the constitutional head of the State.
President
True. Article 52 creates the office and Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President.

points: In a parliamentary system the head of State (President) is nominal and the head of government (PM) is real.
The President must act on the advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the PM (Article 74).

PYQ-POL-APK-36CBE3.lead: Option 3: Article 74(1) provides a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at the head to aid and advise the President, who shall act on that advice.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament
False. Parliament controls the ministry, but it does not advise the President under Article 74.
Lok Sabha
False. The Council of Ministers is responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), but the Lok Sabha itself does not advise the President.
Council of Ministers with the PM at the head
True. This is the wording of Article 74(1).
PM or Deputy PM
False. The advice is of the whole Council headed by the PM; the post of Deputy PM is not mentioned in the Constitution.

points: The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the advice binding on the President.
The 44th Amendment (1978) let the President send the advice back once for reconsideration, but the reconsidered advice is binding.

PYQ-POL-APK-4360E4.lead: Option 2: Article 112 says the Annual Financial Statement is a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the Government of India for that year.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Statement of the financial condition of the country
False. It covers the Government's own estimates, not the whole country's finances.
Estimated receipts and expenditure of GoI for that year
True. This is the wording of Article 112(1).
Surplus income of the previous year
False. It looks forward to the coming year; it is an estimate, not a report on past surplus.
Presentation of the Economic Survey
False. The Economic Survey is a separate Finance Ministry review of the economy and is not a constitutional document.

points: The Constitution never uses the word 'Budget'; the Budget is the popular name of the Annual Financial Statement.
It is laid before Parliament by the President's direction; expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund is shown separately.

PYQ-POL-APK-4A8AB6.lead: Option 1: Under Article 72(1)(a) only the President can pardon punishments given by a court-martial.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The President of India
True. Article 72 extends his pardoning power to court-martial sentences.
The Governor of a state
False. The Governor's power (Article 161) covers only offences against state laws and does not include court-martial sentences.
The Prime Minister
False. The PM has no pardoning power; he only advises the President.
The Chief Minister
False. The CM has no pardoning power; he only advises the Governor.

points: Two powers only the President has: pardon of court-martial sentences and full pardon of a death sentence.
Memory hook: military court = Union subject, so only the President.

PYQ-POL-APK-51931E.lead: Option 2: President's rule was imposed in Andhra Pradesh in January 1973.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: December 1975
False. No President's rule was imposed in Andhra Pradesh then; it was the time of the national Emergency.
January 1973
True. It was imposed on 18 January 1973 after the Jai Andhra agitation and lasted until 10 December 1973.
January 1974
False. By then the state had a popular government again.
December 1974
False. No President's rule was imposed in Andhra Pradesh then.

points: The Jai Andhra agitation (1972-73) demanded a separate Andhra state; Chief Minister P.V. Narasimha Rao resigned.
When the rule ended, Jalagam Vengala Rao became Chief Minister.

PYQ-POL-APK-519324.lead: All three statements are true, so option 1 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Articles 256-263 in Part XI deal with administrative relations
True
Chapter II of Part XI (Articles 256 to 263) is titled 'Administrative Relations' between the Union and the states.
2. Centre can direct states on means of communication of national or military importance
True
Article 257(2) lets the Union direct a state to build and maintain such means of communication.
3. Article 365: failure to obey Union directions
True
Article 365 says the President may then hold that the state cannot be carried on as per the Constitution, which opens the way to Article 356.

points: Option 2 (only 2 and 3) wrongly drops statement 1.
Option 3 (only 1 and 3) wrongly drops statement 2.
Option 4 (only 1 and 2) wrongly drops statement 3.

PYQ-POL-APK-606966.lead: Option 3: Under Article 111 a Bill becomes an Act after both Houses pass it and the President gives assent.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Passed by Lok Sabha and assented to
False. Passing by one House is not enough; both Houses must pass it.
An Act becomes a Bill...
False. This reverses the terms: a draft (Bill) becomes law (Act), never the other way.
Passed by both Houses and assented to by the President
True. This is the process in Articles 107 and 111.
Passed by Rajya Sabha and assented to
False. Again only one House; the Lok Sabha must also pass it.

points: A 'Bill' is a proposed law; it becomes an 'Act' only after assent.
Even a Money Bill goes to the Rajya Sabha, which can hold it only 14 days; it is then deemed passed by both Houses.

PYQ-POL-APK-71CDB5.lead: Option 1: The President is a constitutional authority because the office is created by the Constitution itself (Article 52).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Constitutional authority
Created directly by the Constitution and changeable only by amending it, e.g. President, Election Commission, CAG. Article 52 says 'There shall be a President of India'.
Statutory authority
Created by an ordinary Act of Parliament or a state, e.g. NHRC (1993 Act). No Act created the President's office.
Administrative authority
An officer or body that only carries out day-to-day government work, e.g. a District Collector. The President is the head of the State, not a mere administrator.
Non-executive authority
A body with no executive power, e.g. an advisory committee. Article 53 vests the executive power of the Union in the President, so this does not fit.

points: Article 52 creates the office; Article 53 gives it the executive power of the Union.
He is the nominal head; real power lies with the Council of Ministers led by the PM (Article 74).

PYQ-POL-APK-761AEA.lead: Option 2: Article 352 lets the President proclaim a National Emergency when the security of India is threatened by war, external aggression or armed rebellion.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 350
False. It gives every person the right to submit a representation for redress of grievances in any language used in the Union or state.
Article 352
True. It is the National Emergency provision.
Article 376
False. It is a transitional provision about High Court judges at the commencement of the Constitution.
Article 321
False. It lets a legislature extend the functions of a Public Service Commission.

points: The 44th Amendment (1978) replaced 'internal disturbance' with 'armed rebellion'.
The President proclaims it only on the written advice of the Union Cabinet (44th Amendment).

PYQ-POL-APK-9A5B41.lead: Option 1: Article 352 is the National Emergency provision.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 352
True. National Emergency on grounds of war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
Article 356
False. It is President's Rule (state emergency) on failure of constitutional machinery in a state.
Article 360
False. It is Financial Emergency, when the financial stability or credit of India is threatened.
Article 365
False. It is the effect of a state's failure to obey Union directions, which can lead to Article 356.

points: Three emergencies in Part XVIII: 352 National, 356 State, 360 Financial.
Memory hook: 352 - 356 - 360, gaps of four.

PYQ-POL-APK-A3045C.lead: Option 3: Under Article 80 the President nominates 12 members to the Rajya Sabha.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: False. No such number appears in Article 80.
False. This was the number of Anglo-Indians the President could nominate to the Lok Sabha (Article 331), a provision now ended.
True. Article 80(1)(a) and 80(3): 12 persons with special knowledge or practical experience.
False. No such number appears in Article 80.

points: The 12 must have special knowledge or experience in literature, science, art and social service.
The 104th Amendment (2019) ended the Lok Sabha Anglo-Indian nominations.

PYQ-POL-APK-B47923.lead: Option 3: Under Article 356 the Governor of the state sends the report on failure of constitutional machinery to the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Chief Minister
False. The CM heads the very government whose failure is being reported; Article 356 gives him no role.
Home Minister
False. Article 356 does not mention a Home Minister.
Governor
True. The President may act on the Governor's report or otherwise.
Home Secretary
False. A civil servant has no constitutional role under Article 356.

points: The President can act even without a Governor's report ('or otherwise').
S.R. Bommai case (1994): President's rule is subject to judicial review.

PYQ-POL-APK-B57028.lead: Option 4: Under Article 61 the impeachment charge is preferred by either House of Parliament.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: CBI
False. The CBI is an investigating agency under the Union government; it has no role in impeachment.
CVC
False. The CVC is a vigilance body for public servants; it has no role in impeachment.
NIA
False. The NIA investigates terror offences; it has no role in impeachment.
Either House of Parliament
True. One House prefers the charge, and the other House investigates it.

points: The charge must be signed by one-fourth of the members of the House and 14 days' notice given to the President.
Each House must pass the resolution by two-thirds of its total membership.

PYQ-POL-APK-B6FA3A.lead: Option 2: Under Article 65 the Vice-President acts as President when there is a vacancy in the office.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Chief Justice of India
False. The CJI acts only when both the President's and the Vice-President's offices are vacant (President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969).
Vice-President
True. Article 65(1) makes him act as President until a new President takes office.
Speaker of Lok Sabha
False. The Speaker has no role in this succession.
Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha
False. He acts as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha when the Vice-President acts as President, but does not act as President.

points: A vacancy caused by death, resignation or removal must be filled within six months (Article 62).
While acting as President, the Vice-President does not perform the duties of Rajya Sabha Chairman.

PYQ-POL-APK-BACE53.lead: Option 4: CJI M. Hidayatullah was the first Chief Justice to act as President, from 20 July to 24 August 1969.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Zakir Hussain
False. He was the elected President who died in office in May 1969, creating the vacancy.
V.V. Giri
False. He was Vice-President and acted as President first, then resigned to contest the election.
Fakhruddin Ali Ahmed
False. He was an elected President (1974-77), never a CJI.
M. Hidayatullah
True. With both offices vacant, the CJI acted as President.

points: Hidayatullah later became Vice-President (1979), elected unopposed.
Memory hook: 1969 - Husain died, Giri resigned, Hidayatullah acted.

PYQ-POL-APK-C3FE68.lead: Option 3: President's Rule can be extended for a maximum of three years, with Parliament's approval every six months.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: One year
False. One year is the limit for continuing beyond which special conditions are needed, not the maximum.
Two years
False. No such limit exists in Article 356.
Three years
True. Article 356(4) allows extension up to three years in six-month spells.
Four years
False. Under Article 356, President's Rule can be extended to a maximum of three years, not four.

points: Beyond one year it can continue only if a National Emergency is in force and the Election Commission certifies that elections cannot be held (44th Amendment).
Each approval needs a simple majority of each House.

PYQ-POL-APK-C4CC03.lead: Option 4: Under Article 61 the only ground for impeaching the President is 'violation of the Constitution'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Any criminal offence
False. Not a ground; and Article 361 protects the President from criminal proceedings during his term.
Moral degradation
False. Not a ground mentioned in Article 61.
Unsoundness of mind
False. Not a ground for impeachment, though it matters for some other offices.
Violation of the Constitution
True. This is the single ground in Article 61.

points: The Constitution does not define 'violation of the Constitution'.
No President has so far been impeached.

PYQ-POL-APK-D05836.lead: Option 1: Under Article 72 the President can pardon or reduce a sentence, including a death sentence.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President of India
True. Article 72 gives him power to pardon, commute or remit, and he alone can fully pardon a death sentence.
Prime Minister
False. The PM has no pardoning power; the Cabinet only advises the President.
Chief Justice of India
False. The courts impose sentences; pardon is an executive power, not a judicial one.
Vice-President
False. He has no pardoning power unless he is acting as President.

points: The Governor (Article 161) can suspend, remit or commute a death sentence but cannot pardon it.
The President exercises this power on the advice of the Union Cabinet.

PYQ-POL-APK-DA7524.lead: Option 3: The electoral college has elected MPs of both Houses and elected MLAs of the states, Delhi and Puducherry.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: All members of Parliament and all MLAs
False. 'All' wrongly includes nominated members.
Elected MPs and all MLAs
False. Nominated MLAs do not vote, and the UT Assemblies are left out.
Elected MPs, elected MLAs of states, Delhi and Puducherry
True. This matches Article 54 as amended by the 70th Amendment (1992).
All MPs and elected MLAs of states
False. 'All MPs' wrongly includes nominated MPs, and Delhi and Puducherry are left out.

points: Members of state Legislative Councils do not vote.
Article 54 gives the electoral college; Article 55 gives the method of voting.

PYQ-POL-APK-E88DC3.lead: Option 3: Article 103 says the President must obtain the Election Commission's opinion and act according to it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Obtain EC opinion, may or may not accept it
False. The opinion is binding, not just advisory.
President decides without any opinion
False. Article 103(2) makes taking the EC's opinion compulsory.
Obtain EC opinion and act according to it
True. This is the wording of Article 103(2).

PYQ-POL-WEB-1755FB.lead: Option 1, Article 257(1), is correct: the executive power of every State must be used so that it does not impede or prejudice the Union's executive power.

President's Rule when the constitutional machinery in a State fails; it is the remedy for breakdown, not the general rule on executive power.

PYQ-POL-WEB-77C1B2.lead: Option 2 is correct: under Article 123 the President can issue ordinances only when both Houses, or either House, are not in session.

False. The Lok Sabha only agrees to a resolution already passed by the Rajya Sabha.

False. 'Either House' is the rule for the President's impeachment, not the VP.

Rajya Sabha alone ✓
True. Passed there by effective majority after 14 days' notice, then agreed to by Lok Sabha by simple majority.

PYQ-POL-WEB-C035D3.lead: Option 2: members of both Houses of Parliament elect the Vice-President.

What it is / means
Correct?

PYQ-POL-011A533AF4D9.lead: Option 4: the 91st Amendment Act, 2003 capped the total number of ministers, including the PM, at 15% of the Lok Sabha's total strength.

PYQ-POL-16CF77A3BDA7.lead: Option 4: Article 75(3) says the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (House of the People).

What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong. The Rajya Sabha can question and criticise ministers but cannot remove the ministry by a no-confidence vote.
The President

The Lok Sabha
Correct as per Article 75(3); the directly elected House can vote the whole ministry out.

points: Collective responsibility means ministers 'swim and sink together': a no-confidence vote in the Lok Sabha forces all ministers, even Rajya Sabha members, to resign.

PYQ-POL-1FEF003E3E38.lead: Option 2: Clement Attlee of the Labour Party was the British Prime Minister when India became independent on 15 August 1947.

PYQ-POL-22C6703812A6.lead: Option 4: Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers with the Prime Minister at its head to aid and advise the President.

Article 74
Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President; the President must act on its advice.

points: The 42nd Amendment (1976) made the advice binding; the 44th Amendment (1978) let the President send it back once for reconsideration.
Articles 74–75 together form the core of the Union Council of Ministers.

PYQ-POL-2B6BA16F3F6F.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are functions of the Cabinet Secretariat; statement 3 is not. Answer: option 3 (1 and 2 only).

False

points: Option 1 misses statement 2; options 2 and 4 wrongly include statement 3.

PYQ-POL-3467F373FE2A.lead: Option 4: in February 2020 D.V. Sadananda Gowda was Union Minister of Chemicals and Fertilizers in Modi's second ministry.

Sadananda Gowda's portfolio from 2019 until the July 2021 reshuffle.

PYQ-POL-34B59BFFEF70.lead: Option 3: Article 77 deals with the conduct of business of the Government of India.

Correct?

PYQ-POL-3C8E56F75F4C.lead: Option 1: the Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers, which holds the real executive power.

Correct?

No such post: the Rajya Sabha has a Chairman (the Vice-President), not a Speaker.

Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha; not part of the Council of Ministers.
President
The nominal (de jure) executive who acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

points: In a parliamentary system the head of State is nominal, and the head of government (PM) is real.

PYQ-POL-47604F3B6BB7.lead: Option 3: Article 75(2) says ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President.

PYQ-POL-5396248EF37B.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (both 1 and 2).

True/False

True

PYQ-POL-APK-5F2B3D.lead: Option 1: under Article 75(1) the President appoints the PM, and the other ministers on the PM's advice.

PYQ-POL-APK-80F030.lead: Option 4: the death of a sitting Prime Minister automatically dissolves the Council of Ministers, because the Council cannot exist without its head.

PYQ-POL-APK-F99525.lead: Option 3: Article 75(1A) caps the total number of ministers, including the PM, at 15% of the total members of the Lok Sabha.

Correct, added by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003.

PYQ-POL-CEBEECB9A33A.lead: Official key: option 2 (Jennings). Laxmikanth credits the phrase 'key stone of the cabinet arch' to Lord Morley (not an option); Jennings called the PM 'the key-stone of the constitution', the nearest match.

Correct?
rows: Laski
Called the PM 'the pivot around which the entire governmental machinery revolves'.
Jennings
Called the PM 'a sun around which planets revolve' and 'the key-stone of the constitution'.
✓ (key)
Wheare
K.C. Wheare called India 'quasi-federal'; no such remark on the PM.
Bryce
Not associated with this description of the PM.

points: Lord Morley: 'primus inter pares' and 'key stone of the cabinet arch'.
Lowell called the Cabinet (not the PM) 'the keystone of the political arch'.
Since Morley is not an option, Jennings ('key-stone') is the best available answer.

PYQ-POL-D88B524384F8.lead: Option 1: the President appoints the Prime Minister under Article 75(1).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The President appoints the Prime Minister
True: Article 75(1) says the President appoints the PM; the PM is not elected by Parliament or the Lok Sabha as such.
The PM is elected by Parliament
False; there is no election of the PM by Parliament.
The PM is elected by the Lok Sabha
False; he is appointed, though he must keep Lok Sabha majority support.
The PM functions as Leader of the Parliamentary Party in the Lok Sabha
Not always true: a PM from the Rajya Sabha (e.g. Manmohan Singh) does not lead the party in the Lok Sabha.

points: Appointment is constitutional; majority support is a political condition.

PYQ-POL-F18ACCE39FB9.lead: Option 1: a non-member can be appointed PM but must become a member of either House within six months.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Need not be an MP; must join either House within six months
Correct as per Article 75(5), which covers the PM too.
Must join the Lok Sabha within six months
Too narrow; membership of the Rajya Sabha is also enough.
Must be a member of either House
Too strict; a non-member can be appointed for six months.
Must be a member of the Lok Sabha
Too strict; neither prior membership nor Lok Sabha membership is required.

points: Unlike India, in Britain the PM should definitely be a member of the House of Commons.
Example: Manmohan Singh was PM as a Rajya Sabha member.

PYQ-POL-F2C024486B4F.lead: Option 3: the Cabinet form of government is a device of parliamentary democracy to make the government collectively responsible to the people through their elected House.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Minimising criticism of the government
Wrong; parliamentary government actually exposes the government to constant criticism through questions and motions.
Speeding up government activities
Speed is not the principle; cabinet government works through deliberation and consultation.
Ensuring collective responsibility of the Government to the people
Correct; under Article 75(3) ministers stand or fall together before the Lok Sabha, which represents the people.
Strengthening the head of government whose hold is declining
Wrong; the system rests on collective, not one-person, power.

points: Collective responsibility is the bedrock principle of parliamentary government.

PYQ-POL-F3215C03B831.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true, statement 2 is false, so the answer is option 4 (1 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Permanent Chairman of Chiefs of Staff Committee
True
The CDS is the permanent Chairman of the Chiefs of Staff Committee.
2. Military command over the three Service Chiefs
False
The CDS does not exercise military command over the three Service Chiefs, including over himself as Chairman.
3. Principal Military Advisor to the Defence Minister on tri-service matters
True
He advises the Defence Minister on all tri-service matters; Service Chiefs still advise on their own Service.

points: Options 1 and 2 wrongly include statement 2; option 3 drops statement 1 and includes statement 2.
General Bipin Rawat became the first CDS on 1 January 2020.

PYQ-POL-F8195A2CE744.lead: Official key: option 2 (Agricultural Policy Wing). But the three wings of the Cabinet Secretariat are Civil, Military and Intelligence, so option 3 (Military Wing) is the correct study answer.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Social Policy Wing
The Cabinet Secretariat has three wings: Civil, Military and Intelligence; there is no Social Policy Wing among them.
Agricultural Policy Wing
Official key, but no such wing exists in the Cabinet Secretariat.
Official key
Military Wing
One of the three wings (Civil, Military, Intelligence); it handles defence matters for Cabinet committees.
✓ (study answer)
Fiscal Policy Wing
Fiscal policy is handled by the Finance Ministry, not by a wing of the Cabinet Secretariat, whose wings are Civil, Military and Intelligence.

points: The Cabinet Secretariat works directly under the Prime Minister and is headed by the Cabinet Secretary.
Hook: 'C-M-I' — Civil, Military, Intelligence.
PYQ-POL-F8195A2CE744.also: Disputed key: the Cabinet Secretariat wings are Civil, Military and Intelligence; there is no Agricultural Policy Wing, so option 3 (Military Wing) is correct.

PYQ-POL-FE3258365574.lead: Official key: option 3. But per Laxmikanth the order is Cabinet Minister > Minister of State > Deputy Minister, so option 3 is false; option 2 (Cabinet Ministers are superior) is the correct study answer.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: All the Ministers are equal
False; the three categories differ in rank, emoluments and political importance.
Cabinet Ministers are superior to other Ministers
True; they head key ministries and are members of the Cabinet (also named in Article 352).
✓ (study answer)
Deputy Ministers above Ministers of State
False; Deputy Ministers come next below Ministers of State and only assist them or Cabinet Ministers.
Official key
Ministers without portfolio are lowest
False; rank depends on category, not on holding a portfolio — the lowest category is the Deputy Minister.

points: Strictly, the Constitution does not classify ministers; the ranks come from convention.
PYQ-POL-FE3258365574.also: Disputed key: Ranks are Cabinet > Minister of State > Deputy Minister (Laxmikanth); Deputy Ministers are not above MoS. Option 2 is the only true statement (Cabinet also named in Art 352).

PYQ-POL-WEB-0A2898.lead: Option 3: the Constitution places no bar on a nominated member being appointed a Union minister.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only Rajya Sabha can have nominated members
False; the Lok Sabha had two nominated Anglo-Indian members (Article 331) until 2020.
Two Anglo-Indians nominated to Rajya Sabha
False; Anglo-Indian nomination was to the Lok Sabha, not the Rajya Sabha.
No bar on a nominated member becoming Union minister
True; any member of either House can be a minister.
Nominated member votes in both President and VP elections
False; nominated members vote in the Vice-Presidential election but not in the Presidential election.

points: The 104th Amendment (2019) ended Anglo-Indian nomination to the Lok Sabha from January 2020.

PYQ-POL-WEB-0DBE3A.lead: Option 4: the Cabinet Mission (1946) proposed an interim government in which all portfolios, including War, would be held by Indian leaders.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Simon Commission
1927–28 commission of only British members to review the 1919 Act; no proposal for an all-Indian Executive Council.
Simla Conference
1945 conference on the Wavell Plan; the Viceroy and Commander-in-Chief (who held War) were to stay British.
Cripps Proposal
1942 offer of dominion status after the war; defence was to remain with the British.
Cabinet Mission
1946 plan; it led to the Interim Government of September 1946 with all portfolios held by Indians.

points: The Interim Government was headed by Nehru as Vice-President of the Executive Council.

PYQ-POL-WEB-10A18E.lead: Option 1: Article 75(1) says the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 75
Appointment of the PM and other ministers.
Article 66
Article 66 deals with the election of the Vice-President, not with the appointment of the PM, which is in Article 75.
Article 62
Time of holding election to fill a vacancy in the office of President.
Article 71
Disputes relating to election of the President or Vice-President.

points: Article 74 creates the Council of Ministers; Article 75 says how its members are appointed.

PYQ-POL-WEB-1FC995.lead: Option 2: Gulzarilal Nanda served only 13 days each time as acting PM (1964 and 1966), the shortest tenure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Atal Bihari Vajpayee
His first term in 1996 lasted 16 days — short, but longer than Nanda's.
Gulzarilal Nanda
Acting PM for 13 days after Nehru's death (1964) and again after Shastri's death (1966).
Chandra Shekhar
About 7 months (November 1990–June 1991).
Charan Singh
About 5.5 months (July 1979–January 1980).

points: Among regular (non-acting) PMs, Vajpayee's 16-day term of 1996 is the shortest.

PYQ-POL-WEB-2EA99A.lead: Option 1: Article 75(1) says the other ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the PM — the only one of these powers written in the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Advising the President on appointing other Ministers
Article 75(1) expressly says other ministers are appointed by the President on the PM's advice, so this power is written into the Constitution.
Allocating business among Ministers
Formally done by the President through rules under Article 77(3); the PM's role is by practice.
Summoning Cabinet meetings
A convention; the Constitution does not say who calls Cabinet meetings.
Transferring a Minister between Departments
A convention of parliamentary government, not written in the Constitution.

points: Many of the PM's powers come from conventions borrowed from Britain, not from the text.

PYQ-POL-WEB-33C9FE.lead: Option 4: in a parliamentary democracy, the President is the nominal head and the Council of Ministers under the PM is the real executive.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Federalism
Division of power between the Centre and the States; it says nothing about who holds executive power inside the Union.
Representative Legislature
A law-making body elected by the people; it answers who makes laws, not who holds executive power.
Universal Adult Franchise
Every citizen aged 18 or above can vote (Article 326); it concerns voting rights.
Parliamentary Democracy
Executive is drawn from and responsible to the legislature; the President acts on ministers' advice (Article 74).

points: Laxmikanth: President = nominal (de jure) executive; PM = real (de facto) executive.

PYQ-POL-WEB-48886E.lead: Neither statement is correct, so the answer is option 4.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. All Cabinet Ministers must be sitting Lok Sabha members
False
Ministers may be from either House; a non-member can also be a minister for six months (Article 75(5)).
2. Cabinet Secretariat works under the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs
False
The Cabinet Secretariat functions directly under the Prime Minister.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 accept at least one false statement.

PYQ-POL-WEB-499F24.lead: Option 3: Chandra Shekhar (November 1990–June 1991, about 7 months) served the shortest tenure among these four.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: H.D. Deve Gowda
June 1996–April 1997, about 10.5 months.
V.P. Singh
December 1989–November 1990, about 11 months.
Chandra Shekhar
About 7 months; he resigned in March 1991 when Congress withdrew support and continued as caretaker till June 1991.
I.K. Gujral
I.K. Gujral held office from April 1997 to March 1998, about 11 months, which is longer than Chandra Shekhar's roughly seven months.

points: Gujral's term technically included a caretaker period after the Lok Sabha was dissolved in December 1997.

PYQ-POL-WEB-4C3B19.lead: Option 4 — A is false but R is true.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
False
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible only to the Lok Sabha, not to the Rajya Sabha (Article 75(3)).
R
True
Members of either House, Lok Sabha or Rajya Sabha, can be Union ministers.
