Option 1 fails: A is false.
Option 2 fails: A is false.
Option 3 fails: A is false.

PYQ-POL-WEB-4D3450.lead: Option 1: 15%. The 91st Amendment (2003) caps the Council of Ministers at 15% of the total strength of the House, including the Prime Minister.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct: 15% is the only ceiling written in the Constitution, in Article 75(1A) for the Union and Article 164(1A) for the States.
Wrong: 20% does not appear anywhere in the Constitution as a limit on ministers.
Wrong: 12 is the minimum number of ministers in a State (Article 164(1A)), not a percentage cap.
Wrong: 10% is not a ceiling on ministers; it is a common distractor with no constitutional basis.

points: Caution: the stem says 'Assembly of States' (Rajya Sabha), but the 15% is actually counted on Lok Sabha strength for the Union (Article 75(1A)) and on Legislative Assembly strength for a State.
The 91st Amendment, 2003 added these caps to stop very large ministries.
Memory hook: '15 and 12' - 15% maximum, 12 ministers minimum in a State.

PYQ-POL-WEB-52E60E.lead: Option 2: Jawaharlal Nehru headed the Interim Government of 1946 as Vice-President of the Viceroy's Executive Council.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Rajendra Prasad
Wrong: Dr. Rajendra Prasad was a member holding Food and Agriculture; he later presided over the Constituent Assembly.
2. Jawaharlal Nehru
Correct: Nehru was Vice-President of the Council, holding External Affairs and Commonwealth Relations, and functioned as head of the government.
3. Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
Wrong: Sardar Patel was a member in charge of Home and Information and Broadcasting.
4. Rajagopalachari
Wrong: C. Rajagopalachari was a member in charge of Education and Arts.

points: The Interim Government was formed on 2 September 1946 under the Cabinet Mission Plan.
Its members were members of the Viceroy's Executive Council; the Viceroy remained its formal head.

PYQ-POL-WEB-58DE44.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Ministries/Departments are created by the Prime Minister on the advice of the Cabinet Secretary.
False
Ministries are created and business allocated under rules made by the President (Article 77(3)) on the Prime Minister's advice; the Cabinet Secretary does not advise the PM to create them.
2. Each Ministry is assigned to a Minister by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.
True
The President allocates portfolios under the Allocation of Business Rules, always acting on the Prime Minister's advice (Articles 74 and 77(3)).

points: Option 1 fails because statement 1 is false.
Option 3 fails because it includes the false statement 1.
Option 4 fails because statement 2 is true.

PYQ-POL-WEB-5D137F.lead: Option 4: the 44th Amendment (1978) allows the President to send advice back once for reconsideration.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong: the 39th Amendment (1975) dealt with disputes about the election of the President, Vice-President, PM and Speaker, not ministerial advice.
Wrong: the 40th Amendment is not the provision on the President's power to return advice.
Wrong: the 42nd Amendment (1976) made the advice of ministers binding on the President; it gave no power to send it back.
Correct: the 44th Amendment added a proviso to Article 74(1) letting the President require reconsideration once; he must then act on the advice tendered after reconsideration.

points: Sequence to remember: 42nd made advice binding, 44th softened it by allowing one return.
This is called the President's 'suspensive veto' over ministerial advice.

PYQ-POL-WEB-5DC4E7.lead: Option 3: the Prime Minister has full discretion in choosing his ministers; the President only formally appoints them on his advice.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. is free to choose his ministers only from among those who are members of either House of the Parliament
Wrong: a non-member can also be made a minister, but must enter either House within six months (Article 75(5)).
2. can choose his cabinet colleagues after due counselling by the President of India in this regard
Wrong: the President has no constitutional role in counselling the PM on whom to choose.
3. has full discretion in the choice of persons who are to serve as ministers in his cabinet
Correct: under Article 75(1) the President appoints ministers on the PM's advice, so the real choice is the PM's.
4. has only limited powers in the choice of his cabinet colleagues because of the discretionary power vested with the President of India
Wrong: the President has no discretionary power over the choice of ministers, so the PM's power is not limited by him.

points: Article 75(1): the PM is appointed by the President, and other ministers on the PM's advice.
In practice, coalition partners and party politics may shape the choice, but constitutionally the discretion is the PM's.

PYQ-POL-WEB-663492.lead: Option 3: Article 166 deals with the conduct of business of the Government of a State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 164
Wrong: Article 164 covers other provisions about ministers (appointment by the Governor, collective responsibility, 15% cap).
2. Article 167
Wrong: Article 167 lays down the Chief Minister's duty to communicate decisions and furnish information to the Governor.
3. Article 166
Correct: Article 166 says all executive action is taken in the Governor's name and the Governor makes rules for allocation of business among ministers.
4. Article 177
Wrong: Article 177 gives ministers and the Advocate General the right to speak in the Houses of the State Legislature.

points: The Union counterparts are Article 77 (conduct of business) and Article 78 (PM's duties).
Memory hook: State numbers = Union numbers + 89 (77 to 166, 78 to 167).

PYQ-POL-WEB-6AE8A5.lead: Option 2: six months. A person who is not an MP can be a minister, but must become a member of either House within six consecutive months (Article 75(5)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Six weeks
Wrong: six weeks is the period an ordinance survives after Parliament reassembles, not this limit.
2. Six months
Correct: Article 75(5) allows a non-member minister for six consecutive months; if he does not get elected or nominated, he ceases to be a minister.
3. Nine months
Wrong: nine months is not a period found in this provision.
4. One year
Wrong: one year is not the limit; the Constitution fixes six months.

points: The same rule applies to State ministers under Article 164(4).
A non-member PM is also possible under this rule.

PYQ-POL-WEB-731DA0.lead: Option 2: 15% of Lok Sabha members, including the Prime Minister (Article 75(1A)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 10% of Lok Sabha Members
Wrong: 10% is not the constitutional ceiling.
2. 15% of Lok Sabha Members
Correct: the 91st Amendment, 2003 limited the total number of ministers, including the PM, to 15% of the total strength of the Lok Sabha.
3. 33.33% of Lok Sabha Members
Wrong: one-third (33.33%) is not a limit on ministers in the Constitution.
4. 25% of Lok Sabha Members
Wrong: 25% is not a limit on ministers in the Constitution.

points: The same 91st Amendment put the State cap at 15% of the Assembly, with a minimum of 12 (Article 164(1A)).
It also disqualifies a defector from holding a ministerial post until re-elected.

PYQ-POL-WEB-8E86CF.lead: Option 3 (official): representation of all parts of India in the Council of Ministers is followed only as a convention; it is not written in the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The finance minister is to be a Member of the Lower House
Wrong: no rule or settled convention requires the Finance Minister to sit in the Lok Sabha; several Finance Ministers have been Rajya Sabha members.
2. The Prime Minister has to resign if he loses majority in the Lower House

Arguably also unwritten: the Constitution only says the ministry is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)); resignation on losing majority follows from that, so examiners treat it as a constitutional consequence.
3. All the parts of India are to be represented in the Council of Ministers
Correct: giving every region and major group a place in the ministry is a political convention with no constitutional text behind it.

4. In the event of both the President and the Vice-president demitting office simultaneously before the end of their tenure the Speaker of the Lower House of the Parliament will officiate as the President
Wrong: if both offices are vacant, the Chief Justice of India (not the Speaker) acts as President, under the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969.

points: A convention is an unwritten practice that is regularly followed; it is not enforceable in court.
Option 2 is the reason this key is debated, but option 3 is the purest example of a convention, so it is kept.
PYQ-POL-WEB-8E86CF.also: Disputed key: option 2 is also not written in the Constitution in so many words; option 3 is kept as the study answer.

PYQ-POL-WEB-8FF104.lead: Option 3: ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister (Article 75(1)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. According to the Constitution of India, the total number of members of the Council of Ministers cannot exceed 20% of the total number of Members of the House of the People
Wrong: the ceiling is 15%, not 20%, of the Lok Sabha (Article 75(1A)).
2. The rank of the different Ministers is determined by the President
Wrong: the rank of ministers (Cabinet, Minister of State, Deputy) is decided by the Prime Minister, not by the President.
3. The Ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister
Correct: Article 75(1) says the President appoints other ministers on the PM's advice.
4. Only a member of either House of Parliament can be appointed as a Minister
Wrong: a non-member can be appointed but must become an MP within six months (Article 75(5)).

points: The President acts only formally; the real choice and ranking belong to the PM.

PYQ-POL-WEB-B75364.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true and 2 is false, so the answer is option 4 (1 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Nehru was in his fourth term as PM when he died.
True
Nehru became PM in 1947 and was re-appointed after the 1952, 1957 and 1962 elections, so he was in his fourth term when he died on 27 May 1964.
2. Nehru represented Rae Bareli as an MP.
False
Nehru represented Phulpur (Allahabad) in Uttar Pradesh; Rae Bareli was represented by Feroze Gandhi and later Indira Gandhi.
3. The first non-Congress PM took office in 1977.
True
Morarji Desai of the Janata Party became PM in March 1977, the first PM not from the Congress.

points: Option 1 fails because it includes the false statement 2.
Option 2 fails because it leaves out the true statement 1.
Option 3 fails because it leaves out the true statement 3.
PYQ-POL-WEB-B75364.also: Nehru died in office on 27 May 1964.

PYQ-POL-WEB-BD5F8D.lead: Option 4 is the wrong statement: even during a National Emergency, the President has no discretion and must act on ministerial advice.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A Council of Ministers must always exist to advise the President.
True: Article 74(1) requires a Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President at all times.
2. Even after the dissolution of Lok Sabha, Council of Ministers exists to advise the President.
True: ministers continue after Lok Sabha dissolution until a new government is formed.
3. Even after the resignation of the Prime Minister, Council of Ministers exists to advise the President.
True: the outgoing ministry continues as caretaker until a new PM is sworn in.
4. During the period of National Emergency, the President acquires discretionary powers, and can take independent decisions.
False (answer): the 42nd Amendment (1976) made ministerial advice binding, even during a National Emergency.

points: U.N.R. Rao (1971): the Council of Ministers must always exist.

PYQ-POL-WEB-C909FB.lead: All three statements are correct, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Rajya Sabha members sit on PAC and COPU, but the Estimates Committee is wholly from the Lok Sabha.
True
PAC and the Committee on Public Undertakings each have 15 Lok Sabha and 7 Rajya Sabha members, while all 30 Estimates Committee members are from the Lok Sabha.
2. The Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs works under the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs.
True
The Ministry functions under the overall direction of the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs, which plans the government's business in Parliament.
3. The Minister of Parliamentary Affairs nominates MPs to government committees, councils and boards.
True
Nominating MPs to bodies set up by various ministries is one of the listed functions of the Ministry of Parliamentary Affairs.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out one correct statement, so they fail.
PYQ-POL-WEB-C909FB.also: Estimates Committee: 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, elected every year by proportional representation.

PYQ-POL-WEB-D030C1.lead: Option 1: Article 164(2) makes the State Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Legislative Assembly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct: Article 164 deals with ministers in the States, and clause (2) states collective responsibility to the Assembly.
Wrong: Article 163 says there shall be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the Governor.
Wrong: Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor.
Wrong: Article 169 deals with abolition or creation of Legislative Councils.

points: Union counterpart: Article 75(3), responsibility to the Lok Sabha.
Collective responsibility means the whole ministry resigns if the Assembly passes a no-confidence motion.
PYQ-POL-WEB-D030C1.also: Union counterpart: Article 75(3), responsibility to the Lok Sabha.

PYQ-POL-WEB-EA4DA0.lead: Option 1: a Rajya Sabha member cannot vote in the Lok Sabha, so such a PM cannot vote on a no-confidence motion, which is moved only in the Lok Sabha.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. he will not be able to vote in his favour in the event of a no confidence motion
Correct: ministers may speak in either House but may vote only in the House of which they are members (Article 88).
2. he will not be able to speak on the Budget in the Lower House
Wrong: under Article 88 every minister can speak in both Houses, including on the Budget in the Lok Sabha.
3. he can make statements only on the Upper House
Wrong: he can make statements in both Houses, not only the Upper House.
4. he has to become a member of the Lower House within six months after being sworn in as the Prime Minister
Wrong: membership of either House is enough; there is no rule to shift to the Lok Sabha within six months.

points: Indira Gandhi (1966) and Manmohan Singh (2004-14) were PMs while in the Rajya Sabha.
PYQ-POL-WEB-EA4DA0.also: Manmohan Singh was PM for 10 years as a Rajya Sabha member.

PYQ-POL-WEB-FC989E.lead: Option 1: the Prime Minister chairs the National Water Resources Council.

What it is / means
Correct?

Correct: the PM is chairman of bodies like NITI Aayog, the Inter-State Council, the National Integration Council and the National Water Resources Council.

Wrong: the Environment and Forests Minister does not head this Council.

Wrong: the Science and Technology Minister has no role as head of this Council.

What it is / means
Correct?

2. the President of India

PYQ-POL-0B6015AE7C94.lead: Official key: Option 2 (Five times). Documented records show three spells, so 'Three times' (option 3) is the better answer.

What it is / means
Correct?

False

True

IV
False

Correct?

A constituency electing several members. India now has only single-member constituencies, so this cannot be the reason.

True. The 1947 Act proclaimed the lapse of British paramountcy, so princely states could choose.
4. Extension of franchise to about 50% of population
False. Extension of franchise was a 1935 Act feature, and it covered only about 14% of the population, not 50%.

points: The 1947 Act created two independent dominions, India and Pakistan, from 15 August 1947.
Options 1 and 4 are features of the 1935 Act; examiners mix the two Acts often.
Universal adult franchise came only with the Constitution in 1950.

PYQ-POL-APK-962B1F.lead: Answer: option 1. The President appoints the Chief Justice of India under Article 124(2).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President
Correct. Article 124(2) says every Supreme Court judge, including the CJI, is appointed by the President.
Prime Minister
The PM advises the President but does not appoint.
Law Minister
The Law Minister starts the process and sends the name, but has no power to appoint.
Supreme Court Collegium
The collegium recommends judges; the CJI post itself goes by seniority, and the appointment is made by the President.

points: The President consults such judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts as he deems necessary.
By convention, upheld in the Second Judges case (1993), the senior-most Supreme Court judge is appointed CJI.
This convention was broken in 1973 (A.N. Ray) and 1977 (M.H. Beg).

PYQ-POL-APK-9B7F35.lead: Answer: option 1. Justice P.N. Bhagwati is credited with introducing Public Interest Litigation (PIL) in India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: P.N. Bhagwati
Correct. Along with Justice V.R. Krishna Iyer he relaxed the rule of locus standi so that any public-spirited person could approach the court for others.
D.Y. Chandrachud
CJI from 2022 to 2024; known for privacy and other later judgments, not for starting PIL.
H.J. Kania
The first Chief Justice of India (1950-51), long before PIL began.
S.H. Kapadia
CJI from 2010 to 2012; not connected with the start of PIL.

points: PIL began in the late 1970s and early 1980s; S.P. Gupta v Union of India (1981) is the key case on relaxed locus standi.
'Locus standi' means the right to bring a case; normally only the affected person can sue, but PIL allows others to sue on behalf of the poor.
Even a letter or postcard to the court can be treated as a petition (epistolary jurisdiction).

PYQ-POL-APK-AAAA9B.lead: Answer: option 1. The Sarkaria Commission on Centre-State relations was set up in 1983 under retired Supreme Court judge R.S. Sarkaria.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Sarkaria Commission
Set up in 1983 on Centre-State relations, headed by Justice R.S. Sarkaria; it reported in 1988 with 247 recommendations.
Punchhi Commission
Also on Centre-State relations, but set up in 2007 under retired CJI M.M. Punchhi.
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
Set up in 1957 on Panchayati Raj; it recommended the three-tier system.
Ashok Mehta Committee
Set up in 1977 on Panchayati Raj; it recommended a two-tier system.

points: Two clues in the stem: 'Centre-State relations' removes options 3 and 4, and '1983' removes option 2.
Laxmikanth notes that the Centre has implemented 180 of Sarkaria's 247 recommendations.

PYQ-POL-APK-AF5892.lead: Answer: option 1. In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Supreme Court held that the Preamble is a part of the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
Held the Preamble is part of the Constitution and laid down the basic structure doctrine.
Minerva Mills (1980)
Held that limited amending power and the balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles are part of the basic structure.
Golaknath (1967)
Held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; later overruled in Kesavananda.
A.K. Gopalan (1950)
Took a narrow view of personal liberty under Article 21; nothing about the Preamble.

points: Kesavananda overruled the Berubari opinion (1960), which had said the Preamble is not part of the Constitution.
Because the Preamble is part of the Constitution, it can be amended under Article 368, but not in a way that damages the basic structure.
PYQ-POL-APK-AF5892.also: In LIC of India case (1995) the Court again said the Preamble is an integral part of the Constitution.

PYQ-POL-APK-CE8E1F.lead: Answer: option 3. Article 32 lets a person move the Supreme Court directly when a Fundamental Right is violated.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 15
Prohibits discrimination on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth; it is a right, not a remedy.
Article 19
Guarantees six freedoms such as speech and movement; again a right, not a remedy.
Article 32
Right to constitutional remedies: the Supreme Court can issue writs to enforce Fundamental Rights, and the person can come directly.
Article 36
Defines 'State' for Part IV (Directive Principles).

points: Dr B.R. Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, so the Supreme Court cannot refuse to hear such a petition merely because the High Court is also available.
High Courts have similar but wider writ power under Article 226.

PYQ-POL-APK-EFAB27.lead: Answer: option 4. Article 137 gives the Supreme Court power to review its own judgments or orders.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 135
Gives the Supreme Court the jurisdiction the Federal Court had under existing law.
Article 136
Special leave to appeal from any court or tribunal, except military tribunals.
Article 141
Law declared by the Supreme Court is binding on all courts in India.
Article 137
Review of judgments or orders by the Supreme Court, subject to law and rules made under Article 145.

points: Review lets the Court correct an error apparent on the record in its own decision.
Memory hook: '137 = Review; 136 = Special leave; 141 = Binding law'.
PYQ-POL-APK-EFAB27.also: The curative petition, a remedy after review is dismissed, was evolved in Rupa Ashok Hurra case (2002).

PYQ-POL-APK-F1A38E.lead: Answer: option 3. India has single citizenship, so dual citizenship is not a feature of the Indian Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Supremacy of Constitution
India has it: the Constitution is the highest law, and any law against it can be struck down.
Independent Judiciary
India has it: security of tenure, fixed salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund and other safeguards keep courts free.
Dual Citizenship
India does NOT have it. Dual citizenship means being a citizen of the country and also of one's State, as in the USA.
Division of Powers
India has it: powers are divided between Centre and States through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists (Seventh Schedule).

points: The question asks which is NOT a feature, so the one India lacks is the answer.
Single citizenship was taken from the British model; every Indian is a citizen of India only.
PYQ-POL-APK-F1A38E.also: Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) is not true dual citizenship; it gives no voting rights.

PYQ-POL-APK-F60F6F.lead: Answer: option 2. On 15 February 2024 the Supreme Court struck down the Electoral Bond Scheme as unconstitutional.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Upheld as constitutional
Wrong. The Court unanimously held the scheme unconstitutional.
Struck down as unconstitutional
Correct. A 5-judge bench held that secret donations violated voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a).
Modified to include more transparency
Wrong. The Court did not modify the scheme; it struck it down completely.
Deferred for further reviews
Wrong. The Court gave a final decision, not a deferral.

points: Case: Association for Democratic Reforms v Union of India (2024), 5-judge Constitution Bench led by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud.
SBI was told to stop issuing bonds and to give donor details to the Election Commission for publication.
Link to earlier rulings: voters' right to know about candidates and parties comes from Article 19(1)(a).

PYQ-POL-APK-FCCC2E.lead: Answer: option 1. Article 50, a Directive Principle, asks the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.
Organise agriculture and animal husbandry on scientific lines and prohibit cow slaughter.
Defines 'State' for the purposes of Part IV.
Early childhood care and education for children below six years (wording after the 86th Amendment, 2002).

points: Article 50 is in Part IV (Directive Principles), so it is not enforceable in courts but is fundamental in governance.
Separation ensures that magistrates who try cases are not under executive officers like the Collector.
Memory hook: 'Fifty = Fair judge' (judiciary separate).

PYQ-POL-B28937D09D32.lead: Answer: option 4. In State of Tamil Nadu v K. Balu (December 2016) the Court used Article 142 to ban liquor shops near highways.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Validity of defamation law
Wrong. In Subramanian Swamy v Union of India (2016) the Court upheld criminal defamation, without Article 142 directions.
Regulatory mechanism for legal profession
Wrong. This was not the 2016 Article 142 case asked about.
Right of disabled people to live with dignity
Wrong. This was not the 2016 Article 142 directions case.
Ban on liquor shops near highways
Correct. The Court banned liquor sale within 500 metres of national and state highways to reduce drunk driving deaths.

points: Article 142 lets the Supreme Court pass any decree or order needed to do 'complete justice' in a case, even where no law covers the point.
Critics call such orders judicial legislation, because they work like a law made by the Court.

PYQ-POL-B2F270CA26E2.lead: Answer: option 4. The Supreme Court is the custodian (guardian) of the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The President of India
Takes an oath to 'preserve, protect and defend' the Constitution, but cannot interpret it with final authority.
The Prime Minister of India
Head of government; bound by the Constitution, but not its custodian.
The Lok Sabha Secretariat
An administrative office of the Lok Sabha; it has no constitutional guardian role.
The Supreme Court of India
The final interpreter and guardian of the Constitution; it strikes down laws that violate it (judicial review).

points: Through judicial review the Court tests laws and executive orders against the Constitution.
Its interpretation binds all courts under Article 141.

PYQ-POL-B3BA406F8E0D.lead: Answer: option 4. S.R. Bommai v Union of India (1994) laid down limits on President's Rule under Article 356.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Golaknath (1967)
Held Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights; not about President's Rule.
Maneka Gandhi (1978)
Gave a wide meaning to 'personal liberty' in Article 21; not about President's Rule.
Minerva Mills (1980)
Held limited amending power and the FR-DPSP balance are basic structure; not about President's Rule.
S.R. Bommai (1994)
Held that a proclamation under Article 356 is open to judicial review and the majority must be tested on the floor of the House.

points: Bommai also held that secularism is a basic feature, and that the Assembly should not be dissolved until Parliament approves the proclamation.
After Bommai, misuse of Article 356 reduced sharply.

PYQ-POL-BBBE20AD62C2.lead: Answer: option 1. Article 140 is titled 'Ancillary powers of Supreme Court'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 140
Parliament may give the Supreme Court supplementary powers needed to use its jurisdiction more effectively.
Article 138
Enlargement of the Supreme Court's jurisdiction on Union List matters by Parliament.
Article 143
Advisory jurisdiction: President can seek the Court's opinion.
Article 150
Form of accounts of the Union and States, prescribed on the CAG's advice; not about the Supreme Court.

points: 'Ancillary' means helping or supporting: these are extra powers that help the Court use its existing jurisdiction.
Difference: Article 138 adds new subjects to the Court's jurisdiction; Article 140 adds helper powers.

PYQ-POL-C2EACC028FD5.lead: Answer: option 3. The main function of original jurisdiction (Article 131) is to settle disputes between the Centre and States.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: To review state laws
This is judicial review, a separate power exercised in many kinds of cases, not specially the original jurisdiction.
To handle criminal appeals
Criminal appeals come under appellate jurisdiction (Article 134).
To settle disputes between Centre and States
Correct. Federal disputes start directly in the Supreme Court and only it can decide them.
To hear election disputes
Election petitions for Parliament and State Legislatures go first to the High Courts; the Supreme Court hears appeals.

points: 'Original' means the case begins in the Supreme Court; 'appellate' means it comes from a lower court.
Federal disputes include Centre vs States and State vs State.

PYQ-POL-C749400FFD5D.lead: Answer: option 3. The 2007 interim stay on the 27% OBC quota in central educational institutions came on Ashoka Kumar Thakur's petition.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Ravichandran
Not the petitioner in the 2007 OBC education quota case.
Indra Sawhney
The 1992 Mandal case on OBC reservation in government jobs; it fixed the 50% ceiling and creamy layer.
Ashoka Kumar Thakur
Challenged the Central Educational Institutions (Reservation in Admission) Act, 2006; the Court stayed the OBC quota in March 2007.
Keshavananda
The 1973 basic structure case; not about OBC reservation.

points: In April 2008 the Court finally upheld the 27% OBC quota but excluded the creamy layer.
Clue: the stem says 'educational institutions', which rules out Indra Sawhney (jobs).

PYQ-POL-CA80E32ED25C.lead: Official key: option 1 (A and B only). But statements C and D are also true, so option 4 (A, B, C and D) is the better answer.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. NJAC made by the 99th Constitutional Amendment
True
The 99th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2014 and the NJAC Act, 2014 created the NJAC.
B. Struck down by the Supreme Court in 2015
True
In the Fourth Judges case (16 October 2015) the Court held both the amendment and the Act void by 4:1.
C. Six-member body including the CJI
True
Members: the CJI (chair), two senior-most Supreme Court judges, the Union Law Minister and two eminent persons.
D. Collegium system revived after NJAC was struck down
True
Laxmikanth: 'Consequently, the earlier collegium system became operative again.'

points: Option 1 (official) leaves out C and D, which are both true.
Option 2 leaves out D; option 3 leaves out C.
The Court struck down NJAC because it said the Law Minister and eminent persons could affect judicial independence.
PYQ-POL-CA80E32ED25C.also: Disputed key: the official key is option 1 (A and B only), but statements C and D are also true — NJAC had 6 members (CJI, 2 senior SC judges, Law Minister, 2 eminent persons) and the collegium became operative again after the 2015 verdict.

PYQ-POL-D3794AD563FB.lead: Answer: option 2. Disputes between States start directly in the Supreme Court under Article 131, which is its original jurisdiction.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Appellate Jurisdiction
The Court hears an APPEAL against a judgment of a lower court, mostly a High Court; a State-State dispute does not come from a lower court.
Original Jurisdiction
The case STARTS in the Supreme Court itself; for federal disputes it is exclusive (Article 131).
Advisory Jurisdiction
The Court gives an OPINION when the President asks (Article 143); there are no contesting parties.
Writ Jurisdiction
The Court issues writs to enforce Fundamental Rights (Article 32); this concerns citizens, not States.

points: 'Exclusive' means no other court can decide it; 'original' means it is heard first here, not by way of appeal.
The dispute must involve a legal right; political questions are excluded.
PYQ-POL-D3794AD563FB.also: Inter-State river water disputes are excluded (Article 262).

PYQ-POL-D7157D034932.lead: Statement A is true and B is false, so the answer is option 1 (A only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. Covers disputes between States, or Union and States
True
Article 131 gives the Supreme Court exclusive original jurisdiction over such federal disputes.
B. Original jurisdiction means cases first started in other courts
False
It is the opposite: original means the case begins in the Supreme Court itself. Cases that start elsewhere and come up later are appellate.

points: Option 2 (B only) and option 3 (Both) wrongly accept B.
Option 4 (Neither) wrongly rejects A.
Memory hook: original = 'origin' is in the Supreme Court.

PYQ-POL-DA0FFA0E5DCD.lead: Answer: option 3. Original jurisdiction lets the Supreme Court settle disputes between the Union and the States (Article 131).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Reviews decisions of tribunals
Hearing appeals against tribunal decisions is appellate jurisdiction (e.g. special leave under Article 136), not original.
Grants pardons to criminals
Courts do not grant pardons; the President (Article 72) and the Governor (Article 161) do.
Settles disputes between Union and States
Correct. These federal disputes begin in the Supreme Court and only it can decide them.
Deals only with criminal appeals
Wrong twice: criminal appeals are appellate, and the Court also hears civil and constitutional appeals.

points: Key difference: original = the case begins in the Supreme Court; appellate = it comes from a lower court.
The word 'only' in option 4 is a common trap; the Supreme Court's work is never limited to one type of case.

PYQ-POL-DCB43019D8A0.lead: Answer: option 1. The Supreme Court is called the guardian of the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Supreme Court
The final interpreter and guardian of the Constitution; its rulings bind all courts (Article 141).
High Court
Also does judicial review in its State, but its decisions can be appealed to the Supreme Court, so it is not the final guardian.
District Court
Decides ordinary civil and criminal cases in a district; it has no power of constitutional review like the higher courts.
Lok Adalat
A forum for settling disputes by compromise under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987; not a constitutional court.

points: It can strike down laws and executive actions that violate the Constitution (judicial review).
It is also called the guarantor of Fundamental Rights because of Article 32.

PYQ-POL-E198AFE11F5A.lead: Answer: option 2. Justice M. Fathima Beevi became the first woman judge of the Supreme Court in 1989.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Sujata Manohar
Second woman judge of the Supreme Court (1994).
Fathima Beevi
First woman judge of the Supreme Court (1989); she later became Governor of Tamil Nadu.
Ruma Pal
Third woman judge of the Supreme Court (2000).
Indu Malhotra
First woman appointed to the Supreme Court directly from the Bar (2018), not the first woman judge.

points: Fathima Beevi was from Kerala and was appointed after retiring from the Kerala High Court.
Trap: 'first woman directly from the Bar' (Indu Malhotra) is a different record.

PYQ-POL-E1C39ECFB81E.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true and 2 and 4 are false, so the answer is option 1 (1 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. President must consult the CJI while appointing SC judges
True
Under Article 124(2) consultation with the CJI is obligatory for appointing any judge other than the CJI.
2. SC judges can be removed by the CJI only
False
Removal is by the President after Parliament passes an address by special majority (Article 124(4)); the CJI has no power to remove.
3. Salaries charged on the Consolidated Fund, not voted
True
Salaries and expenses of the Supreme Court are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India; Parliament can discuss but not vote on them.
4. SC staff appointed by Government after consulting CJI
False
The CJI himself appoints the officers and servants of the Court without executive interference (Article 146).

points: Option 2 (3 and 4) and option 3 (4 only) wrongly accept statement 4.
Option 4 (all) wrongly accepts statements 2 and 4.
Each true statement protects independence: consultation limits the executive, charged salaries protect from budget pressure.
PYQ-POL-E1C39ECFB81E.also: Judges' salaries cannot be reduced to their disadvantage after appointment, except during a financial emergency.

PYQ-POL-E65ABD744601.lead: Answer: option 4. In Vishaka v State of Rajasthan (1997) the Court laid down guidelines to prevent sexual harassment of women at the workplace.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Illegal detentions
Guidelines on arrest and detention came in D.K. Basu v State of West Bengal (1996), not Vishaka.
Torture in police custody
Also covered by D.K. Basu (1996), not Vishaka.
Atrocities against SC/STs
Covered by the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989, not by Vishaka.
Sexual harassment of working women at workplaces
Correct. The Vishaka guidelines required every employer to prevent and redress sexual harassment.

points: The Court used Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21 and the international convention CEDAW, since there was no law then.
The guidelines were later replaced by the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (POSH) Act, 2013.

PYQ-POL-EA1094A75D21.lead: Answer: option 4. Under Article 140 Parliament, by law, can confer ancillary powers on the Supreme Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President of India
The President cannot confer such powers on his own; Article 140 gives this power to Parliament.
Law Commission of India
An advisory body that only recommends legal reforms; it cannot give powers to the Court.
Minister of Law and Justice
A member of the executive; he can propose a Bill but cannot confer powers himself.
Parliament of India
Correct. Article 140 lets Parliament give supplementary powers to help the Court use its jurisdiction.

points: Ancillary powers are helper powers, not new subjects of jurisdiction.
Pattern: Parliament can add to the Supreme Court's powers (Articles 138, 139, 140) but cannot curtail them.
PYQ-POL-EA1094A75D21.also: Parliament can also enlarge the Court's jurisdiction on Union List matters (Article 138).

PYQ-POL-WEB-029698.lead: Answer: option 2. Under Article 124(4) a Supreme Court judge can be removed only for proved misbehaviour or incapacity.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Disrespect of the Constitution
Not a ground of removal. The Constitution names only two grounds, and this vague phrase is not one of them.
Proven misbehaviour or incapacity
These are the only two grounds. Misbehaviour means wrong conduct; incapacity means inability to work (for example, illness). Both must be proved by an inquiry committee.
Murder charges
A criminal charge by itself is not a ground. Only misbehaviour that is proved through the inquiry can lead to removal.
Lack of knowledge
Not a ground in the Constitution; judges are not removed for lacking knowledge.

points: A removal motion needs 100 Lok Sabha or 50 Rajya Sabha members' signatures; a three-member committee then inquires (Judges Enquiry Act, 1968).
Each House must pass it by special majority (majority of total membership and two-thirds present and voting); then the President orders removal.
The word 'proved' is key: an accusation alone is never enough.
PYQ-POL-WEB-029698.also: No Supreme Court judge has been removed so far; the first impeachment attempt was against Justice V. Ramaswami (1991-93).

PYQ-POL-WEB-030949.lead: Answer: option 3. Under Article 124(3) a distinguished jurist, in the President's opinion, can be appointed a Supreme Court judge.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Advocate for 10 years in any court
Wrong. The rule is 10 years as an advocate of a High Court (or High Courts in succession), not of any court.
High Court judge for 3 years
Wrong. The requirement is 5 years as a High Court judge.
Distinguished jurist in the President's opinion
Correct. This is one of the three alternative qualifications in Article 124(3).
Judicial office for 15 years
Wrong. This is not a qualification for the Supreme Court.

points: The person must also be a citizen of India.
Memory hook: 5 (HC judge) - 10 (HC advocate) - jurist.
PYQ-POL-WEB-030949.also: The Constitution fixes no minimum age for appointment as a Supreme Court judge.

PYQ-POL-WEB-05609E.lead: Both statements were correct when asked, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Judges (Inquiry) Bill, 2006 proposed a Judicial Council for complaints
True
The 2006 Bill proposed a National Judicial Council to receive and inquire into complaints against Supreme Court judges and High Court Chief Justices and judges.
2. Under the DV Act, 2005, a woman can petition a First Class Judicial Magistrate
True
An aggrieved woman applies to the Magistrate under the Act, and 'Magistrate' there means a Judicial Magistrate of the First Class.

points: Options 1 and 2 each reject one true statement; option 4 rejects both.
The 2006 Bill lapsed and was never enacted; complaints about judges are still dealt with under the in-house procedure and the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968.

PYQ-POL-WEB-0BE156.lead: Answer (as per the exam): option 1. When this question was set, the Supreme Court had the Chief Justice and not more than 33 other judges.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct at exam time. The 2019 Amendment Act raised the strength to 34 (CJI plus 33).
This is the 2026 TOTAL strength including the CJI, not the number of 'other judges'.
Parliament has never fixed 35 as the number of other judges; after the 2019 Act the figure is 33 plus the CJI.
This is the 2026 figure: after the 2026 amendment the Court has the CJI plus 37 other judges. It was not the answer when this question was asked.

points: Original strength was CJI plus 7; Parliament raised other judges to 10 (1956), 13 (1960), 17 (1977), 25 (1986), 30 (2008), 33 (2019).
Parliament changes this number by an ordinary law under Article 124(1).
Read the stem carefully: 'other judges' excludes the CJI, so 34 total means 33 others.
PYQ-POL-WEB-0BE156.also: 2026 update: after an ordinance in May 2026, Parliament passed the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Bill, 2026, raising the strength to 38 (CJI plus 37). In a new exam, 37 would be the answer.

PYQ-POL-WEB-0D7DBD.lead: Answer: option 1. In Swaraj Abhiyan v Union of India (2016) the Supreme Court issued guidelines on drought management.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Swaraj Abhiyan v Union of India
Correct. The Court directed the Centre to update the Drought Management Manual and set up a national disaster mitigation fund.
PUCL v Union of India
Known for the right to food (mid-day meals, ration) and telephone tapping cases, not 2016 drought guidelines.
Common Cause v Union of India
Known for passive euthanasia and living wills (2018).
Mahipal Singh Rana v State of UP
A 2016 case on contempt by an advocate and regulation of the legal profession.

points: The Court linked drought relief to the right to life under Article 21.

PYQ-POL-WEB-1973B6.lead: Option 2: the salaries and allowances of Supreme Court judges are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India, so Parliament cannot vote them down.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Judicial fund of India
Wrong: there is no fund called the 'Judicial Fund of India'; the Constitution creates only the Consolidated Fund, the Contingency Fund and the Public Account.
2. Consolidated fund of India
Correct: Article 112(3) lists judges' salaries as 'charged' expenditure on the Consolidated Fund of India; Parliament may discuss it but does not vote on it.
3. Contingent fund of India
Wrong: the Contingency Fund (Article 267) is only an imprest for urgent, unforeseen spending, later made good from the Consolidated Fund; regular salaries are not paid from it.
4. Government Salaries fund
Wrong: no 'Government Salaries Fund' exists in the Constitution; this option is invented.

points: Charging the salaries on the Consolidated Fund protects judicial independence, because the legislature cannot cut them by refusing a vote.
Under Article 125, salaries cannot be reduced to a judge's disadvantage after appointment, except during a Financial Emergency (Article 360).
PYQ-POL-WEB-1973B6.also: High Court judges' salaries are charged on the State's Consolidated Fund; their pensions are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

PYQ-POL-WEB-1C3A25.lead: Option 3: legislators can either pass a fresh law that removes the basis of the judgment, or amend the Constitution to get around it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Pass a law challenging the decision
Partly right but incomplete: Parliament can pass a law that cures the defect the Court found (it cannot simply overrule the judgment), but this is only one of the two routes.
2. Pass a constitutional amendment that circumvents the decision
Partly right but incomplete: a constitutional amendment under Article 368 can circumvent a ruling (for example, the 1st Amendment after Champakam Dorairajan), but this too is only one route.
3. Both are options, pass a constitutional amendment that circumvents the decision or pass a law challenging the decision
Correct: both routes are available, so the option that combines them is the full answer.
4. No options are there before the legislators and executives
Wrong: the legislature is not helpless; it has both the law-making and the amending power, subject to judicial review and the basic structure.

points: A new law must remove the legal basis of the judgment; a bare law saying 'the judgment shall not apply' is struck down.
Amendments are themselves limited by the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).

PYQ-POL-WEB-1EE3FA.lead: Option 3: under Article 124(2) every Supreme Court judge, including the Chief Justice, is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. the Supreme Court Collegium
Wrong: the collegium (CJI and four senior-most judges) only recommends names; the formal appointing authority is the President.
2. the Cabinet
Wrong: the Cabinet advises the President, but the Constitution gives the appointment power to the President, not to the Cabinet.
3. the President of India
Correct: Article 124(2) says every judge shall be appointed by the President after consultation with such judges as he deems necessary.
4. the Lok Sabha

Created village courts, not Lok Adalats.

points: Before 1987 Lok Adalats were voluntary with no legal backing.
No appeal lies against a Lok Adalat award.

PYQ-POL-53B97BDCC22A.lead: Official key Option 1: Justice B.S. Chauhan chaired the 21st Law Commission (2015–2018).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Justice B.S. Chauhan
Justice B.S. Chauhan, a former Supreme Court judge, chaired the 21st Law Commission (2015–18), so this is correct.
Justice A.P. Shah
Chairman of the 20th Law Commission (after D.K. Jain).
Justice D.K. Jain
First chairman of the 20th Law Commission.
Justice Madan B. Lokur
A former Supreme Court judge, not a chairman of the 20th or 21st Commission.

points: Options 2 and 3 both belong to the 20th Commission — a common trap.
PYQ-POL-53B97BDCC22A.also: Justice Ritu Raj Awasthi chaired the 22nd Law Commission.

PYQ-POL-67AF0A4A026A.lead: Option 3: Articles 323A and 323B (Part XIV-A) deal with tribunals.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Emergency provisions
These are in Part XVIII, Articles 352–360, not 323A/323B.
Distribution of tax revenues
Distribution of tax revenues is in Part XII (Articles 268–281), while Articles 323A and 323B deal with tribunals.
Tribunals
Part XIV-A: Article 323A (administrative tribunals) and 323B (tribunals for other matters).
Scheduled Tribes
STs are dealt with by Article 342 and the Fifth and Sixth Schedules, not Part XIV-A.

points: Part XIV-A was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

PYQ-POL-APK-1E852F.lead: Official key Option 1: the Legal Services Authorities Act was passed in 1987.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

No legal-services law was passed then; Article 39A itself came only in 1976.

1978 is the year of the 44th Amendment; it has nothing to do with legal services.

points: The Act came into force on 9 November 1995.
PYQ-POL-APK-1E852F.also: Free legal aid is in Article 39A (42nd Amendment, 1976).

PYQ-POL-APK-53C5ED.lead: Official key Option 3: the Armed Forces Tribunal has no Regional Bench at Bhopal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Jabalpur
Jabalpur has an AFT Regional Bench serving Madhya Pradesh.
Guwahati
Guwahati has an AFT Regional Bench serving the North-East.
Bhopal
Bhopal has no AFT Regional Bench; it is a seat of the National Green Tribunal instead.
Jaipur
Jaipur has an AFT Regional Bench serving Rajasthan.

points: Trap: Bhopal is a seat of the NGT, not AFT.
PYQ-POL-APK-53C5ED.also: AFT was set up under the Armed Forces Tribunal Act, 2007.

PYQ-POL-BE07B677BE24.lead: Option 2: CAT decides recruitment and service matters of public servants.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: National Green Tribunal
Set up under the NGT Act, 2010 for environmental cases, not service matters.
Central Administrative Tribunal
Set up under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 (Article 323A) for recruitment and service matters of public servants.
Armed Forces Tribunal
Handles service matters of members of the armed forces only, under the AFT Act, 2007.
Income Tax Appellate Tribunal
Hears appeals in income-tax matters, a taxation subject, not service disputes.

points: CAT was set up in 1985 under Article 323A.

PYQ-POL-E7355730E6A9.lead: Option 1: Article 323B permits tribunals for matters such as taxation, land reforms and labour disputes.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Taxation, land reforms, labour disputes
True: these are among the matters listed in Article 323B.
Only for the armed forces
False: Article 323B has a wide list of civil matters; armed forces tribunals are not its subject.
Exclusively environmental matters
False: environment is not a 323B entry; the NGT was made under a separate 2010 Act.
States set up tribunals for local government
False: local government is not a 323B entry, and both Parliament and States hold this power.

points: Both Parliament and State legislatures can act under 323B.
PYQ-POL-E7355730E6A9.also: Article 323A is only for service matters and only Parliament.

PYQ-POL-FAA410DAA1A3.lead: Third-party key Option 2: only statement 2 is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Only civil, not criminal cases
False
LX: a Gram Nyayalaya exercises the powers of both criminal and civil courts and follows summary procedure in criminal trials.
2. Social activists as mediators/conciliators
True
The Act tells the Gram Nyayalaya to settle disputes by conciliation using appointed conciliators, who can include local social workers.

points: Option 1 selects only the false statement.
Option 3 wrongly includes statement 1; Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 2.
A Gram Nyayalaya is presided over by a Nyayadhikari, a judicial officer appointed by the State in consultation with the High Court.

PYQ-POL-WEB-287756.lead: Option 4: the Charter Act, 1833 led to the first Law Commission (1834).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Government of India Act, 1858
It transferred the rule of India from the Company to the Crown; it did not create a Law Commission.
Indian Councils Act, 1861
It began associating Indians with law-making and gave the Viceroy ordinance power; no Law Commission.
Regulating Act, 1773
It provided for a Supreme Court at Calcutta and made the Governor of Bengal Governor-General; no Law Commission.
Charter Act, 1833
It provided for codification of laws, leading to the first Law Commission in 1834.

points: The first Law Commission was chaired by Lord Macaulay.
It drafted the Indian Penal Code, which was enacted in 1860.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. CAT set up under PM Lal Bahadur Shastri
False
CAT came in 1985 when Rajiv Gandhi was PM; Shastri was PM in 1964–66, before Article 323A (1976) even existed.
2. Members from judicial and administrative streams
True
LX states CAT members are drawn from both judicial and administrative streams.

points: Option 1 selects only the false statement 1.
Option 3 wrongly includes statement 1; Option 4 wrongly rejects the true statement 2.

PYQ-POL-WEB-4F1817.lead: Official key Option 1: only statement I is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Set up under the NGT Act, 2010
True
The National Green Tribunal was established under the National Green Tribunal Act, 2010.
II. Bound by CPC, 1908
False
Like CAT, the NGT is not bound by the CPC; it is guided by the principles of natural justice.
III. Six places of sitting
False
It sits at five places: New Delhi (principal), Bhopal, Pune, Kolkata and Chennai.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 all include a false statement (II or III).
PYQ-POL-WEB-4F1817.also: NGT must try to dispose of cases within six months.

PYQ-POL-WEB-F1F619.lead: Option 4: all three statements are wrong, so 'none of the above' is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only pre-litigation, not pending matters
False: LX says a Lok Adalat deals with both cases pending before any court and disputes at pre-litigation stage.
Only civil, not criminal matters
False: compoundable criminal matters are also settled; only non-compoundable offences are barred.
Only serving or retired judicial officers
False: a Lok Adalat has judicial officers 'and other persons' — usually a lawyer and a social worker.
None of the above is correct
True, because statements 1, 2 and 3 are all false.

points: Each wrong statement uses the word 'only' — a warning sign; the real rules are wider.
Key limit to remember: no jurisdiction over non-compoundable offences.

PYQ-POL-04F9743E9273.lead: Option 1 (official key): The 76th Amendment, 1994 placed the Tamil Nadu reservation Act (69 per cent) in the Ninth Schedule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: IX
Correct. The Ninth Schedule, protected by Article 31B, shields listed laws from Fundamental Rights challenges.
X
Wrong. The Tenth Schedule contains the anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985).
XI
Wrong. The Eleventh Schedule lists 29 subjects for Panchayats (73rd Amendment, 1992).
XII
Wrong. The Twelfth Schedule lists 18 subjects for Municipalities (74th Amendment, 1992).

points: The 69% figure crossed the 50% ceiling of Indra Sawhney (1992), which is why protection was sought.
As a post-24 April 1973 insertion, it remains open to basic-structure review (I.R. Coelho, 2007).

PYQ-POL-081155950B58.lead: Option 1 (official key): Laxmikanth says the scope of judicial review in India is narrower than in the USA.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Narrower than the USA
True. India follows 'procedure established by law', so courts mainly test whether a law is within power; the US 'due process of law' lets courts also test reasonableness.
Lies with Supreme Court only
False. High Courts also have judicial review power, for example under Article 226.
The word appears in Article 134
False. The phrase 'judicial review' is not used anywhere in the Constitution; Article 134 deals with criminal appeals.
The Constitution defines the term
False. The Constitution neither uses nor defines the term; the power is implied from Articles 13, 32, 226 and others.

points: Because of 'due process', critics called the US Supreme Court a 'third chamber' of the legislature.
India is a synthesis of American judicial supremacy and British parliamentary supremacy.

PYQ-POL-121EB5644B06.lead: Option 4 (official key): The Constitution gives the power of judicial review to both the Supreme Court and the High Courts.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Explicitly mentioned in Article 13
False. Article 13 makes inconsistent laws void, but the phrase 'judicial review' is not used anywhere in the Constitution.
Only after approval by Parliament
False. Courts review laws already in force on a challenge; no prior approval of Parliament is needed.
Only the Supreme Court
False. High Courts can also declare laws unconstitutional.
Both SC and HCs can strike down laws
True. This is Laxmikanth's statement of the Indian position.

points: Points 1 and 3 are common traps: the power is explicit in effect but the term itself is absent.
PYQ-POL-121EB5644B06.also: Supreme Court acts via Article 32; High Courts via Article 226.

PYQ-POL-2B489090B8F2.lead: Option 1 (official key): Judicial review means the power of the judiciary to pronounce on the constitutionality of laws and executive orders.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Pronounce on constitutionality of laws and executive orders
Correct. This matches Laxmikanth's definition.
Question the wisdom of laws
Wrong. Indian courts test validity, not the wisdom, suitability or policy of a law.
Review all Bills before assent
Wrong. Courts review enacted laws; the only pre-enactment route is an advisory opinion if the President refers a question under Article 143.
Review its own earlier judgments
Wrong. That is the Supreme Court's review power under Article 137, a different concept.

points: Keep three words apart: judicial review (laws/orders), review of judgment (Art. 137), advisory opinion (Art. 143).

PYQ-POL-86AC4EF80897.lead: Only statement (ii) is correct, so option 2 (official key).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: (i) Explicitly mentioned in the Constitution
False
The phrase 'judicial review' is not used anywhere in the Constitution, though Articles 13, 32, 226 and others confer the power.
(ii) Part of the basic structure
True
The Supreme Court has declared judicial review a basic feature (Minerva Mills, 1980; L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).
(iii) Can be curtailed by ordinary law
False
Since it is part of the basic structure, it cannot be curtailed even by a constitutional amendment, much less by an ordinary law.

points: Option 1 wrongly adds (iii).
Option 3 picks only the false statement (i).
Option 4 includes both false statements.

PYQ-POL-A7159FA84112.lead: Option 1: The primary purpose of judicial review is to examine whether laws (and executive orders) are constitutional.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Examine the constitutionality of laws
Correct. Courts declare laws violating the Constitution null and void.
Appoint ministers
Wrong. Ministers are appointed by the President on the Prime Minister's advice (Article 75).
Elect judges
Wrong. Judges in India are appointed by the President, not elected.
Amend the Constitution
Wrong. Amendment is Parliament's power under Article 368; courts only test amendments.

points: Laxmikanth's three reasons for judicial review: supremacy of the Constitution, federal equilibrium, protection of Fundamental Rights.

PYQ-POL-DF48AF800814.lead: Statement I is true and II is false, so option 1 (I only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Limited judicial review
True
Courts can review a pardon decision on limited grounds such as mala fides, arbitrariness or irrelevant considerations (Maru Ram, 1980; Epuru Sudhakar, 2006), but not on its merits.
II. Without Central Government advice
False
Under Article 74 the President exercises the pardoning power on the advice of the Union Council of Ministers, and that advice is binding.

points: Option 2 wrongly accepts II and rejects I.
Option 3 wrongly accepts II.
Option 4 wrongly rejects I.
PYQ-POL-DF48AF800814.also: Pardoning power: President under Article 72, Governor under Article 161.

PYQ-POL-WEB-1E7C32.lead: Option 4 (official key): Judicial review protects the division of powers between Centre and States, which is the core of a federal government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliamentary Government
Wrong. This describes how the executive answers to the legislature; Britain has it without judicial review of Acts.
Presidential Government
Wrong. This is about a President separate from the legislature; it is not what judicial review symbolises.
Unitary Government
Wrong. A unitary system has no power division to guard; the UK has parliamentary sovereignty.
Federal Government
Correct. A federation needs an independent court to keep each government within its powers; Laxmikanth lists 'federal equilibrium' as a purpose.

points: Judicial review began in the federal USA (Marbury v. Madison, 1803).

PYQ-POL-WEB-BA9EAE.lead: Option 2: Article 32 (Supreme Court) and Article 226 (High Courts) give the courts power to issue writs, the clearest expression of judicial review.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 21 and Article 446
Wrong. Article 21 is the right to life and liberty; there is no Article 446 (the Constitution ends at Article 395).
Article 32 and Article 226
Correct. Both empower courts to issue directions, orders or writs against unconstitutional laws and actions.
Article 44 and Article 152
Wrong. Article 44 is the Uniform Civil Code directive; Article 152 defines 'State' for Part VI.
Article 17 and Article 143
Wrong. Article 17 abolishes untouchability; Article 143 is the President's power to seek the Supreme Court's advice.

points: Article 13 is also a key provision, but it is not among these options.

PYQ-POL-4AD5961F5CBE.lead: Option 1 (USA): the concept of judicial activism originated and developed in the USA; the term was coined in 1947 by Arthur Schlesinger Jr.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: USA
Laxmikanth: judicial activism originated and developed in the USA; Arthur Schlesinger Jr., an American historian, coined the term in 1947.
India
India adopted judicial activism later, in the mid-1970s; it did not originate here.
UK
The UK follows parliamentary sovereignty, where courts cannot strike down Acts of Parliament, so activism did not arise there.
USSR
The Soviet system had no independent judiciary with power to check the other organs, so activism could not originate there.

points: In India the foundations were laid by Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer, P.N. Bhagwati, O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai.
Memory hook: judicial review and judicial activism both came from the USA.

PYQ-POL-BA4E93E88A7D.lead: Option 1: judicial activism means the judiciary voluntarily stepping in, on its own initiative where needed, to protect public interest and rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Voluntary intervention in public interest
Activism is the assertive role of courts acting for public interest, often through PIL or suo motu action.
Passive interpretation of laws
Passive interpretation is judicial restraint, the opposite of activism.
Strictly enforcing only existing laws
Applying the law strictly without creative interpretation is also restraint; activism departs from strict precedent.
Declaring elections null and void
Setting aside an election on an election petition is a routine judicial function under election law, not a sign of activism.

points: Laxmikanth: activism forces the legislature and executive to discharge their constitutional duties (LX p437).
PIL is the most popular form of judicial activism (LX p445).

PYQ-POL-0DB21DF7CD3C.lead: Option 2: PIL in India is primarily associated with judicial activism; Laxmikanth calls PIL the most popular form of judicial activism.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Judicial review
The power of courts to test laws against the Constitution; it existed before PIL and is not its main link.
Judicial activism
PIL is an outcome and the most popular manifestation of judicial activism.
Election Commission
The body that conducts elections under Article 324; unrelated to PIL.
Police investigation
Inquiry into crimes by police; it is an executive function, not PIL.

points: PIL relaxed locus standi so courts could act for the poor; this active role is judicial activism.

PYQ-POL-2F4A7E41090F.lead: Option 2 (1979): Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar (1979), on undertrial prisoners, is regarded as the first reported PIL in India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: No PIL milestone is fixed to this year; by then PIL was already established.
Hussainara Khatoon was filed and decided in 1979, leading to the right to speedy trial under Article 21.
Not the year of the first PIL; PIL had already begun before this.
Judicial activism was emerging in the mid-1970s, but the first PIL case is dated 1979.

points: Laxmikanth says PIL was introduced in the early 1980s, when S.P. Gupta (1981) firmly established liberal locus standi; Hussainara (1979) is the earliest case usually cited.

PYQ-POL-4DED62278ED3.lead: A and C are true, B is false, so the answer is option 1 (A and C only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A. PIL is also known as Social Action Litigation
True
Laxmikanth lists Social Action Litigation (SAL) as another name of PIL.
B. PIL is an outcome of judicial restraint
False
Laxmikanth says PIL is an outcome of judicial activism, which is the opposite of restraint.
C. Krishna Iyer and Bhagwati were pioneers
True
Laxmikanth names Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati as the pioneers of PIL.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 fail because each includes the false statement B.

PYQ-POL-WEB-1524E4.lead: Option 1: Justice P.N. Bhagwati was a pioneer of Public Interest Litigation in India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Public Interest Litigation
Bhagwati, with Krishna Iyer, pioneered PIL by accepting letters as writ petitions and widening locus standi.
Judicial review
Judicial review is written into the Constitution (Articles 13, 32, 226); it existed before him.
Fundamental rights
These are in Part III of the Constitution, made by the Constituent Assembly, not pioneered by a judge.
Land reforms
These were laws made by legislatures to end intermediaries and redistribute land, not a judicial innovation.

points: He wrote the S.P. Gupta (1981) judgment that widened locus standi.
PYQ-POL-WEB-1524E4.also: He was Chief Justice of India in 1985-86 (LX list of CJIs).

PYQ-POL-WEB-3008C1.lead: Option 3 (USA): PIL originated and developed in the USA in the 1960s.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Switzerland
Known for direct democracy (referendum, initiative), not for the origin of PIL.
Iceland
Iceland has no link with the origin of PIL, which began in the USA.
USA
In the USA, PIL was designed in the 1960s to give legal representation to unrepresented groups such as the poor, consumers, environmentalists and minorities.
New Zealand
New Zealand has no link with the origin of PIL, which began in the USA.

points: India introduced PIL in the late 1970s and early 1980s.
Memory hook: judicial review, judicial activism and PIL all came from the USA.

PYQ-POL-WEB-3C2D8C.lead: Option 2: PIL is linked with judicial activism; Laxmikanth calls PIL an outcome of judicial activism.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Judicial review
A power of courts to test laws; PIL uses courts but is not defined by this power.
Judicial activism
PIL is the most popular form of judicial activism, where courts act for the poor and voiceless.
Judicial intervention
A general phrase for a court stepping into a matter; it is not the standard textbook link for PIL.
Judicial sanctity
Not a recognised constitutional concept.

points: The standard pairing in exams is PIL = judicial activism.

PYQ-POL-WEB-DBFE6D.lead: Option 3: this is the Supreme Court's definition of Public Interest Litigation, quoted by Laxmikanth.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Judicial Review
A power of courts to test laws and actions against the Constitution, not a kind of legal action.
Judicial Activism
An approach or attitude of courts, not a kind of legal action.
Public Interest Litigation
A legal action for public or general interest where a class of the community has pecuniary or other interest affecting their legal rights; the exact SC definition.
Proxy Litigation
Not a recognised category of constitutional litigation in India.

points: The stem describes a type of case; only PIL is a type of case among the options.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Launched 1952, holistic aim
True
Statement 1 is true: the CDP started on 2 October 1952 with a holistic rural development aim.
2. Top-down, minimal local role
False
Its design aimed at people's participation
3. Infra, education, health, agriculture
True
Statement 3 is true: the CDP was a multi-sector programme covering infrastructure, education, health and agriculture.

points: Options 2 and 4 include false 2; option 1 leaves out true 3.

PYQ-POL-APK-B0DAE2.lead: Balwant Rai Mehta chaired the committee appointed in January 1957 to review the CDP and NES.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Jayaprakash Narayan
Sarvodaya leader; led the 1974–75 'Total Revolution' movement
Balwant Rai Mehta
Chairman; report November 1957 recommended democratic decentralisation
V.K. Krishna Menon
V.K. Krishna Menon was a diplomat and Defence Minister (1957–62), not this committee's chairman.
Karpuri Thakur
Socialist leader, Chief Minister of Bihar

points: The committee found the CDP failed because people did not participate, so it proposed elected three-tier bodies (Panchayati Raj).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Rajasthan began Panchayati Raj at Nagaur
Planning Commission set up; Constitution in force
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee appointed and reported
The CDP was launched on 2 October 1952 with 55 projects, so 1952 is correct.

points: Sequence: CDP 1952 → NES 1953 → BRM 1957 → NDC 1958 → Nagaur 1959.

PYQ-POL-62EBB8936A81.lead: Balwant Rai Mehta (1957) → Dantwala (1978) → L.M. Singhvi (1986) → Gadgil (1988): d,b,c,a, option 4.

head: Committee
Year
Concept
rows: d. Balwant Rai Mehta
The BRM Committee (1957) recommended three-tier Panchayati Raj, the earliest of the four.
b. Dantwala
The Dantwala Committee (1978) dealt with block-level planning.
c. L.M. Singhvi
Constitutional recognition, Gram Sabha as direct democracy
a. Gadgil
The Gadgil Committee (1988) became the basis of the 64th Amendment Bill (1989), the latest of the four.

points: Option 1 (d,b,a,c) swaps Singhvi and Gadgil.
Options 2 and 3 misplace Dantwala/Gadgil; BRM must come first as the oldest.

PYQ-POL-7A0EA2362763.lead: Panchayat Raj: the Balwant Rai Mehta report (1957) recommended 'democratic decentralisation', which came to be known as Panchayati Raj.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Panchayat Raj
The three-tier local self-government the report recommended
Community Development
The programme (1952) the committee was asked to review; the report is remembered for its outcome, Panchayati Raj
Planning Commission
Body set up in 1950 for national planning; not the report's subject
Zonal Councils
Created by the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 for inter-state cooperation

points: The committee was appointed in January 1957 to review the CDP and NES, but its key recommendation was Panchayati Raj.
Rajasthan first implemented it at Nagaur on 2 October 1959.

PYQ-POL-APK-047B96.lead: The NDC (January 1958) did not insist on a single rigid pattern; it left states free to evolve patterns suited to local conditions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Single, rigid pattern for all states
The NDC expressly refused to insist on a single rigid pattern, so this is wrong.
Detailed, uniform functions for all PRIs
Functions varied from state to state; only broad principles were common
Flexibility for states to develop own patterns
Exactly what the NDC said; basic principles to be identical
Centralised control over PRIs
Centralised control is the opposite of democratic decentralisation, which the NDC accepted.

points: Result: states differed in tiers (Tamil Nadu two, Rajasthan three, West Bengal four) and in which tier was powerful.
Local government is a State subject (Entry 5, State List), so flexibility suited the federal scheme.

PYQ-POL-APK-31C0E4.lead: Balwant Rai Mehta Committee (1957) recommended the three-tier system.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Ashok Mehta Committee
The Ashok Mehta Committee (1977–78) recommended a two-tier system, not three tiers.
Narasimhan Committee
Narasimham committees (1991, 1998) on banking sector reforms
Balwant Rai Mehta Committee
Gram panchayat (village), panchayat samiti (block), zila parishad (district)
Raj Committee
K.N. Raj Committee (1972) on agricultural income taxation

points: The three tiers were to be linked through indirect elections.
Hook: Balwant = three (B-R-M, three letters); Ashok = two.

PYQ-POL-APK-66BCB0.lead: BRM made the block-level Panchayat Samiti the executive body.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Panchayat Samiti
Block tier; executive body that carries out development work
Nyaya Panchayat
Village court for petty cases — judicial, not executive
Zila Panchayat
District tier; only advisory, coordinating and supervisory under BRM
Gram Panchayat
Village tier with directly elected members; not named the executive

points: The block was then the unit of the Community Development Programme, so BRM placed executive power there.
Ashok Mehta later reversed this and made the zila parishad executive.

PYQ-POL-APK-824037.lead: Statement 4 is correct: BRM wanted the District Collector to chair the zila parishad.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Village panchayat indirectly elected
False — village panchayat was to be directly elected
Panchayat samiti advisory
False: BRM made the panchayat samiti the executive body, not an advisory one.
Zila parishad executive
False — zila parishad was advisory, coordinating and supervisory
Collector chairs zila parishad
True: BRM recommendation 5 made the district collector the chairman of the zila parishad.

points: Options 1-3 swap the roles of the tiers; remember: samiti = executive, zila parishad = advisory.
Samiti and zila parishad members were indirectly elected.

PYQ-POL-APK-9D2322.lead: BRM recommended three tiers: gram panchayat (village), panchayat samiti (block), zila parishad (district).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Two-tier
A two-tier system was the Ashok Mehta Committee's (1978) idea, not BRM's.
Four-tier
Adopted by West Bengal; not a BRM recommendation
Three-tier: village, block, district
BRM's first recommendation was a three-tier system: village, block and district.
Single-tier
A single-tier system was not recommended by any major committee.

points: The tiers were to be organically linked through indirect elections.

PYQ-POL-APK-BFDD76.lead: BRM wanted adequate resources transferred to PRIs to enable them to discharge their functions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Fully dependent on state grants
Full dependence on state grants was not BRM's view; it would kill local autonomy.
Independent authority to collect taxes
Compulsory taxation powers was an Ashok Mehta (1978) idea, not BRM's
Adequate resources to be transferred
BRM recommendation 7 said adequate resources should be transferred to these bodies.
Direct central funding
Not recommended; local government is a State subject

points: BRM paired this with 'a genuine transfer of power and responsibility' — powers without money would be empty.

PYQ-POL-APK-EF5812.lead: Statement 3 is INCORRECT: BRM never gave PRIs power to levy income tax; income tax is a Union subject.

head: Option
What it is / means

False

3. Constitution has not fixed the term of Rajya Sabha members
True
The Constitution leaves it to Parliament; the Representation of the People Act, 1951 fixes the term at six years.

points: Option 1 (Only 2 and 3) is wrong because statement 2 is false.
Option 2 (Only 2) is wrong because statement 2 is false and it leaves out true statement 3.
Option 4 (1, 2 and 3) is wrong because statements 1 and 2 are both false.
PYQ-POL-APK-571C00.also: One-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every second year.

PYQ-POL-APK-6622D7.lead: Option 4: the Inter-State Council Secretariat was set up in 1991, is headed by a Secretary to the Government of India, and since 2011 also works as the secretariat of the Zonal Councils.

Correct: Laxmikanth states exactly these facts about the Secretariat.

points: Members: PM (Chairman), all Chief Ministers, CMs of UTs with legislatures, Administrators of other UTs, Governors of States under President's Rule and six Union Cabinet ministers including the Home Minister.

PYQ-POL-APK-6622D7.also: The ISC was set up by a Presidential order in 1990 under Article 263.

PYQ-POL-APK-6965C4.lead: Option 1: NITI Aayog has no Article in the Constitution; it was created by an executive (Cabinet) resolution in 2015.

Correct?

Wrong: the Comptroller and Auditor General is provided for in Article 148.

Wrong: the Finance Commission is provided for in Article 280.

PYQ-POL-APK-818EDF.lead: The answer is option 3: Article 244A allows an autonomous state within Assam for certain tribal areas.

Correct: the Rajamannar Committee was appointed by the Tamil Nadu government in 1969 to study Centre-State relations.

PYQ-POL-APK-C33705.lead: Option 4: the Sixth Schedule can be amended by a simple majority of Parliament, like an ordinary law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Effective majority
More than half of the House's effective strength (total minus vacancies); used for removing the Vice-President or the Speaker.
Absolute majority
More than half of the total membership of the House; it is used only as one part of the special majority.
Special majority
Majority of total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting; needed for most amendments under Article 368.
Simple majority
More than half of members present and voting, as for an ordinary bill; para 21 of the Sixth Schedule says such laws are not Art 368 amendments.

points: Laxmikanth lists the Fifth and Sixth Schedules among provisions amendable by simple majority 'outside the scope of Article 368'.
Hook: tribal schedules (5th and 6th) need flexibility, so they are amended easily.

PYQ-POL-APK-C84C8D.lead: The answer is option 4: Nagaland is not under the Sixth Schedule.

Mizoram
Has Sixth Schedule autonomous districts (three).
Nagaland
Not covered by the Sixth Schedule; its special protection comes from Article 371A.

points: The Sixth Schedule covers only four states: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram (memory hook: AMTM).
There are ten tribal areas in all; Tripura has one.

PYQ-POL-C1C94D9DD745.lead: Option 2: only the Inter-State Council is provided for directly in the Constitution, in Article 263.

PYQ-POL-C5CC85BB95FE.lead: Option 2: the Indian Foreign Service works only for the Union government in a Union subject (foreign affairs), so it is a Central Service.

Correct?

Correct: Central Services work under the exclusive control of the Central government; the Indian Foreign Service is a Group A Central Service.

Wrong: a State Service works only under a State government, e.g. a Deputy Collector; foreign affairs is never a State job.

Wrong: Local Service means employees of local bodies such as municipalities and panchayats.

PYQ-POL-C6A9A9383493.lead: Option 3 is the NOT-true statement: Article 262 lets Parliament bar courts over the water dispute itself, but the Supreme Court is not completely shut out.

Correct?

Wrong choice: this is true; Article 262 is the Article on inter-State water disputes.

Correct: this statement is not true, because the Supreme Court can still deal with related matters, such as appeals by special leave (Cauvery judgment, 2018) and enforcement of awards.
