POL-6.1.9-P102-05.lead: Option 1: Article 18(4) covers all three — any present, emolument or office from or under a foreign State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct: Article 18(4) says no person holding an office of profit or trust under the State shall accept any present, emolument or office of any kind from a foreign State without the President's consent (LX p127).
2. 1 and 2 only
Wrong: it leaves out office, which is also covered.
3. 2 only
Wrong: it leaves out present and office.
4. 3 only
Wrong: it leaves out present and emolument.

points: Article 18(4) applies to both citizens and foreigners who hold an office of profit or trust under the State (LX p127).

POL-6.1.9-P102-06.lead: Option 3: untouchability in Article 17 means caste-based social disability, so barring a person from a public well because of caste is the clear case.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Avoiding physical contact during an infectious illness solely for medical reasons
Not untouchability: avoiding contact for medical reasons has nothing to do with birth in a caste.
2. Limiting entry to a private family function to invited guests, without any caste-based exclusion
Not untouchability: inviting only chosen guests to a private function, without caste exclusion, is not a caste disability.
3. Excluding a person from a public well because that person’s caste is treated as ritually polluting
Untouchability (correct): exclusion from a public well because the caste is treated as polluting is the historical practice Article 17 abolishes.
4. Temporarily closing a public well to everyone because its water is contaminated
Not untouchability: closing the well to everyone for contamination applies equally to all, with no caste basis.

points: 'Untouchability' is not defined in the Constitution or the Act; courts read it as the practice as it developed historically — disabilities imposed because of birth in certain castes (LX p127).
Article 17 applies against private individuals too (PUDR case, 1982) (LX p127).

POL-6.1.9-P102-07.lead: Option 4: Article 17 itself abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice; enforcing any disability from it is an offence punishable in accordance with law (LX p127).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Untouchability remains constitutionally permissible until Parliament abolishes it by statute.
Wrong: abolition took effect from the Constitution itself; it did not wait for a statute.
2. Article 17 itself fixes the same two-year sentence for every offence involving untouchability.
Wrong: Article 17 fixes no punishment; Parliament makes the punishing law under Article 35.
3. Article 17 merely permits each State to decide whether untouchability should be abolished.
Wrong: States have no choice; the abolition is absolute and applies everywhere.
4. Article 17 itself abolishes untouchability and forbids its practice; enforcement of disabilities arising from it is punishable in accordance with law.
Correct: this is the text of Article 17 — abolition is constitutional, punishment is statutory.

points: Laws made: Untouchability (Offences) Act, 1955 (now PCR Act) and SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 (LX p127).

POL-6.1.9-P102-08.lead: Option 2: Article 18(1) prohibits the State from conferring titles on anybody, citizen or foreigner.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The proposal is permissible because the recipient is a foreign national.
Wrong: the ban covers 'any body, whether a citizen or a foreigner' (LX p127).
2. The proposal is prohibited: Article 18(1) does not limit its prohibition to citizen recipients.
Correct: Article 18(1) puts no citizenship limit on the recipient.
3. The proposal becomes permissible if the President consents under Article 18(3).
Wrong: Article 18(3) is about foreigners accepting titles from foreign States; President's consent cannot permit the Indian State to confer a title.
4. The proposal is governed only by Article 18(2), which concerns titles conferred by the Indian State.
Wrong: Article 18(2) is about citizens accepting titles from foreign States, not about titles given by the Indian State.

points: Clause (1) restricts the State as giver; clauses (2)–(4) restrict persons as receivers (LX p127).

POL-6.1.9-P103-01.lead: Only statement 1 is true. So the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why

In Balaji Raghavan (1995) the Supreme Court held that national awards are not 'titles' under Article 18, which bars only hereditary titles of nobility (LX p127).
False
The same judgment said the awards must not be used as prefixes or suffixes; otherwise the awardee should forfeit the award (LX p127).

Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement 2 which is false.

POL-6.1.9-P103-03.lead: Option 2 (a, b, c, g) is correct: speech is 19(1)(a), assembly (b), association (c), profession (g).

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Speech and expression
a. Speech
19(1)(a): freedom of speech and expression, including the press.
B. Peaceful assembly
b. Assembly
19(1)(b): assemble peaceably and without arms.
C. Associations
c. Association
19(1)(c): form associations, unions or cooperative societies.
D. Profession, trade
g. Profession

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong: it reverses the order — (e) is residence and (d) is movement.

3. c and e
Wrong: (c) is the right to form associations, unions or co-operative societies.
4. d and e
Correct: (d) = move freely throughout India; (e) = reside and settle in any part of India (LX p128).

Order of 19(1): (a) speech, (b) assembly, (c) association, (d) movement, (e) residence, (g) profession.

POL-6.1.9-P103-05.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true; statement 3 is false. So the answer is option 3 (1 and 2 only).

True/False
Why

The 44th Amendment Act, 1978 deleted Article 19(1)(f) and Article 31, and inserted Article 300A in Part XII (LX p128).
True
Article 19 originally had seven rights; with (f) deleted it now guarantees six (LX p128).

POL-6.1.9-P104-01.lead: Option 2: freedom of the press is not mentioned separately but is implied in freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a) (LX p130).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It is protected solely by occupational freedom under Article 19(1)(g).
Wrong: the press is protected mainly by Article 19(1)(a), not solely by the occupational freedom of 19(1)(g).
2. It is implicit in the freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).
Correct: courts read press freedom into 19(1)(a) — e.g. Romesh Thappar (1950) and Sakal Papers (1962).
3. It is expressly enumerated as a separate freedom alongside speech in Article 19(1)(a).
Wrong: the Constitution does not expressly list press freedom; it is implicit.
4. It is a freedom exclusively of journalists, unavailable to other citizens under Article 19(1)(a).
Wrong: Article 19 rights belong to all citizens; journalists have no special separate right.

points: Laxmikanth lists freedom of the press among the implied parts of 19(1)(a) (LX p130).

POL-6.1.9-P104-02.lead: Option 3: 'general public interest' is not a ground in Article 19(2); it appears in Articles 19(5) and 19(6).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Public order; security of the State
Both listed: public order and security of the State are grounds in Article 19(2).
2. Defamation; contempt of court
Both listed: defamation and contempt of court are grounds in Article 19(2).
3. General public interest; friendly relations with foreign States
Correct: friendly relations with foreign States is a ground, but 'general public interest' is not.
4. Sovereignty and integrity of India; decency or morality; incitement to an offence
All listed: sovereignty and integrity of India, decency or morality and incitement to an offence are 19(2) grounds.

points: The eight 19(2) grounds: sovereignty and integrity, security of the State, friendly relations with foreign States, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation, incitement to an offence (LX p130).
The First Amendment (1951) added public order, friendly relations and incitement; the 16th (1963) added sovereignty and integrity.

POL-6.1.9-P104-03.lead: Option 4: commercial speech is protected under Article 19(1)(a), subject to reasonable restrictions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Commercial purpose alone removes all Article 19(1)(a)protection.
Wrong: a profit motive does not remove protection; Tata Press v. MTNL (1995) held commercial advertisement is part of free speech.
2. Every advertisement is immune from regulation once it contains a price.
Wrong: protection is not immunity; false or misleading ads can still be regulated.
3. Only political advertisements can qualify as speech.
Wrong: protection is not limited to political ads.
4. Commercial speech can be protected under Article 19(1)(a), subject to the applicable constitutional restrictions.
Correct: truthful commercial ads are protected but remain subject to Article 19(2) restrictions.

points: Laxmikanth lists 'freedom of commercial advertisements' within 19(1)(a) (LX p130).

POL-6.1.9-P104-04.lead: Option 1: Bijoe Emmanuel (1986) held that respectful silence during the national anthem, for genuine religious belief, is protected; not singing is not disrespect.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Correct: the Court protected the Jehovah's Witness children under Articles 19(1)(a) (includes right to remain silent) and 25 (conscience).
2. Article 25(1) protects only organised religious ceremonies and cannot protect a pupil’s conscientious silence.
Wrong: Article 25 protects freedom of conscience, not only organised ceremonies.
3. Article 19(1)(a) protects the choice of spoken words but excludes a choice to remain silent.
Wrong: free speech includes the freedom of silence (LX p130).
4. Respect for the anthem requires singing in every case, even when the pupils stand respectfully without disruption.
Wrong: no law requires singing; standing respectfully is enough.

points: Laxmikanth lists 'freedom of silence' among the rights within 19(1)(a) (LX p130).

POL-6.1.9-P104-05.lead: Both statements are true. So the answer is option 4 (Both 1 and 2).

True/False

True

Option 2 (2 only) is wrong: it leaves out true statement 1.
Option 3 (Neither 1 nor 2) is wrong: it leaves out true statements 1 and 2.

POL-6.1.9-P104-06.lead: Option 2: candidate A is elected, because NOTA votes are counted but never defeat a candidate.

What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong: no fresh poll is ordered even if NOTA gets the most votes.
2. Candidate A is declared elected as the highest-polling contesting candidate.
Correct: the candidate with the most votes among the candidates (A with 30,000) is declared elected.
3. The seat remains vacant until NOTA falls below a candidate’s total.
Wrong: the seat is not left vacant; the result is declared.
4. Both candidates are automatically disqualified from contesting again.
Wrong: NOTA leading has no disqualification effect.

POL-6.1.9-P104-07.lead: Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — airwaves are public property, so their use can be regulated.

True/False
Why

True
Right to telecast does not give an unrestricted right to any frequency.
R
True
Airwaves are public property, to be regulated by a public authority in public interest.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Annoyance is a listed 19(2) ground

False. Article 19(2) lists only sovereignty and integrity, security of State, friendly relations, public order, decency or morality, contempt of court, defamation and incitement to an offence; 'annoyance' is not one of them.
2. Small penalty cures vagueness
False. The defect is that no one knows what is forbidden; a light sentence does not tell citizens or police where the line lies.
3. Vague, overbroad wording chills speech and allows arbitrary enforcement
True. The Court held that undefined words like 'annoying' or 'inconvenient' catch protected speech, so people self-censor and police can arrest at will.

False. The internet may be regulated differently in procedure, but it does not add a ground beyond the eight listed in Article 19(2).

head: Option
What it is / means

False. IPC Section 124A ('sedition', based on 'disaffection towards Government') was not copied; the BNS has a differently worded offence.

True. Section 152 targets secession, armed rebellion, subversive activities and separatism that endanger the nation, rather than hostility to the Government.
3. No provision against secession or armed rebellion
False. Section 152 expressly covers exciting secession, armed rebellion and subversive activities.
4. Every criticism of Government is sedition
False. The Explanation to Section 152 excludes lawful comments disapproving government measures with a view to their alteration by lawful means.

points: The focus shifted from protecting the Government to protecting the nation's sovereignty, unity and integrity.

POL-6.1.9-P105-04.lead: Option 1: lawful criticism of government measures that does not excite the listed activities is not an offence under Section 152.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Such comments are not an offence

True. The Explanation says comments disapproving measures or administrative or other action of the Government, aimed at lawful change and not exciting the listed activities, do not constitute the offence.
2. Covers only proposed measures, not action already taken
False. The Explanation expressly covers 'administrative or other action of the Government' as well as measures.
3. Lawful means insufficient until Government accepts the change
False. Nothing requires Government acceptance; seeking change by lawful means is itself the protected activity.
4. Written criticism stays outside the Explanation
False. The Explanation applies to comments whether spoken or written, as long as they do not excite the listed activities.

points: Concept: democracy needs the freedom to oppose government policy; the line is crossed only when one excites secession, armed rebellion, subversion or separatism.
This mirrors the old idea that 'disapprobation' of Government action is not sedition.

What it is / means
Correct?

False. Article 19(1)(a) protects unpopular and even shocking views; otherwise free speech would protect only the majority.
3. Examine statutory ingredients; disagreement alone is not enough
True. In Khushboo the Supreme Court quashed many complaints over her remarks because no ingredient of any offence was made out.
4. Article 19 bars prosecution for every statement
False. Speech is still subject to reasonable restrictions under Article 19(2), such as defamation or incitement.

points: Lesson: the court asks 'which legal ingredients are proved?', not 'how many people are upset?'.
Free speech is not absolute (option 4 fails), but it is also not lost just because it is unpopular (options 1, 2 fail).

False. The Court has held since All India Bank Employees (1962) that Article 19(1)(c) protects forming the union, not every activity, such as strikes, used by it.
2. Association protection does not guarantee a right to strike
True. Rangarajan held government employees have no fundamental, legal, moral or equitable right to go on strike.
3. Silence of Article 19 makes strike a Fundamental Right
False. Fundamental Rights must be found in the text or its interpretation; absence of a ban does not create a right.
4. Statutory permission makes it a Fundamental Right
False. A right given by a statute (e.g. industrial law) stays a legal right; only the Constitution creates Fundamental Rights.

False. That was exactly the law struck down: forcing new members on the Hindi Sahitya Sammelan destroyed the voluntary body.
4. Covers continuing with voluntarily agreed membership, subject to valid restrictions
True. An association is its members; changing them by force means it is no longer the association they formed.

points: The right also includes the negative right not to join an association (LX).
Recognition of an association is not a Fundamental Right.

POL-6.1.9-P106-13.lead: Option 1: the majority quashed the pre-publication scrutiny order against the newspaper 'Organiser' because the original Article 19(2) did not include public order.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Quashed the scrutiny order under 19(2) as it then stood
True. Pre-censorship was a restriction on press freedom, and it could not be saved because 'public order' was not then a 19(2) ground.
2. Upheld it on the public order ground
False. Public order was added to 19(2) only by the First Amendment in 1951, after this case.
3. Film certification was the main issue
False. The case was about a newspaper; film censorship was decided in K.A. Abbas (1970).
4. Pre-scrutiny is not a press restriction
False. The Court held that pre-censorship is clearly a restriction on liberty of the press.

points: Brij Bhushan and Romesh Thappar (1950) prompted the First Amendment (1951) to add public order, friendly relations and incitement to an offence to 19(2).

POL-6.1.9-P106-14.lead: Option 3: flying the National Flag with respect and dignity is part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a), subject to reasonable restrictions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only a Flag Code privilege with no constitutional basis
False. The Court rooted the right in Article 19(1)(a); the Flag Code is only executive instructions regulating it.
2. Fundamental Duty under 51A enforceable by writ
False. Respecting the Flag is a duty under 51A(a), but duties are not enforceable by writ and the claim here was a right.
3. Part of 19(1)(a), with respect and subject to reasonable restrictions
True. This is the holding of Naveen Jindal (2004).
4. Absolute and unregulable
False. No 19(1) right is absolute; Article 19(2) restrictions and the 1971 Act apply.

points: After this case, the Flag Code of India, 2002 allowed private citizens to fly the flag on all days.

POL-6.1.9-P107-01.lead: Option 3: Article 19(6) expressly lets the State prescribe professional or technical qualifications for practising any profession or trade.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Qualifications only for government jobs
False. 19(6)(i) applies to practising any profession or carrying on any occupation, private or public.
2. Only if the profession is a State monopoly
False. State monopoly is a different limb, 19(6)(ii); qualifications under 19(6)(i) do not need it.
3. 19(6) expressly permits prescribing professional or technical qualifications
True. A medical degree requirement is a classic example under 19(6)(i).
4. Registration allowed but no educational qualification
False. Educational qualifications are exactly what 19(6)(i) allows.

points: 19(6) has three parts: interests of general public, qualifications (i), and State trade or monopoly (ii).
Reason: public safety — an untrained doctor endangers life.

POL-6.1.9-P107-02.lead: Option 1: Article 20(1) bars conviction under a criminal law that did not exist when the act was done (no ex post facto law).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 20(1)
No conviction except for violating a law in force when the act was done, and no greater penalty than that law allowed.
2. Article 20(2)
Double jeopardy: no one can be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once.
3. Article 20(3)
Self-incrimination: an accused cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself.
4. Article 19(1)(c)
Right to form associations, unions or co-operative societies; unrelated to criminal convictions.

points: Here the act was lawful in 2024, so a 2025 law cannot make it a crime backwards.
Article 20 protects any person — citizen, foreigner or company (LX).
POL-6.1.9-P107-02.also: Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency (44th Amendment).

POL-6.1.9-P107-03.lead: Option 4: under Article 20(1), no penalty greater than that prescribed when the offence was committed can be imposed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Automatically impose five years
False. The five-year maximum came after the offence, so it cannot apply.
2. New maximum applies if trial began after amendment
False. The relevant date is the date of the act, not the date of trial.
3. New maximum applies to serious offences
False. Article 20(1) has no exception for seriousness.
4. Cannot exceed the maximum when the offence occurred
True. The maximum stays two years for this offence.

points: Article 20(1) has two limbs: (i) no conviction under a later law, (ii) no greater penalty than at the time of the act.
Key date to remember: date of commission of the act.

POL-6.1.9-P107-04.lead: Option 2 (A-2, B-3, C-1) is correct: Article 20 has three clauses for accused persons.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. No greater retrospective penalty
Article 20(1) bars ex post facto criminal laws: no one can be convicted for an act that was not an offence when done, or given a greater penalty than the law then allowed, so A matches 2.
B. No double punishment
Article 20(2) is the protection against double jeopardy: no person shall be prosecuted and punished for the same offence more than once, so B matches 3.
C. No compelled self-incrimination
20(3): an accused cannot be forced to be a witness against himself.

points: Option 1 fails: A-1 (20(3)) is wrong, A matches 2; B-2 (20(1)) is wrong, B matches 3; C-3 (20(2)) is wrong, C matches 1.
Option 3 fails: A-3 (20(2)) is wrong, A matches 2; B-1 (20(3)) is wrong, B matches 3; C-2 (20(1)) is wrong, C matches 1.
Option 4 fails: B-1 (20(3)) is wrong, B matches 3; C-3 (20(2)) is wrong, C matches 1.
Hook: 20(1) past law, 20(2) twice, 20(3) self.

POL-6.1.9-P107-05.lead: Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — Article 20(2) protects only against a second criminal prosecution and punishment.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
A departmental dismissal does not bar later criminal prosecution.
R
True
Article 20(2) applies only when a person was prosecuted and punished in criminal proceedings for the same offence.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. A departmental inquiry is not 'prosecution' before a court, so the double-jeopardy bar is not triggered.
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A, so "does not explain" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.
POL-6.1.9-P107-05.also: Maqbool Hussain (1953): customs confiscation is not prosecution by a judicial tribunal.

POL-6.1.9-P107-06.lead: Option 3: forcing an accused to give testimonial answers admitting guilt engages protection against self-incrimination, Article 20(3).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Protection against second prosecution and punishment
This is Article 20(2), double jeopardy; no second trial is involved here.
2. Protection against retrospective penalty
This is Article 20(1); no change in law is involved here.
3. Protection against compelled self-incrimination
Article 20(3): an accused cannot be compelled to be a witness against himself, which covers forced testimonial answers.
4. Protection against every physical identification
False. Lawful fingerprints, signatures and blood samples are not 'being a witness' (Kathi Kalu Oghad, 1961).

points: Test: does the material come from the accused's mind (testimony — protected) or from the body (physical evidence — not protected)?

POL-6.1.9-P107-07.lead: Grounds 1 and 2 are in Article 19(5), so the answer is option 3 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Interests of the general public
True
Article 19(5) allows restrictions on movement and residence in the interests of the general public.
2. Protection of interests of Scheduled Tribes
True
It allows restricting outsiders' entry into tribal areas to protect their culture, language and customs (LX).
3. Contempt of court
False
Contempt of court is a ground only in Article 19(2), for speech.

points: Option 1 drops statement 2; options 2 and 4 wrongly include statement 3.
19(5) covers 19(1)(d) movement and 19(1)(e) residence.

POL-6.1.9-P107-08.lead: Option 1: Article 19(6)(ii) permits laws for trade, business, industry or service by the State or a State-owned or controlled corporation, with complete or partial exclusion of citizens.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 19(6)(ii) permits State trade including complete or partial exclusion
True. This is the express text, which allows a State transport monopoly.
2. Only if every citizen keeps a share
False. The clause expressly allows complete exclusion of citizens.
3. 19(6)(ii) is about qualifications only
False. Qualifications are in 19(6)(i); 19(6)(ii) deals with State trade.
4. 19(1)(g) bars every State-run competing business
False. 19(6)(ii) saves such laws from challenge under 19(1)(g).

points: Clause (ii) was added by the First Amendment (1951) to allow nationalisation.
Such a monopoly law need not be separately proved 'reasonable' as to its exclusion.

POL-6.1.9-P107-09.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 4 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 20(1) forbids benefit of a later lighter penalty
False
Article 20(1) only stops a greater penalty; it does not bar a lighter one, and T. Barai (1983) allowed the benefit.
2. Depends on the legislation and any savings clause
True
Whether the reduced punishment applies is a question of the new law, e.g. whether it saves earlier penalties.

points: Article 20(1) is a shield for the accused, not a sword against him.
Options 1 and 2 wrongly accept statement 1; option 3 rejects the true statement 2.

POL-6.1.9-P107-10.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 2 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. General public interest is a ground for 19(1)(g)
True
Article 19(6) expressly allows reasonable restrictions in the interests of the general public.
2. Restrictions confined to qualifications
False
19(6) also covers general public interest and State trade or monopoly, not just qualifications.
3. Morality separately listed in 19(6)
False
Morality appears in 19(2) (as 'decency or morality') and 19(4), not in 19(6).

points: Options 1 and 4 wrongly accept statement 2; option 3 wrongly includes statement 3.
Immoral trades (like trafficking) can still be banned, as there is no right to carry on an immoral trade (LX).

POL-6.1.9-P107-11.lead: Option 3: the State must protect lawful expression and deal with the threatened violence, not yield to intimidation (S. Rangarajan, 1989).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Ban because threat creates a valid restriction
False. A threat by a hostile group is not a 19(2) ground; the danger must be proximate and directly linked to the expression.
2. Need approval from the threatening group
False. That would give a 'heckler's veto' to anyone willing to threaten violence.
3. Protect expression and address the violence
True. The Court said freedom of expression cannot be suppressed on account of threats; maintaining law and order is the State's duty.
4. Withdraw protection because some disagree
False. Disagreement does not remove Article 19(1)(a) protection.

points: Case: the Tamil film 'Ore Oru Gramathiley' on reservation policy.
Heckler's veto = silencing a speaker because the audience threatens trouble; Indian courts reject it.
POL-6.1.9-P107-11.also: Freedom of expression cannot be held to ransom by threats of violence.

POL-6.1.9-P107-12.lead: Option 4: Article 20(1) does not make a later change of procedure or court unconstitutional merely because it came after the act; other safeguards still apply.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Every criminal provision must stay unchanged
False. Laxmikanth: 20(1) prohibits only conviction or sentence under an ex post facto law, not the trial.
2. Makes change valid even if it violates other rights
False. The change can still be tested under Article 14 or Article 21.
3. Guarantees trial only by the court competent on the date of offence
False. No one has a vested right in a particular court or procedure (Rao Shiv Bahadur Singh, 1953).
4. Not unconstitutional merely on that ground; other safeguards apply
True. Only a new offence or a greater penalty is barred by 20(1).

points: Remember: 20(1) = what you are punished for and how much, not how or where you are tried.

POL-6.1.9-P108-01.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 20(1) invalidates every retrospective civil law
False
Laxmikanth: the limitation applies only to criminal laws; civil liability or tax can be imposed retrospectively.
2. A retrospective tax law can be tested under other provisions
True
It may still be challenged under Articles 14, 19(1)(g) or 265 if arbitrary.

points: Options 1 and 3 wrongly accept statement 1; option 4 rejects the true statement 2.
POL-6.1.9-P108-01.also: Parliament and legislatures can make retrospective civil and tax laws.

POL-6.1.9-P108-02.lead: Option 4: a lawfully taken fingerprint is physical identification material, not compelled testimony.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A forced oral confession
Compelled testimony from personal knowledge; barred by Article 20(3).
2. A compelled account admitting participation
Compelled testimony, as it reveals what the accused knows; barred.
3. Answers forcibly revealing personal knowledge
Compelled testimony, as it reveals what the accused knows; barred by Article 20(3).
4. Fingerprint taken under lawful authority
Physical evidence used only for comparison; it conveys no personal knowledge, so 20(3) does not apply (Kathi Kalu Oghad, 1961).

points: Laxmikanth: 20(3) does not extend to thumb impressions, specimen signatures, blood specimens or exhibition of the body.
POL-6.1.9-P108-02.also: Criminal Procedure (Identification) Act, 2022 governs taking such measurements.

POL-6.1.9-P108-03.lead: Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — Article 20(3) covers compelled statements outside court too.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Protection against self-incrimination can apply during police interrogation.
R
True
Article 20(3) is not limited to statements in court.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Since the protection covers compulsion outside court too, it reaches police questioning (Nandini Satpathy, 1978).
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A, so "does not explain" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.
POL-6.1.9-P108-03.also: An accused includes one formally accused in an FIR at the time of statement.

POL-6.1.9-P108-04.lead: Option 3: Article 21 protects all persons, citizens and non-citizens alike.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Requires permanent residence
False. Article 21 says 'no person', with no residence condition.
2. Depends on reciprocity
False. Fundamental Rights do not depend on how another country treats Indians.
3. Available to citizens and non-citizens
True. Laxmikanth: this right is available to both.
4. Only foreigners employed in India
False. No employment condition exists; a tourist is covered.

points: Rights for all persons: Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23-28. Citizens only: 15, 16, 19, 29, 30.

POL-6.1.9-P108-05.lead: Option 2: Article 21 uses the expression 'procedure established by law'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Due process of law
The phrase of the US Constitution (5th and 14th Amendments); the framers did not adopt it.
2. Procedure established by law
The actual words of Article 21, borrowed from the Japanese Constitution.
3. Procedure approved by the executive
Not in the Constitution; executive approval alone cannot deprive liberty.
4. Procedure established by constitutional convention
Not in the Constitution; conventions are unwritten practices.

points: Gopalan (1950) read it literally; Maneka Gandhi (1978) required the procedure to be fair, just and reasonable.

POL-6.1.9-P108-06.lead: Option 4: after Maneka Gandhi (1978), the procedure must also be fair, just and reasonable, not merely enacted.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Any enacted procedure satisfies Article 21
False. This was the Gopalan (1950) view that Maneka Gandhi overruled.
2. Only executive action can be tested
False. Maneka extended protection against arbitrary legislative action too (LX).
3. Fairness matters only for citizens
False. Article 21 covers every person, citizen or foreigner, so fairness is not only for citizens.
4. Procedure must be fair, just and reasonable
True. It must follow natural justice and not be arbitrary or oppressive.

points: Articles 14, 19 and 21 are read together (the 'golden triangle').
Laxmikanth: in effect, Maneka introduced 'due process of law'.

POL-6.1.9-P108-07.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Voluntary tests allowed with safeguards
True
Selvi allowed narcoanalysis, polygraph and BEAP tests with consent, a lawyer present and NHRC guidelines.
2. Consent alone makes results admissible
False
The results themselves are not admissible as evidence; only facts later discovered with their help may be used.

points: Options 2 and 3 wrongly accept statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
POL-6.1.9-P108-07.also: Information discovered because of a voluntary test may be admitted (then Section 27, Evidence Act; now BSA Section 23 proviso).

POL-6.1.9-P108-08.lead: Option 3: common facts are not enough; the ingredients of the two offences must be compared to see if they are the 'same offence' under Article 20(2).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Bars every later case from the same incident
False. One incident can give rise to legally distinct offences, each of which can be tried.
2. Different labels always mean different offences
False. A mere change of name does not decide it; ingredients do.
3. Compare ingredients, not just facts
True. S.L. Apte (1961) held the test is identity of offences, not of facts.
4. Applies only after departmental dismissal
False. Laxmikanth: 20(2) applies only to proceedings before a court or judicial tribunal, not departmental ones.

points: 'Same offence' = same ingredients. Example: cheating and forgery can come from the same act but are different offences.

POL-6.1.9-P108-09.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Applies only if earlier prosecuted and punished
True
Article 20(2) says no person shall be 'prosecuted and punished' for the same offence more than once (autrefois convict).
2. Also bars retrial after acquittal
False
Article 20(2) needs prior punishment; the bar after acquittal comes from procedure law (old CrPC s.300, now BNSS s.337).

points: Options 2 and 3 wrongly accept statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
The protection applies only before a court or judicial tribunal, not departmental inquiries (LX).

POL-6.1.9-P108-10.lead: Option 2: substantial psychological pressure that overbears free will can amount to compulsion under Article 20(3).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. No physical injury means no compulsion
False. Nandini Satpathy held compulsion may be physical or psychological, such as threats or prolonged intimidation.
2. Serious psychological coercion can make testimony compelled
True. What matters is whether free choice was overborne, not whether a blow was struck.
3. Relevant only when repeated before a judge
False. The protection extends to police interrogation of an accused, not just court testimony.
4. Every question to an accused is banned
False. Only answers that tend to incriminate the accused are protected; others may be required.

points: Article 20(3) applies from the stage of police questioning (Section 161 CrPC, now BNSS Section 180).

POL-6.1.9-P108-11.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Tests are physical evidence because machines are used
False
Using scientific equipment does not change the fact that the results come from the subject's mind.
2. Results are testimonial as they convey personal knowledge
True
Selvi held that these test results are testimonial, so compelling them violates Article 20(3).
3. Public interest alone allows dilution
False
The Court held Article 20(3) is a non-derogable right and cannot be diluted for investigation needs.

points: Option 2 wrongly includes statement 1; option 3 wrongly includes statement 3; option 4 includes both false ones.
Forced tests also violate personal liberty and mental privacy under Article 21.

POL-6.1.9-P108-12.lead: Items 1, 2 and 4 are non-testimonial, so the answer is option 3 (1, 2 and 4 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Specimen handwriting
True
It is used only to compare with a disputed document and conveys no personal knowledge (Kathi Kalu Oghad).
2. Specimen signature
True
Laxmikanth lists specimen signatures as outside 20(3).
3. Compelled written account of how the offence was done
False
This is a written confession conveying personal knowledge, so it is testimonial and barred.
4. Blood sample for forensic comparison
True
Blood specimens are physical material, not testimony (LX).

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 all wrongly include item 3; option 1 also drops items 2 and 4.
Being a witness means imparting personal knowledge — documents can be testimonial, physical samples are not.

POL-6.1.9-P108-13.lead: Option 4: Nandini Satpathy was decided in 1978 and Selvi in 2010.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Nandini Satpathy is correctly 1978, but Selvi was decided in 2010, not 2014, so this option fails.
Selvi is correctly 2010, but Nandini Satpathy was decided in 1978, not 1988, so this option fails.
Both years are wrong: Nandini Satpathy was 1978 (not 1988) and Selvi was 2010 (not 2014).
Correct: Nandini Satpathy v. P.L. Dani was decided in 1978 and Selvi v. State of Karnataka in 2010, both on Article 20(3).

points: Both cases are on Article 20(3), right against self-incrimination.
Nandini Satpathy: protection applies even at police questioning. Selvi: forced narco-analysis, polygraph and brain-mapping violate Article 20(3).

POL-6.1.9-P109-01.lead: Option 2: A.K. Gopalan (1950) gave the narrow reading of Article 21, which Maneka Gandhi (1978) overruled.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
Laid down the basic structure doctrine limiting Parliament's amending power.
2. A.K. Gopalan (1950)
Held Article 21 protects only against executive action and any law-made procedure is enough.
3. Minerva Mills (1980)
Struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment and protected the balance between Fundamental Rights and DPSP.
4. Shreya Singhal (2015)
Struck down Section 66A of the IT Act for vagueness.

points: Gopalan also treated each Fundamental Right as a separate compartment; Maneka linked Articles 14, 19 and 21.

POL-6.1.9-P109-02.lead: Option 4: the public trust doctrine requires the State, as trustee of natural resources, to justify giving them for exclusive private use.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Polluter-pays principle
The polluter must bear the cost of damage and restoration; it is about liability for pollution, not custody of resources.
2. Precautionary principle
The State must prevent environmental harm even when science is uncertain; it is about risk, not trusteeship.
3. Eminent domain
The State's power to acquire private property for public purpose; the reverse of this situation.
4. Public trust doctrine
Resources like rivers, seashores and forests are held by the State in trust for the public and cannot be handed over for private use freely.

points: Applied in India in M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) over a motel on the Beas river.

POL-6.1.9-P109-03.lead: All four are recognised dimensions of Article 21, so the answer is option 1 (1, 2, 3 and 4).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Living with human dignity
True
Maneka Gandhi and Francis Coralie Mullin (1981) held life means living with dignity (LX).
2. Pollution-free environment
True
Laxmikanth lists decent environment including pollution-free water and air (Subhash Kumar, 1991).
3. Health
True
Right to health and emergency medical aid was recognised in Parmanand Katara (1989).
4. Privacy
True
K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) declared privacy a Fundamental Right under Article 21.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 each wrongly leave out one or more recognised rights.

POL-6.1.9-P109-04.lead: Option 2: her existing passport was impounded under Section 10(3)(c) of the Passports Act, 1967 'in public interest'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Refusal of first passport
False. She already had a passport; the issue was its impounding.
2. Impounding of existing passport under Section 10(3)(c)
True. It was done without a hearing and without reasons, which the Court found unfair.
3. Revocation of citizenship
False. Her citizenship was never in question.
4. Cancellation after a criminal conviction
False. There was no conviction; the order cited only public interest.

points: The Court held the procedure must follow natural justice (right to be heard).
POL-6.1.9-P109-04.also: Satwant Singh Sawhney (1967) had earlier held travel abroad is part of personal liberty.

POL-6.1.9-P109-05.lead: Option 3: M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997) declared the public trust doctrine part of Indian law and quashed the Span Motel lease on the Beas.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Vellore Citizens Welfare Forum (1996)
Tamil Nadu tannery pollution case; accepted precautionary and polluter-pays principles.
2. Indian Council for Enviro-Legal Action (1996)
Bichhri (Rajasthan) chemical pollution case; applied polluter pays.
3. M.C. Mehta v. Kamal Nath (1997)
Public trust doctrine; set aside lease of fragile riverbank land in Himachal Pradesh.
4. M.C. Mehta v. UOI — Oleum Gas Leak (1987)
Laid down absolute liability for hazardous industries.

points: Hook: Kamal Nath — 'Nath' of the river; public trust over the Beas.

POL-6.1.9-P109-06.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Article 21 uses 'procedure established by law'
True
These are the exact words of Article 21, which are still in the text.
2. US 5th and 14th Amendments contain due process clauses
True
The 5th binds the federal government and the 14th the States.
3. Maneka changed the text to 'due process of law'
False
Courts only interpret; the wording can change only by amendment under Article 368, which never happened.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 wrongly include statement 3.
Maneka gave 'due process' in effect by requiring fair, just and reasonable procedure, without altering the words.

POL-6.1.9-P109-07.lead: Option 4 (3–1–2) is correct: Prem Shankar Shukla is on handcuffing, Mohini Jain on education and capitation fees, R. Rajagopal on privacy.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Prem Shankar Shukla (1980)
3. Handcuffing
Routine handcuffing of undertrials violates Article 21.
B. Mohini Jain (1992)
1. Education, capitation fees
Right to education; capitation fees struck down.
C. R. Rajagopal (1994)
2. Privacy
Right to privacy; publication of autobiography.

POL-6.1.9-P109-08.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Precaution and polluter pays are essential features of sustainable development
True
Vellore (1996) said so and called them part of the law of the land.
2. Developer bears onus to show action is benign
True
Under the precautionary principle the burden of proof is on the actor or industrialist.
3. Lack of certainty requires postponing prevention
False
It is the opposite: lack of scientific certainty is no reason to postpone preventive measures.

points: Option 1 drops statement 2; options 3 and 4 wrongly include statement 3.

Correct: LX p139 says 'forced labour' includes compulsion from economic circumstances, that is, working for less than the minimum wage.

False: payment below the statutory minimum is itself treated as forced labour, so part payment does not save the employer.

points: Concept: Article 23 bans traffic in human beings, begar and similar forms of forced labour, and it applies against private persons too (LX p139).

POL-6.1.9-P121-02.lead: Option 1: habeas corpus tests the legality of detention, and lies against private persons as well as public authorities.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Habeas corpus
'To have the body'. Court orders the detainer to produce the person and checks if detention is legal.
✓ — the issue is illegal confinement.
Quo warranto
'By what authority'. Court asks a person to show his right to hold a public office.
✗ — no public office involved.
Certiorari
'To be certified'. Higher court quashes an order of a lower court or tribunal.
✗ — no order to quash.
Prohibition
'To forbid'. Higher court stops a lower court from exceeding jurisdiction.
✗ — no pending case.

points: Habeas corpus can be issued against both public authorities and private individuals (LX p145).

POL-6.1.9-P121-03.lead: Option 4: a bona fide friend may file habeas corpus for a detained person who cannot approach the court.

What it is / means
Correct?

✗ — Habeas corpus protects liberty, so the court accepts a petition from a bona fide friend without any formal authority; the confined person often cannot sign one anyway.
Option 2
Claims the friend must prove a legal right to custody of the detained adult.
✗ — The court only asks whether the detention is illegal; the petitioner does not need any custody right over the adult.
Option 3
Claims only close family members, never a friend, can file for release.
✗ — Standing (locus standi) is relaxed in habeas corpus, so a genuine friend or even a stranger acting in good faith can file.
Option 4
Says a bona fide friend can file habeas corpus for a person who cannot reach the court.
✓ — Correct: because the detenu cannot approach the court, a friend acting in good faith may petition on their behalf.

✓ — Correct: when a competent court has passed a valid sentence and custody is legal, habeas corpus cannot be used to rehear the merits.
Option 3
Claims every convicted prisoner must be freed once a petition is filed.
✗ — release follows only if detention is illegal.
Option 4
Claims there is no remedy at all to challenge the merits of a conviction.
✗ — they can be challenged through appeal or revision.

points: Laxmikanth: habeas corpus is not issued where detention is under a lawful order of a competent court.

POL-6.1.9-P121-05.lead: Option 3: K.S. Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy under Article 21 and overruled ADM Jabalpur.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Minerva Mills (1980)
Limited Parliament's amending power; balance of FRs and DPSPs.
✗ — Limited Parliament's amending power; balance of FRs and DPSPs.
Indra Sawhney (1992)
OBC reservation; 50% ceiling; creamy layer.
✗ — OBC reservation; 50% ceiling; creamy layer.
K.S. Puttaswamy (2017)
Nine-judge Bench: privacy is a Fundamental Right; ADM Jabalpur overruled.
✓ — Nine-judge Bench: privacy is a Fundamental Right; ADM Jabalpur overruled.
Shreya Singhal (2015)
2015 case that struck down Section 66A of the IT Act for violating free speech.
✗ — Shreya Singhal dealt with online speech under Article 19(1)(a); it did not overrule ADM Jabalpur.

points: ADM Jabalpur (1976) had held that no habeas corpus lies during an Article 359 suspension.

POL-6.1.9-P121-06.lead: Option 1: mandamus orders a public authority to perform a legal duty it has refused to do.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Mandamus
'We command'. Court orders a public body to perform its duty.
✓ — the authority refuses a statutory duty.
Habeas corpus
'To have the body'. Tests legality of detention.
✗ — no one is detained.
Quo warranto
'By what authority'. Tests right to a public office.
✗ — 'By what authority'. Tests right to a public office.
Prohibition
'To forbid'. Stops a lower court exceeding jurisdiction.
✗ — 'To forbid'. Stops a lower court exceeding jurisdiction.

points: The court orders the authority to consider the application, not to approve it.
Mandamus does not lie for discretionary duty, against private bodies, or against the President/Governors (LX p145).
POL-6.1.9-P121-06.also: Example: a licensing office sits on a complete licence application — mandamus directs it to decide.

POL-6.1.9-P121-07.lead: Option 2: in Kanubhai Brahmbhatt (1987), the SC said it may, for good reasons, ask the petitioner to approach the High Court first.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Option 1
Immediate adjudication of every petition.
✗ — Kanubhai Brahmbhatt says the Supreme Court may redirect a petitioner to the High Court, so it need not decide every petition at once.
Option 2
Says the SC may, for good reasons, ask the petitioner to approach the High Court first.
✓ — Correct: this is the holding of Kanubhai Brahmbhatt (1987); the SC keeps its Article 32 power but can redirect the petitioner.
Option 3
Claims a High Court decision is a compulsory step before the Supreme Court.
✗ — There is no such constitutional requirement; going to the High Court first is a matter of the SC's discretion, not a precondition.
Option 4
Claims only High Courts can hear such writ petitions.
✗ — Jurisdiction under Article 32 (SC) and Article 226 (HC) is concurrent, not exclusive to High Courts.

points: Article 32 remains a Fundamental Right; this is only judicial management of workload.

POL-6.1.9-P121-08.lead: Option 3: Article 32 gives the SC original jurisdiction to enforce Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Appellate
Hearing appeals from lower courts (Arts 132–134, 136).
✗ — The petitioner went straight to the SC without appealing any lower-court judgment, so appellate jurisdiction is not involved.
Advisory
Opinion on Presidential reference (Art 143).
✗ — Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143 is an opinion on a reference by the President; here a person filed a petition.
Original (writ) for FRs
A person directly petitions the Supreme Court under Article 32 to enforce a Fundamental Right.
✓ — Correct: the case starts in the SC itself, so this is original (writ) jurisdiction for Fundamental Rights.
Exclusive, inter-State disputes
Original jurisdiction under Article 131.
✗ — Article 131 covers disputes between the Centre and States; it does not cover an individual's Fundamental Rights petition.

points: Original but not exclusive: High Courts share it under Article 226.

POL-6.1.9-P121-09.lead: Option 4: Kanu Sanyal (1973) held that physical production is not essential; the court can decide legality without it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Option 1
Claims the court loses jurisdiction if the detainee is not physically produced.
✗ — Kanu Sanyal (1973) held physical production is not essential, so the court keeps jurisdiction without it.
Option 2
Claims the court can release the detainee without examining the legality of custody.
✗ — The very purpose of habeas corpus is to test whether custody is legal; release follows only if it is not.
Option 3
Claims physical production of the detainee is always forbidden.
✗ — Production is not prohibited; the court may still order it in a suitable case.
Option 4
Says physical production is not always essential; legality can be decided without it.
✓ — Correct: this is the Kanu Sanyal (1973) view, which fits the stem where production was dispensed with.

points: The core of habeas corpus is testing legality of custody, not producing the body.

POL-6.1.9-P121-10.lead: Option 2: habeas corpus means 'to have the body' and mandamus means 'we command'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Option 1
Gives 'we command' for habeas corpus and 'to have the body' for mandamus.
✗ — it swaps them: 'we command' is mandamus and 'to have the body' is habeas corpus.
Option 2
Habeas corpus means 'to have the body'; mandamus means 'we command'.
✓ — Correct: both meanings are right and in the order asked (habeas corpus first, then mandamus).
Option 3
Gives the meanings of prohibition ('to forbid') and quo warranto ('by what authority').
✗ — 'to forbid' is prohibition and 'by what authority' is quo warranto, not the two asked.
Option 4
Gives the meanings of quo warranto ('by what authority') and certiorari ('to be certified').
✗ — 'by what authority' is quo warranto and 'to be certified' is certiorari.

points: Other writs: prohibition 'to forbid', certiorari 'to be certified', quo warranto 'by what authority'.

POL-6.1.9-P121-11.lead: Option 4: in the Keshav Singh reference (1964), the SC held legislative origin is not an absolute bar; the High Court can hear habeas corpus.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Option 1
Claims legislative origin of the detention always ends the High Court's jurisdiction.
✗ — The Keshav Singh reference (1964) held legislative origin is not an absolute bar to habeas corpus.
Option 2
Claims the High Court must cancel every sentence passed by the Assembly.
✗ — The High Court only tests the legality of the detention; it does not automatically set aside every sentence.
Option 3
Claims that a High Court hearing such a petition commits contempt of the House.
✗ — In the Keshav Singh reference the SC held that entertaining the petition was not contempt of the House.
Option 4
Says legislative origin is not an absolute bar to High Court habeas corpus.
✓ — Correct: this is the Keshav Singh (1964) view, so the High Court can examine the non-member's detention.

points: Arose when the UP Assembly jailed non-member Keshav Singh for contempt.

POL-6.1.9-P121-12.lead: Option 2: ADM Jabalpur was expressly overruled by the nine-judge Bench in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Option 1
Claims ADM Jabalpur's majority view is still binding law today.
✗ — It was expressly overruled by the nine-judge Bench in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).
Option 2
Says ADM Jabalpur was overruled in K.S. Puttaswamy (2017).
✓ — Correct: the nine-judge Bench in Puttaswamy expressly overruled the ADM Jabalpur majority.
Option 3
Claims Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled ADM Jabalpur.
✗ — Kesavananda (1973) came before ADM Jabalpur (1976), so it could not have overruled it.
Option 4
Claims Maneka Gandhi (1978) affirmed ADM Jabalpur.
✗ — Maneka Gandhi widened Article 21 and did not affirm ADM Jabalpur; the overruling came in Puttaswamy (2017).

points: The 44th Amendment (1978) had already made Articles 20 and 21 non-suspendable.

POL-6.1.9-P122-01.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True
Article 361(1) says the President and Governor are not answerable to any court for the exercise of their official powers and duties. This is a personal immunity of the office-holder.
False

The immunity protects the person, not the government's acts. Actions taken in the name of the President or Governor can still be challenged in court against the Government of India or the State Government.

points: Option 2 and option 3 fail because statement 2 confuses personal immunity with immunity of government action.
Option 4 fails because statement 1 is a correct reading of Article 361(1).
Memory hook: the person is shielded, the action is not.

POL-6.1.9-P122-02.lead: Option 4: private status alone does not decide the matter; the court must see whether a public duty with a public-law element is involved.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Argument always correct for every private body
Claims private bodies can never get mandamus.
✗ — Article 226 reaches 'any person or authority', so a private body performing a public duty can be directed.
2. Every private contract enforceable by mandamus
Claims writs enforce all private contracts.
✗ — Purely contractual or private rights are enforced by civil suit, not by mandamus.
3. Must first become a government department
Claims only government bodies can be directed.
✗ — There is no such condition; the nature of the duty matters, not the label of the body.
4. Examine public duty and public-law element
The correct test for mandamus against a non-State body.

points: Mandamus ('we command') orders performance of a legal public duty that has been refused.
Article 226 is wider than Article 32: it covers Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose', and 'any person or authority'.
So the court looks at the function and duty, not at who owns the body.

POL-6.1.9-P122-03.lead: Option 2: Prohibition is the writ that stops a lower court or tribunal from continuing a case beyond its jurisdiction.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Certiorari
'To be certified'. It quashes a final order already passed without or in excess of jurisdiction.
✗ — Here proceedings are still continuing; nothing final is to be quashed yet.
2. Prohibition
'To forbid'. A higher court stops a lower court or tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction while the case is pending.
3. Quo warranto
'By what authority'. It tests a person's legal right to hold a public office.
✗ — No one's title to office is in question.
4. Mandamus for a favourable decision
'We command'. It orders performance of a public duty.
✗ — Mandamus can never dictate how a case should be decided on merits.

points: Prohibition directs inactivity, while mandamus directs activity.
Prohibition lies only against judicial and quasi-judicial bodies, not administrative ones.
Hook: Prohibition = before the final order; Certiorari = after the final order.

POL-6.1.9-P122-04.lead: Option 3: Certiorari quashes an order already passed without jurisdiction.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Prohibition
'To forbid'. Stops a pending proceeding before the final order.
✗ — The order is already passed; stopping future steps does not remove it.
2. Habeas corpus
'To have the body'. Tests the legality of a person's detention.
✗ — No detention is involved.
3. Certiorari
'To be certified'. A higher court calls up the record and quashes an order passed without or in excess of jurisdiction.
4. Quo warranto
'By what authority'. Tests title to a public office.
✗ — The question is about an order, not an office-holder.

points: Prohibition is preventive; certiorari is curative (corrective).
Both are jurisdictional writs but are used at different stages of the proceedings.
Certiorari now also lies against administrative authorities affecting individual rights.

POL-6.1.9-P122-05.lead: Option 3: the High Court may still hear the writ for breach of natural justice, though relief is discretionary.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Must quash whenever an appeal exists
Says the High Court is bound to quash the order whenever an appeal exists.
✗ — Writ relief is always discretionary; the court weighs the facts.
2. Loses all writ jurisdiction
Says the mere existence of a statutory appeal ousts Article 226 completely.
✗ — An alternative remedy is a rule of self-restraint, not a bar on jurisdiction.
3. May entertain for natural-justice breach; not automatic
Correct statement of the exceptions to the alternative-remedy rule.
4. Only Parliament can permit
Says the High Court can hear the writ only if a law of Parliament allows it.
✗ — Article 226 power comes from the Constitution and cannot depend on Parliament's permission.

points: Recognised exceptions: breach of a Fundamental Right, breach of natural justice, order wholly without jurisdiction, or challenge to the validity of the law.
Here the required hearing was not given, so the natural-justice exception applies.

POL-6.1.9-P122-06.lead: Option 2: the court can direct the authority to exercise its discretion lawfully, but it does not grant the benefit itself.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Discretion excludes all directions
Says 'discretion' puts the authority wholly beyond court directions.
✗ — Refusing even to consider is a failure to exercise discretion, which mandamus can correct.
2. Require lawful exercise; no automatic benefit
Correct: court orders proper consideration only.
3. Applicant automatically gets the benefit
Says the court itself grants the benefit to the applicant.
✗ — The decision still belongs to the authority under the statute.
4. Court substitutes its own policy
Says the court replaces the authority's policy with its own choice.
✗ — Courts review legality; they do not replace the authority's policy choice.

points: In K.S. Jagannathan the Supreme Court held that where a body fails to exercise a discretion vested in it, the court may direct it to do so properly.
Key idea: mandamus commands the duty to decide, not a particular decision.

POL-6.1.9-P122-07.lead: Option 3: certiorari is a supervisory writ, not an appeal for re-weighing evidence.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Rehearing every factual issue
Treats certiorari as a full retrial of every factual issue.
✗ — The court does not rehear facts under certiorari.
2. Substitute preferred factual view
Treats certiorari as an appeal where the court picks its preferred view of evidence.
✗ — A different possible view of evidence is not a ground for certiorari.
3. Supervisory, not an ordinary appeal
Correct description from T.C. Basappa: certiorari is supervisory, not an ordinary appeal.
✓ — Correct: since no jurisdictional or patent legal error is shown, a mere other view of evidence cannot ground certiorari.
4. Never addresses patent error of law
Denies that certiorari can correct an error of law apparent on the record.
✗ — An error of law apparent on the face of the record is a recognised ground.

points: Grounds for certiorari: lack or excess of jurisdiction, breach of natural justice, and error of law apparent on the record.
In this stem none of these exists, so the writ should not issue.

POL-6.1.9-P122-08.lead: Option 3: Prohibition means 'to forbid' and certiorari means 'to be certified'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. To have the body — We command
'To have the body' is habeas corpus and 'we command' is mandamus.
✗ — These are the meanings of two different writs, not prohibition and certiorari.
2. To be certified — To forbid
Gives both correct meanings but in reverse order.
✗ — The question asks prohibition first, then certiorari.
3. To forbid — To be certified
Prohibition means 'to forbid'; certiorari means 'to be certified'.
✓ — Correct: both meanings are right and in the order asked (prohibition first, then certiorari).
4. By what authority — To have the body
'By what authority' is quo warranto and 'to have the body' is habeas corpus.
✗ — Neither meaning belongs to prohibition or certiorari.

points: Five writs: habeas corpus (to have the body), mandamus (we command), prohibition (to forbid), certiorari (to be certified or informed), quo warranto (by what authority or warrant).
Watch the order asked in 'respectively' questions.

POL-6.1.9-P122-09.lead: Option 1: Article 32 relief is available because the authorities' failure threatens Article 21; private origin of pollution does not defeat the claim.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Art 32 addresses authorities' failure
The State's inaction in enforcing pollution laws violates the right to life.
2. Private ownership excludes Art 32
Says private polluters defeat the petition.
✗ — The petition targets the authorities' failure; the Court also directed private polluters to pay.
3. Duties unenforceable if private industry
Says the regulators' statutory duties vanish when the polluters are private industries.
✗ — Statutory duties of regulators remain fully enforceable.
4. Automatic closure
Says every pollution allegation leads automatically to closure of industries.
✗ — The Court acts on evidence and expert reports, not automatically.

points: The Bichhri case involved toxic sludge from chemical units in Rajasthan.
The Court applied the 'polluter pays' principle.
Right to a clean environment is read into Article 21.

POL-6.1.9-P123-01.lead: Quo warranto ('by what authority') tests a person's legal right to hold a public office.

head: Option
Meaning
Fits?
rows: Mandamus
'We command'. Court orders a public official or body to do a legal duty it failed to do.
No — no duty is being refused
Prohibition
'To forbid'. Higher court stops a lower court or tribunal before it exceeds its jurisdiction.
No — no court case to stop
Habeas corpus
'To have the body'. Court orders the detainer to bring the person to court and checks if the detention is legal.
No — no one is detained
Quo warranto
'By what authority'. Court asks a person to show his legal right to hold a public office.
Yes — it tests the right to the office

points: Stem: a person holds a statutory public office without the required qualification — his authority is in doubt.
It lies only for a substantive public office created by statute or Constitution, not a private or ministerial post (Laxmikanth p.161).
Any public-minded person can seek it, not only the aggrieved person.
POL-6.1.9-P123-01.also: Example: a Vice-Chancellor appointed without the qualification the Act requires.

POL-6.1.9-P123-02.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: False
Quo warranto does not require the petitioner to claim the office for himself. It only questions the legality of the present holder's title.
True
Laxmikanth notes that quo warranto can be sought by any public-minded person, not necessarily the aggrieved person.

points: Options 1 and 3 fail because they include statement 1.
Option 4 fails because statement 2 is correct.
Hook: quo warranto has wide locus standi, unlike habeas corpus-type personal claims.

POL-6.1.9-P123-03.lead: Option 1: a mere preference for a more meritorious candidate does not show an unlawful title.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Preference alone not enough
Correct: quo warranto needs lack of legal title.
2. Comparative merit enough
Treats a candidate's greater comparative merit as a ground for quo warranto.
✗ — If rules and qualifications are satisfied, the title is lawful.
3. Better candidate makes appointment void
Treats a lawful appointment as void because a better candidate existed.
✗ — Existence of a better candidate does not break any legal rule.
4. Court replaces suitability judgment
Asks the court to decide who is the more suitable candidate.
✗ — Suitability is for the appointing authority; the court checks only legality.

points: Quo warranto asks 'by what authority' — it checks eligibility and compliance with appointment rules.
It is not a tool to re-run a selection on merit.

POL-6.1.9-P123-04.lead: Option 3: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — quo warranto tests title to a public office only.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Quo warranto does not lie for a purely private office.
R
True
The writ tests the legality of a claim to a public office.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Since the writ exists only to test claims to public office, it cannot apply to private offices.
Option 1 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 2 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.
Option 4 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A, so "does not explain" is wrong.

POL-6.1.9-P123-05.lead: Option 3: judicial orders of civil courts are not amenable to certiorari under Article 226; Article 227 supervision is separate.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 226 and 227 identical
Says Articles 226 and 227 are the same jurisdiction.
✗ — Article 226 is writ jurisdiction; Article 227 is supervisory superintendence over subordinate courts.
2. All civil-court orders open to certiorari
This was the view of Surya Dev Rai (2003).
✗ — Radhey Shyam overruled it on this point.
3. Outside 226; 227 distinct
Correct holding of the three-judge bench.
4. Removes all remedies
Says the ruling leaves the party with no remedy against civil-court orders.
✗ — Appeal, revision and Article 227 supervision remain available.

points: The judges reasoned that civil courts are not 'authorities' to which certiorari issues.
Hook: Civil court order → Article 227, not Article 226 writ.

POL-6.1.9-P123-06.lead: Option 4: Article 32(2) expressly allows directions, orders or writs, 'including' the five writs, for enforcing Part III rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only writ names confer power
Treats the five named writs as an exhaustive list of what the Court can issue.
✗ — The word 'including' makes the list illustrative.
2. Any order for any dispute
Says Article 32 allows any order in any dispute, removing the Part III limit.
✗ — Article 32 is only for enforcing Fundamental Rights.
3. Parliament permits each case
Says Parliament must approve each case before the Court can act.
✗ — The power flows directly from the Constitution.
4. Directions and orders included
Says Article 32(2) covers directions and orders as well as the five writs.
✓ — Correct: the text says 'directions or orders or writs, including' the five writs, so the respondent's narrow reading fails.

points: This flexible power lets the Supreme Court give guidelines and continuing mandamus in PIL cases.
Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right and part of the basic structure.

POL-6.1.9-P123-07.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True
Quo warranto literally means 'by what authority or warrant'.
True
If the holder lacks a lawful title, the court can declare the office vacant and oust him; it prevents illegal usurpation of public office.
False
The writ only removes the unlawful holder. Filling the office is for the appointing authority under the rules, not an automatic gift to the petitioner.

points: Option 1 fails because it leaves out true statement 2.
Options 3 and 4 fail because they include false statement 3.

POL-6.1.9-P124-01.lead: Both statements are correct, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True

Article 33 lets Parliament, by law, decide how far the Fundamental Rights of armed forces, police, intelligence staff and similar forces are restricted or abrogated. State legislatures have no such power.
True
The stated purpose is to ensure proper discharge of their duties and maintenance of discipline among them.

points: Options 1 and 2 fail because each drops one correct statement.
Option 4 fails because both statements are correct.
POL-6.1.9-P124-01.also: Examples of such laws: Army Act 1950, Air Force Act 1950, Navy Act 1957, Police Forces (Restriction of Rights) Act 1966.

POL-6.1.9-P124-02.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 1 (1, 2 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True
Article 33(b) covers forces charged with maintenance of public order, such as police forces.
True
Article 33(c) covers persons in bureaus or organisations set up by the State for intelligence or counter-intelligence.
True
Article 33(d) covers persons employed in telecommunication systems set up for these forces or organisations.
False
Article 33 does not cover every civilian government employee; it is limited to the listed forces and organisations.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 fail because they include statement 4.
Armed forces themselves are covered by Article 33(a).

POL-6.1.9-P124-03.lead: Option 4: Article 34 lets Parliament indemnify acts done to maintain or restore order in a martial-law area.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 35
Gives Parliament exclusive power to make laws giving effect to certain Fundamental Rights.
2. Article 352
Proclamation of National Emergency on war, external aggression or armed rebellion.
✗ — It is an emergency provision, not martial-law indemnity.
3. Article 33
Lets Parliament restrict rights of armed forces, police and similar forces.
4. Article 34
Restriction of rights while martial law is in force; indemnity and validation.

points: Parliament can also validate any sentence, punishment or forfeiture ordered under martial law in that area.
An Act of Indemnity cannot be challenged for violating Fundamental Rights.
POL-6.1.9-P124-03.also: 'Martial law' is not defined anywhere in the Constitution; it is implicit in Article 34.

POL-6.1.9-P124-04.lead: Option 2: under both Article 33 and Article 34, the power belongs to Parliament.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 33 State Legislature / 34 Parliament
Gives the Article 33 power to State Legislatures.
✗ — Article 33 power is with Parliament only.
2. 33 Parliament modifies / 34 Parliament indemnity
Article 33: Parliament may modify FRs of forces; Article 34: Parliament may grant indemnity during martial law.
✓ — Correct: both subjects are in the right articles and the power under both lies with Parliament.
3. Subjects swapped
Places indemnity under 33 and forces under 34.
✗ — The subjects are reversed: modifying rights of forces is Article 33, and indemnity for acts during martial law is Article 34.
4. 34 President grants indemnity
Gives Article 34 power to the executive.
✗ — Indemnity requires a law made by Parliament.

points: Article 33: restrict rights of forces for discipline.
Article 34: indemnify and validate acts in a martial-law area.
Article 35 adds that such laws are made only by Parliament.

POL-6.1.9-P124-05.lead: All three statements are correct, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True
Laxmikanth lists the Police Forces (Restriction of Rights) Act, 1966 among laws made by Parliament under Article 33.
True
A law under Article 33 can exclude courts martial from the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts for enforcement of Fundamental Rights.
True
'Members of the armed forces' also includes non-combatant employees like barbers, carpenters, mechanics and cooks.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out one correct statement, so they fail.

POL-6.1.9-P124-06.lead: Option 2: High Courts can review Armed Forces Tribunal decisions under Article 226, but should do so sparingly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Art 227(4) excludes every review
Says Article 227(4) leaves High Courts no role at all over AFT decisions.
✗ — Article 227(4) only removes superintendence over armed-forces tribunals; it does not touch Article 226 judicial review.
2. 226 review available, sparingly
Correct holding of Parashotam Dass (2023).
3. Rehearing as first appeal
Treats the High Court as a first appellate court rehearing the case.
✗ — Judicial review checks legality, not a full rehearing.
4. Tribunal excludes review by declaring finality
Lets the tribunal shut out review by declaring its own decisions final.
✗ — Judicial review is part of the basic structure and cannot be ousted by the tribunal.

points: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that High Court review of tribunal decisions under Articles 226/227 is part of the basic structure.
POL-6.1.9-P124-06.also: Judicial review is part of the basic structure (L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).

POL-6.1.9-P124-07.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: False
Article 34 allows indemnity for any person in the service of the Union or a State 'or any other person', not only armed-forces members.
True
Parliament may validate any sentence passed, punishment inflicted or forfeiture ordered under martial law in the area.

points: Options 1 and 3 fail because they include false statement 1.
Option 4 fails because statement 2 is correct.

POL-6.1.9-P124-08.lead: Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — aid presupposes a functioning civil authority.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Armed forces called in aid of civil power do not replace civil administration.
R

head: Statement

Why
rows: 1. Citizens aged 18+ on the fixed date can register, subject to disqualifications
True
Article 326 provides adult suffrage for Lok Sabha and Assembly elections: every citizen of at least 18 years, not disqualified by the Constitution or law, can register.
2. Every House must be directly elected by all adult residents including non-citizens
False
Article 326 covers only the Lok Sabha and Legislative Assemblies, and only citizens; Rajya Sabha and Legislative Councils are indirectly elected.
3. It removes all disqualifications
False
Article 326 expressly keeps disqualifications such as non-residence, unsoundness of mind, crime or corrupt practice.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 wrongly include statement 2 or 3.
The voting age was reduced from 21 to 18 by the 61st Amendment Act, 1988.

POL-6.1.9-P128-07.lead: Option 3 (1–2–3) is correct: A. Article 265 → Part XII; B. Article 301 → Part XIII; C. Article 326 → Part XV.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Article 265 – taxation only by authority of law
1 – Part XII
Part XII covers Finance, Property, Contracts and Suits (Articles 264-300A).
B. Article 301 – freedom of trade and commerce
2 – Part XIII
Part XIII is Trade, Commerce and Intercourse within India (Articles 301-307).
C. Article 326 – adult suffrage
3 – Part XV
Part XV is Elections (Articles 324-329A).

points: Hook: XII money, XIII trade, XV elections – Article numbers rise with the Part numbers.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-2, B-1 (correct: A-1, B-2).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives B-3, C-2 (correct: B-2, C-3).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-3, C-1 (correct: A-1, C-3).

POL-6.1.9-P128-08.lead: Option 4 (A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3) is correct: A. Swaran Singh Committee → Fundamental Duties; B. B.P. Mandal Commission → Identification of socially and educationally backward classes; C. M.N. Venkatachaliah Commission → Review of the working of the Constitution; D. Ram Nandan Prasad Committee → Creamy layer criteria among OBCs.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
