2 – Fundamental Duties
Its report led the 42nd Amendment to add Part IVA (Article 51A).
B. B.P. Mandal Commission (1979)
4 – Identification of socially and educationally backward classes
Second Backward Classes Commission; recommended 27% OBC reservation.
C. M.N. Venkatachaliah Commission (2000)
1 – Review of the working of the Constitution
National Commission to Review the Working of the Constitution (NCRWC).
D. Ram Nandan Prasad Committee (1993)
3 – Creamy layer criteria among OBCs
Set up after Indra Sawhney (1992) to identify the creamy layer.

points: Mandal identified the OBCs; Ram Nandan decided who among them is 'creamy' – do not swap these two.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives B-3, D-4 (correct: B-4, D-3).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A-1, C-2 (correct: A-2, C-1).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-4, B-2 (correct: A-2, B-4).

POL-6.1.9-P128-09.lead: Option 1: the NCRWC proposed that the State should, by suitable legislation, secure rural wage employment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Oblige the State to enact law for rural wage employment
NCRWC suggested a new right to rural wage employment for a minimum of 80 days a year, secured by law.
Omit Article 41 (right to work)
False; the commission wanted to strengthen the right to work, not delete it.
Move rural employment to the Union List
False; it made no such change in the division of subjects.
Leave it to market forces
False; this is the opposite of its proposal for a legal guarantee.

points: NCRWC listed new rights it wanted added, including the right to rural wage employment for at least 80 days in a year.
Later, the MGNREGA, 2005 gave a statutory guarantee of 100 days of wage employment, which shows the same idea.

POL-6.1.9-P129-01.lead: Option 2 (A–1, B–2) is correct: A. Shankari Prasad → First Amendment; B. Sajjan Singh → Seventeenth Amendment.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Shankari Prasad (1951)
1 – First Amendment
Upheld the 1st Amendment; held Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368.
B. Sajjan Singh (1965)
2 – Seventeenth Amendment
Upheld the 17th Amendment (1964) on land reform, repeating Shankari Prasad's view.

points: Both cases favoured Parliament; Golaknath (1967) later reversed this view.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-2, B-1 (correct: A-1, B-2).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives B-1 (correct: B-2).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-2 (correct: A-1).

POL-6.1.9-P129-02.lead: Option 3: Golak Nath (1967) held that Parliament cannot take away or abridge Fundamental Rights by amendment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Shankari Prasad (1951)
Held that Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368; an amendment is not 'law' under Article 13.
Sajjan Singh (1965)
Followed Shankari Prasad and upheld the 17th Amendment.
Golak Nath (1967)
Held that an amendment is 'law' under Article 13, so Fundamental Rights cannot be abridged.
A.K. Gopalan (1950)
A case on preventive detention and the meaning of 'procedure established by law' in Article 21.

points: Parliament answered Golak Nath with the 24th Amendment (1971); Kesavananda Bharati (1973) overruled Golak Nath and gave the basic structure doctrine.
Memory hook: Shankari and Sajjan said 'Yes, amend'; Golak Nath said 'No'.

POL-6.1.9-P129-03.lead: Option 4: Kesavananda Bharati was decided by 13 judges by a 7 to 6 majority.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 11 judges; 6–5
This is the Golak Nath (1967) bench size and split.
9 judges; 5–4
Does not match Kesavananda; 9-judge benches decided cases like Indra Sawhney.
13 judges; unanimous
Bench size is right, but the court was sharply divided, not unanimous.
13 judges; 7–6
The largest bench in Indian history; a 7–6 majority laid down the basic structure doctrine.

points: The case was decided on 24 April 1973 and presided over by Chief Justice S.M. Sikri.
It held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, but not its basic structure.

POL-6.1.9-P129-04.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so the answer is option 4 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Section 14 struck down for blocking disclosure of grounds
True
The Court held Section 14 of the Preventive Detention Act, 1950 invalid because it stopped the detenue from disclosing the grounds of detention to the court.
2. This made the whole Act invalid
False
Section 14 was severable, so the rest of the Act stood; this is the doctrine of severability under Article 13.

points: Option 1 (2 only) and option 2 (both) wrongly accept statement 2; option 3 wrongly rejects statement 1.
Gopalan is also known for its narrow reading of 'procedure established by law' in Article 21, later changed by Maneka Gandhi (1978).

POL-6.1.9-P129-05.lead: Option 2: Prospective overruling — the Golak Nath rule applied only to future amendments.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Pith and substance
Used to decide which list (Union/State) a law truly belongs to.
Prospective overruling
A new ruling applies only to the future and does not undo past decisions or laws.
Colourable legislation
What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly; tests legislative competence.
Territorial nexus
Allows a State law to apply to things outside the State if there is a real connection.

points: In Golak Nath, the Court used prospective overruling so that the 1st, 4th and 17th Amendments stayed valid, but future amendments could not abridge Fundamental Rights.
The doctrine prevents chaos that would follow if old amendments were suddenly void.

POL-6.1.9-P129-06.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 4 (both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Shankari Prasad separated ordinary law from amendments
True
In 1951 the Court held that 'law' in Article 13 means only ordinary law, not an amendment made under Article 368.
2. Golak Nath treated an amendment as 'law'
True
In 1967 the Court held that an amendment is 'law' under Article 13, so it cannot abridge Fundamental Rights.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each reject a true statement.
The 24th Amendment (1971) then added Article 13(4) to say Article 13 does not apply to amendments, restoring the Shankari Prasad view.

POL-6.1.9-P129-07.lead: Option 3: Chief Justice S.M. Sikri presided over the 13-judge Kesavananda Bharati bench.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: K. Subba Rao
Chief Justice who led the Golak Nath bench (1967).
Patanjali Sastri
Early Chief Justice (1951–1954); Shankari Prasad was decided in his time.
S.M. Sikri
Chief Justice 1971–1973; presided over Kesavananda Bharati.
Y.V. Chandrachud
Longest-serving Chief Justice (1978–1985); Minerva Mills was under him.

points: Kesavananda was decided in April 1973, at the end of Sikri's term.
Hook: Subba Rao = Golak Nath; Sikri = Kesavananda; Chandrachud = Minerva Mills.

POL-6.1.9-P129-08.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 1 (both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Majority followed Shankari Prasad and upheld the 17th Amendment
True
In Sajjan Singh (1965) the Court held that Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights under Article 368.
2. Justice Mudholkar raised doubt about changing basic features
True
In his separate opinion he asked whether basic features of the Constitution could be changed by amendment, an idea later used in Kesavananda.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 each reject a true statement.
Mudholkar J.'s question is seen as the seed of the basic structure doctrine.

POL-6.1.9-P130-01.lead: Option 2: Minerva Mills (1980) held that balance between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: DPSPs can never influence interpretation
False; courts use DPSPs to interpret laws and rights.
Rights and DPSPs must be balanced; harmony is basic structure
Minerva Mills struck down part of the 42nd Amendment that gave all DPSPs priority over Articles 14 and 19.
Parliament cannot amend Part IV
False; Parliament can amend Part IV under Article 368.
Part IV amendments are immune from review
False; judicial review itself is part of the basic structure.

points: The 42nd Amendment (1976) extended Article 31C to all DPSPs; Minerva Mills said this destroyed the balance.
The Court said Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are like two wheels of a chariot.

POL-6.1.9-P130-02.lead: Option 4: Indra Sawhney (1992) upheld the 27% OBC reservation, subject to exclusion of the creamy layer.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: M.R. Balaji (1963)
Held that reservation should generally not exceed 50%.
Janhit Abhiyan (2022)
Upheld the 10% EWS reservation (103rd Amendment).
State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh (2024)
Allowed sub-classification within Scheduled Castes.
Indra Sawhney (1992)
The Mandal case; upheld 27% OBC quota with creamy-layer exclusion and the 50% ceiling.

points: The 27% quota came from the Mandal Commission recommendations, implemented in 1990.
Conditions: creamy layer excluded, total reservation normally within 50%, no reservation in promotions (later changed by the 77th Amendment).

POL-6.1.9-P130-03.lead: Option 1: the First Amendment, 1951 inserted both Articles 31A and 31B.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: First Amendment, 1951
Added Articles 31A (saving of land reform laws) and 31B with the Ninth Schedule.
Fourth Amendment, 1955
Changed Article 31(2) to bar challenges on adequacy of compensation.
Seventeenth Amendment, 1964
Widened 'estate' in Article 31A and added laws to the Ninth Schedule.
Twenty-fourth Amendment, 1971
Affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights (Article 13(4)).

points: The First Amendment protected zamindari abolition laws from challenge under Fundamental Rights.
Article 31B with the Ninth Schedule shields listed laws; after I.R. Coelho (2007) laws added after 24 April 1973 can be reviewed.

POL-6.1.9-P130-04.lead: Option 4: compensation must be at least the market value for self-cultivated land within the ceiling.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: No acquisition at all
False; acquisition is allowed if market-value compensation is paid.
Only original purchase price
False; the proviso requires market value, not purchase price.
Compensation may be omitted
False; this protected portion is exactly where compensation is compulsory.
Compensation not less than market value
The second proviso to Article 31A(1), added by the 17th Amendment, guarantees this.

points: Article 31A protects land reform laws, but small cultivators' own land within the ceiling must get market-value compensation.
This protects the personal land of farmers while allowing reforms on large estates.

POL-6.1.9-P130-05.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so the answer is option 3 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Challenge on inadequacy of compensation barred
True
The 4th Amendment (1955) made the adequacy of compensation non-justiciable in courts.
2. It removed public purpose and authority of law
False
Acquisition still needed a public purpose and authority of law; only the adequacy question was closed.

points: Option 1 and option 2 accept the false statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
Later the 25th Amendment (1971) replaced the word 'compensation' with 'amount'.

POL-6.1.9-P130-06.lead: Option 2: the 24th Amendment made it compulsory for the President to give assent to an amendment bill.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Return for reconsideration
Allowed only for ordinary bills (Article 111); not for amendment bills.
Shall give assent
The 24th Amendment (1971) amended Article 368 to make assent compulsory.
Refer to a referendum
India has no referendum system for amendments.
Obtain Supreme Court approval
No such step exists; courts review only after the law is made.

points: So the President has neither an absolute veto nor a suspensive veto on a constitutional amendment bill.
The same amendment also added Article 13(4) and 368(3).

POL-6.1.9-P130-07.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 2 (both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Mohini Jain decided in 1992
True
Mohini Jain v. State of Karnataka (1992) said the right to education flows from Article 21.
2. Unni Krishnan decided in 1993
True
Unni Krishnan (1993) limited it: free education until 14 years; after that subject to State capacity.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 each reject a true date.
Article 21A (free and compulsory education for 6–14 years) was added later by the 86th Amendment, 2002.

POL-6.1.9-P130-08.lead: Option 4: Unni Krishnan recognised free education till 14; after that it depends on the State's economic capacity.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: No connection between education and Article 21
False; the Court read the right to education into Article 21.
Confined to 6–14 by applying Article 21A
False; Article 21A did not exist in 1993 (added in 2002).
Free education at every level regardless of capacity
False; the student's claim is exactly what the Court rejected.
Free till 14, then subject to State capacity
This is the actual holding, which also partly overruled Mohini Jain.

points: The Court drew on Article 45 (DPSP on free education) to fix the age of 14.
Higher and professional education is a right only within the State's economic limits.

POL-6.1.9-P130-09.lead: Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — limited amending power is itself basic (Minerva Mills).

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Parliament cannot turn its limited amending power into an unlimited one.
R
True
Minerva Mills held that limited amending power is itself a basic feature.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. If limited power is basic, an attempt to make it unlimited would destroy a basic feature.
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A, so "does not explain" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.

POL-6.1.9-P131-01.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 26th Amendment (1971) abolished privy purses
True
It ended the privy purses and privileges of former rulers of princely States.
2. It inserted Article 363A
True
Article 363A says recognition of rulers shall cease and privy purses are abolished.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each reject a true statement.
The 26th Amendment also omitted Articles 291 and 362 relating to privy purses and rulers' rights.

POL-6.1.9-P131-02.lead: Option 3: the 97th Amendment Act is of 2011, and it came into force in 2012.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Act year is right, but it did not come into force in 2011.
Gives 2012 for both; the Act year is wrong because the Act is titled 2011.
✗ — The Act is of 2011; only its coming into force was in 2012.
Passed and assented in 2011; came into force on 15 February 2012.
Gives 2012 as the Act year and 2013 as the start year.
✗ — Both years are wrong: the Act is of 2011 and it came into force on 15 February 2012.

points: The 97th Amendment made forming cooperative societies a Fundamental Right (Article 19(1)(c)), added Article 43B (DPSP) and Part IXB.
In 2021 the Supreme Court struck down Part IXB as far as it covered State cooperatives.

POL-6.1.9-P131-03.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 'Amount' replaced 'compensation'
True
The 25th Amendment (1971) used the word 'amount' so courts could not test it as fair compensation.
2. No challenge on the ground of non-cash payment
True
The amended clause said the law cannot be questioned because the amount is given otherwise than in cash.
3. Removed public purpose and authority of law
False
Acquisition still required a public purpose and authority of law.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.
The 25th Amendment also added Article 31C, protecting laws implementing Article 39(b) and (c).

POL-6.1.9-P131-04.lead: Option 4 (2–3–1) is correct: A. Omission of provisions → Articles 291 and 362; B. Insertion of the abolition provision → Article 363A; C. Substitution of the definition of 'Ruler' → Article 366(22).

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Omission of provisions
2 – Articles 291 and 362
291 (privy purse sums) and 362 (rights of rulers) were deleted.
B. Insertion of the abolition provision
3 – Article 363A
New 363A ended recognition of rulers and abolished privy purses.
C. Substitution of the definition of 'Ruler'
1 – Article 366(22)
Article 366 is the definitions clause; clause (22) was rewritten.

points: The 26th Amendment (1971) came after the Supreme Court struck down the Presidential order de-recognising princes (Madhav Rao Scindia, 1970).
Option 1 is wrong: it gives B-1, C-3 (correct: B-3, C-1).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A-3, B-2 (correct: A-2, B-3).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-1, C-2 (correct: A-2, C-1).

POL-6.1.9-P132-01.lead: Option 3: the Court quashed the criminal cases because no offence was made out; moral disapproval is not a crime.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Upheld complaints because views offended morality
False; the Court said offending social morality is not by itself an offence.
Free expression can never be restricted
False; Article 19(2) allows reasonable restrictions.
Quashed proceedings; morality is not criminality
The Court found no prima facie offence and protected free expression.
Every live-in relationship equals marriage
False; the Court did not give such a ruling.

points: The case shows that unpopular views are protected by Article 19(1)(a) unless they fall under Article 19(2).
Criminal law should not be used to punish opinions simply because many people dislike them.

POL-6.1.9-P87-01.lead: Option 2: a legal right is one that the law recognises and courts can enforce.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Approval by the community
Creates a social or moral expectation, not a legal right.
Recognition and enforceability under law
This is what makes a claim a legal right.
Longstanding observance
Long custom alone does not make a right enforceable.
Connection with ethics
Moral rights depend on conscience, not on courts.

points: The courtesy in the stem is a moral or social right; the statute's entitlement is a legal right.
Fundamental Rights are legal rights with the highest protection because the Constitution guarantees them.

POL-6.1.9-P87-02.lead: Option 2 (A–3, B–4, C–1, D–2) is correct: A. Civil → Equal civic standing without discrimination; B. Political → Voting, contesting, holding office; C. Economic → Basic needs, livelihood; D. Cultural → Language and culture.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Civil
3 – Equal civic standing without discrimination
Civil rights protect the person's equal status and freedom in society.
B. Political
4 – Voting, contesting, holding office
Political rights let a citizen take part in government.
C. Economic
1 – Basic needs, livelihood
Economic rights concern work, wages and freedom from want.
D. Cultural
2 – Language and culture
Cultural rights protect a group's language, script and culture.

points: Ask: does the right protect my person (civil), my vote (political), my bread (economic) or my culture (cultural)?
Option 1 is wrong: it gives B-1, C-4 (correct: B-4, C-1).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-2, D-3 (correct: A-3, D-2).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives C-2, D-1 (correct: C-1, D-2).

POL-6.1.9-P88-01.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Part III covers Articles 12 to 35
True
Fundamental Rights are listed in Part III, Articles 12 to 35.
2. Article 300A is a Fundamental Right
False
Article 300A is in Part XII; the 44th Amendment (1978) made property a legal (constitutional) right, not a Fundamental Right.

points: Options 2 and 3 accept the false statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
Property was removed from Part III by deleting Articles 19(1)(f) and 31.

POL-6.1.9-P88-02.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so the answer is option 4 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Issued in 1215 under King John in Latin; limited royal power
True
Magna Carta was the charter of rights the barons got from King John in 1215.
2. A universal modern charter of equal rights for all
False
It protected mainly barons and free men; it was a medieval feudal document, not a modern universal charter.

points: Options 1 and 2 accept the false statement 2; option 3 rejects the true statement 1.
Magna Carta is called the first written document on fundamental rights of citizens.

POL-6.1.9-P88-03.lead: Option 3: suspension of Fundamental Rights during Emergency was borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: United States
Source of Fundamental Rights, judicial review, independent judiciary.
Ireland
Source of Directive Principles and nomination to Rajya Sabha.
Weimar Germany
Source of the provision to suspend Fundamental Rights during Emergency.
Canada
Source of federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Centre.

points: In India this is under Articles 358 and 359.
Hook: Weimar = Emergency suspension.

POL-6.1.9-P88-04.lead: Option 1: the Commonwealth of India Bill, 1925 included free elementary education among fundamental rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Commonwealth of India Bill, 1925
Drafted under Annie Besant; it listed rights such as free speech and free elementary education.
Government of India Act, 1919
Introduced dyarchy in provinces; no bill of rights.
Indian Councils Act, 1909
Morley-Minto reforms; separate electorates for Muslims.
Government of India Act, 1858
Transferred power from the Company to the Crown.

points: This was one of the early Indian demands for written rights; later came the Nehru Report (1928).
None of the British Acts gave a bill of Fundamental Rights.

POL-6.1.9-P88-05.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is option 4 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Guaranteed and protected by the Constitution
True
They are 'fundamental' because the Constitution guarantees them and courts protect them (Article 32).
2. Essential for all-round development
True
They are most essential for the material, intellectual, moral and spiritual development of individuals.
3. Never subject to restriction
False
Fundamental Rights are not absolute; the State can impose reasonable restrictions.

points: Options 2 and 3 include the false statement 3; option 1 leaves out the true statement 2.
Two reasons for 'fundamental': supreme law guarantees them, and they are vital for human development.

POL-6.1.9-P89-01.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. First ten US amendments = Bill of Rights
True
The Bill of Rights is the first ten amendments of the US Constitution (1791).
2. Part III inspired by the US Bill of Rights
True
The Fundamental Rights in Part III were inspired by the US Constitution, i.e. the Bill of Rights.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each reject a true statement.
Part III is often called the Magna Carta of India.

POL-6.1.9-P89-02.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so the answer is option 4 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Guaranteed right to approach the Supreme Court for Part I rights
True
The Sub-Committee's Part I listed justiciable rights, with a guaranteed remedy in the Supreme Court.
2. Part II principles directly enforceable
False
Part II contained non-justiciable policy principles, which later became the Directive Principles.

points: Options 1 and 2 accept the false statement 2; option 3 rejects the true statement 1.
This split (justiciable vs non-justiciable) is the origin of Part III vs Part IV.

POL-6.1.9-P90-01.lead: Option 2: Article 14 is for all persons, but Article 19(1)(g) is only for citizens.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Both confined to citizens
False; Article 14 uses the word 'any person'.
Article 14 for foreigner; 19(1)(g) for citizens
Correct division of who holds which right.
Both extend to foreigners equally
False; Article 19 freedoms are for citizens only.
19(1)(g) for foreigners, not 14
Gives Article 19(1)(g) to foreigners but denies them Article 14.
✗ — Article 14 covers 'any person', including foreigners, while Article 19(1)(g) is only for citizens; the option inverts this.

points: Rights for citizens only: Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, 30.
Rights for all persons: Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25 to 28.

POL-6.1.9-P90-02.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Clauses (1) and (2) not for enemy aliens
True
Article 22(3) says these protections do not apply to an enemy alien.
2. Same exclusion for preventive detainees
True
Article 22(3) also excludes persons detained under a preventive detention law.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each reject a true statement.
Clauses (1) and (2) give the right to know grounds, to consult a lawyer, and to be produced before a magistrate within 24 hours.

POL-6.1.9-P90-03.lead: Option 1 (20, 21A, 23, 24) is correct: A. Protection in respect of conviction → Article 20; B. Free and compulsory education 6-14 → Article 21A; C. Traffic in human beings and forced labour → Article 23; D. Child labour below 14 in hazardous work → Article 24.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Protection in respect of conviction
Article 20
No ex-post-facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination.
B. Free and compulsory education 6-14
Article 21A
Article 21A, added by the 86th Amendment, 2002, makes free and compulsory education for children aged 6 to 14 a Fundamental Right, so B matches Article 21A.
C. Traffic in human beings and forced labour
Article 23
Article 23 prohibits traffic in human beings, begar (forced unpaid labour) and other forms of forced labour, so C matches Article 23.
D. Child labour below 14 in hazardous work
Article 24
Bans employment of children below 14 in factories, mines, hazardous jobs.

POL-6.1.9-P92-01.lead: Option 2 (14–18; 19–22; 25–28; 29–30) is correct: A. Equality → 14–18; B. Freedom → 19–22; C. Freedom of religion → 25–28; D. Cultural and educational rights → 29–30.

POL-6.1.9-P94-01.lead: Doctrine of severability (option 3): only the invalid part is struck down and the separable valid part survives.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Doctrine of eclipse
Applies to a pre-Constitution law that violates Fundamental Rights; it becomes dormant, not dead, and revives if the conflict is removed.
Doctrine of waiver
The idea that a person may give up a right; the Supreme Court held it does not apply to Fundamental Rights.
Doctrine of severability
When one provision violates a Fundamental Right and can be separated, only that provision is void and the rest of the law continues.
Doctrine of prospective overruling
A court applies its new ruling only to future cases, leaving past actions undisturbed (Golaknath, 1967).

points: Article 13 declares laws void 'to the extent of' inconsistency — these words are the textual basis of severability.
Memory hook: severability = 'cut off the bad part, keep the good part'.

POL-6.1.9-P94-02.lead: Option 2: Article 14 cannot be waived; Basheshar Nath (1959) held that waiver does not apply to Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Personal benefit, written consent can relinquish
False — Article 14 is a command to the State placed in the Constitution on grounds of public policy, not a private benefit one can sign away.
Cannot be waived in this manner
True — no individual can authorise the State to discriminate arbitrarily against him.
Valid if part of voluntary financial settlement
False — a settlement is still a waiver; voluntariness does not change the constitutional bar.
Valid if a benefit was already received
False — accepting a benefit does not make arbitrary discrimination lawful or estop the person from challenging it.

points: Concept: Fundamental Rights limit State power in the public interest, so the State cannot escape them by private agreement.
Memory hook: Basheshar Nath — 'No waiver of Fundamental Rights'.

POL-6.1.9-P94-03.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True
In Kesavananda Bharati (1973) the Court upheld the 24th Amendment (1971), accepting that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.
False
Although Articles 13(4) and 368(3) say an amendment is not 'law' under Article 13, Kesavananda held that Parliament cannot alter the basic structure, so an amendment destroying it is invalid.

points: Option 2 (2 only) and option 3 (both) wrongly accept statement 2; option 4 (neither) wrongly rejects statement 1.
Concept: excluding amendments from Article 13 removes only the Article 13 test; the basic-structure limit on Article 368 still applies.

POL-6.1.9-P94-04.lead: Option 3: an indivisible scheme cannot be saved by artificial separation; the whole falls.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Remainder must always survive
False — the remainder survives only if it can stand on its own and still carry out the legislature's intent.
Severability label permits judicial rewriting
False — courts may cut out the invalid part but cannot rewrite a law; rewriting is the legislature's job.
Indivisible scheme cannot be saved
True — when valid and invalid parts are so interwoven that one cannot exist without the other, the entire scheme is void.
Invalid provision becomes valid
False — severability never cures the invalid part; it only decides how much of the rest can be saved.

points: Concept: severability works only when the valid part is separable; if separation would leave a law Parliament never intended, the whole law falls.
Test: would the legislature have enacted the remainder by itself? If not, nothing survives.

POL-6.1.9-P94-05.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

True/False
Why

L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held that the power of judicial review of the High Courts (Article 226) and the Supreme Court (Article 32) is part of the basic structure.
False
Tribunals can only supplement, not supplant, the High Courts; tribunal decisions remain subject to review by a High Court Division Bench, so review cannot be removed by creating a tribunal.

points: Option 2 (2 only) and option 3 (both) wrongly accept statement 2; option 4 (neither) wrongly rejects statement 1.
Concept: the clauses of Articles 323A and 323B that excluded High Court jurisdiction were struck down for this reason.

Year
Why in this order

The Court held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights, treating an amendment as 'law' under Article 13.
2. 24th Amendment

1. Kesavananda Bharati
The Court upheld the 24th Amendment but laid down the basic-structure limit.

points: Option 1 reverses the order; option 2 puts the amendment before the case it overturned; option 4 puts Kesavananda before the 24th Amendment it reviewed.

POL-6.1.9-P94-07.lead: Ultra vires (option 2): an act done beyond the powers given by law is void.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Res judicata
A matter finally decided by a competent court cannot be reopened between the same parties.
Ultra vires
Latin for 'beyond the powers'; an authority that exceeds the powers given by its parent statute acts ultra vires and the act is void.
Parens patriae
The State or court acting as guardian of persons unable to protect themselves, such as minors.
Prospective overruling
A new judicial ruling applies only to future cases, not to past transactions.

points: Concept: a statutory authority has only the powers its Act gives it; anything beyond is invalid and can be quashed by writs such as certiorari.

POL-6.1.9-P94-08.lead: Option 2: Articles 13(4) and 368(3) were inserted by the 24th Amendment (1971).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

13(1) deals with pre-Constitution laws; 368(4) was added by the 42nd Amendment (1976) and struck down in Minerva Mills.

What it is / means
Correct?

True — Fundamental Rights are placed in the Constitution as a matter of public policy, so the doctrine of waiver does not apply.
Waivable if in writing
False — the form of the waiver makes no difference; no Fundamental Right can be waived.

False — the Court recognised no such exception for Article 19 or any other right.
Lost if not asserted in time
False — a Fundamental Right is not lost by mere delay, though a court may decline relief for undue delay.

Correct?

False. It only removes the 50% ceiling for the backlog; other limits continue.

POL-6.1.9-P99-05.lead: Option 1: the proviso to Article 335 allows relaxed qualifying marks or lower evaluation standards for SC/ST reservation in promotion.

POL-6.1.9-P99-07.lead: Option 3: under the catch-up rule, when the senior general employee A is later promoted, A regains seniority over B in the promoted grade.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

False. A is promoted in normal course; the rule only decides seniority between them.
3. A regains seniority over B
True. This is the catch-up rule: an accelerated roster promotion does not carry permanent seniority.
4. B keeps seniority permanently
False. This describes consequential seniority, the opposite rule, later restored by the 85th Amendment for SCs/STs.

points: Catch-up rule came from Virpal Singh Chauhan (1995) and Ajit Singh (1996).
Memory hook: catch-up = the senior 'catches up' and gets his seniority back.

POL-651-P143-008.lead: Option 2: Article 46 asks the State to promote the educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially SCs and STs, and to protect them from social injustice and exploitation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only cultural rights of religious minorities
False. Cultural and educational rights of minorities are Fundamental Rights in Articles 29 and 30, not Article 46.
2. Educational and economic interests of weaker sections, especially SCs/STs; protection from injustice and exploitation
True. This is almost the exact wording of Article 46, a Gandhian Directive Principle.
3. Help confined exclusively to SCs and STs
False. Article 46 covers all 'weaker sections of the people'; SCs and STs are only named as the special focus ('in particular').
4. Only employment reservations, no education
False. Article 46 starts with educational interests; job reservation for backward classes is in Article 16(4), a Fundamental Right.

points: Article 46 has two parts: a positive duty (promote education and economic interests) and a protective duty (shield from social injustice and all forms of exploitation).
Laxmikanth lists Article 46 among the Gandhian principles because uplift of the weak was part of Gandhi's programme.
Memory hook: '46 = weak sections' (4+6 = 10 fingers that lift the weak).

D. Uniform civil code

Article 44 directs the State to try to secure a uniform civil code for citizens throughout India; it is a liberal-intellectual principle, so D matches 2.

True

False

True

POL-651-P144-002.lead: Option 4: Article 50 directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Separate legislature from executive
False. India has a parliamentary system where the executive sits in the legislature; Article 50 says nothing about this.
2. Separate judiciary from legislature
False. Article 50 names the executive, not the legislature.
3. Separate Union and State judicial services
False. No such split exists in Article 50; India has a single integrated judiciary.
4. Separate judiciary from executive in public services
True. This is the exact wording of Article 50.

points: The aim is to stop executive officers (like Collectors) from also acting as judges, so that justice is impartial.
The Criminal Procedure Code, 1973 gave effect to it by separating judicial magistrates from executive magistrates.
Article 50 is a liberal-intellectual principle.

POL-651-P144-003.lead: Option 4: Article 51 does not make treaties automatically part of Indian law; it only asks the State to foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Article 51(a) directs the State to promote international peace and security, so this is a real directive and not the answer.
2. Maintain just and honourable relations between nations
Article 51(b) directs the State to maintain just and honourable relations between nations, so it is a real directive.
3. Encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration
Article 51(d) directs the State to encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration, so it is a real directive.
4. Give treaties automatic force of law
Not in Article 51. In India a treaty needs a law of Parliament (Article 253) to be enforced domestically.

points: The question asks for what is NOT a directive, so the false statement (option 4) is the answer.
Article 51(c) speaks of 'respect for international law and treaty obligations' — respect, not automatic enforcement.
Article 51 is classed as a liberal-intellectual principle.

head: Statement
True/False
Why

True
Article 41 directs the State to secure the right to work; NREGA turned it into a legal guarantee of 100 days of wage work.
2. Replaced by VB-G RAM G Act, 2025 from 1 July 2026 with 125 days
True
The Viksit Bharat – Guarantee for Rozgar and Ajeevika Mission (Gramin) Act, 2025 replaced MGNREGA from 1 July 2026 and raised the guarantee to 125 days.
3. Made right to work a Fundamental Right in Part III
False

POL-651-P149-001.lead: Option 4: under Suk Das (1986), failing to inform a poor accused of free legal aid violates fair trial under Article 21, even if he never applied.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Formal application is indispensable
False. Suk Das held that a poor, often illiterate accused cannot be expected to apply for a right he does not know of.
2. Inform only after conviction
False. Legal aid is needed at trial; telling him afterwards cannot cure an unfair trial.
3. Pleading not guilty without counsel is a waiver
False. A waiver must be informed; silence by someone who was never told cannot be a waiver.
4. No application does not excuse failure to inform; Article 21 is breached
True. This is the ratio of Suk Das; the conviction was set aside.

points: Suk Das v. Union Territory of Arunachal Pradesh (1986): the court has a duty to tell the accused of his right to free legal aid.
It built on Hussainara Khatoon (1979) and Khatri (1981), which read free legal aid into Article 21.
Article 39A (directive) and Article 21 (Fundamental Right) together give this protection.

POL-651-P149-002.lead: Option 2: in MRF v. Inspector, Kerala (1998), Article 43 helped judge whether the restriction was reasonable under Article 19(6); it gave no blanket immunity.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 43 makes every welfare law immune
False. Only Article 31C gives limited immunity, and only for laws under Article 39(b) and (c).
2. Article 43 relevant for reasonableness under Article 19(6)
True. The Court upheld the paid-holidays law as a reasonable restriction, using the welfare goals of Articles 42-43.
3. Courts must ignore Article 43
False. DPSPs are not enforceable, but courts use them to interpret laws and test reasonableness.
4. Paid-holiday laws are automatically unconstitutional
False. Article 19(1)(g) is subject to reasonable restrictions in the public interest under 19(6).

points: Article 43 directs a living wage and decent conditions of work for workers.
Concept: DPSPs cannot be enforced in court, but a law that gives effect to them is more likely to be held reasonable.
Same idea as in Kasturi Lal (1980) and Bijoy Cotton Mills (1955).

POL-651-P149-003.lead: Option 4: Pannalal Bansilal Pitti (1996) held that reform may be gradual; the legislature can tackle one community's problems first.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Must wait for a UCC
False. The Court said waiting for a uniform law is not required before reforming one area.
2. All communities on an identical timetable
False. The Court said a uniform law at one stroke may be counter-productive to unity.
3. Article 44 directly enforceable
False. Article 44 is a Directive Principle and cannot be enforced in court (Article 37).
4. Reform may proceed in stages
True. This is the holding; the AP law on Hindu religious endowments was upheld.

points: Pannalal Bansilal Pitti v. State of Andhra Pradesh (1996) upheld the AP Charitable and Hindu Religious Institutions and Endowments Act, 1987.
Concept: equality (Article 14) does not demand that every community be reformed at once.
Link to Article 44: UCC is a goal to be reached gradually.

POL-651-P149-004.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Talaq-e-biddat set aside by 3:2
True
In Shayara Bano v. Union of India (2017) the five-judge bench set aside instant triple talaq by a 3:2 majority.
2. Every judge reached an identical finding under Articles 14, 15, 21 and 25
False
The judges split: Justice Nariman and Lalit held it arbitrary under Article 14; Justice Kurian Joseph held it un-Islamic; the CJI Khehar and Justice Nazeer dissented.

points: Option 2 and 3 wrongly accept statement 2; option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1.
Concept: a majority result can rest on different reasons given by different judges.
Hook: 3:2 — three against triple talaq.
POL-651-P149-004.also: Parliament then passed the Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Marriage) Act, 2019.

POL-651-P149-005.lead: Option 3: in Sarla Mudgal (1995), the second marriage is void while the first Hindu marriage is not legally dissolved.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Conversion automatically dissolves first marriage
False. A Hindu marriage can be ended only by a decree under the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955.
2. Conversion alone validates second marriage
False. The Court held the second marriage void and the husband liable for bigamy (Section 494 IPC).
3. Second marriage invalid while first subsists
True. This is the ratio of Sarla Mudgal.
4. Valid on first wife's consent
False. Consent cannot dissolve a marriage; only a court decree can.

points: Sarla Mudgal v. Union of India (1995) stopped conversion being used to escape the bar on bigamy.
The Court also urged the government to take steps towards a Uniform Civil Code under Article 44.

POL-651-P149-006.lead: Option 2: in Shah Bano (1985), religion did not exclude a divorced Muslim woman from maintenance under Section 125 CrPC.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Personal law excluded her
False. The Court held Section 125 is a secular provision that applies to all religions.
2. Not excluded by religion
True. This is the holding in Mohd. Ahmed Khan v. Shah Bano Begum (1985).
3. Divorce removes her from 'wife'
False. The explanation to Section 125 includes a divorced woman who has not remarried.
4. Maintenance never beyond iddat
False. The Court allowed maintenance beyond iddat if she cannot maintain herself.

points: Section 125 CrPC aims to prevent destitution, so it applies whatever the religion.
The Court also lamented that Article 44 (UCC) had remained a dead letter.
POL-651-P149-006.also: The Muslim Women (Protection of Rights on Divorce) Act, 1986 followed; Danial Latifi (2001) upheld it.

PRAC-POL-E4B11472E7F5.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are Gandhian, so the answer is option 3 (1 and 3 only).

True/False

True (Gandhian)
Article 48's cow-protection part is listed by Laxmikanth among Gandhian principles.
2. Protect environment, forests and wildlife
False (not Gandhian)
Article 48A (42nd Amendment, 1976) is a liberal-intellectual principle.
3. Cottage industries in rural areas
True (Gandhian)
Article 43's cottage-industry part reflects Gandhi's village self-reliance (village swaraj).

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 wrongly include statement 2.
Other Gandhian directives: village panchayats (40), co-operatives (43B), weaker sections (46), prohibition of intoxicants (47).
Note: Article 48's 'modern and scientific agriculture' part is liberal-intellectual, but its cow-protection part is Gandhian.

POL-652-N001.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct; statement 3 reverses the sanctions. So the answer is option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True
Fundamental Rights are negative because they stop the State from doing certain things, while DPSPs are positive because they ask the State to act.
True
DPSPs need laws or executive action to be implemented, while Fundamental Rights are generally operative on their own.
False
It is the reverse: Fundamental Rights have legal sanction (enforceable in court), while DPSPs have only moral and political sanction.

points: Option 2 (2 and 3 only) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement 3 which is false; it leaves out true statement 1.
Option 3 (1 and 3 only) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement 3 which is false; it leaves out true statement 2.

POL-652-N002.lead: Option 3 is correct: Fundamental Rights promote individual welfare, while Directive Principles promote community welfare.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Fundamental Rights: community; Directive Principles: individual
Wrong: this is the reverse of the correct pairing.
2. Fundamental Rights: individual; Directive Principles: individual
Wrong: DPSPs are societarian and aim at community welfare, not individual welfare.
3. Fundamental Rights: individual; Directive Principles: community
Correct: FRs are personal and individualistic, while DPSPs are societarian and socialistic.
4. Fundamental Rights: community; Directive Principles: community
Wrong: FRs protect each person's freedoms, so they mainly promote individual welfare.

points: This is a standard row of Laxmikanth's FR vs DPSP comparison table.

POL-652-N003.lead: Option 4 is correct: a law cannot be struck down only because it conflicts with a Directive Principle, since Article 37 makes DPSPs non-enforceable.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The law is void under Article 13, which invalidates every law that is inconsistent with the provisions of Part IV.
Wrong: Article 13 voids laws inconsistent with Part III (Fundamental Rights), not Part IV.
2. The law is void because Article 37 declares the Directive Principles fundamental in the governance of the country.
Wrong: Article 37 calls DPSPs fundamental in governance, but expressly says they shall not be enforced by any court.
3. The law survives only if the President certifies that it advances the objectives of Part IV of the Constitution.
Wrong: no presidential certification system exists for laws under Part IV.
4. The law cannot be struck down merely for conflict with a Directive Principle, as Article 37 bars court enforcement.
Correct: without an FR violation or other constitutional defect, the law survives.

points: Non-justiciable means courts cannot enforce a provision or strike down laws for breaching it.

POL-652-N004.lead: Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — FRs are enforceable and DPSPs are not, so FRs prevailed in Champakam.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
True. In Champakam Dorairajan (1951) the Court held that DPSPs must conform to and run subsidiary to the Fundamental Rights.
R
True
True. Article 37 makes DPSPs unenforceable, while Fundamental Rights are enforceable through writs under Article 32.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. The Court's reasoning was that enforceable rights cannot give way to unenforceable directives; so the enforceability difference in R is the basis of A. This led to the 1st Amendment (Article 15(4)).
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A, so "does not explain" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.
POL-652-N004.also: The 1st Amendment, 1951 added Article 15(4) after this case.

POL-652-N005.lead: Option 2 (2–3–4–1) is correct: Champakam 1951, 25th Amendment 1971, 42nd Amendment 1976, Minerva Mills 1980.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong: it puts the 25th Amendment (1971) before Champakam (1951).
Correct: Champakam (1951), 31C inserted (1971), 31C extended (1976), Minerva Mills (1980).
Wrong: it puts the 42nd Amendment (1976) before the 25th (1971).
Wrong: it puts Minerva Mills (1980) before the 42nd Amendment extension it struck down (1976).

points: Champakam held that FRs prevail over DPSPs; Minerva Mills restored the balance between them.

POL-652-N006.lead: Option 4: A is false, but R is true — only the second provision (excluding judicial review) was struck down.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
False
False. Kesavananda struck down only the second provision of 31C (which barred courts from examining whether a law actually gave effect to the DPSP). The first provision was upheld.
R
True
True. Judicial review is a basic feature and cannot be taken away.

points: Does R explain A? Does not arise, because A is false. R does explain why the second provision fell, but not a strike-down 'in its entirety'.
Option 1 (Both A and R are true, and R explains A) fails: A is false, so "both true" is wrong.
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: A is false, so "both true" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: it reverses the truth values: R is the true one, A the false one.

POL-652-N007.lead: Both statements are correct. So the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True
As inserted by the 25th Amendment (1971), Article 31C protected 39(b) and (c) laws from being void for violating Articles 14, 19 or 31.
True
The 44th Amendment (1978) omitted Article 31 (right to property) and removed its reference from Article 31C.

points: Option 1 (1 only) is wrong: it leaves out true statement 2.
Option 2 (2 only) is wrong: it leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) is wrong: it leaves out true statements 1 and 2.
Property became a constitutional legal right under Article 300A.

POL-652-N008.lead: Option 4 (3–1–4–2) is correct: A. Champakam → DPSPs subsidiary to FRs; B. Golak Nath → No amendment can abridge FRs; C. Kesavananda → First part of 31C valid, review bar invalid; D. Minerva Mills → Harmony of Parts III and IV is basic structure.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Champakam (1951)
3 – DPSPs subsidiary to FRs
Champakam Dorairajan (1951) held that the Directive Principles must conform to and run subsidiary to the Fundamental Rights, so A matches 3.
B. Golak Nath (1967)
1 – No amendment can abridge FRs
Golak Nath (1967) held that Parliament cannot amend Fundamental Rights to take away or abridge them, so B matches 1.
C. Kesavananda (1973)
4 – First part of 31C valid, review bar invalid
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) upheld the first part of Article 31C but struck down its second part, which barred courts from reviewing such laws, so C matches 4.
D. Minerva Mills (1980)
2 – Harmony of Parts III and IV is basic structure
Minerva Mills (1980) held that the balance and harmony between Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles is part of the basic structure, so D matches 2.

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-1, B-3 (correct: A-3, B-1).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives C-2, D-4 (correct: C-4, D-2).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives B-4, C-1 (correct: B-1, C-4).

POL-652-N009.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3 (1 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. FRs may be amended to implement DPSPs within the basic structure
True
After Minerva Mills (1980), Parliament can amend Fundamental Rights to implement Directive Principles as long as the amendment does not damage the basic structure.
2. Minerva Mills struck down original Article 31C
False

Minerva Mills struck down only the 42nd Amendment (1976) extension of 31C to all Directive Principles; the original first provision (Article 39(b) and (c)) had already been upheld in Kesavananda Bharati (1973).
3. Property Owners Association (2024): 31C as upheld in Kesavananda still operates
True
In November 2024 the nine-judge bench held that Article 31C, in the form upheld in Kesavananda Bharati, continues to be in force even though the 1976 extension was struck down.

points: Option 1 and option 4 fail because they include the false statement 2; option 2 fails for the same reason and also drops the true statement 1.
Remember the three steps: 25th Amendment (1971) inserts 31C → Kesavananda (1973) strikes its second provision (no judicial review) → Minerva (1980) strikes the 42nd Amendment extension.

POL-652-N010.lead: Option 2: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A — non-enforceability does not explain the difference in aims of the two Parts.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
True. Fundamental Rights establish political democracy; DPSPs aim at social and economic democracy (a welfare State).
R
True
True. Article 37 makes DPSPs non-enforceable by any court.

points: Does R explain A? No. The difference in aims comes from the content of the two Parts (individual rights vs social-economic goals), not from whether they are enforceable.
Option 1 (Both A and R are true, and R explains A) fails: R is true but is not the reason for A.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.

POL-652-N011.lead: Option 1: Article 31C protects such a law only against challenges under Articles 14 and 19, so ground (i) fails but ground (ii) remains open.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: (i) only
Article 19(1)(g) is one of the rights from which 31C gives immunity to a law implementing Article 39(b) or (c).
(ii) only
Article 25 (freedom of religion) is not mentioned in Article 31C, so the law gets no protection on this ground.
Both (i) and (ii)
Wrong because 31C does not cover Article 25; the immunity is limited to Articles 14 and 19.
Neither (i) nor (ii)
Wrong because the law meets all conditions: it implements Article 39(c) and, being a State law, has the President's assent.

points: Article 31C (25th Amendment, 1971) says a law giving effect to Article 39(b) or (c) shall not be void for violating Article 14 or 19 (Article 31 was also listed until it was deleted in 1978).
Its proviso says a State law gets this protection only if it is reserved for the President and receives his assent; that condition is met here.
Memory hook: 31C = shield of 14 and 19 only; every other Fundamental Right, such as Article 25, can still be used to challenge the law.

POL-652-N012.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Article 15(2) binds only the State
False

Article 15(2) says no citizen shall be subjected to any disability on grounds of religion, race, caste, sex or place of birth in access to shops, restaurants, hotels and public places; it applies against private persons as well as the State.
2. Articles 17, 23 and 24 operate against private persons
True
Abolition of untouchability (Article 17), the ban on forced labour and human trafficking (Article 23) and the ban on child labour in factories (Article 24) bind private individuals too.

points: Options 1 and 3 fail because they accept the false statement 1.
Option 4 fails because statement 2 is true.
Contrast: Article 15(1) bars only the State from discriminating, while 15(2) bars both the State and private persons.

POL-652-N013.lead: Option 3: A is true, but R is false — Golak Nath did not make DPSPs enforceable; it treated amendments as 'law'.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
True. Golak Nath (1967) held that Parliament cannot take away or abridge Fundamental Rights even to implement DPSPs.
R
False
False. Golak Nath never held DPSPs enforceable; Article 37 keeps them non-justiciable.

points: Does R explain A? Does not arise, because R is false. Golak Nath's reasoning was that an amendment is 'law' under Article 13, not that DPSPs are enforceable.
Option 1 (Both A and R are true, and R explains A) fails: R is false, so it cannot be true or explain A.
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R is false, so "both true" is wrong.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: it reverses the truth values: A is the true one, R the false one.

POL-652-N014.lead: Pairs 1 and 3 are correct; Golak Nath was decided in 1967, not 1971. Answer: option 4.

head: Pair
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Champakam Dorairajan – 1951
True
Led to the 1st Amendment (Article 15(4)).
2. Golak Nath – 1971
False
Decided 1967 (11 judges); 1971 is the 24th Amendment that answered it.
3. Minerva Mills – 1980
True
Struck down parts of the 42nd Amendment.

points: Option 1 includes the wrong pair 2.
Option 2 includes the wrong pair 2 and leaves out pair 1.
Option 3 includes the wrong pair 2.
POL-652-N014.also: 1971 is the year of the 24th and 25th Amendments.

LX-PQ-163.lead: Option 4: the Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended incorporating Fundamental Duties.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Shah Commission
Appointed in 1977 by the Janata government to inquire into the excesses committed during the Emergency.
First Administrative Reforms Commission
Set up in 1966 to suggest reforms in public administration; it did not deal with citizens' duties.
Santhanam Committee
The 1962–64 committee on prevention of corruption, which led to the Central Vigilance Commission.
Swaran Singh Committee
Set up by the Congress Party in 1976; its advice led to Part IVA through the 42nd Amendment.

points: The 42nd Amendment, 1976 added Part IVA (Article 51A) with ten duties.
The Committee recommended eight duties; Parliament added ten.

LX-UPSC-2017-Q05.lead: Neither statement is true, so the answer is option 4 (neither 1 nor 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. A legislative process is provided to enforce the duties
False
The Constitution provides no machinery to enforce the duties; they are non-justiciable, though Parliament is free to enforce some of them by ordinary law.
2. They are correlative to legal duties
False
Fundamental Duties are moral and civic obligations; the Constitution does not tie each of them to a matching legal duty with a legal sanction.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 fail because each accepts at least one false statement.
Note the difference: 'Parliament may enforce them by law' (true) is not the same as 'the Constitution provides a process to enforce them' (false).

POL-661-C001.lead: Option 1: the 2023 amendment renamed the Act as the Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Van (Sanrakshan Evam Samvardhan) Adhiniyam, 1980
The new name, meaning Forest (Conservation and Augmentation) Act; it stresses increasing forests as well as conserving them.
Bharatiya Van Adhiniyam, 1980
Not a real name; the 1927 Indian Forest Act was not renamed this way.
Van Adhikar Adhiniyam, 1980
'Van Adhikar' means forest rights, which is the subject of the separate Forest Rights Act, 2006.
Paryavaran (Sanrakshan) Adhiniyam, 1980
This would mean Environment (Protection) Act, which is a different law of 1986.

points: The Forest (Conservation) Amendment Act, 2023 changed the name of the Forest (Conservation) Act, 1980.
Forest laws support Article 51A(g), the duty to protect and improve the natural environment including forests, and Article 48A, the matching Directive Principle.

POL-661-CH-001.lead: Option 2: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A — Article 13, not the separate Part numbers, makes every law answerable to Fundamental Rights.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
True. A law meant to promote a Fundamental Duty must still satisfy Fundamental Rights; courts may use the duty to judge whether a restriction is reasonable.
R
True
True. Duties are in Part IVA and rights in Part III.

points: Does R explain A? No. Every law is tested against Fundamental Rights because of Article 13, whatever its aim. Being in different Parts is not the reason.
Option 1 (Both A and R are true, and R explains A) fails: R is true but is not the reason for A.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.
POL-661-CH-001.also: Courts may use a Fundamental Duty to judge whether a restriction on a right is reasonable.

POL-661-CH-002.lead: Option 3 (3–4–1–2) is correct: A. UDHR → 1948; B. Part IVA commencement → 3 January 1977; C. 86th Amendment Act date → 12 December 2002; D. 51A(k) commencement → 1 April 2010.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. UDHR
The UN General Assembly adopted the Universal Declaration of Human Rights in 1948, so A matches 3.
B. Part IVA commencement
4 – 3 January 1977
Part IVA with the original ten duties, added by the 42nd Amendment, came into force on 3 January 1977, so B matches 4.
C. 86th Amendment Act date
1 – 12 December 2002
The Constitution (Eighty-sixth Amendment) Act is dated 12 December 2002, even though its education provisions began later, so C matches 1.
D. 51A(k) commencement
2 – 1 April 2010
Article 51A(k) came into force on 1 April 2010, the same day as Article 21A and the RTE Act, so D matches 2.

points: The trap is C vs D: the Act is dated 2002 but its education parts came into force only in 2010.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives C-2, D-1 (correct: C-1, D-2).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A-4, B-3 (correct: A-3, B-4).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives B-1, C-4 (correct: B-4, C-1).

POL-661-CH-003.lead: Option 1: the environmental duty does not cancel the duty to safeguard public property and abjure violence; a citizen must follow both.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Environmental duty does not displace 51A(i)
Correct, because Article 51A(g) (protect the environment) and Article 51A(i) (safeguard public property, abjure violence) stand side by side and both bind the citizen.
Invoking 51A(g) protects damage to buses
Wrong, because no Fundamental Duty gives a licence to break another duty or the criminal law.
Weigh benefit against damage only
Wrong, because it ignores that 51A(i) separately asks citizens to reject violence, whatever the cause.
Non-justiciable, so property laws cannot apply
Wrong, because non-justiciability only means courts cannot enforce the duty itself; ordinary laws against damaging property still apply fully.

points: All eleven duties are meant to be read together; one duty is never a defence for violating another.
Peaceful protest is protected, but destroying public property is both against 51A(i) and punishable under ordinary law.

POL-661-CH-004.lead: Statements 1 and 2 make the case for balance, so the answer is option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Rights without concern for others encourage irresponsibility
True
If people only claim rights and ignore others, society suffers; duties remind citizens of what they owe to others.
2. Duties without protecting freedom reduce people to subordination
True
If the State only imposes duties and does not protect liberty, citizens become mere subjects; this is why rights remain guaranteed.
3. Duties may always extinguish rights when the State finds it convenient
False
This destroys the balance; Indira Gandhi herself said duties are 'not to smother rights' but to create a democratic balance, and any limit on a right must pass constitutional tests.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 fail because each includes statement 3, which argues for domination of duties rather than balance.

POL-661-N001.lead: Option 1: Both A and R are true, and R explains A — Parliament rejected the Committee's tax-paying proposal.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
True. Paying taxes is not in Article 51A.
R
True
True. The Swaran Singh Committee proposed it, but it was not accepted when Part IVA was inserted in 1976.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. It is missing from the list exactly because Parliament rejected that proposal. R explains A.
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A, so "does not explain" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.
POL-661-N001.also: Committee proposed 8 duties; the 42nd Amendment (1976) added 10.

POL-661-N002.lead: Proposals 1 and 2 were not incorporated, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Parliament may impose penalty for not observing duties
True (not incorporated)
Laxmikanth lists this among the Committee recommendations the Congress Party did not accept.
2. Penalty law cannot be questioned for violating Fundamental Rights
True (not incorporated)
This court-immunity proposal was also rejected, so any such law remains open to judicial review.
3. A separate chapter on Fundamental Duties
False (it was incorporated)
This was accepted: the 42nd Amendment created Part IVA with Article 51A.

points: Option 1 misses proposal 2; options 3 and 4 wrongly include proposal 3, which was actually adopted.
The third rejected proposal was the duty to pay taxes.

POL-661-N003.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3 (1 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 42nd Amendment enacted during the internal Emergency
True
The 42nd Amendment Act was passed in 1976 while the Emergency proclaimed in June 1975 was in force.
2. Committee set up after Janata Party came to power in 1977
False
The Swaran Singh Committee was set up by the Congress Party in 1976; the Janata government came later and only chose not to remove the duties.
3. Part IVA came into force before the Emergency was revoked
True
Part IVA came into force on 3 January 1977, while the internal Emergency was revoked only in March 1977.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 fail because each includes the false statement 2.
The Janata government's 43rd and 44th Amendments reversed many 42nd Amendment changes but kept the Fundamental Duties.

POL-661-N004.lead: Items 1, 3 and 4 are duties, so the answer is option 2 (1, 3 and 4 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Uphold sovereignty, unity and integrity
True
True: upholding the sovereignty, unity and integrity of India is Fundamental Duty 51A(c).
2. Promote educational and economic interests of weaker sections
False
This is Article 46, a Directive Principle addressed to the State, not a citizen's duty.
3. Promote harmony and common brotherhood
True
True: promoting harmony and the spirit of common brotherhood is Fundamental Duty 51A(e).
4. Develop scientific temper, humanism, spirit of inquiry and reform
True
True: developing scientific temper, humanism and the spirit of inquiry and reform is Fundamental Duty 51A(h).

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 fail because they include item 2, which belongs to Part IV (DPSP).
Tip: if the sentence begins 'The State shall…' in the Constitution, it is a Directive Principle; 51A begins 'It shall be the duty of every citizen'.

POL-661-N005.lead: Option 4: the notice is wrong because Article 51A(i) speaks only of public property, not private houses.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 51A(i) covers public and private property
Wrong, because the text is 'to safeguard public property and to abjure violence'; private property is not mentioned.
Article 300A lays down a duty to protect property
Wrong, because Article 300A (Part XII) is the constitutional right to property: no one shall be deprived of property save by authority of law.
No clause of 51A refers to property
Wrong, because 51A(i) does refer to public property.
51A(i) refers to public property only
Correct; the notice misquotes the duty by extending it to private houses.

points: Article 51A(i) pairs two ideas: safeguard public property and abjure (give up) violence.
Private property is protected by ordinary law and Article 300A, not by a Fundamental Duty.

POL-661-N006.lead: Option 1 (A–3, B–4, C–1, D–2) is correct: A. Public assistance in old age, sickness → Article 41; B. Population control, family planning → Concurrent List; C. Interests of SCs, STs, weaker sections → Article 46; D. Compassion for living creatures → Article 51A(g).

Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Public assistance in old age, sickness
3 – Article 41
Public assistance in cases of unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement is a Directive Principle in Article 41, so A matches 3.
B. Population control, family planning
4 – Concurrent List
Population control and family planning is Entry 20A of the Concurrent List, added by the 42nd Amendment, so B matches 4.
C. Interests of SCs, STs, weaker sections
1 – Article 46
Promotion of educational and economic interests of SCs, STs and other weaker sections is a Directive Principle in Article 46, so C matches 1.
D. Compassion for living creatures
2 – Article 51A(g)
Compassion for living creatures is part of the Fundamental Duty in Article 51A(g), so D matches 2.

Option 3 is wrong: it gives B-2, D-4 (correct: B-4, D-2).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-4, B-3 (correct: A-3, B-4).

POL-661-P134-001.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 1950 Constitution contained Directive Principles
True
Part IV (Articles 36–51) on Directive Principles has been in the Constitution since 26 January 1950.
2. 1950 Constitution contained Part IVA on duties
False
The original Constitution had no Fundamental Duties; Part IVA was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

points: Options 2 and 3 fail because they accept statement 2; option 4 fails because statement 1 is true.
Laxmikanth notes that the framers put the duties of the State (DPSPs) in the original text but not the duties of citizens.

POL-661-P134-002.lead: Option 2: claiming one's own freedoms while respecting others' freedoms and public property shows that rights and responsibilities complement each other.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Duties replace all enforceable rights
Wrong, because Fundamental Rights remain enforceable under Article 32 even after duties were added.
Rights and social responsibilities complement each other
Correct: the association enjoys rights and also performs duties, which is the idea of balance behind Part IVA.
Rights exist only after every duty is performed
Wrong, because the Constitution does not make Fundamental Rights conditional on first performing duties.
Public responsibilities belong only to government
Wrong, because citizens also have duties, for example 51A(i) to safeguard public property.

points: Rights and duties are correlative: my right is meaningful only if others respect it as their duty.

POL-661-P134-003.lead: Option 1: a legal duty is backed by law and its breach can be punished by the State; a moral duty rests only on conscience and social approval.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Legal duty backed by law; moral duty on conscience
Correct: a legal duty has a legal sanction (fine, penalty), while breaking a moral duty brings only social disapproval or guilt.
Moral duty enforced by courts, legal duty not
Wrong, because it reverses the two; courts enforce legal duties, not moral ones.
Both enforceable by writ under Article 32
Wrong, because Article 32 writs enforce Fundamental Rights, not moral duties, and even Fundamental Duties are non-justiciable.
A duty is legal only if listed in Article 51A
Wrong, because any valid law (for example a tax law) creates a legal duty; 51A duties themselves have no direct legal sanction.

points: Laxmikanth says some Fundamental Duties are moral (cherish ideals of the freedom struggle) and some civic (respect the Flag and Anthem).

POL-661-P134-004.lead: Option 1: the Fundamental Duties were inspired by the Constitution of the former USSR.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Former USSR
Socialist constitutions gave equal importance to rights and duties; India borrowed Fundamental Duties and the ideal of justice in the Preamble from it.
Canada
India borrowed a federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Centre from Canada.
Australia
India borrowed the Concurrent List, freedom of trade and commerce, and the joint sitting from Australia.
Ireland
India borrowed the Directive Principles of State Policy from Ireland.

points: The USSR Constitution said the exercise of rights is inseparable from performing duties.
Major democracies like the USA, Canada and Australia have no list of citizens' duties.
POL-661-P134-004.also: Among major democracies, Japan's Constitution also lists citizens' duties.

POL-661-P134-005.lead: Option 3: Mahatma Gandhi said that the true source of rights is duty.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Jawaharlal Nehru
First Prime Minister; moved the Objectives Resolution, but this quotation is not his.
B.R. Ambedkar
Chairman of the Drafting Committee; he stressed rights and their remedies (Article 32 as the 'heart and soul'), not this saying.
Mahatma Gandhi
He believed that if everyone does his duty, rights follow automatically; this is his well-known view.
Sardar Swaran Singh
Chaired the 1976 committee on Fundamental Duties, but the quotation is Gandhi's.

points: Gandhi's idea, that rights flow from duties well performed, is often cited to justify Part IVA.

POL-661-P134-006.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

True/False
Why

True

2. Several duties express values from Indian tradition
True
Laxmikanth says the duties refer to values that have been part of Indian tradition, mythology, religions and practices.
3. Tradition makes every breach punishable under 51A
False
Article 51A itself carries no legal sanction; a breach is punishable only if a separate valid law makes it so.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 fail because they include the false statement 3.

POL-661-P134-007.lead: Option 2: social duties are responsibilities towards others in general, while Fundamental Duties are those given specific recognition in the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong, because many genuine social and moral duties exist outside the Constitution.
Social duties are wider; Fundamental Duties are constitutionally recognised
Correct: the forum's duties are real social duties even if not listed, while 51A names a selected set.
Trust exists only where every failure is criminally punished
Wrong, because trust and respect rest on conscience and community, not on criminal punishment.
Constitutional recognition makes moral and legal duties identical
Wrong, because a duty in 51A is still non-justiciable and differs from a legal duty enforced by law.

POL-661-P134-008.lead: Option 4: a tax validly imposed by law must be paid; it does not have to be listed as a Fundamental Duty.

What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong, because ordinary laws create many enforceable duties without any mention in 51A.

Wrong, because the tax's force comes from the law under Article 265, not from Part IVA.

Wrong, because Article 265 says no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
A statutory obligation need not be an express duty
Correct: the person is bound by the valid tax law itself.

Correct match (List-II)

True/False

True
51A(e) asks citizens to promote harmony and brotherhood across religious, linguistic, regional or sectional diversities and to renounce practices against the dignity of women.
2. The women's dignity duty is only in 51A(k)
False
51A(k), added in 2002, is about parents providing education to children aged 6–14.

POL-661-P135-004.lead: Option 2: Article 51A begins, 'It shall be the duty of every citizen of India'.

What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong, because 51A is not limited to government employees; it covers all citizens.
Every citizen of India
Correct; Fundamental Duties are confined to citizens.

Wrong, because foreigners are not covered, unlike some Fundamental Rights such as Articles 14 and 21 which apply to all persons.

head: Option
What it is / means

False: the 'ordinary residence since migration' route under Article 6(b)(i) was only for those who came before 19 July 1948.
