Parliament has no role in voting for Council members.

points: The same PR-STV method is used for the Rajya Sabha and for the President's election.
Hence Council members are indirectly elected; the people do not vote for them directly.

POL-721-AR-02.lead: Option 4: Article 81 now allows at most 550 members – up to 530 from the States and up to 20 from the Union Territories.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 543 is the present actual strength of elected Lok Sabha seats, not the constitutional maximum.
545 was the actual strength including the two nominated Anglo-Indian members, before 2020.
552 was the old maximum (530 + 20 + 2 Anglo-Indians); it fell when the 104th Amendment ended Anglo-Indian nomination from 25 January 2020.
550 is the maximum after the 104th Amendment: 530 from States + 20 from Union Territories.

points: Do not confuse the maximum (550) with the present strength (543).
In April 2026 the Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill to raise the Lok Sabha limit (to about 850) failed to get a two-thirds majority in the Lok Sabha, so Article 81 is unchanged.

POL-721-CH-01.lead: Option 3: Tamil Nadu has no Legislative Council; it abolished its Council in 1986.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Karnataka
Karnataka is one of the six bicameral States.
2. Maharashtra
Maharashtra is one of the six bicameral States.
3. Tamil Nadu
Tamil Nadu abolished its Council in 1986; the Tamil Nadu Legislative Council Act, 2010 for its revival never came into force.
4. Telangana
Telangana has had a Council since its formation in 2014.

points: Six bicameral States: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Uttar Pradesh, Bihar, Maharashtra and Karnataka.
Memory hook: 'AT-UB-MK'. The J&K Council was abolished by the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019.

POL-721-CH-02.lead: Option 1 — Both A and R are true, and R explains A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
A law of Parliament creating (or abolishing) a Legislative Council is not treated as an amendment of the Constitution under Article 368.
R
True
Article 169(3) expressly says so, once the State Assembly has passed the required special-majority resolution.

points: Does R explain A? Yes — A states the rule and R points to the clause that creates it. Because Article 169(3) itself removes such laws from Article 368, R explains A.
Option 2 fails: R actually does explain A.
Option 3 fails: R is in fact true.
Option 4 fails: A is in fact true.

POL-721-CH-03.lead: Option 3: after the second passage by the Assembly, the bill is deemed passed by both Houses; there is no joint sitting in States.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The bill is permanently defeated
Wrong: the Council cannot permanently defeat an ordinary bill; it can only delay it.
2. A joint sitting is compulsory
Wrong: joint sitting (Article 108) is only for Parliament; State legislatures have no such device.
3. The Assembly can ultimately prevail; there is no joint sitting
Correct: under Article 197 the Assembly's version prevails after the Council's delay of at most four months in all.
4. The Governor must dissolve both Houses
Wrong: the Council is a permanent House and cannot be dissolved; disagreement on a bill never leads to dissolution.

points: This shows the Council is only a revising and delaying chamber, much weaker than the Rajya Sabha.
Also note: a bill that starts in the Council and is rejected by the Assembly simply dies.

POL-721-CH-04.lead: Option 1: both Rajya Sabha and a Legislative Council are permanent Houses, but the Council is much weaker against its Assembly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Both are continuing chambers, but the Council is constitutionally weaker than the Assembly
Correct: neither House is dissolved (one-third retire every second year), but the Council can only delay ordinary bills while the Rajya Sabha has near-equal power.
2. Both can be dissolved by the President
Wrong: neither the Rajya Sabha nor a Council can be dissolved by anyone.
3. Both possess equal powers with their lower Houses
Wrong: the Rajya Sabha has nearly equal power on ordinary bills, but the Council does not; on money bills both are weaker.
4. Both are directly elected by the people
Wrong: both are indirectly elected (and partly nominated), not directly elected by the people.

points: Rajya Sabha deadlocks are solved by a joint sitting, where the Lok Sabha's larger size usually wins; Council deadlocks are solved by the Assembly simply passing the bill again.
The Council's very existence depends on the Assembly's wish (Article 169), unlike the Rajya Sabha.

POL-721-P213-01.lead: Option 1: Article 79 says Parliament consists of the President and two Houses – the Rajya Sabha and the Lok Sabha.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. President, Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha
Correct: the President, the Council of States and the House of the People together form Parliament.
2. Prime Minister, Lok Sabha and Supreme Court
Wrong: the Prime Minister heads the executive and the Supreme Court is the judiciary; neither is part of Parliament.
3. President and Lok Sabha only
Wrong: it leaves out the Rajya Sabha, which Article 79 names as one of the two Houses.
4. Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha only
Wrong: it leaves out the President, who is an integral part of Parliament.

points: The President is not a member of either House, but a bill becomes law only with his assent, he summons and prorogues the Houses and dissolves the Lok Sabha.
This follows the British pattern, where the Crown is part of Parliament.

POL-721-P219-01.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Not subject to dissolution
True
Article 83(1) makes the Rajya Sabha a continuing chamber; it is never dissolved.
2. One-third retire every second year
True
Members serve six years and about one-third retire every second year, so seats are filled by biennial elections.

points: Options 1 and 2 fail because each leaves out one true statement.
Option 4 fails because both are true.
Contrast: the Lok Sabha has a five-year term and can be dissolved earlier.

POL-721-P356-01.lead: Option 1: under Article 168, a unicameral State legislature consists of the Governor and the Legislative Assembly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Governor and Legislative Assembly
Correct: in a State with one House, the legislature is the Governor plus the Assembly.
2. Legislative Assembly alone
Wrong: it leaves out the Governor, who is an integral part of the State legislature.
3. Governor and Legislative Council
Wrong: the State has no Council, and the Assembly cannot be left out.
4. Governor, Assembly and Council
Wrong: this is the bicameral pattern; the State in the stem has no Council.

points: The Governor is not a member of the House, but bills need his assent and he summons, prorogues and dissolves the Assembly.
This is the State-level copy of Article 79 for Parliament.

POL-721-P356-02.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are required; 4 is not, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Majority of total membership of Assembly
True
This is half of the 'special majority' Article 169 requires for the Assembly's resolution.
2. Two-thirds of members present and voting
True
This is the other half of the special majority; both conditions must be met together.
3. A law of Parliament
True
Article 169(1) says Parliament may by law create or abolish the Council once the Assembly so requests.
4. Ratification by half the States
False
Article 169(3) says such a law is not an amendment under Article 368, so no State ratification is needed.

points: Option 1 fails because it leaves out the law of Parliament.
Options 3 and 4 fail because they include ratification by States.
Parliament passes the law by a simple majority.

POL-721-P357-01.lead: Option 1. Local authorities elect about one-third of the Legislative Council.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Local authorities - one-third
Right: one-third of members are elected by local authorities under Article 171(3).
Graduates - one-third
Wrong: graduates elect only one-twelfth of the members.
Teachers - one-sixth
Wrong: teachers elect one-twelfth of the members, not one-sixth.
Nominees - one-third
Wrong: the Governor nominates one-sixth of the members, not one-third.

points: 1/3 local bodies + 1/3 MLAs + 1/12 graduates + 1/12 teachers + 1/6 nominated = whole House.

POL-721-P358-01.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Maximum strength is one-third of the Assembly
True
Article 171(1) says the Council's total members shall not exceed one-third of the Assembly's total strength.
2. A continuing chamber
True
Article 172(2) says the Council is not subject to dissolution.
3. All members retire together after six years
False
Members serve six years, but one-third of them retire every second year, so they never all retire together.

points: Options 3 and 4 fail because they include false statement 3.
Option 1 fails because it leaves out true statement 2.
The minimum strength is 40 members.

POL-721-REC-STAGE-001.lead: All three statements are true, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Minimum strength 40
True
Article 171(1) says the Council shall have not less than 40 members.
2. One-twelfth elected by graduates
True
Article 171(3)(b): graduates of three years' standing residing in the State elect one-twelfth.
3. One-twelfth elected by teachers
True
Article 171(3)(c): teachers of three years' standing in institutions not lower than secondary school elect one-twelfth.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 fail because each leaves out at least one true statement.
The maximum is one-third of the Assembly strength.
Remaining categories: one-third by local bodies, one-third by MLAs, one-sixth nominated by the Governor.

POL-721-REC-STAGE-002.lead: Option 1: four categories (local authorities, graduates, teachers, MLAs) are elected; the Governor nominates experts in the remaining one-sixth.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Local-authority, graduate, teacher and MLA categories are elected; the Governor nominates persons with specified knowledge or practical experience
Correct: this matches Article 171(3) and (5).
2. Every category is elected directly by all voters
Wrong: no category is directly elected by all voters; Council members are indirectly elected or nominated.
3. Teachers are nominated by the Chief Minister and graduates by the Governor
Wrong: teachers and graduates both elect their own members; the Chief Minister nominates no one.
4. The Governor nominates the local-authority and MLA categories
Wrong: local authorities and MLAs elect their members; the Governor only nominates persons from literature, science, art, co-operative movement and social service.

points: 5/6 indirectly elected + 1/6 nominated.
All elected categories use proportional representation by single transferable vote (Article 171(4)).

POL-R21-SREM-AP-reserved-seats.lead: Option 1: of 175 Andhra Pradesh Assembly seats, 29 are reserved for SCs and 7 for STs.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. SC 29; ST 7
Correct: after the 2008 delimitation and the 2014 bifurcation, the AP Assembly has 29 SC and 7 ST seats.
2. SC 25; ST 9
Wrong: 25 SC and 9 ST does not match the AP figures.
3. SC 7; ST 29
Wrong: this reverses the two numbers; SCs are far larger in AP's population than STs.
4. SC 34; ST 7
Wrong: AP has 29 SC seats, not 34; the ST figure of 7 alone is right.

points: Article 332 reserves Assembly seats for SCs and STs in proportion to their population in the State.
Total AP reserved seats = 36 of 175; the rest (139) are general.

POL-R21-SREM-APTS-2017-legal-opinion.lead: Option 3: Section 26 of the AP Reorganisation Act, 2014 is 'subject to' Article 170, which freezes the total Assembly seats until the first census after 2026.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Both State Assemblies rejected the increase by resolution
Wrong: neither Assembly rejected the increase; both actually wanted it.
2. The Election Commission has no power to delimit constituencies
Wrong: delimitation is done by a Delimitation Commission, but the real block is the constitutional freeze, not the Election Commission's powers.
3. The provision is subject to Article 170, which freezes the total number of Assembly seats until the figures of the first census after 2026 are published
Correct: Article 170(3), as amended by the 84th Amendment (2001), freezes the total number of seats till the post-2026 census, and the Act itself is made subject to it.
4. The Supreme Court struck down the provision as unconstitutional
Wrong: the Supreme Court did not strike down the provision; in 2025 it declined to order delimitation for AP and Telangana ahead of the national exercise.

points: So the increase (175 to 225 in AP, 119 to 153 in Telangana) needs either a constitutional amendment or the delimitation after the first post-2026 census.
In 2017 the Attorney General also opined that the seats could not be increased without amending Article 170.

POL-R21-SREM-Assembly-population-bases.lead: Option 3: total seats are frozen on the 1971 census, while constituencies are redrawn on the 2001 census, until the first census after 2026.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. (i) 2001 census; (ii) 1971 census
Wrong: 2001 is the basis for boundaries, not for the total number of seats.
2. (i) 1971 census; (ii) 2011 census
Wrong: 2011 census has not been used for delimitation.
3. (i) 1971 census; (ii) 2001 census
Correct: the 42nd (1976) and 84th (2001) Amendments froze total seats on the 1971 census, and the 87th Amendment (2003) made the 2001 census the basis for drawing constituency boundaries.
4. (i) 2011 census; (ii) 2011 census
Wrong: 2011 census is not used for either purpose.

points: Reason for the freeze: States that controlled population growth should not lose seats.
The Constitution (131st Amendment) Bill, 2026 to change this was defeated in the Lok Sabha in April 2026, so the freeze still stands.

POL-R21-SREM-Assembly-population-princip.lead: Option 1: Article 170(2) requires the population-to-seat ratio to be, as far as practicable, the same throughout the State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. So far as practicable, the ratio between each constituency’s population and its allotted seats should be the same throughout the State
Correct: each constituency should have roughly the same population per seat, so that each vote carries about equal weight.
2. Every constituency should have equal geographical area, even where population density differs
Wrong: the Constitution uses population, not geographical area.
3. Each constituency should contain the same number of registered electors, regardless of its population
Wrong: the rule is based on population (census figures), not the number of registered electors.
4. The population-to-seat ratio should be identical between all States, rather than within each State
Wrong: Article 170(2) applies within each State; equality between States is the rule for Lok Sabha seats (Article 81).

points: This gives effect to 'one person, one vote, one value'.
'Population' here means the population in the last census whose figures are taken for delimitation (2001 for boundaries).

POL-R21-SREM-Assembly-reservation-basis.lead: Option 2: Article 332 reserves Assembly seats for SCs and STs in proportion to their population; Article 171 gives no SC/ST reservation in the Council.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 332 applies the same population-based SC/ST seat-reservation scheme to both the Assembly and the Council
Wrong: Article 332 covers only the Legislative Assembly, not the Council.

2. Article 332 generally provides SC/ST reservation in Assemblies in population proportion, subject to constitutional exceptions; Article 171’s Council categories do not prescribe corresponding SC/ST-reserved Council seats
Correct: Assembly reservation is population-based (with special rules for some north-eastern States), while the Council's categories under Article 171 carry no SC/ST quota.
3. Article 171 prescribes SC/ST-reserved Council seats, while Article 332 provides only for Governor-nominated Assembly members
Wrong: this reverses the Articles; Article 171 has no SC/ST seats, and Article 332 is about reservation, not nomination.
4. The Council’s local-authority seats are SC/ST-reserved seats in the same proportions as Assembly seats
Wrong: Council local-authority seats are not reserved for SCs or STs.

points: Reservation in the Lok Sabha is under Article 330 and in Assemblies under Article 332; the Rajya Sabha and Councils have none.
The reservation lasts until 2030 after the 104th Amendment (2019).

POL-R21-SREM-Council-law-authority.lead: Option 2: Article 171 is the Council-composition Article; clause (2) lets Parliament provide otherwise by law, and clause (3)(a) lets Parliament specify the local authorities.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 170; the State Legislature may prescribe the Council’s electoral categories by law
Wrong: Article 170 deals with the composition of the Legislative Assembly, not the Council.
2. Article 171; Parliament may provide a different composition scheme by law under clause (2), and specify local authorities under clause (3)(a)

Correct: Article 171(2) says the Council's composition shall be as Parliament may by law provide (until then, clause (3) applies), and 171(3)(a) refers to local authorities Parliament specifies by law.
3. Article 171; the State Government may change the constitutional composition by notification after consulting the Election Commission
Wrong: no State Government notification can change the composition fixed by the Constitution.
4. Article 169; the State Assembly’s special-majority resolution itself changes the Council’s electoral categories
Wrong: Article 169 only lets the Assembly request creation or abolition of a Council; it does not change electoral categories.

points: So the Constitution gives the scheme but Parliament controls the details – another example of Parliament's role over Councils.
Memory hook: 168 – structure, 169 – create/abolish Council, 170 – Assembly, 171 – Council.

POL-R21-SREM-Punjab-UP-SC-count-share.lead: Option 2: reserved constituencies use a joint electorate – all electors vote, but only Scheduled Caste candidates can contest.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only Scheduled Caste voters vote, and only Scheduled Caste candidates may contest
Wrong: that would be a separate electorate, which the Constitution rejected; all voters of the constituency vote.
2. All electors of the constituency vote, but only Scheduled Caste candidates may contest
Correct: under Article 332 and the RPA, every elector in the constituency votes, but candidates must be from the Scheduled Castes.
3. All electors vote and anyone may contest, but Scheduled Caste candidates receive weighted votes
Wrong: there is no weighted voting; every vote counts the same.
4. The member is nominated by the Governor from among the Scheduled Castes
Wrong: members of reserved seats are elected, not nominated by the Governor.

points: Separate electorates were the colonial device; the Poona Pact (1932) replaced them with reserved seats in a joint electorate.
An SC candidate may also contest a general seat.

POL-R21-SREM-ST-special-allocation.lead: Option 1: in Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland, 59 of the 60 Assembly seats are reserved for Scheduled Tribes.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Arunachal Pradesh and Nagaland
Correct: both these tribal-majority States reserve 59 of 60 seats for STs, leaving just one general seat (Itanagar in Arunachal and Dimapur-I in Nagaland).
2. Meghalaya and Mizoram
Wrong: Meghalaya reserves 55 seats for STs and Mizoram 39 of its 40.
3. Manipur and Tripura
Wrong: Manipur reserves 19 of 60 for STs and Tripura 20 of 60.
4. Sikkim and Mizoram
Wrong: Sikkim has 32 seats with 12 for Bhutia-Lepcha, and Mizoram has only 40 seats.

points: Article 332(3A) gives special rules for ST reservation in Arunachal, Meghalaya, Mizoram and Nagaland.
This is a special arrangement for States where tribal people form the large majority.

POL-R21-SREM-State-delegated-electoral-r.lead: Option 2: an MLC can be appointed a Minister or even Chief Minister, because Article 164 allows ministers from either House of the State legislature.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Vote in the election of the President of India
Wrong: only elected MLAs (and elected MPs) form the electoral college for the President; MLCs are excluded (Article 54).
2. Be appointed as a Minister or as the Chief Minister of the State
Correct: a minister must be a member of the State legislature, which includes the Council; many Chief Ministers have been MLCs.
3. Vote in the election of the State's representatives to the Rajya Sabha
Wrong: Rajya Sabha members from a State are elected only by the elected MLAs (Article 80(4)); MLCs do not vote.
4. Vote on a no-confidence motion against the State Council of Ministers
Wrong: the Council of Ministers is responsible only to the Assembly (Article 164(2)); a no-confidence motion is moved and voted only there.

points: This shows the Council's limited role: it shares in the ministry but not in making or unmaking it.
Example: Uttar Pradesh and Maharashtra Chief Ministers have held office as MLCs.

POL-R21-SREM-teachers-electorate.lead: Option 3: the teachers' electorate is persons teaching for at least three years in institutions not lower than secondary school (Article 171(3)(c)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Teachers of government primary schools with at least one year of service
Wrong: primary school teachers are excluded, and the period is three years, not one.
2. All university graduates of at least three years' standing residing in the State
Wrong: this describes the separate graduates' electorate (Article 171(3)(b)), not the teachers'.
3. Persons engaged for at least three years in teaching in educational institutions not lower in standard than a secondary school
Correct: Article 171(3)(c) says teachers of three years' standing in educational institutions not lower in standard than a secondary school elect one-twelfth.
4. Only university and college teachers nominated by the Governor
Wrong: teachers are not nominated; they vote as an electorate, and it includes school teachers too.

points: Graduates' and teachers' constituencies each elect one-twelfth of the Council.
Memory hook: both need 'three years' – of being a graduate, or of teaching.

POL-R21-STATE-AP-TS-Council-allocation.lead: Option 4: an Assembly resolution under Article 169 only requests Parliament; without a law of Parliament nothing is abolished.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Council stood abolished from the date of the resolution
Wrong: the resolution does not abolish the Council by itself.
2. The Council stood abolished as soon as the Governor gave assent
Wrong: the Governor has no role in assenting to such a resolution; abolition needs a law of Parliament.
3. The Council's sittings stood suspended until Parliament took a decision
Wrong: the Council's sittings are not suspended; it keeps working until Parliament's law takes effect.
4. By itself it abolished nothing: abolition needs a law of Parliament, and the Council continued (the Assembly withdrew the resolution in 2021)
Correct: Parliament passed no law, the AP Council continued, and the AP Assembly withdrew the resolution in November 2021.

points: Article 169: Assembly special-majority resolution → Parliament's law (simple majority) → abolition.
This is why the Council is called dependent on the Assembly's wish but also on Parliament's action.

POL-R21-STATE-Council-MLA-share.lead: Option 3: one-third of 60 is 20; MLAs elect them from among persons who are not members of the Assembly (Article 171(3)(d)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Five; only sitting MLAs
Wrong: five would be one-twelfth, and MLAs cannot elect sitting MLAs.
2. Ten; only members of local bodies
Wrong: ten is one-sixth (the Governor's nominees), and local bodies form a separate category.
3. Twenty; persons who are not members of the Assembly
Correct: Article 171(3)(d) gives one-third to members elected by the MLAs from persons who are not Assembly members.
4. Thirty; only serving government teachers
Wrong: thirty is half, which is not any category, and teachers are a separate one-twelfth category.

points: For a 60-member Council: 20 local bodies, 5 graduates, 5 teachers, 20 by MLAs, 10 nominated = 60.
The bar on electing MLAs stops a person sitting in both Houses.

POL-R21-STATE-Council-age-term-rotation.lead: Option 2: an MLC must be at least 30 years old, serves six years, and about one-third retire every second year.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 25 years; five-year term; all members retire together
Wrong: 25 years is the age for the Assembly, five years is the Assembly's term, and Council members never retire together.
2. 30 years; six-year term; as nearly as possible one-third retire every second year
Correct: Article 173 fixes 30 years for the Council, and Article 172(2) gives a six-year term with one-third retiring every second year.
3. 30 years; three-year term; one-half retire every year
Wrong: the term is six years, not three, and one-third (not half) retire every two years.
4. 35 years; six-year term; one-third retire every third year
Wrong: 35 years is the age for President and Governor, and retirement is every second year, not third.

points: The rotation makes the Council a permanent House that is never dissolved.
Same pattern as the Rajya Sabha: 30 years, six years, one-third every two years.

POL-R21-STATE-Council-delay-periods.lead: Option 2: the Council can hold an ordinary bill for three months the first time and one month the second time – four months in all.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. (i) One month; (ii) three months
Wrong: the order is reversed; Article 197 gives three months first and one month second.
2. (i) Three months; (ii) one month
Correct: Article 197 gives three months at the first stage and one month at the second; after that the bill is deemed passed by both Houses.
3. Fourteen days at each stage
Wrong: 14 days is the limit for a Money Bill, not an ordinary bill.
4. Six months at each stage
Wrong: six months is the period after which a joint sitting can be called for Parliament (Rajya Sabha), not the Council's limit.

points: So the Council is only a delaying chamber; the Assembly always prevails.
Memory hook: '3 + 1 = 4 months' for an ordinary bill, '14 days' for a Money Bill.

POL-R21-STATE-Council-nomination-fields.lead: Option 1: Article 171(5) lists literature, science, art, co-operative movement and social service.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Literature, science, art, co-operative movement and social service
Correct: these five fields are listed in Article 171(5) for the Governor's nominees.
2. Literature, science, art, electoral management and defence administration
Wrong: electoral management and defence administration are not listed.
3. Science, engineering, commerce, taxation and electoral management
Wrong: engineering, commerce, taxation and electoral management are not listed.
4. Literature, social service, military command, diplomacy and taxation
Wrong: military command, diplomacy and taxation are not listed.

points: The Rajya Sabha list (Article 80(3)) has only four fields: literature, science, art and social service; the Council list adds 'co-operative movement'.
Memory hook: Council = Rajya Sabha list + Co-operation.

POL-R21-STATE-Council-total-pattern.lead: Option 1: the Council elects its Chairman from among its members and can remove him by a resolution of a majority of all the then members (Articles 182–183).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Elected by the Council from among its members; removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members of the Council
Correct: the Chairman is elected by the Council and removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members, after 14 days' notice.
2. Appointed by the Governor; removed by the Governor at his discretion
Wrong: the Governor neither appoints nor removes the Chairman.
3. The Governor is the ex-officio Chairman, just as the Vice-President is of the Rajya Sabha
Wrong: unlike the Vice-President for the Rajya Sabha, there is no ex-officio Chairman; the Governor is not a member of the Council.
4. Elected by the Legislative Assembly; removed by a resolution of the Assembly
Wrong: the Assembly elects its own Speaker; it has no role in choosing or removing the Council Chairman.

points: The Chairman is a member of the Council, so he votes only in case of a tie (casting vote).
Deputy Chairman is elected and removed the same way.

POL-R21-STATE-bicameral-constituents.lead: Option 1: Article 168 says a bicameral State legislature consists of the Governor, the Legislative Assembly and the Legislative Council.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 168: Governor, Assembly and Council; the Governor is a constituent but not an ordinary member of either House.
Correct: the Governor is part of the legislature but is not a member of either House.
2. Article 168: Assembly and Council only; the Governor automatically becomes Council Chairman.
Wrong: it leaves out the Governor, and the Governor never becomes Council Chairman; the Council elects its own.
3. Article 169: Chief Minister, Assembly and Council; the Governor is an elected Assembly member.
Wrong: Article 169 is about creating or abolishing Councils, the Chief Minister is not a constituent, and the Governor is never an Assembly member.
4. Article 170: Governor, Assembly and High Court; the Council is outside the legislature.
Wrong: Article 170 is about the Assembly's composition, and the High Court is part of the judiciary, not the legislature.

points: Memory hook: 168 – who forms the legislature, 169 – create/abolish Council, 170 – Assembly, 171 – Council.
This mirrors Article 79 for Parliament (President + two Houses).

LX-PQ-001.lead: Option 3: the Speaker is not the chairman of the Estimates Committee; its chairman is appointed by the Speaker from among its members.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Business Advisory Committee
The Speaker chairs the Business Advisory Committee, which fixes the time-table of House business.
2. Rules Committee
The Speaker chairs the Rules Committee, which considers matters of procedure.
3. Estimates Committee
Correct: the Estimates Committee's chairman is appointed by the Speaker from among its members, and he is invariably from the ruling party.
4. General Purposes Committee
The Speaker chairs the General Purposes Committee, which deals with House matters not covered by other committees.

points: The Speaker presides over the Business Advisory, Rules and General Purposes Committees ex-officio.
Financial committees (Estimates, Public Accounts, Public Undertakings) have chairmen appointed by the Speaker, not the Speaker himself.

LX-PQ-002.lead: Option 2: Zero Hour is not mentioned in the Rules of Procedure; it is an informal device.

head: Option

rows: 1. A private member's bill is one moved by a nominated MP
False

A private member is any MP who is not a minister, whether elected or nominated. A nominated member who is a minister would move a government bill, and an elected backbencher moves a private member's bill.
2. A private member's bill was recently passed for the first time
False
Fourteen private members' bills have been passed by both Houses and became law; the last one was in 1970. So it would not be a first in history.

points: Public (government) bill = introduced by a minister; private member's bill = introduced by any non-minister MP, usually on Fridays.
Option 1 and option 3 fail because statement 1 confuses 'private member' with 'nominated member'.
Option 2 fails because statement 2 is historically wrong.

LX-UPSC-2018-Q10.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Swatantra Party was the largest opposition party in the first Lok Sabha
False
In the first Lok Sabha (1952) the largest opposition group was the Communist Party of India. The Swatantra Party was formed only in 1959.
2. A Leader of the Opposition was first recognised in 1969
True
The first official Leader of the Opposition in Lok Sabha was recognised in 1969 (Ram Subhag Singh, Congress (O)). The post got statutory status in 1977.
3. A party needs at least 75 members for its leader to be LoP
False
The rule is that the party must hold at least one-tenth of the total strength of the House, which is about 55 in Lok Sabha, not 75.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 all include statement 1 or 3, which are false.
The Leader of the Opposition gets the salary and facilities of a cabinet minister (Salary and Allowances of Leaders of Opposition in Parliament Act, 1977).
Memory hook: LoP needs '1/10 of the House', the same fraction as quorum.

LX-UPSC-2019-Q13.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Ended Company trade monopoly except tea and trade with China
True
The Charter Act of 1813 threw Indian trade open to all British merchants, but kept the Company's monopoly over trade in tea and trade with China.
2. Asserted Crown sovereignty over Company territories
True
The Act for the first time asserted the sovereignty of the British Crown over the Company's Indian territories.
3. Indian revenues now controlled by British Parliament
False
The 1813 Act did not transfer control of Indian revenues to Parliament. Direct Crown control of finances came only with the Government of India Act, 1858.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 fail because each includes the false statement 3.
The 1813 Act also allowed Christian missionaries into India and set aside ₹1 lakh a year for the education of Indians.
Memory hook: 1813 = 'trade opened, Crown asserted'; 1833 = monopoly fully ended.

LX-UPSC-2022-Q03.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (2 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. A Constitution Amendment Bill needs prior recommendation of the President
False
Article 368 does not require the President's prior recommendation. Such a bill can be introduced by a minister or even a private member in either House.
2. The President must give assent
True
After the 24th Amendment Act, 1971, the President is bound to give assent to a Constitution Amendment Bill; he can neither withhold assent nor return it.
3. Special majority in both Houses; no joint sitting
True
Each House must pass it separately by a special majority, and if the Houses disagree there is no joint sitting; the bill simply fails.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 fail because each includes the false statement 1.
Bills affecting federal provisions also need ratification by half of the State Legislatures by simple majority.
Contrast: Money Bills need prior presidential recommendation; amendment bills do not.

POL-722-AR-01.lead: Prorogation by the President ends a session, but the Lok Sabha itself continues; option 2 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Adjournment
Ends only a sitting for some hours or days; the session continues. Done by the presiding officer.
Prorogation
Ends the session; the House remains alive and is later summoned again. Done by the President.
Dissolution
Ends the life of the Lok Sabha itself, leading to fresh elections.
Quorum call
Only checks whether one-tenth members are present; it ends nothing.

points: Pending bills do not lapse on prorogation, but some do lapse on dissolution.
Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and is never dissolved.

POL-722-AR-02.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Demands for grants are voted only by Lok Sabha
True
Article 113 gives the power to assent to or refuse demands for grants to the Lok Sabha; Rajya Sabha can only discuss the budget.
2. Charged expenditure is submitted to vote
False
Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India can be discussed but is not submitted to vote of Parliament (Article 113(1)).

points: Options 2 and 3 fail because statement 2 is false; option 4 fails because statement 1 is true.
Charged items include the President's emoluments, salaries of Supreme Court judges and the CAG, and debt charges.

POL-722-CH-01.lead: Article 108 joint sitting cannot be held for a Money Bill, because the Lok Sabha has overriding power over it; option 3 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Ordinary Bill
Joint sitting is available when the Houses disagree on it.
Financial Bill category I
Joint sitting is available; after introduction it is treated like an ordinary bill.
Money Bill
No joint sitting; Rajya Sabha can only recommend within 14 days and Lok Sabha decides.
A bill with amendments disputed by both Houses
This is one of the three situations that allow a joint sitting under Article 108.

points: Constitution Amendment Bills also cannot go to a joint sitting.
Joint sittings have been held only three times: 1961, 1978 and 2002.

POL-722-CH-02.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Moved only in Lok Sabha
True
The Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)), so the motion is only in Lok Sabha.
2. Must specify reasons
False
A no-confidence motion need not state any reasons; it simply says the House has no confidence in the ministry.
3. Concerns collective responsibility of the Council of Ministers
True
It is moved against the whole Council of Ministers, which must resign if it is passed.

points: Option 1 leaves out the true statement 3; options 3 and 4 include the false statement 2.
Contrast: a censure motion must state reasons and can be against one minister.

POL-722-P234-01.lead: The Speaker of Lok Sabha presides over a joint sitting of the two Houses, so option 2 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Chairman of Rajya Sabha
Wrong. The Chairman is not a member of either House and does not preside at a joint sitting.
Speaker of Lok Sabha
Correct. Article 118(4) and the joint-sitting rules give this role to the Speaker.
President
Wrong. The President only summons the joint sitting under Article 108.
Prime Minister
Wrong. The PM is a member of a House, not a presiding officer.

points: In the Speaker's absence, the Deputy Speaker presides; if he is absent, the Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha.
Decisions at a joint sitting are by majority of total members present and voting.

POL-722-P236-01.lead: Effective strength = 245 − 20 = 225; more than half of 225 is 113, so option 1 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct. 225 ÷ 2 = 112.5, and the smallest whole number above it is 113.
Wrong. 114 is a majority, but not the minimum.
Wrong. 123 is the absolute majority of total membership (245), not of effective strength.
Wrong. This is more than any needed majority.

points: Effective majority = majority of total membership minus vacancies.
It is used to remove the Vice-President, the Rajya Sabha Deputy Chairman, and the Speaker and Deputy Speaker.

POL-722-P237-01.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Introduced only in Lok Sabha
True
Article 109 says a Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha, and only with the President's recommendation.
2. Rajya Sabha must return it within 14 days
True
Rajya Sabha must return it with or without recommendations within 14 days; otherwise it is deemed passed by both Houses.
3. Rajya Sabha may reject it
False
Rajya Sabha cannot reject or amend a Money Bill; it can only make recommendations that Lok Sabha may accept or reject.

points: Option 1 leaves out the true statement 2; options 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.
The Speaker certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill, and his decision is final (Article 110(3)).

POL-722-P255-01.lead: After demands for grants are voted, the Appropriation Bill is passed to allow withdrawal of money from the Consolidated Fund; option 3 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: General discussion
Comes before voting, right after presentation of the budget.
Committee scrutiny
Departmental standing committees examine demands before they are voted.
Appropriation Bill
Follows voting on demands; no money can be withdrawn without it (Article 114).
Budget presentation
The very first stage of the budget process.

points: Order: presentation → general discussion → committee scrutiny → voting on demands → Appropriation Bill → Finance Bill.
The Finance Bill gives effect to the tax proposals.

POL-722-P257-01.lead: A token cut motion asks that the demand be reduced by ₹100 to raise a specific grievance; option 3 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Policy cut
Asks that the demand be reduced to Re 1; shows disapproval of the policy behind the demand.
Economy cut
Asks for reduction by a stated amount to bring economy in expenditure.
Token cut
Asks for reduction by ₹100 to ventilate a specific grievance within the government's responsibility.
Guillotine
Not a cut motion; on the last day the Speaker puts all remaining demands to vote together.

points: Cut motions are moved only in Lok Sabha during voting on demands for grants.
Memory hook: Policy = 1, Token = 100, Economy = 'some amount'.

POL-722-P260-01.lead: Under Article 100(3), quorum is one-tenth of the total number of members of the House, including the presiding officer; option 2 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: One-fifth
Wrong. No House of Parliament uses this fraction.
One-tenth
Correct. Lok Sabha quorum is 55 and Rajya Sabha is 25.
One-third
Wrong. Article 100(3) fixes quorum at one-tenth, not one-third, of the total members.
Fifty members
Wrong. Fifty is the support needed for leave of a no-confidence motion, not quorum.

points: If there is no quorum, the presiding officer must adjourn the House or suspend the meeting.
Quorum means the minimum number of members needed for the House to transact business.

POL-722-REC-STAGE-001.lead: Article 84 sets minimum age 25 years for Lok Sabha and 30 years for Rajya Sabha; option 1 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Lok Sabha 25; Rajya Sabha 30
Correct; Article 84 with the RPA fixes 25 years for Lok Sabha and 30 years for Rajya Sabha.
Lok Sabha 30; Rajya Sabha 25
Wrong. The ages are reversed: Lok Sabha needs 25 and Rajya Sabha needs 30.
Both 25
Wrong. Lok Sabha needs 25 years, but Rajya Sabha requires 30 years.
Both 30
Wrong. Lok Sabha requires only 25 years.

points: The upper House needs a higher age because it is meant to be a body of more mature members.
Same pattern in States: Assembly 25, Council 30.

POL-722-REC-STAGE-002.lead: Under Article 83(2), during a national emergency Parliament may extend the Lok Sabha by law one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the emergency ends; option 1 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament may extend it one year at a time, but not beyond six months after the emergency ends
Correct. This is the exact rule of Article 83(2).
The President may extend it indefinitely
Wrong. Only Parliament can extend it, by law, and only one year at a time.
Rajya Sabha alone may extend it for six years
Wrong. Rajya Sabha has no power to extend the Lok Sabha; only Parliament can do so by law under Article 83(2).
Its term can never be extended
Wrong. Extension is allowed during a national emergency.

points: Normal term of Lok Sabha is five years from its first meeting.
The fifth Lok Sabha was extended in 1976 during the internal emergency.

POL-722-REC-STAGE-003.lead: In Sita Soren v. Union of India (2024), a seven-judge bench held that Articles 105(2) and 194(2) do not protect legislators from prosecution for bribery, overruling P.V. Narasimha Rao (1998); option 1 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: No immunity for bribery; P.V. Narasimha Rao overruled
Correct. Bribery is complete when the bribe is accepted, so it is not part of the speech or vote that is protected.
Every act remotely connected with a vote is immune
Wrong. The Court rejected this wide reading.
Only MPs, not State legislators, may claim immunity
Wrong. The ruling covers both MPs (Article 105) and MLAs (Article 194), and neither gets immunity for bribery.
A House privilege proceeding permanently bars criminal prosecution
Wrong. House action and criminal prosecution can both proceed.

points: Privilege protects freedom of speech and voting in the House, not crimes committed to influence that speech or vote.

POL-N16-CUR-003.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3 (1, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 87th Amendment shifted boundary basis from 1991 to 2001
True
The 84th Amendment (2001) allowed readjustment of constituencies on the 1991 census; the 87th Amendment (2003) changed this to the 2001 census.
2. Boundary rationalisation required an increase in every State's seat total
False
The readjustment only redrew boundaries within each State; the total seats of each State stayed frozen.
3. Freeze lasts until figures of the first census after 2026 are published
True
The freeze ends only when the figures of the first census taken after 2026 are published, not merely when the year 2026 arrives.

points: Options 1 and 2 include the false statement 2; option 4 leaves out the true statement 3.
The freeze was meant to avoid penalising States that controlled population.

POL-N16-CUR-004.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 4 (2, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Election petition is first filed in the Supreme Court
False
Under the RPA 1951, an election petition is filed first in the High Court; an appeal then lies to the Supreme Court.
2. President calls constituencies to elect through the notification
True
Section 14 of the RPA 1951 says the President, by notification, calls upon constituencies to elect members for a new Lok Sabha.
3. RPA 1951 covers conduct of elections and qualifications; rolls are in RPA 1950
True
The 1950 Act deals with allocation of seats and preparation of electoral rolls; the 1951 Act deals with conduct of elections, qualifications, disqualifications and disputes.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 include the false statement 1.
Memory hook: 1950 = seats and rolls; 1951 = elections and disputes.

POL-N16-CUR-006.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 1 (1, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Both resolutions need two-thirds of members present and voting
True
Article 249 and Article 312 each require a Rajya Sabha resolution supported by two-thirds of members present and voting.
2. An Article 249 law continues indefinitely after the resolution lapses
False
A law made under Article 249 ceases to have effect six months after the resolution ceases to be in force.
3. Art 249 = national interest on State List; Art 312 = All India Services
True
These are the correct subjects of the two Articles.

points: Option 2 leaves out the true statement 3; options 3 and 4 include the false statement 2.
An Article 249 resolution is valid for one year and can be renewed any number of times.

POL-N16-CUR-007.lead: All three statements are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1, 2, 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Art 252: two or more State resolutions enable Parliament to legislate for them
True
When two or more State Legislatures pass resolutions, Parliament can make a law on a State List matter for those States.
2. Art 253: Parliament may implement international agreements
True
Parliament can make any law to implement a treaty or international agreement, even on a State List subject.
3. Another State may later adopt the Art 252 Act
True
Article 252 lets any other State adopt the law later by passing a resolution of its own Legislature.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 each leave out a true statement.
An Article 252 law can be amended or repealed only by Parliament, not by the States.

POL-N16-CUR-008.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3 (2, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. An Art 250 law continues indefinitely after the emergency
False
A law made under Article 250 becomes inoperative six months after the National Emergency ceases.
2. Art 250 lets Parliament legislate on State List matters during national emergency
True
While a proclamation of national emergency is in operation, Parliament can make laws on any State List subject.
3. Arts 356–357 are a separate route under President's Rule
True
Under Article 357, during President's Rule in a State, the State's law-making powers are exercised by or under the authority of Parliament.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 include the false statement 1.
Difference: Article 250 covers the whole country in a national emergency; Article 357 covers only the State under President's Rule.

POL-N16-CUR-011.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 4 (1, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Art 71(3) lets Parliament regulate election matters
True
Parliament, subject to the Constitution, may by law regulate matters relating to the election of the President or Vice-President; it did so by the 1952 Act.
2. Disputes are decided by the Election Commission
False
Article 71(1) says all doubts and disputes about the election are decided by the Supreme Court, whose decision is final.
3. Regulating and deciding disputes are distinct functions
True
Regulation is a legislative function (Parliament); deciding disputes is a judicial function (Supreme Court).

points: Options 1 and 3 include the false statement 2; option 2 leaves out the true statement 3.
The Election Commission only conducts the presidential election; it does not decide its disputes.

POL-N16-CUR-012.lead: All three statements are correct, so the answer is option 1 (1, 2, 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Chairman and four other members
True
Article 280 provides for a Finance Commission consisting of a chairman and four other members.
2. The President constitutes it
True
The President constitutes the Finance Commission every five years or earlier.
3. Parliament determines qualifications and manner of selection
True
Parliament fixed these by the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951; e.g., the chairman must have experience in public affairs.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 each leave out a true statement.
Its recommendations are advisory and not binding on the government.

POL-N16-CUR-013.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Concerns a definite matter of urgent public importance; interrupts business
True
An adjournment motion draws attention of the House to a definite matter of urgent public importance and sets aside normal business.
2. May be admitted on a sub judice matter
False
An adjournment motion cannot be raised on a matter pending before a court (sub judice).
3. Has an element of censure; not used in Rajya Sabha
True
It is seen as an extraordinary device with an element of censure against the government, so Rajya Sabha does not use it.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 include the false statement 2.
It needs support of 50 members to be admitted, and discussion lasts at least two and a half hours.

POL-N16-CUR-014.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3 (2, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. A token cut reduces the demand to Re 1
False
Reducing the demand to Re 1 is a policy cut; a token cut reduces it by ₹100.
2. Defeat on a central financial measure shows loss of support
True
If the government is defeated on a money matter, it shows the ministry has lost Lok Sabha's confidence, which may lead to its resignation.
3. A cut motion is a budget device, not a constitutional amendment
True
Cut motions are moved during voting on demands for grants to reduce a demand.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 include the false statement 1.
Memory hook: Policy = Re 1, Token = ₹100.

POL-N16-CUR-015.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Art 265: no tax without authority of law
True
Article 265 says no tax shall be levied or collected except by authority of law.
2. Art 292: Parliament may limit Union borrowing and guarantees
True
The Union can borrow on the security of the Consolidated Fund of India within limits fixed by Parliament by law.
3. Art 292: Union may borrow only within India
False
Article 292 has no territorial limit, so the Union can borrow abroad too; the 'within India' restriction applies to States under Article 293.

points: Options 1 and 3 include the false statement 3; option 2 leaves out the true statement 2.
A State cannot borrow without Centre's consent while it owes money to the Centre (Article 293(3)).

POL-N16-CUR-016.lead: All three statements are correct, so the answer is option 1 (1, 2, 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Art 112: annual financial statement laid before both Houses
True
The President causes the budget to be laid before both Houses of Parliament.
2. Advances from Contingency Fund pending authorisation
True
The Contingency Fund is at the President's disposal for unforeseen expenditure, and Parliament authorises it later (Article 267).
3. Voting on demands belongs to Lok Sabha
True
Article 113 gives only Lok Sabha the power to vote on demands for grants.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 each leave out a true statement.
Contingency Fund advances do not bypass Parliament; they are only made before its approval.

POL-N16-CUR-017.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (2, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Other Election Commissioners removed like a Supreme Court judge
False
Under Article 324(5), other Election Commissioners can be removed by the President on the recommendation of the Chief Election Commissioner; they do not have judge-like protection.
2. CAG removed like a Supreme Court judge
True
Article 148 gives the CAG the same removal manner and grounds as a Supreme Court judge.
3. CEC removed like a Supreme Court judge
True
The CEC can be removed only on the same grounds and in the same manner as a Supreme Court judge.

Judge-like removal means proved misbehaviour or incapacity, through an address by special majority in both Houses.

POL-N16-CUR-019.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3 (1, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Lok Sabha chooses Speaker and Deputy Speaker from its members
True
Article 93: the Lok Sabha elects its Speaker and Deputy Speaker from amongst its members.
2. The Deputy Speaker resigns to the President
False
Article 94: the Deputy Speaker resigns by writing to the Speaker, and the Speaker resigns to the Deputy Speaker.
3. Rajya Sabha chooses its Deputy Chairman from its members
True
Article 89(2): Rajya Sabha elects its Deputy Chairman from amongst its members; the Chairman is the Vice-President ex officio.

points: Options 1 and 2 include the false statement 2; option 4 leaves out the true statement 3.

POL-N16-CUR-020.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 4 (2, 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Rajya Sabha may hold a Money Bill for 30 days
False
Rajya Sabha must return a Money Bill within 14 days (Article 109); otherwise it is deemed passed.
2. Art 110(3) gives disputed classification to the Speaker
True
If a question arises whether a bill is a Money Bill, the decision of the Lok Sabha Speaker is final.
3. Rajya Sabha Chairman is not the certifier
True
Only the Speaker endorses the certificate on a Money Bill sent to Rajya Sabha and the President.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 include the false statement 1.

POL-N16-CUR-021.lead: Option 1 (1, 3 only): statement(s) 1, 3 true, statement(s) 2 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The Constitution provides a special approval arrangement involving Rajya Sabha while Lok Sabha is dissolved.
True
True. The proviso to Article 352(4) says that if Lok Sabha is dissolved (or dissolves within the 30 days) without approving the proclamation, it survives if Rajya Sabha has approved it.
2. Under Article 352(4), the proclamation can continue beyond thirty days after the reconstituted Lok Sabha first sits without that House approving it.
False
False. In that case the proclamation ceases 30 days after the reconstituted Lok Sabha first sits unless Lok Sabha also approves it within those 30 days; Rajya Sabha approval alone is not enough.
3. Article 352(7) requires revocation if Lok Sabha passes the specified disapproval resolution.
True
True. Article 352(7), added by the 44th Amendment, 1978, obliges the President to revoke the proclamation if Lok Sabha passes a resolution disapproving its continuation (simple majority).

points: Option 2 (1 only) leaves out true statement 3.
Option 3 (1, 2 only) wrongly includes false statement 2 and leaves out true statement 3.
Option 4 (2, 3 only) wrongly includes false statement 2 and leaves out true statement 1.
Lok Sabha has the final word: it alone can end the emergency by a disapproval resolution, and its approval is required once it is reconstituted.

POL-N16-CUR-022.lead: Option 2 (1, 2, 3): statement(s) 1, 2, 3 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. While a National Emergency is in operation, Parliament may by law extend the Lok Sabha's term by not more than one year at a time.
True
True. Under Article 83(2), during a National Emergency Parliament can extend Lok Sabha's term by law for one year at a time, and not beyond six months after the emergency ends.
2. Lok Sabha’s ordinary five-year period runs from the date appointed for its first meeting.
True
True. Article 83(2) counts the five years from the date appointed for the first meeting of the House, not from the date of the election result.
3. Earlier dissolution of Lok Sabha is constitutionally possible.
True
True. The President can dissolve Lok Sabha earlier on the advice of the Council of Ministers, so the five years are a maximum, not a fixed term.

Option 3 (1, 3 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 4 (2, 3 only) leaves out true statement 1.
Memory hook: Rajya Sabha is permanent, Lok Sabha is 5 years maximum, extendable only during emergency.

POL-N16-CUR-023.lead: Option 3 (1, 2, 3): statement(s) 1, 2, 3 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. A substantive motion is an independent, self-contained proposal for the House to express a decision or opinion.
True
True. A substantive motion is a self-contained independent proposal dealing with a very important matter, such as an impeachment or a no-confidence motion.
2. A substitute motion proposes an alternative which supersedes the original if adopted.
True
True. A substitute motion is moved in place of an original motion and offers an alternative to it; if adopted, it supersedes the original motion.
3. An amendment is one of the categories of subsidiary motions.
True
True. Subsidiary motions are of three kinds: ancillary, superseding and amendment, so an amendment is one category of subsidiary motion.

points: Option 1 (1, 3 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 2 (2, 3 only) leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2, 3.
Laxmikanth divides motions into three types: substantive, substitute and subsidiary.

POL-N16-CUR-024.lead: Option 4 (1, 2 only): statement(s) 1, 2 true, statement(s) 3 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. An ancillary motion assists the regular transaction of business, such as a bill’s committee referral.
True
True. An ancillary motion is recognised as the regular way of proceeding with various kinds of business, for example a motion to refer a bill to a committee.
2. A superseding motion seeks to displace the proceeding then under discussion.
True
True. A superseding motion is moved during the debate on another issue and seeks to displace that issue, for example a motion to postpone the matter.
3. Once an amendment to a motion is moved, the original motion lapses automatically.
False
False. An amendment only seeks to modify or substitute part of the original motion; the original motion stays before the House and does not lapse when an amendment is moved.

points: Option 1 (1, 2, 3) wrongly includes false statement 3.
Option 2 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 3 (1, 3 only) wrongly includes false statement 3 and leaves out true statement 2.
Remember the three subsidiary motions: ancillary, superseding, amendment.

POL-N16-CUR-025.lead: Option 1 (2, 3 only): statement(s) 2, 3 true, statement(s) 1 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Every resolution, once adopted by the House, is always legally binding on the government.
False
False. Most resolutions only express the opinion of the House and are not binding on the government; only statutory resolutions passed under a law have legal effect.
2. A private member’s resolution is moved by a member who is not a minister.
True
True. A private member's resolution is moved by a private member, that is, any member other than a minister.
3. A government resolution is moved by a minister; a statutory resolution may be moved by a minister or private member under its legal provision.
True

POL-R21-ELECT-byelection-time-exceptions.lead: Option 1: within six months of the vacancy, unless less than one year of the term remains (Section 151A, RPA).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Correct: Section 151A fixes six months; exceptions are a remaining term under one year, or ECI certifying with the Centre that holding it is difficult.

Wrong: there is no three-month rule, and the law does allow exceptions.

Wrong: the limit is six months, not one year.

Wrong: the ECI has no open discretion; it must follow the six-month limit.

What it is / means
Correct?

False, because Section 100(1)(b) makes voiding the election compulsory once a corrupt practice by the candidate is proved.

False, because the Election Commission has no power to set aside an election; only an election petition before the High Court can do so.
High Court shall declare the election void
True: election petitions are tried by the High Court, and proof of bribery by the returned candidate leaves the court no choice but to void it.
Every incorrect affidavit gives same result
False, because an incorrect affidavit is not automatically a corrupt practice; the petitioner must prove a specific ground under Section 100.

points: Article 329(b): an election can be questioned only by an election petition as provided by law; appeal lies to the Supreme Court.
'Shall' in Section 100 means the court has no discretion once the ground is proved.

What it is / means
