LX-UPSC-2017-Q18.lead: Option 3: the main advantage of parliamentary government is that the executive remains responsible to the legislature, which can question and remove it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Executive and legislature work independently
This describes separation of powers, a presidential feature; in the parliamentary system they are fused.
Continuity of policy and more efficient
Stability and definiteness of policy are merits of the presidential system; LX lists 'no continuity of policies' as a demerit of the parliamentary system.
Executive responsible to the legislature
'Responsible government' is a listed merit of the parliamentary system; ministers face questions, motions and no-confidence votes daily.
Head of government cannot be changed without election
False for parliamentary systems: a PM can be replaced mid-term if he loses majority support.

points: Dr Ambedkar: the British system gives more responsibility but less stability; India preferred responsibility.
Other merits: harmony between legislature and executive, prevents despotism, wide representation.

LX-UPSC-2020-Q10.lead: Option 2: in a parliamentary system the Government is responsible to Parliament and can be removed by it through a vote of no-confidence.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: All parties represented in Government
That is an all-party/national government, an occasional arrangement; normally the majority party alone forms the government.
Responsible to Parliament and removable by it
Exactly the parliamentary principle: the ministry stays in office only as long as it has the confidence of the popular House.
Elected by people and removable by them
Describes a directly elected executive, as in a presidential system; and removal by the people (recall) is not part of it.
Chosen by Parliament but not removable before fixed term
A fixed term independent of legislative confidence is a presidential-type feature; it contradicts responsibility.

points: Key words to spot: 'collective responsibility', 'confidence of the House', 'no-confidence motion' = parliamentary.
In India, Article 75(3): Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

POL-731-CH-01.lead: Option 2: the Union Council of Ministers answers to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)) and a State Council of Ministers to the Legislative Assembly (Article 164(2)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Union—Rajya Sabha; State—Legislative Council
Wrong. The indirectly elected upper Houses cannot remove a ministry by a no-confidence vote.
Union—Lok Sabha; State—Legislative Assembly
Correct. Responsibility is always to the directly elected lower House.
Union—President; State—Governor personally
Wrong. Ministers hold office at their pleasure (individual responsibility), but collective responsibility is to the House.
Both—Supreme Court
Wrong. Courts can review legality of actions but ministries are not politically responsible to the judiciary.

points: Logic: the popular House represents the people, so the government must keep its confidence.
Ministers from the upper House are still collectively responsible to the lower House.

POL-731-CH-02.lead: Option 1 (1 only): a parliamentary ministry depends on the confidence of the popular House; a presidential executive has a fixed tenure and does not fall on losing a majority.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Parliamentary ministry must resign or seek dissolution
True
Under collective responsibility the ministry must quit if it loses the confidence of the popular House, or the PM may advise dissolution of the House.
2. Presidential executive automatically loses its tenure
False
In a presidential system the executive is elected for a fixed term and is not responsible to the legislature; it can be removed only by impeachment, not by losing a majority.

points: Option 2 picks only the false statement.
Option 3 wrongly includes statement 2.
Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1, the core rule of responsible government.

POL-731-P152-01.lead: Option 3: a fixed executive tenure independent of legislative confidence belongs to the presidential system, so it is inconsistent with parliamentary government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Political responsibility to the popular House
A core parliamentary feature (collective responsibility).
Fusion of legislature and executive
A parliamentary feature; Bagehot called the cabinet the hyphen and buckle that joins the two.
Fixed executive tenure independent of confidence
Presidential feature: the US President serves a fixed four-year term whatever Congress thinks. Inconsistent with parliamentary system.
Ministers drawn from the legislature
A parliamentary feature called double membership.

points: LX Table 13.1: parliamentary features are dual executive, majority party rule, collective responsibility, political homogeneity, double membership, PM leadership, dissolution of lower House, fusion of powers.

POL-731-P152-02.lead: Option 4: a fixed-tenure executive independent of the legislature is a presidential feature; the Assembly rejected it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Familiarity under British rule
A real reason. K.M. Munshi argued that India's constitutional traditions had already become parliamentary.
Preference for more responsibility over stability
A real reason. Dr Ambedkar said the Draft Constitution preferred more responsibility to more stability.
Avoid legislative–executive conflicts
A real reason. The framers felt an infant democracy could not risk the constant conflicts seen in the US system.
Desire for fixed-tenure executive
NOT a reason. This is what the presidential system offers, which the Assembly turned down.

points: The fourth LX reason is the nature of Indian society: a plural society needs wide representation in government.

POL-731-P152-03.lead: Option 4: responsible government is a merit of the parliamentary system, not a demerit.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Unstable government
A demerit: a ministry can fall when it loses majority support, e.g. coalition breakdowns.
Lack of continuity of policies
A demerit: a change of government can reverse earlier policies.
Dictatorship of the Cabinet
A demerit: with an absolute majority the cabinet can become autocratic (Laski, Ramsay Muir).
Responsible government
A merit: the ministry is answerable to Parliament through questions, motions and no-confidence votes.

points: LX demerits: unstable government, no continuity of policies, dictatorship of cabinet, against separation of powers, government by amateurs.

POL-731-P153-01.lead: Option 2: Article 75(3) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Rajya Sabha
Cannot remove the ministry; it has no power of no-confidence motion, though ministers answer questions there.
Lok Sabha
Correct: the ministry stays only while it has the Lok Sabha's confidence, and a no-confidence motion passed there removes it.
Parliament in a joint sitting
Joint sittings (Article 108) are only for resolving deadlocks on ordinary bills.
Supreme Court
The judiciary reviews legality, but the ministry is not politically responsible to it.

points: Even ministers from Rajya Sabha are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha.
The ministry swims and sinks together: a Lok Sabha defeat removes all ministers.

POL-731-P153-02.lead: Option 1: a nominal head (President) plus a real executive (PM-led Council) is a dual executive, a mark of parliamentary government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Dual executive with nominal and real parts
Correct: the President is head of State with formal powers; the PM and ministers actually govern.
Directly elected executive
Wrong: the Indian President is indirectly elected, and real executive power comes from Lok Sabha majority, not direct election.
Judicial supremacy
Wrong: this is about courts' final say on law, unrelated to who heads the executive.
Hereditary cabinet
Wrong: ministers are appointed on the PM's advice and depend on the House's confidence; nothing is inherited.

points: Presidential system has a single executive: the President is both head of State and head of Government.
Article 74(1): the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

POL-731-P153-03.lead: Option 1: cabinet solidarity (collective responsibility) requires every minister to support Cabinet decisions publicly or resign.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Cabinet solidarity
Directly strained: a minister who disagrees must resign; he cannot stay and oppose the decision in public.
Judicial review
Power of courts to strike down unconstitutional acts; not involved in an internal ministerial disagreement.
Bicameralism
Having two Houses of legislature; not affected by a minister's statement.
Federal supremacy
Union-State relations; unrelated to ministers' conduct inside the cabinet.

points: LX: if a minister does not agree with a cabinet decision and is not prepared to defend it, he or she must resign.
Example: Dr B.R. Ambedkar resigned from the Cabinet in September 1951 over the Hindu Code Bill; C.D. Deshmukh resigned over states reorganisation.

POL-731-P153-04.lead: Option 2: a common minimum programme gives coalition partners a shared policy base, and collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha continues.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Differences automatically end collective responsibility
False: Article 75(3) applies to every ministry; party differences do not suspend it.
Consensus gives common basis while responsibility continues
True: coalition ministers agree on a programme, then defend Cabinet decisions together, or resign.
Responsible only to the Rajya Sabha
False: responsibility is always to the Lok Sabha, whatever the party composition.
Decisions bind only largest party's ministers
False: Cabinet decisions bind all ministers, irrespective of party.

points: Political homogeneity is a feature of parliamentary government; in a coalition it is replaced by consensus on a common programme.
The whole ministry still stands or falls together on a no-confidence motion.

POL-731-P153-05.lead: Option 1 (1 only): the President administers the oaths; cabinet secrecy does not free ministers from answering Parliament.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. President administers oaths of office and secrecy
True
Article 75(4): before a minister enters office, the President administers the oaths of office and secrecy (Third Schedule forms).
2. Secrecy means no duty to answer Parliament on announced policy
False
The oath of secrecy only bars disclosing confidential matters; ministers remain answerable to Parliament (questions, motions) for policy under collective responsibility.

points: Option 2 picks only the false statement; option 3 wrongly adds it.
Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1, which is a direct constitutional rule.

POL-731-P153-06.lead: Jennings: Cabinet is the core; Crossman and Mackintosh: Prime Ministerial government; Bagehot: buckle; Ramsay Muir: dictatorship of the Cabinet — option 2 (A–4, B–1, C–2, D–3).

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Ivor Jennings
4. Cabinet as the core
Jennings saw the Cabinet as the core around which the British constitutional system works.
B. Crossman and Mackintosh
1. Prime Ministerial Government
R.H. Crossman and J.P. Mackintosh argued that after World War II the PM dominated, so it is 'Prime Ministerial government'.
C. Bagehot
2. Buckle binding executive and legislature
Bagehot: the Cabinet is the hyphen and buckle binding the executive and legislature (fusion of powers).
D. Ramsay Muir
3. Dictatorship of the Cabinet
Ramsay Muir (How Britain is Governed) warned that the Cabinet's huge powers amount to a 'dictatorship of the Cabinet'.

points: Option 1 (A–1, B–4, C–2, D–3) is wrong: it gives A→1 (Prime Ministerial Government); B→4 (Cabinet as the core).
Option 3 (A–4, B–2, C–1, D–3) is wrong: it gives B→2 (Buckle binding executive and legislature); C→1 (Prime Ministerial Government).
Option 4 (A–4, B–1, C–3, D–2) is wrong: it gives C→3 (Dictatorship of the Cabinet); D→2 (Buckle binding executive and legislature).

POL-731-P154-01.lead: Option 2: under Article 75(5) a minister who is not an MP for six consecutive months ceases to be a minister.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Three months
Wrong: Article 75(5) allows a non-member minister six consecutive months, not three, to enter Parliament.
Six months
Correct: a non-member can be a minister for up to six consecutive months, within which he must enter either House.
One year
Too long; the Constitution fixes six months.
Until Lok Sabha is dissolved
Wrong: the six-month limit applies regardless of the life of the House.

points: The same rule applies to the PM and to State ministers (Article 164(4)).
This is one difference from Britain, where usually only MPs become ministers.
POL-731-P154-01.also: Supreme Court, S.R. Chaudhuri v State of Punjab (2001): a non-member cannot be reappointed minister repeatedly without getting elected.

POL-731-P154-02.lead: Option 2: India combines parliamentary government with a supreme written Constitution and judicial review; Britain follows parliamentary sovereignty.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Unlimited parliamentary sovereignty
False for India: Parliament's powers are limited by the written Constitution, federalism, judicial review and Fundamental Rights.
Parliamentary government with constitutional supremacy and judicial review
True: this is a key distinction listed by LX.
Britain has a written supreme constitution identical to India's
False: Britain has an unwritten constitution and Parliament is sovereign.
Judicial review absent in India
False: Articles 13, 32 and 226 give courts power to strike down unconstitutional laws.

points: Other differences: India is a republic (elected head) vs British monarchy; Indian PM can be from either House; no shadow cabinet in India.

POL-731-P154-03.lead: Option 3: the shadow cabinet is formed by the Opposition to balance the ruling cabinet and prepare its members for future ministerial office.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Inner committee of the governing Cabinet
False: that describes an inner/kitchen cabinet, not the shadow cabinet.
Judicial committee that countersigns decisions
False: no such body; and countersigning is a matter of legal responsibility of ministers, not courts.
Opposition team scrutinising departments and preparing alternative ministry
True: each shadow minister watches a ministry and is ready to take over if the Opposition wins.
Second executive appointed by the monarch
False: the monarch appoints no second executive; the government continues during dissolution.

points: LX: the shadow cabinet is a unique institution of the British cabinet system; there is no such institution in India.

POL-731-P154-04.lead: Option 1: the Indian PM may belong to either House; the British PM must, by convention, be from the House of Commons.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: India either House; Britain Commons
True: LX lists this as a difference between the two models.
Both from upper Houses
False: the British PM sits in the Commons (lower House), and Indian PMs have mostly been Lok Sabha members.
India requires Lok Sabha membership
False: Rajya Sabha members have been PM, e.g. Indira Gandhi (1966), Manmohan Singh.
Neither system links ministry with legislature
False: both have double membership; in India a non-member must enter Parliament within six months.

points: Example: Manmohan Singh was PM (2004-2014) as a Rajya Sabha member.

POL-731-P155-01.lead: Option 3: in the US presidential system neither side can end the other's term over a policy disagreement; both serve fixed terms.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President may dissolve the House
False: the US President has no power to dissolve Congress ('no dissolution of lower House').
Congress can end term by no-confidence
False: the President is not responsible to Congress; he can be removed only by impeachment for serious offences.
Neither can dissolve or remove; fixed terms continue
True: this is separation of powers with a fixed-term executive.
Cabinet becomes collectively responsible to Congress
False: US secretaries are responsible only to the President, not to Congress.

points: Result: legislative-executive deadlock can continue, which is why India's framers avoided the presidential model.

LX-PQ-038.lead: Option 4 is the wrong statement (the answer): the President can withdraw an ordinance at any time (on ministerial advice).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Co-extensive with Parliament's legislative power
Correct statement: ordinances can be issued only on subjects Parliament can legislate on, with the same limits.
Laid down in Article 123
Correct statement: Article 123 is indeed the source of the President's ordinance-making power, so it is not the answer.
Ceases six weeks after reassembly
Correct statement: an ordinance lapses six weeks after Parliament reassembles unless approved earlier.
Cannot be withdrawn at any time
Incorrect statement: Article 123(2)(b) allows the President to withdraw it at any time.

points: Maximum life of an ordinance without approval: six months and six weeks.
The power is not discretionary; it is used on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

LX-PQ-061.lead: Option 2: Article 113(3) says no demand for a grant shall be made except on the recommendation of the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Prime Minister
Leads the government but the Constitution vests the recommendation formally in the President.
President
Correct: Article 113(3) says no demand for a grant can be made except on the President's recommendation.
Finance Minister
Presents the budget, but the constitutional recommendation is the President's.
CAG
Audits expenditure after it is made; has no role in recommending demands.

points: This ensures that only the executive (through the President) can initiate demands for spending; the Lok Sabha can only accept, reduce or reject them.

LX-PQ-065.lead: Option 3: the President is elected by the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected members of State Legislative Assemblies (Article 54).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Members of Parliament and state legislatures
Wrong: nominated members are excluded, and Legislative Councils are excluded.
Elected members of Parliament and state legislatures
Wrong: 'state legislatures' would include Legislative Councils, whose members do not vote.
Elected MPs and elected MLAs of State Assemblies
Correct (Article 54): the electoral college is the elected members of both Houses of Parliament and the elected MLAs of States (and Delhi, Puducherry).
Elected LS members, all RS members and Assemblies
Wrong: nominated Rajya Sabha members do not vote.

points: Nominated members do take part in the impeachment of the President.
LX-PQ-065.also: 70th Amendment (1992) added elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry.

LX-PQ-072.lead: Option 4 — A is false but R is true.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
False
Under Article 57, a person who holds or has held the office of President is eligible for re-election. There is no limit on terms.
R
True
Under Article 58, a person must be qualified to be a member of the Lok Sabha to be elected President.

points: Does R explain A? Not needed — A is false, so there is nothing for R to explain.
Option 1 fails: A is false.
Option 2 fails: A is false.
Option 3 fails: A is false.

LX-PQ-151.lead: Option 4: the executive officer of a cantonment board is appointed by the President of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President of the board
Heads the board (the station commander) but does not appoint the executive officer.
Defence Secretary
Senior bureaucrat of the Defence Ministry; not the appointing authority.
Chief Secretary of the state
Cantonments are under the Union Defence Ministry, not the State government.
President of India
Correct: the executive officer belongs to a central cadre and is appointed by the President.

points: Cantonment boards are set up under the Cantonments Act, 2006 (earlier 1924), for civil administration of cantonment areas.

LX-PQ-164.lead: Option 2: both statements are true, but Statement-II (the procedure) does not explain Statement-I (the ground for impeachment).

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: Statement-I
True
Article 61: the President can be impeached only for 'violation of the Constitution'.
Statement-II
True
Article 61 lays down the procedure: charges by 1/4 members with 14 days' notice, two-thirds of total membership in each House.

points: Does II explain I? No. I tells WHY (ground) a President can be impeached; II only says the Constitution lays down HOW (procedure). Having a procedure is not the reason for the ground.
Option 1 is wrong because it claims a causal link that does not exist.
Options 3 and 4 are wrong because both statements are true.
LX-PQ-164.also: Impeachment needs a two-thirds majority of total membership of each House.

LX-PQ-178.lead: Option 3 (1 and 2): ordinance power is in Article 123 and co-extensive with Parliament's power; statements 3 and 4 are false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Article 123
True
Article 123 gives the President ordinance-making power.
2. Co-extensive with Parliament
True
LX: the power is coextensive, as regards all matters except duration, with Parliament's law-making power.
3. Only when Lok Sabha not in session
False
He can promulgate when both Houses or either House is not in session; the condition is not tied to the Lok Sabha alone.
4. Discretionary power
False
LX: it is not a discretionary power; he acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

points: Option 1 and option 2 wrongly include statement 4.
Option 4 wrongly includes statement 3.

LX-PQ-184.lead: Option 4 (1, 2 and 3): the Indian President has pocket, absolute and suspensive veto, but not a qualified veto.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Pocket veto
True
He may keep a bill pending indefinitely, as Article 111 fixes no time limit (e.g. Zail Singh, Post Office Bill 1986).
2. Absolute veto
True
He may withhold assent, e.g. for private members' bills or when a ministry resigns.
3. Suspensive veto
True
He may return a bill once for reconsideration; Parliament can override by ordinary majority.
4. Qualified veto
False
Overridable only by a higher majority; possessed by the US President, not the Indian.

points: Option 1 (2, 3) omits pocket veto.
Options 2 and 3 wrongly include qualified veto.

LX-UPSC-2024-Q02.lead: Option 4: Dr Sachchidananda Sinha, the oldest member, was elected temporary chairman (provisional President) of the Constituent Assembly on 9 December 1946.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: C. Rajagopalachari
Later the last Governor-General; not the provisional President.
Dr B.R. Ambedkar
Dr B.R. Ambedkar was Chairman of the Drafting Committee, not the provisional President of the Constituent Assembly.
T.T. Krishnamachari
T.T. Krishnamachari was a member of the Drafting Committee, not the provisional President of the Constituent Assembly.
Dr Sachchidananda Sinha
Correct: chosen as the oldest member, following the French practice.

points: Dr Rajendra Prasad was elected permanent President on 11 December 1946.

POL-732-CH-01.lead: Option 1: the election must be held within six months, and the new President gets a full five-year term.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Election within six months; the successor receives a full five-year term

Correct: Article 62(2) requires the election to fill a vacancy caused by death, resignation or removal within six months, and the person elected holds office for a full five years from the date he enters office.
2. Election within one year; the successor serves only the remainder
Wrong: the limit is six months, not one year, and the successor does not merely complete the remaining term; he gets a fresh five-year term.
3. Immediate direct election; the successor serves six years
Wrong: the President is never directly elected by the people; he is elected indirectly by an electoral college (Article 54), and the term is five years, not six.
4. No election is needed until the next general election
Wrong: there is no 'next general election' for the President; the vacancy must be filled by a fresh election within six months.

points: Until the new President is elected, the Vice-President acts as President (Article 65).
Contrast: for the Vice-President's office too, a successor gets a full five-year term, unlike a by-election to the Lok Sabha where the member serves only the remainder.
Memory hook: 'six months to elect, five full years to serve'.

POL-732-CH-02.lead: Option 2: elected MLAs vote in the presidential election but have no role in impeachment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Nominated MPs vote in election but not impeachment
Wrong: nominated MPs do not vote in the presidential election, but they do take part in impeachment, which is the exact opposite of this statement.
2. Elected State MLAs vote in election but do not participate in impeachment

Correct: elected members of State Legislative Assemblies are part of the electoral college (Article 54), but impeachment takes place only in the two Houses of Parliament (Article 61), so MLAs play no part in it.
3. State Legislative Council members participate in both
Wrong: members of State Legislative Councils take part in neither the election nor the impeachment of the President.
4. Nominated MPs and State MLAs participate in both
Wrong: nominated MPs vote only in impeachment, and MLAs only in the election, so neither group takes part in both.

points: Article 54: electoral college = elected MPs of both Houses + elected MLAs of States (and of Delhi and Puducherry, after the 70th Amendment, 1992).
Article 61: impeachment is a process of Parliament alone, so every MP, elected or nominated, can vote on it.
Memory hook: 'Election = elected only; Impeachment = Parliament only'.

POL-732-P156-01.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Elected members of both Houses of Parliament
True
Article 54 includes the elected members of both the Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha in the electoral college.
2. Elected members of State Legislative Assemblies
True
Article 54 includes elected MLAs of all States; the 70th Amendment (1992) added elected MLAs of Delhi and Puducherry.
3. Nominated members of the Rajya Sabha
False
Nominated members of either House do not vote in the presidential election, because they do not represent the people through election.
4. Members of State Legislative Councils
False
Members of State Legislative Councils (MLCs), elected or nominated, are not part of the electoral college.

points: Option 2 is wrong because it wrongly adds statement 3 (nominated Rajya Sabha members).
Option 3 is wrong because it drops statement 1 and wrongly adds statement 4 (MLCs).
Option 4 is wrong because it includes both excluded groups, 3 and 4.

POL-732-P157-01.lead: Option 2: Article 55(3) says the President is elected by proportional representation by means of the single transferable vote, and the voting is by secret ballot.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. First-past-the-post with open ballot
Wrong: first-past-the-post (whoever gets the most votes wins) is used for Lok Sabha seats, not for the President, and the presidential vote is secret, not open.
2. Proportional representation by single transferable vote with secret ballot
Correct: each elector ranks candidates by preference; a candidate must reach a fixed quota of votes, and lower preferences are transferred until someone reaches it. The ballot is secret.
3. List proportional representation by voice vote
Wrong: India does not use list proportional representation for the President, and there is no voice vote.
4. Direct popular election by simple majority
Wrong: the President is elected indirectly by an electoral college, not directly by the people.

points: Quota = (total valid votes ÷ 2) + 1, so the winner needs an absolute majority of votes, not just the largest share.
The same method is used for electing the Vice-President and Rajya Sabha members.
LX notes the term 'proportional representation' is a misnomer here, since only one seat is filled; it is really a preferential (majoritarian) system.

POL-732-P158-VALUE-01.lead: Option 3: an MLA's vote value uses the 1971 census population of the State and the number of elected members of its Legislative Assembly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Current population and total Legislative Council membership
Wrong: the current population is not used, and the Legislative Council plays no part in the presidential election.
2. 2011 census population and nominated Assembly membership
Wrong: the 2011 census is not the base, and nominated members are never counted in the calculation.
3. 1971 census population and elected Legislative Assembly membership
Correct: value of an MLA's vote = (State population ÷ total elected MLAs) ÷ 1000, with population frozen at the 1971 census.
4. Current electorate and total MPs
Wrong: MLA vote value is calculated from State population and elected MLAs, not from the electorate or the number of MPs.

points: The 84th Amendment (2001) kept the 1971 census as the base until the first census after 2026, so that States which controlled population are not penalised.
Because populations and Assembly sizes differ, the value of an MLA's vote differs from State to State (e.g. Uttar Pradesh has the highest).

POL-732-P159-MP-01.lead: Option 1: the value of an MP's vote is the total value of all MLAs' votes divided by the total number of elected MPs, so every MP gets the same value.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. MP value is derived from aggregate MLA vote value divided among elected MPs
Correct: one single formula is used for all MPs; this makes the Union side (MPs) equal in total weight to the States side (MLAs), and every MP's vote has the same value.
2. The Constitution gives each MP one ordinary vote without valuation
Wrong: votes in the presidential election are weighted; the Constitution does not give MPs an unvalued 'one man one vote'.
3. Rajya Sabha alone fixes MP values annually
Wrong: the Rajya Sabha does not fix vote values; they are worked out by the formula in Article 55.
4. State population is ignored in all calculations
Wrong: State population is the base of the MLA vote value, and through it, of the MP vote value too.

points: Article 55 aims at two kinds of parity: uniformity among States, and parity between the Union and the States as a whole.
MLA values differ because State populations and Assembly sizes differ; MP values are all equal because they come from one national total.

POL-732-P160-01.lead: Option 3: under Article 71, all doubts and disputes about the President's election are decided by the Supreme Court, and its decision is final.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Election Commission
Wrong: the Election Commission conducts the presidential election (Article 324), but it cannot decide disputes about it.
2. Parliament
Wrong: Parliament can regulate other matters of the election by law, but it does not decide election disputes.
3. Supreme Court
Correct: the Supreme Court alone inquires into and decides disputes about the election of the President (and Vice-President), and its decision is final.
4. Chief Justice acting alone administratively
Wrong: the dispute is decided by the Supreme Court as a court, not by the Chief Justice acting alone in an administrative capacity.

points: If the election is declared void, acts already done by that President remain valid (Article 71(2)).
The election cannot be challenged on the ground that the electoral college was incomplete because of vacancies (Article 71(4)).

POL-732-P160-ELECT-SAFE-01.lead: Both statements are false, so the answer is option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Election invalid merely because the electoral college had a vacancy
False
Article 71(4) says the election cannot be challenged on the ground of any vacancy in the electoral college, for example a dissolved Assembly.
2. Official acts before the decision become invalid if the election is declared void
False
Article 71(2) protects such acts: things done by the President before the Supreme Court's decision remain valid.

points: Option 1 is wrong because statement 1 is false (Article 71(4)).
Option 2 is wrong because statement 2 is false (Article 71(2)).
Option 3 is wrong because neither statement is true.
Concept: these rules keep the office stable, so the country's work is not undone by a later court decision.

POL-732-P161-QUAL-01.lead: Option 2: a 40-year-old Indian citizen who is a Governor qualifies, because a Governor is not treated as holding an office of profit for this purpose.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A 34-year-old Indian citizen serving as a Union Minister
Wrong: being a Union Minister is not a bar (it is exempted from the office-of-profit rule), but the person is only 34 and the minimum age is 35 (Article 58).
2. A 40-year-old Indian citizen serving as a State Governor

Correct: the person is a citizen and over 35, and Article 58 says the Governor of a State, like the sitting President, Vice-President and Union or State Ministers, is not deemed to hold an office of profit.
3. A 40-year-old foreign citizen serving as a university professor
Wrong: only a citizen of India can be elected President (Article 58), so a foreign citizen is ineligible whatever his age.
4. A 30-year-old Indian citizen holding no office
Wrong: the person holds no office, but at 30 he is below the minimum age of 35.

points: Article 58 qualifications: citizen of India, at least 35 years old, qualified for election to the Lok Sabha, and not holding an office of profit.
Memory hook: Lok Sabha member 25, Rajya Sabha 30, President and Vice-President 35.

POL-732-P162-NOM-01.lead: All three are required, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. At least 50 electors as proposers
True
The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections Act, 1952 (as amended in 1997) requires the nomination to be subscribed by at least 50 electors as proposers.
2. At least 50 electors as seconders
True
The same law requires at least 50 electors as seconders, to keep out non-serious candidates.
3. The prescribed security deposit
True
Each candidate must deposit ₹15,000 in the Reserve Bank of India; it is forfeited if he fails to get one-sixth of the votes polled.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 are wrong because each leaves out at least one condition that the law actually requires.
These conditions are laid down by Parliament's law, not by the Constitution itself (Article 71(3) lets Parliament regulate the election).

POL-732-P162-OATH-01.lead: Option 3: the President takes oath before the Chief Justice of India and resigns by writing to the Vice-President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Oath—Speaker; resignation—Prime Minister
Wrong: the Speaker administers no oath to the President, and the President's resignation does not go to the Prime Minister.
2. Oath—Vice-President; resignation—Chief Justice
Wrong: the Vice-President receives the resignation; he does not administer the oath, and the Chief Justice does not receive the resignation.
3. Oath—Chief Justice of India; resignation—Vice-President

Correct: Article 60 says the oath is taken before the Chief Justice of India (or, in his absence, the senior-most available judge of the Supreme Court); Article 56(1)(a) says the resignation is addressed to the Vice-President.
4. Oath—Prime Minister; resignation—Parliament
Wrong: the Prime Minister does not administer the President's oath, and the resignation is not addressed to Parliament.

points: The Vice-President must at once inform the Speaker of the Lok Sabha about the resignation (Article 56(2)).
The Vice-President resigns by writing to the President (Article 67(a)).
Memory hook: the two highest offices resign to each other.

POL-732-P163-01.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Either House may initiate it
True
Under Article 61(1) the impeachment charge can be started in either the Lok Sabha or the Rajya Sabha.
2. The ground is violation of the Constitution
True
Article 61(1) gives only one ground: 'violation of the Constitution'.
3. Final resolution needs two-thirds of members present and voting only
False
Article 61 needs a majority of two-thirds of the total membership of the House, which is harder than two-thirds of those present and voting.

points: Option 1 is wrong because it leaves out the true statement 2.
Option 3 is wrong because it leaves out statement 1 and wrongly includes statement 3.
Option 4 is wrong because statement 3 is false.

POL-732-P163-IMM-01.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Not answerable to any court for official acts
True
Article 361(1): the President is not answerable to any court for the exercise and performance of the powers and duties of his office.
2. No criminal proceedings during the term
True
Article 361(2): no criminal proceedings can be instituted or continued against the President in any court during his term, even for personal acts.
3. Civil proceedings for personal acts without prior notice
False
Article 361(4): civil proceedings for personal acts can be started only after two months' written notice has been given to him.

points: Option 1 is wrong because it leaves out the true statement 2.
Options 3 and 4 are wrong because they include the false statement 3.
Also: no arrest or imprisonment can be ordered against him during his term (Article 361(3)).

POL-732-P163-IMP-PROC-01.lead: Both conditions apply, so the answer is option 1 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Signed by at least one-fourth of the total members of that House
True
Article 61(2)(a) requires the resolution moving the charge to be signed by at least one-fourth of the total members of the House.
2. At least fourteen days' notice to the President
True
Article 61(2)(a) also requires at least 14 days' written notice to the President before the resolution is moved.

points: Options 2 and 3 are wrong because each drops one of the two conditions in Article 61(2)(a).
Option 4 is wrong because both conditions are required.
After this, the resolution must be passed by two-thirds of the total membership of that House, and the other House investigates the charge.

POL-732-P165-EXEC-01.lead: Option 3: the President formally makes appointments under the Constitution, but acts through set procedures and on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Every appointment is an unrestricted personal choice
Wrong: the President cannot make unrestricted personal choices; Article 74 makes ministerial advice binding.
2. Parliament makes every executive appointment by joint sitting
Wrong: Parliament does not make executive appointments, and joint sittings are only for resolving deadlocks on bills (Article 108).
3. Appointments are constitutionally made by the President, generally within specified procedures and ministerial advice
Correct: Article 53 vests executive power in the President, but under Article 74 he acts on ministerial advice, and many appointments follow fixed procedures (for example, judges after consultation).
4. Courts administer the Union executive
Wrong: courts can review executive action, but they do not administer the Union executive.

points: This is the core idea of parliamentary government: the President is the nominal head, the Council of Ministers is the real executive.
Examples: the President appoints the PM, Attorney General, CAG, CEC, Governors and judges, but in practice on advice.

POL-732-P166-LEG-01.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 4 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The President is a constituent part of Parliament
True
Article 79: Parliament consists of the President and the two Houses.
2. The President may summon and prorogue Parliament
True
Article 85 gives the President power to summon and prorogue the Houses.
3. The President may dissolve the Rajya Sabha
False
The Rajya Sabha is a permanent House and cannot be dissolved; the President can dissolve only the Lok Sabha (Article 85(2)(b)).

points: Option 1 is wrong because it leaves out the true statement 2.
Options 2 and 3 are wrong because they include the false statement 3.
One-third of Rajya Sabha members retire every second year, which is why it is never dissolved as a whole.

POL-732-P167-01.lead: Option 1: Article 123 lets the President issue an ordinance when Parliament is not in session and immediate action is needed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 123 ordinance
Correct: an ordinance is a temporary law made by the President on the Cabinet's advice when one or both Houses are not in session; it has the same force as an Act of Parliament.
2. Article 61 impeachment
Wrong: Article 61 is the procedure for removing the President, not for making laws.
3. Article 72 pardon
Wrong: Article 72 is the President's power to pardon, reprieve, respite, remit or commute punishment.
4. Article 368 referendum
Wrong: Article 368 is about amending the Constitution, and the Indian Constitution has no provision for a referendum.

points: An ordinance must be laid before Parliament when it reassembles and ceases six weeks after reassembly unless approved earlier.
Maximum life of an ordinance: six months and six weeks.

POL-732-P168-ORD-LIM-01.lead: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are correct, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Same force as a parliamentary Act while it lasts
True
Article 123(2) says an ordinance has the same force and effect as an Act of Parliament.
2. It may amend the Constitution
False
An ordinance can only deal with subjects on which Parliament can make ordinary laws; the Constitution can be amended only under Article 368.
3. It is subject to judicial review
True
In the Cooper case (1970) the Court held the President's satisfaction can be questioned; the 44th Amendment (1978) removed the 38th Amendment's bar on review.
4. It ceases six weeks after Parliament reassembles
True
Article 123(2)(a): it lapses six weeks after reassembly unless Parliament approves it earlier, or it is disapproved or withdrawn.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 are wrong because they include the false statement 2.
Option 1 also leaves out statements 3 and 4; option 2 leaves out statements 1 and 3.

POL-732-P169-01.lead: Option 4: the Indian President has no qualified veto.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Absolute veto
Wrong: the absolute veto (withholding assent, so the bill ends) is available to the Indian President.
2. Suspensive veto
Wrong: the suspensive veto (returning a bill once for reconsideration) is available, though not for Money Bills.
3. Pocket veto
Wrong: the pocket veto (keeping a bill pending indefinitely) is available because the Constitution fixes no time limit for assent.
4. Qualified veto
Correct: a qualified veto is one that the legislature can override by a higher (special) majority; it exists in the USA, not in India.

points: In India, if Parliament re-passes a returned bill, even by a simple majority, the President must assent; so the Indian suspensive veto is weaker than a qualified veto.
Memory hook: India has A-S-P (Absolute, Suspensive, Pocket), not Q.

POL-732-P169-POCKET-TIME-01.lead: Option 4: the pocket veto exists because the Constitution fixes no time limit for the President to give or withhold assent.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Every bill lapses after fourteen days
Wrong: no bill lapses after fourteen days; the 14-day period relates to the Rajya Sabha's handling of Money Bills.
2. The Rajya Sabha alone controls assent
Wrong: assent to bills is given by the President (Article 111), not by the Rajya Sabha.
3. The Supreme Court must first approve every bill
Wrong: the Supreme Court does not pre-approve bills; it can only review laws after they are made.
4. The Constitution prescribes no time limit for presidential assent or withholding
Correct: since Article 111 sets no deadline, the President can simply keep a bill pending, which is called the pocket veto.

points: Giani Zail Singh used the pocket veto on the Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill, 1986.
The US President must act within 10 days, so the Indian President's pocket veto is wider.

POL-732-P169-STATE-01.lead: Option 2: under Article 201, the President is not bound to assent to a State bill re-passed after reconsideration.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The President must assent as with a reconsidered Union ordinary bill
Wrong: the 'must assent' rule of Article 111 applies only to Union ordinary bills re-passed by Parliament, not to reserved State bills.
2. The President may still withhold assent; the Union-bill reconsideration rule does not bind this case
Correct: when a reserved State bill is returned and re-passed, it is again presented to the President, who may still withhold assent; so he has an absolute veto over State bills.
3. The Governor alone must assent
Wrong: once the Governor reserves a bill for the President, the decision rests with the President, not the Governor.
4. The bill automatically becomes law after fourteen days
Wrong: no bill becomes law automatically by the passing of time; assent is always needed.

points: If the President returns the bill, the State Legislature must reconsider it within six months (Article 201).
Concept: this shows the Union's control over State legislation in a federation with a unitary bias.

POL-732-P169-VETO-LIM-01.lead: Option 1: a Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration, and assent cannot be withheld from a duly passed Constitution Amendment Bill.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration; assent cannot be withheld from a duly passed Constitution Amendment Bill

Correct: a Money Bill is introduced only with the President's prior recommendation, so he either assents or withholds assent but cannot return it; and the 24th Amendment (1971) made assent to amendment bills compulsory.
2. Both bills may be returned once
Wrong: neither bill can be returned; the suspensive veto does not apply to Money Bills or to Constitution Amendment Bills.
3. Assent may be withheld permanently from both
Wrong: assent cannot be withheld from a Constitution Amendment Bill at all, because of Article 368(2) as amended by the 24th Amendment.
4. Only a Constitution Amendment Bill may be returned
Wrong: a Constitution Amendment Bill cannot be returned either; the President must give assent.

points: The President normally assents to a Money Bill, since it comes with his prior permission.
Memory hook: amendment bill = no veto of any kind.

POL-732-P170-01.lead: Option 2: commutation means replacing one form of punishment with a lighter form.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Remission
Wrong: remission reduces the period of a sentence without changing its nature (e.g. 2 years' rigorous imprisonment cut to 1 year's rigorous imprisonment).
2. Commutation
Correct: commutation substitutes a lighter form of punishment, for example death to rigorous imprisonment, or rigorous to simple imprisonment.
3. Reprieve
Wrong: reprieve is a temporary stay of the execution of a sentence, especially a death sentence, so the convict can seek pardon or commutation.
4. Respite
Wrong: respite means awarding a lesser sentence than the original because of a special fact, such as physical disability or pregnancy of the offender.

points: All these powers come under Article 72 (President) and Article 161 (Governor).
Pardon removes both the sentence and the conviction completely.

POL-732-P170-FIN-01.lead: Option 3: all three items in option 3 are genuine financial powers of the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Passing the Appropriation Bill; certifying a Money Bill; voting demands for grants
Wrong: passing the Appropriation Bill and voting demands for grants are done by Parliament (Lok Sabha), and certifying a Money Bill is done by the Speaker (Article 110(3)).
2. Deciding tax appeals; auditing Union accounts; fixing GST rates alone
Wrong: tax appeals are decided by tribunals and courts, auditing is done by the CAG, and GST rates are recommended by the GST Council.
3. Prior recommendation for a Money Bill; causing the Budget to be laid; constituting the Finance Commission
Correct: Money Bills need his prior recommendation (Article 117), he causes the Budget to be laid (Article 112), and he constitutes the Finance Commission every five years (Article 280).
4. Preparing CAG reports; levying taxes by decree; dissolving the Rajya Sabha
Wrong: CAG reports are prepared by the CAG, taxes need a law of Parliament (Article 265), and the Rajya Sabha cannot be dissolved.

points: Other financial powers: no demand for grants can be made except on his recommendation, and the Contingency Fund of India is at his disposal.
Concept: the President's financial role is formal; the actual taxing and spending decisions are Parliament's.

POL-732-P171-CLEM-CMP-01.lead: Option 2: only the President can grant clemency in court-martial cases and pardon a death sentence; the Governor cannot.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only the Governor can act in court-martial cases
Wrong: it is the President, not the Governor, who can act in court-martial cases (Article 72(1)(a)).
2. The President can grant pardon in court-martial cases and can pardon a death sentence; the Governor cannot exercise court-martial clemency
Correct: Article 72 covers court-martial sentences, offences against Union laws and death sentences; under Article 161 the Governor has no court-martial power and cannot pardon a death sentence.
3. Neither can commute a sentence
Wrong: both the President and the Governor can commute a sentence, including a death sentence.
4. The Governor's power extends to every Union-law offence
Wrong: the Governor's power extends only to offences against laws on matters to which the State's executive power extends.

points: The Governor can suspend, remit or commute a death sentence, but only the President can pardon it.
Both act on the advice of the Council of Ministers (Maru Ram case, 1980).

POL-732-P172-MIL-01.lead: Option 4: the President's supreme command of the defence forces is regulated by law and is exercised within responsible government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Military power is exercised without law or ministerial responsibility
Wrong: military power is not exercised without law or ministerial responsibility; the Cabinet is answerable to Parliament for it.
2. It permits unilateral constitutional amendment during war
Wrong: no war gives the President power to amend the Constitution alone; amendment always needs Article 368.
3. The title transfers command to the Chief Justice
Wrong: the title does not pass command to the Chief Justice, who heads the judiciary and has no military role.
4. Exercise is regulated by law and operates within responsible government
Correct: Article 53(2) says the supreme command is vested in the President, but its exercise is regulated by law made by Parliament, and he acts on ministerial advice.

points: The President appoints the chiefs of the Army, Navy and Air Force and can declare war or conclude peace, subject to Parliament's approval.
Concept: a civilian, nominal head commands the forces, but real control lies with the elected government.

POL-732-P173-01.lead: Option 1: if the Council of Ministers sends the same advice again, the President must act on it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The President must act on the reiterated advice
Correct: the proviso to Article 74(1), added by the 44th Amendment (1978), lets the President return advice once for reconsideration, but he is bound by the reconsidered advice.
2. The President may reject it permanently
Wrong: the President cannot reject reiterated advice permanently; that would defeat responsible government.
3. The Supreme Court must approve it first
Wrong: the Supreme Court has no role in approving ministerial advice; under Article 74(2) courts cannot even inquire into what advice was given.
4. The Rajya Sabha decides by simple majority
Wrong: the Rajya Sabha does not decide on advice given to the President.

points: The 42nd Amendment (1976) first made ministerial advice binding; the 44th added the one-time reconsideration.
Concept: the President can pause and question, but finally the elected government decides.

POL-732-P173-SIT-01.lead: Option 3: in a hung Lok Sabha, the President appoints the person most likely to win the House's confidence and asks for a floor test where needed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Personally govern until the next election
Wrong: the President cannot govern personally; Article 74 requires a Council of Ministers to aid and advise him at all times.
2. Choose any preferred policy programme
Wrong: the President does not choose policies; policy is made by the Council of Ministers.
3. Appoint the person most likely to command House confidence and require a floor test where necessary
Correct: this is situational discretion: he invites the leader most likely to command a majority and can ask him to prove it on the floor of the House.
4. Transfer appointment power to the Supreme Court
Wrong: the appointment of the PM is never transferred to the Supreme Court.

points: S.R. Bommai (1994) held that majority must be tested on the floor of the House.
Charan Singh (1979), appointed in such a situation, resigned without facing the Lok Sabha.

POL-732-P175-HIST-01.lead: Option 4: Rajendra Prasad is the only President to serve two full terms (1950-62).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Droupadi Murmu – first President
Wrong. The first President was Rajendra Prasad. Murmu (2022) is the first President from a Scheduled Tribe.
2. N. Sanjiva Reddy – first woman President
Wrong. Sanjiva Reddy (1977) is the only President elected unopposed. The first woman President was Pratibha Patil (2007).
3. Pratibha Patil – elected unopposed
Wrong. She won a contested election in 2007; the unopposed one was Sanjiva Reddy.
4. Rajendra Prasad – two full terms
Right. He was elected in 1952 and 1957, and no one else has served two terms.

points: The options shuffle real 'firsts' among the wrong people, so learn each record with its person: Prasad = two terms, Reddy = unopposed, Patil = first woman, Murmu = first ST.

POL-733-CH-01.lead: Option 1 is correct: a Vice-President elected after a mid-term vacancy gets a full five-year term from the date he takes office.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A fresh full five-year term
True. Article 67 counts five years from the date he enters office.
Only the remaining term
False. There is no rule of finishing the predecessor's term.
Six months pending approval
False. No such interim term or parliamentary approval exists.
Ends with the current Lok Sabha
False. The term is not linked to the Lok Sabha's life.

points: The same rule applies to the President when elected to fill a vacancy.

POL-733-CH-02.lead: Option 2 is correct: nominated MPs vote in the Vice-President's election, while State MLAs do not.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Nominated MPs in both elections
False. Nominated MPs vote only in the Vice-President's election; they are excluded from the President's (Art 54).
2. Nominated MPs in VP election; MLAs not
True. The VP's college is all MPs (elected and nominated) only (Art 66); MLAs are not included.
3. State MLAs in both elections
False. MLAs vote only in the President's election.
4. MLCs only in VP election
False. Members of State Legislative Councils vote in neither the presidential nor the vice-presidential election.

points: President = elected MPs + elected MLAs; Vice-President = all MPs (both elected and nominated).

POL-733-P180-01.lead: Option 1 (1 and 2 only) is correct: the Vice-President is elected by all members of both Houses of Parliament only.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Elected Lok Sabha members
True. All MPs are in the VP's electoral college.
2. Nominated Rajya Sabha members
True. Nominated MPs are included, unlike in the President's election.
3. Elected State MLAs
False. MLAs have no part in the VP's election.
4. State MLCs
False. Members of State Legislative Councils vote in neither election; the VP's electoral college is only MPs of both Houses.

points: Options 3 and 4 wrongly include MLAs; option 2 wrongly drops nominated members.
Election is by proportional representation by single transferable vote, with secret ballot (Art 66).

POL-733-P180-02.lead: Option 2 is correct: under Article 71, the Supreme Court alone decides disputes over the Vice-President's election, and its decision is final.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Election Commission
It conducts the election (Art 324) but does not decide disputes.
Supreme Court
Article 71 gives it sole jurisdiction over such disputes.
Parliament
It forms the electoral college but does not decide election disputes.
Rajya Sabha Chairman
This is the VP himself; he cannot judge his own election.

points: If the election is declared void, acts already done by him remain valid.

POL-733-P180-NOM-01.lead: Option 3 is correct: a VP nomination needs at least 20 proposers, 20 seconders and a security deposit of ₹15,000.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. At least 20 proposers
True. Nomination must be subscribed by at least 20 electors as proposers.
2. At least 20 seconders
True. It must also have at least 20 electors as seconders.
3. Security deposit
True. Every candidate deposits ₹15,000 in the Reserve Bank of India.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each leave out a true statement.
For the President, the figures are 50 proposers and 50 seconders.

POL-733-P181-01.lead: Option 3 is correct: Article 66(3) requires the Vice-President to be qualified for election to the Rajya Sabha.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Lok Sabha
This is the requirement for the President (Art 58), not the Vice-President.
Either State Legislative House only
False. The Constitution refers to a House of Parliament, not a State House.
Rajya Sabha
True. The VP is the ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, so he must be qualified for it.
Either House of Parliament
False. The Constitution names only the Rajya Sabha.

points: Other qualifications: citizen of India, completed 35 years, no office of profit.

POL-733-P181-02.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct and 4 is false, so option 4 (1, 2 and 3 only) is the answer.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Originates only in Rajya Sabha
True. The resolution can be introduced only in the Rajya Sabha.
2. Majority of all then members of RS
True. It is an effective majority of the Rajya Sabha.
3. Lok Sabha must agree
True. The Lok Sabha must agree by a simple majority.
4. It is impeachment
False. Laxmikanth notes that no formal impeachment is needed; it is simple removal.

points: Option 1 drops statement 3; option 2 wrongly includes statement 4; option 3 drops statement 1 and includes 4.

POL-733-P181-COND-01.lead: Option 1 is correct: under Article 66(2), if an MP or MLA becomes Vice-President, his seat is deemed vacated on entering office.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Seat deemed vacated
True. The Constitution treats the seat as vacated on the day he enters the office.
Retains both offices
False. A VP cannot be a member of any House of Parliament or State legislature.
President decides case by case
False. Article 66(2) makes the MP's seat vacant automatically on entering the VP's office; the President has no discretion.
Only a Lok Sabha seat is vacated
False. A Rajya Sabha or State legislature seat is also vacated.

points: He must also not hold any other office of profit.

POL-733-P181-OATH-01.lead: Option 4 is correct: under Article 69, the Vice-President takes his oath before the President or a person appointed by him.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Chief Justice of India only
False. The CJI administers the President's oath (Art 60), not the VP's.
Chairman of Election Commission
False. No such office administers this oath.
Prime Minister
False. The PM takes his own oath before the President.
President, or person appointed
True. Article 69: the VP takes oath before the President or a person appointed by him for that purpose.

points: In the oath, the VP swears to faithfully discharge his duties.

POL-733-P181-REMOVE-PROC-01.lead: Statement 1 alone is correct, so option 1 is the answer.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 14 days' notice needed
True. No resolution can be moved without at least 14 days' advance notice.
2. Violation of Constitution as only ground
False. The Constitution mentions no ground for the VP's removal.

points: Options 2 and 3 wrongly accept statement 2; option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1.
'Violation of the Constitution' is the ground for impeaching the President.

POL-733-P181-VAC-01.lead: Option 2: a Vice-President vacancy must be filled 'as soon as possible' (Article 68), while a President vacancy must be filled within six months (Article 62).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Both must be filled within exactly six months
False. Only the President's vacancy has a six-month limit; the Constitution fixes no time limit for the Vice-President.
VP vacancy filled as soon as possible; six months fixed for the President ✓
True. Article 68(2) says 'as soon as possible' for the VP, and Article 62(2) says 'not later than six months' for the President.
Neither vacancy requires an election
False. Both vacancies are filled only by a fresh election by the respective electoral college.
VP successor serves only the predecessor's remainder
False. The newly elected Vice-President gets a full five-year term from the date he enters office.

points: Concept: the President's office cannot be left vacant long, because the Vice-President is only acting; so a hard six-month limit exists. The VP's office has no such urgency.
In both cases the new office-holder gets a full five-year term, not the unexpired term.
Memory hook: President = six months; Vice-President = as soon as possible.

POL-733-P182-01.lead: Option 1: the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, because the Vice-President cannot chair the Rajya Sabha while acting as President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha ✓
The Rajya Sabha's own elected deputy presiding officer. While the VP acts as President, the Deputy Chairman performs the Chairman's duties (Article 91).
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The presiding officer of the Lok Sabha only. He has no role in conducting Rajya Sabha business.
Prime Minister
Head of the government and a member of the executive. He never presides over either House.
Chief Justice of India
Head of the judiciary. He may act as President in a double vacancy, but never chairs the Rajya Sabha.

points: Article 64: while acting as President, the Vice-President does not perform the duties of Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (LX p305).
This keeps the two roles separate: one person cannot be head of state and presiding officer of a House at the same time.

POL-733-P182-02.lead: Option 2: as Chairman, the Vice-President has only a casting vote, used when votes are equally divided.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: On every bill before debate
False. The Chairman does not vote in the first instance on any bill (Article 100(1)).
Only when votes are equally divided ✓
True. A casting vote is given only in case of a tie, to break the deadlock (Article 100(1)).
Only on a Money Bill
False. A Money Bill gives the Chairman no special vote; the tie rule is the same for all matters.
Whenever the Council of Ministers requests
False. The presiding officer must be neutral; the government cannot ask him to vote.

points: The Vice-President is not a member of the Rajya Sabha, so he does not vote as an ordinary member; his only vote is the casting vote.
This is the same as the Lok Sabha Speaker's casting vote — the purpose is to resolve a deadlock, not to take sides.

POL-733-P182-ACT-LIMIT-01.lead: Option 2: six months, because a new President must be elected within six months of the vacancy (Article 62(2)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Three months
False. No three-month limit exists in the Constitution for a presidential vacancy.
Six months ✓
True. The election must be held within six months, so the Vice-President can act as President for at most six months (LX p305).
One year
False. One year would exceed the six-month limit of Article 62(2).
The entire unexpired presidential term
False. That is the American system, where the VP becomes President for the rest of the term; in India the VP only acts.

points: Article 65(1): the VP acts as President only until the newly elected President enters office.
The new President gets a full five-year term, not the balance of the old term.

POL-733-P182-DUAL-VAC-01.lead: Option 4: under the President (Discharge of Functions) Act, 1969, the Chief Justice of India acts as President; if that office is also vacant, the senior-most available Supreme Court judge acts.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Prime Minister
Head of the government (real executive). He is never placed in the line to act as President.
Lok Sabha Speaker
Presiding officer of the Lok Sabha. The Act gives him no role in discharging presidential functions.
Attorney General of India
The Union government's chief law officer (Article 76). He has no role in presidential succession.
CJI, or senior-most available SC judge ✓
True. The 1969 Act made by Parliament under Article 70 names the CJI, then the senior-most available judge (LX p282).

points: Example: in 1969, after President Zakir Husain died and acting President V.V. Giri resigned, CJI M. Hidayatullah acted as President from 20 July to 24 August 1969 (LX p282 footnote).
The person so acting enjoys all the powers and immunities of the President.

POL-733-P182-EMOL-01.lead: Option 3: the Constitution fixes no salary for the Vice-President as such; he is paid as ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, and gets the President's emoluments while acting as President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A separate salary solely for being VP
False. The Constitution has not fixed any emoluments for the Vice-President in that capacity (LX p305).
No remuneration in any capacity
False. He draws a regular salary as Chairman of the Rajya Sabha, fixed by Parliament under Article 97.
Paid as RS Chairman; President's emoluments while acting ✓
True. While acting as President, he gets the President's salary and allowances, not the Chairman's (Articles 64 proviso and 65(3)).
Lok Sabha Speaker's salary always applies
False. The Speaker's salary is for the Lok Sabha's presiding officer; the VP's pay comes from the Rajya Sabha Chairman's post.

points: In 2018 Parliament raised the Rajya Sabha Chairman's salary to ₹4 lakh per month (LX p305).
Key idea: the VP's pay is attached to the job he actually does — chairing the Rajya Sabha.

POL-733-P182-TEMP-INCAP-01.lead: Option 3: when the President is temporarily unable to work (absence, illness), the Vice-President discharges his functions until he resumes duty (Article 65(2)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A fresh President must be elected immediately
False. An election is needed only when the office is vacant; here the President still holds office.
The Prime Minister becomes President
False. The PM is head of government and has no constitutional role in replacing the President.
VP discharges functions until President resumes ✓
True. Article 65(2) provides exactly this temporary arrangement.
The Lok Sabha Speaker serves for five years
False. The Speaker has no role, and nobody gets a new five-year term when there is no vacancy.

points: Distinguish: vacancy (death/resignation/removal) → VP 'acts as' President up to six months under Article 65(1); temporary inability → VP 'discharges the functions' under Article 65(2).
During this period too, the Deputy Chairman presides over the Rajya Sabha.

POL-733-P183-01.lead: Option 3 is the incorrect description: the Vice-President has no routine executive power of his own.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Ex-officio Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Correct description. Article 64 makes him ex-officio Chairman; this is his normal function.
A source of continuity for presidential duties
Correct description. Under Article 65 he acts as or discharges the functions of the President when needed.
Independent routine executive authority parallel to the PM ✓
Incorrect — so this is the answer. The Constitution gives the VP no executive functions; real executive power lies with the PM and Council of Ministers (Article 74).
A constitutional office created by Article 63
Correct description. Article 63 says 'There shall be a Vice-President of India'.

points: Because the Constitution gives him no significant function in his own capacity, some scholars call him 'His Superfluous Highness' (LX p305).
The office exists to maintain political continuity of the Indian State.

POL-733-P183-2025-ELECTION-OATH.lead: Option 4: Jagdeep Dhankhar resigned in July 2025 by writing to the President (Article 67(a)); C.P. Radhakrishnan was elected in September 2025.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Death of the incumbent
False. Dhankhar did not die in office; he resigned, citing health reasons.
Removal by a Rajya Sabha resolution
False. No removal resolution under Article 67(b) was passed; no VP has ever been removed.
Expiry of the five-year term
False. Dhankhar took office in August 2022, so his term would have run to 2027.
Resignation addressed to the President ✓
True. A Vice-President resigns by a letter addressed to the President (Article 67(a)).

points: After a resignation, the election is held 'as soon as possible' (Article 68(2)), which is why it came within about two months.
The newly elected VP gets a full five-year term from the date he enters office (LX p304).

POL-733-P183-HIST-1962-1967.lead: Option 2: G.S. Pathak (VP 1969–74) never became President; the other three moved from Vice-President to President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Zakir Husain
VP 1962–67, then elected President in 1967 (LX p1063).
G.S. Pathak ✓
VP 1969–74 only. He was never elected President.
V.V. Giri
VP 1967–69, then elected President in 1969 after acting as President.
R. Venkataraman
VP 1984–87, then elected President in 1987.

points: Other VPs who later became President: S. Radhakrishnan, Shankar Dayal Sharma and K.R. Narayanan.
Memory hook: Pathak sits between Giri and Jatti in the VP list — a 'gap' who never moved up.

POL-733-P183-UNOPPOSED-1952-1987.lead: Option 3: the 1952, 1957, 1979 and 1987 Vice-Presidential elections were all unopposed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong set. 1962 was contested — Zakir Husain defeated N. Samant Singh (LX p302).
Wrong set. 1967 was contested — V.V. Giri defeated Prof. Habib.
Correct. S. Radhakrishnan (1952, 1957), M. Hidayatullah (1979) and Shankar Dayal Sharma (1987) were elected unopposed.
Wrong set. 1974 (B.D. Jatti vs N.E. Horo) and 1984 (R. Venkataraman vs B.C. Kambley) were contested.

points: Only four VP elections so far were unopposed, per LX Table 19.1.

POL-733-P183-US-01.lead: Option 4: the Indian Vice-President only acts as President until a new one takes office, while the American Vice-President actually becomes President for the rest of the term.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Both automatically serve the predecessor's remaining term
False. Only the US VP does this; in India a new President must be elected within six months (Article 62).
Neither office is elected indirectly
False. India's VP is elected indirectly by an electoral college of members of both Houses of Parliament (Article 66).
Only India has an upper-house presiding role
False. The US VP is also the presiding officer (President) of the Senate, the US upper house.
India: acts until successor; US: becomes President ✓
True. This is the key difference noted by Laxmikanth (LX p305).

points: Similarity: both chair the upper house; India's office was modelled on the American one (LX p301).
Difference: succession — the US VP succeeds; the Indian VP only acts.

POL-733-P184-01.lead: Option 4: S. Radhakrishnan (1952–62) and M. Hamid Ansari (2007–17) each served two terms as Vice-President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Krishan Kant and Bhairon Singh Shekhawat
Wrong. Krishan Kant (1997–2002) died in office, and Shekhawat (2002–07) served one term.
V.V. Giri and B.D. Jatti
Wrong. Giri (1967–69) resigned to contest the presidency, and Jatti (1974–79) had one term.
K.R. Narayanan and R. Venkataraman
Wrong. Each served a single term as VP (1992–97 and 1984–87) before becoming President.
S. Radhakrishnan and M. Hamid Ansari ✓
Correct. Radhakrishnan was elected in 1952 and 1957; Ansari in 2007 and 2012 (LX p302, p1063).

points: Memory hook: the first VP and the 12th VP are the only two with two terms.

LX-PQ-004.lead: Option 2: a calling attention notice calls a minister's attention to a matter of urgent public importance and seeks an authoritative statement from him.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Half-an-hour discussion
A discussion on a matter of public importance already much debated, whose answer needs clarification on facts; no formal motion or vote (LX p353).
Calling attention notice ✓
A member calls a minister's attention to an urgent public matter and seeks his statement. Indian innovation, since 1954 (LX p351).
Short duration discussion
A 'two-hour discussion' on an urgent public matter; no formal motion or vote; since 1953.
Adjournment motion
Draws the attention of the House (not a minister) to a definite urgent matter; needs 50 members; involves censure, so not allowed in the Rajya Sabha.

points: Key word in the stem: 'attention of minister' → calling attention.
Unlike zero hour, calling attention is mentioned in the Rules of Procedure.

LX-PQ-008.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true; 4 and 5 are false — so option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Calls attention of a minister to urgent public matter
True
This is the definition of the calling attention motion (LX p351).
2. Main purpose: authoritative statement from minister
True
The member seeks an authoritative statement from the minister on that matter.
3. No censure against government
True
Unlike an adjournment motion, it carries no element of censure.
4. Indian innovation since 1952
False
It is an Indian innovation, but in existence since 1954, not 1952.
5. Not mentioned in the Rules
False
Unlike zero hour, it is mentioned in the Rules of Procedure.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes statement 4 (wrong year).
Option 2 includes only the two false statements.
Option 3 wrongly includes statement 5.

LX-PQ-049.lead: Option 2: the 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 first made it obligatory for the President to act on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 24th amendment
1971; made it compulsory for the President to give assent to Constitution Amendment Bills — not about ministerial advice.
42nd amendment ✓
1976; amended Article 74(1) to make ministerial advice binding on the President for the first time.
44th amendment
1978; allowed the President to send advice back once for reconsideration — it came later, so not 'first time'.
54th amendment
1986; increased salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges.

points: Sequence: 42nd (1976) made advice binding → 44th (1978) added one reconsideration, after which the advice binds.

LX-PQ-064.lead: Statements 2, 4 and 5 are features of the parliamentary system — option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Independent judiciary
False
It is not a feature special to parliamentary government; presidential systems like the USA also have it.
2. Collective responsibility
True
Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75); this is the bedrock principle (LX p207).
3. Written Constitution
False
Not a parliamentary feature — Britain, the home of the parliamentary system, has no written Constitution.
4. De jure and de facto executives
True
President is nominal executive, PM the real executive (LX p206).
5. Double membership
True
Ministers are members of both the legislature and the executive (LX p207).

points: Option 1 wrongly includes 3 and drops 5.
Option 2 wrongly includes 1 and drops 5.
Option 4 wrongly includes 1.

LX-PQ-071.lead: Option 2 — Both A and R are true but R is not a correct explanation of A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
India has adopted the parliamentary form of government at the Centre and in the States.
R
True
The President is the nominal (titular) head of State, while the Council of Ministers headed by the Prime Minister is the real executive.

points: Does R explain A? No — R describes one feature of the parliamentary system; it is not the reason India adopted that system. India chose it for responsibility and familiarity with the British model, so Laxmikanth keys R as not explaining A.
Option 1 fails: R does not explain A.
Option 3 fails: R is in fact true.
Option 4 fails: A is in fact true.

LX-PQ-116.lead: Option 3: the word 'Cabinet' appears only in Article 352, inserted by the 44th Amendment (1978).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 74
Provides a Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President; does not use the word 'Cabinet'.
Article 75
Deals with appointment and responsibility of ministers; speaks of the Council of Ministers, not the Cabinet.
Article 352 ✓
National Emergency; it defines the Cabinet as the PM and Cabinet-rank ministers, whose written decision is needed for an emergency (LX p319).
Not mentioned
False — it is mentioned once, in Article 352.

points: The original Constitution did not mention 'Cabinet' at all; its role still rests on British conventions.

LX-PQ-118.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are correct; 4 is wrong — option 4.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Censure needs reasons; no-confidence does not
True
LX Table 23.2: a censure motion must state reasons; a no-confidence motion need not.
2. No-confidence only against whole council
True
Censure can target one minister, a group or the whole council; no-confidence only the entire council.
3. Govt must resign only on no-confidence
True
If a no-confidence motion passes the council must resign; on a censure motion it need not.
4. Censure in both Houses, no-confidence only Lok Sabha
False
Both motions are Lok Sabha devices, since the council is responsible only to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)).

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each wrongly include statement 4.

LX-PQ-128.lead: Statement I is incorrect and Statement II is correct — option 4.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: Statement I: PM can dismiss a minister
False
