Under Article 75(2), ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President; the PM can only ask a minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss him (LX p309).
Statement II: President appoints ministers on PM's advice
True
Article 75(1): other ministers are appointed by the President on the advice of the Prime Minister.

points: Since Statement I is false, the question of II explaining I does not arise.
Options 1 and 2 fail because they treat Statement I as correct.
Option 3 fails because it reverses the truth of the two statements.

LX-PQ-185.lead: Option 4: the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 governs the present relationship — advice is binding, but the President may send it back once for reconsideration.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 42nd Amendment Act
1976; made advice binding with no option to return it — later modified, so not the present rule.
48th Amendment Act
Extended President's rule in Punjab beyond one year; not about ministerial advice.
54th Amendment Act
The 54th Amendment Act (1986) increased the salaries of Supreme Court and High Court judges; it did not touch President-ministry relations.
44th Amendment Act ✓
1978; added a proviso to Article 74(1): one reconsideration, after which the President must act on the advice (LX p1024).

points: Present position: the reconsidered advice binds the President.

LX-UPSC-2013-Q03.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are implied in parliamentary government; 3 is not — option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Cabinet members are MPs
True
Double membership: a minister who is not an MP for six consecutive months ceases to be a minister (Article 75(5)).
2. Ministers hold office while they enjoy confidence
True
Collective responsibility means the ministry stays only as long as it has the Lok Sabha's confidence.
3. Cabinet headed by the Head of State
False
The Cabinet is headed by the Prime Minister (head of government); the President is only the nominal head.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 all wrongly include statement 3; option 2 also drops 1 and 2.

LX-UPSC-2013-Q04.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are correct; 1 is wrong — option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Collectively responsible to Parliament
False
Article 75(3) says the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the House of the People (Lok Sabha), not to the whole Parliament.
2. Ministers hold office during President's pleasure
True
Article 75(2) says ministers hold office during the pleasure of the President.
3. PM communicates legislative proposals to President
True
Article 78 makes it the PM's duty to communicate decisions and proposals for legislation to the President.

points: Option 1 picks only the false statement.
Option 3 wrongly includes statement 1.
Option 4 wrongly includes statement 1.

LX-UPSC-2014-Q07.lead: Option 3 (1 and 2 only): statement(s) 1, 2 true, statement(s) 3 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Preparation of agenda for Cabinet Meetings
True
True. The Cabinet Secretariat prepares the agenda for Cabinet meetings and keeps the record of their proceedings.
2. Secretarial assistance to Cabinet Committees
True
True. It also provides secretarial assistance to the Cabinet Committees, besides the full Cabinet.
3. Allocation of financial resources to the Ministries Select the correct answer using the code given below.
False
False. Allocating financial resources to ministries is done through the Budget, prepared by the Ministry of Finance and voted by Parliament; it is not a Cabinet Secretariat function.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 2 (2 and 3 only) wrongly includes false statement 3 and leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (1, 2 and 3) wrongly includes false statement 3.
The Cabinet Secretariat works under the Prime Minister and is headed by the Cabinet Secretary; its role is coordination and servicing, not funding.

LX-UPSC-2014-Q10.lead: Option 1 (1 only): statement(s) 1 true, statement(s) 2 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The President shall make rules for the more convenient transaction of the business of the Government of India, and for the allocation among Ministers of the said business.
True
True. Article 77(3) empowers the President to make rules for the more convenient transaction of Government of India business and for its allocation among ministers.
2. All executive actions of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the Prime Minister.
False
False. Article 77(1) says all executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President, not the Prime Minister.

points: Option 2 (2 only) wrongly includes false statement 2 and leaves out true statement 1.
Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) wrongly includes false statement 2.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) leaves out true statement 1.
The President is the formal (nominal) executive, so orders run in his name even though ministers actually decide.

LX-UPSC-2021-Q03.lead: Option 2 (2 only): statement(s) 2 true, statement(s) 1 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. N. Gopalaswamy Iyengar Committee suggested that a minister and a secretary be designated solely for pursuing the subject of administrative reform and promoting it.
False
False. The answer key treats this statement as incorrect: this recommendation is not credited to the N. Gopalaswamy Ayyangar Committee.
2. In 1970, the Department of Personnel was constituted on the recommendation of the Administrative Reforms Commission, 1966, and this was placed under the Prime Minister’s charge.
True
True. The Department of Personnel was set up in 1970 on the recommendation of the Administrative Reforms Commission (1966) and was placed under the Prime Minister's charge.

points: Option 1 (1 only) wrongly includes false statement 1 and leaves out true statement 2.
Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) wrongly includes false statement 1.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) leaves out true statement 2.
The personnel function has stayed with the PM since then; today it is the Department of Personnel and Training under the Ministry of Personnel.

LX-UPSC-2022-Q04.lead: Option 2 (2 only): statement(s) 2 true, statement(s) 1 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The Constitution of India classifies the ministers into four ranks viz. Cabinet Minister, Minister of State with Independent Charge, Minister of State and Deputy Minister.
False
False. The Constitution does not classify ministers at all; the three/four ranks (Cabinet, MoS independent charge, MoS, Deputy Minister) come from convention and practice.
2. The total number of ministers in the Union Government, including the Prime Minister, shall not exceed 15 percent of the total number of members in the Lok Sabha.
True
True. Article 75(1A), added by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003, caps the total number of ministers, including the PM, at 15% of the total strength of Lok Sabha.

points: Option 1 (1 only) wrongly includes false statement 1 and leaves out true statement 2.
Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) wrongly includes false statement 1.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) leaves out true statement 2.
The Constitution speaks only of a 'Council of Ministers' (Article 74); the word 'Cabinet' appears only in Article 352.

LX-UPSC-2022-Q09.lead: Option 1 (1 and 3 only): statement(s) 1, 3 true, statement(s) 2, 4 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. As per the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in Lok Sabha, the election of Deputy Speaker shall be held on such date as the Speaker may fix.
True
True. Rule 8 of the Lok Sabha Rules says the election of the Deputy Speaker is held on a date fixed by the Speaker.
2. There is a mandatory provision that the election of a candidate as Deputy Speaker of Lok Sabha shall be from either the principal opposition party or the ruling party.
False
False. There is no mandatory rule about the party of the Deputy Speaker; giving the post to the opposition is only a convention, not a binding provision.
3. The Deputy Speaker has the same power as of the Speaker when presiding over the sitting of the House and no appeal lies against his rulings.
True
True. While presiding, the Deputy Speaker has all the powers of the Speaker, and no appeal lies against his rulings in that capacity.
4. The well established parliamentary practice regarding the appointment of Deputy Speaker is that the motion is moved by the Speaker and duly seconded by the Prime Minister.
False
False. The Speaker, as presiding officer, does not move the motion; motions proposing a member's name for Deputy Speaker are moved by members of the House.

points: Option 2 (1, 2 and 3) wrongly includes false statement 2.
Option 3 (3 and 4 only) wrongly includes false statement 4 and leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (2 and 4 only) wrongly includes false statement 2, 4 and leaves out true statement 1, 3.

POL-734-CH-01.lead: Option 2: collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha means the whole ministry stands or falls together.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Individual responsibility to the Rajya Sabha
Ministers are individually responsible to the President (Article 75(2)); Rajya Sabha cannot remove a government.
2. Collective responsibility to the Lok Sabha
Article 75(3) makes the Council of Ministers collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, so loss of its confidence removes the whole ministry.
3. Judicial review under Article 74(2)
Article 74(2) bars courts from asking what advice ministers gave; it has nothing to do with the ministry resigning.
4. Administrative responsibility of secretaries
Secretaries are civil servants answerable to their ministers, not to the House; their responsibility cannot bring down a government.

points: 'Ministers swim and sink together': a no-confidence vote in Lok Sabha ends the entire Council, not just the PM.

POL-734-CH-02.lead: Option 2: the minister is the political head and the secretary is the administrative head of a ministry.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Minister - administrative head; Secretary - political head
Reverses the roles: the secretary is a civil servant, not a political head.
2. Minister - political head; Secretary - administrative head
Correct: the minister makes policy and answers to Parliament; the secretary is the senior civil servant who runs the ministry and advises the minister.
3. Prime Minister - administrative head; Cabinet Secretary - political head
The PM is the political head of the government, and the Cabinet Secretary is the senior-most civil servant, not a political head.
4. President - political head; Minister - judicial head
The President is the nominal executive head, not a ministry's political head, and no minister is a 'judicial head'.

points: Political executive = elected and temporary (ministers); permanent executive = civil servants (secretaries).

POL-734-LAX-01.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2): statement(s) 1, 2 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Union executive action is expressed in the President's name.
True
True. Article 77(1) says all executive action of the Government of India shall be expressed to be taken in the name of the President.
2. Properly authenticated instruments cannot be challenged merely because the President did not personally make them.
True
True. Article 77(2) says orders authenticated as per the rules cannot be called in question on the ground that they were not made or executed by the President.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 2 (2 only) leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) leaves out true statement 1, 2.
Article 77(2) protects routine government orders so that their validity does not depend on the President personally signing each one.

POL-734-LAX-02.lead: Option 1: no; Article 88 lets a minister speak in the other House but not vote there.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. No, voting is confined to the House of membership
Correct: Article 88 gives every minister the right to speak and take part in both Houses and their committees, but voting is only in the House of which he is a member.
2. Yes, every minister votes in both Houses
Wrong: the proviso to Article 88 expressly denies a vote in a House of which the minister is not a member.
3. Yes, but only on Money Bills
Wrong: Money Bills are not an exception; a Rajya Sabha member cannot vote in Lok Sabha on any bill.
4. No, and the minister may not speak there either
Wrong: Article 88 does allow the minister to speak and take part in Lok Sabha proceedings.

points: The same right under Article 88 is also given to the Attorney General of India.

POL-734-LAX-03.lead: Option 1: the Prime Minister heads the Council of Ministers, so when the head goes the whole Council goes.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Council is constitutionally headed by the Prime Minister
Correct: Article 74(1) provides a Council of Ministers 'with the Prime Minister at the head', so the Council cannot survive his exit.
2. Every minister has an independent fixed term
Wrong: ministers have no fixed term; under Article 75(2) they hold office during the pleasure of the President.
3. The President becomes head of the Council
Wrong: the President never heads the Council of Ministers; he is the head of state who acts on its advice.
4. Lok Sabha is automatically dissolved
Wrong: the PM's death or resignation does not dissolve Lok Sabha; only the President can dissolve it.

points: A minister's resignation only creates a vacancy; the PM's resignation or death dissolves the entire Council.

POL-734-LAX-04.lead: Option 4 (1, 2 and 3): statement(s) 1, 2, 3 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Article 75 says the President appoints the Prime Minister.
True
True. Article 75(1) says the Prime Minister shall be appointed by the President.
2. Normally the appointee is the leader able to command Lok Sabha confidence.
True
True. By convention the President appoints the leader of the majority party or coalition that commands the confidence of the Lok Sabha.
3. A hung House creates a limited field for presidential judgment, followed by a floor test.
True
True. When no party has a clear majority, the President uses limited personal discretion to appoint a PM and asks him to prove his majority on the floor within a time.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2, 3.
Option 2 (1 and 2 only) leaves out true statement 3.
Option 3 (2 and 3 only) leaves out true statement 1.
Example: in 1979 President Sanjiva Reddy appointed Charan Singh in a hung situation.

POL-734-LAX-05.lead: Option 1: the Cabinet is a small inner group of senior ministers within the larger Council of Ministers and is its real decision-making centre.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Cabinet is the smaller inner body of senior ministers and the principal decision-making nucleus
Correct: the Cabinet has only Cabinet-rank ministers and takes the key decisions that bind the whole Council.
2. The Cabinet includes every minister
Wrong: the Council includes all three categories; the Cabinet is only a part of it.
3. Only the Council is collectively responsible
Wrong: collective responsibility under Article 75(3) applies to the whole Council of Ministers, and the Cabinet decides in its name.
4. The Constitution fixes separate five-year terms for Cabinet members
Wrong: no minister has a fixed constitutional term; all hold office during the President's pleasure.

points: Council of Ministers is a wider body with no meetings as a whole; the Cabinet meets regularly and directs policy.

POL-734-LAX-06.lead: Option 1: the President administers the oaths of office and secrecy to the PM and all ministers (Article 75(4)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. President
Correct: Article 75(4) says the President shall administer the oaths of office and secrecy to a minister before he enters office.
2. Chief Justice of India
The CJI administers the oath to the President, not to the PM.
3. Speaker
The Speaker presides over Lok Sabha and has no role in the oath of ministers.
4. Outgoing Prime Minister
The outgoing PM has no constitutional role in swearing in the new PM.

points: The forms of these oaths are given in the Third Schedule.

POL-734-LAX-07.lead: Option 4 (1, 2 and 3): statement(s) 1, 2, 3 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. recommends ministerial appointments
True
True. The President appoints only those persons as ministers whom the PM recommends.
2. allocates and reshuffles portfolios
True
True. The PM allocates portfolios among ministers and can reshuffle them.
3. may seek a minister's resignation.
True
True. The PM can ask a minister to resign or advise the President to dismiss him in case of difference of opinion.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2, 3.
Option 2 (1 and 2 only) leaves out true statement 3.
Option 3 (2 and 3 only) leaves out true statement 1.
These powers make the PM the real head of the Council of Ministers.

POL-734-LAX-08.lead: Option 1: advising the President on summoning and proroguing Parliament is part of the PM's role in relation to Parliament.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Advising the President on summoning and proroguing Parliament
Correct: the PM advises the President on summoning and proroguing sessions and can recommend dissolution of Lok Sabha.
2. Appointing Supreme Court judges alone
Wrong: judges are appointed by the President under Article 124 after consultation (collegium system); the PM does not appoint them alone.
3. Certifying every Money Bill
Wrong: the Speaker of Lok Sabha certifies whether a bill is a Money Bill (Article 110(3)).
4. Removing the Speaker
Wrong: the Speaker is removed by a resolution of Lok Sabha passed by an effective majority (Article 94).

points: The PM is also the leader of the House in Lok Sabha and announces government policies on the floor.

POL-734-LAX-09.lead: Option 1: in India a presidential order need not be countersigned by a minister to be valid.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A presidential act need not be countersigned by a minister to be valid
Correct: unlike Britain, India has no rule that a minister must countersign the President's orders.
2. Every presidential act must be countersigned
Wrong: countersignature is a British practice that India did not adopt.
3. Courts may always compel disclosure of advice
Wrong: Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring whether, and what, advice was given.
4. Each minister has a constitutionally fixed personal veto
Wrong: no minister has a personal veto; decisions are taken collectively by the Council.

points: So legal responsibility of ministers is weak in India: there is no provision for it like in Britain.

POL-734-LAX-10.lead: Option 1: a kitchen cabinet is an informal group of a few trusted colleagues and advisers around the PM.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. An informal group of trusted advisers around the Prime Minister
Correct: it is an informal inner body of the PM and two to four influential colleagues (and sometimes friends or family) where real decisions may be discussed.
2. A constitutionally mandated committee
Wrong: it has no constitutional or legal basis.
3. All Cabinet ministers in formal session
Wrong: that is the formal Cabinet meeting, a different body.
4. The Cabinet Secretariat's permanent staff
Wrong: the Cabinet Secretariat staff are civil servants, not a group of political advisers.

points: Indira Gandhi's kitchen cabinet was well known; the term shows how the PM may bypass the formal Cabinet.

POL-734-LAX-11.lead: Option 1: a caretaker government is the outgoing ministry that continues by convention, doing routine work and avoiding major policy decisions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A conventional continuing ministry expected to handle routine business and avoid major new policy except necessity
Correct: after dissolution the ministry stays in office (Article 74 needs a Council at all times) but by convention avoids big new policies.
2. A body expressly created by a separate constitutional article
Wrong: no separate Article creates a caretaker government; it rests on convention.
3. A government with no Council of Ministers
Wrong: there is always a Council of Ministers, as held in U.N.R. Rao (1971).
4. A ministry free from parliamentary conventions
Wrong: a caretaker ministry is bound even more strictly by parliamentary conventions.

points: It may still take decisions in an emergency or genuine necessity.

POL-734-LAX-12.lead: Option 1: the bar lasts till the end of the member's term or till he is re-elected, whichever is earlier.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Until the original term ends or the member is re-elected earlier, whichever occurs first
Correct: Article 75(1B), added by the 91st Amendment (2003), uses exactly this formula.
2. For life
Wrong: Article 75(1B) does not impose a lifelong bar; it ends with the term or re-election.
3. For exactly six months
Wrong: Article 75(1B) has no fixed six-month period; the six-month rule in Article 75(5) is about a non-member minister.
4. Only until the Speaker records the order
Wrong: the bar continues for the remaining term unless he is re-elected; it does not end on the Speaker's order.

points: The 91st Amendment also added the 15% cap on ministers (Article 75(1A)).

POL-734-LAX-13.lead: Option 1: no; Cabinet Committees can take final decisions, though the Cabinet can review them.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. No; committees may take decisions, subject to Cabinet review
Correct: Cabinet Committees not only sort out issues but also take decisions, which the Cabinet may review.
2. Yes, always
Wrong: their decisions do not always need separate ratification by the full Cabinet.
3. Only the President may ratify them
Wrong: the President has no role in ratifying their decisions.
4. They can only make non-binding suggestions
Wrong: they are decision-making bodies, not merely advisory.

points: They are extra-constitutional, set up under the Transaction of Business Rules, and reduce the Cabinet's workload.

POL-734-LAX-14.lead: All four pairs are correct, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2, 3 and 4).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Political Affairs – political and Centre-State issues
True
It deals with domestic and foreign policy and Centre-State relations; it is called the 'super-cabinet'.
2. Security – defence and internal security
True
It handles defence, national security and related appointments.
3. Appointments – senior appointments
True
It decides top appointments in the Central Secretariat, PSUs and banks.
4. Parliamentary Affairs – government business in Parliament
True
It watches the progress of government business in Parliament.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out at least one correct pair, so they are incomplete.
Cabinet committees are extra-constitutional: set up by the PM under the Rules of Business; most are chaired by the PM.

POL-734-LAX-15.lead: Option 1: the Economic Affairs Committee directs and coordinates government activity in the economic sphere.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Economic Affairs Committee — directs and coordinates government activity in the economic sphere
Correct pair: this is exactly the function of the Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs.
2. Political Affairs Committee — decides senior appointments in the Central Secretariat and public enterprises
Wrong pair: senior appointments belong to the Appointments Committee; Political Affairs deals with domestic and foreign policy matters.
3. Appointments Committee — looks after the progress of government business in Parliament
Wrong pair: business in Parliament is looked after by the Parliamentary Affairs Committee; the Appointments Committee decides higher-level appointments.
4. Parliamentary Affairs Committee — deals with defence and national security policy
Wrong pair: defence and security belong to the Committee on Security; Parliamentary Affairs looks after government business in Parliament.

points: The Political Affairs Committee is the most powerful, called a 'Super-Cabinet'.

POL-734-LAX-16.lead: Option 2 (1 and 2 only): statement(s) 1, 2 true, statement(s) 3 false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. They are ad hoc coordination bodies for specific issues.
True
True. GoMs are ad hoc bodies formed to advise on specific emergent issues and critical problem areas.
2. Some may decide on behalf of the Cabinet while others only recommend.
True
True. Some GoMs are empowered to decide on behalf of the Cabinet, while others only make recommendations.
3. They must continue permanently after advice is finalised.
False
False. GoMs are disbanded once their advice is crystallised; they are not permanent.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 3 (2 and 3 only) wrongly includes false statement 3 and leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (1, 2 and 3) wrongly includes false statement 3.

POL-734-LAX-17.lead: Option 4 (1, 2 and 3): statement(s) 1, 2, 3 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Non-Cabinet ministers may be members or special invitees.
True
True. Cabinet Committees usually include Cabinet ministers, but non-Cabinet ministers can also be members or special invitees.
2. A senior Cabinet minister may chair a committee when the Prime Minister is not a member.
True
True. Most are headed by the PM, but sometimes a senior Cabinet minister acts as chairman.
3. If the Prime Minister is a member, the Prime Minister presides.
True
True. If the PM is a member of a committee, he invariably presides over it.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2, 3.
Option 2 (1 and 2 only) leaves out true statement 3.
Option 3 (2 and 3 only) leaves out true statement 1.

POL-734-LAX-18.lead: Option 3: the Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs is chaired by a senior Cabinet minister, not the PM.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs
Chaired by the PM; deals with domestic and foreign policy matters and is the most powerful committee.
2. Cabinet Committee on Economic Affairs
Chaired by the PM; directs and coordinates economic activity.
3. Cabinet Committee on Parliamentary Affairs
Correct: chaired by a senior minister (earlier the Home Minister, currently the Defence Minister); it looks after government business in Parliament.
4. Appointments Committee of the Cabinet
Chaired by the PM; decides higher appointments, and has only the PM and Home Minister as members.

points: LX: 'mostly headed by the PM ... sometimes other senior Cabinet ministers act as chairman'.

POL-734-LAX-19.lead: Option 3: the committees on Investment and Growth and on Employment and Skill Development were created in 2019.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Committee on Security and Committee on Political Affairs
Wrong: the Committee on Security and the Committee on Political Affairs both existed well before 2019; they were part of the original six.
2. Committee on Accommodation and Committee on Parliamentary Affairs
Wrong: the Committee on Accommodation and the Committee on Parliamentary Affairs were among the six committees that existed before 2019.
3. Committee on Investment and Growth and Committee on Employment and Skill Development
Correct: these two were added in 2019, raising the total to eight.
4. Committee on Economic Affairs and Appointments Committee
Wrong: the Economic Affairs Committee and the Appointments Committee are among the oldest standing committees, not 2019 additions.

points: The eight: Political Affairs, Economic Affairs, Appointments, Parliamentary Affairs, Security, Accommodation, Investment and Growth, Employment and Skill Development.

POL-734-LAX-20.lead: Option 1: the Second ARC said GoMs should be used selectively, with clear authority to decide and a fixed time limit.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Use them selectively with clear decision authority and prescribed time limits
Correct: it found too many GoMs slowed decisions, so it asked that they be few, empowered and time-bound.
2. Make every GoM permanent
Wrong: GoMs are ad hoc by nature and are disbanded once advice is crystallised; the ARC never recommended making them permanent.
3. Prohibit them from coordinating ministries
Wrong: coordinating ministries is the very purpose of GoMs.
4. Require every GoM to include all Cabinet ministers
Wrong: a GoM has only the ministers concerned with the subject, not the whole Cabinet.

POL-734-LAX-21.lead: Option 1: U.N.R. Rao (1971) held that the Council of Ministers continues even after Lok Sabha is dissolved.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Council of Ministers continues because Article 74 requires one
Correct: Article 74 is mandatory, so the President can never exercise executive power without a Council's aid and advice.
2. The Council automatically ceases
Wrong: the Court rejected the claim that the Council ceases on dissolution, because Article 74 always requires a Council.
3. The President governs without advice
Wrong: the Court said any exercise of power without aid and advice would be unconstitutional.
4. Rajya Sabha becomes the Council of Ministers
Wrong: Rajya Sabha is a House of Parliament and never acts as the Council of Ministers; the outgoing ministry continues instead.

POL-734-LAX-22.lead: Option 1: in Shamsher Singh (1974) the Supreme Court held that the 'satisfaction' of the President means the satisfaction of the Council of Ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Council of Ministers
Correct: the President exercises his powers on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers, so 'satisfaction' is theirs.
2. President personally in every case
Wrong: personal satisfaction applies only in a few exceptional discretionary situations.
3. Chief Justice of India
Wrong: the CJI has no role in executive satisfaction.
4. Lok Sabha Speaker
Wrong: the Speaker belongs to the legislature and has no role in executive decisions.

points: A seven-judge bench decided this; it applies to the Governor too.

POL-734-LAX-23.lead: Option 1: upholding the sovereignty and integrity of India is a part of the oath of office.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India
Correct: the oath of office includes bearing true faith to the Constitution and upholding the sovereignty and integrity of India.
2. Never reveal any matter under consideration
Part of the oath of secrecy: the minister swears not to reveal matters that come before him as a minister.
3. Keep every Cabinet paper forever secret from courts
In neither oath; courts can call for documents, subject only to Article 74(2) on advice.
4. Disclose all internal dissent to Parliament
In neither oath; ministers keep internal differences confidential under collective responsibility.

points: Both oath forms are in the Third Schedule and are given by the President (Article 75(4)).

POL-734-LAX-24.lead: Option 1: Article 75(6) says ministers' salaries and allowances are determined by Parliament by law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Parliament
Correct: Parliament fixes them by law under Article 75(6).
2. President acting alone
Wrong: the President does not fix ministers' salaries on his own; Article 75(6) gives this to Parliament.
3. Finance Commission
Wrong: the Finance Commission deals with sharing of taxes between Union and States (Article 280).
4. Supreme Court
Wrong: the Supreme Court has no role in fixing ministers' salaries.

points: Ministers get the salary and allowances of an MP plus additional allowances.

POL-734-LAX-25.lead: Option 1: under collective responsibility, a minister who cannot support a Cabinet decision must resign.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Resign
Correct: every minister must own Cabinet decisions; one who disagrees must resign.
2. Remain and publicly disown it
Wrong: publicly disowning a decision breaks collective responsibility.
3. Ask the President to veto it personally
Wrong: the President acts on the Council's advice and cannot veto Cabinet decisions on a minister's request.
4. Vote against it in every House regardless of membership
Wrong: a minister votes only in his own House (Article 88) and must support Cabinet decisions.

points: Example: Dr B.R. Ambedkar resigned in 1951 over differences on the Hindu Code Bill.

POL-734-LAX-26.lead: Option 1: Article 352(3) defines the Cabinet as the PM and other Cabinet-rank ministers appointed under Article 75.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Prime Minister and ministers of Cabinet rank appointed under Article 75
Correct: this is the definition added by the 44th Amendment (1978).
2. Every Union minister of every rank
Wrong: Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers are not of Cabinet rank, so they are excluded from this definition.
3. Prime Minister alone
Wrong: the decision must be of the Cabinet, not of the PM alone; the 44th Amendment was made after the 1975 emergency was declared on the PM's advice alone.
4. Cabinet Secretariat officials
Wrong: Cabinet Secretariat officials are civil servants who service the Cabinet; they are not ministers and are not part of the Cabinet.

points: The President can proclaim National Emergency only on the written advice of the Cabinet.

POL-734-LAX-27.lead: Option 3: there are eight Cabinet Committees; the number became eight when two were added in 2019.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Six
Wrong: six was the number before 2019, when the committees on Investment and Growth and on Employment and Skill Development were added.
2. Seven
Wrong: seven is not the current count; after the 2019 additions the total is eight.
3. Eight
Correct: Political Affairs, Economic Affairs, Appointments, Parliamentary Affairs, Security, Accommodation, Investment and Growth, and Employment and Skill Development.
4. Nine
Wrong: there is no ninth Cabinet Committee; Groups of Ministers are ad hoc bodies and are not counted as Cabinet Committees.

POL-734-LAX-28.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2): statement(s) 1, 2 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The Security Committee comprises the Prime Minister and the Home, Defence, Finance and External Affairs Ministers.
True
True. The Cabinet Committee on Security consists of the PM and the ministers of Home, Defence, Finance and External Affairs.
2. The Appointments Committee comprises the Prime Minister and Home Minister.
True
True. The Appointments Committee of the Cabinet has only two members: the PM and the Home Minister.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 2 (2 only) leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) leaves out true statement 1, 2.
The CCS deals with defence, law and order, internal security and atomic energy.

POL-734-LAX-29.lead: Option 1: Article 77(3) lets the President make rules for convenient transaction of Union business and its allocation among ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Convenient transaction of Union business and its allocation among ministers
Correct: these are the Allocation of Business Rules and Transaction of Business Rules, 1961.
2. Election of the Prime Minister by Parliament
Wrong: Parliament does not elect the PM; the President appoints him under Article 75(1).
3. Judicial review of Cabinet advice
Wrong: Article 74(2) bars courts from inquiring into advice; Article 77(3) is about business rules.
4. Removal of ministers without the Prime Minister's advice
Wrong: ministers are appointed and removed on the PM's advice (Article 75(1)).

POL-734-LAX-30.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2): statement(s) 1, 2 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. communicate Council decisions and legislative proposals to the President
True
True. Article 78(a) requires the PM to communicate to the President all decisions of the Council of Ministers on administration and proposals for legislation.
2. furnish information relating to Union administration and legislative proposals when the President calls for it.
True
True. Article 78(b) requires the PM to furnish information on administration and legislative proposals when the President calls for it.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 2 (2 only) leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) leaves out true statement 1, 2.
Article 78(c) adds a third duty: to place before the Council any matter decided by a single minister if the President so requires.

POL-734-LAX-31.lead: Option 1: under Article 78(c) the President may require the PM to place the matter before the Council of Ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Prime Minister must place the matter before the Council
Correct: this ensures a decision taken by one minister becomes a collective decision.
2. The Supreme Court must approve the decision
Wrong: Article 78 involves only the President, the PM and the Council; the Supreme Court has no role in approving executive decisions.
3. The minister automatically loses office
Wrong: Article 78(c) does not remove the minister; it only sends his decision to the Council for collective consideration.
4. The Rajya Sabha must ratify the decision
Wrong: Rajya Sabha has no power to ratify executive decisions; the Council of Ministers is responsible to Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)).

POL-734-P187-01.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2): statement(s) 1, 2 true; all statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The President may require the Council of Ministers to reconsider its advice.
True
True. The proviso to Article 74(1), added by the 44th Amendment (1978), lets the President ask the Council to reconsider its advice once.
2. After reconsideration, the President must act according to that advice.
True
True. After reconsideration the President must act according to the advice.

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2.
Option 2 (2 only) leaves out true statement 1.
Option 4 (Neither 1 nor 2) leaves out true statement 1, 2.
The 42nd Amendment (1976) first made the advice binding.

POL-734-P188-01.lead: Option 3: Article 75(1A) caps ministers, including the PM, at 15% of Lok Sabha's total strength.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 10 per cent
Wrong: 10% is not the figure in Article 75(1A); the cap fixed by the 91st Amendment is 15%.
2. 12 per cent
Wrong: 12 is the minimum number of ministers in a state (Article 164(1A)), not a percentage.
3. 15 per cent
Correct: Article 75(1A), inserted by the 91st Amendment Act, 2003, fixes the ceiling at 15% of the total strength of Lok Sabha.
4. 20 per cent
Wrong: 20% is not the figure; the constitutional ceiling is 15%.

points: For states the cap is 15% of the Assembly, with a minimum of 12 ministers.

POL-734-P189-01.lead: Option 4: Article 78 lists the PM's duties to communicate decisions and furnish information to the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 74
Article 74 provides for a Council of Ministers headed by the PM to aid and advise the President; it does not list the PM's duties of communication.
2. Article 75
Article 75 deals with appointment, tenure, collective responsibility, oath and salaries of ministers, not the PM's duty to inform the President.
3. Article 77
Article 77 deals with conduct of business: action in the President's name, authentication of orders and business rules.
4. Article 78
Correct: Article 78 sets out the duties of the Prime Minister as respects furnishing information to the President.

POL-734-P190-01.lead: Option 3 is the incorrect statement: the PM does not necessarily remain in office for five full years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Constitution does not prescribe a fixed five-year term
Correct statement: the Constitution gives the PM no fixed term.
2. Continuation depends on Lok Sabha majority support
Correct statement: he stays as long as he enjoys Lok Sabha majority support.
3. A Prime Minister necessarily remains in office for five full years
Incorrect statement (answer): his term is not fixed; he may resign, lose confidence or be removed earlier.
4. Loss of Lok Sabha confidence can require resignation
Correct statement: loss of confidence in Lok Sabha requires resignation.

points: Five years is the normal term of Lok Sabha (Article 83(2)), not of the PM.

POL-734-P192-01.lead: Option 2: the Deputy PM is an extra-constitutional, merely descriptive designation with no special powers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It is a constitutional office under Article 75
Wrong: Article 75 provides only for the Prime Minister and other ministers; the Deputy PM is not mentioned anywhere in the Constitution.
2. It is an extra-constitutional designation without special constitutional powers
Correct: the Supreme Court (Devi Lal case, 1990) held the title is descriptive and gives no powers of the PM.
3. Its holder automatically succeeds the Prime Minister
Wrong: there is no automatic succession; if the PM leaves, the whole Council goes and the President appoints a new PM.
4. Its holder must be a Rajya Sabha member
Wrong: there is no membership requirement for the title; like any minister, the holder may belong to either House, and holders have come from Lok Sabha.

points: Sardar Patel was India's first Deputy PM.

POL-734-P193-01.lead: Option 2: under Article 75(5), the minister ceases to be a minister after six consecutive months without membership of either House.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The minister automatically becomes a Rajya Sabha member
Wrong: Rajya Sabha membership comes only by election by the State Assembly members (or nomination); it is never automatic.
2. The minister ceases to hold office
Correct: Article 75(5) says a minister who is not an MP for six consecutive months ceases to be a minister at the end of that period.
3. The minister continues until the Lok Sabha dissolves
Wrong: Article 75(5) ends his office after six months; it does not let him continue till Lok Sabha is dissolved.
4. The President must seek the Supreme Court's opinion
Wrong: no Supreme Court reference is involved; the loss of office follows automatically from Article 75(5).

POL-734-P193-02.lead: Option 2: Article 74(2) protects the question of whether advice was given and what that advice was from judicial inquiry.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The legality of every executive order
Wrong: Article 74(2) protects only the advice; the legality of executive orders remains open to judicial review.
2. Whether advice was tendered to the President and what that advice was
Correct: courts cannot inquire into whether any advice was tendered and, if so, what advice.
3. The qualifications of ministers
Wrong: ministers must be MPs or become MPs within six months (Article 75(5)); questions of membership and qualification are not covered by Article 74(2).
4. The numerical strength of the Council of Ministers
Wrong: the size of the Council is limited by Article 75(1A) to 15% of Lok Sabha, and that limit is not shielded by Article 74(2).

POL-734-P194-02.lead: Option 2 is the incorrect statement: the Constitution does not define the three ranks of ministers; they come from parliamentary convention.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: They reflect political-administrative practice
True. The three-tier classification is based on conventions of parliamentary government developed in Britain.
✗ (true statement)
The Constitution expressly defines all three ranks
False. Articles 74 and 75 speak only of a 'Council of Ministers'; its size and classification are not mentioned in the Constitution.
✓ (the incorrect one)
Their roles differ in participation and departmental charge
True. Cabinet Ministers attend Cabinet meetings; Ministers of State may hold independent charge or be attached; Deputy Ministers only assist.
✗ (true statement)
They remain within the wider Council of Ministers
True. The Council of Ministers is the wider body containing all three categories; the Cabinet contains only Cabinet Ministers.
✗ (true statement)

points: The question asks for the INCORRECT statement, so the false claim is the answer.
The classification has legislative sanction only through the Salaries and Allowances of Ministers Act, 1952, which defines 'minister' to include a deputy minister — not through the Constitution.
Memory hook: Constitution = 'Council of Ministers' only; ranks = convention.

POL-734-P195-02.lead: Option 2: a minister is individually responsible to the President (holds office during his pleasure, Article 75(2)), and the Council is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Individual—Lok Sabha; collective—President
Reverses the two. The Lok Sabha enforces collective, not individual, responsibility, and collective responsibility is not owed to the President.
Individual—President's pleasure; collective—Lok Sabha
Matches Article 75(2) (individual) and Article 75(3) (collective).
Individual—Rajya Sabha; collective—Supreme Court
Neither body enforces ministerial responsibility; the Rajya Sabha cannot vote a ministry out and the Supreme Court is a court, not a political forum.
Individual—Election Commission; collective—President
The Election Commission conducts elections and has no role in ministerial responsibility.

points: Individual responsibility: the President can remove a minister, but only on the PM's advice.
Collective responsibility: when the Lok Sabha passes a no-confidence motion, all ministers, including those from the Rajya Sabha, must resign.
Hook: 'one minister — President; whole team — Lok Sabha'.

POL-734-P197-01.lead: All three statements are true, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. They are extra-constitutional
True
They are not mentioned in the Constitution; the Rules of Business provide for their establishment.
2. They are set up by the Prime Minister
True
The PM sets them up as the situation requires, so their number, names and membership change from time to time.
3. They may be standing or ad hoc
True
Standing committees are permanent; ad hoc committees are formed for a special problem and dissolved when the task is done.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out at least one true statement, so they fail.
Cabinet Committees reduce the Cabinet's workload; they can take decisions, but the Cabinet can review them.
Example: Cabinet Committee on Political Affairs, Appointments Committee of the Cabinet.

POL-E44-CUR-734-001.lead: Option 1: beyond chairing the Council of Ministers, the PM is the leader of the nation — shaping foreign policy, representing the government politically and leading in crises.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Shapes India's position in international affairs, represents the Union government politically, and supplies national and crisis leadership
This describes the PM's wider roles listed by Laxmikanth: leader of the nation, chief spokesman of the Union government, crisis manager and key role in foreign policy.
Acts as the formal non-partisan head of State, authenticating executive action while remaining outside party government
This is the President, the nominal (de jure) head of State; the PM is a party leader and the real executive.
Functions only as the minister in charge of external affairs, without responsibility for whole-government coordination
Wrong: the PM coordinates the work of all ministries; foreign policy is only one of his roles.
Serves as the permanent civil-service coordinator who implements policy without political responsibility to Parliament
This describes a senior civil servant such as the Cabinet Secretary; the PM is a politician answerable to the Lok Sabha.

points: The PM is the real (de facto) executive, while the President is the nominal (de jure) executive.
Laxmikanth also lists the PM as leader of the party in power and political head of the services.

LX-PQ-055.lead: Option 4: the Charter Act of 1833 made the Governor-General of Bengal the Governor-General of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Government of India Act of 1858
Wrong: the 1858 Act changed the title to Viceroy of India and ended Company rule.
2. Indian Councils Act of 1861
Wrong: the Indian Councils Act, 1861 began associating Indians with law-making and restored legislative powers to Bombay and Madras.
3. Pitts India Act of 1784
Wrong: Pitt's India Act, 1784 created the Board of Control and dual government; it did not create this office.
4. Charter Act of 1833
Correct: the 1833 Act vested all civil and military powers in the Governor-General of India; Lord William Bentinck was the first.

points: The 1833 Act was the final step towards centralisation in British India.
Memory hook: Regulating Act 1773 = GG of Bengal; Charter 1833 = GG of India; 1858 = Viceroy.

LX-PQ-062.lead: Statements 1, 3 and 5 are features of the 1858 Act, so the answer is option 4.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Crown rule replaced Company rule.
True
The Government of India Act, 1858 transferred the government of India from the East India Company to the British Crown.
2. A Board of Control was set up over the Court of Directors.
False
The Board of Control was created by Pitt's India Act, 1784; the 1858 Act abolished both the Board and the Court of Directors.
3. A Council of India was established.
True
The 1858 Act created a 15-member Council of India to advise the Secretary of State.
4. Legislative and executive functions of the Governor-General were separated.
False
This was done by the Charter Act of 1853, not the 1858 Act.
5. A new office of Secretary of State for India was created.
True
The 1858 Act created the Secretary of State, a member of the British cabinet, with full control over Indian administration.

points: Options 1 and 2 fail because they include the false statement 4 (and option 2 also statement 2).
Option 3 fails because it leaves out the true statement 3.

LX-PQ-089.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true and 4 is false, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The executive power of the State is vested in him.
True
Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor.
2. He must have attained 35 years of age.
True
Article 157 requires a Governor to be a citizen of India who has completed 35 years.
3. He holds office during the pleasure of the President.
True
Article 156(1) says the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President.
4. The grounds for his removal are laid down in the Constitution.
False
The Constitution lays down no grounds and no procedure for removing a Governor; he can be removed at the President's pleasure.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 fail because each includes the false statement 4.

LX-PQ-100.lead: Option 2: the 7th Amendment, 1956 allowed the same person to be Governor of two or more States.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 4th Amendment
Wrong: the 4th Amendment (1955) dealt with compensation for acquired property, not Governors.
2. 7th Amendment
Correct: the 7th Amendment added a proviso to Article 153 permitting one Governor for two or more States.
3. 11th Amendment
Wrong: the 11th Amendment (1961) changed the Vice-President's election to an electoral college instead of a joint sitting.
4. 24th Amendment
Wrong: the 24th Amendment (1971) affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights.

points: The 7th Amendment is also the States Reorganisation amendment of 1956.
When one Governor serves two States, the President decides the sharing of emoluments (Article 158(3A)).

LX-PQ-101.lead: Option 1: 'officers subordinate' under Article 154 includes the Chief Minister and all the ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. All the ministers and the Chief Minister
Correct: the Governor acts through the Council of Ministers headed by the CM, so the CM and ministers are among the officers subordinate to him for this purpose.
2. All the ministers except the Chief Minister
Wrong: the CM is the head of the Council of Ministers and cannot be left out.
3. Only the Chief Minister and the Deputy Chief Minister
Wrong: limiting it to the CM and Deputy CM has no basis; Deputy CM is not even a constitutional post.
4. Only the Cabinet Ministers
Wrong: Ministers of State and Deputy Ministers are also part of the ministry, so 'only Cabinet Ministers' is too narrow.

points: Article 154(1): executive power is exercised by the Governor directly or through officers subordinate to him.
This is the Laxmikanth practice-question answer.

LX-PQ-106.lead: Option 1 — Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Under Article 164(1), the Chief Minister holds office during the pleasure of the Governor.
R
True
Under Article 164(1), the Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor.

points: Does R explain A? Yes — the authority that appoints an office holder also holds the 'pleasure' over him. Since the Governor appoints the CM, the CM serves during the Governor's pleasure, so R explains A.
Option 2 fails: R actually does explain A.
Option 3 fails: R is in fact true.
Option 4 fails: A is in fact true.

LX-PQ-109.lead: Option 1 — Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
The Governor is the nominal (titular) executive head of the State; real power lies with the Council of Ministers.
R
True
The Constitution provides a parliamentary system of government in the States, as at the Centre.

points: Does R explain A? Yes — in a parliamentary system the head of State is nominal and the ministry is the real executive. Because States follow this system, the Governor is a nominal head, so R explains A.
Option 2 fails: R actually does explain A.
Option 3 fails: R is in fact true.
Option 4 fails: A is in fact true.

LX-PQ-110.lead: Option 1 — Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Under Article 156, the Governor holds office during the pleasure of the President.
R
True
Under Article 155, the Governor is appointed by the President.

points: Does R explain A? Yes — the authority that appoints an office holder also holds the 'pleasure' over him. Since the President appoints the Governor, the Governor serves during the President's pleasure, so R explains A.
Option 2 fails: R actually does explain A.
Option 3 fails: R is in fact true.
Option 4 fails: A is in fact true.

LX-PQ-115.lead: Option 4: 'during the pleasure of the Governor' really means as long as the ministry enjoys the majority of the Legislative Assembly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Pleasure of the President
Wrong: the President's pleasure applies to the Governor himself (Article 156), not to the State ministry.
2. Pleasure of the Prime Minister
Wrong: the Prime Minister has no role in the life of a State ministry.
3. Pleasure of the Chief Minister
Wrong: the CM can advise dropping individual ministers, but the ministry as a whole survives only with Assembly support.
4. Pleasure of the Legislative Assembly
Correct: because the ministry is collectively responsible to the Assembly (Article 164(2)), the Governor cannot dismiss it while it has a majority.

points: Article 164(1) says ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure; Article 164(2) gives this its real meaning.

LX-PQ-131.lead: Option 1 (LX key): both statements are true and Statement-II explains Statement-I.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: Statement-I
True
The Governor is the constitutional (de jure) head; all executive action is taken in his name (Article 166).
Statement-II
True
The Chief Minister heads the Council of Ministers that actually runs the government, so he is the real (de facto) head.

points: Does II explain I? In a parliamentary system real power lies with the ministry headed by the CM; because the CM exercises the real power, the Governor remains only a nominal head. That link is why the book treats II as the explanation.
Option 2 fails on the book's view, which treats the two as cause and effect of the same system.
Options 3 and 4 fail because both statements are true.
LX-PQ-131.also: Disputed key: some treat the two statements as parallel facts (option 2); the LX key 1 is kept.

LX-PQ-137.lead: Option 2: ordinance-making (Article 213) is the Governor's most important legislative power.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Nominating members to the state legislative council.
Wrong: nominating one-sixth of Council members (Article 171) is a legislative power but a minor one, and exists only in States with a Council.
2. Issuing ordinances
Correct: under Article 213 the Governor can make laws himself when the legislature is not in session; an ordinance has the same force as an Act.
3. Assenting bills passed by the state legislature
Wrong: assent to Bills (Article 200) is important, but the Governor only approves laws made by others.
4. Dissolving the state legislative Assembly
Wrong: dissolution (Article 174) is done on the CM's advice and does not make law.

points: An ordinance must be approved within six weeks of the legislature reassembling or it lapses.
The Governor can promulgate only when the House is not in session and he is satisfied immediate action is needed.

LX-PQ-138.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A). The CM heads the Council, so he is its link with the Governor.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Article 167 makes the CM communicate all Council decisions to the Governor and furnish information the Governor asks for.
R
True
Article 163: there is a Council of Ministers with the CM at its head.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Because the CM leads the Council, he is the natural single voice between it and the Governor; Article 167 puts that duty on him for this very reason.
Option 2 (both true, R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: R is true.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: A is true.

LX-PQ-168.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A). Because the CM can remove a minister, a minister serves only while the CM trusts him.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Ministers hold office during the Governor's pleasure (Art 164(1)), and the Governor uses it on the CM's advice, so in practice a minister lasts only while the CM trusts him.
R
True
The CM can ask a minister to resign or advise the Governor to dismiss him.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. A minister depends on the CM's confidence precisely because the CM can get him removed at any time.
Option 2 (both true, R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: R is true.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: A is true.

LX-PQ-189.lead: Statements 2 and 4 are correct, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The Governor can pardon court-martial sentences, the President cannot.
False
It is the reverse: only the President can pardon sentences by court martial (Article 72); the Governor has no such power.
2. The President can pardon a death sentence, the Governor cannot.
True
Under Article 72 the President can pardon a death sentence; the Governor under Article 161 can suspend, remit or commute it but cannot pardon it.
3. The Governor can pardon a death sentence, the President cannot.
False
This reverses the correct position stated in statement 2.
4. The President can pardon court-martial sentences, the Governor cannot.
True
Article 72(1)(a) covers court-martial sentences for the President only.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 fail because each includes a false statement (1 or 3).

LX-UPSC-2013-Q12.lead: Option 3: the Constitution lays down no procedure for removing a Governor.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. In India, the same person cannot be appointed as Governor for two or more States at the same time
False: the 7th Amendment (1956) allows one person to be Governor of two or more States (Article 153).
2. The Judges of the High Court of the States in India are appointed by the Governor of the State just as the Judges of the Supreme Court are appointed by the President
False: High Court judges are appointed by the President (Article 217), not by the Governor.
3. No procedure has been laid down in the Constitution of India for the removal of a Governor from his/her post
True: the Governor holds office during the President's pleasure (Article 156) and no removal procedure or grounds are laid down.
4. In the case of a Union Territory having a legislative setup, the Chief Minister is appointed by the Lt. Governor on the basis of majority support
False: in Delhi and Puducherry the Chief Minister is appointed by the President, not by the Lt. Governor.

points: B.P. Singhal (2010): the pleasure cannot be used arbitrarily or for political reasons.

LX-UPSC-2023-Q10.lead: Option 4: the Charter Act of 1833 designated the Governor-General of Bengal as Governor-General of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Regulating Act
Wrong: the Regulating Act, 1773 made the Governor of Bengal the Governor-General of Bengal (Warren Hastings).
2. The Pitt’s India Act.
Wrong: Pitt's India Act, 1784 set up the Board of Control (dual government), not this title.
3. The Charter Act of 1793
Wrong: the Charter Act of 1793 mainly renewed the Company's charter; it did not create this office.
4. The Charter Act of 1833
Correct: the 1833 Act gave the Governor-General of India all civil and military powers; Lord William Bentinck was the first.

points: Memory hook: 1773 Bengal, 1833 India, 1858 Viceroy.
LX-UPSC-2023-Q10.also: Charter Act 1833 was the final step towards centralisation in British India.

POL-735-CH-01.lead: Option 2: in a hung Assembly, the Governor appoints the person most likely to command a majority and asks for proof on the floor of the House.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Governor personally selects a government for the full term without a confidence vote
Wrong: a government cannot run without a confidence vote; majority must be shown in the House, not judged privately by the Governor.
2. The Governor appoints a person likely to command a majority and requires proof on the floor of the House
Correct: the Governor uses limited discretion to choose the likely leader and then requires a floor test within a fixed time.
3. The President directly appoints the Chief Minister
Wrong: the Chief Minister is appointed by the Governor (Article 164(1)), not by the President.
4. The outgoing Chief Minister must continue for five years
Wrong: an outgoing CM only continues as caretaker until a new ministry is sworn in; no five-year rule exists.

points: S.R. Bommai (1994): the floor of the House is the proper place to test majority.
POL-735-CH-01.also: S.R. Bommai (1994): the floor of the House is the proper place to test majority.

POL-735-CH-02.lead: All three routes are available, so the answer is option 4.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Assent.
True
Article 200 lets the Governor assent to a Bill, after which it becomes law.
2. Reserve the Bill for the President.
True
Article 200 lets the Governor reserve a Bill for the President's consideration.
3. Withhold assent and return a non-Money Bill for reconsideration.
True
The 2025 opinion said withholding must be coupled with returning the Bill to the House with comments; a Money Bill cannot be returned.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out at least one available route.
The Court rejected an indefinite 'pocket veto' of simply sitting on a Bill.

POL-735-LAX-01.lead: All three conditions are correct, so the answer is option 4.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Not a member of Parliament or a State Legislature.
True
Article 158(1) says the Governor shall not be a member of either House of Parliament or of a State Legislature.
2. Not hold any other office of profit.
True
Article 158(2) bars the Governor from holding any other office of profit.
3. A legislator appointed Governor vacates his seat on entering office.
True
Article 158(1) deems the seat vacated on the date he enters office as Governor.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out a correct condition.
POL-735-LAX-01.also: Governor's emoluments cannot be reduced during the term (Article 158(4)).

POL-735-LAX-02.lead: Option 1: a Money Bill can be introduced only in the Assembly and only on the Governor's recommendation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Money Bill
Correct: Article 207(1) requires the Governor's recommendation for a Money Bill, and Article 198 allows its introduction only in the Assembly.
2. Ordinary private member's resolution
Wrong: a private member's resolution is not a financial measure and needs no recommendation.
3. Motion of thanks
Wrong: the Motion of Thanks is a discussion on the Governor's address, not a financial measure.
4. Adjournment motion
Wrong: an adjournment motion draws attention to an urgent public matter; it needs no recommendation.

points: The Governor also causes the State Budget to be laid before the Legislature (Article 202).
POL-735-LAX-02.also: The Governor causes the State Budget to be laid before the Legislature (Article 202).

POL-735-LAX-03.lead: Option 3: the Governor's report on breakdown of constitutional machinery is the basis for President's Rule under Article 356.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 123
Wrong: Article 123 is the President's ordinance power.
2. Article 213
Wrong: Article 213 is the Governor's ordinance power.
3. Article 356
Correct: under Article 356 the President may proclaim emergency on the Governor's report or otherwise.
4. Article 360 only
Wrong: Article 360 is financial emergency and does not depend on a Governor's report.

points: The proclamation must be approved by Parliament within two months.
POL-735-LAX-03.also: Proclamation must be approved by Parliament within two months.

POL-735-LAX-04.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct and 3 is wrong, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Selecting a CM where no party has a clear majority.
True
In a hung Assembly the Governor uses limited discretion to choose the person most likely to win a confidence vote.
2. Requiring a floor test when majority is credibly disputed.
True
S.R. Bommai (1994) held that majority must be tested on the floor of the House.
3. Dismissing a majority government because of disliking its policy.
False
A ministry with Assembly majority cannot be dismissed; the Governor must act on its advice on policy.

points: Option 1 leaves out statement 2.
Options 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.

POL-735-LAX-05.lead: Option 1: yes, the proviso to Article 153 allows one Governor for two or more States.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Yes, the Constitution permits it
Correct: the 7th Amendment, 1956 added this proviso.
2. No, never
Wrong: it is clearly permitted and often done.
3. Only during a national emergency
Article 153, as amended by the 7th Amendment (1956), allows one person to be Governor of two or more States at any time; no emergency is required.
4. Only if every State Legislature elects that person
Wrong: the Governor is appointed by the President (Article 155), not elected by State legislatures.

points: When one Governor serves two States, the President decides how salary is shared (Article 158(3A)).
POL-735-LAX-05.also: When one Governor serves two States, the President decides how salary is shared (Article 158(3A)).

POL-735-LAX-06.lead: Option 1: the Governor resigns by writing addressed to the President (Article 156(2)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. President
Correct: since the President appoints the Governor and he holds office at the President's pleasure, the resignation goes to the President.
2. Chief Minister
Wrong: the Chief Minister heads the State ministry and has no power to appoint or accept the resignation of the Governor.
3. Chief Justice of the High Court
Wrong: the Chief Justice of the High Court only administers the oath (Article 159).
4. State Legislature
Wrong: the State Legislature does not appoint or remove the Governor.

points: Memory hook: resign to the one who appoints.

POL-735-LAX-08.lead: All three powers belong to the Governor, so the answer is option 4.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Summon the State Legislature.
True
Article 174(1) lets the Governor summon each House from time to time.
2. Prorogue it.
True
Article 174(2)(a) lets the Governor prorogue the House or either House.
3. Dissolve the Legislative Assembly.
True
Article 174(2)(b) lets the Governor dissolve the Assembly (only the Assembly, not the Council).

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out a correct power.
The gap between two sessions cannot exceed six months.

POL-735-LAX-09.lead: Option 1: the Governor nominates one-sixth of the Legislative Council members (Article 171(3)(e)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. One-sixth
Correct: nominees have special knowledge or experience in literature, science, art, co-operative movement and social service.
2. One-third
Wrong: one-third is the share elected by local bodies, and another one-third by MLAs.
3. One-half
Wrong: one-half is not any share in the Council's composition.
4. All members
Wrong: most members are elected; only one-sixth are nominated.

points: Composition: 1/3 local bodies, 1/3 MLAs, 1/12 graduates, 1/12 teachers, 1/6 nominated.
POL-735-LAX-09.also: One-twelfth each are elected by graduates and by teachers.

POL-735-LAX-11.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Courts may issue a limited mandamus for prolonged, unexplained inaction.
True
The 2025 opinion allowed limited judicial review for prolonged, unexplained delay, directing the Governor to decide without commenting on merits.
2. Courts may replace the Governor's decision on the merits.
False
The Court said it cannot substitute its own decision for the Governor's on the merits of a Bill.
3. The Constitution has a general rule of deemed assent after a judicial deadline.
False
The Court held courts cannot fix timelines, and 'deemed assent' is not permitted by the Constitution.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 fail because each includes a false statement.

POL-735-LAX-12.lead: Option 1: the Constitution specifies no grounds and no impeachment process for removing a Governor.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Constitution specifies no grounds and provides no impeachment process
Correct: the Governor holds office during the President's pleasure (Article 156(1)).
2. Removal requires State Assembly impeachment
Wrong: there is no impeachment of a Governor; impeachment exists only for the President (Article 61).
3. Removal requires Supreme Court conviction
Wrong: no court conviction is needed; removal is by the President's order.
4. A five-year term is absolutely guaranteed
Wrong: the five-year term (Article 156(3)) is subject to the President's pleasure, so it is not guaranteed.

points: B.P. Singhal (2010): removal cannot be arbitrary, capricious or mala fide.
POL-735-LAX-12.also: B.P. Singhal (2010): removal cannot be arbitrary, capricious or mala fide.

POL-735-LAX-13.lead: Option 1: unlike the President, the Governor has no diplomatic, military or emergency powers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Diplomatic, military and national-emergency powers
Correct: these powers belong only to the President.
2. Executive and legislative powers
Wrong: the Governor has executive (Article 154) and legislative powers like the President.
3. Financial and judicial powers
Wrong: the Governor has financial (Money Bills, Contingency Fund) and judicial (Article 161) powers.
4. Ordinance and clemency powers
Wrong: the Governor has ordinance (Article 213) and clemency (Article 161) powers.

points: LX: the Governor's powers are similar to the President's except diplomatic, military and emergency powers.

POL-735-LAX-14.lead: Option 1: the Governor appoints the State Election Commissioner, who can be removed only like a High Court judge (Article 243K(2)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Governor; removal only in the manner and on grounds of a High Court judge
Correct: this protects the Commissioner's independence; service conditions cannot be varied to his disadvantage.
2. President; removal at pleasure
Wrong: the President has no role, and removal is not at pleasure.
3. Chief Minister; removal by simple Assembly vote
Wrong: the CM does not appoint him, and a simple Assembly vote cannot remove him.
4. Election Commission of India; removal by Governor alone
Wrong: the Election Commission of India conducts Union and State elections, not local ones; it does not appoint him.

points: The State Election Commission conducts panchayat and municipal elections.

POL-735-LAX-15.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct and 3 is wrong, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Address the Legislature at specified sessions.
True
Article 176 requires a special address at the first session after each general election and the first session of each year.
2. Send messages to the House or Houses.
True
Article 175(2) lets the Governor send messages to the House on a pending Bill or otherwise.
3. Vote as an ordinary member.
False
The Governor is not a member of the Legislature (Article 158(1)), so he cannot vote.

points: Option 1 leaves out statement 2.
Options 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.
POL-735-LAX-15.also: Special address is given at the first session after elections and each year's first session.

POL-735-LAX-16.lead: Option 1: a Governor's ordinance lapses six weeks after the Legislature reassembles (Article 213(2)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Six weeks
Correct: it ends earlier if the Assembly disapproves it or the Governor withdraws it.
2. Six months
Wrong: six months is the maximum gap between sessions, not the ordinance limit.
3. Thirty days
Wrong: thirty days is not the constitutional period.
4. One year
Wrong: one year is not the constitutional period.

points: If the Houses reassemble on different dates, six weeks count from the later date.
POL-735-LAX-16.also: Maximum life of an ordinance is six months plus six weeks.

POL-735-LAX-17.lead: Option 1: the Governor constitutes a State Finance Commission every five years (Articles 243I and 243Y).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Every five years
Correct: it reviews the finances of panchayats (243I) and municipalities (243Y).
2. Every year
Article 243-I requires the Governor to constitute a State Finance Commission every five years, not every year.
3. Every ten years
Wrong: it is not formed every ten years.
4. Only during President's Rule
Wrong: it is not linked to President's Rule.

points: The report goes to the Governor, who lays it before the Legislature.

POL-735-LAX-18.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2): the Governor has no court-martial power, but can act on a death sentence under a State law (by suspending, remitting or commuting it).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Article 161 does not extend to court-martial sentences.
True
Only the President, under Article 72, can deal with sentences given by a court martial (military court); the Governor has no such power.
2. Article 161 may apply to a death sentence for an offence within the State executive field.
True
The Governor cannot pardon a death sentence, but can suspend, remit or commute it when the offence is against a law within the State's executive power.

points: Option 1 and Option 2 each leave out one true statement.
Option 4 is wrong because both statements are true.
Key difference: only the President can fully pardon a death sentence; the Governor can only reduce or suspend it.

POL-735-LAX-19.lead: Option 1: once a Bill is reserved, the decision belongs to the President under Article 201.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. President
Correct: the President may give assent, withhold assent, or (for a non-Money Bill) ask the Governor to return it to the House for reconsideration.
2. Governor again
Wrong: after reserving the Bill, the Governor has no further say on assent; even a re-passed Bill goes back to the President.
3. Chief Minister alone
Wrong: the Chief Minister has no constitutional power to decide on a reserved Bill.
4. State High Court
Wrong: the High Court plays no part in the assent process for Bills.

points: Article 200 gives the Governor four choices: assent, withhold, return (non-Money Bill) or reserve for the President.
If the House passes a returned Bill again, it goes back to the President, who is still not bound to assent.
POL-735-LAX-19.also: If the House passes it again, it goes back to the President, who is not bound to assent.

POL-735-LAX-20.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2): Article 213 needs both conditions together before the Governor can issue an ordinance.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Legislature (or both Houses in a bicameral State) must not be in session.
True
Article 213(1) allows an ordinance only when the Assembly, or both Houses where there is a Council, are not in session; if even one House is sitting, the normal law-making route must be used.
2. Circumstances must require immediate action.
True
The Governor must be satisfied that circumstances exist which make immediate action necessary; this satisfaction is the second condition.

points: Options 1 and 2 each drop one of the two required conditions.
Option 4 is wrong because both conditions are stated in Article 213.
The power is not discretionary: the Governor acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers.

POL-735-LAX-21.lead: Option 1: Article 161 covers offences against laws on matters to which the State's executive power extends.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Matters to which the State's executive power extends
Correct: this is the exact limit in Article 161 — the Governor's clemency follows the State's executive field.
2. Every court-martial offence
Wrong: court-martial sentences are outside the Governor's power; only the President can deal with them (Article 72).
3. Only Union List offences
Wrong: offences against Union List laws fall under the President's power, not the Governor's.
4. Every offence throughout India
Wrong: the Governor's power is limited to the State's field; it does not cover every offence in India.

points: Memory hook: President = Union laws + court martial + death sentence pardon; Governor = State-field laws only.

POL-735-P330-01.lead: Option 2: under Article 155, the President appoints the Governor by warrant under the President's hand and seal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. By election in the State Legislature
Wrong: the Governor is not elected by the State Legislature or the people.
2. By the President through a warrant under the President's hand and seal
Correct: Article 155 says the President appoints the Governor by warrant under hand and seal; in practice on Union Cabinet advice.
3. By the Chief Justice of India
Wrong: the Chief Justice of India has no role in appointing a Governor.
4. By the Union Cabinet through a parliamentary resolution
Wrong: no parliamentary resolution is needed; the appointment is an executive act of the President.
