points: The Constituent Assembly chose appointment over direct election, following the Canadian model, to avoid a clash with the elected Chief Minister.
The Supreme Court has called the office an independent constitutional office, not an employee of the Union.

POL-735-P331-01.lead: Option 2 (1 and 2 only): Article 157 asks only for Indian citizenship and completed age of 35 years.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Citizen of India
True
Article 157 makes Indian citizenship a qualification for the Governor.
2. At least 35 years of age
True
Article 157 requires the person to have completed 35 years of age.
3. Resident of the State concerned
False
This is not a constitutional condition; by convention a Governor is usually an outsider to the State, as the Sarkaria Commission also preferred.

points: Option 1 misses statement 2.
Options 3 and 4 wrongly include statement 3, which is not in the Constitution.

POL-735-P331-02.lead: Option 2: the Governor holds office for five years, subject to the President's pleasure, and continues until the successor takes charge.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A fixed five-year term immune from removal
Wrong: the term is not immune; the President can remove the Governor at any time (Article 156(1)).
2. Five years, subject to the President's pleasure, with continuation until a successor assumes office
Correct: Article 156 gives a five-year term at the President's pleasure, and the Governor stays until a successor assumes office.
3. A term coterminous with the State Assembly
Wrong: the Governor's term is not linked to the State Assembly's term.
4. Six years, subject to impeachment
Wrong: there is no six-year term and no impeachment process for a Governor.

points: B.P. Singhal case (2010): the President's pleasure cannot be used arbitrarily or only because of a change of government at the Centre.

POL-735-P332-01.lead: Option 3: the Chief Justice of the State High Court administers the Governor's oath (Article 159).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. President of India
Wrong: the President does not swear in Governors; the President's own oath is given by the Chief Justice of India.
2. Chief Minister
Wrong: the Chief Minister takes oath from the Governor, not the other way round.
3. Chief Justice of the State High Court
Correct: Article 159 names the Chief Justice of the High Court; in his absence, the senior-most available judge of that court.
4. Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
Wrong: the Speaker administers oaths to no one in this process; MLAs take oath before the Governor or a person appointed by him.

points: Memory hook: President — CJI; Governor — High Court Chief Justice.

POL-735-P333-01.lead: Option 2: Article 154 vests the executive power of the State in the Governor.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 153
Wrong: Article 153 only says there shall be a Governor for each State.
2. Article 154
Correct: Article 154 vests the State's executive power in the Governor, exercised directly or through subordinate officers.
3. Article 161
Wrong: Article 161 is the Governor's pardoning power.
4. Article 168
Wrong: Article 168 deals with the composition of the State Legislature.

points: The Governor is the nominal (constitutional) head; the real executive is the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister.
Union counterpart: Article 53 for the President.

POL-735-P333-02.lead: Option 3: Article 213 contains the Governor's ordinance-making power.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 174
Wrong: Article 174 is about summoning, proroguing and dissolving the State Legislature.
2. Article 200
Wrong: Article 200 is about assent to State Bills.
3. Article 213
Correct: Article 213 lets the Governor issue ordinances when the Legislature is not in session.
4. Article 356
Wrong: Article 356 deals with President's Rule in a State.

points: An ordinance ceases six weeks after the Legislature reassembles, unless withdrawn or disapproved earlier.
Union counterpart: Article 123 for the President.

POL-735-P333-03.lead: Option 2 (1 and 2 only): the Governor appoints both, but SPSC members can be removed only by the President.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The Governor appoints the Advocate General.
True
Article 165 lets the Governor appoint the Advocate General, who holds office during the Governor's pleasure.
2. The Governor appoints State Public Service Commission members.
True
Article 316 gives the Governor power to appoint the Chairman and members of the SPSC.
3. The Governor may remove those members at personal pleasure.
False
Under Article 317 only the President can remove SPSC members, on the grounds and procedure in the Constitution; the Governor can only suspend during a Supreme Court inquiry.

points: Option 1 misses statement 2.
Options 3 and 4 wrongly include statement 3.

POL-735-P334-02.lead: Option 3: a Bill that would endanger the High Court's position must be reserved for the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Assent immediately
Wrong: immediate assent is barred for such a Bill.
2. Return it only to the Legislative Council
Wrong: returning a Bill is for reconsideration by the House(s), and it is not a route for this case.
3. Reserve it for the President
Correct: the second proviso to Article 200 makes reservation compulsory for a Bill that would so derogate from the powers of the High Court as to endanger its constitutional position.
4. Refer it to the Election Commission
Wrong: the Election Commission has no role in State Bills.

points: This is the one case where reservation is obligatory; in other cases reservation is the Governor's discretion.
The aim is to protect judicial independence from State law.

POL-735-P337-01.lead: Option 2: Article 161 contains the Governor's clemency power.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 72
Wrong: Article 72 is the President's pardoning power.
2. Article 161
Correct: Article 161 lets the Governor grant pardons, reprieves, respites, remissions, and suspend, remit or commute sentences for State-field offences.
3. Article 200
Wrong: Article 200 is about assent to State Bills.
4. Article 361
Wrong: Article 361 gives personal protection to the President and Governors.

points: Memory hook: 72 = President, 161 = Governor.

POL-735-P338-01.lead: Option 3 is the incorrect statement: Article 361 protects the Governor personally, not every government action.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It provides specified personal protection to a serving Governor
Correct statement (so not the answer): Article 361 gives personal immunity to a serving Governor.
2. A Governor is not answerable to a court for official acts while in office
Correct statement (so not the answer): Article 361(1) says the Governor is not answerable to any court for official acts.
3. It makes every official action completely immune from judicial review
Incorrect statement, so this is the answer: courts can still review the legality of the government's action itself; only the Governor personally is protected.
4. Its protection must be distinguished from review of the underlying government action
Correct statement (so not the answer): the personal immunity of the Governor is separate from judicial review of the underlying action.

points: Also, no criminal proceedings can be started or continued against a Governor during the term (Article 361(2)).
The question asks for the INCORRECT statement — read 'incorrect' carefully.

PRAC-POL-48C909E04FA6.lead: Option 1 (1 only): reserving a Bill is a constitutional discretion, and choosing a CM in a hung House is a situational discretion, so statement 2 is false.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The Governor can reserve a State Bill for the President at own discretion.
True
Reservation of a Bill under Article 200 is listed as a constitutional discretion of the Governor.
2. The Governor cannot appoint a Chief Minister at own discretion.
False
When no party has a clear majority, or the CM dies with no obvious successor, the Governor chooses the CM in his own discretion (situational discretion).

points: Option 2 and Option 3 wrongly treat statement 2 as true.
Option 4 is wrong because statement 1 is true.

LX-PQ-016.lead: Article 32 = SC writs, 300 = suits against government, 226 = HC writs, 13 = judicial review — option 3 (4 3 2 1).

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. SC writ jurisdiction
4. Article 32
Art 32: the right to move the SC for enforcing Fundamental Rights through writs; itself a Fundamental Right.
B. Suits against government
3. Article 300
Art 300: the Government of India and the States can sue and be sued, like the old East India Company.
C. HC writ jurisdiction
2. Article 226
Art 226: High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and 'any other purpose', so their writ power is wider.
D. Judicial review
1. Article 13
Art 13: laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void — the textual basis of judicial review.

points: Code 5 (Article 166, conduct of State business) fits none of these.
Option 1 (4 3 5 1) is wrong: it gives C→5 (Article 166).
Option 2 (3 4 2 5) is wrong: it gives A→3 (Article 300); B→4 (Article 32); D→5 (Article 166).
Option 4 (5 4 3 2) is wrong: it gives A→5 (Article 166); B→4 (Article 32); C→3 (Article 300); D→2 (Article 226).

LX-PQ-198.lead: Answer: option 4. Statement I is incorrect because formally the Governor, not the Chief Minister, dismisses a minister; Statement II is correct.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: Statement I
False
Ministers hold office during the pleasure of the Governor (Article 164(1)); the CM can only ask a minister to resign or advise the Governor to dismiss him.
Statement II
True
Article 163(1) provides a Council of Ministers with the Chief Minister at its head.

points: Does II explain I? Being the head of the Council gives the CM real influence, but it does not give him the legal power to dismiss; that formal power stays with the Governor.
Options 1 and 2 fail because they treat Statement I as correct.
Option 3 fails because it reverses the truth values.
Exam tip: 'in practice' the CM gets a minister removed; 'legally' the Governor removes him.

LX-UPSC-2018-Q04.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: True
An MLA's vote value is the State's population divided by the number of elected MLAs, divided by 1000, so it differs from State to State.

Why
rows: 1. Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 followed the Sanyal Committee
True
The H.N. Sanyal Committee (1961, report 1963) led to the 1971 Act.
2. Constitution empowers SC and HC to punish for contempt
True
Article 129 (Supreme Court) and Article 215 (High Courts) make them courts of record with power to punish contempt of themselves.
3. Constitution defines civil and criminal contempt
False
The definitions are in the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, not in the Constitution.
4. Parliament makes laws on contempt of court
True
Contempt of the Supreme Court is in the Union List and contempt of other courts in the Concurrent List.

points: Options 3 and 4 include the false statement 3; option 1 leaves out the true statement 4.

POL-741-AT-acting-cji.lead: Option 4: under Article 126 the President appoints another Supreme Court judge to act as CJI.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Senior-most judge takes over without appointment
There is no automatic takeover; Article 126 requires the President to appoint a judge to perform the duties.
President appoints a High Court judge directly
Article 126 allows only a Supreme Court judge; a High Court judge can sit only as an ad hoc judge under Article 127.
Full Court elects an acting CJI
The judges do not elect anyone; Article 126 gives the choice to the President.
President appoints another SC judge
Article 126 says the duties are performed by such other judge of the Court as the President may appoint.

points: Article 127 deals with ad hoc judges; Article 128 with retired judges sitting again.

POL-741-AT-adhoc-conditions.lead: All three conditions apply, so the answer is option 3 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Lack of quorum
True
Article 127 applies when there is a lack of quorum of permanent judges to hold or continue a session.
2. Previous consent of the President
True
The CJI may appoint only with the President's previous consent.
3. Consult the Chief Justice of the High Court
True
The CJI must consult the Chief Justice of the High Court concerned.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each leave out a required condition.
The judge chosen must be qualified for appointment as a Supreme Court judge.

POL-741-AT-adhoc-priority.lead: Option 1: under Article 127(2) Supreme Court attendance has priority over the judge's other duties.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: SC attendance has priority
Article 127(2) says it is the duty of the judge to attend in priority to the other duties of his office.
High Court assignment prevails
This reverses Article 127(2); the Supreme Court work comes first, not the High Court work.
Attendance is optional
Once validly requested, attending is the judge's duty under Article 127(2), not a choice.
Judge loses all judicial powers
The opposite is true: while attending he has all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of a Supreme Court judge.

points: During attendance the judge has all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of a Supreme Court judge.

POL-741-AT-administrative-charge.lead: Option 2: Article 146(3) charges the Supreme Court's administrative expenses on the Consolidated Fund of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Charged on every State's Consolidated Fund
The Supreme Court is a Union institution, so Article 146(3) charges its costs on the Union's fund, not on State funds.
Charged on the Consolidated Fund of India
Article 146(3) charges salaries, allowances and pensions of the Court's officers and staff on the Consolidated Fund of India.
Need annual Lok Sabha vote
Charged expenditure may be discussed but is not voted by Parliament, which protects the Court's independence.
Court fees belong to the CJI
Fees and other money taken by the Court form part of the Consolidated Fund of India; they are not anyone's personal property.

points: Judges' salaries are also charged on the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 125).

POL-741-AT-advisory-two-classes.lead: Option 4: under Article 143(1) the Court 'may' report; under Article 143(2) it 'shall' report.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Court must answer every reference
Wrong for clause (1): there the Court 'may' report, so it can decline, as it did in the Ayodhya reference.
Clause 1 private appeals; clause 2 criminal appeals
Article 143 is the advisory jurisdiction on references by the President; it has nothing to do with appeals.
Clause 1 gives binding decrees
An advisory opinion is not a decree and does not bind the President, and clause (2) does give an opinion.
Clause 1 'may'; clause 2 'shall'

Clause (1) covers any question of law or fact of public importance (Court may report); clause (2) covers disputes from pre-Constitution treaties excluded by the proviso to Article 131 (Court shall report).

points: The Ram Janmabhoomi reference (1993) was returned unanswered in 1994 (Ismail Faruqui case).

POL-741-AT-age-determination-law.lead: Option 4: Article 124(2A) lets Parliament by law fix the authority and manner for determining a judge's age.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Governor
The Governor is a State executive head and has no role regarding Supreme Court judges.
The CJI by personal direction
Article 124(2A) speaks of a law made by Parliament, so a personal administrative direction is not enough.
The State Legislature
Supreme Court matters are Union subjects; a State Legislature has no power over them.
Parliament
Article 124(2A) says the age is decided by such authority and in such manner as Parliament may by law provide.

points: Clause (2A) was added by the 15th Amendment, 1963.

POL-741-AT-aid-authorities.lead: Option 2: Article 144 says all civil and judicial authorities in India must act in aid of the Supreme Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only High Court judges
Too narrow: Article 144 binds every civil and judicial authority, not only High Court judges.
All civil and judicial authorities in India
Article 144 requires all civil and judicial authorities in the territory of India to act in aid of the Supreme Court.
Only Union ministries
Wrong: State authorities are equally bound; Article 144 says all authorities in India.
Only those named in an Article 143 reference
Article 144 is a general rule for all of the Court's work, not limited to advisory references.

points: It backs up Article 142, under which SC decrees are enforceable throughout India.

POL-741-AT-appointment-authority.lead: Option 1: the President appoints Supreme Court judges by warrant under his hand and seal (Article 124(2)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President of India
Article 124(2) says every judge is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal.
CJI alone
The CJI heads the collegium that recommends names, but the formal appointment is by the President.
Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Speaker presides over the Lok Sabha and has no role in appointing judges.
Union Law Minister alone
The Law Ministry processes the file, but the minister has no power to appoint.

points: In practice the collegium recommends names.
POL-741-AT-appointment-authority.also: The NJAC (99th Amendment) was struck down in 2015, restoring the collegium.

POL-741-AT-civil-appeal-certificate.lead: Both findings are required, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Substantial question of law of general importance
True
Article 133(1)(a) requires the High Court to certify that the case involves a substantial question of law of general importance.
2. HC thinks the question needs SC decision
True
Article 133(1)(b) also requires the High Court's opinion that the question needs to be decided by the Supreme Court.

points: Options 1 and 2 drop a condition; option 4 denies both.
The certificate is given under Article 134A.
POL-741-AT-civil-appeal-certificate.also: The valuation test (Rs 20,000) was removed by the 30th Amendment, 1972.

POL-741-AT-common-question-withdrawal.lead: Option 3: under Article 139A(1) the Supreme Court may withdraw such cases and dispose of them itself.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Automatically quash both
Article 139A does not allow quashing; the Court must decide the common questions of law.
Transfer only with every State's consent
No State consent is needed; the Court acts on its own motion or on application by the Attorney-General or a party.
Withdraw and dispose of them itself
Article 139A(1) lets the Court withdraw the cases and dispose of them itself, so the law is settled once for all.
Direct HCs to ignore and bar withdrawal
This is the opposite of the provision, which exists precisely to allow withdrawal.

points: The SC may act on its own motion or on application by the Attorney-General or a party.
It may also return the cases to the High Courts after deciding the questions of law.
POL-741-AT-common-question-withdrawal.also: Article 139A was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

POL-741-AT-constitutional-appeal.lead: Option 2: Article 132 can apply to a criminal case too, if the High Court gives a certificate under Article 134A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It is unavailable because the proceeding is criminal
Wrong: Article 132 covers civil, criminal or other proceedings, so the criminal nature of the case does not shut this route.
2. It may apply with the requisite High Court certificate under Article 134A
Correct: if the High Court certifies that the case involves a substantial question of law on interpreting the Constitution, an appeal lies to the Supreme Court under Article 132.
3. It requires every case to involve a death sentence
Wrong: a death sentence matters only for the criminal-appeal route of Article 134; Article 132 is about constitutional questions, whatever the sentence.
4. It requires the President to refer the appeal
Wrong: the President has no role in sending an appeal; the trigger is the High Court's certificate, not a presidential reference.

points: Concept: Article 132 = appeal in constitutional matters; the test is 'substantial question of law as to the interpretation of the Constitution'.
Article 133 = civil appeals, Article 134 = criminal appeals, Article 134A = how the High Court grants the certificate.
Memory hook: 132 asks 'Is the Constitution in question?', not 'Is it civil or criminal?'.

POL-741-AT-constitutional-location.lead: Option 3: Part V, Articles 124–147 deal with the Union judiciary (the Supreme Court).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Part VI, Articles 214–231
Wrong: Part VI, Articles 214–231 deal with the High Courts, which belong to the State judiciary.
2. Part XIV-A, Articles 323A–323B
Wrong: Part XIV-A, Articles 323A–323B deal with tribunals, added by the 42nd Amendment (1976).
3. Part V, Articles 124–147
Correct: Articles 124 to 147 in Part V (Chapter IV, 'The Union Judiciary') deal with the organisation, jurisdiction and powers of the Supreme Court.
4. Part III, Articles 12–35
Wrong: Part III, Articles 12–35 contain the Fundamental Rights, not the court structure.

points: Part V is 'The Union' (President, Parliament, Union judiciary), so the Supreme Court sits there.
Part VI is 'The States', so High Courts (Articles 214–231) sit there.

POL-741-AT-curative-boundary.lead: Option 1: the litigant is wrong; a curative petition is an exceptional remedy, not a second appeal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Incorrect: curative jurisdiction is exceptional and subject to stringent safeguards
Correct: after a review petition is dismissed, the Supreme Court may reconsider only on narrow grounds such as violation of natural justice, bias of the judge or gross miscarriage of justice.
2. Correct: every dismissed review must receive a full fresh appeal
Wrong: there is no right to a full fresh hearing on the same merits; that would defeat the finality of Supreme Court judgments.
3. Correct: a curative petition lies directly to the President
Wrong: a curative petition is filed in the Supreme Court itself; the President has no role in it.
4. Incorrect only because curative petitions are a High Court remedy
Wrong: the curative petition is a Supreme Court remedy created by the Supreme Court, not a High Court remedy.

points: The Supreme Court created the curative petition in Rupa Ashok Hurra v. Ashok Hurra (2002), using its inherent power to cure gross miscarriage of justice.
Order to remember: judgment → review petition (Article 137, within 30 days) → curative petition (rare, limited grounds).

POL-741-AT-enlargement-agreement.lead: Option 1: under Article 138(2), a Union–State special agreement works only if Parliament also provides for it by law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Parliament must by law provide for exercise of that jurisdiction
Correct: Article 138(2) needs two things — a special agreement between the Government of India and a State, and a law of Parliament providing for the exercise of that jurisdiction.
2. Only the Governor’s private approval is needed
Wrong: the Governor has no role in enlarging the Supreme Court's jurisdiction; there is no 'private approval' step.
3. No further condition exists
Wrong: the agreement alone is not enough; the Article itself demands a parliamentary law.
4. Every State Assembly must ratify it as a constitutional amendment
Wrong: no constitutional amendment or ratification by all State Assemblies is needed; an ordinary law of Parliament is sufficient.

points: Article 138(1): Parliament by law can enlarge jurisdiction on Union List matters.
Article 138(2): for other matters, a Centre–State special agreement plus a law of Parliament.
Parliament can enlarge, but cannot curtail, the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.

POL-741-AT-family-appeal-boundary.lead: Option 3 (1 only): only a contested final judgment is appealable; consent decrees and interlocutory orders are not.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Contested final judgment in a spousal-property dispute
True
Section 19(1) allows one appeal to the High Court, on facts and law, from a final judgment or order of a Family Court that is not interlocutory.
2. Valid consent decree
False
Section 19(2) says no appeal lies from a decree or order passed with the consent of the parties, because the parties themselves agreed to it.
3. Interlocutory order
False
Section 19(1) excludes interlocutory (in-between) orders, so that the case is not delayed by repeated appeals.

points: Option 1 (1 and 2) fails because it wrongly allows an appeal against a consent decree.
Option 2 (2 and 3) fails because it picks both non-appealable items and drops the only appealable one.
Option 4 (all three) fails for the same reasons as options 1 and 2.
Laxmikanth: the Act provides for only one right of appeal, which lies to the High Court.

POL-741-AT-family-establishment.lead: Option 3 (both): Family Courts are set up by the State Government after consulting the High Court, and are compulsory in cities above one million.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. State Government acts after consulting the High Court
True
The Act provides for establishment of Family Courts by State Governments in consultation with the High Courts.
2. Obligatory in a city or town above one million
True
The Act makes it obligatory for the State Government to set up a Family Court in every city or town with a population exceeding one million.

points: Options 1 and 2 fail because each drops one true statement; option 4 fails because both are true.
In other areas the State may set up Family Courts if it thinks necessary (optional, not compulsory).

POL-741-AT-family-representation.lead: Option 4: parties have no right to a lawyer as of right, but the Court may take a legal expert's help as amicus curiae.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Every party has an unconditional statutory right to a lawyer
Wrong: section 13 says the opposite — no party is entitled as of right to be represented by a legal practitioner.
2. Legal expertise can never assist the Court
Wrong: the Court may, in the interest of justice, seek the help of a legal expert as amicus curiae ('friend of the court').
3. Only advocates may file or conduct any proceeding
Wrong: parties normally appear and conduct their own case; advocates are not the only ones who can act.
4. There is no representation entitlement as of right; the Court may seek a legal expert as amicus curiae
Correct: this states section 13 exactly — no representation as of right, but amicus curiae help is allowed.

points: Reason: Family Courts aim at an informal, conciliatory atmosphere, not a lawyer-driven adversarial fight.
Amicus curiae = a lawyer who assists the court, not a lawyer for either party.

POL-741-AT-family-settlement.lead: Option 1: section 9 asks the Family Court to try, in the first instance, to help and persuade parties to settle, where the case allows.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Assist and persuade parties toward settlement, consistently with the case circumstances
Correct: the Court must endeavour to assist and persuade parties towards a settlement, consistent with the nature and circumstances of the case.
2. Compel a settlement regardless of consent or circumstances
Wrong: a settlement needs the parties' agreement; the Court cannot force one on them.
3. Refuse every contested case because only settlements are possible
Wrong: if settlement fails, the Family Court hears and decides the contested case on merits.
4. Transfer every matter immediately to a Lok Adalat
Wrong: the Act does not require sending every matter to a Lok Adalat; conciliation is done by the Family Court itself, with counsellors if needed.

points: Laxmikanth: it is obligatory for the Family Court to endeavour, in the first instance, to effect reconciliation or settlement; at that stage rigid procedure does not apply.
Key word: 'persuade', not 'compel'.

POL-741-AT-gram-appeal-routes.lead: Option 2: criminal appeals go to the Court of Session and civil appeals go to the District Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. District Court — Court of Session
Wrong: this reverses the two forums; the District Court hears civil appeals and the Court of Session hears criminal appeals.
2. Court of Session — District Court
Correct: under the Act, a criminal appeal lies to the Court of Session and a civil appeal to the District Court, each to be decided within six months.
3. High Court — Supreme Court
Wrong: appeals from a Gram Nyayalaya go first to the district-level courts, not directly to the High Court or Supreme Court.
4. Gram Sabha — District Collector
Wrong: the Gram Sabha and the District Collector are not courts and have no appellate power.

points: Logic: a Gram Nyayalaya is a court of a Judicial Magistrate first class, so its appeals go to the next court above it in each stream.
Memory hook: 'Session for Sin (crime), District for Dispute (civil)'.

POL-741-AT-gram-appointment.lead: Option 1: the State Government appoints the Nyayadhikari in consultation with the High Court, and he must be eligible to be a Judicial Magistrate first class.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. State Government in consultation with High Court — eligible as Judicial Magistrate first class
Correct: a Gram Nyayalaya is a court of a Judicial Magistrate of the first class, and its presiding officer is appointed by the State Government in consultation with the High Court.
2. Gram Sabha alone — elected sarpanch
Wrong: the Nyayadhikari is a judicial officer, not an elected sarpanch, and the Gram Sabha does not appoint him.
3. President alone — qualified Supreme Court judge
Wrong: the President does not appoint Nyayadhikaris, and Supreme Court qualifications are irrelevant to a grassroots court.
4. District Collector alone — any revenue officer
Wrong: the Collector does not appoint him, and a revenue officer is an executive officer, not a judicial officer.

points: Nyayadhikaris draw the same salary and powers as First Class Magistrates working under High Courts.
This keeps the court judicial and independent, even though it sits at panchayat level.

POL-741-AT-gram-commencement.lead: Option 3: the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 came into force on 2 October 2009.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 2 October 2008
Wrong: 2 October 2008 is a year too early; the Act was passed by Parliament in 2008 but not brought into force then.
2. 26 January 2009
Wrong: 26 January 2009 is Republic Day, not the commencement date of this Act.
3. 2 October 2009
Correct: the Act was brought into force on 2 October 2009, Gandhi Jayanti, linking 'justice at the doorstep' with Gandhi's idea of village self-rule.
4. 15 August 2010
Wrong: 15 August 2010 is Independence Day and has no link with this Act.

points: Purpose: access to justice for citizens at their doorstep, based on the Law Commission's 114th Report and Article 39A.
Gram Nyayalayas are set up for each intermediate-level panchayat or a group of them.

POL-741-AT-gram-mobile-scope.lead: Option 4 (both): a Gram Nyayalaya is a mobile court and has both civil and criminal jurisdiction.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Mobile court proceedings near the parties
True
The Act makes the Gram Nyayalaya a mobile court; from its seat at the intermediate panchayat headquarters it goes to villages to hear and dispose of cases.
2. Both civil and criminal jurisdiction
True
It exercises the powers of both criminal and civil courts, over the cases listed in the First and Second Schedules to the Act.

points: Options 1 and 2 fail because each drops one true statement; option 3 fails because both are true.
It follows summary procedure in criminal trials and is guided by natural justice, not bound by the Evidence Act.

POL-741-AT-inauguration.lead: Option 2: the Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 26 January 1950
Wrong: 26 January 1950 is when the Constitution came into force and the Court legally came into existence; the inauguration came two days later.
2. 28 January 1950
Correct: the Supreme Court was inaugurated on 28 January 1950, succeeding the Federal Court of India set up under the Government of India Act, 1935.
3. 15 August 1947
Wrong: 15 August 1947 is Independence Day; the Federal Court, not the Supreme Court, functioned then.
4. 26 November 1949
Wrong: 26 November 1949 is the date the Constitution was adopted, not when the Court began.

points: The Supreme Court also replaced the British Privy Council as the highest court of appeal.
Memory hook: Constitution starts 26 Jan; Court opens two days later, 28 Jan.

POL-741-AT-inquiry-committee.lead: Option 1: the inquiry committee has the CJI or a Supreme Court judge, a High Court Chief Justice, and a distinguished jurist.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A CJI/other Supreme Court judge, a High Court Chief Justice and a distinguished jurist
Correct: this is the three-member committee the Speaker or Chairman constitutes after admitting a removal motion.
2. The CJI and the two senior-most Supreme Court judges
Wrong: the committee is not a panel of the CJI and two senior Supreme Court judges; it mixes the Supreme Court, a High Court and a jurist.
3. The Speaker, Union Law Minister and Attorney-General
Wrong: the Speaker, Law Minister and Attorney-General are not members; the inquiry is kept judicial, away from political executives.
4. A High Court Chief Justice and two Members of Parliament
Wrong: Members of Parliament are not on the committee; MPs only vote on the motion after the committee reports.

points: If the committee finds misbehaviour or incapacity, the House takes up the motion; if not, the motion fails.
Mix to remember: one SC, one HC, one jurist.

POL-741-AT-inquiry-notice.lead: Option 3: the notice needs 100 Lok Sabha members or 50 Rajya Sabha members.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong: 50 and 25 are half the actual numbers.
Wrong: Rajya Sabha needs only 50 signatures, not 100.
Correct: under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968, a removal motion is signed by 100 members in the Lok Sabha or 50 members in the Rajya Sabha and given to the Speaker/Chairman.
Wrong: this reverses the numbers; the larger House (Lok Sabha) needs the larger number.

points: The Speaker/Chairman may admit or refuse the motion.
Final removal needs a special majority in each House and then the President's order; no Supreme Court judge has been removed so far.

POL-741-AT-integrated-hierarchy.lead: Option 3: in India one single hierarchy of courts enforces both Union and State laws.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Separate court hierarchies exclusively administer Union and State laws
Wrong: separate Union and State court systems is the American model (double system of courts), not India's.
2. Only the Supreme Court may apply Union laws
Wrong: High Courts and subordinate courts also apply Union laws every day.
3. The same judicial hierarchy administers both Union and State laws
Correct: the Supreme Court, then High Courts, then subordinate courts form one single system, taken from the Government of India Act, 1935, that enforces both Central and State laws.
4. Every subordinate judge is appointed directly by the Supreme Court
Wrong: subordinate judges are not appointed by the Supreme Court; district judges, for example, are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court.

points: India is federal but has a unified (integrated) judiciary, unlike the USA.
Keyword: 'integrated' = one ladder of courts for all laws.

POL-741-AT-no-minimum-age.lead: Option 1: Article 124(3) prescribes no minimum age for a Supreme Court judge.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. No minimum age is prescribed
Correct: Article 124(3) asks only for Indian citizenship plus one of three — 5 years as HC judge, 10 years as HC advocate, or distinguished jurist in the President's opinion; no age is mentioned.
2. Thirty-five years
Wrong: 35 years is the minimum age for the President (and Vice-President), not for judges.
3. Forty years
Wrong: no 40-year limit appears in Article 124(3).
4. Forty-five years
Wrong: no 45-year limit appears either; the only age fixed for judges is the retirement age of 65.

points: Laxmikanth: 'the Constitution has not prescribed a minimum age for appointment as a judge of the Supreme Court'.
Trap: students confuse minimum age (none) with retirement age (65).

POL-741-AT-oath-authority.lead: Option 4: the oath is made before the President or a person appointed by him, in the form in the Third Schedule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. CJI alone — Second Schedule
Wrong: the CJI does not administer it by law, and the Second Schedule deals with salaries and emoluments, not oaths.
2. Speaker or nominee — Fourth Schedule
Wrong: the Speaker administers no oath to judges, and the Fourth Schedule allots Rajya Sabha seats.
3. Prime Minister — Third Schedule
Wrong: the Prime Minister has no role in administering a judge's oath, though the Schedule named is correct.
4. President or presidential appointee — Third Schedule
Correct: Article 124(6) requires the oath or affirmation before the President or someone he appoints, in the form set out in the Third Schedule.

points: The Third Schedule holds forms of oaths for Ministers, MPs, judges, CAG and others.
The judge swears true faith to the Constitution, to uphold India's sovereignty and integrity, to act without fear or favour, and to uphold the Constitution and laws.

POL-741-AT-open-majority-dissent.lead: Option 4 (both): Article 145 requires judgments in open court and lets the majority decide while allowing dissent.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. No judgment except in open court
True
Article 145 requires every judgment to be delivered in open court, so justice is seen to be done publicly.
2. Majority decides; a non-concurring judge may dissent
True
Judgments are by majority, but a judge who does not agree may deliver a dissenting judgment or opinion.

points: Options 1 and 2 fail because each drops one true statement; option 3 fails because both are true.
A famous dissent: Justice H. R. Khanna in ADM Jabalpur (1976).

POL-741-AT-original-private-party.lead: Option 2: a private company is not one of the parties Article 131 covers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 131 necessarily applies whenever the Union is sued
Wrong: Article 131 does not apply just because the Union is a party; both sides must be units of the federation.
2. The private company does not satisfy Article 131’s specified-party requirement
Correct: Article 131 covers only disputes between the Centre and States, or between States; a suit by a private party against the Centre or a State cannot be entertained under it.
3. Every Union contract dispute is an Article 143 reference
Wrong: Article 143 is the President's advisory reference, not a route for contract disputes.
4. Article 131 becomes available only after the company first appeals from a High Court
Wrong: Article 131 is original jurisdiction (first hearing), so it never depends on an appeal from a High Court.

points: The dispute must also involve a legal right (law or fact), so political questions are excluded.
The company can sue in an ordinary civil court or file a writ where a right is affected.

POL-741-AT-parliament-conduct.lead: Option 3: Parliament may discuss a judge's conduct only on a motion for an address to the President praying for removal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Any question-hour question
Wrong: question hour is not an exception; questions about a judge's conduct in duties are barred.
2. Any ordinary budget debate
Wrong: a budget debate is not an exception either.
3. A motion for presenting an address to the President praying for removal
Correct: Article 121 bars discussion of a Supreme Court or High Court judge's conduct in duties, except on a motion for presenting an address praying for removal.
4. A State Minister’s request
Wrong: a minister's request cannot create an exception to a constitutional bar.

points: This protects judicial independence: judges are not criticised in the legislature for their decisions.
Article 211 bars State Legislatures from discussing such conduct, with no removal exception, since States cannot remove judges.

POL-741-AT-postretirement-practice.lead: Option 4: Article 124(7) bars a retired Supreme Court judge from pleading or acting in any court or before any authority in India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It is allowed whenever the tribunal is outside Delhi
Wrong: the bar covers the whole territory of India, not only Delhi.
2. It is allowed after a two-year waiting period
Wrong: there is no waiting period; the bar is permanent.
3. It is allowed if the CJI informally agrees
Wrong: the CJI cannot relax a constitutional bar, formally or informally.
4. Pleading or acting before an authority in India is barred
Correct: a tribunal is a court or authority in India, so the retired judge cannot plead there.

points: Purpose: a sitting judge should not favour anyone in the hope of future work after retirement.
Compare: a retired High Court judge may plead in the Supreme Court and other High Courts (Article 220).

POL-741-AT-removal-grounds.lead: Option 3: the facts show neither proved misbehaviour nor incapacity, so there is no ground for removal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Unpopularity alone is an additional constitutional ground
Wrong: Article 124(4) gives only two grounds; unpopularity is not one of them.
2. The Union Cabinet may dismiss the judge for loss of confidence
Wrong: judges do not hold office at the pleasure of the Cabinet; they can be removed only by the President after a special-majority address by Parliament.
3. The stated facts do not establish either constitutional removal ground
Correct: without proved misbehaviour or incapacity, Article 124(4) cannot be used.
4. A simple resolution of one House removes the judge automatically
Wrong: removal needs an address passed by both Houses, each by special majority, in the same session, followed by the President's order.

points: Security of tenure protects judges who give unpopular but lawful decisions.
No Supreme Court judge has been removed so far; the V. Ramaswami motion (1993) failed in the Lok Sabha.

POL-741-AT-retired-attendance.lead: Option 2: a retired judge can sit under Article 128 only with the President's previous consent and the person's own consent.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The person must serve even without consent
Wrong: the retired judge's consent is required, so he cannot be forced to serve.
2. Previous presidential consent and the person’s consent are required
Correct: the CJI may request a retired judge to sit, with the previous consent of the President and of that person.
3. The person automatically receives a fresh permanent appointment
Wrong: he is not deemed a regular judge of the Supreme Court; it is a temporary arrangement.
4. The person may sit only after election by both Houses
Wrong: Parliament does not elect judges at all.

points: While sitting, he gets allowances fixed by the President and has all the powers of a Supreme Court judge.
Contrast: Article 127 (ad hoc judge) uses a sitting HC judge; Article 128 uses a retired judge.

POL-741-AT-rules-approval.lead: Option 3: the Supreme Court makes its rules with the President's approval, subject to any law of Parliament.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Rules are made by each Governor for the Supreme Court
Wrong: Governors are State executives and have no role in Supreme Court rules.
2. Rules need no presidential approval and override parliamentary law
Wrong: presidential approval is needed, and the rules are subject to laws made by Parliament.
3. The Court makes rules with presidential approval, subject to parliamentary law
Correct: Article 145(1) lets the Court, with the President's approval, make rules on its practice and procedure, subject to parliamentary law.
4. Only the Lok Sabha Speaker may issue procedural rules
Wrong: the Speaker regulates Lok Sabha business, not the Supreme Court.

points: The rules cover matters such as who may practise, how appeals are heard, and bench sizes.
Hook: Court drafts, President approves, Parliament can override.

POL-741-AT-seat.lead: Option 4: the CJI may appoint another place as the Supreme Court's seat, with the President's approval.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Governor alone selects the place
Wrong: a Governor has no role in the Supreme Court's seat.
2. A State Assembly resolution is sufficient
Wrong: a State Assembly resolution has no constitutional effect on this.
3. The Union Cabinet alone relocates the Court
Wrong: the Cabinet cannot relocate the Court alone; the decision belongs to the CJI with the President's approval.
4. The CJI appoints the place with the President’s approval
Correct: Article 130 makes Delhi the seat but lets the CJI, with the President's approval, appoint other places.

points: The provision is only optional; no court can order the President or the CJI to choose another seat.

POL-741-AT-specialleave-character.lead: Option 4: Article 136 is a discretionary power and is not limited to final High Court judgments.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. An automatic appeal as of right in every case
Wrong: special leave is discretionary and cannot be claimed as a matter of right.
2. A power confined to final High Court judgments in civil suits
Wrong: it covers any judgment, final or interlocutory, in any matter — constitutional, civil, criminal, tax, labour and more.
3. An appeal available only after a presidential reference
Wrong: it needs no presidential reference; the Supreme Court acts on a petition by the aggrieved party.
4. A discretionary power that is not confined to final High Court judgments
Correct: it can be granted against any court or tribunal in India (except military courts/tribunals), whether or not the order is final.

points: The Court itself says this power should be used sparingly, only in special and extraordinary situations.
It is the widest appellate power of the Supreme Court.

POL-741-AT-staff-appointment.lead: Option 1: the CJI, or another judge or officer he directs, appoints Supreme Court staff.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The CJI, or another judge or officer directed by the CJI
Correct: Article 146(1) gives the CJI the power to appoint officers and servants, so the executive cannot interfere.
2. The Union Law Minister on the Attorney-General’s recommendation
Wrong: the Law Minister and the Attorney-General have no appointing role.
3. The President in every case, without any role for the CJI
Wrong: the President's role is limited to the proviso — he may require UPSC consultation for specified posts.
4. The UPSC alone for every staff post
Wrong: the UPSC is consulted only where the President's rule requires it; it does not appoint all staff.

points: Freedom to appoint its own staff is one of the safeguards of the Supreme Court's independence.

POL-741-AT-staff-financial-rules.lead: Option 3: rules on salaries, allowances, leave or pensions of Supreme Court staff need the President's approval.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Approval of the Governor
Wrong: a Governor has nothing to do with Supreme Court staff.
2. Approval of the Lok Sabha Speaker
Article 146(2) proviso requires the President's approval for staff rules on salaries, allowances, leave or pensions; the Lok Sabha Speaker has no role.
3. Approval of the President
Correct: the proviso to Article 146(2) requires the President's approval for rules about salaries, allowances, leave or pensions.
4. No approval because all staff rules are entirely exempt
Wrong: these money-related rules are not exempt; the proviso specifically covers them.

points: Reason: these rules involve public money, so the executive head approves them.
These staff expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.

POL-741-AT-tenure-resignation.lead: Option 2: a Supreme Court judge retires at 65 and resigns by writing to the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 62 years — Governor
Wrong: 62 is the High Court retirement age, and the Governor is not the addressee.
2. 65 years — President
Correct: Article 124(2) fixes 65 years, and the judge resigns by writing to the President, who appointed him.
3. 65 years — CJI
Wrong: the age is right, but resignation goes to the President, not the CJI.
4. 62 years — President
Wrong: the addressee is right, but 62 is the High Court age.

points: Memory hook: SC 65, HC 62 — both resign to the President.

POL-741-AT-union-list-enlargement.lead: Option 2: Article 138(1) lets Parliament by law enlarge the Supreme Court's jurisdiction on Union List matters.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A unilateral State executive order under Article 162
Wrong: Article 162 is about a State's executive power; a State cannot enlarge the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.
2. Parliamentary law under Article 138(1)
Correct: Parliament by law can confer further jurisdiction on any Union List matter under Article 138(1).
3. Only a presidential advisory reference under Article 143
Wrong: Article 143 is only for advisory opinions sought by the President.
4. Only an informal agreement of all High Courts
Wrong: High Courts have no power to enlarge the Supreme Court's jurisdiction.

points: For other matters, Article 138(2) needs a Centre–State special agreement plus a law of Parliament.

POL-741-CH-01.lead: Option 2: a President's request for opinion invokes advisory jurisdiction under Article 143.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Original jurisdiction under Article 131
Wrong: Article 131 is for disputes between the Centre and States, not for opinions.
2. Advisory jurisdiction under Article 143
Correct: under Article 143 the President may seek the Court's opinion on a question of law or fact of public importance.
3. Review jurisdiction under Article 137
Wrong: Article 137 is review of the Court's own judgments.
4. Writ jurisdiction under Article 32
Wrong: Article 32 is for enforcing Fundamental Rights through writs.

points: The opinion is advisory and does not bind the President.
On a question of public importance the Court may refuse; on a pre-Constitution treaty dispute it must give its opinion.

POL-741-CH-02.lead: Option 2: Article 145(3) needs at least five judges for a substantial question of constitutional interpretation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Three judges
Wrong: three judges are not enough under Article 145(3).
2. Five judges
Correct: such cases, and Article 143 references, are heard by at least five judges (a Constitution Bench).
3. Seven judges
Wrong: seven is a larger bench used by choice, not the minimum.
4. Nine judges
Wrong: nine is also a larger bench, not the minimum.

points: Other cases are heard by single judges and division benches.
Larger benches are formed when an earlier ruling must be reconsidered.

POL-741-HIST-adm-khanna-dissent.lead: Option 3: Justice H. R. Khanna was the sole dissenting judge in ADM Jabalpur (1976).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A. N. Ray
Wrong: A. N. Ray was the Chief Justice and led the majority.
2. M. H. Beg
Wrong: M. H. Beg was part of the majority.
3. H. R. Khanna
Correct: Khanna held that the right to life survives even when its enforcement is suspended during an Emergency.
4. Y. V. Chandrachud
Wrong: Y. V. Chandrachud joined the majority.

points: The majority held that habeas corpus petitions were not maintainable during the 1975 Emergency.
Khanna was later superseded for Chief Justice in 1977 and resigned.

POL-741-HIST-statutory-origin-constituti.lead: Option 3: the Supreme Court legally came into existence on 26 January 1950.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 28 January 1950
Wrong: 28 January 1950 is the ceremonial inauguration date.
2. 26 November 1949
Wrong: 26 November 1949 is when the Constitution was adopted; most provisions were not yet in force.
3. 26 January 1950
Correct: the Supreme Court was created by the Constitution, so it came into existence when the Constitution came into force on 26 January 1950.
4. 15 August 1947
Wrong: 15 August 1947 is Independence Day; the Federal Court functioned then.

points: Remember the difference: 26 Jan = legal existence, 28 Jan = inauguration.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. 1956 Act
11. 11 judges in total
The 1956 Act raised the SC from 8 (7 + CJI) to 11 (10 + CJI).
B. 1960 Amendment
14. 14 judges in total
The 1960 amendment raised it to 13 judges + CJI, a total of 14.
C. 1977 Amendment
18. 18 judges in total
The 1977 amendment raised it to 17 judges + CJI, a total of 18.

points: Original strength in 1950 was 8 (7 + CJI).
Option 1 (14–11–18) is wrong: it gives A→14 (14 judges in total); B→11 (11 judges in total).
Option 3 (11–18–14) is wrong: it gives B→18 (18 judges in total); C→14 (14 judges in total).
Option 4 (18–14–11) is wrong: it gives A→18 (18 judges in total); C→11 (11 judges in total).

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. 1986 Amendment
26. 26 judges in total
The 1986 amendment raised it to 25 judges + CJI, a total of 26.
B. 2008 Amendment
31. 31 judges in total
The 2008 amendment raised it to 30 judges + CJI, a total of 31.
C. 2019 Amendment
34. 34 judges in total
The 2019 amendment raised it to 33 judges + CJI, a total of 34.

points: Article 124(1) lets Parliament raise the number by ordinary law.
Option 1 (31–26–34) is wrong: it gives A→31 (31 judges in total); B→26 (26 judges in total).
Option 2 (26–34–31) is wrong: it gives B→34 (34 judges in total); C→31 (31 judges in total).
Option 3 (34–31–26) is wrong: it gives A→34 (34 judges in total); C→26 (26 judges in total).
POL-741-HIST-strength-1986-2008-2019.also: In 2026 an ordinance and then the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act raised the total to 38 (37 + CJI).

POL-741-HIST-supersession-pairs.lead: Option 2: in 1973 A. N. Ray superseded Shelat, Hegde and Grover; in 1977 M. H. Beg superseded H. R. Khanna.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 1973: A. N. Ray over H. R. Khanna; 1977: M. H. Beg over J. M. Shelat, K. S. Hegde and A. N. Grover.
Wrong: it swaps the superseded judges between the two years.
2. 1973: A. N. Ray over J. M. Shelat, K. S. Hegde and A. N. Grover; 1977: M. H. Beg over H. R. Khanna.
Correct: Ray, fourth in seniority, was made CJI in 1973 over three senior judges, and Beg was made CJI in 1977 over Khanna.
3. 1973: M. H. Beg over J. M. Shelat, K. S. Hegde and A. N. Grover; 1977: A. N. Ray over H. R. Khanna.
Wrong: it swaps the two Chief Justices between the years.
4. 1973: A. N. Ray over J. M. Shelat, K. S. Hegde and A. N. Grover; 1977: Y. V. Chandrachud over H. R. Khanna.
Wrong: 1977 is right except the name; Beg, not Chandrachud, was appointed in 1977.

points: Both broke the convention (1950–1973) of appointing the senior-most judge.
The Second Judges Case (1993) restored seniority for the CJI post.

POL-741-P286-01.lead: Option 1: Article 124(1) sets up the Supreme Court with a CJI and other judges.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 124(1)
Correct: Article 124(1) establishes the Court and fixes its composition, with Parliament able to raise the number by law.
2. Article 129
Wrong: Article 129 makes the Supreme Court a court of record.
3. Article 131
Wrong: Article 131 is original jurisdiction.
4. Article 145(3)
Wrong: Article 145(3) is the minimum five-judge bench.

points: Originally 8 judges (CJI + 7); now 34 (CJI + 33) after a 2019 Act.

POL-741-P290-01.lead: Option 4 (all three): any one of these, plus citizenship, qualifies a person.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Five years as a High Court judge
True
Article 124(3)(a) accepts five years as a judge of a High Court or High Courts in succession.
2. Ten years as a High Court advocate
True
Article 124(3)(b) accepts ten years as an advocate of a High Court or High Courts in succession.
3. Distinguished jurist in the President's opinion
True
Article 124(3)(c) accepts a distinguished jurist in the President's opinion.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 fail because each leaves out at least one valid route.
Citizenship is required in every case.

POL-741-P291-01.lead: Option 3: each House needs a special majority — majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Simple majority of members present and voting
Wrong: a simple majority is too low for removing a judge.
2. Two-thirds of total membership only
Wrong: the two-thirds requirement is of members present and voting, alongside a majority of total membership.
3. Majority of total membership plus at least two-thirds present and voting
Correct: both conditions must be met in each House in the same session.
4. Unanimous vote of both Houses
Article 124(4) needs a special majority (majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting), not a unanimous vote.

points: After the address, the President issues the removal order.

POL-741-P293-01.lead: Option 2: Article 131 gives the Supreme Court original jurisdiction in Centre–State disputes.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 32
Wrong: Article 32 is for enforcing Fundamental Rights.
2. Article 131
Correct: Article 131 covers disputes between the Centre and States or between States, and it is exclusive.
3. Article 136
Wrong: Article 136 is special leave to appeal.
4. Article 143
Wrong: Article 143 is for advisory opinions.

points: Exclusive means no other court can hear these disputes; original means first hearing, not appeal.
The first suit was West Bengal v. Union (1961).

POL-741-P294-01.lead: Option 3: special leave does not apply to tribunals under Armed Forces laws.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A High Court
Wrong: High Court judgments are the most common subject of special leave.
2. A civil court
Wrong: civil courts are covered as courts in India.
3. A tribunal constituted under a law relating to the Armed Forces
Correct: Article 136(2) excludes courts or tribunals under any law relating to the Armed Forces.
4. A consumer commission
Wrong: consumer commissions are tribunals covered by Article 136.

points: Reason: military discipline is kept separate from ordinary appeal routes.

POL-741-P295-01.lead: Option 1: Article 32 guarantees the right to move the Supreme Court for writs to enforce Fundamental Rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 32
Correct: Article 32 is itself a Fundamental Right, giving the Court writ power for enforcing Fundamental Rights.
2. Article 129
Wrong: Article 129 makes the Court a court of record.
3. Article 137
Wrong: Article 137 is review of judgments.
4. Article 226
Wrong: Article 226 gives writ power to High Courts, not the Supreme Court.

points: Ambedkar called Article 32 the 'heart and soul' of the Constitution.
High Court writs (Article 226) are wider in scope.

POL-741-P295-02.lead: Option 2: Article 129 declares the Supreme Court a court of record with power to punish contempt.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 124
Wrong: Article 124 deals with establishment and composition.
2. Article 129
Correct: Article 129 makes it a court of record and gives power to punish for its contempt.
3. Article 136
Article 136 gives the Supreme Court power to grant special leave to appeal; the court-of-record and contempt power is in Article 129.
4. Article 141
Wrong: Article 141 makes Supreme Court law binding on all courts.

points: Court of record: its records have evidentiary value and are precedents.
Article 215 gives the same status to High Courts.

POL-741-P296-01.lead: Option 2: Article 137 empowers the Supreme Court to review its own judgments.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 136
Wrong: Article 136 is special leave to appeal.
2. Article 137
Correct: Article 137 allows review, filed within thirty days, on grounds like error on the face of the record.
3. Article 142
Wrong: Article 142 enables complete justice orders.
4. Article 145
Wrong: Article 145 deals with rules and procedure.

points: After review, a curative petition is possible on narrow grounds.

POL-741-PROC-cji-recommendation-route.lead: Option 1: the Law Minister forwards the recommendation to the Prime Minister, who advises the President to appoint.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Outgoing CJI recommendation → Union Law Minister → Prime Minister advises → President appoints.
Correct: under the Memorandum of Procedure, the Law Minister puts the outgoing CJI's recommendation to the PM, who advises the President.
2. Outgoing CJI recommendation → Prime Minister → Union Law Minister advises → President appoints.
Wrong: it swaps the roles of the Law Minister and PM.
3. Outgoing CJI recommendation → Union Law Minister → President advises → Prime Minister appoints.
Wrong: the President appoints; the PM does not.
4. Outgoing CJI recommendation → President → Prime Minister advises → Union Law Minister appoints.
Wrong: the Law Minister never appoints a CJI.

points: Article 124(2) gives the President the power to appoint judges.
Since 1993, the senior-most judge is appointed CJI.

POL-741-REM-adhoc-eligibility-powers.lead: Option 2 (both): an ad hoc judge must be qualified for the Supreme Court and has full Supreme Court powers while attending.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Must be qualified for Supreme Court appointment
True
Article 127 requires the High Court judge chosen to be qualified for appointment as a Supreme Court judge.
2. Full jurisdiction, powers and privileges while attending
True
While attending, he enjoys all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of a Supreme Court judge.

points: Options 1 and 4 fail because each drops one true statement; option 3 fails because both are true.
The CJI appoints him only after consulting the High Court Chief Justice and with the President's previous consent.

POL-741-REM-advisory-five.lead: Article 145(3) requires at least five judges for Article 143 references.
points: The same five-judge minimum applies to cases involving a substantial question of constitutional interpretation.
Two, three or seven are not the constitutional minimum.

POL-741-REM-citizenship.lead: Option 4: the citizenship requirement remains; being a distinguished jurist does not waive it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The President’s jurist assessment alone dispenses with citizenship
Wrong: the President's opinion replaces only the experience requirement, not citizenship.
2. Residence in India automatically substitutes for citizenship under this clause
Wrong: residence is not the same as citizenship.
3. Taking the judicial oath later cures the absence of citizenship at appointment
Wrong: eligibility is tested at appointment, so a later oath cannot cure it.
4. The citizenship requirement remains; distinguished-jurist status does not waive it
Correct: Article 124(3) requires every appointee to be an Indian citizen.

points: The distinguished-jurist route is an alternative only to HC judge or advocate experience.

POL-741-REM-composition.lead: Option 2: Article 124(1) provides for a CJI and other judges, with Parliament empowered to increase the number by law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The CJI and seven other judges, with Parliament unable to enlarge that number
Wrong: CJI plus seven was the original strength, but Parliament has raised it several times.
2. The CJI and other judges, with Parliament empowered to prescribe a larger number by law
Correct: Parliament increased the strength by law in 1956, 1960, 1977, 1986, 2008 and 2019.
3. The CJI and other judges whose number may be enlarged by presidential executive order alone
Wrong: the number is changed by a law of Parliament, not by executive order.
4. The CJI and every serving High Court Chief Justice as ex officio members
Wrong: High Court Chief Justices are not ex officio Supreme Court members.

points: Current strength: CJI plus 33 (2019 Act).

POL-741-REM-judges-residuals.lead: Option 3 (both): both correctly describe the Second (1993) and Third (1998) Judges Cases.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Second Judges Case: CJI consults two senior-most judges
True
In 1993, the Court held that the CJI's advice binds the President, but the CJI must consult two of his senior-most colleagues.
2. Third Judges Case: non-compliant recommendations not binding
True
In 1998, the Court held that the CJI's recommendation without the consultation norms is not binding on the Government.

points: Options 1 and 2 fail because each drops one true statement; option 4 fails because both are true.
The Third Judges Case widened the collegium to the CJI plus four senior-most judges.

POL-741-REM-oath-faith.lead: Option 1: the judge swears true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and to uphold it and the laws.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the Constitution and the laws
Correct: these are part of the Third Schedule oath.
2. Give the elected government’s policy priority over the Constitution whenever the two conflict
Wrong: the oath places the Constitution above government policy.
3. Treat every parliamentary enactment as immune from constitutional scrutiny
Wrong: judges must test laws against the Constitution through judicial review.
4. Maintain the secrecy of every judicial decision even after it is delivered in open court
Wrong: judgments are delivered in open court; no such secrecy is sworn.

points: Oath items: true faith to the Constitution, uphold sovereignty and integrity, act without fear or favour, uphold the Constitution and the laws.

POL-741-REM-removal-order.lead: Option 2: once both Houses pass the address by special majority, the judge is removed only by an order of the President (Article 124(4)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A joint notification by the Lok Sabha Speaker and Rajya Sabha Chairman alone
Wrong: the Speaker and the Chairman only present the address to the President; they have no power to remove a judge.
2. An order of the President
Correct: Article 124(4) says a judge shall not be removed except by an order of the President passed after an address by each House.
3. A disciplinary order of the CJI without a presidential order
Wrong: the CJI has no disciplinary power to remove a fellow Supreme Court judge; removal is a constitutional process ending with the President.
4. A recommendation by the inquiry committee itself
Wrong: the three-member inquiry committee under the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 only reports whether the charges are proved; it cannot remove anyone.

points: Order of steps: notice signed by MPs, admission by Speaker/Chairman, inquiry committee report, special-majority address in both Houses, then President's order.
Memory hook: Parliament 'asks', the President 'acts'.

POL-741-REM-retired-sitting-status.lead: Option 3: under Article 128 a retired judge who sits on request has all the jurisdiction, powers and privileges of a Supreme Court judge, but is not otherwise deemed to be a judge of that Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only advisory functions may be performed; judicial powers remain with permanent judges
Wrong: the person does real judicial work, not just advisory work; Article 128 gives full jurisdiction and powers while sitting.
2. The request itself restores permanent Supreme Court membership for all purposes
Wrong: the request is only for a temporary sitting; it does not make the person a permanent member of the Court.
3. The person has a Supreme Court judge’s jurisdiction, powers and privileges while so acting, but is not otherwise deemed a judge of that Court
Correct: this is the exact position under Article 128: full powers while acting, but not a judge for other purposes.
4. Judicial powers may be exercised only if separately delegated by the Union Law Minister
Wrong: the Law Minister has no role; the powers come directly from Article 128 itself.

points: The CJI may make the request only with the previous consent of the President and of the retired judge.
Such a judge gets allowances fixed by the President.

POL-741-REM-state-discussion.lead: Option 3: Article 211 bars the State Legislature from discussing the conduct of any Supreme Court or High Court judge in discharge of duties, and it has no removal-motion exception.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The claim is correct because Article 211 reproduces the parliamentary exception
Wrong: Article 211 does not copy Article 121; Article 121 has an exception for a removal motion in Parliament, Article 211 has none.
2. The discussion becomes permissible whenever the Governor gives prior consent
Wrong: there is no Governor's consent route; the bar in Article 211 is absolute.
3. Article 211 prohibits the stated discussion and does not contain that identical removal-motion exception
Correct: only Parliament can remove judges, so only Parliament (Article 121) needs the exception; a State Legislature never discusses a judge's conduct.
4. Article 211 restricts discussion only of district judges, not Supreme Court or High Court judges
Wrong: Article 211 expressly covers judges of the Supreme Court and High Courts, not only district judges.

points: Article 121: no discussion in Parliament on a judge's conduct except on a removal motion.
Article 211: the same bar for State Legislatures, without the exception, because States have no role in removing judges.

POL-741-SUPP-aor-filing-and-appearance.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is Option 1 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Only an Advocate-on-Record may file an appearance or act for a party.
True
Under Order IV of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013, only an Advocate-on-Record (AoR) can file pleadings and act for a party in the Supreme Court.
2. A non-AoR advocate may appear and plead when instructed by the AoR or permitted by the Court.
True
Other advocates can argue a case in the Supreme Court, but only when instructed by an AoR or allowed by the Court.

points: Option 2 and Option 3 are wrong because each leaves out one true statement.
Option 4 is wrong because both statements are true.
Concept: 'acting/filing' is reserved for AoRs; 'pleading/arguing' is open to other advocates on instruction.

POL-741-SUPP-apex-replacement.lead: Option 3: the Supreme Court took over the roles of the Federal Court of India and the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Federal Court and every State High Court
Wrong: High Courts were not replaced; they continue as the top courts of the States under Article 214.
2. Calcutta High Court and the Election Commission
Wrong: the Calcutta High Court still exists, and the Election Commission is not a court at all.
3. Federal Court and Judicial Committee of the Privy Council
Correct: the Federal Court (set up in 1937 under the Government of India Act, 1935) and the Privy Council in London were the earlier apex courts; the Supreme Court replaced both on 28 January 1950.
4. Constituent Assembly and Public Service Commission
Wrong: the Constituent Assembly made the Constitution and the Public Service Commission recruits civil servants; neither was a court.

points: The Federal Court heard federal disputes; the Privy Council heard final appeals from India.
Memory hook: one Supreme Court in place of 'Federal + Privy'.

POL-741-SUPP-building-architect.lead: Option 1: the Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026 raised the strength from 34 to 38 (the CJI plus 37 other judges).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct: the 2026 law raised the number of other judges from 33 to 37, so the total including the CJI is 38.
Wrong: 36 would mean an increase of only two judges, which is not what the 2026 law did.
Wrong: 40 is not the figure fixed by the 2026 law.
Wrong: 42 is not the figure fixed by the 2026 law.

points: Article 124(1) lets Parliament change the number of judges by ordinary law, without a constitutional amendment.
Earlier step: the 2019 Act had made it 34 (CJI + 33).

POL-741-SUPP-cji-seniority-fitness.lead: Option 3: under the Memorandum of Procedure (MoP), the senior-most Supreme Court judge considered fit to hold the office is appointed CJI.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Every retiring High Court Chief Justice must be elected CJI
Wrong: High Court Chief Justices are not elected or automatically made CJI; the CJI comes from the Supreme Court itself.
2. Seniority is irrelevant in all circumstances
Wrong: seniority is the main rule; it was departed from only in rare cases (1973 and 1977), which drew strong criticism.
3. The senior-most Supreme Court judge considered fit is the conventional choice
Correct: the MoP follows the seniority convention, with the condition that the judge is considered fit.
4. The Constitution requires a nationwide judicial election
Wrong: the Constitution has no election for judges; Article 124(2) says the President appoints them.

points: The outgoing CJI recommends his successor and the Law Minister sends it to the Prime Minister and the President.
Memory hook: CJI = senior-most + fit.

POL-741-SUPP-contempt-classification.lead: Option 4: A is civil contempt, B is criminal contempt (Contempt of Courts Act, 1971, Sec 2).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A criminal; B civil
Swaps the two. Breaking a promise to the court is civil; prejudicing a trial is criminal.
Both automatically immune
No such immunity; the Act gives only limited defences like fair and accurate reporting.
Both only civil
B harms the administration of justice itself, so it is criminal, not civil.
A civil; B criminal
Civil contempt = wilful disobedience of an order or breach of an undertaking (Sec 2(b)); criminal contempt = scandalising, prejudicing proceedings or obstructing justice (Sec 2(c)).

points: Simple test: civil contempt hurts a party by disobeying the court; criminal contempt hurts the court and justice itself.
Example A: a person promises the court to vacate a house and does not. Example B: a paper prints matter that sways a pending trial.
Arts 129 and 215 make the SC and HCs courts of record with power to punish contempt.

POL-741-SUPP-court-record-evidence.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and statement 3 is false, so the answer is Option 3 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Its records are kept for perpetual memory and have evidentiary value that cannot be questioned.
True
This is the first feature of a court of record: its judgments are accepted as evidence and cannot be questioned when produced before any court.
2. It has the power to punish for contempt of itself.
True
Article 129 gives the Supreme Court power to punish for contempt of itself; this is the second feature of a court of record.
3. Under the Constitution, High Courts are not courts of record.
False
Article 215 expressly makes every High Court a court of record with the same power to punish for contempt.

points: Option 1 is wrong because it leaves out true statement 2.
Option 2 is wrong because it includes false statement 3 and leaves out statement 1.
Option 4 is wrong because statement 3 is false.

POL-741-SUPP-criminal-appeal-1970.lead: Option 1: Parliament used Article 134(2) to pass the 1970 Act, which gives an appeal as of right when a High Court reverses an acquittal and sentences the accused to life imprisonment or at least ten years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The 1970 Act also provides the specified life-or-at-least-ten-years statutory route
Correct: the Supreme Court (Enlargement of Criminal Appellate Jurisdiction) Act, 1970 covers exactly this ten-year case.
2. No statutory enlargement is constitutionally possible
Wrong: Article 134(2) itself allows Parliament to enlarge the Supreme Court's criminal appellate jurisdiction by law.
3. Only the President can commute this into an appeal
Wrong: the President's pardoning power (Article 72) can reduce a sentence but cannot create a right of appeal.
4. Every sentence of any length has an automatic appeal
Wrong: not every sentence gets an automatic appeal; other cases need a High Court certificate or special leave.

points: Article 134(1) gives appeal as of right only in certain death-sentence cases.
So the claim 'only death sentence gives appeal' ignores the 1970 statutory route.

POL-741-SUPP-fair-criticism-final-case.lead: Option 1: Section 5 of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1971 protects fair comment on the merits of a case that has been heard and finally decided.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Fair comment on the merits of a case heard and finally decided
Correct: once a case is decided, a fair, good-faith comment on the judgment is not contempt.
2. Wilful disobedience of a court order
Wrong: wilful disobedience of a court order is 'civil contempt' under the Act, so it is punishable, not protected.
3. Threatening a witness to obstruct a pending trial
Wrong: threatening a witness interferes with the course of justice, which is 'criminal contempt'.
4. Every publication about any pending case irrespective of its effects
Wrong: a publication about a pending case is protected only in limited situations (for example innocent publication), not in every case.

points: Concept: courts can be criticised fairly after a decision, but justice must not be obstructed.
Truth as a defence was added by a 2006 amendment.

POL-741-SUPP-family-gram-act-years.lead: Option 2: the Family Courts Act is of 1984 and the Gram Nyayalayas Act is of 2008.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Family Courts 1987—Gram Nyayalayas 2008
Wrong: 1987 is the year of the Legal Services Authorities Act, not the Family Courts Act.
2. Family Courts 1984—Gram Nyayalayas 2008
Correct: Family Courts Act, 1984 and Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008 are the right short-title years.
3. Family Courts 2008—Gram Nyayalayas 1984
The Family Courts Act is of 1984 and the Gram Nyayalayas Act of 2008, so this option reverses the two years.
4. Family Courts 1984—Gram Nyayalayas 1987
Wrong: Family Courts 1984 is right, but 1987 is not the Gram Nyayalayas year.

points: Family Courts deal with marriage and family disputes; Gram Nyayalayas are village-level courts.
Memory hook: Family '84, Legal Services '87, Gram Nyayalayas '08.

POL-741-SUPP-fathima-supreme-service.lead: Option 3: Justice M. Fathima Beevi was appointed the first woman judge of the Supreme Court in 1989.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Justice Leila Seth
Wrong: Justice Leila Seth was the first woman Chief Justice of a State High Court (Himachal Pradesh), not a Supreme Court judge.
2. Justice Ruma Pal
Wrong: Justice Ruma Pal became a Supreme Court judge later, in 2000.
3. Justice M. Fathima Beevi
Correct: Justice Fathima Beevi from Kerala was the first woman judge of the Supreme Court (1989).
