4. Justice Sujata V. Manohar
Wrong: Justice Sujata V. Manohar was the second woman Supreme Court judge (1994), not the first.

points: She later served as Governor of Tamil Nadu.
Memory hook: Fathima = First.

POL-741-SUPP-financial-emergency-directi.lead: Option 2: Article 360(4)(b) lets the President direct a cut in salaries and allowances of Supreme Court and High Court judges during a Financial Emergency.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The President may reduce High Court judges’ pay but Supreme Court judges are expressly excluded.
Wrong: Supreme Court judges are not excluded; Article 360 names both Supreme Court and High Court judges.
2. The President may direct reduction of the salaries and allowances of Supreme Court and High Court judges.
Correct: the President may reduce salaries of all Union employees and of Supreme Court and High Court judges.
3. A Governor may independently direct reduction of Supreme Court judges’ salaries.
Wrong: a Governor has no such power; directions under Article 360 come from the President (the Union).
4. Judges’ salaries and allowances are expressly exempt from every direction under the Financial Emergency provision.
Wrong: judges are expressly included in Article 360, so they are not exempt.

points: Normally judges' salaries cannot be reduced to their disadvantage after appointment; a Financial Emergency is the only exception.
No Financial Emergency has been declared in India so far.

POL-741-SUPP-first-two-chief-justices.lead: Option 2: Harilal J. Kania was the first CJI (1950-51) and M. Patanjali Sastri was the second (1951-54).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. M. Patanjali Sastri—Harilal Kania
Wrong: this option reverses the correct order.
2. Harilal Kania—M. Patanjali Sastri
Correct: Kania was the first and Patanjali Sastri the second Chief Justice of India.
3. S. R. Das—M. H. Kania
Wrong: S. R. Das came after Patanjali Sastri and Mehr Chand Mahajan, so he was not first or second.
4. Mehr Chand Mahajan—Y. V. Chandrachud
Wrong: Mehr Chand Mahajan was the third CJI and Y. V. Chandrachud was the 16th.

points: Kania died in office in 1951, so Patanjali Sastri took over.
POL-741-SUPP-first-two-chief-justices.also: Y. V. Chandrachud had the longest tenure as CJI (1978–85).

POL-741-SUPP-gram-natural-justice.lead: Option 4: a Gram Nyayalaya is not bound by the Indian Evidence Act, 1872; it is guided by natural justice, subject to rules made by the High Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It is strictly bound by the rules of evidence in the Indian Evidence Act, 1872
Wrong: the Act frees Gram Nyayalayas from the strict rules of evidence so that justice is quick and simple.
2. It decides cases only according to local custom, without any written procedure
Wrong: they are not custom-based courts; they follow the Act, natural justice and High Court rules.
3. It follows the procedure laid down by the District Collector
Wrong: the District Collector has no role in laying down court procedure.
4. It is not bound by the rules of evidence in the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 but is guided by the principles of natural justice, subject to rules made by the High Court
Correct: this is the procedure stated in the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008.

points: Natural justice means: hear both sides and the judge must not be biased.
Aim: cheap, fast justice at the doorstep of villagers.

POL-741-SUPP-judges-cases-principles.lead: Option 4 (2–3–1): First case - consultation is not concurrence; Second - primacy of the CJI-led judiciary; Third - CJI must consult four senior-most judges.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. First Judges Case (S.P. Gupta, 1981)
2. Consultation did not mean concurrence
The executive could differ from the CJI; 'consultation' under Art 124 was not binding.
B. Second Judges Case (SCAORA, 1993)
3. Primacy of judicial opinion symbolised by the CJI
Overruled the First case; 'consultation' means concurrence, and the collegium system was born.
C. Third Judges Case (Presidential Reference, 1998)
1. CJI must consult the four senior-most puisne judges
Opinion on Art 143 reference widened the collegium to CJI + 4 for SC appointments.

points: Option 1 (1–2–3) gives A-1 and C-3: it reverses the First and Third cases.
Option 2 (2–1–3) gives B-1 and C-3: the four-judge collegium came in 1998, not 1993.
Option 3 (3–2–1) gives A-3 and B-2: CJI primacy was the Second case, which overruled the First.

POL-741-SUPP-legislative-irregularity-il.lead: Option 4: Articles 122 and 212 protect only 'irregularity of procedure'; courts can still examine substantive illegality or unconstitutionality.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. All legislative acts are immune even if constitutionally illegal
Wrong: legislative acts that are unconstitutional or illegal can be checked by courts.
2. Courts may annul every proceeding for any minor procedural departure
Wrong: a minor procedural slip is exactly what Articles 122 and 212 protect from court inquiry.
3. Legislative privilege automatically overrides the entire Constitution
Wrong: privileges exist under the Constitution and cannot override it.
4. Mere procedural irregularity is different from substantive illegality or constitutional violation
Correct: Raja Ram Pal (2007) drew this line between mere irregularity and illegality.

points: Concept: the House controls its own procedure, but it is not above the Constitution.

POL-741-SUPP-notice-admission-discretion.lead: Option 1: the Speaker may admit or refuse the motion after consulting persons and considering material, as Section 3 of the Judges (Inquiry) Act, 1968 provides.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. No; the Speaker may admit or refuse it after the statutory consideration
Correct: signatures only make the notice valid; the Speaker still decides whether to admit it.
2. Yes; signatures themselves remove the judge
Wrong: signatures cannot remove a judge; only the President's order after a special-majority address can (Article 124(4)).
3. Yes; the Speaker has no admission decision
Wrong: the Act expressly gives the Speaker the power to admit or refuse.
4. No; only the Chief Election Commissioner may admit it
Wrong: the Chief Election Commissioner has nothing to do with removal of judges.

points: Needed signatures: 100 Lok Sabha members or 50 Rajya Sabha members.
If admitted, a three-member inquiry committee is formed.

POL-741-SUPP-oath-duties.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are part of the oath; statement 3 is not, so the answer is Option 4 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India.
True
The oath in the Third Schedule asks the judge to uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India.
2. Perform duties without fear or favour, affection or ill-will.
True
The oath requires the judge to perform duties without fear or favour, affection or ill-will.
3. Always support the governing political party.
False
No such words exist; party loyalty would destroy judicial independence.

points: Option 1 is wrong because it leaves out statement 2.
Option 2 and Option 3 are wrong because they include false statement 3.

POL-741-SUPP-ordinary-bench-two.lead: Option 3: under the Supreme Court Rules, 2013, a case is ordinarily heard by a Bench of not less than two judges.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. One judge
Wrong: single-judge hearing is only for some limited matters, not the ordinary rule.
2. Three judges
Wrong: three-judge benches are used when a matter is referred, but they are not the minimum.
3. Two judges
Correct: the ordinary minimum Bench (Division Bench) is two judges.
4. Five judges
Wrong: five judges is the minimum for a Constitution Bench under Article 145(3), needed for a substantial question of constitutional interpretation.

points: Article 145 lets the Supreme Court make rules for its own practice and procedure.

POL-741-SUPP-original-eight.lead: Option 2: the original strength was 8 — one Chief Justice and seven other judges.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong: 7 was only the number of other judges; the total including the CJI was 8.
Correct: Article 124(1) originally provided one CJI plus not more than seven other judges.
The original strength was 8 (CJI plus 7 judges); 11 came only after Parliament raised the number in 1956.
14 was reached only after the 1960 increase, so it is not the original strength of 8 envisaged in 1950.

POL-741-SUPP-original-eight.also: Supreme Court (Number of Judges) Amendment Act, 2026 raised the strength from 34 to 38 (CJI + 37).

POL-741-SUPP-preconstitution-federal-exc.lead: Option 4: Article 143(2) lets the President refer such excluded disputes to the Supreme Court, which must give its opinion.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 32 as a private writ appeal
Wrong: Article 32 is the writ route for enforcing Fundamental Rights, not a presidential reference.
2. Article 136 as an ordinary appeal as of right
Wrong: Article 136 is special leave to appeal, which is discretionary and never an appeal as of right.
3. Article 124 as a judicial appointment
Wrong: Article 124 creates the Court and deals with appointment and removal of judges.
4. Article 143(2) reference
Correct: Article 143(2) covers disputes arising from pre-Constitution treaties, agreements, sanads etc., which the Article 131 proviso excludes.

points: Under Article 143(1) the Court may refuse to give an opinion; under 143(2) it must give one.
In both cases the opinion is not binding on the President.
POL-741-SUPP-preconstitution-federal-exc.also: Under 143(1) the Court may refuse an opinion; under 143(2) it must give one.

POL-741-SUPP-retired-judge-allowances.lead: Option 2: under Article 128 the President decides the allowances of a retired judge sitting in the Supreme Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Governor of the former High Court State
Wrong: the Governor has no role in Supreme Court matters.
2. The President
Correct: Article 128 says such a judge is entitled to allowances as the President may by order determine.
3. The Lok Sabha Speaker
Under Article 128 the allowances of a retired judge asked to sit are determined by the President's order; the Speaker has no role.
4. The retired judge unilaterally
Wrong: the judge cannot fix his own allowances.

points: The CJI makes the request, with prior consent of the President and of the retired judge.
While sitting, the person has the Court's powers but is not otherwise deemed a judge.

POL-741-SUPP-review-thirty-days.lead: Option 3: a review petition must ordinarily be filed within 30 days of the judgment or order.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 15 days
Wrong: 15 days is not the limit in the Supreme Court Rules.
2. 60 days
Under the Supreme Court Rules a review petition must ordinarily be filed within 30 days of the judgment, so 60 days is wrong.
3. 30 days
Correct: Order XLVII of the Supreme Court Rules, 2013 fixes 30 days.
4. 90 days
Wrong: 90 days is the limit for some special leave petitions, not for review.

points: The power of review comes from Article 137.
After review is dismissed, the last remedy is a curative petition.
POL-741-SUPP-review-thirty-days.also: Special leave petitions have different limitation periods (e.g., 90 days in civil matters).

POL-741-SUPP-senior-advocate-designation.lead: Option 2: under Section 16(2) of the Advocates Act, 1961, the Supreme Court or a High Court designates Senior Advocates.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Bar Council of India
Wrong: the Bar Council of India regulates the profession but does not designate Senior Advocates.
2. The Supreme Court or a High Court
Correct: the Supreme Court or a High Court does it, with the advocate's consent, on the basis of ability, standing at the Bar or special knowledge.
3. The Union Ministry of Law and Justice
Wrong: the Law Ministry is the Government, and designation is kept away from it to protect independence.
4. The President on the advice of the Chief Justice of India
Wrong: the President has no role in this designation.

points: A Senior Advocate cannot file cases directly; he appears with an AoR or another advocate.

POL-741-SUPP-state-psc-reference.lead: Option 1: under Article 317(1), the President refers the case of misbehaviour of any PSC member, even a State PSC member, to the Supreme Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. President
Correct: removal for misbehaviour needs a Supreme Court inquiry on the President's reference, and then a President's order.
2. Governor acting alone
Wrong: the Governor appoints State PSC members but cannot make the reference; he can only suspend the member during the inquiry (Article 317(2)).
3. Chief Minister
Wrong: the Chief Minister has no constitutional role here.
4. State Assembly Speaker
Wrong: the Speaker has no role in removing PSC members.

points: This protects PSC members from State government pressure.
POL-741-SUPP-state-psc-reference.also: State PSC members are appointed by the Governor but removable only by the President.

PRAC-POL-D84E97734BE0.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is Option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Administrative expenses, salaries, allowances and pensions of the Court's staff are charged on the Consolidated Fund of India.
True
Article 146(3) charges these expenses on the Consolidated Fund, so Parliament discusses but does not vote on them; this protects independence.
2. Fees and other moneys taken by the Court form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.
True
Article 146(3) also says that fees or other moneys taken by the Court form part of the Consolidated Fund of India.

points: Option 1 and Option 2 are wrong because each leaves out one true statement.
Option 4 is wrong because both are true.

LX-PQ-142.lead: Option 4: Article 217(3) says the President decides the age of a High Court judge after consulting the Chief Justice of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Chief Justice of the concerned High Court
Wrong: the Chief Justice of the concerned High Court is consulted for appointments (Article 217(1)), but not on a dispute about a judge's age under Article 217(3).
2. The Governor of the concerned state
Wrong: the Governor is consulted in appointing High Court judges, but Article 217(3) does not give him any role in deciding age.
3. The Attorney-General of India
Wrong: the Attorney-General is the Centre's chief law officer and advises the government; he is not the person named in Article 217(3).
4. The Chief Justice of India
Correct: Article 217(3) requires the President to consult the Chief Justice of India, and the President's decision is final.

points: The judge's age matters for the retirement age of 62.

LX-PQ-190.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. It is laid down in Article 200.
True
Article 200 gives the Governor four options on a Bill passed by the State Legislature, one of which is reserving it for the President.
2. It is not a discretionary power.
False
Reserving a Bill for the President (outside the compulsory case) is in the Governor's discretion, so the statement is false.
3. It is compulsory if the bill endangers the High Court.
True
The second proviso to Article 200 makes reservation compulsory if the Bill would endanger the position of the High Court.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes 2.
Option 2 misses 1.
Option 4 wrongly includes 2.

POL-742-CH-01.lead: Option 4: Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for 'any other purpose'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 32 only
Wrong: Article 32 is a Supreme Court remedy only for enforcing Fundamental Rights, and it is not a High Court power.
2. Article 136
Wrong: Article 136 is the Supreme Court's special leave to appeal, not a writ power of the High Court.
3. Article 215
Wrong: Article 215 makes the High Court a court of record with contempt power; it does not give writ jurisdiction.
4. Article 226
Correct: Article 226 lets a High Court issue writs for Fundamental Rights and also 'for any other purpose', such as enforcing an ordinary legal right.

points: So High Court writ power is wider than the Supreme Court's.
POL-742-CH-01.also: Article 32 is itself a fundamental right; Article 226 is not.

POL-742-CH-02.lead: Option 4: Article 235 vests control over district and subordinate courts in the High Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 227
Wrong: Article 227 gives the High Court superintendence over all courts and tribunals in its territory, but the specific control over district courts is Article 235.
2. Article 231
Wrong: Article 231 lets Parliament set up a common High Court for two or more States.
3. Article 233
Wrong: Article 233 is about the Governor appointing district judges in consultation with the High Court.
4. Article 235
Correct: Article 235 vests control over district courts and subordinate courts, including postings, promotions and leave, in the High Court.

points: Article 235 supports judicial independence.

POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-01.lead: Option 2: Guntur (1954) → Hyderabad (1956) → common court (2014) → Amaravati (2019).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 1954 Andhra State court at Hyderabad → 1956 Andhra Pradesh court at Guntur → 2014 common court at Hyderabad → 2019 separate Andhra Pradesh court at Amaravati
Wrong: the 1954 Andhra State High Court sat at Guntur, and the 1956 Andhra Pradesh High Court sat at Hyderabad, so the places are swapped.
2. 1954 Andhra State court at Guntur → 1956 Andhra Pradesh court at Hyderabad → 2014 common court at Hyderabad → 2019 separate Andhra Pradesh court at Amaravati
Correct: Andhra State High Court at Guntur (1954); Andhra Pradesh High Court at Hyderabad (1956); common court at Hyderabad (2014); separate court at Amaravati (2019).
3. 1954 Andhra Pradesh court at Guntur → 1956 Andhra State court at Hyderabad → 2014 common court at Hyderabad → 2019 separate Andhra Pradesh court at Amaravati
Wrong: the places are right but the names are swapped; Andhra Pradesh did not exist in 1954, it was formed in 1956.
4. 1954 Andhra State court at Guntur → 1956 Andhra Pradesh court at Hyderabad → 2014 separate Andhra Pradesh court at Amaravati → 2019 common court at Hyderabad
Wrong: it reverses 2014 and 2019; the common court came first (2014) and Amaravati followed on 1 January 2019.

points: Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953.
POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-01.also: The 2014 common court was the High Court of Judicature at Hyderabad for Telangana and Andhra Pradesh.

POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-02.lead: Option 2: a High Court can issue a writ to an outside authority if the cause of action arises wholly or partly within its territory.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Supreme Court gives it prior permission
Wrong: the Constitution does not require Supreme Court permission for a High Court to issue writs.
2. The cause of action arises, wholly or in part, within its territorial jurisdiction
Correct: Article 226(2), added by the 15th Amendment (1963), lets a High Court issue writs to an authority outside its territory if the cause of action arises wholly or partly within it.
3. The petitioner is a permanent resident of that State
Wrong: the petitioner's residence is not the test; the test is where the cause of action arises.
4. The Governor of the State authorises it
Wrong: the Governor has no role in the High Court's writ jurisdiction.

points: Article 226(2) widened access to justice.

POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-03.lead: (2) The High Court — since the 19th Amendment (1966), election petitions about MPs and MLAs are tried first by the High Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Election Commission of India
The body that conducts elections (Art 324); it does not decide election petitions after the result.
The High Court
Hears election petitions about MPs and MLAs in its original jurisdiction; appeal lies to the Supreme Court.
The Supreme Court
Decides disputes about the election of the President and Vice-President directly (Art 71), and hears appeals in MP/MLA cases, but not the first trial.
A special Election Tribunal appointed by the President
Election Tribunals existed earlier, but the 19th Amendment Act, 1966 abolished them and gave the power to the High Courts.

points: "First instance" means the court where the case starts — for MP/MLA election petitions that is the High Court.
Memory hook: President/VP election → Supreme Court; MP/MLA election → High Court.

POL-742-HC-PRACTICE-04.lead: (3) The removal is invalid — the address of Parliament must be presented to the President in the same session.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The President can remove the judge because the required votes cure the timing defect.
False: the special majority and the same-session rule are separate conditions; meeting one does not cure the other.
The President can remove the judge if the State Legislature confirms the addresses.
False: the State Legislature has no role in removing a High Court judge; only Parliament acts.
The addresses do not meet the same-session requirement for a presidential removal order.
True: Art 124(4), applied to HC judges by Art 217(1)(b), requires presentation in the same session.
The President may waive the timing requirement on the Chief Justice of India's recommendation.
False: it is a constitutional requirement; neither the President nor the CJI can waive it.

points: Removal needs: proved misbehaviour or incapacity, a special majority in each House, and presentation to the President in the same session.
The procedure is regulated by the Judges Enquiry Act, 1968; no High Court judge has been impeached so far.

POL-742-P312-01.lead: (4) Article 231 — Parliament may by law establish a common High Court for two or more States.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 214
Says there shall be a High Court for each State.
Article 216
Says every High Court has a Chief Justice and other judges as the President decides.
Article 226
Article 226 gives High Courts power to issue writs; the common High Court for two or more States is under Article 231.
Article 231
Lets Parliament by law set up a common High Court for two or more States (and a Union territory).

points: The power was added by the 7th Amendment Act, 1956; Art 214 is the general rule (one HC per State) and Art 231 is the exception.
Example: the Punjab and Haryana High Court serves Punjab, Haryana and Chandigarh.

POL-742-P312-02.lead: (1) Article 214 — it lays down the basic rule that there shall be a High Court for each State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 214
Says there shall be a High Court for each State.
Article 216
Says every High Court has a Chief Justice and other judges as the President decides.
Article 219
Deals with the oath of High Court judges, taken before the Governor.
Article 227
Gives the High Court power of superintendence over courts and tribunals in its territory.

points: Art 214 is the rule; Art 231 (common High Court) is the exception to it.
Memory hook: Part VI on High Courts begins at Art 214 with 'one State, one High Court'.

POL-742-P313-01.lead: (2) The President — under Art 216 the President decides from time to time how many judges a High Court needs.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament

POL-742-P316-01.lead: (2) Article 215 — every High Court is a court of record with power to punish for its contempt.

True/False

3. FC 1 yr/Rs 10,000; SC 3 yrs/Rs 50,000
This swaps the two classes; the first class, being the higher court, must have the larger power.
4. FC 3 yrs/Rs 50,000; SC 1 yr/Rs 10,000
These are the BNSS limits for the two classes of Judicial Magistrates.

points: The imprisonment limits (3 years and 1 year) are the same as in the CrPC; only the fine limits rose.
Ladder of criminal courts: Judicial Magistrate II (1 yr) → Judicial Magistrate I (3 yrs) → Chief Judicial Magistrate (7 yrs) → Sessions Judge (any sentence; death needs High Court confirmation).
LX p523 also gives 7 years for the CJM and 3 years for the Judicial Magistrate.

POL-743-A18.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so the answer is option 2 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. First- and second-class magistrates can award community service
True
The BNSS (Section 23) newly adds community service as a sentence both classes of Judicial Magistrates may pass for minor offences.
2. First-class magistrate can award up to 7 years
False
A first-class Judicial Magistrate can award only up to 3 years; seven years is the limit of the Chief Judicial Magistrate (LX p523).

points: Option 1 (both) fails because statement 2 is false.
Option 3 (2 only) picks the false statement and drops the true one.
Option 4 (neither) fails because statement 1 is true.
Community service is unpaid work for the benefit of society, ordered instead of jail for petty offences.

POL-743-A19.lead: Option 1: BNSS Section 6 provides Courts of Session, Judicial Magistrates of the first class, Judicial Magistrates of the second class and Executive Magistrates.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Sessions, JM-I, JM-II, Executive Magistrates
Exactly the four classes listed in the BNSS, besides High Courts and courts under other laws.
2. Includes Metropolitan Magistrates
Metropolitan Magistrates existed under the CrPC, 1973 but the BNSS dropped them as a separate class; this option also leaves out second-class magistrates.
3. Assistant Sessions Courts, Small Causes Courts
The BNSS no longer has Assistant Sessions Judges or Metropolitan Magistrates, and a Small Causes Court is a civil court, not a criminal court.
4. City Civil, Small Causes, Family Courts
These are civil-side or special courts, not the criminal courts created by a criminal-procedure law.

points: The BNSS replaced the CrPC, 1973 from 1 July 2024.
Hook: 'two judicial classes + sessions + executive' = four classes; no metropolitan, no assistant sessions.

POL-743-A20.lead: Option 3: the BNSS repeals the CrPC but its savings clause lets trials, appeals, inquiries and investigations pending on 1 July 2024 continue under the CrPC, 1973.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. BNSS applies automatically
Wrong, because the savings clause specifically keeps pending matters under the old Code to avoid confusion midway.
2. Judge chooses the law
Procedure is fixed by law, not by the judge's choice; a judge has no such option.
3. CrPC continues via savings clause
Correct; a savings clause preserves the old law for matters already started.
4. Trial must restart
Nothing in the BNSS cancels pending trials; restarting would waste time and harm the accused and victims.

points: A 'repeal and savings' clause ends an old law for the future but saves what is already pending under it.
Memory hook: 'old case, old Code; new case, new Sanhita'.

POL-743-A21.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is option 4 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. In-service officers eligible with 7 years' combined advocate/judicial experience
True
The Constitution Bench allowed in-service judicial officers to compete for direct recruitment if their practice as advocate plus service as judicial officer adds up to seven years.
2. Minimum age 35 years
True
The Court fixed a minimum age of 35 years on the date of application for this direct-recruitment route.
3. Entitled to appointment without selection
False
Meeting the eligibility thresholds only allows a person to apply; he must still pass the selection process conducted under Article 233.

points: Option 1 and option 2 wrongly include statement 3.
Option 3 (all three) fails for the same reason.
Concept: eligibility ≠ entitlement. Art 233(2) earlier read as letting only practising advocates use the 7-year route; Rejanish opened it to serving judges.

POL-743-A22.lead: Option 2: the Court made the ruling prospective — it applies from the date of judgment and does not disturb selections already completed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Retrospective, cancelling earlier appointments
Prospective overruling was chosen exactly to avoid unsettling judges already appointed.
2. Prospective from judgment date
This is what the Constitution Bench directed.
3. Only to past selections
This is the reverse of prospective application; a new rule cannot apply only to the past.
4. Only after Parliament amends Art 233
The Court interpreted Article 233 itself, so no amendment was needed for the ruling to take effect.

points: 'Prospective' means 'from now on'; 'retrospective' means 'reaching back into the past'.
Courts use prospective effect when undoing past actions would cause chaos.

POL-743-A23.lead: Option 1: Article 233(1) itself says the appointment, posting and promotion of district judges are made by the Governor in consultation with the High Court, so the proposal is wrong.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Clause covers appointment, posting and promotion
Correct reading of the text of Article 233(1) (LX p522).
2. Only State PSC consulted
The State PSC plays no part for district judges; it is consulted under Article 234 only for other judicial posts.
3. Mentions appointment alone
False; the clause expressly adds posting and promotion.
4. Governor can drop it by circular
A constitutional requirement cannot be removed by an executive circular; only a constitutional amendment could change it.

points: Consultation with the High Court protects judicial independence at every stage of a district judge's career.

POL-743-A24.lead: Statement 1 is true and 2 is false, so the answer is option 3 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Protects specified pre-Twentieth-Amendment appointments and acts
True

Article 233A, inserted by the 20th Amendment (1966), validates district-judge appointments made before that amendment and the judgments and orders passed by those judges, even if Arts 233/235 were not followed.
2. Blanket validation of future unlawful appointments
False
Article 233A only looks backward; any future appointment must follow Article 233 fully.

points: Option 1 (both) fails because statement 2 is false.
Option 2 picks only the false statement; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
Background: in Chandra Mohan v. State of UP (1966) the Court struck down irregular appointments, and the amendment saved them (LX p900 lists the case).

POL-743-A25.lead: All three are named in Article 235, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Posting
True
Article 235 expressly names posting of judicial officers below district judge as under High Court control (LX p522).
2. Promotion
True
Promotion is also expressly named in Article 235.
3. Grant of leave
True
Grant of leave is the third matter expressly named in Article 235.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out one matter that the Article expressly lists.
Hook: 'P-P-L' — Posting, Promotion, Leave — all with the High Court.

POL-743-A26.lead: Option 1: Article 237 lets the Governor, by public notification, apply the chapter to chosen classes of magistrates from a date he fixes, with exceptions and modifications.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Date and exceptions contemplated; not automatic
Article 237 lets the Governor apply the chapter to magistrates from a date he fixes, with exceptions and modifications, so it need not be uniform.
2. Immediate, to all magistrates, no exception
False; the Article lets the Governor choose classes, a date and exceptions.
3. Only Parliament fixes the date
False; the Governor fixes the date in his notification.
4. Creates an All India Judicial Service
False; an AIJS can only be created under Article 312 by Parliament, after a Rajya Sabha resolution.

points: Purpose: to bring magistrates under the same High Court control as civil judges, separating the judiciary from the executive (Article 50).
LX p522: 'The Governor may direct that the above provisions... apply to any class or classes of magistrates'.

POL-743-A27.lead: Option 2: a Court of Small Causes decides small-value civil cases summarily; its decision is final, but the High Court can revise it (LX p523).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Tries offences punishable with death
Death-penalty cases are tried by the Sessions Judge; a Small Causes Court is a civil court.
2. Small civil cases, summary, final subject to HC revision
A Court of Small Causes decides small-value civil cases by summary procedure; its decision is final, subject to High Court revision.
3. Hears appeals from district judge
Appeals from the district judge go to the High Court; a Small Causes Court is lower, not higher.
4. Tribunal under Art 323B
It is a regular civil court set up by State law, not a tribunal under Article 323B.

points: 'Summary' means quick, simplified procedure; 'revision' means the High Court can check whether the law was applied correctly.

POL-743-CH-01.lead: Option 3: Article 50 directs the State to separate the judiciary from the executive in the public services of the State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 39A
Equal justice and free legal aid (added by 42nd Amendment, 1976).
Article 44
Uniform Civil Code for citizens throughout India.
Article 50
Separation of the judiciary from the executive.
Article 51
Promotion of international peace and security.

points: The CrPC, 1973 carried out Article 50 by separating judicial magistrates from executive magistrates.
Hook: '50 = fifty-fifty split' between judiciary and executive.

POL-743-CH-02.lead: Option 3: Article 235 vests control over district courts and subordinate courts in the High Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 233
Appointment, posting and promotion of district judges by the Governor.
Article 234
Recruitment of persons other than district judges, after consulting the State PSC and High Court.
Article 235
High Court control over subordinate courts, including posting, promotion and leave below district judge.
Article 237
Governor may extend these provisions to classes of magistrates.

points: Hook for 233-237: Appoint DJ, other judges, Control, Definitions (236), magistrates (237).
LX p522.

POL-743-CH-03.lead: Option 2: Article 236(a) includes the sessions judge (and additional and assistant sessions judges) in 'district judge'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Attorney General
The Union's highest law officer under Article 76; a lawyer, not a judge.
Sessions judge
The district judge sitting on the criminal side; listed in Article 236(a).
Comptroller and Auditor General
Auditor of public accounts under Article 148; not a judicial office.
Tribunal chairperson
Head of a statutory tribunal; tribunals are outside the district judiciary.

points: Article 236 list: city civil court judge, additional/joint/assistant district judge, chief judge of small cause court, chief presidency magistrate, additional chief presidency magistrate, sessions, additional and assistant sessions judge (LX p522).
Same person: called district judge in civil cases and sessions judge in criminal cases (LX p523).

POL-743-CH-04.lead: Option 2: Article 236(b) defines 'judicial service' as a service of persons intended to fill the post of district judge and civil judicial posts below it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only High Court posts
High Court judges are constitutional office-holders appointed under Article 217, not members of a 'service'.
District judge and lower civil judicial posts
Exact definition in Article 236(b) (LX p522).
All civil-service posts
General administrative posts such as IAS or State services are not judicial service.
All tribunals and commissions
Tribunals are created under Part XIV-A or statutes and are outside this definition.

points: The word 'exclusively' means only judicial posts — no administrative posts are mixed in.

POL-743-CH-05.lead: Option 3: under Article 237 the Governor extends these provisions to specified classes of magistrates by public notification.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President
The President has no role here; subordinate courts are a State matter.
Parliament
Article 237 does not require any law of Parliament.
Governor
Named in Article 237 as the authority issuing the notification (LX p522).
High Court alone
The High Court controls subordinate courts under Article 235 but does not issue the Article 237 notification.

points: Throughout Articles 233-237 the Governor is the formal authority and the High Court is the controlling or consulted body.

POL-743-CH-06.lead: Option 2: the 20th Amendment Act, 1966 inserted Article 233A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 7th Amendment, 1956
Reorganised States on linguistic lines and abolished Part A/B/C/D classification.
20th Amendment, 1966
Inserted Article 233A to validate district-judge appointments struck down in Chandra Mohan v. State of UP (1966).
42nd Amendment, 1976
Added tribunals (Part XIV-A) and the All India Judicial Service in Article 312, not Article 233A.
44th Amendment, 1978
Removed the right to property from Fundamental Rights and changed emergency safeguards.

points: Hook: 'Twenty saved the judges' — case and amendment both in 1966 (LX p900 lists Chandra Mohan, 1966).

POL-743-P323-01.lead: Option 2: under Article 233 the Governor appoints district judges in consultation with the High Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President
Appoints Supreme Court and High Court judges (Arts 124, 217), not district judges.
Governor
Named in Article 233 as the appointing authority (LX p522).
Chief Minister
The Constitution gives the Chief Minister no role in Article 233.
State Public Service Commission
Consulted under Article 234 for judicial posts below district judge, not for district judges.

points: Direct recruit: advocate or pleader of at least 7 years, not already in government service, recommended by the High Court (LX p522).

POL-743-P323-02.lead: Both bodies are consulted, so the answer is option 3 (both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. State Public Service Commission
True
Article 234 requires the Governor to consult the State PSC before making rules for recruiting judicial officers other than district judges (LX p522).
2. High Court
True
Article 234 also requires consultation with the High Court exercising jurisdiction in the State.

points: Options 1 and 2 each leave out one body; option 4 denies both.
Contrast: for district judges (Art 233) only the High Court is consulted; for lower judges (Art 234) both PSC and High Court.

POL-743-P324-01.lead: Option 2: Article 312(3) says an All India Judicial Service shall not include any post inferior to that of a district judge.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: High Court judge
HC judges are constitutional office-holders, not service posts, so this is not the floor.
District judge
The lowest post an AIJS may include; anything below it is barred.
Civil judge senior division
A post below district judge, so it cannot be included — but it is not the level named in Art 312(3).
Judicial magistrate
Also below district judge; excluded, but not the reference level.

points: The 42nd Amendment (1976) added the AIJS to Article 312.
Creating an AIJS needs a Rajya Sabha resolution (two-thirds present and voting) followed by a law of Parliament; none has been created so far.

POL-743-P324-02.lead: Option 2: the structure, jurisdiction and names of subordinate courts are laid down by the States, so they differ slightly from State to State (LX p523).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Municipal bodies
Local bodies have no power to create or name courts.
State laws
States decide their subordinate court structure, so names and arrangements vary.
Parliament annually
Parliament does not choose court arrangements every year.
Supreme Court uniformly
The Supreme Court decides cases; it does not prescribe a single court structure for all States.

points: Example: some metropolitan cities have city civil courts, and some States have small causes courts (LX p523).

POL-743-SJ-PRACTICE-01.lead: Option 2: X was tried by an Additional Sessions Judge, so his appeal goes to the High Court; Y was tried by a Chief Judicial Magistrate with a sentence under 7 years, so his appeal goes to the Court of Session.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. X — Session; Y — HC
Reverses the rule: a Sessions-level trial cannot be appealed to a Sessions Court.
2. X — HC; Y — Session
Correct under BNSS Section 415 (old CrPC Section 374).
3. Both to Session (≤7 years)
The 7-year test applies only to trials by Magistrates; any trial by a Sessions or Additional Sessions Judge goes to the High Court, whatever the sentence.
4. Both to HC (confirmation)
Confirmation by the High Court is required only for death sentences, not for five-year terms (LX p523).

points: Rule: appeal goes one step up the ladder — Magistrate → Sessions Court → High Court.
A Magistrate's conviction goes directly to the High Court only if the sentence exceeds seven years.

LX-PQ-075.lead: Option 4: CAT exercises original jurisdiction over recruitment and all service matters of the public servants it covers (LX p525).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Recruitment matters
Covered, but only one part of its jurisdiction.
Promotion matters
Covered as a service matter, but incomplete as an answer.
Disciplinary matters
Covered as a service matter, but incomplete as an answer.
Recruitment and all service matters
Complete description from Article 323A and the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985.

points: 'Service matters' means all conditions of service — pay, promotion, seniority, discipline, pension and so on.
When one option includes all the others, it is usually the complete answer.

LX-UPSC-2013-Q07.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Free, competent legal services to weaker sections on equal opportunity
True
This is the stated aim of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, under which NALSA was constituted (LX p522-ch38).
2. Issues guidelines to State Legal Services Authorities
True
NALSA lays down policies and principles, and State Authorities give effect to its directions.

points: Options 1 and 2 each drop a true statement; option 4 rejects both.
The Act was passed in 1987 but came into force on 9 November 1995 (LX).
Constitutional basis: Article 39A (free legal aid).

LX-UPSC-2018-Q14.lead: Only statement 2 is true, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. NGT by Act, CPCB by executive order
False
Both are statutory: NGT under the NGT Act, 2010 and CPCB under the Water (Prevention and Control of Pollution) Act, 1974.
2. NGT gives environmental justice; CPCB improves water and air quality
True
This matches their mandates: NGT decides environmental cases quickly, while CPCB works to keep streams and wells clean and improve air quality.

points: Option 1 and option 3 include the false statement 1; option 4 rejects the true statement 2.
Statutory = created by an Act; executive = created by a government order.

LX-UPSC-2019-Q15.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are true, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. PNGRB was the first regulator
False
Regulators such as SEBI (1992) and TRAI (1997) existed long before PNGRB (2006).
2. Ensures competitive gas markets
True
Promoting competitive markets for gas is one of PNGRB's tasks under the PNGRB Act, 2006.
3. Appeals go to the Appellate Tribunal for Electricity
True
The PNGRB Act makes APTEL the appellate tribunal for PNGRB decisions.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 include the false statement 1.

POL-744-A01.lead: Option 1: tribunals give specialised, quasi-judicial decisions within a limited, defined subject area.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Specialised quasi-judicial adjudication
Tribunals use expert members and simple procedure for technical and service disputes.
2. Unlimited jurisdiction
Tribunals have only the jurisdiction their Act gives; ordinary courts handle the rest.
3. Only non-binding advice
Tribunal decisions bind the parties; giving advice only is the role of advisory bodies like the Law Commission.
4. Private arbitration panels
Tribunals are set up by law, not chosen by contracting parties.

points: 'Quasi-judicial' means acting like a court — hearing both sides and deciding — without being a regular court.

POL-744-A02.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Civilian defence posts can be covered
True
CAT covers civilian employees of the defence services (LX p525).
2. Uniformed forces covered
False
Members of the defence forces are expressly excluded; their disputes go to the Armed Forces Tribunal.
3. SC staff and Parliament secretariat excluded
True
Section 2 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 excludes them (LX p525).

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 include the false statement 2.

POL-744-A03.lead: Option 4: denial of promotion is a service dispute (CAT); a theft trial is a criminal prosecution (criminal court).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Promotion — criminal; theft — service
Denial of promotion is a service matter and theft is a crime, so this option swaps the two categories.
2. Both CAT matters
Being a government employee does not make a crime a service matter; CAT has no criminal jurisdiction.
3. Neither concerns a forum
Both go to a forum — service dispute to the tribunal, theft to a criminal court.
4. Promotion — service; theft — criminal
Promotion denial concerns conditions of service (a CAT-type dispute), while theft is a crime tried in criminal courts, so this pairing is correct.

points: Service disputes concern conditions of employment; criminal prosecution concerns an offence against the law.

POL-744-A04.lead: Option 2: the applicant may appear in person or through a legal practitioner of his choice (LX p526).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only govt presenting officer
A presenting officer appears for the government, not for the applicant.
2. In person or lawyer of choice
Allowed under Section 23 of the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985.
3. Only a senior advocate
No such requirement; any lawyer or the applicant himself may appear.
4. No lawyer allowed
False: the CAT procedure lets an applicant appear in person or take the help of a legal practitioner of his choice.

points: CAT keeps procedure cheap and simple: a nominal fee of Rs 50 and freedom from the CPC (LX p526).

POL-744-A05.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true, so the answer is option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Centre establishes SAT on State request
True
The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 lets the Central government set up an SAT on the specific request of the State (LX p526).
2. JAT for two or more States
True
The Act provides for a Joint Administrative Tribunal for two or more States (LX p526).
3. JAT only for municipal tax
False
A JAT exercises all the service-matter powers of administrative tribunals for those States; tax is not its subject.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.

POL-744-A06.lead: Option 2: taxation, foreign exchange/import-export, industrial and labour disputes and land reforms are all listed in Article 323B (LX p526).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Citizenship, passports, recruitment, taxation
Citizenship and passports are not in Art 323B; recruitment belongs to Art 323A.
2. Taxation, forex, labour, land reforms
Taxation, foreign exchange and import/export, industrial and labour disputes, and land reforms are all expressly listed in Article 323B.
3. Promotion, citizenship, divorce, land reforms
Only land reforms is in 323B; promotion is a 323A service matter.
4. Impeachment, pardons, passports, taxation
Impeachment and pardons are constitutional processes, not tribunal subjects; only taxation fits.

points: Art 323B list: taxation; forex, import-export; industrial and labour; land reforms; urban property ceiling; elections; food stuffs; rent and tenancy.
Art 323B tribunals can be made by Parliament or State legislatures within their legislative competence.

POL-744-A07.lead: All four are in Article 323B, so the answer is option 4.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Ceiling on urban property
True
Ceiling on urban property is one of the subjects expressly listed in Article 323B (LX p526), so this is true.
2. Food-stuffs
True
Food-stuffs (production, supply and distribution) are expressly listed in Article 323B (LX p527), so this is true.
3. Rent and tenancy
True
Added by the 75th Amendment, 1994, which provided for rent tribunals (LX p1014).
4. Elections to Parliament and State legislatures
True
Listed, subject to the Article's exclusions (LX p526).

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out at least one listed subject.

POL-744-A08.lead: Option 2: Article 323A allows only one tribunal for the Centre and one for each State (or two or more States), with no hierarchy, while Article 323B allows a hierarchy (LX p527).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 323A hierarchy; 323B single
This reverses the position: Article 323A has no hierarchy of tribunals, while Article 323B allows a hierarchy.
2. 323A no hierarchy; 323B hierarchy
Laxmikanth's third difference: Article 323A has one tribunal for the Centre and per State with no hierarchy, while 323B allows a hierarchy.
3. 323A by States; 323B only Parliament
Reversed: 323A tribunals only by Parliament; 323B by Parliament and State legislatures.
4. 323A taxation; 323B service
Reversed: 323A is for service matters; 323B for taxation, land reforms etc.

points: Three differences: subject (service vs other), who creates (Parliament only vs both), hierarchy (no vs yes).
Each wrong option simply flips one of these differences.

POL-744-A09.lead: Option 1: legal-services institutions provide free legal services, organise Lok Adalats and run legal-awareness camps (LX ch38).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Free services, Lok Adalats, awareness
These are the core functions under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
2. Awareness alone
Incomplete; they also give help in litigation.
3. Court fees, prosecution, compulsory arbitration
They pay court fees for the poor rather than collect them; prosecution is the State's job.
4. Lok Adalats alone, on decided appeals
Lok Adalats settle pending and pre-litigation disputes, not cases already finally decided.

points: Lok Adalat = 'people's court' for amicable settlement.

POL-744-A10.lead: Option 4: free legal services include lawyers, certified copies, and preparation of appeal paper-books including printing and translation (LX ch38).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only oral advice
Free services include a lawyer in proceedings and payment of fees, not just advice.
2. Certified copies excluded
Supplying certified copies is expressly included.
3. Appeals excluded after trial
Preparation of an appeal paper-book is expressly included.
4. Litigation assistance included
Free legal services cover litigation-related help such as counsel, certified copies and translation of an appeal paper-book, so this is correct.

points: The four listed services: court and process fees; lawyer; certified copies; appeal paper-book with printing and translation.

POL-744-A11.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Women and children specified
True
Section 12 names a woman or a child as eligible for free legal services.
2. SC/ST specified
True
Members of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe are a listed category.
3. All need income ceiling
False
Income is a separate category; a woman, child or SC/ST person qualifies regardless of income.

points: Options 1 omits a true statement; options 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.
Section 13 adds that the person must have a prima facie case to prosecute or defend.

POL-744-A12.lead: Option 3: industrial workmen, persons in custody and victims of trafficking or begar are all categories named in Section 12 of the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Every salaried employee, property owner and taxpayer
None of these is a Section 12 category; being salaried or owning property says nothing about need for free legal aid.
Only convicted prisoners, excluding undertrials
Wrong: the category is 'persons in custody', which covers undertrials too, not just convicts.
Industrial workmen, persons in custody, trafficking/begar victims
All three are expressly listed eligible categories in Section 12.
Only unemployed persons below the income ceiling
Section 12 uses an income limit, not unemployment; and income is only one of several categories, so 'only' is wrong.

points: Section 12 lists: SC/ST members, trafficking or begar victims, women and children, persons with disability, victims of mass disaster/caste atrocity/flood/drought/earthquake/industrial disaster, industrial workmen, persons in custody, and persons below the notified income limit.
The idea: free legal aid (Article 39A) goes to weaker sections, chosen by vulnerability, not by job or property.
Memory hook: 'workers, women, weak, in custody, in calamity'.

POL-744-A13.lead: Option 4: no fee is charged in a Lok Adalat, and any court fee already paid is refunded when the case is settled there.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Fresh Lok Adalat fee compulsory; old fee forfeited
Wrong on both counts: Lok Adalat charges no fee, and the old fee is refunded, not forfeited.
Earlier court fee must be paid again
Wrong: nothing is paid twice; the fee already paid comes back to the party.
Only the winner may claim a new filing fee
Wrong: Lok Adalat settles by compromise, so there is no 'winner', and no new filing fee exists.
No fee; paid court fee refunded on settlement
Correct: this is the refund rule in the proviso to Section 21(1), linked to the Court Fees Act, 1870.

points: Lok Adalat aims at free, quick, friendly justice, so it removes the cost barrier.
The Supreme Court listed 'no court fee, and refund of fee already paid' as a key benefit.
POL-744-A13.also: A Lok Adalat award is final and binding; no appeal lies against it.

POL-744-A14.lead: Option 1: a Permanent Lok Adalat has a chairman who is or was a district/additional district judge (or held higher judicial office) plus two persons experienced in public utility services.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Standing forum: judicial chair + two public-utility experts
This is exactly the composition laid down by the 2002 amendment.
Three serving district judges, no non-judicial member
Wrong: only the chair is judicial; the other two are public-utility experts, not judges.
Temporary bench, utility officer as chair, two police officers
Wrong: it is permanent, its chair is a judicial officer, and police have no place in it.
Administrative chair and four elected local representatives
Wrong: chair must be judicial, total strength is three, and no elected representatives sit.

points: The 2002 amendment (Chapter VI-A) created PLAs for public utility disputes.
Mix of law (judicial chair) and field knowledge (two utility experts) lets it settle or even decide such disputes.

POL-744-A15.lead: Option 2: water supply, sanitation (public conservancy), hospital services and insurance are all listed public utility services for PLAs.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Tax, urban land ceiling, food prices, rent
These are Article 323B tribunal subjects, not public utility services.
Water supply, sanitation, hospitals, insurance
All four are in the PLA list (supply of power, light or water; public conservancy or sanitation; hospital or dispensary services; insurance).
Recruitment, transfers, promotion, discipline
These are service matters, handled by administrative tribunals like CAT under Article 323A.
Inheritance, divorce, adoption, partition
These are personal/family or civil property matters; divorce goes to Family Courts.

points: Full LX list: transport of passengers/goods by air, road, water; postal, telegraph, telephone; power, light, water supply; public conservancy or sanitation; hospitals or dispensaries; insurance.
A public utility is a service supplied to the public at large — a test that rules out options 1, 3 and 4.

POL-744-A19.lead: Option 3: SCLSC handles Supreme Court matters, DLSA works at district level and the Taluk Legal Services Committee at taluk level.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: SCLSC — district cases; DLSA — Supreme Court cases
Roles swapped: SCLSC is for the Supreme Court and DLSA for the district.
Taluk committee — all-India policy; NALSA — one village
Reversed: NALSA (national) lays down policy; the taluk committee works at taluk level.
SCLSC — Supreme Court; DLSA — district; Taluk committee — taluk
The SCLSC handles Supreme Court matters, the DLSA works at district level and the Taluk committee at taluk level, so each body matches its level.
SLSA — Parliament's service disputes; SCLSC — transfers
Invented roles: SLSA runs legal aid in the State; service disputes go to tribunals, not legal-services bodies.

points: Ladder: NALSA (national) → SLSA (State) and HCLSC (High Court) → DLSA (district) → Taluk committee; SCLSC serves the Supreme Court.
All give free legal services and organise Lok Adalats under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

POL-744-A20.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is Option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Persons with disability
True
Persons with disability are an express Section 12 category (LX lists 'disabled persons').
2. Victims of mass disaster or caste atrocity in undeserved want
True
Section 12 covers victims of mass disaster, ethnic violence, caste atrocity, flood, drought, earthquake or industrial disaster.
3. Only persons whose dispute is finally decided
False
Legal aid is meant for filing or defending cases; a person whose case is already over gains nothing from it, and no such condition exists.

points: Option 2 (2 and 3) wrongly includes statement 3 and drops statement 1.
Option 3 (1 and 3) wrongly includes statement 3 and drops statement 2.
Option 4 (all) wrongly includes the false statement 3.

POL-744-A21.lead: Option 4: CAT was set up in 1985 with its principal bench at New Delhi.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1976 — Mumbai
1976 is the 42nd Amendment year that added Article 323A; Mumbai is only a regular bench.
1987 — Chennai
1987 is the Legal Services Authorities Act year; Chennai is only a regular bench.
1995 — Kolkata
1995 is when the Legal Services Act came into force; Kolkata is only a regular bench.
1985 — New Delhi
CAT was set up under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, principal bench New Delhi.

points: Chain: Article 323A (1976) → Administrative Tribunals Act (1985) → CAT (1985).
CAT has 19 regular benches; the principal bench is at New Delhi.

POL-744-A22.lead: Option 1: the first Lok Adalat camp after independence was held in Gujarat in 1982.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Gujarat
The first post-independence Lok Adalat camp was organised here in 1982.
Maharashtra
Lok Adalats spread here later; it was not the first.
Karnataka
The first Lok Adalat camp in 1982 was held in Gujarat, not Karnataka.
Tamil Nadu
The first Lok Adalat camp in 1982 was held in Gujarat, not Tamil Nadu.

points: The camp's success spread Lok Adalats across India, at first without statutory backing.
Statutory status came with the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 (in force 9 November 1995).

POL-744-A23.lead: Option 3: Lok Adalats can be organised by SLSA, DLSA, SCLSC, HCLSC and Taluk Legal Services Committees.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only DLSA, excluding court committees
Wrong: the SCLSC and HCLSC (court committees) can also organise them.
Only Supreme Court and High Court committees
Wrong: State, District and Taluk bodies also organise them.
Court committees plus State, District and Taluk institutions
Correct: all five bodies named in Section 19 can organise Lok Adalats.
Only private bar associations
Wrong: bar associations are not statutory organisers.

points: Section 19: any of these bodies may organise Lok Adalats 'at such intervals and places' as it thinks fit.
A Lok Adalat usually has a judicial officer as chairman, with a lawyer and a social worker as members.

POL-744-A24.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is Option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Carriage of passengers/goods by air, road or water
True
Transport service by air, road or water is the first listed public utility service.
2. Postal, telegraph or telephone services
True
These are expressly listed public utility services.
3. Only government-owned providers
False
The list speaks of services, e.g. supply of power, light or water 'by any establishment'; private providers like private insurers are covered too.

points: Option 1 (1 only) misses the true statement 2.
Option 3 (2 and 3) drops statement 1 and wrongly includes statement 3.
Option 4 (all) wrongly includes statement 3.

POL-744-CH-01.lead: Option 2: the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 sets up NALSA, SLSAs, DLSAs and gives Lok Adalats statutory status.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985
Made under Article 323A to set up CAT and State Administrative Tribunals for service disputes.
Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
Creates legal-services authorities and gives Lok Adalats statutory backing.
Family Courts Act, 1984
Provides family courts for marriage and family disputes.
Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008
Provides village-level courts (Gram Nyayalayas).

points: The 1987 Act gives effect to Article 39A (free legal aid).
Memory: 1984 family, 1985 tribunals, 1987 legal services, 2008 village courts.
POL-744-CH-01.also: The 1987 Act came into force on 9 November 1995 — National Legal Services Day.

POL-744-CH-02.lead: A Lok Adalat cannot take up a non-compoundable offence.

head: Option
Meaning
Fits?
rows: A pending compoundable dispute
A case already in court that the law lets parties settle (e.g. minor hurt, cheque bounce).
No - allowed
A pre-litigation civil matter
A dispute not yet filed in court (e.g. unpaid bill).
No - allowed
A non-compoundable offence
A serious crime the parties cannot settle by compromise (e.g. murder, rape); only the court can decide.
Yes
A bank-recovery settlement
A loan dues dispute settled by agreement; common in Lok Adalats.
No - allowed

points: Lok Adalat works only by compromise, so it can take only matters that can be settled.
Section 19(5), Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 bars non-compoundable offences.

POL-744-CH-03.lead: Option 2: unlike an ordinary Lok Adalat, a Permanent Lok Adalat may decide the dispute on merits if conciliation fails.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Must return every such dispute undecided
This is what an ordinary Lok Adalat does; a PLA has extra power to decide.
May decide the eligible dispute on merits
Correct: if parties fail to agree, the PLA 'shall decide the dispute on merits'.
May act only after the dispute is filed in a regular court
Wrong: an application to a PLA is made before the dispute is brought to any court.
May decide any non-compoundable criminal charge
Wrong: a PLA has no jurisdiction over offences not compoundable under any law.

points: Ordinary Lok Adalat = settlement only; PLA = conciliation first, then adjudication.
A PLA award is final, binding and made by majority.
POL-744-CH-03.also: A PLA award is final and binding on all parties.

POL-744-FACET-01.lead: Supply of power, light or water to the public is a listed public utility service.
points: Section 22A(b) of the Legal Services Authorities Act lists power, light or water supply by any establishment.
Election symbols, citizenship and judicial recruitment are state functions, not public utilities.

POL-744-FACET-02.lead: Option 2: the Administrative Tribunals Act excludes court staff and the secretarial staff of legislatures.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: All State civil servants
Not excluded: State employees' service disputes can go to State Administrative Tribunals under the same Act.
High Court/subordinate-court staff and legislature secretariat staff
Excluded: the Act does not apply to officers and servants of courts or to secretarial staff of legislatures, to protect their independence.
All civilian defence staff
Not excluded: CAT jurisdiction expressly covers civilian employees of the defence services.
All employees of government-controlled societies
Not excluded: the Central Government can bring such societies under CAT by notification (Section 14(2)).

points: LX: members of the defence forces, officers and servants of the Supreme Court and secretarial staff of Parliament are not covered by CAT.
Do not confuse: uniformed defence forces are excluded (they go to AFT), but civilian defence employees are covered.

POL-744-FACET-03.lead: HCLSC handles High Court cases; SLSA is the State-level authority.
points: The High Court Legal Services Committee works under Section 8A.
The State Legal Services Authority under Section 6 heads legal aid in the State.
Neither handles elections, service tribunals or national policy.

POL-744-LX36-CAT-LIMITATION.lead: Option 3: under Section 21, an application to CAT must be made within one year of the final order.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Three months
Not the limitation period under Section 21.
Six months
Six months appears only as the waiting time after filing an appeal that is not decided; it is not the limitation period.
One year
Correct: one year from the date the final order is made.
Two years
Two years is longer than the limit; under the Administrative Tribunals Act the ordinary period to apply to CAT is one year from the final order.

points: If an appeal is filed and not decided, the year runs after six months from the appeal.
CAT may admit a late application if the applicant shows sufficient cause for delay.

POL-744-LX36-CAT-REMEDIES.lead: Option 2: under Section 20, CAT ordinarily does not admit an application until available service-rule remedies are exhausted.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: CAT must admit once filed
Wrong: admission is not automatic; CAT first checks that remedies are exhausted.
Remedies under service rules must ordinarily be exhausted
Correct: the applicant must first use the departmental appeal/representation available.
Memorial to the President first for everyone
Wrong: a memorial is not a compulsory step for every applicant.
Only after a High Court certifies exhaustion
Wrong: no High Court certificate is involved; CAT itself decides.

points: Logic: let the department correct its own mistake first, then the tribunal steps in.
The word 'ordinarily' means CAT may relax the rule in fit cases.

POL-744-LX36-CAT-REVIEW.lead: Option 2: CAT can review its own decisions, and its orders can be challenged before a Division Bench of the High Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: CAT has no power to review
Wrong: the Act gives CAT a civil court's power to review its own decisions.
CAT reviews its own decision; HC Division Bench judicial review
Correct: Chandra Kumar (1997) held High Court judicial review is basic structure.
Only the President reviews CAT orders
Wrong: the President has no role in reviewing tribunal orders.
Only UPSC reviews CAT orders
Wrong: UPSC is a recruiting body, not an appellate body.

points: Originally appeals lay only to the Supreme Court; Chandra Kumar struck down that bar.
Now an aggrieved servant must first go to the High Court Division Bench, not directly to the Supreme Court.

POL-744-LX38-NALSA-EVALUATION.lead: Option 2: the Chief Justice of the High Court is Patron-in-Chief of the SLSA, and the District Judge is ex officio Chairman of the DLSA.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Governor; District Collector
Executive heads have no such role; legal-services bodies are headed by the judiciary.
Chief Justice of HC; District Judge
Correct: the Act makes the High Court Chief Justice Patron-in-Chief of the SLSA and the District Judge Chairman of the DLSA.
Chief Minister; District Judge
Second part right, but the Chief Minister is not Patron-in-Chief of the SLSA.
CJI; Chief Judicial Magistrate
The CJI is Patron-in-Chief of NALSA, not the SLSA; the CJM does not chair the DLSA.

points: Pattern: NALSA — CJI; SLSA — CJ of the High Court; DLSA — District Judge.
The executive chairman of an SLSA is a serving or retired High Court judge.

POL-744-LX38-ORDINARY-NO-SETTLEMENT.lead: Option 1: P goes back to the referring court and resumes from the stage reached; in Q the parties are advised to seek a court remedy.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: P resumes at old stage; Q parties advised
Correct: s.20(5),(7) for pending cases and s.20(6) for pre-litigation matters.
Both automatically become pending in the same court
Wrong: Q was never filed, so no case automatically arises.
P restarts from the beginning; Q advised
Wrong on P: the court continues from the stage before referral, not a fresh trial.
P closed and refiled; Q sent to court
Wrong: P is returned, not closed; Q is only given advice.

points: Failed settlement must not waste time already spent in court.
A pre-litigation matter has no court to return to, so parties are told to go to court.

POL-744-LX38-ORDINARY-PENDING-REFERRAL.lead: Option 4: when only one party applies, the court must give the parties a reasonable opportunity to be heard before referring.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Refer immediately
Wrong: one party's request alone does not allow immediate referral.
Obtain a signed settlement first
Wrong: settlement is the goal of the Lok Adalat, not a pre-condition.
Send it as a pre-litigation matter
Wrong: the case is already pending in court, so it is not pre-litigation.
Hear the parties first
Correct: s.20(1) proviso requires a reasonable opportunity of being heard.

points: LX: referral is possible when parties agree, one party applies, or the court is satisfied.
Hearing both sides is natural justice — the other party may not want a compromise.

POL-744-LX38-PLA-AWARD-MAJORITY.lead: Option 2: a Permanent Lok Adalat award is made by a majority of its members, so two of three suffices.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: All three must agree
The Act does not require all three members to agree; an award can be made by the majority of the Permanent Lok Adalat.
Two-member majority
Correct: the award is made by a majority of the persons constituting the PLA (s.22E).
Chair's view alone
Wrong: the chair has one voice like the others.
Parties choose which view
Wrong: parties cannot pick; the forum decides by majority.

points: A PLA has a chairman and two members, so majority means two.
POL-744-LX38-PLA-AWARD-MAJORITY.also: PLA awards are final and binding and are deemed civil-court decrees.

POL-744-LX38-PLA-PARALLEL-COURT.lead: Option 3: once a PLA application is made, no party to it may invoke any court's jurisdiction in the same dispute.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Yes, until settlement signed
Wrong: the bar starts from the application, not from signing.
Only the respondent may
Wrong: the bar applies to every party to the application.
No, neither party
Section 22C(2) bars both parties from invoking a civil court's jurisdiction in the same dispute once the application is made.
Yes, with consent
Wrong: consent does not lift a statutory bar.

points: Purpose: avoid parallel cases and conflicting results.
Insurance is a listed public utility service, so the PLA has jurisdiction.

POL-744-LX38-PLA-SIGNED-TERMS.lead: Option 1: the PLA must pass an award in terms of the signed agreement and give a copy to each party.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Award in agreed terms; copy to each party
Section 22C(7) says that when the parties sign a settlement, the Permanent Lok Adalat passes an award in its terms and gives each party a copy.
Send to civil court
Wrong: the PLA itself makes the award; no court is involved.
Award only after deciding merits
Wrong: merits are decided only if the parties fail to agree (s.22C(8)).
Close without award
Wrong: a signed settlement must be turned into an award so it is enforceable.

points: Order: conciliation → if agreed, award on terms; if not, decision on merits.

POL-744-P307-01.lead: Option 2: Article 39A (DPSP) directs the State to secure equal justice and free legal aid.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 32
Right to move the Supreme Court for enforcing Fundamental Rights.
Article 39A
Article 39A, a Directive Principle added by the 42nd Amendment (1976), directs the State to promote equal justice and free legal aid.
Article 50
DPSP: separation of judiciary from executive.
Article 226
Article 226 gives High Courts the power to issue writs; it has nothing to do with free legal aid, which is Article 39A.

points: The Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 was made to give effect to Article 39A.
POL-744-P307-01.also: Article 39A was added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.

POL-744-P307-02.lead: Option 3 is the incorrect statement: no appeal lies to any court against a Lok Adalat award.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Deemed a civil-court decree
True: s.21(1) — so it can be executed like a decree.
Final and binding
Section 21(2) says a Lok Adalat award is final and binding, so this statement is correct and not the answer.
An ordinary appeal lies
False: no appeal lies to any court — this is the statement asked for.
Binds the parties
True: binding on all parties to the dispute.

points: The award is based on consent, so an appeal makes no sense.
A party alleging fraud etc. can only use a writ petition.

POL-744-P327-01.lead: Option 2: the 42nd Amendment, 1976 inserted Part XIV-A (Articles 323A, 323B).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 24th Amendment (1971)
Affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part, including Fundamental Rights.
42nd Amendment (1976)
The 42nd Amendment (1976) inserted Part XIV-A 'Tribunals' with Articles 323A and 323B, so this is correct.
44th Amendment (1978)
Removed the right to property from Fundamental Rights.
75th Amendment (1994)
Provided for State rent control tribunals.

points: The original Constitution had no tribunal provisions.
POL-744-P327-01.also: Part XIV-A was added on the Swaran Singh Committee's recommendation.

POL-744-P327-02.lead: Option 1: only Parliament can provide for administrative tribunals under Article 323A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament
Correct: Article 323A empowers Parliament alone.
State legislatures
Wrong: they act only under Article 323B.
Supreme Court
Courts do not create tribunals; Article 323A gives this power to Parliament alone.
Parliament and States jointly
Wrong: joint power exists under 323B, not 323A.

points: Under 323A Parliament passed the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985.
Even State Administrative Tribunals are set up by the Centre on a State's request.

POL-744-P328-01.lead: CAT follows principles of natural justice, not the CPC.

head: Option
Meaning
Fits?
rows: Parliamentary privilege
Special rights of MPs/MLAs (e.g. free speech in the House).
No
Natural justice
Basic fairness: hear both sides, and no one judges his own case.
Yes
Cabinet secrecy
Ministers keep Cabinet talks secret (oath of secrecy).
No
Strict liability
Liability for harm even without fault (e.g. hazardous industry).
No

points: The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 frees CAT from the CPC, 1908.
So CAT procedure is simple and quick, but still fair.

POL-744-P329-01.lead: Option 2: L. Chandra Kumar (1997) held High Court judicial review over tribunals to be basic structure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
Kesavananda Bharati (1973) laid down the basic structure doctrine itself, but it did not deal with judicial review of tribunal decisions.
L. Chandra Kumar (1997)
Restored High Court review over tribunal decisions.
S.R. Bommai (1994)
S.R. Bommai (1994) dealt with President's Rule under Article 356 and secularism, not with tribunals.
Minerva Mills (1980)
Held limited amending power is basic structure.

points: After this case, CAT orders go first to a High Court Division Bench.

POL-744-P329-02.lead: Option 3: under Article 323B both Parliament and State legislatures may establish tribunals within their own legislative competence.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament only
Parliament alone acts under Article 323A; Article 323B lets both Parliament and State legislatures set up tribunals.
State legislatures only
Under Article 323B both Parliament and State legislatures may set up tribunals within their competence, not States alone.
Parliament and State legislatures
Correct: each may create tribunals for matters within its own legislative competence.
High Courts only
Courts do not create tribunals; under Article 323B only legislatures (Parliament and States) can establish them.

points: Subjects include taxation, foreign exchange, labour, land reforms, urban property ceiling and elections.

PRAC-POL-DFACEE89986D.lead: Option 1: NALSA is constituted under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987
The Act under which NALSA is constituted.
Legal Services Act, 1990
No 'Legal Services Act, 1990' created NALSA; it was set up under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
Judicial Services Act, 1980
No 'Judicial Services Act, 1980' created NALSA; it was set up under the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992
NALSA is a statutory body, not created by a constitutional amendment.

points: The Act came into force on 9 November 1995.
The Chief Justice of India is NALSA's Patron-in-Chief.
PRAC-POL-DFACEE89986D.also: The Act gives effect to Article 39A.

POL-751-AT-article251-temporary.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is Option 3 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. State keeps its power to legislate
True
Article 251 says nothing in Articles 249/250 restricts a State legislature's power to make laws it could otherwise make.
2. Conflicting State provision inoperative while Union law has effect
True
Under Article 251, the State law is inoperative only to the extent of repugnancy and only so long as Parliament's law has effect.
3. Entire State Act permanently void
False
The State law is only suspended, not void; it becomes operative again when Parliament's temporary law ceases.

points: Option 1 misses the true statement 2.
Options 2 and 4 wrongly include statement 3.
Articles 249 (Rajya Sabha resolution) and 250 (Emergency) let Parliament make temporary laws on State List subjects; such laws lapse six months after the resolution or emergency ends.

POL-751-AT-article31b-limited-shield.lead: Option 2: the lawyer is wrong — Article 31B shields Ninth Schedule laws only from Part III (Fundamental Rights) challenges.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct: overrides the whole Constitution
Wrong: Article 31B speaks only of laws being void for inconsistency with Part III rights; it gives no wider immunity.
