Incorrect: shield is limited to Part III objections
Correct: a law lacking legislative competence can still be struck down even if placed in the Ninth Schedule.
Correct: listed Acts become constitutional provisions
Wrong: Ninth Schedule laws stay ordinary laws; listing only protects them from Part III challenge.
Incorrect because it protects only executive orders
Wrong reason: the Ninth Schedule lists Acts and Regulations, not executive orders.

points: I.R. Coelho (2007): laws placed in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can be challenged for violating basic structure, including Articles 14, 15, 19 and 21.
So 31B is a limited shield, not a blanket immunity.

POL-751-AT-certificate-consideration.lead: Option 2: the High Court must determine, as soon as may be, whether the certificate can be given.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Grant automatically
Wrong: the High Court must apply the legal tests of the Article concerned; there is no automatic certificate.
Determine as soon as may be
Correct: Article 134A requires the High Court to decide the certificate question as soon as may be after the judgment.
Reject because oral
Wrong: Article 134A expressly allows an oral application made immediately after the judgment.
Wait for the President
Wrong: the President has no role; certificates are given by the High Court itself.

points: Article 134A (44th Amendment, 1978) covers certificates for appeal to the Supreme Court under Articles 132(1), 133(1) and 134(1)(c).
The High Court may also act on its own motion.

POL-751-AT-coelho-finalised-transactions.lead: Option 3: Coelho said actions taken and transactions finalised under the impugned Acts would not be open to challenge.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: All pending and future disputes barred
Wrong: Coelho did the opposite — it opened post-1973 Ninth Schedule laws to basic-structure review.
All completed transactions reopened
Wrong: reopening settled matters would cause chaos; the Court expressly protected them.
Actions taken and finalised transactions saved
Correct: this was the express saving in the judgment.
Only President-approved transactions saved
Wrong: the saving had no such condition; the President plays no role here.

points: I.R. Coelho v. State of Tamil Nadu (2007) was a nine-judge bench ruling on Ninth Schedule laws.
Prospective-style saving: the law can be tested in future, but completed acts stay valid.

POL-751-AT-coelho-impact-not-form.lead: Option 2: In I.R. Coelho (2007) the Supreme Court said the test is the actual effect of the law on Fundamental Rights (the 'impact' or 'rights' test), not the form of the amendment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Schedule label alone gives conclusive immunity
Wrong. Coelho held there is no blanket immunity; putting a law in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 does not by itself protect it.
Examine actual effect on rights and whether the basic structure is damaged
Correct. The court looks at the real impact on Part III rights (especially Articles 14, 19 and 21) and asks whether that impact damages the basic structure.
Invalidate every Part III infringement automatically
Wrong. Coelho said a law abridging Part III rights may or may not damage the basic structure, so the court must still do the basic-structure inquiry.
Look only at the statute's title
Wrong. This is the very 'form' approach Coelho rejected; the consequence of the law, not its label or title, decides validity.

points: Coelho: 'the form of an amendment is not the relevant factor, but the consequence thereof would be the determinative factor'.
The cut-off is 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment.
Memory hook: Coelho = effect, not form.

POL-751-AT-coelho-invalid-reinserted.lead: Option 1: Under Coelho, a law put in the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 can still be challenged on the ground that its effect on rights damages the basic structure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Open to challenge for basic-structure damage on the rights test
Correct. Coelho held that Ninth Schedule protection after 24 April 1973 is not blanket; the law is tested by the rights test on the touchstone of the basic structure.
Insertion cures every constitutional defect
Wrong. If insertion cured every defect, Parliament could defeat judicial review at will; Coelho held judicial review is a basic feature that cannot be removed this way.
Earlier adverse ruling gives permanent immunity
Wrong. An earlier ruling striking the law down is a reason for concern, not a shield; nothing in Coelho turns a court's adverse ruling into immunity.
Only Parliament may examine validity
Wrong. Deciding constitutional validity is the job of the courts under Articles 32 and 226, not of Parliament.

points: Coelho (2007) confirmed Waman Rao (1980): laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973 are valid only if they do not damage the basic structure.
Laws placed before that date keep their protection under Article 31B.
POL-751-AT-coelho-invalid-reinserted.also: 24 April 1973 is the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment.

POL-751-AT-concurrent-repugnancy.lead: Option 4: Under Article 254(1), when a State law on a Concurrent List subject conflicts with a valid central law, the central law prevails and the State law is void only to the extent of the conflict.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: State law always prevails because it is later
Wrong. The 'later law wins' rule does not apply between Centre and State; a State law prevails only through presidential assent under Article 254(2).
Governor may disregard the parliamentary law
Wrong. The Governor has no power to set aside a law of Parliament; the conflict is settled by Article 254 itself.
Whole State Act fails even where separable
Wrong. Article 254(1) says the State law is void 'to the extent of the repugnancy', so separable parts survive.
Parliamentary law prevails; State law void to the extent of repugnancy
Correct. This is the text and effect of Article 254(1).

points: Repugnancy means a direct conflict: both laws cannot be obeyed at the same time.
Article 254(2) exception: a State law reserved for and assented to by the President prevails in that State, but Parliament can later amend or repeal it.

POL-751-AT-countermajoritarian-criticism.lead: Option 4: The counter-majoritarian difficulty is the objection that unelected judges can strike down laws made by the people's elected representatives.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Every decision needs a referendum
Wrong. No one proposes this; courts decide cases without public votes, and the criticism is about judges overruling legislatures, not about referendums.
Only the executive can interpret the Constitution
Wrong. This is not the criticism; in India the Supreme Court is the final interpreter of the Constitution.
Constitution forbids courts examining statutes
Wrong. The Indian Constitution does the opposite: Articles 13, 32 and 226 let courts test statutes.
Unelected judges may invalidate laws of elected representatives
Correct. This is the democratic worry: a few unelected judges override the majority's will expressed through the legislature.

points: The phrase was made popular by the US scholar Alexander Bickel.
The usual answer to the criticism: the Constitution itself is the people's higher will, and courts protect it, especially minority rights, against temporary majorities.

POL-751-AT-criminal-constitutional-route.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so option 4 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. HC reverses acquittal and sentences to death
True
Article 134(1)(a) gives an appeal to the Supreme Court as of right when a High Court on appeal reverses an acquittal and sentences the accused to death.
2. HC withdraws a case, convicts and sentences to death
True
Article 134(1)(b) covers a High Court that withdraws a case from a subordinate court, tries it itself and sentences the accused to death.
3. Every criminal conviction
False
Clauses (a) and (b) cover only these death-sentence situations; other criminal appeals need a High Court certificate under Article 134(1)(c) or special leave under Article 136.

points: Option 1 (1 only) and option 2 (2 only) each drop one true clause.
Option 3 wrongly includes statement 3.
Memory hook: Article 134(1)(a) and (b) = death sentence passed by the High Court itself.

POL-751-AT-delegated-legislation-review.lead: Option 3: Delegated (subordinate) legislation is subject to judicial review; courts check whether it is within the parent Act and whether it violates the Constitution.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Succeeds whenever a Minister signed the rule
Wrong. A Minister's signature gives the rule no immunity; it is still tested like any other law under Article 13.
Only Acts of Parliament can be reviewed
Wrong. Judicial review covers legislation of Parliament and State Legislatures and also subordinate legislation.
Reviewable; authority and constitutional validity may be examined
Correct. A rule beyond the parent Act is ultra vires, and a rule violating Fundamental Rights is void.
The rule becomes a constitutional amendment
Wrong. Only Parliament acting under Article 368 can amend the Constitution; a rule is a lower form of law.

points: Article 13(3) defines 'law' to include rules, regulations, orders and notifications, so they too are void if they violate Fundamental Rights.
Justice Quadri's second category of judicial review includes subordinate legislation.

POL-751-AT-extraterritorial-operation.lead: Option 4: Article 245(2) says no law made by Parliament shall be deemed invalid on the ground that it would have extra-territorial operation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Every such law is automatically void
Wrong. This is the opposite of Article 245(2), which saves Parliament's laws from this objection.
Only a State Legislature may make such a law
Wrong. State laws operate only within the State (Article 245(1)); the extra-territorial power belongs to Parliament.
The Constitution contains no relevant rule
Wrong. Article 245(2) is exactly the relevant rule.
That ground alone does not invalidate the law; other requirements remain
Correct. The law can still be struck down on other grounds such as lack of legislative competence or violation of Fundamental Rights.

points: Extra-territorial operation means the law applies to Indian citizens and their property anywhere in the world.
Article 245(1): Parliament legislates for the whole or any part of India; a State for the whole or any part of the State.

POL-751-AT-federal-government-party-comb.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are covered and 3 is not, so option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Union and States vs other States
True
Article 131(b) covers a dispute between the Government of India and one or more States on one side and one or more other States on the other.
2. Two or more States
True
Article 131(c) covers a dispute between two or more States.
3. Private company vs private company
False
Article 131 is a federal jurisdiction only between governments; private parties go to ordinary courts or use writ jurisdiction.

points: Option 2 and option 3 both wrongly include statement 3.
Option 4 includes all three, so it also fails on statement 3.
Article 131(a) covers the Union versus one or more States; the dispute must involve a question of legal right.

POL-751-AT-federal-residual-jurisdiction.lead: Option 3: Article 135 lets the Supreme Court exercise the jurisdiction and powers of the Federal Court under any pre-constitution law, where Articles 133 and 134 do not apply, until Parliament provides otherwise.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 131
Wrong. Article 131 is the Supreme Court's original jurisdiction in Centre-State and inter-State disputes.
Article 134A
Wrong. Article 134A deals with the High Court certificate for appeal to the Supreme Court.
Article 135
Correct. It carries over the old Federal Court's jurisdiction under pre-constitution laws.
Article 143
Wrong. Article 143 is the advisory jurisdiction: the President may seek the Supreme Court's opinion.

points: The Federal Court (set up under the Government of India Act, 1935) was replaced by the Supreme Court in 1950; Article 135 avoids a gap in its old powers.
Laxmikanth lists Article 135 among the provisions supporting judicial review.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Sentinel on the qui vive
1. V.G. Row - Patanjali Sastri
CJ Patanjali Sastri in State of Madras v. V.G. Row (1952) called the court the 'sentinel on the qui vive' (ever-alert guard) of FRs.
B. FRs a mere adornment without remedies
2. Minerva Mills - Y.V. Chandrachud
CJ Chandrachud in Minerva Mills (1980): without judicial review FRs become a 'mere adornment'.
C. Ultimate interpreter of constitutional limits
3. State of Rajasthan v. Union - P.N. Bhagwati
Justice Bhagwati in State of Rajasthan v. Union (1977): the Court is the ultimate interpreter of the Constitution.

points: Option 2 is wrong: it gives A-2, B-1 (should be A-1, B-2).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives B-3, C-2 (should be B-2, C-3).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-3, C-1 (should be A-1, C-3).

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. List I
2. Parliament
List I (Union List): only Parliament - Art 246(1).
B. List II
3. State Legislatures
List II (State List): State Legislatures, subject to the Constitution - Art 246(3).
C. List III
1. Parliament and State Legislatures
List III (Concurrent): both - Art 246(2).

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-1, B-2, C-3 (should be A-2, B-3, C-1).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-3, B-2 (should be A-2, B-3).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives B-1, C-3 (should be B-3, C-1).

POL-751-AT-marbury-year.lead: Marbury v. Madison was decided in 1803.
points: Chief Justice John Marshall gave the judgment, founding judicial review in the USA.
1776 is US independence; 1787 is the US Constitution; 1865 ended the Civil War.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. First Amendment, 1951
3. Arts 31A, 31B and Ninth Schedule
1st Amendment (1951) inserted Arts 31A, 31B and the Ninth Schedule.
B. 24th Amendment, 1971
24th (1971) inserted Art 13(4) and 368(3): Art 13 does not apply to amendments.
C. 42nd Amendment, 1976
42nd (1976) inserted Art 368(4),(5) barring courts - struck down in Minerva Mills (1980).

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-1, B-3 (should be A-3, B-1).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives B-2, C-1 (should be B-1, C-2).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-2, C-3 (should be A-3, C-2).

POL-751-AT-ninth-insertion-mechanism.lead: Option 3: The Ninth Schedule is part of the Constitution, so a law can be added to it only by Parliament through a constitutional amendment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: State declaration alone amends the Schedule
Wrong. A State Legislature has no power to amend the Constitution; Article 368 gives that power to Parliament.
Governor may insert it by assent
Wrong. Governor's assent only makes the State Bill an Act; it cannot change a Schedule of the Constitution.
Insertion needs a parliamentary constitutional amendment
Correct. For example, the 76th Amendment (1994) placed the Tamil Nadu reservation Act in the Ninth Schedule.
Every State land law enters automatically
Wrong. Only laws named in the Schedule by an amendment are protected under Article 31B; there is no automatic entry.

points: Article 31B protects laws in the Ninth Schedule from challenge on Fundamental Rights grounds, subject to the basic-structure test for post-24 April 1973 entries.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Article 31A
1. Acquisition of estates
Art 31A saves laws for acquisition of estates (land reform) from Arts 14, 19.
B. Article 31B
2. Ninth Schedule laws
Art 31B validates Acts placed in the Ninth Schedule.
C. Article 31C
3. Certain Directive Principles
Art 31C saves laws giving effect to Art 39(b),(c) Directive Principles.

points: Option 2 is wrong: it gives A-2, B-1 (should be A-1, B-2).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives B-3, C-2 (should be B-2, C-3).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A-3, C-1 (should be A-1, C-3).

POL-751-AT-ninth-lettered-entry.lead: Option 4: The 76th Amendment Act, 1994 placed the Tamil Nadu reservation Act, which provided 69 per cent reservation, in the Ninth Schedule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 73rd Amendment, 1992
Wrong. It gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions (Part IX).
77th Amendment, 1995
Wrong. It allowed reservation in promotions for SCs and STs (Article 16(4A)).
81st Amendment, 2000
Wrong. It allowed unfilled reserved vacancies of a year to be treated as a separate class (carry-forward), free of the 50% ceiling.
76th Amendment, 1994
Correct. It shielded the 69% reservation law, which crossed the 50% limit set in Indra Sawhney (1992).

points: Because it was placed after 24 April 1973, this law can still be tested on the basic structure (I.R. Coelho, 2007).

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Shankari Prasad (1951)
2. Amendment not 'law'; 1st Amendment upheld
Shankari Prasad (1951): an amendment is not 'law' under Art 13; First Amendment upheld.
B. Waman Rao (1981)
3. Post-24 April 1973 Ninth Schedule laws open to challenge
Waman Rao (1981): Ninth Schedule laws after 24 April 1973 (Kesavananda date) can be challenged.
C. L. Chandra Kumar (1997)
1. Judicial review is basic structure
L. Chandra Kumar (1997): judicial review under Arts 32 and 226/227 is basic structure.

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives A-1, B-2, C-3 (should be A-2, B-3, C-1).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A-3, B-2 (should be A-2, B-3).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives B-1, C-3 (should be B-3, C-1).

POL-751-AT-ninth-original-count.lead: Option 4: When the 1st Amendment, 1951 created the Ninth Schedule, it contained only 13 Acts and Regulations.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong. This is not the original count; the original Schedule had 13 entries.
Wrong. This is not the original count; the original Schedule had 13 entries.
Wrong. This is not the original count; the original Schedule had 13 entries.
Correct. Laxmikanth: 'Originally (in 1951), the Ninth Schedule contained only 13 acts and regulations'.

points: The number has now grown to 282 (Laxmikanth).
State laws in it mainly deal with land reforms and abolition of zamindari; Parliament's laws deal with other matters.
POL-751-AT-ninth-original-count.also: Laws added after 24 April 1973 can be tested on the basic structure (Waman Rao, 1980; I.R. Coelho, 2007).

POL-751-AT-nonstate-territory.lead: Option 1: Article 246(4) lets Parliament make laws on any matter, even a State List matter, for any part of India not included in a State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 246(4) permits it
Correct. Areas outside any State, such as Union Territories, have no State Legislature, so Parliament fills the gap.
Article 246 always prohibits Parliament
Wrong. The State List bars Parliament only for State territory; clause (4) expressly allows it for non-State areas.
Only a constitutional amendment can permit it
Wrong. The power already exists in Article 246(4); no amendment is needed.
Only a High Court may legislate
Wrong. Courts do not make laws; legislating is the job of Parliament and State Legislatures.

points: Article 246 also divides subjects: Union List (clause 1), Concurrent List (clause 2), State List (clause 3).

POL-751-AT-preconstitutional-continuance.lead: Option 2: Article 372(1) keeps laws in force before 26 January 1950 alive, subject to the Constitution, until altered, repealed or amended by a competent authority.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Becomes a constitutional amendment
Wrong. An old law stays an ordinary law; it does not become part of the Constitution.
Continues subject to the Constitution until competently changed
Correct. This is the text of Article 372(1); it avoids a legal vacuum on the commencement of the Constitution.
Necessarily lapsed on 26 January 1950
Wrong. Article 372 exists precisely so that existing laws did not lapse.
Immune from Fundamental Rights review
Wrong. Article 13(1) says pre-constitution laws inconsistent with Fundamental Rights are void to that extent.

points: Example: the Indian Penal Code, 1860 continued after 1950 under Article 372.
Laxmikanth lists Article 372 among the judicial-review provisions.

POL-751-AT-presidential-assent-repugnanc.lead: Statement 1 is true and 2 is false, so option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Assented State law may prevail in that State
True
Under Article 254(2), a State law on a Concurrent subject that is reserved for the President and gets his assent prevails in that State over an earlier central law.
2. Parliament permanently barred thereafter
False
The proviso to Article 254(2) lets Parliament later make a law on the same matter, including one that adds to, amends, varies or repeals the State law.

points: Option 2 wrongly accepts statement 2 and rejects 1.
Option 3 wrongly accepts statement 2.
Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1.

POL-751-AT-territorial-law-range.lead: Option 1: Article 245(1) says Parliament may make laws for the whole or any part of India, and a State Legislature for the whole or any part of the State.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament: whole or part of India; State: whole or part of State
Correct. This is the exact wording of Article 245(1).
Parliament: only Union Territories
Wrong. Parliament legislates for the whole country, not only for Union Territories.
Parliament: whole of India only, never a part
Wrong. Article 245(1) expressly allows laws for 'any part' of India, and a State may also legislate for part of the State.
State: adjoining States with Governor's consent
Wrong. A State law cannot extend beyond the State, and a Governor's consent cannot widen this limit.

points: Article 245(2): Parliament's laws are not invalid for extra-territorial operation; State laws have no such protection.

POL-751-CH-01.lead: All three are true, so option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Constitutional amendments
True
Amendments are tested on the basic structure doctrine (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973); e.g. the 99th Amendment (NJAC) was struck down in 2015.
2. Legislation
True
Laws of Parliament, State Legislatures and subordinate legislation can be struck down if unconstitutional.
3. Administrative action
True
Actions of the Union, States and authorities under the State can be quashed through writs.

points: This is Justice Syed Shah Mohamed Quadri's three-fold classification quoted by Laxmikanth.
Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out at least one true category.
POL-751-CH-01.also: Articles 13, 32 and 226 are key sources of judicial review.

POL-751-CH-02.lead: Option 4: Laxmikanth gives three purposes of judicial review: supremacy of the Constitution, federal equilibrium and protection of Fundamental Rights. Executive supremacy is not one of them.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Constitutional supremacy
A real purpose: the Constitution is the highest law, and courts strike down laws against it. So it is not the answer.
Federal equilibrium
A real purpose: courts keep the Centre and States within their own Lists. So it is not the answer.
Protection of fundamental rights
A real purpose: courts void laws and actions that violate Part III. So it is not the answer.
Executive supremacy
Not a purpose, so it is the answer. Judicial review checks the executive too; it never places the government above the Constitution.

points: The question asks which is NOT a purpose, so the keyed option is the odd one out.

POL-751-CH-03.lead: Option 1: Article 13 declares laws inconsistent with or in derogation of Fundamental Rights void to the extent of the inconsistency.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 13
Correct. It is the main textual basis of judicial review of laws in India.
Article 32
Wrong. Article 32 is the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of Fundamental Rights; it gives the remedy, not the voidness rule.
Article 136
Wrong. Article 136 lets the Supreme Court grant special leave to appeal from any court or tribunal (except military ones).
Article 226
Wrong. Article 226 lets High Courts issue writs for Fundamental Rights and for any other purpose.

points: Article 13(1) covers pre-constitution laws; Article 13(2) bars the State from making new laws that abridge Fundamental Rights.
'To the extent' means only the offending part is void (doctrine of severability).
POL-751-CH-03.also: Article 13(2) bars the State from making laws that take away or abridge FRs.

POL-751-CH-04.lead: Option 2: Article 32 lets a person go directly to the Supreme Court, and Article 226 to a High Court, for writs to enforce rights.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Articles 14 and 19
Wrong. These are rights themselves (equality; six freedoms), not routes to a court.
Articles 32 and 226
Correct. They give the writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts.
Articles 72 and 161
Wrong. These are the pardoning powers of the President and the Governor.
Articles 123 and 213
Wrong. These are the ordinance powers of the President and the Governor.

points: Article 226 is wider than Article 32: High Courts can issue writs for Fundamental Rights and 'for any other purpose'.
Article 32 itself is a Fundamental Right; Ambedkar called it the heart and soul of the Constitution.

POL-751-CH-05.lead: All three are valid grounds, so option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Violates fundamental rights
True
A law that infringes Part III is void under Article 13.
2. Exceeds legislative competence
True
A law made by an authority outside its powers, such as a State legislating on a Union List subject, is invalid.
3. Repugnant to a constitutional provision
True
The Constitution is supreme, so a law conflicting with any of its provisions is invalid.

points: These are exactly the three grounds Laxmikanth lists under 'Scope of judicial review'.
Options 1, 2 and 3 each drop at least one valid ground.

POL-751-CH-06.lead: Option 1: The 1st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951 added Article 31B and the Ninth Schedule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: First Amendment, 1951
Correct. It was made to protect land reform and zamindari abolition laws from Fundamental Rights challenges.
Seventh Amendment, 1956
Wrong. It reorganised the States (abolishing Part A, B, C, D classes) after the States Reorganisation Act, 1956.
Twenty-fourth Amendment, 1971
Wrong. It affirmed Parliament's power to amend any part of the Constitution, including Fundamental Rights, after the Golaknath case.
Forty-second Amendment, 1976
Wrong. Called the 'mini-Constitution', it added 'socialist', 'secular' and 'integrity' to the Preamble and Fundamental Duties.

points: Article 31B saves Ninth Schedule laws from challenge on Fundamental Rights grounds, but post-24 April 1973 entries face the basic-structure test.

POL-751-CH-07.lead: Option 3: Waman Rao (1980) held that laws added to the Ninth Schedule after 24 April 1973, the date of the Kesavananda Bharati judgment, are valid only if they do not damage the basic structure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 26 January 1950
Wrong. This is the date the Constitution came into force, not the Ninth Schedule cut-off.
18 June 1951
Wrong. This is the date of the 1st Amendment, which created the Ninth Schedule; it is not the review cut-off.
24 April 1973
Correct. The basic structure doctrine was laid down on this date, so later insertions are tested against it.
25 June 1975
Wrong. This is the date of the internal Emergency proclamation, unrelated to the cut-off.

points: I.R. Coelho (2007) reaffirmed the same cut-off.
Logic: Parliament could not be bound by a doctrine before the court announced it, so the date of announcement is the line.

POL-751-P297-01.lead: Option 2: Judicial review is the power of the judiciary (Supreme Court and High Courts) to examine the constitutionality of laws and executive orders of both the Centre and the States.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament setting aside SC judgments
Wrong. This reverses the idea; judicial review is a power of courts over the other organs, not of Parliament over courts.
SC and HCs examine laws and executive orders of Centre and States
Correct. This is Laxmikanth's definition; unconstitutional acts are declared null and void.
SC alone, only Parliament's laws
Wrong on two counts: High Courts also have the power, and it covers State laws and executive orders too.
President seeking SC opinion
Wrong. That is the advisory jurisdiction under Article 143, not judicial review.

points: Judicial review in India is conferred by the Constitution itself, unlike the USA where it was declared by the court in Marbury v. Madison (1803).

POL-751-P297-DOCTRINE-01.lead: Option 2: Under pith and substance, the court looks at the true nature and character of a law; if that falls within the legislature's List, an incidental effect on another List does not invalidate it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Any incidental overlap invalidates the whole law
Wrong. Some overlap is unavoidable in a federal division of powers; the doctrine exists to tolerate incidental encroachment.
Incidental effect alone need not invalidate a law within competence
Correct. This is the core of the doctrine.
Governor's assent transfers Parliament's powers
Wrong. Assent only completes the making of a State Act; legislative powers are fixed by Article 246 and the Seventh Schedule.
Ignore the object; examine only the title
Wrong. The doctrine looks at the substance of the law, not its title or label.

points: Leading case: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951), where a prohibition law (State List) was upheld though it touched imports (Union List).
POL-751-P297-DOCTRINE-01.also: Leading case: State of Bombay v. F.N. Balsara (1951).

POL-751-P297-ORIGIN-01.lead: Option 3: Judicial review was first propounded in Marbury v. Madison (1803) by Chief Justice John Marshall of the US Supreme Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Marbury v. Madison - John Jay
Wrong pair. The case is right, but John Jay was the first Chief Justice (1789-1795), not the one who decided Marbury.
Dred Scott v. Sandford - Roger Taney
Wrong. This is a real pairing, but the case was decided in 1857 and concerned slavery, not the 1803 affirmation.
Marbury v. Madison - John Marshall
Correct. Marshall's 1803 judgment held that courts can declare laws contrary to the Constitution void.
McCulloch v. Maryland - Charles Evans Hughes
Wrong. McCulloch (1819) was also decided by Marshall; Hughes was Chief Justice much later, in the 1930s.

points: Laxmikanth: the doctrine 'originated and developed in the USA' and was 'propounded for the first time' in Marbury.

POL-751-P298-01.lead: Option 2: Kesavananda Bharati (1973) held that Parliament can amend any part of the Constitution but cannot alter its basic structure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A.K. Gopalan (1950)
Wrong. It took a narrow view of personal liberty under Article 21, treating each Fundamental Right separately.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973)
Correct. It laid down the basic structure doctrine, limiting the amending power under Article 368.
Maneka Gandhi (1978)
Wrong. It widened Article 21: a law depriving liberty must be just, fair and reasonable.
S.R. Bommai (1994)
Wrong. It limited the misuse of Article 356 (President's Rule) and held secularism a basic feature, but it did not create the doctrine.

points: Judgment date 24 April 1973 is also the Ninth Schedule cut-off used in Waman Rao and Coelho.

POL-751-P299-01.lead: Option 1: The Supreme Court has held judicial review to be a basic feature of the Constitution, and the basic structure cannot be destroyed even by a constitutional amendment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Judicial review is a basic feature
Correct. Laxmikanth: the power of judicial review 'cannot be curtailed or excluded even by a constitutional amendment' (Minerva Mills, 1980; L. Chandra Kumar, 1997).
Every amendment requires a referendum
Wrong. India has no referendum for amendments; Article 368 uses special majorities and, for some provisions, State ratification.
Courts may veto any policy
Wrong. Courts test legality and constitutionality, not the wisdom of policy.
Article 368 prohibits all amendments
Wrong. Article 368 is the very power to amend; it only cannot be used to destroy the basic structure.

points: So an amendment abolishing judicial review would be struck down as violating the basic structure.

POL-761-A01.lead: Statement 1 is true and 2 is false, so option 3 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Indian foundations by Krishna Iyer, Bhagwati, Chinnappa Reddy, Desai
True
Laxmikanth: the doctrine was introduced in India in the mid-1970s and these four judges laid its foundations.
2. Originated in Britain
False
Judicial activism originated and developed in the USA; the term was coined in 1947 by Arthur Schlesinger Jr.

points: Option 1 wrongly accepts statement 2.
Option 2 accepts the false statement and rejects the true one.
Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1.

POL-761-A02.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are Wadehra's reasons and 4 is not, so option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Citizens look to the judiciary for rights
True
Wadehra's reason (ii): citizens look up to the judiciary, putting pressure on it to help the suffering masses.
2. Judicial enthusiasm for social reform
True
Wadehra's reason (iii): judges like to take part in social reforms, which encourages PIL and liberal locus standi.
3. Constitution gives room for an active role
True
Wadehra's reason (v): the Constitution itself has provisions giving the judiciary scope to play an active role.
4. Unlimited authority to disregard limits
False
This is not in Wadehra's list; courts themselves derive power from the Constitution and must act within it.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 all include the false statement 4.
Wadehra's other reasons: near collapse of responsible government, and legislative vacuum.

POL-761-A03.lead: All three appear in Kashyap's list, so option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Legislature fails its responsibilities
True
Kashyap's first eventuality is when the legislature fails to discharge its responsibilities.
2. Weak government in a hung legislature
True
Kashyap's second eventuality: a hung House gives a weak, insecure government unable to take decisions that displease any group.
3. Failure to protect basic rights
True
Kashyap includes cases where the legislature and executive fail to protect basic rights such as a decent life and healthy surroundings.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out at least one listed situation.
Kashyap also lists courts' own craze for populism and publicity as a cause.

head: Item
Matches
Why
rows: A Ideological
Fear of usurping other institutions
B Epistemic
Courts lack technical/economic expertise
C Management
Workload and case arrears

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Legitimation
2. Authority depleted when PIL orders are ignored
Legitimation fear: courts' authority erodes when PIL orders are ignored.
B. Democratic
3. PIL's effect on democracy's future
Democratic fear: is PIL nurturing or depleting democracy?
C. Biographic
1. Judge's post-retirement standing
Biographic fear: the judge's standing after retirement.

points: Option 2 is wrong: it gives A-3, B-2 (should be A-2, B-3).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A-1, C-2 (should be A-2, C-1).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives B-1, C-3 (should be B-3, C-1).

Consumer rights groups

Bar-based groups
In the list (group 12): they raise autonomy and accountability of the judiciary. So not the answer.
Legislature parties of the ruling coalition
Not in the list, so it is the answer. Ruling parties hold power; they are not activist groups that push courts to act against the State.

points: Baxi lists 15 groups, including environmental, child rights, women's rights, media autonomy groups and individual petitioners.

POL-761-A11.lead: Option 2: In Aravali Golf Club (2007) the Supreme Court held that courts cannot direct creation of a post that was never sanctioned and regularise workers against it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Examine an existing statutory entitlement
Normal judicial work: courts may enforce rights already given by law. So not the answer.
Create the unsanctioned post and regularise workers
Beyond jurisdiction, so it is the answer. Creating posts is an executive or legislative function involving money and policy.
Read the governing service rules
Normal judicial work: interpreting rules is the core of a court's job. So not the answer.
Distinguish actual work from a sanctioned post
Normal judicial work: it is a factual and legal inquiry within the court's power. So not the answer.

points: The judgment (Justices A.K. Mathur and Markandey Katju) warned against judicial overreach and stressed separation of powers.

POL-761-A12.lead: Option 3: The Court warned that if judges encroach on the other organs, politicians may react by demanding closer control over the judiciary, threatening its independence.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Independence requires abandoning review
Wrong. Restraint means staying within limits, not giving up judicial review, which is a basic feature.
All executive decisions must be immune
Wrong. Executive action remains reviewable for legality; the case only asked courts not to take over executive functions.
Encroachment can provoke demands for political control of judges
Correct. Self-restraint protects the judiciary's own independence and credibility.
Judges chosen by referendum
Wrong. Nothing in the case or the Constitution suggests electing judges.

points: Lesson: judicial restraint and judicial independence support each other.

POL-761-A13.lead: Option 4: Judicial restraint is linked with respect for precedent and the framers' original intent, staying within lawful interpretation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Purposive development of remedies
Wrong. Moulding law to changing social needs is the mark of judicial activism.
Judge's policy preference decisive
Wrong. Letting personal policy views decide is a definition of activism, and beyond lawful options it becomes overreach.
Refusing all review whenever policy is invoked
Wrong. That is abdication of duty, not restraint; courts must still test legality.
Precedent and original intent
Correct. Restraint means self-control: follow established law and leave policy to the legislature and executive.

points: Laxmikanth: activism departs from 'strict adherence to judicial precedent'; restraint is its antithesis.

POL-761-ACTIVISM-REMEDIAL-AUTHORITY.lead: Option 2: 'Judicial activism' is a description of a style, not a legal power; the court must find an existing power for the order and respect its limits.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Label is an independent source of power
Wrong. Courts get power only from the Constitution and laws, not from how commentators describe past judgments.
Identify an existing legal power and apply its limits
Correct. For example Articles 32, 142 or 226, or a statute, each with its own limits.
Need a statute using the term
Wrong. No law needs to use the word 'activism'; the relief depends on an existing power, whatever it is called.
Decide solely by public policy goal
Wrong. A good policy aim cannot create judicial authority; that would be overreach.

points: Memory hook: labels describe, Articles empower.

POL-761-CH-01.lead: Option 2: The term 'judicial activism' was first coined in 1947 by the American historian Arthur Schlesinger Jr.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A. V. Dicey
Wrong. Dicey, a British jurist, is known for the concept of 'rule of law'.
Arthur Schlesinger Jr.
Correct. He used it in a 1947 Fortune magazine article on the US Supreme Court.
John Marshall
Wrong. Marshall was the US Chief Justice who propounded judicial review in Marbury v. Madison (1803).
Montesquieu
Wrong. The French thinker is known for the theory of separation of powers.

points: Judicial activism originated in the USA; in India it began in the mid-1970s.

POL-761-CH-02.lead: Option 1: Laxmikanth says judicial activism is also known as 'judicial dynamism'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Judicial activism
Correct. The proactive role of courts in protecting rights and pushing other organs to do their duties.
Judicial restraint
Wrong. Restraint is self-control by courts, the antithesis of activism.
Judicial review
Wrong. Review is the power to test laws against the Constitution; activism is one way of using it.
Judicial overreach
Wrong. Overreach is activism that crosses limits and takes over the work of other organs.

points: Dynamism and activism both suggest an active, moving court; restraint suggests holding back.

POL-761-CH-03.lead: Option 2: Laxmikanth names two aspects of Indian judicial activism: directions to government authorities (as in PIL) and expansion of Fundamental Rights by interpretation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Taxation and elections
Wrong. Taxation is a legislative function and elections are run by the Election Commission.
Directions to authorities and expansion of rights
Correct. E.g. Vishaka (1997) guidelines, and the wide reading of Article 21 after Maneka Gandhi (1978).
Treaties and budgets
Wrong. Treaties are made by the executive and budgets passed by the legislature.
Appointments and audits
Wrong. Audit is done by the CAG; these are not the forms of activism named in the book.

points: The rights expanded are mainly Articles 14, 19 and 21.

POL-761-CH-04.lead: Option 1: Laxmikanth says courts expanded Articles 14 (equality), 19 (freedoms) and 21 (life and liberty) through activist interpretation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct. Often called the 'golden triangle' of Fundamental Rights.
Wrong. These are the President's pardon power and the ordinance powers of the President and Governor.
Wrong. These are the CAG, the Finance Commission and the Election Commission.
Wrong. These are the three emergency provisions: national, State (President's Rule) and financial.

points: Coelho also treats Article 21 read with Articles 14 and 19 as reflecting the basic structure.

POL-761-CH-05.lead: Option 1: a legislative vacuum (no law on an urgent issue) and failure of the other organs to do their duty are the accepted grounds for a more active judicial role.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Legislative vacuum and institutional failure
When Parliament has made no law on a pressing matter, or the executive fails to act, courts step in to protect rights until the proper organ acts.
A desire to contest elections
Judges do not contest elections; electoral politics has nothing to do with the judicial role and cannot justify activism.
Routine replacement of every policy
Replacing every government policy would be overreach, because making and running policy is the work of the legislature and executive.
Judicial control of the budget
The budget is passed by Parliament (Articles 112-117); courts have no power to control it, so this cannot justify activism.

points: Laxmikanth defines judicial activism as the proactive role of the judiciary that forces the legislature and executive to discharge their constitutional duties.
Activism is justified when there is a gap or failure elsewhere; it is not a licence to take over the other organs' work.
Memory hook: activism fills a vacuum, it does not replace the government.

POL-761-CH-06.lead: Option 2: Hussainara Khatoon (1979) dealt with undertrial prisoners in Bihar jails kept for years without trial, and the Court held that speedy trial is part of Article 21.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Pollution of the Ganga by tanneries
This is the M.C. Mehta (Ganga pollution) litigation, a later environmental PIL, not Hussainara Khatoon.
Undertrial prisoners and speedy trial
Newspaper reports showed undertrials in Bihar jailed longer than the maximum sentence for their offence; the Court ordered their release and read speedy trial into Article 21.
Sexual harassment at the workplace
This was decided in Vishaka v. State of Rajasthan (1997), which laid down workplace harassment guidelines.
Appointment and transfer of HC judges
This was the subject of S.P. Gupta v. Union of India (1981), the First Judges case, which also widened locus standi.

points: Hussainara Khatoon is widely called the first reported PIL in India; it was filed on behalf of prisoners who could not approach the court themselves.
Concept: PIL lets someone else go to court for people too poor or helpless to do so.
Memory hook: Hussainara = undertrials = speedy trial (Article 21).

POL-761-CH-07.lead: Option 2: when a court permanently runs policy administration, it does the executive's work, which breaks the separation of powers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Collective responsibility
Ministers are collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha (Article 75(3)); this concerns minister-legislature relations, not courts.
Separation of powers
Each organ works in its own field: the legislature makes laws, the executive implements them and the judiciary decides disputes. A court running administration enters the executive's field.
Universal adult franchise
Every adult citizen has the right to vote (Article 326); court activity does not affect who can vote.
Bicameralism
A legislature with two Houses, such as Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha; it has nothing to do with courts taking over administration.

points: Supervising a remedy for a short time is accepted; permanently taking over administration is judicial overreach.
Laxmikanth records the Supreme Court's warning that judicial activism must not become judicial adventurism (LX p440).

POL-761-CH-08.lead: Option 3: judicial restraint means courts keep the power of review but use it with self-control, respecting the roles of the legislature and executive.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: It abolishes judicial review
False. Judicial review is part of the basic structure; restraint only guides how it is used, it does not remove it.
It requires silence in every rights case
False. Even a restrained court must act when a fundamental right is clearly violated, because Articles 32 and 226 make that its duty.
It permits review while respecting institutional limits
True. The court reviews laws and actions but does not substitute its own view on policy matters that belong to elected organs.
It transfers interpretation to the executive
False. Final interpretation of the Constitution stays with the courts; restraint does not hand it to the government.

points: Laxmikanth: judicial activism is the antithesis of judicial restraint, which means the self-control exercised by the judiciary.
Memory hook: restraint = brakes, not removal of the engine.

POL-761-P302-01.lead: Option 2: judicial activism is the proactive role of the judiciary in protecting citizens' rights and making the legislature and executive discharge their constitutional duties.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Refusal of courts to examine government policy
This is judicial abdication or extreme restraint, the opposite of activism.
Proactive role protecting rights and pushing other organs to act
This is exactly Laxmikanth's definition of judicial activism.
Parliament overriding Supreme Court judgments
This describes a legislative power, not any approach of the judiciary, so it cannot define judicial activism.
Strict following of precedent and framers' intent
This is judicial restraint; Laxmikanth notes activism departs from strict adherence to precedent in favour of progressive social policy.

points: Judicial activism is also called judicial dynamism (LX p437).
In India it began in the mid-1970s with Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer, P.N. Bhagwati, O. Chinnappa Reddy and D.A. Desai.

POL-761-P303-01.lead: Option 3: continuously replacing executive administration is judicial overreach, because the court is doing the executive's job instead of reviewing it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Testing constitutionality
This is ordinary judicial review of laws and executive actions, a core and legitimate court function.
Protecting a proven right
Enforcing a fundamental right once violation is shown is the court's duty under Articles 32 and 226.
Continuously replacing executive administration
Here the court itself runs government work on a continuing basis, crossing into the executive's field.
Following binding precedent
Courts are bound by earlier rulings of higher courts; under Article 141 Supreme Court law binds all courts, so this is normal.

points: Overreach (also called judicial adventurism) is activism that goes beyond the court's proper role.
The Supreme Court warned that judicial activism must not become judicial adventurism (LX p440).

POL-762-A01.lead: Option 1: Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati were the pioneers of PIL in India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati
Laxmikanth names these two Supreme Court judges as the pioneers of PIL; they accepted letters and relaxed locus standi.
John Marshall and Arthur Schlesinger Jr.
Marshall was the US Chief Justice of Marbury v. Madison (judicial review); Schlesinger coined 'judicial activism' in 1947.
A.V. Dicey and Montesquieu
Dicey explained the rule of law; Montesquieu explained separation of powers. Neither was an Indian judge.
M.C. Setalvad and C.K. Daphtary
They were eminent Attorneys-General of India (Setalvad the first), i.e. government lawyers, not PIL-pioneering judges.

points: PIL in India grew in the late 1970s and early 1980s out of judicial activism.
Memory hook: 'Iyer-Bhagwati' = PIL pair.

POL-762-A02.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Social Interest Litigation
True
Laxmikanth lists Social Interest Litigation (SIL) as another name of PIL.
2. Class Action Litigation
True
Laxmikanth also lists Class Action Litigation (CAL) as another name, because a whole class of people is represented.

points: Options 1 and 2 are wrong because each leaves out one correct name.
Option 4 is wrong because both names are recognised.
The third name is Social Action Litigation (SAL).

POL-762-A03.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so the answer is option 4 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Petitioner, authority and court cooperate
True
Laxmikanth: PIL is essentially a co-operative effort of the petitioner, the State or public authority and the court to secure rights of vulnerable sections.
2. Flexibility removes fairness and proof
False
The court has flexibility, but whatever procedure it adopts must still be one known to judicial tenets; fairness is not removed.

points: Option 1 (both) and option 2 (2 only) wrongly accept statement 2.
Option 3 (neither) wrongly rejects statement 1.
Concept: PIL is non-adversarial, but it is still a judicial proceeding.

POL-762-A04.lead: Option 2: the letter-PIL categories include non-payment of minimum wages, exploitation of casual workers and labour-law violations, except in individual cases.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Every individual service dispute must be PIL
Wrong. Individual cases are expressly excluded, and service matters are in the list of matters not entertained as PIL.
Minimum-wage, casual-worker and labour-law complaints, except individual cases
This is the exact wording of category 3 of the Supreme Court's 1988 guidelines (modified 1993 and 2003).
Only employers may raise minimum-wage complaints
Wrong. PIL exists so that workers or public-spirited persons can complain on behalf of exploited workers; it is not limited to employers.
Labour category excludes every collective complaint
Wrong. Collective exploitation is precisely what the category covers; only individual cases are left out.

points: Reason: PIL is for wrongs affecting many weak people, not a personal service grievance.
Individual disputes go to labour courts or ordinary writs.

POL-762-A05.lead: All three are listed letter-PIL categories, so the answer is option 1 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Neglected children
True
It is category 2 in the Supreme Court's list of letters or petitions ordinarily entertained as PIL.
2. Harassment/torture of SC/ST or backward villagers
True
Category 7 covers harassment or torture of villagers by co-villagers or police, from SC, ST and economically backward classes.
3. Petitions from riot victims
True
Category 9 is petitions from riot-victims.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 each leave out one true statement, so they fail.
Other categories: bonded labour, minimum wages, jail petitions, police excesses, atrocities on women, environment and family pension.

POL-762-A06.lead: All three are listed categories, so the answer is option 3 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Police refusal to register, harassment, custodial death
True
Category 5 covers petitions against police for refusing to register a case, police harassment and death in police custody.
2. Atrocities on women
True
Category 6 covers atrocities on women, such as harassment of brides, bride-burning, rape, murder and kidnapping.
3. Pollution, drugs, adulteration, heritage, forests, wildlife
True
Category 8 covers environmental pollution, ecological balance, drugs, food adulteration, heritage and culture, antiques, forest and wildlife and other matters of public importance.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each omit one true statement.
The list was framed in 1988 and modified in 1993 and 2003.

POL-762-A07.lead: Option 4: in Sunil Batra (II) v. Delhi Administration (1980), the Supreme Court treated a prisoner's letter about the torture of a fellow inmate in Tihar Jail as a writ petition.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Kharak Singh v. State of U.P.
A 1963 case on police surveillance and domiciliary visits, linked to personal liberty and privacy, not a letter petition.
A.D.M. Jabalpur v. Shivkant Shukla
The 1976 Emergency case holding that habeas corpus could not be sought while Article 21 enforcement was suspended.
Nilabati Behera v. State of Orissa
A 1993 case awarding compensation for a custodial death under Article 32; it is not the Tihar letter case.
Sunil Batra v. Delhi Administration
Prisoner Sunil Batra wrote to the Court about torture of a co-prisoner; Justice Krishna Iyer treated the letter as a habeas corpus petition.

points: This is epistolary (letter) jurisdiction, a key feature of PIL.
Sunil Batra (I) in 1978 dealt with solitary confinement (LX case list); the letter case is the second one.

POL-762-A08.lead: Option 2: D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997) began as a letter from the Legal Aid Services, West Bengal, on custodial deaths, and produced binding arrest and detention guidelines.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Joginder Kumar v. State of U.P. (1994)
This case held that police must justify an arrest and inform a friend or relative, but it was not the legal-aid letter case.
D.K. Basu v. State of West Bengal (1997)
A letter on custodial deaths was treated as a writ petition, and the Court issued detailed guidelines (arrest memo, informing relatives, medical check-up).
Lalita Kumari v. Govt of U.P. (2013)
This case held that registering an FIR is mandatory when a complaint discloses a cognizable offence.
Arnesh Kumar v. State of Bihar (2014)
This case restrained automatic arrests in offences punishable up to seven years, especially dowry-harassment cases.

points: D.K. Basu shows how a letter-PIL can protect Article 21 rights of people in custody.
Memory hook: 'Basu = Bureau of legal aid letter = arrest guidelines'.

POL-762-A09.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are in the excluded list and bonded labour is an included category, so the answer is option 1 (1, 2 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Landlord-tenant disputes
True (excluded)
Landlord-tenant matters are item 1 of the matters not entertained as PIL, because they are private disputes.
2. Service, pension and gratuity
True (excluded)
Service matters and those on pension and gratuity are item 2 of the excluded list; they are individual grievances.
3. Admission to medical/educational institutions
True (excluded)
Admission matters are item 4 of the excluded list.
4. Bonded labour petitions
False (not excluded)
Bonded labour is category 1 of the matters ordinarily entertained as PIL.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 fail because each includes statement 4 (bonded labour), which is a core PIL subject.
Note: family pension is an included category, while service pension is excluded.

POL-762-A10.lead: Guruvayur gave PIL principles; BALCO said PIL is no panacea; Chaufal gave guidelines.

head: Case
Year
Associated idea
rows: A. Guruvayur Devaswom v. C.K. Rajan
2 — PIL principles framework
B. BALCO Employees Union
1 — PIL not a panacea
C. Balwant Singh Chaufal
3 — misuse-control guidelines

points: So the order is 2-1-3.
POL-762-A10.also: BALCO was decided on 10 December 2001; it is reported as (2002) 2 SCC 333.

POL-762-A11.lead: Option 4: whether res judicata applies in a PIL depends on the nature of the petition and the facts and circumstances of the case.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: It never applies to any PIL
Wrong. Procedural laws do apply to PIL, so res judicata is not ruled out completely.
It automatically bars every later petition
Wrong. It is not automatic; the court looks at the nature of the petition first.
The PIL label reopens every final judgment
Wrong. Calling a case PIL does not defeat finality of judgments.
Depends on nature of petition and facts
This is principle 6 laid down in Guruvayur Devaswom Managing Committee v. C.K. Rajan (2003).

points: Res judicata means a matter finally decided by a competent court cannot be reopened by the same parties; it exists for finality in litigation.
In PIL the court applies it flexibly, case by case.

POL-762-A12.lead: Option 2: in a fit case the court may look at the wider public wrong, but a purely private quarrel does not become a PIL just by its label (Guruvayur Devaswom, 2003).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Any private origin permanently bars inquiry
Too rigid; Guruvayur allows the court to examine wider public affairs in the interest of justice.
Court may examine broader affairs; private quarrel is not PIL by label
Exactly Guruvayur's qualification: substance decides, not the title.
Every personal grievance must be admitted as PIL
Opposite error; PIL is for public interest, not private disputes.
Personal gain alone proves public interest
Personal gain is a ground to reject a PIL, not to prove one.

points: Guruvayur (2003) laid down principles on when a PIL is maintainable.
The court looks at substance: is there a genuine public injury or public duty failure?

POL-762-A13.lead: Option 1: in special situations the court may appoint a commission or other body to investigate allegations and find facts.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Appoint a commission or body to find facts
Principle 9 of the Guruvayur principles allows this; the court may even direct management of a public institution taken over by such a commission.
Treat allegations as proved
Wrong. Relaxing who can file (locus standi) does not relax proof; facts must still be verified.
Hand permanent departmental power to petitioner
Wrong. The court cannot give executive power to a private petitioner; that would break separation of powers.
Reject all fact-finding
Wrong. PIL often needs facts, which is exactly why commissions are appointed.

points: Poor victims cannot collect evidence themselves, so the court gathers facts through commissions.

POL-762-A14.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are true and 1 is false, so the answer is option 3 (2 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Each judge invents own PIL procedure
False
The guideline says the opposite: instead of every judge devising his own procedure, each High Court should formulate rules.
2. High Courts should frame proper PIL rules
True
Guideline 2 asks each High Court to frame rules encouraging genuine PIL and discouraging PIL with oblique motives.
3. Larger public interest, gravity and urgency get priority
True
Guideline 6 says such petitions must be given priority over other petitions.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 fail because each includes the false statement 1.
Other guidelines: verify the petitioner's credentials, check the petition's contents, and impose exemplary costs on busybodies.

POL-762-A15.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 4 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 'Paisa Interest Litigation' = money motive
True
Laxmikanth lists it among labels of PIL misuse, where a public-interest petition actually serves private monetary gain.
2. 'Middle-class Interest Litigation' is no ban on genuine middle-class petitioners
True
It is a criticism that PIL is drifting to middle-class concerns; it is not a rule that stops any genuine petitioner.

points: Options 1 and 2 each leave out a true statement; option 3 rejects both.
Other misuse labels: Publicity, Politics and Private Interest Litigation.

POL-762-CH-01.lead: Option 1: PIL is also known as Social Action Litigation (SAL).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Social action litigation
Laxmikanth lists SAL as another name of PIL: litigation used as social action for poor and voiceless groups.
Fiscal litigation
Cases about taxes and public finance; it is not a name for PIL.
Electoral adjudication
Deciding election disputes through election petitions; it has nothing to do with PIL.
Private arbitration
Private parties settling a dispute before an arbitrator outside court; PIL is the opposite, a public court case.

points: Other names: Social Interest Litigation (SIL) and Class Action Litigation (CAL).
POL-762-CH-01.also: Pioneers in India: Justices V.R. Krishna Iyer and P.N. Bhagwati.

POL-762-CH-02.lead: Option 1: PIL is filed under Article 32 in the Supreme Court and Article 226 in the High Courts.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Articles 32 and 226
Writ jurisdiction of the Supreme Court and High Courts; Laxmikanth says courts entertain PIL in exercise of these powers.
Articles 72 and 161
Pardoning powers of the President and the Governor; unrelated to litigation.
Articles 123 and 213
Ordinance-making powers of the President and the Governor; these are executive law-making powers.
Articles 148 and 280
The Comptroller and Auditor General and the Finance Commission; these are constitutional bodies, not court routes.

points: PIL is a form of writ petition, so it travels through the writ Articles.
Memory hook: 32 = Supreme Court, 226 = High Court.

POL-762-CH-03.lead: Option 2: epistolary jurisdiction means a court may treat a letter or postcard addressed to it as a writ petition.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Decide appeals only on written briefs
This is a mode of hearing, not epistolary jurisdiction.
Treat a letter or postcard as a writ petition
'Epistolary' means 'by letter'; courts accept letters or telegrams as PIL in matters of public importance.
Advisory opinion to the President by letter
Advisory jurisdiction is under Article 143, on a reference by the President, not a letter from a citizen.
Transfer a case between High Courts
Transfer of cases is a separate Supreme Court power and has nothing to do with letters.

points: Example: in Sunil Batra (II) (1980), a prisoner's letter was treated as a writ petition.
The court relaxes procedural law and pleadings in such cases.

POL-762-CH-04.lead: Option 1: requiring the petitioner to be the person whose own right is violated is the old locus standi rule; PIL is the exception to it, so it is NOT a feature of PIL.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Petitioner must be the person personally harmed
This is the traditional locus standi rule that PIL relaxes; any public-spirited person can file for others.
Court is active and may appoint commissions
A real feature: the court is assertive and may appoint commissions to find facts.
Proceedings not strictly adversarial
A real feature: PIL is a co-operative effort, not a fight between two parties.
Procedural technicalities are relaxed
A real feature: the court relaxes procedure and pleadings, even accepting letters.

points: In a NOT-question, the right answer is the one statement that contradicts PIL.

POL-762-CH-05.lead: Option 2: any public-spirited person or social organisation can file a PIL for people who cannot approach the court themselves.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Article 73
Extent of the executive power of the Union.

Inter-State Council set up by the President.

What it is / means
Correct?

No such Act exists; the 1956 law under Art 262 for dispute tribunals is the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act.
National Water Policy Act
No such Act exists; the National Water Policy is a government policy, not a law.

POL-8.1.2-Q24.lead: Option 3: under Art 263 the President can establish an Inter-State Council.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Prime Minister
The PM chairs the Council but does not create it.
The Parliament
No law of Parliament is needed; the Council is set up by a Presidential order.
The President
Art 263 empowers the President to set up the Council if public interest needs it; one was set up in 1990.
The Union Home Minister
The Union Home Minister is only a member of the Council; the power to set it up lies with the President under Art 263.

points: It was set up in 1990 on the Sarkaria Commission's recommendation.

POL-8.1.2-Q25.lead: Option 4 is NOT a function: the Inter-State Council (ISC) only inquires and advises; it cannot give binding awards on river water disputes.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Inquiring into and advising on disputes between states
Art 263(a): the ISC may inquire into and advise on disputes between states. This is a listed duty.
2. Investigating subjects of common interest
Art 263(b): the ISC may investigate and discuss subjects of common interest to states or the Centre. This is a listed duty.
3. Recommending better coordination of policy
Art 263(c): the ISC may make recommendations for better coordination of policy and action. This is a listed duty.
4. Adjudicating inter-state river water disputes with binding awards
Binding adjudication of inter-state river water disputes is done by tribunals set up under Art 262 and the Inter-State River Water Disputes Act, 1956, not by the ISC.

points: Art 263 lets the President set up an ISC with three duties (a), (b) and (c) — all are advisory in nature.
An advisory body recommends; it cannot decide a dispute with a final, binding award.
Memory hook: 262 = water tribunals (decide); 263 = council (advise).

POL-8.1.2-Q26.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct and 3 is wrong, so the answer is option 4 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. First set up in 1990 on Sarkaria's recommendation
True
The Sarkaria Commission (1983-88) recommended a permanent ISC, and the V.P. Singh government set it up by presidential order in 1990.
2. Chaired by the Prime Minister
True
The Prime Minister is the ex-officio Chairman of the ISC.
3. Members are only CMs and UT Administrators
False
Members also include six Union Cabinet ministers (including the Home Minister) nominated by the PM, Governors of states under President's Rule, and CMs of UTs having legislatures.

points: Option 1 (1, 2 and 3) and option 3 (1 and 3 only) fail because they include the wrong statement 3.
Option 2 (2 and 3 only) fails because it drops the true statement 1 and adds the false statement 3.
The word 'only' in statement 3 is the trap: the ISC is a wider body than CMs and Administrators.

POL-8.1.2-Q27.lead: Option 4: the Chief Justice of India is not a member; the ISC is an executive coordination body, so no judge sits on it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Chief Ministers of UTs having legislative assemblies
The CMs of UTs having legislative assemblies (e.g. Delhi, Puducherry) are members of the ISC.
2. Governors of states under President's Rule
Governors of states under President's Rule are members, because during President's Rule they run the state government.
3. Six Union Cabinet Ministers nominated by the Prime Minister
Six Union Cabinet ministers, including the Home Minister, nominated by the PM are members.
4. The Chief Justice of India
The CJI heads the judiciary; he is not part of the ISC, which is made up only of political executives of the Centre, states and UTs.

points: Full ISC list: PM (Chairman), CMs of all states, CMs of UTs with legislatures, Administrators of UTs without legislatures, Governors of states under President's Rule, and six Union Cabinet ministers.
Keeping judges out protects separation of powers: the ISC advises on policy, and courts may later have to decide disputes.
POL-8.1.2-Q27.also: Permanent invitees: five Cabinet-rank ministers / Ministers of State (independent charge) nominated by the PM.

False

Option 3 (both) fails because of statement 2; option 4 (neither) fails because statement 1 is a correct reading of Art 307.

POL-8.1.2-Q30.lead: Option 4: the Indian Foreign Service is a Central Service, not an All-India Service.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Indian Administrative Service
IAS is an All-India Service; in 1947 the ICS was replaced by the IAS.
2. Indian Police Service
IPS is an All-India Service; in 1947 the Indian Police was replaced by the IPS.
3. Indian Forest Service
The Indian Forest Service (IFoS) was created in 1963 and came into existence in 1966 as the third All-India Service.
4. Indian Foreign Service
The Indian Foreign Service officers work only under the Union (Ministry of External Affairs) and are not allotted to state cadres, so it is a Central Service.

points: An All-India Service officer is recruited by the Centre but serves in a state cadre, under both Centre and state.
Only three All-India Services exist today: IAS, IPS and IFoS.
Trap: the abbreviation 'IFS' can mean Foreign Service or Forest Service — only the Forest Service is an AIS.

POL-8.1.2-Q31.lead: Statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is wrong, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

True/False
Why

True
All-India Service officers are recruited through UPSC and trained by the Centre.
2. Ultimate control lies with the state
False
Ultimate control lies with the Centre; the state where the officer serves has only immediate (day-to-day) control.

points: Option 2 and option 3 fail because both accept statement 2, which reverses the position.
Option 4 fails because statement 1 is true.
Example: a state can suspend an IAS officer, but major penalties like dismissal can be imposed only by the Centre.

POL-8.1.2-Q32.lead: Correct order is 2, 4, 1, 3 (option 3): IAS 1947 → Art 258A 1956 → IFoS 1966 → ISC 1990.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

4,2,1,3 is wrong because it puts the 7th Amendment (1956) before the IAS (1947).
2,4,1,3 is correct: ICS→IAS 1947, 7th Amendment adds Art 258A 1956, IFoS comes into existence 1966, ISC set up 1990.
2,4,3,1 is wrong because it puts the ISC (1990) before the IFoS (1966).

points: ICS was replaced by IAS in 1947.
The 7th Amendment Act, 1956 inserted Art 258A (states entrusting functions to the Union).
IFoS was created in 1963 and came into existence in 1966; the ISC was set up in 1990 after the Sarkaria report.

POL-8.1.2-Q33.lead: Option 2: under Art 312 the Rajya Sabha resolution must be supported by two-thirds of members present and voting.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A simple majority of members present
A simple majority is used for ordinary business; Art 312 needs a special majority.
2. Two-thirds of members present and voting
Two-thirds of members present and voting is exactly what Art 312 requires for creating a new All-India Service.
3. An absolute majority of total membership
An absolute majority of total membership is not the test in Art 312.
4. Two-thirds of total membership
Two-thirds of total membership is not the test either; only those present and voting are counted.

points: The Rajya Sabha represents states, so its special resolution is needed before the Centre creates a service that will work in the states.
After the resolution, Parliament creates the service by an ordinary law.
POL-8.1.2-Q33.also: The same majority is used under Art 249 for laws on State List subjects in the national interest.

POL-8.1.2-Q34.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A). Central control over State officers is why AIS is called anti-federal.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
All-India Services are criticised as violating the spirit of federalism.
R
True
IAS/IPS officers hold top State posts but are recruited, and ultimately controlled, by the Centre.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Central control over officers running State administration is the precise federal objection.
Option 2 (both true, R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: R is true.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: A is true.
POL-8.1.2-Q34.also: Justification: high standards, uniformity, coordination; Ambedkar backed AIS for strategic posts.

POL-8.1.2-Q35.lead: Option 3: SPSC members are appointed by the Governor but can be removed only by the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Governor
The Governor appoints, and may suspend a member pending the Supreme Court inquiry on misbehaviour, but cannot remove.
2. The Chief Minister
The Chief Minister has no power to remove SPSC members.
3. The President
The President alone can remove them, on grounds and in the manner given in Art 317.
4. The state legislature
The state legislature has no role in removing SPSC members.

points: Art 317: removal is by the President; for misbehaviour, only after an inquiry by the Supreme Court.
Purpose: to protect the SPSC from pressure from the state government that appointed it.

POL-8.1.2-Q36.lead: Both statements are correct, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Parliament can create a JSPSC for two or more states on their request
True
Art 315(2): Parliament can provide for a Joint State PSC when the legislatures of the states concerned pass resolutions; its members are appointed by the President.
2. UPSC can serve a state on the Governor's request with the President's approval
True
Art 315(4): UPSC can serve the needs of a state on the request of the Governor and with the approval of the President.

points: Options 1 and 2 fail because each drops one true statement.
Option 4 fails because both statements are true.
Note: a JSPSC is a statutory body (created by Parliament's law), unlike UPSC and SPSC which are constitutional bodies.
POL-8.1.2-Q36.also: UPSC also assists states in joint recruitment for posts needing special qualifications.

POL-8.1.2-Q37.lead: Option 2: under Art 217, HC judges are appointed by the President after consulting the CJI and the Governor of the state.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Chief Minister and the state Law Minister
The Chief Minister and state Law Minister are not named consultees in Art 217.
2. The Chief Justice of India and the Governor of the state
The CJI and the Governor are the consultees named in Art 217 (plus the HC Chief Justice for other judges).
3. The Union Law Minister only
The Union Law Minister is not a constitutional consultee for HC appointments.
4. The state Public Service Commission
The SPSC selects state civil servants and has no role in appointing judges.

points: For a judge other than the Chief Justice, the Chief Justice of that High Court is also consulted.
In practice, after the Judges cases, names come through the collegium of the Supreme Court.
POL-8.1.2-Q37.also: The President can also transfer HC judges (Art 222) and removes them on Parliament's address.

POL-8.1.2-Q38.lead: Option 2: Art 231 lets Parliament, by law, establish a common High Court for two or more states.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Supreme Court
The Supreme Court decides cases; it has no power to create courts.
2. The Parliament by law
Parliament by law can set up a common High Court for two or more states and a UT (Art 231).
3. The two state legislatures jointly
State legislatures cannot jointly create a High Court; establishing a common HC is Parliament's power.
4. The Inter-State Council
The Inter-State Council only advises (Art 263) and cannot set up courts.

points: Normally each state has its own HC (Art 214), but Art 231 is the exception.
Examples: Bombay HC (Maharashtra, Goa, and UTs of Dadra and Nagar Haveli and Daman and Diu); Punjab and Haryana HC (with Chandigarh); Gauhati HC (Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, Arunachal Pradesh).

POL-8.1.2-Q39.lead: Option 4: Andhra Pradesh and Telangana no longer share a High Court; AP got its separate High Court in 2019.

What it is / means
Correct?

The Bombay High Court serves both Maharashtra and Goa, so this pair does share a HC.
2. Punjab and Haryana
The Punjab and Haryana High Court serves both states and Chandigarh, so this pair shares a HC.
3. Assam and Nagaland
The Gauhati High Court serves Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram and Arunachal Pradesh, so this pair shares a HC.
4. Andhra Pradesh and Telangana
Since 1 January 2019, Andhra Pradesh has its own High Court (at Amaravati), and the Hyderabad HC became the Telangana HC.

points: After the 2014 bifurcation, the two states first shared the High Court at Hyderabad.
The common HC is created by Parliament under Art 231.
