POL-8.1.2-Q41.lead: Option 2: Art 353(a) extends the Union's executive power to giving directions to any state on any matter during a National Emergency.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 352
Art 352 is the proclamation of National Emergency itself, not the power of directions.
2. Article 353
Art 353 gives the effect of the proclamation: the Centre can direct any state on any matter (353(a)), and Parliament can legislate on any matter (353(b)).
3. Article 354
Art 354 allows the President to modify the distribution of revenues between Centre and states during an Emergency.
4. Article 358
Art 358 suspends the Art 19 freedoms during an Emergency declared on war or external aggression.

points: During a National Emergency, the state governments are not suspended, but they come under the complete control of the Centre.
Memory hook: 352 declares, 353 directs, 354 money, 358 Art 19.

POL-8.1.2-Q42.lead: Option 2: a direction to reduce salaries of state employees is a Financial Emergency power under Art 360.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. President's Rule under Article 356
Under President's Rule the Centre takes over state functions, but salary-cut directions are not the Art 356 power.
2. Financial Emergency under Article 360
During a Financial Emergency (Art 360) the Centre can direct states to observe financial propriety, including reduction of salaries of persons serving the state.
3. Directions under Article 256
Art 256 obliges states to comply with Parliament's laws; it is not a salary-cut provision.
4. National Emergency under Article 352
Art 352/353 allow directions on 'any' matter, but the Constitution specifically names salary reduction as a Financial Emergency direction.

points: Art 360 is meant for a threat to the financial stability or credit of India.
The Centre can also ask states to reserve money bills for the President's consideration during a Financial Emergency.
POL-8.1.2-Q42.also: Art 360 also lets the President direct reduction of salaries of SC and HC judges. A Financial Emergency has never been declared in India.

POL-8.1.2-Q43.lead: Option 2: Art 355 lays down the duty of the Union to protect every state against external aggression and internal disturbance.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 352
Art 352 deals with proclamation of National Emergency, not the general duty of protection.
2. Article 355
Art 355 imposes two duties on the Centre: protect every state, and ensure each state is governed according to the Constitution.
3. Article 356
Art 356 is President's Rule, the remedy used when a state's constitutional machinery fails.
4. Article 365
Art 365 says that failure to obey Union directions allows the President to treat it as a breakdown of constitutional machinery.

points: Art 355 is the 'duty'; Arts 352 and 356 are the 'tools' to discharge it.
The Centre can deploy armed forces in a state in aid of civil power under Union List Entry 2A.

POL-8.1.2-Q44.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A). President's Rule flows from the Article 355 duty.

True/False

True
President's Rule (Article 356) can be imposed when State government cannot be carried on per the Constitution.
R
True
Article 355 makes it the Union's duty to ensure every State is governed per the Constitution.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Article 356 is the means by which the Union carries out its Article 355 duty.
Option 2 (both true, R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: R is true.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: A is true.

POL-8.1.2-Q45.lead: Statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is wrong, so the answer is option 1.

2. Governor can remove the SEC at pleasure

The security of tenure keeps the SEC independent while conducting panchayat and municipal elections.

POL-8.1.2-Q46.lead: Option 4: the Finance Commission is a constitutional body (Art 280); the other three are not created by the Constitution.

Correct?

POL-8.2.1-Q02.lead: Option 3: the Rajamannar Committee (appointed by Tamil Nadu, 1969) recommended that residuary powers be allocated to the states.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Sarkaria Commission
The Sarkaria Commission (1983) said residuary taxation should stay with Parliament and other residuary powers should go to the Concurrent List — not to the states.
2. Punchhi Commission
The Punchhi Commission (2007) did not recommend giving residuary powers to the states.
3. Rajamannar Committee
The Rajamannar Committee (1969-71) recommended allocating residuary powers to the states, as part of its demand for maximum state autonomy.
4. First Administrative Reforms Commission
The First Administrative Reforms Commission (1966) studied administration and did not recommend residuary powers for the states.

points: Under Art 248 and Union Entry 97, residuary power is with Parliament (Canadian model).
Rajamannar also wanted the ISC set up immediately, Arts 356, 357 and 365 omitted, and All-India Services abolished; the Centre ignored its report.
POL-8.2.1-Q02.also: The Anandpur Sahib Resolution (1973) also demanded residuary powers for the states.

POL-8.2.1-Q03.lead: Option 4: India has a single integrated judiciary, so judicial power is not divided between the Centre and the states.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Legislative power
Legislative power is divided through the Union, State and Concurrent Lists of the Seventh Schedule.
2. Executive power
Executive power is divided on the same lines as legislative power.
3. Financial power
Financial (taxing) power is divided: some taxes are levied by the Centre and some by the states.
4. Judicial power
Judicial power is not divided: one hierarchy of courts — SC, HCs, subordinate courts — enforces both Central and state laws.

points: In the USA, federal laws are enforced by federal courts and state laws by state courts (double judiciary).
The integrated judiciary is a unitary feature of the Indian Constitution.

POL-8.2.1-Q04.lead: Statement 1 is correct and statement 2 is wrong, so the answer is option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. A Parliamentary law cannot be invalid just because it operates outside India
True
Art 245(2) protects extra-territorial operation of Parliamentary laws; they can apply to Indian citizens and their property anywhere in the world.
2. A state can legislate for any part of India in its interest
False
Art 245(1) limits a state legislature to the whole or any part of that state; it cannot legislate for other states.

points: Options 2 and 3 fail because they accept the false statement 2.
Option 4 fails because statement 1 is true.
A state law reaching outside its territory is valid only if there is a sufficient territorial nexus with the state.

POL-8.2.1-Q05.lead: Option 4: a law that acts on things done abroad is saved by Art 245(2), which allows extra-territorial legislation by Parliament.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Art 252 – consent of states
Art 252 is about Parliament legislating on State List matters when two or more states request it; it has nothing to do with acts abroad.
2. Art 246(3) – State List
Art 246(3) gives states power over State List subjects; it does not deal with territorial reach.
3. Art 248 – residuary power

POL-8.2.1-Q44.lead: Option 2: under Art 254(1) the Union law prevails, and the state law is void only to the extent of the repugnancy.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: the state law prevails
Wrong as a general rule; the state law can prevail only under the Art 254(2) exception, when it was reserved for and received the President's assent.
✗ Wrong
the Union law prevails and the state law is void to that extent
Correct: the Union law overrides, and only the conflicting part of the state law becomes void, not the whole law.
✓ Correct
both laws become void
Wrong, because repugnancy does not destroy the Union law; the Union law continues to operate.
✗ Wrong
the Supreme Court must refer it to the President
Wrong; Art 254 needs no reference to the President, and the courts themselves decide repugnancy.
✗ Wrong

points: Repugnancy means a Union law and a state law on the same Concurrent List subject cannot stand together.
'To the extent of repugnancy' means the rest of the state law survives.

POL-8.2.1-Q45.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. An assented state law repugnant to an earlier Union law prevails in that state
True
Art 254(2): if a state law on a Concurrent List matter is reserved for the President and receives his assent, it prevails in that state.
2. Parliament can never later override that state law
False
The proviso to Art 254(2) lets Parliament later make a law adding to, amending, varying or repealing that state law.

points: Option 2 and option 3 fail because they treat statement 2 as true.
Option 4 fails because statement 1 is a correct statement of the Art 254(2) exception.
Hook: the President's assent gives the state law life, but Parliament keeps the last word.

POL-8.2.1-Q46.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
If the President later assents to such an Act, the missing previous sanction does not make it invalid.
R
True
Art 255 treats recommendation and previous sanction as matters of procedure only.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Since sanction is only procedure, a later assent can cure the defect; that is why the Act stays valid.
Option 2 fails: R is not a separate fact here; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.
Procedure defect + later assent = valid Act (Art 255).

POL-8.2.1-Q47.lead: The money-lending law is a State List law in its true nature; touching promissory notes is only incidental. So Pith and Substance saves it.

head: Option
Meaning
Fits?
rows: Colourable Legislation
a law that looks valid in form but in substance does what the legislature has no power to do. 'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.'
No - the state is not hiding a Union law; the overlap is incidental
Pith and Substance ✓
look at the true nature (core) of a law to decide which List it belongs to; small incidental overlap with another List is ignored.
Yes - core = money-lending (State List)
Repugnancy
a clash between a Central and a state law on a Concurrent subject; under Art 254 the Central law usually prevails.
No - this is State vs Union List, not a Concurrent List clash
Territorial Nexus
a state law can reach a person or thing outside the state if there is a real link (nexus) with the state. Example: taxing a company registered in the state on its total business.
No - no outside-state element

points: Laxmikanth p. 922: if the pith and substance of a law is within a List, incidental encroachment on another List does not make it invalid.
Classic case: Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee (1947), Bengal money-lending law.

POL-8.2.1-Q48.lead: Option 1: in State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara (1951) the Supreme Court used pith and substance to uphold the Bombay Prohibition Act, 1949.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: State of Bombay v F.N. Balsara
The Act was challenged as encroaching on a matter in the Union List; the Court held its true nature lay in the State List, so the incidental effect did not invalidate it.
✓ Correct
K.C. Gajapati Narayan Deo v State of Orissa
The leading case on the doctrine of colourable legislation, not pith and substance.
✗ Wrong
State of West Bengal v Union of India
A 1962 case on whether the Union could acquire property belonging to a state; it is about federal character, not this Act.
✗ Wrong
S.R. Bommai v Union of India
The 1994 case that limited the misuse of Art 356 (President's Rule).
✗ Wrong

points: Pith and substance: find the true nature of a law; if it falls in the legislature's own List, incidental overlap with another List is ignored.
LX also cites Prafulla Kumar Mukherjee (1947) and State of Rajasthan v G. Chawla (1959) for this doctrine.

POL-8.2.1-Q49.lead: 'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly' is the base of the doctrine of Colourable Legislation.

head: Option
Meaning
Fits?
rows: Pith and Substance
look at the true nature (core) of a law to decide which List it belongs to; small incidental overlap with another List is ignored.
No - it is a test of a law's true nature, not this maxim
Colourable Legislation ✓
a law that looks valid in form but in substance does what the legislature has no power to do. 'What cannot be done directly cannot be done indirectly.'
Yes - Laxmikanth states this exact maxim
Residuary Powers
subjects in none of the three Lists; Parliament alone can make laws on them (Art 248).
No - it is about leftover subjects
Territorial Nexus
a state law can reach a person or thing outside the state if there is a real link (nexus) with the state. Example: taxing a company registered in the state on its total business.
No - it is about territory

points: Laxmikanth p. 925: the whole doctrine rests on 'you cannot do indirectly what you cannot do directly'.
Such a law is declared void even though it looks valid in form.

POL-8.2.1-Q50.lead: Option 1 (A-3, B-4, C-1, D-2) is correct.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept

B. Colourable Legislation
4. Disguised transgression struck down
Colourable legislation: a disguised transgression is struck down.
C. Repugnancy
1. Direct Union-State clash
Repugnancy (Art 254): direct clash of Union and State laws on a Concurrent subject - Union law prevails.
D. Residuary Powers

POL-8.2.1-Q51.lead: Option 1: when a Union law and a state law on the same Concurrent List subject cannot stand together, the doctrine of repugnancy under Art 254 resolves it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Repugnancy – Art 254
Repugnancy is a direct conflict between a Union and a state law on a Concurrent subject; Art 254 says the Union law prevails, except under Art 254(2).
✓ Correct
Pith and Substance – Art 246
This doctrine decides which List a law truly belongs to; it is used when a law overlaps another List, not to settle a Concurrent clash.
✗ Wrong
Colourable Legislation – Art 245
This doctrine strikes down a law that does indirectly what the legislature has no power to do; it is about lack of competence, not a clash.
✗ Wrong
Residuary Powers – Art 248
Residuary power covers matters in none of the three Lists and belongs to Parliament; it has nothing to do with a Concurrent clash.
✗ Wrong

points: The key words 'same Concurrent List subject' and 'cannot stand together' point to repugnancy.
Hook: 254 = 'tie-break' rule for Concurrent List conflicts.

POL-8.2.1-Q52.lead: Both statements are correct, so option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The Governor can reserve certain state bills for the President
True
Art 200 lets the Governor reserve certain bills passed by the state legislature for the President's consideration.
2. The President has an absolute veto over reserved state bills
True
Under Art 201 the President can withhold assent, and the state legislature has no way to override that refusal.

points: Option 1 fails because statement 2 is also true; option 2 fails because statement 1 is true; option 4 rejects both true statements.
This reserving power is one way the Centre controls state legislation, often cited as a unitary feature.

POL-8.2.1-Q53.lead: Option 3: the proviso to Art 304(b) says a state bill imposing reasonable restrictions on trade can be introduced only with the President's previous sanction.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Art 301
Declares that trade, commerce and intercourse shall be free throughout India; it states the freedom, not the sanction rule.
✗ Wrong
Art 302
Lets Parliament impose restrictions on trade in the public interest; it is about Parliament's power, not state bills.
✗ Wrong
Art 304(b)
Lets a state impose reasonable restrictions on trade in the public interest, and its proviso requires the President's previous sanction for such a bill.
✓ Correct
Art 307
Lets Parliament appoint an authority to carry out the purposes of Arts 301 to 304; it does not deal with sanction.
✗ Wrong

points: The President's previous sanction is a form of Central control over state legislation.
Hook: 301 freedom, 302 Parliament limits, 304 state limits (with sanction).

POL-8.2.1-Q54.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. In a Financial Emergency the President can direct states to reserve money bills
True
Art 360(4) lets the Centre direct states to reserve all money bills and other financial bills for the President's consideration during a Financial Emergency.
2. The Governor needs instructions before an ordinance that would have needed Presidential sanction as a bill
True
The proviso to Art 213(1) requires the President's instructions before the Governor promulgates such an ordinance.
3. These controls apply only to Concurrent List matters
False
These controls cover state bills and ordinances generally, including State List matters such as money bills, so they are not limited to the Concurrent List.

points: Option 2 (2 and 3) and option 3 (1 and 3) fail because they include the false statement 3.
Option 4 fails for the same reason: statement 3 is false.

POL-8.2.1-Q55.lead: Option 1: the Sarkaria Commission said Art 356 should be used very sparingly, in extreme cases, as a last resort when all alternatives fail.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 356 should be used very sparingly, only as a last resort
This is a listed Sarkaria recommendation.
✓ Correct
The All-India Services should be abolished
Opposite of Sarkaria: it wanted the All-India Services strengthened and more such services created. Abolition was demanded by Rajamannar and the West Bengal memorandum.
✗ Wrong
Governors should be directly elected by the people of the State
Sarkaria did not recommend election; it dealt with how Governors should be appointed, keeping appointment by the President.
✗ Wrong
The Inter-State Council should be abolished
Opposite of Sarkaria: it recommended a permanent Inter-State Council under Art 263, set up in 1990.
✗ Wrong

points: Sarkaria (appointed 1983, report 1988) made 247 recommendations and favoured a strong Centre without over-centralisation.

POL-8.2.1-Q56.lead: Both statements are correct, so option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Art 249 power over State List in normal times is non-federal
True
Under Art 249 Parliament can legislate on a State List subject even without any Emergency, which cuts into the states' own field, so it is called a non-federal (unitary) feature.
2. State legislatures cannot initiate a constitutional amendment
True
Under Art 368 an amendment bill can be introduced only in either House of Parliament; states can at most ratify some amendments.

points: Option 1 and option 2 each drop one true statement; option 4 rejects both.
In a true federation, the units usually share the power to start amendments.

POL-8.2.2-Q02.lead: Option 2: on Concurrent List subjects, executive power ordinarily stays with the states; the Union gets it only where the Constitution or a law of Parliament specifically gives it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. The Union only
Wrong: even when Parliament makes a law on a concurrent subject, the states normally carry it out.
2. The States, unless the Constitution or a Parliamentary law gives it to the Union
This is the rule: execution of concurrent laws is with the states except where the Constitution or Parliament directs otherwise.
3. Both Union and States equally at all times
There is no rule of equal sharing; execution is with the states by default.
4. The President on the advice of the Inter-State Council
The Inter-State Council is only a recommendatory body under Article 263; it has no executive power.

points: Legislative power on concurrent subjects is shared, but executive power follows a default rule in favour of the states.
Example: the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 is a Parliamentary law that lets the Centre exercise executive control over production, supply and distribution of certain commodities.

POL-8.2.2-Q03.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Art 256: states must use executive power to ensure compliance with Parliament's laws
True
Article 256 places this general obligation on every state, and the Centre may give directions for this purpose.
2. Art 365: non-compliance with Union directions lets the President hold that the state machinery has failed
True
Article 365 says it is lawful for the President to hold so, which opens the way to President's Rule under Article 356.

points: Option 1 (1 only) and option 2 (2 only) each leave out a true statement.
Option 4 (Neither) is wrong because both are correct statements of the Constitution.
Concept: Article 256 creates the duty; Article 365 is the coercive sanction that makes Union directions effective.

POL-8.2.2-Q04.lead: Option 4: collection of land revenue is not a matter on which Article 257 lets the Union direct a state; land revenue is a State List subject handled by the state itself.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Construction of means of communication of national importance
Article 257(2) lets the Centre direct the construction and maintenance of communications declared to be of national or military importance.
✗ (is a listed matter)
2. Maintenance of means of communication of military importance
Also covered by Article 257(2): the Centre can direct the construction and maintenance of communications of military importance.
✗ (is a listed matter)
3. Protection of railways within the state
Article 257(3) lets the Centre direct measures for protecting railways in the state.
✗ (is a listed matter)
4. Collection of land revenue in the state
Not in Article 257; land revenue is a State List subject the state collects on its own.
✓ (NOT a listed matter)

points: Article 257(1) also says a state's executive power must not impede or prejudice the Union's executive power.
Other Union directions in the Constitution cover mother-tongue instruction for linguistic minorities (Art 350A) and welfare schemes for Scheduled Tribes (Art 339).

POL-8.2.2-Q10.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Art 258: President, with the state's consent, entrusts Union functions to the state
True
Article 258 allows the President to entrust Union executive functions to a state government with that government's consent.
2. Art 258A (7th Amendment, 1956): Governor, with the Union's consent, entrusts state functions to the Union
True
Article 258A was added by the 7th Amendment, 1956 and works in the reverse direction, with the consent of the Central government.

points: Options 1 and 2 each drop one correct statement; option 4 denies both.
Concept: legislative powers cannot be delegated between Centre and states, but executive functions can be entrusted by mutual consent to avoid deadlock.
Only the Centre can also delegate without consent, through a law of Parliament on a Union List subject; a state legislature cannot do this.

POL-8.2.2-Q11.lead: Option 4: under Article 258A the Governor of the state entrusts the function, and the consent needed is that of the Union (Central) Government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Governor; consent of the High Court
The Governor is right, but the High Court has no role in executive delegation.
2. President; consent of the state legislature
This mixes up Article 258 (Union to state, by the President) and wrongly adds the legislature.
3. Chief Minister; consent of Parliament
The Constitution gives this power to the Governor, not the Chief Minister, and Parliament's consent is not required.
4. Governor; consent of the Union Government
Exactly the text of Article 258A: the Governor, with the consent of the Government of India, entrusts state functions to it.

points: Mirror rule: Art 258 = President entrusts Union functions to a state, with the state government's consent; Art 258A = Governor entrusts state functions to the Union, with the Union government's consent.
The delegation may be conditional or unconditional.

POL-8.2.2-Q13.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Full faith and credit to public acts, records and judicial proceedings of the Union and every state
True
This is Article 261(1); 'public acts' include legislative and executive acts, and 'public records' include official registers made by public servants.
2. Manner of proving them is decided by Parliament's law
True
Article 261(2) leaves the mode of proof and the effect of such acts and records to laws made by Parliament.

points: Options 1 and 2 each omit a true clause; option 4 denies both.
Concept: since each state's jurisdiction stops at its border, Article 261 makes sure one state's official acts and records are recognised in another.
Article 261(3) adds that final civil judgments can be executed anywhere in India.

POL-8.2.2-Q14.lead: Option 2: only the final civil money decree can be executed anywhere in India; the full faith and credit rule does not oblige other states to enforce one state's penal (criminal) law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Both must be enforced by courts of every other state
Wrong, because the rule applies only to civil judgments, not criminal ones.
2. Only the civil decree is executable anywhere in India
Correct: final civil judgments and orders can be executed anywhere in India without a fresh suit.
3. Only the criminal conviction is enforceable elsewhere
This reverses the rule; criminal judgments are the ones excluded.
4. Neither can be executed outside Telangana
Wrong, because Article 261(3) makes civil decrees executable throughout India.

points: Article 261(3) speaks of final judgments or orders of civil courts.
A state's courts are not required to enforce the penal laws of another state.
Memory hook: money travels, punishment does not.

True/False

POL-8.2.2-Q42.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

POL-8.2.2-Q44.lead: Option 3: a statutory body is created by an Act of Parliament; only the North-Eastern Council was created this way, by the North-Eastern Council Act, 1971.

POL-8.2.2-Q45.lead: Option 1: the States Reorganisation Act, 1956 created five Zonal Councils: Northern, Central, Eastern, Western and Southern.

POL-8.2.2-Q48.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

POL-8.2.2-Q49.lead: Correct option: 1 (A-4, B-3, C-2, D-1). Articles 260–263 are the last four Articles of Part XI on administrative relations, in this order.

What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong: the State List has taxes like tax on agricultural income, but not corporation tax.

Wrong: there are no tax entries in the Concurrent List.

Wrong: the GST Council only recommends on GST; it cannot levy any tax, and corporation tax is not GST.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Dealt with service tax levied by the Centre; it was omitted by the 101st Amendment when service tax merged into GST.
Article 269A
Deals with GST on inter-state supplies (IGST): levied and collected by the Centre and shared as Parliament provides on GST Council advice. It is a revenue-sharing rule, not the law-making power.
Article 279A
Creates the GST Council, which only recommends; it does not give law-making power to legislatures.
Article 246A
The special law-making power on GST given to both Parliament and the State Legislatures.

POL-8.2.3-Q05.lead: (3) Article 265 — no tax can be levied or collected except by authority of law, so an executive order alone cannot impose a levy.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Says no person shall be deprived of property save by authority of law; it is the constitutional right to property, not the rule on taxation.

Creates the Consolidated Funds and Public Accounts of India and the States; it says where money goes, not how a tax may be imposed.
Article 265
Every tax must be backed by a law passed by the legislature; an executive order is not a law.
Article 282
Allows the Centre or a state to give discretionary grants for any public purpose; it has nothing to do with imposing taxes.

POL-8.2.3-Q06.lead: (4) 1, 2 and 3 — all three statements correctly restate Articles 266 and 283.

head: Statement
True/False
Why

True
Art 266(1): all revenues, all loans raised and all money received in repayment of loans form the Consolidated Fund of India.

True
Art 266(2): all other public money (provident funds, small savings, deposits) is credited to the Public Account of India; the government holds it as a banker.

True
Art 283(1) says custody and withdrawal are regulated by law of Parliament and, until such law is made, by rules made by the President.

POL-8.2.3-Q07.lead: (4) 1950 — Parliament enacted the Contingency Fund of India Act in 1950 under Article 267.

Correct?

POL-8.2.3-Q08.lead: (3) Article 268 — duties levied by the Centre but collected and kept by the states, such as stamp duties on bills of exchange and cheques.

What it is / means
Correct?

Centre levies and collects; entire proceeds assigned to the states.

True/False

Correct?

Wrong: Art 279A has no such reference; disputes go to a mechanism set up by the Council.

Correct?

Correct?

Laxmikanth: it audits economy, efficiency and effectiveness and appraises how far social and economic objectives were achieved and at what cost.
Audit of stores and stock
Checks the accounts of stores and stock kept in government offices; it is a regularity check, not an outcome check.

head: Part
True/False
Why

True

R
True
Under Art 317 the Supreme Court's advice is binding: the President cannot ignore it.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. The President has to remove the member only because the Supreme Court's finding binds him. If the advice were optional, as under Art 143, removal would not have to follow. So the binding nature in R is what makes the removal in A compulsory.

What it is / means
Correct?

True/False
Why

True

True/False
Why

True

R
True

POL-8.3.3-Q04.lead: Option 4: Article 318 empowers the Governor to make regulations on members' conditions of service and staff strength.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 316
Wrong: Article 316 deals with the appointment and term of office of PSC members, not with regulations on their service conditions or staff.
Article 322
Wrong: Article 322 only says the expenses of a PSC are charged on the Consolidated Fund; it gives no regulation-making power.
Article 320
Functions of Public Service Commissions.
Article 318
Power to make regulations as to conditions of service of members and staff.

points: For UPSC the President makes these regulations; for an SPSC the Governor does.

POL-8.3.3-Q05.lead: Option 3: an SPSC member holds office for six years or till 62 years of age, whichever is earlier.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 5 years or till 62
Wrong: the SPSC term under Article 316(2) is six years or age 62, whichever is earlier; five years is not the term.
6 years or till 65
Wrong: six years or age 65 is the UPSC term; for SPSC members the age limit is 62.
6 years or till 62
Correct: under Article 316(2) an SPSC member holds office for six years or till age 62, whichever is earlier (the same applies to a Joint SPSC).
6 years or till 60
60 was the original age limit; the 41st Amendment (1976) raised it to 62.

points: UPSC 65, SPSC 62 — the term of six years is common.

POL-8.3.3-Q06.lead: Option 3: the 41st Amendment Act, 1976 raised the SPSC retirement age from 60 to 62.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 15th Amendment, 1963
It added the acting-chairman provision and raised High Court judges' age to 62; not the SPSC age.
42nd Amendment, 1976
The 'mini-Constitution' amendment (Preamble words, Fundamental Duties etc.), not this change.
41st Amendment, 1976
Correct: the 41st Amendment Act, 1976 amended Article 316(2) to raise the SPSC retirement age from 60 to 62.
44th Amendment, 1978
Changed emergency provisions and removed property as a Fundamental Right.

points: Hook: 41 → SPSC 62. Both 41st and 42nd are from 1976, so watch the number.

POL-8.3.3-Q07.lead: Correct option: 1 (A-2, B-1, C-1). UPSC 65; SPSC and JSPSC both 62.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. UPSC
2. 65 years
Members of the UPSC hold office for 6 years or until the age of 65, whichever is earlier, so A matches 2.
B. SPSC
1. 62 years
Members of a State PSC hold office for 6 years or until the age of 62, whichever is earlier, so B matches 1.
C. Joint SPSC
1. 62 years
JSPSC members follow the SPSC limit, 62 years.

points: Option 2 fails: A-1 gives "UPSC" → "62 years" (correct: 65 years); B-2 gives "SPSC" → "65 years" (correct: 62 years); C-2 gives "Joint SPSC" → "65 years" (correct: 62 years).
Option 3 fails: B-3 gives "SPSC" → "60 years (original SPSC limit)" (correct: 62 years).
Option 4 fails: C-3 gives "Joint SPSC" → "60 years (original SPSC limit)" (correct: 62 years).
60 years was the SPSC limit before the 41st Amendment, 1976; it is a trap.
Code 1 is used twice.

POL-8.3.3-Q08.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. An SPSC member resigns to the Governor.
True
SPSC members are appointed by the Governor and address their resignation to the Governor.
2. A JSPSC member resigns to the Governor of the largest state.
False
JSPSC members are appointed by the President and resign to the President.

points: Option 2 picks the false statement; option 3 includes it; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.

POL-8.3.3-Q09.lead: Option 4: the 15th Amendment Act, 1963 added the provision for an acting chairman (Article 316(1A)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 7th Amendment, 1956
Reorganised states into states and UTs; not this provision.
41st Amendment, 1976
Wrong: the 41st Amendment, 1976 only raised the SPSC age limit from 60 to 62; the acting-chairman clause came with the 15th Amendment, 1963.
24th Amendment, 1971
Affirmed Parliament's power to amend Fundamental Rights.
15th Amendment, 1963
Added the acting-chairman provision for both UPSC and SPSC.

points: Acting chairman is appointed when the chairman's office is vacant or the chairman is unable to act.

POL-8.3.3-Q10.lead: Option 4: when the chairman is absent, the Governor can appoint one of the SPSC members as acting chairman.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The President appoints a UPSC member
The President appoints the UPSC acting chairman, not one for an SPSC.
The state legislature elects an acting chairman
Wrong: the state legislature has no role in choosing a PSC chairman; under Article 316(1A) the Governor appoints a member as acting chairman.
The senior-most member automatically becomes chairman
There is no automatic succession; an appointment by the Governor is needed.
The Governor appoints one of the SPSC members
Article 316(1A) allows this when the chairman is unable to act due to absence or other reason.

points: The acting chairman must be a member of the same SPSC.
POL-8.3.3-Q10.also: Acting chairman serves until a new chairman joins or the original resumes.

POL-8.3.3-Q11.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Art 316: the Governor appoints SPSC members, but he cannot remove them.
R
True
Art 317: an SPSC member can be removed only by the President, on the grounds and in the manner given there.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. The Constitution gives the removal power only to the President, so the Governor, though he appoints, has no power to remove. This split protects members from pressure by the State Government.
Option 2 fails: R is not a separate fact here; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.
Appointment: Governor (Art 316). Removal: President (Art 317).

POL-8.3.3-Q12.lead: Option 3: misbehaviour is the only ground that needs a Supreme Court enquiry before removal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Being adjudged insolvent
The President can remove directly on this ground.
Engaging in paid employment outside duties
A direct ground for removal without enquiry.
Misbehaviour
The President must refer it to the Supreme Court; its advice is binding.
Infirmity of mind or body
A direct ground, decided by the President's opinion.

points: Three objective grounds = direct removal; misbehaviour = SC enquiry first.

POL-8.3.3-Q13.lead: Option 4: in 1993 the Supreme Court held that the appointment of a blind professor as SPSC member cannot be set aside on the ground of infirmity of body.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Was void as he was unfit under Article 317
The Court did not treat blindness as unfitness that voids the appointment.
Was valid only for a reduced term
The Court said nothing about reducing the term.
Required prior approval of the President
Not a requirement for SPSC appointments, which are made by the Governor.
Could not be set aside merely on grounds of infirmity of body
Correct: this was the 1993 ruling - physical infirmity alone (here, blindness) is not a ground to set aside an SPSC member's appointment.

points: Article 317's 'infirmity' is a ground for removal in the President's opinion, not a bar to a valid appointment.

POL-8.3.3-Q14.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are correct, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The President must refer misbehaviour to the Supreme Court.
True
Article 317(1) requires a Supreme Court enquiry before removal for misbehaviour.
2. The Supreme Court's advice is only recommendatory.
False
The Court's advice is binding on the President.
3. The Governor can suspend the member during the enquiry.
True
Article 317(2): the Governor may suspend an SPSC member pending the President's final order.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 all include the false statement 2.

POL-8.3.3-Q15.lead: Option 4: during the Supreme Court enquiry the Governor can suspend the member, but only the President can remove him.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Can remove the member at once
The Governor never removes SPSC members; removal is by the President.
Can transfer the member to another SPSC
Wrong: the Constitution gives the Governor no power to transfer an SPSC member to another commission; Article 317 speaks only of suspension and removal.
Must wait without any action
Wrong: the Governor need not wait idle, because Article 317(2) allows him to suspend the member while the Supreme Court reference is pending.
Can suspend the member but not remove him
Correct: under Article 317(2) the Governor may suspend the member pending the Supreme Court report, but final removal is by the President.

points: Governor: appoint + suspend. President: remove.

POL-8.3.3-Q16.lead: Option 3: a member is deemed guilty of misbehaviour if he is interested in a government contract, except as an ordinary member of an incorporated company (Article 317(4)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Criticises government policy in public
Wrong: criticising government policy is not in Article 317(4), which defines misbehaviour only in terms of interest in government contracts or agreements.
Holds shares in any incorporated company
Holding shares in common with other members is expressly excepted.
Is interested in a government contract, otherwise than as a member of an incorporated company
Correct: Article 317(4) deems a member guilty of misbehaviour if he is interested in a government contract, except as an ordinary member of an incorporated company.
Contests a cooperative society election
Wrong: contesting a cooperative society election is not mentioned in Article 317(4)'s definition of misbehaviour.

points: The idea is to prevent conflict of interest with government contracts.

POL-8.3.3-Q17.lead: Option 3: SPSC expenses are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State (Article 322), so they are not voted.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Consolidated Fund of India
Wrong: the Consolidated Fund of India bears the expenses of the UPSC; SPSC expenses are charged on the state's fund under Article 322.
Contingency Fund of the State
Wrong: the Contingency Fund of the State is only an imprest for unforeseen urgent spending, not for regular charged expenses like SPSC salaries.
Consolidated Fund of the State
Correct: charged, not subject to vote of the state legislature.
Public Account of the State
Holds money kept in trust, not used for such salaries.

points: Note: SPSC members are removed by the President, but are paid from the state's fund.

POL-8.3.3-Q18.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Its expenses are not voted by the state legislature.
True
They are charged on the Consolidated Fund of the State.
2. Conditions of service cannot be varied to a member's disadvantage.
True
Article 318 proviso protects members after appointment.
3. A member can be reappointed with the President's approval.
False
A member is not eligible for reappointment to that office at all.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.

POL-8.3.3-Q19.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct, so the answer is option 1.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. An SPSC chairman can become UPSC chairman.
True
Article 319(b): eligible as chairman or member of UPSC or chairman of another SPSC.
2. An SPSC member can become chairman of the same SPSC.
True
Article 319(d): a member is eligible as chairman of that SPSC or any other SPSC.
3. An SPSC chairman can become Chief Secretary.
False
Any other employment under the Government of India or a state is barred.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.

POL-8.3.3-Q20.lead: Option 4: a retiring APPSC chairman cannot be reappointed as chairman of the same APPSC.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Member of the UPSC
Allowed: an SPSC chairman can become chairman or member of UPSC.
✗ (eligible)
Chairman of the Karnataka PSC
He is eligible, so not the answer: a retiring SPSC chairman can become chairman of any other SPSC, such as the Karnataka PSC.
✗ (eligible)
Chairman of the UPSC
He is eligible, so not the answer: under Article 319(b) a retiring SPSC chairman can be appointed chairman or member of the UPSC.
✗ (eligible)
Chairman of the Andhra Pradesh PSC again
Not allowed: no reappointment to the same office after the first term.

points: 'Other SPSC' is allowed; 'same SPSC' again is not.

POL-8.3.3-Q21.lead: Option 1: the primary function of an SPSC is to conduct examinations for appointment to the state services (Article 320(1)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Conducting examinations for state services
Correct: under Article 320(1) the primary duty of an SPSC is to conduct examinations for appointment to the services of the state.
Fixing pay scales of state employees
Pay and service conditions are handled by the state's Department of Personnel / GAD.
Conducting elections to local bodies
Done by the State Election Commission (Article 243K).
Deciding reservation percentages
Reservations are excluded from SPSC consultation (Article 320(4)).

points: SPSC is the state's recruiting agency, the 'watchdog of merit system' in the state.

POL-8.3.3-Q22.lead: Option 4: the SPSC is not consulted on classification of services and cadre management, because these are personnel-management matters handled by the Department of Personnel / General Administration Department.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Methods of recruitment to civil posts
Listed advisory matter under Article 320(3)(a); the SPSC advises on how posts are to be filled.
Disciplinary matters of a civil servant
Listed advisory matter under Article 320(3)(c), including memorials and petitions on such matters.
Claims for pension for injuries sustained on duty
Listed advisory matter under Article 320(3)(e), including the amount of such an award.
Classification of services and cadre management
Not an SPSC matter; Laxmikanth says the SPSC is not concerned with classification, pay, service conditions, cadre management or training.

points: Article 320 gives the SPSC six advisory matters: recruitment methods, principles of appointment/promotion/transfer, discipline, legal-expense claims, injury pensions, and any matter referred by the Governor.
Memory hook: the SPSC is the state's recruiting agency; the GAD is the state's personnel agency.

POL-8.3.3-Q23.lead: All three statements are matters on which the SPSC must be consulted, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Reimbursement of legal expenses of a civil servant for acts in official duty
True
This is the fourth listed advisory matter under Article 320(3)(d).
2. Principles for promotions and transfers
True
Article 320(3)(b) covers principles for appointments, promotions and transfers and the suitability of candidates.
3. Any matter referred by the Governor
True
The last clause of Article 320 lets the Governor refer any other matter to the SPSC.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out one true statement, so all of them are incomplete.
For the UPSC the same list applies, but the referring authority is the President instead of the Governor.

POL-8.3.3-Q24.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
A civil servant punished without the SPSC being consulted cannot get relief from a court only on that ground.
R
True
The Supreme Court has held the consultation rule in Art 320 to be directory, not mandatory.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Only breach of a mandatory rule makes the decision void. Since consultation is directory, skipping it does not void the punishment, so the court gives no relief on that ground alone. R is the legal basis of A.
Option 2 fails: R is not a separate fact here; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.
The government must still act fairly, without malafides.

POL-8.3.3-Q25.lead: Option 4: the Supreme Court has held that selection by the PSC does not by itself give a right to the post, but the government must act fairly and without arbitrariness or mala fides.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Selection gives an enforceable right to the post
False; the Court held that selection by the SPSC confers no right to the post on the candidate.
The APPSC can issue the appointment order itself
False; the SPSC only selects and recommends, while the appointment is made by the state government.
The Governor must appoint within six months
False; the Constitution prescribes no such time limit for making an appointment.
No right to the post, but government must act fairly
True; this is exactly the Supreme Court's position noted by Laxmikanth.

points: The PSC's role is advisory and recommendatory; the final decision to appoint stays with the government.
Even so, the government cannot reject a selected candidate arbitrarily or with mala fides, because that would offend fairness (Article 14).

POL-8.3.3-Q26.lead: Option 3: under Article 321 the state legislature, by an Act, can extend the SPSC's functions and place the personnel system of a local authority (such as a municipal corporation) within its jurisdiction.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: An order of the Governor alone
False; extension of SPSC functions needs a law, not an executive order of the Governor.
An Act of Parliament
False; Parliament does this for the UPSC and Union services, not for a State PSC.
An Act of the state legislature
True; Article 321 lets the state legislature add functions and bring local bodies, corporate bodies or public institutions under the SPSC.
A resolution of the SPSC
False; a commission cannot enlarge its own jurisdiction.

points: Rule of thumb: whoever owns the services makes the law; the state legislature for the SPSC, Parliament for the UPSC.
A municipal corporation is a local authority of the state, so its staff come under the SPSC only through a state Act.

POL-8.3.3-Q27.lead: Option 4: under Article 323 the Governor lays the SPSC's annual report before the state legislature with a memorandum explaining cases where the Commission's advice was not accepted and the reasons.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A report of the CAG
False; CAG audit reports are a separate matter under Article 151 and are not attached to the PSC report.
The President's approval
False; the SPSC report goes to the Governor and needs no presidential approval.
The comments of the High Court
False; the High Court has no role in the SPSC annual report.
Memorandum on non-acceptance of advice
True; this keeps the government accountable to the legislature whenever it rejects SPSC advice.

points: The SPSC's advice is not binding, so the memorandum is the check: the government must explain itself to the House.
Same pattern for the UPSC: report to the President, laid before both Houses of Parliament with a similar memorandum.

POL-8.3.3-Q28.lead: Both statements are correct, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. SPSC is not consulted while making reservations for backward classes
True
Laxmikanth lists reservations in favour of backward classes as outside the SPSC's functional jurisdiction.
2. Rosters and number of vacancies are decided by the state government
True
Reservation and posts are government decisions; the SPSC only recruits against the vacancies and rosters notified by the government.

points: Options 1 and 2 each drop one true statement; option 4 wrongly rejects both.
The second limitation is the claims of SCs and STs in appointments, which also need no SPSC consultation.

POL-8.3.3-Q29.lead: Option 3: regulations of the Governor excluding matters from the SPSC's purview must be laid before each House of the state legislature for at least 14 days, and the legislature can amend or repeal them.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 7 days
Not the prescribed period under Article 320(5).
30 days
Not the prescribed period under Article 320(5).
14 days
Correct; the minimum laying period is 14 days, the same as for UPSC regulations made by the President.
6 weeks
Not the prescribed period; 6 weeks is a common distractor taken from other provisions.

points: Laying the regulations before the House lets the legislature control how much the executive removes from the SPSC's advisory role.
For the UPSC, the President makes such regulations and lays them before Parliament for the same 14 days.

POL-8.3.3-Q30.lead: Option 4: the Department of Personnel / General Administration Department is the central personnel agency of a state, while the SPSC is only the central recruiting agency.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: State Public Service Commission
It is the 'watchdog of the merit system' and recruiting agency, but it does not manage classification, pay, cadres or training.
State Finance Commission
A body under Article 243-I that reviews the finances of panchayats and municipalities; it has no personnel role.
State Vigilance Commission
An anti-corruption advisory body consulted in disciplinary cases, not a personnel manager.
Department of Personnel / GAD
Handles classification of services, pay and service conditions, cadre management and training, so it is the personnel agency.

points: Recruiting (who gets in) is the SPSC's job; managing (what happens after) is the GAD's job.
At the Centre the same split is UPSC (recruiting) and DoPT (personnel).

POL-8.3.3-Q31.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. SPSC advice is binding on the state government
False
Laxmikanth: SPSC recommendations are only advisory and not binding; the government may accept or reject them.
2. Government may reject advice but must explain to the legislature
True
Under Article 323 the Governor lays a memorandum explaining non-acceptance of advice along with the annual report.

points: Option 1 and option 3 fail because they accept statement 1.
Option 4 fails because statement 2 is a correct description of Article 323.

POL-8.3.3-Q32.lead: Option 2: the SPSC has an edge over the State Vigilance Commission, because the SPSC is an independent constitutional body.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Vigilance Commission, as a specialised anti-corruption body
False; specialisation does not give it priority over a constitutional body.
SPSC, as an independent constitutional body
True; Laxmikanth says that in conflicting advice the SPSC has the edge because it is constitutional.
Neither; the High Court decides
False; no High Court arbitration exists for conflicting advice; the government decides.
Vigilance Commission, as it reports to the Chief Minister
False; reporting to the executive weakens, not strengthens, its independence.

points: Both bodies are consulted before disciplinary action, which is why the emergence of the SVC reduced the SPSC's role in discipline.
Same logic at the Centre: the UPSC has an edge over the CVC.

POL-8.3.3-Q33.lead: Option 3: while framing rules for appointment to the state judicial service other than district judges, the Governor consults both the SPSC and the High Court (Article 234).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only the High Court
Incomplete; the SPSC must also be consulted for judicial service below district judge.
Only the SPSC
Incomplete; the High Court must also be consulted.
Both the SPSC and the High Court
Correct; Civil Judges (Junior Division) belong to the judicial service below district judge, covered by Article 234.
The UPSC and the Supreme Court
False; these are Union bodies with no role in state subordinate judicial recruitment.

points: District judges are appointed by the Governor in consultation with the High Court under Article 233, without the SPSC.
Below that level, the SPSC conducts the selection and the High Court controls the subordinate courts.

POL-8.3.3-Q34.lead: Option 1: the UPSC may serve all or any of the needs of a state on the request of the Governor and with the approval of the President (Article 315(4)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Governor's request and President's approval
Correct; this is the procedure under Article 315(4).
State legislature resolution and a law of Parliament
False; this is the procedure for creating a Joint State PSC, not for using the UPSC.
An order of the Chief Minister
False; the Chief Minister has no independent power here.
A resolution of the Rajya Sabha
False; no Rajya Sabha resolution is required.

points: Do not mix up the two: UPSC serving a state = Governor + President; Joint SPSC = state legislatures' resolution + Act of Parliament.
A Joint SPSC is therefore a statutory body, while the UPSC and SPSC are constitutional bodies.

POL-8.3.3-Q35.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
A Joint State Public Service Commission (JSPSC) is a statutory body.
R
True
Parliament creates a JSPSC by an Act, on the request of the legislatures of the states concerned (Art 315).

points: Does R explain A? Yes. A body's status depends on how it is created. A JSPSC comes into existence only through an Act of Parliament, which makes it statutory. R explains A.
Option 2 fails: R is not a separate fact here; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.
UPSC and SPSC are created by the Constitution itself, so they are constitutional bodies.

POL-8.3.3-Q36.lead: Correct option: 1 (A-1, B-2, C-3, D-2). JSPSC: Parliament creates, President appoints and accepts resignation, each Governor gets the report.

Why / concept

Option 3 fails: A-2 gives "Creation" → "President" (correct: Parliament); D-3 gives "Resignation addressed to" → "Each concerned Governor" (correct: President).
Option 4 fails: C-2 gives "Annual report submitted to" → "President" (correct: Each concerned Governor).

POL-8.3.3-Q37.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct and statement 3 is wrong, so the answer is option 1.

True/False
Why

True
Laxmikanth: the number of members of a JSPSC and their conditions of service are determined by the President.
2. Expenses shared as fixed by the President
True

A Joint SPSC serves several states, so its cost is shared among them; the key accepts that the President fixes the share (Laxmikanth gives only the President's power over strength and service conditions).
3. Members removable by any participating Governor
False
JSPSC members are appointed by the President and can be suspended or removed only by the President.

JSPSC members hold office for 6 years or till age 62, resign to the President, and the annual report goes to each concerned Governor.

POL-8.3.3-Q38.lead: Option 2: at present no Joint State Public Service Commission is functioning; each state has its own PSC.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

False; each north-eastern state has its own Public Service Commission.
No JSPSC is functioning
True; the JSPSC provision exists in the Constitution but no such commission works today.
AP and Telangana share a JSPSC
False; after bifurcation they have separate commissions, the APPSC and the TGPSC.
JSPSCs exist for all Union Territories
False; Union Territory services are generally recruited through the UPSC, not a JSPSC.

That is why the JSPSC is a statutory body, unlike the constitutional UPSC and SPSC.

POL-8.3.3-Q39.lead: Option 2: retired IPS officer A.R. Anuradha was appointed Chairperson of the APPSC in October 2024.

Term: 6 years or age 62, whichever is earlier; removal only by the President.

POL-8.3.3-Q40.lead: Correct option: 2 (A-3, B-1, C-2). Udaya Bhaskar APPSC; Chakrapani first TSPSC; Venkatesham present TGPSC.

Why / concept
