points: Does R explain A? Yes. Only members listed in Art 279A(2) vote. Since the CBIC Chairperson is an invitee and not a member, he has no vote to count.
Option 2 fails: R is not a separate fact here; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.
Being a non-member, he also does not count for quorum.

POL-8.3.5-Q10.lead: Option 4 is correct: the Union Revenue Secretary (Department of Revenue, Ministry of Finance) is ex-officio Secretary to the Council.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Union Finance Secretary
A senior Finance Ministry officer, but Laxmikanth names the Revenue Secretary, not the Finance Secretary, as Council Secretary.
Chief Economic Adviser
Advises the Finance Ministry on economic policy and prepares the Economic Survey; holds no Council post.
Cabinet Secretary
Heads the civil service and the Cabinet Secretariat; has no formal role in the Council.
Union Revenue Secretary
Heads the Department of Revenue, which deals with taxes, so he serves as ex-officio Secretary.

points: The Council's Secretariat is located at New Delhi.
Ex-officio means the post comes automatically with the office held.

POL-8.3.5-Q11.lead: Option 1 (1 only) is correct: quorum is one-half of total members, but decisions need three-fourths of weighted votes of members present and voting.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Quorum is one-half of total members
True
Laxmikanth: one-half of the total number of members is the quorum for a meeting (Article 279A(7)).
2. Three-fourths of weighted votes of total membership
False
The three-fourths is counted on members present and voting, not on total membership (Article 279A(9)).

points: Option 2 and option 3 accept the false statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
Do not mix the two numbers: 1/2 decides whether a meeting can be held, 3/4 decides whether a proposal passes.

POL-8.3.5-Q12.lead: Option 3 is correct: the Central Government's vote has a weightage of one-third of the total votes cast.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: One-half of votes cast
One-half is the quorum of the Council, not any vote weight.
Two-thirds of votes cast
This is the combined weightage of all State governments, not the Centre.
One-third of votes cast
Laxmikanth: the vote of the central government shall have a weightage of one-third of the total votes cast.
One-fourth of votes cast
Not a weight in the Council; 3/4 is the majority needed, and 1/4 has no role.

points: Centre 1/3 + all States 2/3 = whole vote; a decision needs 3/4, so neither side alone can pass a proposal.
Hook: States get double the Centre's weight.

POL-8.3.5-Q13.lead: Option 4 is correct: the States must supply 5/8 (62.5%) of their combined vote for the proposal to reach three-fourths.

head: Step
Value
Why
rows: Needed to pass
3/4 = 75% of votes cast
Article 279A(9) requires not less than three-fourths of weighted votes present and voting.
Centre's weight
The Centre's vote counts as one-third of total votes cast.
Gap the States must fill
This much must come from the States' two-thirds share.
Share of States' vote
So at least five-eighths of the States' weighted vote must support the proposal.

points: Option 1 (one-half of States) gives only 33.33 + 33.33 = 66.67%, short of 75%.
Option 2 (two-thirds) and option 3 (three-fourths) are more than the minimum needed, so they are not the minimum share.

POL-8.3.5-Q14.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
If the Centre votes against, all the States together cannot pass a decision.
R
True
The States together have two-thirds (about 66.7%) of the weight, below the three-fourths (75%) needed.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Even if every State votes yes, they reach only 66.7%, short of 75%. So without the Centre a decision cannot pass; R explains A by simple arithmetic.
Option 2 fails: R is not a separate fact here; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.
The Centre has a de facto veto; equally, the Centre's one-third alone cannot pass anything.

POL-8.3.5-Q15.lead: Option 4 is correct: lack of the required three-fourths weighted majority is not a protected ground; such a decision is simply not a valid decision.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A vacancy in the Council
Protected: Article 279A(10) says no act is invalid merely because of a vacancy or defect in the constitution of the Council.
A defect in appointment of a member
Protected: a defect in appointing a person as member does not invalidate the act.
A procedural irregularity not affecting the merits
Protected: minor procedural irregularities that do not affect the merits are saved.
A decision without the required 3/4 majority
Not protected: the 3/4 rule in Article 279A(9) is the substance of a decision, not a technical defect.

points: Clause (10) saves acts from technical defects so that Council work is not undone on small grounds.
It cannot save something that was never validly decided.

POL-8.3.5-Q16.lead: Option 2 (1 and 3 only) is correct: statement 2 is false because the Council itself determines its procedure.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Guided by harmonised structure and national market
True
Laxmikanth: the Council is guided by the need for a harmonised GST structure and a harmonised national market (Article 279A(6)).
2. Procedure laid down by Parliament
False
The Council has to determine its own procedure in performing its functions (Article 279A(8)).
3. Mission: IT-driven, user-friendly GST
True
The mission is to evolve, through wider consultation, a GST structure that is information-technology driven and user friendly.

points: Option 1 and option 4 include the false statement 2; option 3 includes statement 2 and leaves out the true statement 1.

POL-8.3.5-Q17.lead: Option 2 is correct: the Council's vision describes it as the first constitutional federal body with power to take all major GST decisions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Statutory tax tribunal
A body created by an ordinary Act to decide tax disputes; the Council is created by the Constitution and makes recommendations, not judgments.
Constitutional federal body
Created by the Constitution (Article 279A) and made up of the Union and all States deciding together, so it is both constitutional and federal.
Inter-State Council
A separate advisory body that the President may set up under Article 263 for Centre-State consultation.
Quasi-judicial tax body
A body with court-like powers to hear cases; the Council does not hear cases.

points: Constitutional = created by the Constitution; federal = Centre and States both sit in it with shared votes.
Its vision aims at the highest standards of co-operative federalism.

POL-8.3.5-Q18.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) is correct: both are matters listed in Article 279A(4).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Taxes, cesses, surcharges to be merged in GST
True
The first listed function is to recommend which Centre, State and local body taxes, cesses and surcharges get merged in GST (Article 279A(4)(a)).
2. Goods and services to be exempted
True
The Council recommends which goods and services may be subjected to GST or exempted from it (Article 279A(4)(b)).

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each reject at least one true statement.
The Council recommends; actual laws are made by Parliament and the State Legislatures.

POL-8.3.5-Q19.lead: Correct option: 1 (A-4, B-2, C-1, D-3). GST is dual: Centre and State each levy on intra-State supply; IGST on inter-State.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. IGST
4. Levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies and imports
IGST: Centre on inter-State supplies and imports (Art 269A).
B. CGST
2. Levied by the Centre on supplies within a State
CGST: Centre on supplies within a State.
C. SGST
1. Levied by a State on supplies within the State
SGST: State on supplies within the State.
D. UTGST
3. Levied on supplies within a Union Territory without a legislature
UTGST is levied on supplies within a Union Territory without a legislature, where it takes the place of State GST, so D matches 3.

points: Option 2 fails: B-3 gives "CGST" → "Levied on supplies within a Union Territory without a legislature" (correct: Levied by the Centre on supplies within a State); D-2 gives "UTGST" → "Levied by the Centre on supplies within a State" (correct: Levied on supplies within a Union Territory without a legislature).

Option 3 fails: A-1 gives "IGST" → "Levied by a State on supplies within the State" (correct: Levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies and imports); C-4 gives "SGST" → "Levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies and imports" (correct: Levied by a State on supplies within the State).

Option 4 fails: A-2 gives "IGST" → "Levied by the Centre on supplies within a State" (correct: Levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies and imports); B-4 gives "CGST" → "Levied by the Centre on inter-State supplies and imports" (correct: Levied by the Centre on supplies within a State).

POL-8.3.5-Q20.lead: Option 2 (GST Council) is correct: recommending the turnover threshold for GST exemption is a Council function under Article 279A(4)(d).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Finance Commission
Recommends sharing of tax proceeds and grants-in-aid under Article 280; it has no role in GST thresholds.
GST Council
Laxmikanth lists 'the threshold limit of turnover below which goods and services may be exempted from GST' among its functions.
CBIC
Administers central GST and customs; it implements thresholds but does not recommend them.
NITI Aayog
A policy think tank that replaced the Planning Commission in 2015; it has no constitutional role in GST.

points: Threshold limits protect small traders from GST compliance burden, so the joint Centre-State body decides them.

POL-8.3.5-Q21.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) is correct: the Council can recommend rates including floor rates with bands, and its 56th meeting approved a 40% rate for sin and luxury goods.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Can recommend rates including floor rates with bands
True
This is listed in Article 279A(4)(e) and in Laxmikanth's list of functions.
2. 56th meeting approved 40% rate
True
In September 2025 the Council approved 'GST 2.0' with 5% and 18% main slabs and a special 40% rate for sin and luxury goods.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each reject at least one true statement.
The new rates applied from 22 September 2025.

POL-8.3.5-Q22.lead: Option 2 (5% and 18%) is correct: GST 2.0 reduced the main structure to a 5% merit slab and an 18% standard slab.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The 12% slab was removed in GST 2.0, so this pair is wrong.
The two main slabs approved at the 56th meeting, effective 22 September 2025.
12% was removed; most 12% items moved to 5%.
28% was removed; most 28% items moved to 18%, and sin/luxury goods to 40%.

points: Earlier structure: 5%, 12%, 18% and 28%; GST 2.0 merged it into two main slabs plus a special 40% rate.

POL-8.3.5-Q23.lead: Option 4 (Andhra Pradesh) is correct: it is not in the Article 279A(4)(g) list of special-provision States.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Sikkim
A north-eastern State named in the list.
Uttarakhand
Wrong: Uttarakhand is one of the Himalayan States named in Article 279A(4)(g) for special GST provisions.
Himachal Pradesh
Wrong: Himachal Pradesh is one of the Himalayan States named in Article 279A(4)(g) for special GST provisions.
Andhra Pradesh
Not named; the list covers only north-eastern and Himalayan States.

points: List: Arunachal Pradesh, Assam, Jammu and Kashmir, Manipur, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Sikkim, Tripura, Himachal Pradesh and Uttarakhand.
Logic: hilly or border areas with special problems get special GST provisions; AP's special category demand did not put it in this list.
POL-8.3.5-Q23.also: Jammu and Kashmir now refers to the Union territory after the J&K Reorganisation Act, 2019.

POL-8.3.5-Q24.lead: Option 3 (LPG) is correct: LPG is not among the five petroleum products whose GST date the Council must recommend.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Aviation turbine fuel
One of the five products; GST applies to it only from a date the Council recommends.
Natural gas
Wrong: natural gas is one of the five petroleum products in Article 279A(5) on which GST applies only from a date the Council recommends.
Liquefied petroleum gas (LPG)
Not in the list; LPG is already taxed under GST.
High speed diesel
Wrong: high speed diesel is one of the five products in Article 279A(5), along with crude, petrol, natural gas and ATF.

points: The five: petroleum crude, high speed diesel, motor spirit (petrol), natural gas and aviation turbine fuel (Article 279A(5)).
These stay outside GST for now because they are large revenue sources for States.

POL-8.3.5-Q25.lead: Option 2 (2 only) is correct: disputes go to a mechanism set up by the Council itself, and that mechanism covers State-versus-State disputes.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Referred to Inter-State Council under Article 263
False
Article 279A(11) asks the GST Council to establish its own mechanism to adjudicate disputes on its recommendations; the Inter-State Council is not involved.
2. Covers disputes between two or more States
True
The mechanism covers Centre vs State(s), Centre and State(s) vs other State(s), and disputes between two or more States.

points: Option 1 and option 3 accept the false statement 1; option 4 rejects the true statement 2.

POL-8.3.5-Q26.lead: Option 2 is correct: a dispute with the Centre and some States on one side and other States on the other is expressly covered by the Council's mechanism under Article 279A(11).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only Centre vs State; goes to Supreme Court
False: the mechanism is not limited to Centre vs State; it covers three kinds of disputes.
Council's adjudication mechanism, Art 279A(11)
True: 'between the centre and any state or states on one side and one or more other states on the other side' is one listed category.
Referred to the Finance Commission
False: the Finance Commission recommends tax sharing under Article 280 and has no dispute role in GST.
Parliament decides by special majority
False: Article 279A gives Parliament no role in deciding such disputes.

points: Centre + Kerala vs Tamil Nadu + Karnataka fits the second category exactly.

POL-8.3.5-Q27.lead: Option 4 (1, 2 and 3) is correct: all three statements are true.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Council recommends five-year compensation
True
Laxmikanth: the Council recommends compensation to States for revenue loss from GST for five years.
2. Given effect by the 2017 Compensation Act
True
On that recommendation Parliament enacted the Goods and Services Tax (Compensation to States) Act, 2017.
3. Five-year period ended 30 June 2022
True
GST began on 1 July 2017, so five years ended on 30 June 2022.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out one true statement.
The Council recommends, but Parliament determines compensation by law; the compensation cess was later extended to repay loans taken for the Covid-period shortfall.

POL-8.3.5-Q28.lead: Option 1 (1 only) is correct: Article 246A gives both Parliament and States GST law power, but inter-State GST is levied and collected by the Centre.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Both Parliament and State Legislatures make GST laws
True
Article 246A gives both the power to make laws on GST imposed by the Union or the State.
2. Inter-State GST levied and collected by States
False
Under Article 269A, GST on inter-State supply is levied and collected by the Centre and then divided as Parliament provides on Council recommendation.

points: Option 2 and option 3 accept the false statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
Parliament has exclusive power over GST on inter-State supply (Article 246A(2)).

POL-8.3.5-Q29.lead: Option 2 is correct: in Mohit Minerals (2022) the Supreme Court held GST Council recommendations have only persuasive value and are not binding.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Binding on Parliament and States
Rejected: the Court said making them binding would upset fiscal federalism, since Article 279A speaks only of recommendations.
Only persuasive, not binding
The Court's holding; Parliament and State Legislatures keep their own GST law-making power under Article 246A.
Bind States but not Parliament
Rejected: the Court treated Centre and States equally; neither is bound.
Binding only if unanimous
No such rule exists; the Council decides by three-fourths weighted vote and its output stays a recommendation.

points: The Court described Indian federalism as a dialogue, both cooperative and uncooperative.
Hook: Council = advice; legislatures = law.

POL-8.3.5-Q30.lead: Option 4: A is false, R is true.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
False
False. GST Council recommendations are not binding on the Union and State legislatures (Mohit Minerals, 2022).
R
True
The GST Council is a constitutional body under Art 279A.

points: Does R explain A? R is true but does not make A true. Being created by the Constitution decides a body's status, not whether its advice binds. Art 279A only uses the word 'recommendations'.
Options 1, 2 and 3 fail: all of them treat A as true, but A is false.
Option 4 fits: A is false and R is a correct statement.
Constitutional body, persuasive advice.

POL-8.3.5-Q31.lead: Option 2 is correct: GST is a destination-based consumption tax, so revenue goes to the State where goods or services are consumed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Origin-based direct tax
Wrong on both counts: GST is indirect, and it goes to the consuming State, not the producing State.
Destination-based consumption tax
Correct: the final consumer bears it and the revenue follows the place of consumption.
Origin-based production tax
Describes old central excise, charged where goods were made; GST replaced that idea.
Destination-based direct tax
Mixed term: GST is not direct, because the seller collects it from the buyer.

points: Direct tax: the person taxed pays it himself (income tax). Indirect tax: the seller collects it from the buyer (GST).
Example: a car made in Tamil Nadu and sold in Andhra Pradesh yields the State share of GST to Andhra Pradesh, the consuming State.

POL-8.3.5-Q32.lead: Option 2 (17) is correct: quorum is one-half of total members; half of 33 is 16.5, so at least 17 must be present.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: One-third of 33; no Council rule uses one-third of members.
The smallest whole number not less than one-half of 33.
Two-thirds of 33, more than the quorum requires.
About three-fourths of 33; three-fourths is the voting majority, not the quorum.

points: 33 = 2 Union members (FM and MoS) + 31 State members (28 States + Delhi, Puducherry, J&K).
Quorum asks how many must be present; majority asks how many must agree.

POL-8.3.5-Q33.lead: Option 3 (Ladakh) is correct: only Union territories with a legislature are treated as States for GST, and Ladakh has none.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Puducherry
A UT with a legislature, so it is a voting member.
Delhi
A UT with a legislature, so it is a voting member.
Ladakh
A UT without a legislature (created by the 2019 Act), so it is not a member.
Jammu and Kashmir
A UT with a legislature under the 2019 Act, so it is a voting member.

points: For Articles 246A, 268, 269A and 279A, 'State' includes a Union territory with a legislature.
UTs without legislature are governed directly by the Centre, so the Union's vote covers them.

POL-8.3.5-Q34.lead: Option 1 (3 only) is correct: the President constituted the Council by order, but the Finance Minister chairs it and the Secretariat is in New Delhi.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. President is Chairperson
False
The Union Finance Minister is Chairperson; the President only constitutes the Council by order.
2. Secretariat at Mumbai
False
Laxmikanth: the Secretariat of the Council is located at New Delhi.
3. Constituted by President's order
True
Article 279A empowered the President to constitute the Council by order, issued on 15 September 2016.

points: Option 2 includes false statement 1; option 3 includes false statement 2; option 4 includes both.

POL-8.3.5-Q35.lead: Option 1 (1 only) is correct: each side can block, but the Centre's one-third alone can never pass a decision.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Both Centre and a large State bloc can block
True
A decision needs 75%; the Centre's 33.33% voting no leaves at most 66.67%, and a State bloc holding more than 25% of votes cast can also block.
2. Centre's one-third alone can pass a decision
False
33.33% is far below the required three-fourths of weighted votes present and voting.

points: Option 2 and option 3 accept the false statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
Concept: this mutual veto forces consensus, which is the heart of cooperative fiscal federalism.

POL-8.3.5-Q36.lead: Option 3 (Both 1 and 2) is correct: GST subsumed many Central and State indirect taxes, and Article 246A created concurrent GST law power.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Subsumed central excise, VAT and others
True
Laxmikanth lists central excise, service tax and others on the Union side, and State VAT/sales tax, entry tax, luxury tax and others on the State side.
2. New Article 246A for concurrent GST power
True
The 101st Amendment inserted Article 246A giving both Parliament and State Legislatures power to make GST laws.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each reject at least one true statement.
The same Amendment also inserted Articles 269A and 279A and deleted Article 268A on service tax.

POL-8.3.6-Q01.lead: NCSC is a constitutional body because it is created directly by Article 338; the other three are statutory.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: National Commission for Women
Set up in 1992 under the NCW Act, 1990, an Act of Parliament, so it is statutory.
National Human Rights Commission
Set up in 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, so it is statutory.
National Commission for Minorities
Set up in 1993 under the NCM Act, 1992, so it is statutory.
National Commission for Scheduled Castes
Established directly by Article 338 of the Constitution, so it is a constitutional body.

points: Constitutional body = created by the Constitution itself; statutory body = created by an Act of Parliament.
NCST (Article 338A) and NCBC (Article 338B) are the other constitutional commissions of this family.

POL-8.3.6-Q02.lead: Correct option: 4 (A-2, B-4, C-1, D-3). NCW 1992, NCM 1993, NCPCR 2007, separate NCSC 2004.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. NCW
The National Commission for Women was set up in 1992 under the NCW Act of 1990, so A matches 2.
B. NCM
The National Commission for Minorities was set up in 1993 under the NCM Act of 1992, so B matches 4.
C. NCPCR

Option 2 fails: A-4 gives "NCW" → "1993" (correct: 1992); B-2 gives "NCM" → "1992" (correct: 1993).
Option 3 fails: C-3 gives "NCPCR" → "2004" (correct: 2007); D-1 gives "NCSC (separate)" → "2007" (correct: 2004).

POL-8.3.6-Q03.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A): An Article (338) creates the NCSC, so only a constitutional amendment can abolish it.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
An ordinary law cannot override the Constitution; removing NCSC needs an Art 368 amendment.
R
True
True. Article 338 itself establishes the NCSC, so it is a constitutional body, not one created by an Act of Parliament.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Because the body is created by the Constitution (R), an ordinary law cannot remove it (A). R is the cause, A is the result.
Option 2 fails: R is not just a separate true fact; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.
Contrast: statutory bodies such as NHRC or NCW are created by Acts, so Parliament can change or abolish them by ordinary law.

POL-8.3.6-Q04.lead: Original Article 338 (1950) provided for a single Special Officer for SCs and STs.

What it is / means
Correct?

Created by the 89th Amendment Act, 2003, which split the combined commission.

True/False

Option 4 wrongly rejects the true statement 1.

POL-8.3.6-Q06.lead: Correct option: 4 (A-2, B-1, C-4, D-3). 1931 Census, 1935 Act, 1990, 2003.

Correct match (List-II)

Option 3 fails: C-3 gives "65th Constitutional Amendment" → "2003" (correct: 1990); D-4 gives "89th Constitutional Amendment" → "1990" (correct: 2003).

POL-8.3.6-Q07.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why

True

Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1.

POL-8.3.6-Q08.lead: Bhola Paswan Shastri headed the 1978 Commission for SCs and STs set up by the Janata Government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

A senior Union Minister of the time; he did not head this commission.

Kunwar Singh
The first Chairperson of the separate National Commission for STs (2004).

POL-8.3.6-Q09.lead: After the 1987 Resolution the commission remained a non-statutory, national-level advisory body.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 all include statement 3, so they fail.
Link: 102nd (2018) = NCBC + Article 342-A; 105th (2021) = State lists restored.

POL-8.3.8-Q10.lead: Option 4: under Article 342-A(1) the President specifies SEBCs for a state after consultation with the Governor of that state.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Chief Minister
Article 342-A does not name the Chief Minister as the authority to be consulted.
The State Legislature
The legislature has no role in the presidential notification; changes to the notified Central List need a law of Parliament.
The NCBC Chairperson
The NCBC advises on policy, but Article 342-A names the Governor for consultation.
The Governor
Article 342-A follows the same pattern as Articles 341 (SCs) and 342 (STs): consultation with the Governor.

points: After the 105th Amendment, 2021, this notification is the Central List, used for the purposes of the Central Government (LX p791).

POL-8.3.8-Q11.lead: Option 3: under Article 342-A(2), any inclusion in or exclusion from the notified Central List can be made only by Parliament by law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The President by a fresh notification
The President issues the first notification, but cannot change it later by another notification.
NCBC by its order
The NCBC can examine requests and advise, but it has no power to alter the list.
Parliament by law
Article 342-A(2) gives this power only to Parliament.
The Supreme Court
Courts can test the validity of a list but do not prepare or amend it.

points: Same rule as for SC and ST lists under Articles 341(2) and 342(2): first notification by the President, later changes only by Parliament.

POL-8.3.8-Q12.lead: Option 4: the definition clause in Article 366, added by the 102nd Amendment, says SEBCs are the backward classes so deemed under Article 342-A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 340
It allows a commission to investigate backward classes; it does not define who they are.
Article 338-B
It creates the NCBC, the body that protects SEBCs; it is not the definition provision.
Article 15(4)
It allows special provisions for SEBCs but does not say who they are.
Article 342-A
The lists notified under it decide which classes are SEBCs, and Article 366 points to it.

points: The Constitution does not name the backward classes itself; it leaves this to the lists notified under Article 342-A (LX p791).

POL-8.3.8-Q13.lead: Option 4: after Article 338-B created a constitutional NCBC, Parliament repealed the 1993 Act through the NCBC (Repeal) Act, 2018.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: It continues to govern the NCBC
False; the NCBC now works under Article 338-B and rules made by the President.
It was struck down by the Supreme Court
False; no court struck it down, Parliament repealed it.
It was converted into a law for State commissions
False; State BC commissions are set up by State laws, like the AP Act of 1993.
It was repealed by Parliament in 2018
True; the statutory basis was no longer needed once the body became constitutional.

points: Statutory to constitutional: the Act that created the old body is repealed because the Constitution itself now creates it.

POL-8.3.8-Q14.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A): Constitutional status under Art 338-B put NCBC on par with NCSC and NCST.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Since 2018 the NCBC has the same constitutional status as NCSC and NCST.
R
True
The 102nd Amendment, 2018 inserted Art 338-B and made NCBC a constitutional body.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. NCSC and NCST are constitutional bodies; once NCBC also became one (R), it stood at par with them (A).
Option 2 fails: R is not just a separate true fact; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.

POL-8.3.8-Q15.lead: Option 3: the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment is the nodal ministry for backward-class matters and the NCBC.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Ministry of Home Affairs
It deals with internal security, Centre-state matters and UTs, not backward-class welfare.
Ministry of Tribal Affairs
Created in 1999 for STs; it is the nodal ministry for the NCST.
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
It handles SC and OBC welfare and is nodal for the NCSC and NCBC.
Ministry of Minority Affairs
It is nodal for the National Commission for Minorities.

points: LX p624 explains that STs were moved to a separate ministry because Social Justice could not handle all SC, ST and backward-class work.

POL-8.3.8-Q16.lead: Option 2: the NCBC consists of a Chairperson, a Vice-Chairperson and three other Members (five persons).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Chairperson and 4 Members
Wrong; the structure has a Vice-Chairperson as a separate post.
Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and 3 Members
Correct, as fixed by Article 338-B(2) (LX p627).
Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and 5 Members
Wrong; there are three other members, not five.
Chairperson and 2 Members
Wrong; this omits the Vice-Chairperson and one member.

points: The NCSC and NCST have the same 1 + 1 + 3 structure, which makes this easy to remember.

POL-8.3.8-Q17.lead: Option 1 (1 only): members are appointed by the President by warrant, and their service conditions are fixed by the President, not by Parliament.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal
True
True: Article 338-B(3) says NCBC members are appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal (LX p627).
2. Service conditions fixed by Parliament by law
False
The President determines them by rule; the NCBC (Conditions of Service and Tenure) Rules, 2018 were made by the President.

points: Option 2 and option 3 wrongly accept statement 2; option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1.

POL-8.3.8-Q18.lead: Option 1: under the 2018 Rules, NCBC members hold office for three years and cannot be appointed for more than two terms.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 3 years, maximum two terms
Correct, as stated in the 2018 Rules made by the President (LX p627).
5 years, one term only
Wrong; neither the length nor the one-term limit matches the Rules.
6 years or 65 years of age
This is the tenure pattern of the CAG, not of the NCBC.
At the pleasure of the Prime Minister
No NCBC tenure depends on the Prime Minister; the President appoints and fixes tenure by rules.

points: Same three-year, two-term rule applies to the NCSC and NCST.

POL-8.3.8-Q20.lead: Option 4 (1, 2 and 3): all three are functions of the NCBC listed in Article 338-B(5).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Investigate and monitor safeguards
True
This is the first function: investigate and monitor all matters relating to safeguards for SEBCs and evaluate their working.
2. Inquire into specific complaints
True
The second function is to inquire into complaints of deprivation of rights and safeguards of SEBCs.
3. Advise on development and evaluate progress
True
The third function is to participate and advise on socio-economic development and evaluate progress under the Union or a state.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out one true statement, so only option 4 is complete.
The other listed functions are reporting to the President, recommending measures, and any other function the President specifies.

POL-8.3.8-Q21.lead: Option 3: the NCBC presents its reports to the President.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Speaker of the Lok Sabha
The Speaker does not receive the report; it reaches Parliament only when the President lays it.
The Prime Minister
The PM is not named in Article 338-B as the recipient.
The President
The commission reports to the President annually and whenever it thinks fit.
The Union Minister of Social Justice
The nodal ministry does not receive the reports under the Constitution.

points: The President lays the reports before Parliament with a memorandum on action taken and reasons for non-acceptance (LX p628).

POL-8.3.8-Q22.lead: Option 3: the statement 'it can report only once every five years' is NOT correct; the NCBC reports annually and whenever it thinks fit.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: It presents an annual report
Correct statement; an annual report is required.
✗ (true)
It may report at any other time it thinks fit
Correct statement; special reports are allowed.
✗ (true)
It can report only once every five years
Wrong statement; there is no five-year limit, so this is the answer.
Reports concern the working of safeguards for SEBCs
Correct statement; that is the subject of the reports.
✗ (true)

points: In a 'NOT correct' question, the answer is the false statement.

POL-8.3.8-Q23.lead: Option 1 (1 only): the NCBC recommends measures, and the President can assign it further functions, so statement 2 is wrong.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Recommends measures for Union and states
True
Article 338-B(5)(e) lets it recommend measures for effective implementation of safeguards for SEBCs.
2. Only the listed functions; no more can be assigned
False
Article 338-B(5)(f) allows such other functions as the President may specify.

points: Option 2 and option 3 accept the false statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.

POL-8.3.8-Q24.lead: Option 2: the reports must be laid with a memorandum explaining the action taken and the reasons for not accepting any recommendation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Comments of the CAG
The CAG audits public accounts and has no role in NCBC reports.
Memorandum on action taken, with reasons for non-acceptance
Required by Article 338-B(6), which makes the government answerable to Parliament.
Opinion of the Attorney General
The Attorney General gives legal advice on request; no opinion is required here.
Approval of the Union Cabinet
No Cabinet approval is required to lay the report.

points: The recommendations are not binding, but the memorandum forces the government to explain why it rejected any of them.

POL-8.3.8-Q25.lead: Option 2: under Article 338-B(7), an NCBC report concerning a state is forwarded to the State Government, not to the Governor.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Governor of the state
This is the rule for NCSC and NCST reports, not for the NCBC.
The State Government
Article 338-B(7) names the State Government, which lays it before the state legislature.
The High Court of the state
Courts do not receive commission reports.
The State Election Commission
It conducts local body elections and has no role here.

points: This is a favourite trap: NCSC and NCST go to the Governor, NCBC goes to the State Government (LX p628).
The report is laid before the legislature with a memorandum on action taken and reasons for non-acceptance.

POL-8.3.8-Q27.lead: Option 4: imposing imprisonment for contempt is not among the NCBC's civil-court powers; those powers only help it collect evidence.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Summoning a person and examining on oath
This is a listed power, so not the answer: Article 338-B(8) gives the NCBC civil-court power to summon a person and examine him on oath.
✗ (listed)
Requiring production of documents
This is a listed power, so not the answer: under Article 338-B(8) the NCBC can require the discovery and production of any document.
✗ (listed)
Receiving evidence on affidavits
This is a listed power, so not the answer: under Article 338-B(8) the NCBC can receive evidence on affidavits.
✗ (listed)
Imposing imprisonment for contempt
Not listed; the NCBC is a fact-finding body and cannot punish.

points: The other listed powers are requisitioning public records, issuing summons for witnesses and documents, and any other matter the President determines.

POL-8.3.8-Q28.lead: Option 1: the NCBC has the power to regulate its own procedure.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Its own procedure
Correct: Article 338-B(4) gives the NCBC power to regulate its own procedure; it does not regulate other bodies.
The Central List of SEBCs
Only Parliament by law can change the Central List under Article 342-A(2).
State reservation laws
These are made by state legislatures; the NCBC can only advise.
Appointment of its members
Members are appointed by the President by warrant.

points: NCSC and NCST also regulate their own procedure; this is a common feature.

POL-8.3.8-Q29.lead: Option 1: under Article 338-B(9) the Union and every state must consult the NCBC on all major policy matters affecting SEBCs.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: All major policy matters affecting SEBCs
Correct: Article 338-B(9) requires the Union and every State to consult the NCBC on all major policy matters affecting SEBCs.
Only recruitment to central services
Too narrow; the clause is not limited to recruitment.
Only budget allocation for OBC welfare
Too narrow; the clause covers all major policy.
Only delimitation of constituencies
Delimitation is done by the Delimitation Commission and is not an NCBC matter.

points: Exception: since the 105th Amendment, 2021, states need not consult the NCBC when preparing their own State lists (LX p628).

POL-8.3.8-Q30.lead: Option 2: in Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra (2021), the Supreme Court struck down the Maratha quota and read Article 342-A as removing states' power to identify SEBCs.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India
The 1992 Mandal case that upheld OBC reservation and set the 50% ceiling.
Jaishri Laxmanrao Patil v. State of Maharashtra
The 2021 Maratha case; it led Parliament to pass the 105th Amendment.
Janhit Abhiyan v. Union of India
The 2022 case that upheld the 10% EWS quota of the 103rd Amendment.
State of Punjab v. Davinder Singh
The 2024 seven-judge case allowing states to sub-classify SCs.

points: Parliament answered this judgment with the 105th Amendment, 2021, which restored State lists.

POL-8.3.8-Q31.lead: Option 2 (2 only): the Court did not strike down Article 342-A; it upheld it and read it narrowly, but it held the Maratha quota breached the 50% ceiling.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Struck down Article 342-A
False
The Court upheld the 102nd Amendment; by 3:2 it only interpreted Article 342-A as taking away states' power to identify SEBCs.
2. Maratha quota breached the 50% ceiling
True
The Court found no exceptional circumstances to cross the 50% limit set in Indra Sawhney (1992).

points: Option 1 and option 3 accept the false statement 1; option 4 rejects the true statement 2.
Key idea: interpreting a provision is different from striking it down.

POL-8.3.8-Q32.lead: Option 4: the 105th Amendment Act, 2021 restored the power of states and UTs to prepare their own SEBC lists.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: It created Article 338-B and Article 342-A; it was the provision that caused the doubt.
It gave 10% reservation for economically weaker sections.
It extended SC/ST seat reservation in legislatures and ended Anglo-Indian nomination (in force 2020).
It amended Articles 338-B, 342-A and 366 so that states can keep their own lists by law.

points: Sequence: 102nd created the confusion, the Maratha judgment exposed it, and the 105th fixed it.

POL-8.3.8-Q33.lead: Option 1 (1 and 2 only): the 105th Amendment restored State lists and exempted them from NCBC consultation, but the Central List is still changed only by Parliament.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Restored State/UT power to keep own lists
True
States and UTs may prepare and maintain their own lists by law, which can differ from the Central List (LX p791).
2. States need not consult the NCBC for State lists
True
The 105th Amendment exempted states from consultation on their own lists (LX p628).
3. Central List changeable by presidential notification
False
Article 342-A(2) still allows changes to the Central List only by a law of Parliament.

points: Option 2 and option 3 include the false statement 3; option 4 includes all three, so it also fails.

POL-8.3.8-Q34.lead: Option 2: after the 105th Amendment, Andhra Pradesh need not consult the NCBC for its own State list.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Must get a presidential notification under Art 342-A(1)
That notification is for the Central List only, used by the Central Government.
Need not consult NCBC
Correct; the 105th Amendment exempted states from consulting the NCBC on their own lists.
Parliament must pass a law
Parliament's law is needed only for the Central List; the State acts by its own law.
NCBC's advice is binding
NCBC advice is never binding, and for State lists it is not even required.

points: The State list and the Central List can differ; State lists govern state jobs and state institutions.

POL-8.3.8-Q35.lead: Option 1 (A-3, B-1, C-2, D-4) is correct. The 338 series plus Article 340.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Article 338
3. NCSC
Article 338 provides for the National Commission for Scheduled Castes, so A matches 3.
B. Article 338-A
1. NCST
Article 338-A, inserted in 2003 by the 89th Amendment, provides for the commission for Scheduled Tribes, so B matches 1.
C. Article 338-B
2. NCBC
Article 338-B, inserted in 2018 by the 102nd Amendment, provides for the commission for Backward Classes, so C matches 2.
D. Article 340
4. Commission to investigate backward classes
Ad hoc commissions such as Kalelkar, Mandal and Rohini.

points: Option 2 fails: it gives A-1 (NCST), B-3 (NCSC); correct is A-3, B-1.
Option 3 fails: it gives B-2 (NCBC), C-1 (NCST); correct is B-1, C-2.
Option 4 fails: it gives A-4 (Commission to investigate conditions of backward classes), D-3 (NCSC); correct is A-3, D-4.
Art 340 is a temporary inquiry commission; Art 338B is a permanent body — do not confuse.

POL-8.3.8-Q36.lead: Option 1 (A-3, B-2, C-1) is correct. The three 'list' articles.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Article 341
3. Scheduled Castes
President specifies SCs for each State/UT.
B. Article 342
2. Scheduled Tribes
Under Article 342 the President specifies the tribes that are Scheduled Tribes for each State or UT, so B matches 2.
C. Article 342-A
1. SEBCs
Central list of SEBCs (102nd, 2018; 105th, 2021 restored State lists).

points: Option 2 fails: it gives A-2 (Scheduled Tribes), B-3 (Scheduled Castes); correct is A-3, B-2.
Option 3 fails: it gives A-1 (Socially and educationally backward classes), C-3 (Scheduled Castes); correct is A-3, C-1.
Option 4 fails: it gives B-1 (Socially and educationally backward classes), C-2 (Scheduled Tribes); correct is B-2, C-1.
Hook: 341 → SC, 342 → ST, 342-A → the newest group, SEBCs.

POL-8.3.8-Q37.lead: Option 1: Justice R.N. Prasad was the first chairman of the statutory NCBC (1993-96).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Justice R.N. Prasad
First NCBC chairman, 1993-96, as listed by Laxmikanth.
Justice K. Puttaswamy
He chaired the Andhra Pradesh Commission for Backward Classes from 1994, not the NCBC.
Hansraj Gangaram Ahir
He became NCBC chairperson in 2022, long after 1993.
Justice G. Rohini
She headed the 2017 commission on sub-categorisation of OBCs.

points: The NCBC began in 1993 as a statutory body under the NCBC Act, 1993, following Indra Sawhney (1992).

POL-8.3.8-Q38.lead: Option 2: Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti took charge as Chairperson of the NCBC in March 2026.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Hansraj Gangaram Ahir
He was the previous chairperson, from December 2022.
Sadhvi Niranjan Jyoti
Took charge as Chairperson in March 2026.
Bhagwan Lal Sahni
He was the first chairperson after the NCBC became constitutional (2019).
Kiran Umesh Mahalle
She took charge as a Member, not the Chairperson, at the same time.

points: The Chairperson is appointed by the President by warrant under Article 338-B(3) for a three-year term.

POL-8.3.8-Q39.lead: Option 1 (1-2-4-3): Kalelkar Commission 1953, Mandal report 1980, Rohini Commission 2017, 105th Amendment 2021.

head: Event
Year
Why / concept
rows: 1. Kaka Kalelkar Commission appointed
First Article 340 commission; it reported in 1955.
2. Mandal Commission report
Second Article 340 commission, appointed 1979, reported 1980.
4. Rohini Commission constituted
Article 340 commission to study sub-categorisation of central OBCs.
3. 105th Amendment enacted
Restored State power to keep their own SEBC lists after the Maratha judgment.

points: Option 2 puts the 105th Amendment (2021) before Rohini (2017); option 3 puts Mandal before Kalelkar; option 4 puts Rohini before Mandal.

POL-8.3.8-Q40.lead: Option 2: the Justice G. Rohini Commission examined sub-categorisation of OBCs in the Central List.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Creamy layer income limit
The creamy-layer ceiling is fixed by government order; it was not this commission's task.
Sub-categorisation of OBCs
Its task was to check whether a few castes were taking most of the 27% benefit and to divide the list into sub-groups.
Reservation in promotions
Promotion reservation under Article 16(4A) is for SCs and STs, not this commission's subject.
EWS quota
The 10% EWS quota came from the 103rd Amendment, 2019.

points: Sub-categorisation means dividing the OBC list into groups so that the less advanced castes get a fair share.

POL-8.3.8-Q41.lead: Option 1 (1 and 2 only): the Rohini Commission was set up under Article 340 for sub-categorisation, but its recommendations are not binding.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Constituted by the President under Article 340
True
Article 340 lets the President appoint a commission to investigate backward classes.
2. Task was sub-categorisation of central OBCs
True
It studied how benefits were spread among castes in the Central List to make the distribution fairer.
3. Recommendations binding on the Union
False
An Article 340 report is only laid before Parliament with an action-taken memorandum; the government may accept or reject it.

points: Option 2 and option 3 include the false statement 3; option 4 includes all three, so it also fails.

POL-8.3.8-Q42.lead: Option 2 (2 only): the AP Commission for Backward Classes is a statutory body under a State Act, and its members are nominated by the State Government for three years.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. It is a constitutional body
False
It was set up under the Andhra Pradesh Commission for Backward Classes Act, 1993, a State law, so it is statutory.
2. State government appoints for 3 years
True
Section 3 of the Act lets the Government nominate members and Section 4 gives a three-year term.

points: Option 1 and option 3 accept the false statement 1; option 4 rejects the true statement 2.
Only the national body (NCBC, Article 338-B) has constitutional status.

POL-8.3.8-Q43.lead: Option 2: under the AP Act, 1993 the Chairperson must be a judge of a High Court or a retired judge of the Supreme Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: IAS officer of Secretary rank
The Act does not make civil servants eligible for the chair.
Judge of a High Court or the Supreme Court
Required by Section 3(2)(a), which gives the body a judicial head.
Member of the state legislature
Legislators are not the qualifying category for the chair.
Professor of social sciences
The Act provides a social scientist as a member, not as the chairperson.

points: Other members include a social scientist and persons with special knowledge of backward classes, plus a Member-Secretary.

POL-8.3.8-Q44.lead: Option 3 (both): the AP Government must consult the State BC Commission when revising the list, and Justice K. Puttaswamy was its first chairman.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. AP must consult the State BC Commission on list changes
True
Section 11(2) of the AP Act, 1993 says the Government shall consult the Commission when revising the lists.
2. Justice K. Puttaswamy was the first chairman
True
He chaired the Commission from January 1994, when it was first constituted under the 1993 Act.

points: Option 1 and option 2 each reject one true statement; option 4 rejects both.
The Commission's advice is not binding: the Government lays a memorandum explaining any non-acceptance before the Assembly.

POL-8.3.8-Q45.lead: Option 1: in Indra Sawhney (1992) the Supreme Court directed permanent bodies to examine inclusion and exclusion in backward-class lists, and the AP Act, 1993 followed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Indra Sawhney v. Union of India (1992)
The Mandal judgment, which directed permanent backward-class commissions.
Champakam Dorairajan (1951)
It struck down a communal reservation order and led to the First Amendment adding Article 15(4).
M. Nagaraj (2006)
It dealt with reservation in promotion for SCs and STs.
Ashoka Kumar Thakur (2008)
It upheld OBC reservation in central educational institutions.

points: The NCBC Act, 1993 at the Centre and State Acts like Andhra Pradesh's in 1993 were the result of this direction.

POL-8.3.8-Q46.lead: Option 2 (1-2-3-4): Indra Sawhney 1992, statutory NCBC 1993, constitutional status 2018, Maratha judgment 2021.

head: Event
Year
Why / concept
rows: 1. Indra Sawhney judgment
It directed a permanent body for backward-class lists.
2. NCBC as statutory body
Set up under the NCBC Act, 1993 to follow that direction.
3. NCBC gets constitutional status
The 102nd Amendment inserted Article 338-B.
4. Maratha reservation judgment
It interpreted Article 342-A, which came with the 2018 amendment.

points: Option 1 puts the statutory NCBC before the judgment that caused it; option 3 puts the Maratha case before the 2018 amendment it interpreted; option 4 puts constitutional status before statutory status.

POL-8.3.8-Q47.lead: Option 4: constitutional status from 1950 is not common; in 1950 Article 338 provided only a Special Officer, and the commissions became constitutional in 1990, 2003 and 2018.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and 3 Members
This is common, so not the answer: each of NCSC, NCST and NCBC has a Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and three other Members.
✗ (common)
Three-year term
Common; rules made by the President give each a three-year term, with at most two terms.
✗ (common)
Powers of a civil court
Common; all three have civil-court powers while inquiring.
✗ (common)
Constitutional status from 1950
Not common; even the SC body was only a Special Officer in 1950, and the NCBC became constitutional only in 2018.

points: Dates: joint SC-ST commission 1990 (65th Amendment), NCST 2003 (89th), NCBC 2018 (102nd).

POL-8.3.8-Q48.lead: Option 1: denial of OBC certificates is a complaint of deprivation of rights, which the NCBC can inquire into under Article 338-B(5)(b).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Inquiring into specific complaints
This NCBC function directly covers a complaint that rights or benefits were denied.
Notifying the Central List
Done by the President under Article 342-A, not by the NCBC.
Laying reports before Parliament
Wrong: the NCBC sends reports to the President, who causes them to be laid before Parliament; it is not the function used for a complaint.
Fixing service conditions of members
Wrong: service conditions of members are fixed by the President by rule (Article 338-B(3)); this has nothing to do with the complaint.

points: While inquiring, the NCBC can summon officers and call for records using its civil-court powers.

POL-8.3.9-Q01.lead: Answer: Option 2 (2 only). The Special Officer was not in the original Constitution; Art 350B was added by the 7th Amendment, 1956.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Original Constitution provided for the Special Officer
False
The original 1950 Constitution had no such provision; it came only after the States Reorganisation Commission (1953–55) recommended it.
2. Art 350B inserted by the 7th Amendment, 1956
True
The 7th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1956 inserted Art 350B in Part XVII.

points: Option 1 and Option 3 wrongly treat statement 1 as true.
Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 2.
The 7th Amendment implemented the reorganisation of States on linguistic lines, so it also added safeguards for linguistic minorities.

POL-8.3.9-Q02.lead: Answer: Option 4, the States Reorganisation Commission (1953–55) — it felt that linguistic minorities in the new linguistic States needed a special officer to watch their safeguards.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Dhar Commission
The Linguistic Provinces Commission (1948) under S.K. Dhar; it advised against forming States on a linguistic basis.
2. Official Language Commission
The 1955 commission under B.G. Kher on the use of Hindi as the official language; it did not propose this officer.
3. JVP Committee
The 1948–49 committee of Nehru, Patel and Pattabhi Sitaramayya; it also rejected language as the basis for States.
4. States Reorganisation Commission
The Fazl Ali Commission (1953–55); on its recommendation the 7th Amendment inserted Art 350B.

points: Logic: when States were drawn on language lines, people speaking another language in each State became minorities, so the SRC wanted a watchdog for them.
The office itself was set up in 1957.
