points: Option 1 fails: it gives A-1 (Serving or retired HC Chief Justice), B-3 (Former CJI or SC Judge), C-4 (Serving or retired SC Judge); correct is A-3, B-4, C-1.
Option 2 fails: it gives A-4 (Serving or retired SC Judge), B-3 (Former CJI or SC Judge); correct is A-3, B-4.
Option 4 fails: it gives A-1 (Serving or retired HC Chief Justice), C-3 (Former CJI or SC Judge); correct is A-3, C-1.

POL-8.4.1-Q10.lead: Option 4: since the 2019 Amendment, the NHRC has three members with knowledge or practical experience of human rights, and at least one of them must be a woman.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: One must be from a Scheduled Caste
Wrong. The Act sets no caste condition for NHRC members; a SC/ST member rule exists for the National Commission for Women, not the NHRC.
All must be nominated by NGOs
Wrong. NGOs have no nominating role; all members are appointed by the President on the recommendation of the six-member committee headed by the Prime Minister.
One must be a retired civil servant
Wrong. No seat is reserved for civil servants; these seats need only knowledge or practical experience in human rights.
At least one must be a woman
Correct. The 2019 Amendment raised these seats from two to three and required at least one woman among them.

points: Full NHRC: Chairperson + 5 members (one SC judge, one HC Chief Justice, three human-rights persons) + 7 ex-officio members.
Before 2019 there were only two human-rights-expert members and no woman condition.
Memory hook: 2019 = 'two became three, one must be she'.

POL-8.4.1-Q11.lead: Option 4: the Central Vigilance Commission is an anti-corruption body, so its head is not one of the seven ex-officio (deemed) members of the NHRC.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: National Commission for Backward Classes
Wrong choice. Its chairperson became an ex-officio NHRC member through the 2019 Amendment.
National Commission for Protection of Child Rights
Wrong choice. Its chairperson was also added as an ex-officio NHRC member in 2019.
Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities
Wrong choice. The CCPD was added as an ex-officio member in 2019.
Central Vigilance Commission
Correct. The CVC deals with corruption in central government offices, not human rights, so it has no seat in the NHRC.

points: Seven ex-officio members: chairpersons of NCM, NCSC, NCST, NCW, NCBC, NCPCR and the CCPD.
The first four were there from 1993; NCBC, NCPCR and CCPD came in 2019.
Logic: the ex-officio members are bodies that protect a vulnerable group; the CVC protects against corruption, not a group.

POL-8.4.1-Q12.lead: Option 3 (A-3, B-1, C-2) is correct. The 2019 Amendment changed all three numbers.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Ex-officio members
Added NCBC, NCPCR and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities.
B. Human-rights expert members
The 2019 Amendment raised human-rights expert members from 2 to 3, and one of them must be a woman, so B matches 1.
C. Tenure
2. 5 years → 3 years
The 2019 Amendment cut the tenure from 5 years to 3 years (or until age 70, whichever is earlier), so C matches 2.

points: Option 1 fails: it gives B-2 (5 years → 3 years), C-1 (2 → 3); correct is B-1, C-2.
Option 2 fails: it gives A-1 (2 → 3), B-3 (4 → 7); correct is A-3, B-1.
Option 4 fails: it gives A-2 (5 years → 3 years), C-3 (4 → 7); correct is A-3, C-2.

POL-8.4.1-Q13.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true, so option 1 (1 and 3 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Chairperson, NCW
True
The National Commission for Women chairperson has been an ex-officio member since the original 1993 Act.
2. Chairperson, NCBC
False
The National Commission for Backward Classes chairperson was made an ex-officio member only by the 2019 Amendment.
3. Chairperson, NCST
True
The National Commission for Scheduled Tribes chairperson was an ex-officio member before 2019 (originally as part of the combined SC/ST commission).
4. Chairperson, NCPCR
False
The child-rights commission chairperson was added only by the 2019 Amendment.

points: Option 2 wrongly includes statement 2 (NCBC, added 2019).
Option 3 includes 2 and 4, both added in 2019, and leaves out the true ones.
Option 4 wrongly includes statement 4 (NCPCR, added 2019).
Pre-2019 four: Minorities, SCs, STs, Women. Added 2019: BCs, Child Rights, Disabilities.

POL-8.4.1-Q14.lead: Option 4: the President appoints the NHRC Chairperson and members, on the recommendation of a six-member committee headed by the Prime Minister.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Prime Minister
Wrong. The PM heads the recommending committee, but the formal appointment is made by the President.
The Union Home Minister
Wrong. The Home Minister is only one member of the six-member committee.
The Chief Justice of India
Wrong. The CJI is not on the committee; he is consulted only when a sitting SC judge or sitting HC Chief Justice is to be appointed.
The President
Correct. Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993, the President appoints them after the committee recommends names.

points: Recommend = committee (PM, LS Speaker, RS Deputy Chairman, two Leaders of Opposition, Home Minister); appoint = President.
For a State Commission, the Governor appoints on a committee headed by the Chief Minister.

POL-8.4.1-Q15.lead: Option 3: the Chief Justice of India is not a member of the six-member committee that recommends NHRC appointments.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha
Wrong choice. He is a member of the committee (note: the Deputy Chairman, not the Chairman/Vice-President).
Union Home Minister
Wrong choice. The Central Home Minister is a member of the committee.
Chief Justice of India
Correct. The CJI is not on the committee; he is only consulted before a sitting SC judge or sitting HC Chief Justice is appointed.
Leader of the Opposition in the Rajya Sabha
Wrong choice. The Leaders of the Opposition of both Houses are members.

points: Committee: PM (head), Speaker of Lok Sabha, Deputy Chairman of Rajya Sabha, Leaders of Opposition in both Houses, Union Home Minister.
Keeping the judiciary off the committee is why the separate CJI consultation for sitting judges exists.

POL-8.4.1-Q16.lead: Option 3: the Prime Minister heads the six-member committee that recommends the NHRC Chairperson and members.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Speaker of the Lok Sabha
Wrong. The Speaker is a member of the committee, not its head.
Vice-President
Wrong. The Vice-President (Rajya Sabha Chairman) is not on the committee; the Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha is.
Prime Minister
Correct. The Act makes the Prime Minister the chairperson of the recommending committee.
Union Law Minister
Wrong. The Law Minister is not on the committee; the Home Minister is.

points: Two common traps: Deputy Chairman (not Vice-President) and Home Minister (not Law Minister).
State parallel: Chief Minister heads the SHRC committee.

POL-8.4.1-Q17.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so option 4 (1 and 2 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Vacancy in committee does not invalidate appointment
True
The Act provides that no appointment is invalid merely because of a vacancy in the selection committee, so a missing member does not stop the process.
2. Sitting SC judge only after consulting CJI
True
A sitting SC judge or sitting HC Chief Justice can be appointed only after consultation with the Chief Justice of India.
3. Parliament must approve the recommendation
False
Parliament has no approval role; the President appoints directly on the committee's recommendation.

points: Option 1 leaves out the true statement 2.
Options 2 and 3 include the false statement 3.

POL-8.4.1-Q18.lead: Option 2: a sitting SC judge or sitting Chief Justice of a High Court can be appointed only after consulting the Chief Justice of India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Consent of the State Governor
Wrong. The Governor has no role in NHRC appointments; he appoints only State Commission members.
Consultation with the Chief Justice of India
Correct. This safeguard protects judicial independence when a serving judge is taken away from the bench.
Resolution of both Houses of Parliament
Wrong. Parliament passes no resolution for NHRC appointments.
Approval of the Supreme Court collegium
Wrong. The collegium appoints judges; it has no role under the Protection of Human Rights Act.

points: The consultation applies only to sitting judges; retired judges need no CJI consultation.
State parallel: a sitting HC judge or District Judge for an SHRC needs consultation with that High Court's Chief Justice.

POL-8.4.1-Q19.lead: Option 3: after the 2019 Amendment, the Chairperson holds office for 3 years or until age 70, whichever is earlier.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 5 years or till 65 years of age
Wrong. 65 was never the NHRC age limit; it is the retirement age of Supreme Court judges.
5 years or till 70 years of age
Wrong. This was the rule before 2019; the 2019 Amendment reduced 5 years to 3.
3 years or till 70 years of age
Correct. The 2019 Amendment cut the term from five to three years, keeping the 70-year age limit.
6 years or till 65 years of age
Wrong. This is the CAG and Chief Election Commissioner pattern, not the NHRC.

points: The same 3 years / 70 years rule applies to SHRC members.
Memory hook: NHRC = 3 and 70.

POL-8.4.1-Q20.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true and 2 is false, so option 4 (1 and 3 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Eligible for re-appointment
True
The Act, as amended in 2019, says the Chairperson and members are eligible for re-appointment.
2. Re-appointment limited to one more term
False
The one-more-term cap existed for members before 2019; the 2019 Amendment removed it, so the Act now simply says they are eligible for re-appointment.
3. No further government employment after office
True
After their tenure they are not eligible for further employment under the Centre or any State, which protects their independence.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 all include the false statement 2.
Option 1 also leaves out true statement 3.

POL-8.4.1-Q21.lead: Statements 1, 2 and 3 are true and 4 is false, so option 1 (1, 2 and 3 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Direct removal for insolvency
True
Being adjudged insolvent is one of the five grounds on which the President removes directly, without any court inquiry.
2. Direct removal for outside paid employment
True
Taking paid employment outside the duties of office is also one of the five direct grounds.
3. Misbehaviour needs SC inquiry
True
For proved misbehaviour or incapacity, the President must refer the matter to the Supreme Court and can remove only if the Court advises so.
4. Every ground needs SC inquiry
False
Only misbehaviour and incapacity need the SC inquiry; the five objective grounds do not.

points: Option 2 wrongly includes 4 and leaves out 2 and 3.
Option 3 wrongly includes 4.
Option 4 includes all, but 4 contradicts 1 and 2.
Logic: objective facts (insolvency, conviction, court-declared unsoundness) need no inquiry; subjective charges (misbehaviour) need the Supreme Court to judge.

POL-8.4.1-Q22.lead: Option 3: proved misbehaviour is not a direct ground; for it the President must first refer the matter to the Supreme Court for inquiry.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Declared of unsound mind by a competent court
Wrong choice. This is a direct ground, because a court has already declared the fact.
Convicted and sentenced to imprisonment for an offence
Wrong choice. Conviction with imprisonment is a direct ground.
Proved misbehaviour
Correct. Misbehaviour (and incapacity) need a Supreme Court inquiry and advice before removal.
Unfit due to infirmity of mind or body
Wrong choice. Infirmity of mind or body making him unfit is one of the five direct grounds.

points: Five direct grounds: insolvency, outside paid employment, infirmity of mind or body, court-declared unsound mind, conviction and imprisonment.
Same removal rules apply to SHRC members, and even they are removed by the President, not the Governor.

POL-8.4.1-Q23.lead: Answer: option 3 (A true, R false): NHRC members are removed by the President after an SC inquiry, not by impeachment.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
For proved misbehaviour, the President removes only after the Supreme Court inquires and upholds the charge.
R
False
False: there is no impeachment in Parliament for the NHRC Chairperson.

points: Does R explain A? No link: R is false. Note the difference: SC judges are removed by Parliament's address; NHRC members by the President on the Supreme Court's report.
Options 1 and 2 fail: they treat R as true, but R is false.
Option 4 fails: A is a correct statement.

POL-8.4.1-Q24.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true and 2 is false, so option 1 (1 and 3 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Resignation in writing to the President
True
The appointing authority is the President, so a member resigns by writing addressed to the President.
2. Salaries fixed by Parliament in a Schedule
False
Salaries, allowances and service conditions are determined by the Central Government, not by a Schedule of the Act.
3. Service conditions cannot be varied to disadvantage
True
After appointment, salary and service conditions cannot be changed to their disadvantage, which protects independence.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 all include the false statement 2.
For SHRC members, the State Government fixes salaries.

POL-8.4.1-Q25.lead: Option 3: the Act makes the Secretary-General the Chief Executive Officer of the NHRC; since 2019 he exercises its administrative and financial powers under the Chairperson's control.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Chairperson
Wrong. The Chairperson heads the Commission and controls the Secretary-General, but is not called its CEO.
The Director-General (Investigation)
Wrong. The Director-General heads the investigation wing that inquires into complaints.
The Secretary-General
Correct. He is the CEO; the 2019 Amendment gave him all administrative and financial powers (except judicial functions and regulation-making), subject to the Chairperson.
The Registrar (Law)
Wrong. The Registrar handles the law division and complaint processing, not the whole administration.

points: In an SHRC, the Secretary plays the same role.
Hook: Chairperson leads, Secretary-General runs the office.

POL-8.4.1-Q26.lead: Option 2: the NHRC can inquire on its own (suo motu), on a petition by a victim or anyone on his behalf, or on an order of a court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only on a petition by the victim
Wrong. A petition is one route, but the NHRC can also act suo motu (for example on a media report) or on a court order.
Suo motu, on a petition, or on a court order
Correct. These are the three routes named in its first function in the Act.
Only on a reference from the Central Government
Wrong. The NHRC does not need a government reference; it was designed to act independently of the government.
Only on a direction of the Supreme Court
Wrong. A court order is one route, but not the only one.

points: It covers both a violation of human rights and negligence of a public servant in preventing such a violation.
'Suo motu' means 'on its own motion', without anyone filing a complaint.

POL-8.4.1-Q27.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so option 3 (1 and 2 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Intervene in court proceedings
True
The NHRC can intervene in any court proceeding involving an allegation of human-rights violation, with the approval of that court.
2. Visit jails
True
It can visit jails and detention places to study living conditions of inmates and make recommendations.
3. Quash a magistrate's detention order
False
The NHRC is not a court and cannot quash any order; it can only recommend action or approach the Supreme Court or High Court for writs.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 all include the false statement 3.
Its role is mainly recommendatory; only courts can set aside orders.

POL-8.4.1-Q28.lead: Option 4: framing rules of criminal procedure is a law-making task of Parliament (and rule-making by governments), not a function of the NHRC.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Reviewing factors, including terrorism, that inhibit human rights
Wrong choice. This is a listed NHRC function: review such factors and recommend remedies.
Studying international treaties and recommending implementation
Wrong choice. Studying treaties and international instruments on human rights is a listed function.
Encouraging NGOs in the human-rights field
Wrong choice. Encouraging NGO efforts is a listed function.
Framing rules of criminal procedure for police
Correct. The NHRC can only review legal safeguards and recommend measures; it cannot make procedural law.

points: Other listed functions: inquiry, court intervention, jail visits, reviewing safeguards, research, human-rights literacy.
Hook: NHRC reviews, studies, recommends and spreads awareness; it does not legislate.

POL-8.4.1-Q29.lead: Option 1: spreading human-rights literacy and promoting awareness of safeguards is one of the functions of the NHRC under the Act.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: National Human Rights Commission
Correct. The Act lists spreading human-rights literacy and awareness of safeguards among its functions.
Central Information Commission
Wrong. The CIC hears appeals and complaints under the Right to Information Act, 2005.
Law Commission of India
Wrong. The Law Commission is an executive body that studies laws and recommends legal reforms.
Inter-State Council
Wrong. It is set up under Article 263 to discuss Centre-State and inter-State issues.

points: The NHRC does this through publications, media, seminars and camp sittings.
The same function is given to State Commissions.

POL-8.4.1-Q30.lead: Option 1: the NHRC's headquarters is in (New) Delhi, and it may set up offices at other places in India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: New Delhi
Correct. The Act fixes the headquarters at Delhi.
Mumbai
Wrong. Mumbai is not the NHRC headquarters; the Commission may open other offices, but its seat is Delhi.
Kolkata
Wrong. Kolkata is not the NHRC headquarters.
Bengaluru
Wrong. Bengaluru is not the NHRC headquarters.

points: It regulates its own procedure and holds camp sittings in different parts of the country.
An SHRC's headquarters is wherever the State Government notifies.

POL-8.4.1-Q31.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are civil-court powers the NHRC has; statement 3 is not, so option 2 (1 and 2 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Summoning and enforcing attendance of witnesses
True
While inquiring, the NHRC has the powers of a civil court, including summoning witnesses and examining them on oath.
2. Requisitioning public records
True
It can requisition any public record or a copy of it from any court or office, as a civil court can.
3. Sentencing a guilty public servant
False
A civil court's powers do not include criminal sentencing, and the NHRC has no power to punish; it can only recommend prosecution.

points: Option 1 leaves out the true statement 2.
Options 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.
Its proceedings have a judicial character, but its final output is a recommendation.

POL-8.4.1-Q32.lead: Answer: option 3 (A true, R false): Proceedings are judicial in character, but its recommendations are not binding.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
NHRC proceedings are deemed judicial proceedings.
R
False
False: NHRC recommendations are not binding on the government.

points: Does R explain A? No link: R is false. Judicial character applies to how it inquires, not to the force of its findings.
Options 1 and 2 fail: they treat R as true, but R is false.
Option 4 fails: A is a correct statement.

POL-8.4.1-Q33.lead: Option 2: besides its own investigating staff, the NHRC may use the services of any officer or investigation agency of the Central or a State Government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Transfer the complaint to the CBI for prosecution
Wrong. The NHRC cannot itself launch prosecution; it can only recommend prosecution to the government.
Use services of officers or investigation agencies of the Centre or State
Correct. The Act expressly allows it to utilise such officers or agencies for investigation.
Ask the Governor to appoint a judicial commission
Wrong. The Act gives no such route; the Governor has no role in NHRC inquiries.
Close the complaint for want of staff
Wrong. Staff shortage is not a ground to close a complaint; the Act provides borrowed agencies for exactly this situation.

points: It also works with NGOs that have first-hand information on violations.
Manpower shortage is one of the problems the NHRC itself has reported.

POL-8.4.1-Q34.lead: Option 2: the NHRC cannot inquire into any matter after one year from the date the violation is alleged to have been committed, so an 18-month-old complaint is time-barred.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: NHRC must inquire as torture has no time limit
Wrong. The one-year bar applies to all matters; the Act makes no exception for torture.
NHRC cannot inquire as one year has passed
Correct. Section 36(2) of the Act sets this one-year limit.
NHRC can inquire only with Supreme Court leave
Wrong. The Act has no 'leave of the Supreme Court' exception to the time limit.
NHRC must transfer it to the State Commission
Wrong. The same one-year limit binds the State Commission, so transfer does not help.

points: The victim can still go to a court (for example by a writ petition), which is not bound by this NHRC limit.
Hook: NHRC looks back only one year.

POL-8.4.1-Q35.lead: Option 4: the NHRC has no power to attach property; its steps are recommendations plus approaching the Supreme Court or High Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Recommend compensation to the victim
Wrong choice. Recommending compensation or damages is one of its four steps.
Recommend prosecution of the guilty public servant
Wrong choice. It can recommend prosecution or other action against the public servant.
Approach the Supreme Court or High Court for writs
Wrong choice. It can approach the SC or HC for directions, orders or writs.
Order attachment of the public servant's property
Correct. Attachment is an enforcement power of courts; the NHRC cannot punish or enforce.

points: Four steps: recommend compensation, recommend prosecution, recommend interim relief, approach SC/HC.
Its recommendations are not binding, but action taken must be reported within one month.

POL-8.4.1-Q36.lead: Only statement 1 is true, so option 2 (1 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Recommend interim relief
True
The NHRC may recommend to the government the grant of immediate interim relief to the victim.
2. Pay monetary relief from its own funds
False
It has no power to award any relief, including monetary relief; the government pays if it accepts the recommendation.
3. Punish a guilty public servant
False
It has no power to punish violators; it can only recommend prosecution or other action.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 wrongly include statement 2 and/or 3.
Key idea: NHRC recommends; the government enforces.

POL-8.4.1-Q37.lead: Option 1: the concerned government must inform the NHRC of the action taken on its recommendations within one month.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: One month
Correct. This is the ordinary time limit for an action-taken report.
15 days
Wrong. 15 days is not the period prescribed for this report.
Three months
Wrong. Three months applies only to armed-forces cases, where the Central Government reports action taken.
Six months
Wrong. Six months is not prescribed for this report.

points: The same one-month rule applies to State Commissions.
Hook: ordinary case 1 month, armed forces 3 months.

POL-8.4.1-Q38.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A): The action-taken report duty makes governments respond.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Recommendations are not binding, but governments cannot simply ignore them.
R
True
The government must inform NHRC of action taken within one month.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Because the government must report back within a month (R), it has to respond to each recommendation and cannot just ignore it (A).
Option 2 fails: R is not just a separate true fact; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.

POL-8.4.1-Q39.lead: Option 2: for the armed forces the NHRC has a limited role; it seeks a report from the Central Government and then makes recommendations.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Investigates directly with its own team
Wrong. In armed-forces cases the NHRC cannot run its own investigation; it must go through the Central Government.
Seeks a report from the Central Government and makes recommendations
Correct. The Act gives this limited procedure, and the Centre must report action taken within three months.
Refers it to the Army court-martial with binding directions
Wrong. The NHRC's recommendations are never binding, and it cannot direct a court-martial.
Cannot take any notice of it
Wrong. Its role is limited, not absent; it can still seek a report and recommend.

points: 'Armed forces' under the Act means the naval, military and air forces and other armed forces of the Union.
Hook: armed forces = report from Centre, reply in three months.

POL-8.4.1-Q40.lead: Option 2 (A-2, B-1) is correct. Normal one-month rule; three months only for armed forces.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Violation by State police
2. One month
Government must report action taken within one month.
B. Violation by armed forces
1. Three months
NHRC has a limited role here; Centre reports within three months.

points: Option 1 fails: it gives A-1 (Three months), B-2 (One month); correct is A-2, B-1.
Option 3 fails: it gives A-1 (Three months); correct is A-2.
Option 4 fails: it gives B-2 (One month); correct is B-1.
Option 3 and 4 give both cases the same period — wrong, armed forces get a longer, special period.

POL-8.4.1-Q41.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so option 1 (1 and 2 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Reports go to the Centre and the State concerned
True
The NHRC sends its annual or special reports to the Central Government and to the State Government concerned.
2. Laid before the legislature with action-taken memorandum
True
The reports are laid before the respective legislatures with a memorandum of action taken on its recommendations.
3. Reasons for non-acceptance need not be stated
False
The memorandum must also give the reasons for not accepting any recommendation; this is a key accountability check.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.
Because the reasons go before the legislature, the government must justify ignoring the NHRC in public.

POL-8.4.1-Q42.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so option 1 (1 and 2 only) is correct.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Recommendations not binding
True
The NHRC's functions are mainly recommendatory, and its recommendations are not binding on the government.
2. One-year limit
True
It cannot inquire into a matter after one year from the date of the alleged violation.
3. No jurisdiction at all over armed forces
False
Its role is limited, not absent; it may seek a report from the Central Government and make recommendations.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 include the false statement 3.
The Centre must report action on armed-forces recommendations within three months.

POL-8.4.1-Q43.lead: Option 1: the Paris Principles (adopted by the UN General Assembly in 1993) say national human rights institutions need adequate funding and staff so that they are independent of the government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Paris Principles
Correct. The NHRC itself cites them: an NHRI must have its own staff and premises and not be under financial control that affects its independence.
Universal Declaration of Human Rights
Wrong. The UDHR (1948) lists human rights; it does not set standards for how national institutions are funded.
Directive Principles of State Policy
Wrong. DPSPs are Part IV guidelines for State policy, not standards for human-rights institutions.
Bangalore Principles of Judicial Conduct
Wrong. These are standards of ethical conduct for judges.

points: The NHRC states that it is compliant with the Paris Principles.
It receives grants-in-aid from the Ministry of Home Affairs.

POL-8.4.1-Q44.lead: Option 1: the NHRC receives its grants-in-aid every year from the Ministry of Home Affairs, its nodal ministry.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Ministry of Home Affairs
Correct. MHA releases the NHRC's grants; the Home Minister also sits on the selection committee.
Ministry of Law and Justice
Wrong. It is a common distractor because NHRC work is legal, but it is not the nodal ministry.
Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment
Wrong. This ministry deals with SC, OBC and disability welfare, not the NHRC.
Ministry of External Affairs
Wrong. It handles foreign relations, including UN human-rights diplomacy, but not the NHRC.

points: Compare: the National Commission for Women's nodal ministry is Women and Child Development.
Human rights complaints are mostly about police and prisons, which is why Home Affairs is linked.

POL-8.4.1-Q45.lead: Option 2: the NHRC does not inquire into a matter already pending before a State Human Rights Commission or any other commission constituted under law (Section 36(1)).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A custodial death reported in the media
Wrong choice. The NHRC can take suo motu notice of media reports, and custodial deaths are a core part of its work.
A matter already pending before a State Human Rights Commission
Correct. To avoid two bodies inquiring into the same matter, the Act bars the NHRC here.
A complaint by a prisoner's relative
Wrong choice. A petition may be filed by the victim or any person on his behalf.
Bonded labour in a brick kiln
Wrong choice. Bonded and child labour are among the issues the NHRC regularly deals with.

points: The bar works both ways: an SHRC also does not take up a case already being inquired into by the NHRC or another statutory commission.
Other bar: matters older than one year.

POL-8.4.1-Q46.lead: Items 1, 2 and 3 are generally not entertained and item 4 is, so option 2 (1, 2 and 3 only) is correct.

head: Item
Entertained?
Why
rows: 1. Sub judice matters
Not entertained
When a matter is already being decided by a court, the NHRC generally does not take it up, to avoid conflict with the court.
2. Service matters
Not entertained
Disputes about government service conditions (pay, promotion, transfer) are not human-rights violations and go to service tribunals or courts.
3. Events older than one year
Not entertained
The Act bars inquiry after one year from the date of the alleged violation.
4. Custodial violence within six months
Entertained
Recent custodial violence is within the one-year limit and is a core human-rights matter.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes item 4 and leaves out 2 and 3.
Options 3 and 4 wrongly include item 4.
The NHRC's procedure regulations also exclude vague, anonymous or frivolous complaints.

POL-8.4.1-Q47.lead: Option 1: after the 2019 Amendment, human-rights functions in the Union Territory of Delhi are dealt with by the NHRC and cannot be conferred on a State Commission.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Delhi
Correct. The 2019 Amendment lets the Centre confer UT functions on SHRCs, except Delhi, which stays with the NHRC.
Puducherry
Wrong. Its functions can be conferred on a State Commission by the Central Government.
Chandigarh
Wrong. Its functions can also be conferred on an SHRC.
Lakshadweep
Wrong. Its functions can also be conferred on an SHRC.

points: J&K and Ladakh are also excluded from conferment by the 2020 adaptation orders; this question asks about the 2019 Amendment's Delhi rule.
Hook: Delhi = home of the NHRC, so the NHRC keeps it.

POL-8.4.1-Q48.lead: Option 2 (A-2, B-1) is correct. 2019 widened both posts to ordinary judges.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept

2. CJI or Judge of the Supreme Court

B. SHRC Chairperson
1. Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court
Before 2019 only a retired HC Chief Justice.

points: Option 1 fails: it gives A-1 (Has been Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court), B-2 (Has been CJI or Judge of the Supreme Court); correct is A-2, B-1.
Option 3 fails: it gives B-2 (Has been CJI or Judge of the Supreme Court); correct is B-1.
Option 4 fails: it gives A-1 (Has been Chief Justice or Judge of a High Court); correct is A-2.
National body → Supreme Court; State body → High Court.

POL-8.4.1-Q49.lead: Option 1: Justice Arun Kumar Mishra (from 2021) was the first NHRC Chairperson who had not been Chief Justice of India; the 2019 Amendment allowed a former Supreme Court judge to be appointed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Justice Arun Kumar Mishra
Correct. He was a Supreme Court judge, never CJI, and became eligible only because of the 2019 Amendment.
Justice H.L. Dattu
Wrong. He was a former Chief Justice of India before chairing the NHRC.
Justice Ranganath Misra
Wrong. He was the first NHRC Chairperson (1993) and a former Chief Justice of India.
Justice K.G. Balakrishnan
Wrong. He too was a former Chief Justice of India.

points: Before 2019, only a retired CJI could be Chairperson.
After 2019: retired CJI or retired SC judge.

POL-8.4.1-Q50.lead: Option 3: Justice V. Ramasubramanian was a former Judge of the Supreme Court, which qualifies a person for Chairperson since the 2019 Amendment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: A former Chief Justice of India
Wrong. He was never CJI; he retired as a Supreme Court judge.
A former Chief Justice of a High Court
Wrong. An HC Chief Justice qualifies only for a member seat in the NHRC, not for Chairperson.
A former Judge of the Supreme Court
Correct. The 2019 Amendment made former SC judges eligible for Chairperson.
A human-rights expert member
Wrong. Human-rights expert seats are member posts, not the Chairperson's post.

points: He succeeded Justice Arun Kumar Mishra, the first non-CJI Chairperson.
Chairperson: retired CJI or SC judge; SHRC Chairperson: retired HC Chief Justice or HC judge.

POL-8.4.1-Q51.lead: Option 2: the State Government, with the concurrence of the Chief Justice of the High Court, may specify a Court of Session in each district as a Human Rights Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Court of the District Munsiff
Wrong. A Munsiff court is a junior civil court; human-rights offences are criminal matters.
Court of Session
Correct. The Court of Session is the principal criminal court of a district, so it is specified for speedy trial of human-rights offences.
Court of the Chief Judicial Magistrate
Wrong. The CJM court is a magistrate's court below the Court of Session.
Family Court
Wrong. Family Courts deal with marriage, custody and maintenance matters.

points: For each such court, a public prosecutor is specified or an advocate with seven years' practice is appointed special public prosecutor.
Purpose: speedy trial of offences arising from human-rights violations.

POL-8.4.1-Q52.lead: Option 2: the NHRC organises camp sittings and open hearings in different parts of the country to take justice to the victims' doorstep.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Lok Adalats
Wrong. Lok Adalats are organised by Legal Services Authorities to settle disputes by compromise.
Camp sittings and open hearings
Correct. The NHRC reports these as very useful for reaching victims away from Delhi.
Gram Nyayalayas
Wrong. These are village-level courts under the Gram Nyayalayas Act, 2008.
Mobile courts of session
Wrong. The NHRC is not a court and does not run sessions courts.

points: Complaints include custodial deaths, torture, fake encounters and bonded labour.
These sittings also spread human-rights awareness, one of its functions.

POL-8.4.1-Q53.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A): A statutory body can be changed by ordinary law.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Parliament can alter NHRC composition by an ordinary law (as done in 2006 and 2019).
R
True
NHRC is created by the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. What an Act creates, a later Act can change (R explains A); no constitutional amendment is needed.
Option 2 fails: R is not just a separate true fact; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.

POL-8.4.2-Q01.lead: Answer: option 4. The Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 provides for both the NHRC and the State Human Rights Commissions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955
The law that punishes the practice of untouchability; it creates no commission.
2. Human Rights Courts Act, 2006
Not the law that creates SHRCs; Human Rights Courts themselves are provided under the PHR Act, 1993.
3. Commissions of Inquiry Act, 1952
Used to set up ad hoc inquiry commissions on specific matters, not permanent SHRCs.
4. Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993
Creates the NHRC, SHRCs and Human Rights Courts.

points: LX p683: the PHR Act, 1993 provides for the NHRC and also an SHRC at state level, which a state government may constitute.

POL-8.4.2-Q02.lead: 1 and 3 are true, 2 is false, so the answer is option 4 (1 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. It is a statutory body
True
It is created by a law (the PHR Act, 1993), not by the Constitution (LX p683).
2. Every state is constitutionally bound to set it up
False
The Act says an SHRC 'may' be constituted by the state government, so it is optional, and there is no constitutional duty (LX p683).
3. Created under an Act of Parliament
True
The PHR Act, 1993 is a Central law made by Parliament (LX p683).

points: Option 1 (1 and 2), option 2 (all three) and option 3 (2 and 3) all include false statement 2.
Contrast: a State Public Service Commission is a constitutional body (Art 315); the SHRC is not.

POL-8.4.2-Q03.lead: Answer: option 3. The SHRC headquarters is at the place the state government specifies by notification.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Always at the state capital
Wrong: the PHRA, 1993 fixes no rule that the SHRC must sit at the state capital; the state government notifies the place.
2. At the seat of the state High Court
The Act does not tie the SHRC to the High Court seat.
3. At a place notified by the state government
Correct: under the PHRA, 1993 the SHRC headquarters is at the place the state government specifies by notification.
4. At a place fixed by the NHRC
The NHRC has no say in where an SHRC sits.

points: LX p686 (footnote): 'The Headquarters of the State Human Rights Commission shall be at such place as the state government may, by notification, specify.'
Contrast: the NHRC's headquarters is in Delhi (LX p680).

POL-8.4.2-Q04.lead: Answer: option 4 (Chairperson and 2 members). The SHRC is a three-member body.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Chairperson, Vice-Chairperson and 3 members
Wrong: the SHRC has no Vice-Chairperson; it is a three-member body of a Chairperson and two members.
2. Chairperson and 4 members
The original 1993 strength; the 2006 Amendment reduced members to two.
3. Chairperson, 5 members and ex-officio members
Wrong: a Chairperson, 5 members and ex-officio members describes the NHRC, not the SHRC.
4. Chairperson and 2 members
Current SHRC composition: one judicial member and one human rights expert.

points: LX p683: Chairperson (retired HC Chief Justice or HC judge) plus two members: an HC judge or District Judge with 7 years' experience, and a human rights expert.

POL-8.4.2-Q05.lead: Answer: option 1 (1, 2, 3). The Act came in 1993, members were cut to two in 2006, and tenure was cut to three years in 2019.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1993 Act, then 2006 Amendment, then 2019 Amendment: correct order.
Puts the 2019 tenure change before the 2006 member change.
Puts an amendment before the Act it amends, which is impossible.
Puts the 2019 change first, before the Act existed.

points: PHR Act enacted in 1993 (LX p683).
The 2006 Amendment Act set SHRC composition at a Chairperson and two members.
The 2019 Amendment reduced the term of NHRC and SHRC members from five to three years (LX p686).
Logic hook: an Act must always come before its amendments, which removes options 3 and 4 at once.

POL-8.4.2-Q06.lead: Answer: option 4. The SHRC Chairperson must have been a Chief Justice or a Judge of a High Court.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. A retired Chief Justice of India
Qualification for NHRC Chairperson, not SHRC.
2. Any eminent human rights activist
Can be the SHRC's expert member, not Chairperson.
3. A District Judge with 7 years' service
Wrong: a District Judge with seven years' service qualifies only as an SHRC member; the Chairperson must be an HC Chief Justice or Judge.
4. A retired Chief Justice or a Judge of a High Court
The SHRC Chairperson rule; the HC judge route was added in 2019.

points: LX p683: Chairperson should be a retired Chief Justice or a Judge of a High Court.
LX p686: the 2019 Amendment added 'a person who has been a judge of a High Court' as eligible.

POL-8.4.2-Q07.lead: Answer: option 2 (both true, R does not explain A): Both are 2019 changes, but tenure does not explain eligibility.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
After the 2019 amendment, a HC judge (not only a Chief Justice) can be SHRC Chairperson.
R
True
The 2019 amendment cut tenure from five years to three.

points: Does R explain A? No. Both changes came in the same Act, but who may be Chairperson (A) and how long he serves (R) are separate rules.
Option 1 fails: R is true, but it does not give the reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both statements are true.

POL-8.4.2-Q08.lead: Answer: option 4 (7 years). A District Judge needs at least seven years' experience as District Judge to be an SHRC member.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. 5 years
Wrong: five years is not prescribed; the Act requires at least seven years' experience as District Judge.
2. 12 years
Wrong: twelve years is not prescribed; the Act requires at least seven years' experience as District Judge.
3. 10 years
Not the SHRC rule; 10 years is a different test (e.g. advocate practice for High Court judgeship under Art 217).
4. 7 years
The prescribed minimum experience as District Judge.

points: LX p683: a member should be a serving or retired HC judge or a District Judge in the state with at least seven years' experience as District Judge.
Hook: the number 7 also appears for the special public prosecutor of a Human Rights Court (LX p685).

POL-8.4.2-Q09.lead: 1 and 2 are true, 3 is false, so the answer is option 3 (1 and 2 only).

True/False
Why

True
This is the SHRC's judicial member seat (LX p683).
2. One member has human rights knowledge or experience
True
This is the SHRC's second member seat (LX p683).
3. At least one member must be a woman
False
The woman-member rule applies to the NHRC's three expert members (2019 Amendment), not to the SHRC (LX p685).

points: Option 1 (1 only) leaves out true statement 2; option 2 (2 and 3) and option 4 (all three) include false statement 3.

POL-8.4.2-Q10.lead: Answer: option 3 (Governor). The Governor appoints the SHRC Chairperson and members on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Chief Minister.

What it is / means
Correct?

Appoints NHRC members and removes SHRC members, but does not appoint SHRC members.
2. Chief Minister
Heads the recommending committee; does not make the appointment.
3. Governor
Correct: the Governor is the appointing authority for the SHRC, acting on a committee headed by the Chief Minister.
4. Chief Justice of the High Court
Is only consulted when a sitting HC judge or District Judge is appointed.

points: LX p683: appointed by the Governor on the recommendations of a committee of the CM, Speaker, state Home Minister and Leader of Opposition.
Hook: Governor appoints, but only the President removes.

POL-8.4.2-Q11.lead: Answer: option 3 (Chief Justice of the High Court). The recommending committee is made of political and executive leaders; the HC Chief Justice is only consulted for sitting judges.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong: the Chief Minister heads the recommending committee, so he is certainly a member.
2. Speaker of the Legislative Assembly
Wrong: the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly is a member of the recommending committee.
3. Chief Justice of the High Court
Not a member; is only consulted before a sitting HC judge or District Judge is appointed.
4. Leader of Opposition in the Assembly
Wrong: the Leader of Opposition in the Assembly is a member of the recommending committee.

points: LX p683: committee = CM (head), Speaker, state Home Minister and Leader of Opposition in the Assembly.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong: a Legislative Council adds two members (its Chairman and its Leader of Opposition), not one, so the total is six, not five.
4 core members + Chairman of the Council + LoP in the Council.
Wrong: the Act names no seventh member; four core members plus two from the Council make six.

POL-8.4.2-Q13.lead: Option 1 (A-2, B-1, C-3) is correct. SHRC selection committee.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Head
2. Chief Minister
The Chief Minister chairs the committee that recommends SHRC chair and members, so the head is item 2.
B. Only in bicameral States
1. Chairman of the Legislative Council
The Chairman of the Legislative Council (and the LoP in the Council) joins only where a Council exists, i.e. in bicameral States.
C. In every State
3. State Home Minister
The State Home Minister is a member of the selection committee in every State, along with the CM, Speaker and LoP in the Assembly.

points: Option 2 fails: it gives A-3 (State Home Minister), C-2 (Chief Minister); correct is A-2, C-3.
Option 3 fails: it gives B-3 (State Home Minister), C-1 (Chairman of the Legislative Council); correct is B-1, C-3.
Option 4 fails: it gives A-1 (Chairman of the Legislative Council), B-2 (Chief Minister); correct is A-2, B-1.
Other members everywhere: Speaker and LoP of the Assembly; bicameral States also add the Council's LoP.

POL-8.4.2-Q14.lead: Answer: option 4. Consulting the HC Chief Justice is required only when a sitting HC judge or a sitting District Judge is appointed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Any human rights expert
An expert member is not a judge, so no judicial consultation is needed.
2. The Secretary of the Commission
The Secretary is an officer of the Commission, not a member, so this rule does not apply.
3. A retired HC Chief Justice
A retired judge has left the judiciary, so no consultation is required.
4. A sitting HC Judge or a sitting District Judge
Taking a serving judge away from the court needs prior consultation with the HC Chief Justice.

points: LX p683: 'a sitting judge of a High Court or a sitting District Judge can be appointed only after consultation with the Chief Justice of the High Court.'
Parallel at NHRC level: a sitting SC judge or sitting HC Chief Justice needs consultation with the CJI (LX p678).

POL-8.4.2-Q15.lead: Answer: option 3. After the 2019 Amendment the term is three years or until age 70, whichever is earlier.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Both figures are wrong: the term is no longer 5 and the age limit is 70.
2. 5 years or 70, whichever is earlier
Wrong: five years or age 70 was the rule before 2019; the 2019 Amendment cut the term to three years.
3. 3 years or 70, whichever is earlier
The present rule for SHRC (and NHRC) members.
4. 6 years or 65 years of age
This pattern belongs to bodies like the CAG, not the SHRC.

points: LX p683: Chairperson and members hold office for three years or until 70, whichever is earlier, and are eligible for re-appointment.
LX p686: the 2019 Amendment reduced the term from five to three years.

POL-8.4.2-Q16.lead: 1 is true and 2 is false, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why

True
The 2019 Amendment cut the term for both bodies to three years (LX p686).
2. Barred reappointment of SHRC members
False
The opposite: the 2019 Amendment made them eligible for re-appointment (LX p686).

points: Option 2 (2 only) and option 3 (both) include false statement 2; option 4 (neither) wrongly rejects true statement 1.

POL-8.4.2-Q17.lead: Answer: option 4. After tenure, a former SHRC Chairperson or member cannot take further employment under a state government or the Central government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Reappointment to the SHRC
Allowed: since 2019 they are eligible for re-appointment.
2. Legal practice in a private capacity
The Act bars only government employment, not private work.
3. Writing on human rights
Not barred: writing on human rights is private activity, while the Act bars only further employment under a state or Central government.
4. Further employment under the Central government
Barred, along with employment under a state government.

points: LX p683: 'After their tenure, the chairperson and members are not eligible for further employment under a state government or the Central government.'
The bar protects independence: a member should not favour a government hoping for a later job.

POL-8.4.2-Q18.lead: Answer: option 3 (Governor). The resignation is addressed to the Governor, the appointing authority.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. President
Has the power to remove, but the resignation goes to the appointing authority.
2. Chief Minister
Wrong: the Chief Minister only heads the recommending committee; resignation goes to the Governor, the appointing authority.
3. Governor
Appoints the SHRC Chairperson, so the resignation is addressed to the Governor.
4. Chairperson of NHRC
The NHRC has no control over SHRC appointments.

points: LX p683: the SHRC Chairperson and members are appointed by the Governor.
General rule: a resignation goes to the authority that appointed the person.

POL-8.4.2-Q19.lead: Answer: option 3 (President). Although the Governor appoints SHRC members, only the President can remove them.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Governor
Wrong: the Governor appoints SHRC members but has no power to remove them; only the President can.
2. State Legislature
Wrong: the State Legislature has no role in removing an SHRC Chairperson; removal is by the President.
3. President
Removes on the listed grounds, and for misbehaviour or incapacity after a Supreme Court inquiry.
4. Chief Justice of the High Court
Wrong: the HC Chief Justice has no removal power; only the President can remove an SHRC Chairperson.

points: LX p683: 'they can be removed only by the President (and not by the governor)', on the same grounds as NHRC members.
Same pattern as a State Public Service Commission member: appointed by the Governor, removed by the President.

POL-8.4.2-Q20.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A): The Act gives removal power only to the President.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
The Governor appoints the SHRC Chairperson but cannot remove him.
R
True
The PHRA gives the power of removal only to the President.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. The Governor cannot remove because the law places that power with the President alone (R).
Option 2 fails: R is not just a separate true fact; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.
Same split as a State PSC member: Governor appoints, President removes.

POL-8.4.2-Q21.lead: Answer: option 4 (Proved misbehaviour). For misbehaviour or incapacity the President must first refer the matter to the Supreme Court for inquiry.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Adjudged an insolvent
A direct ground: the President can remove without the Supreme Court.
2. Convicted and sentenced to imprisonment
A direct ground, no Supreme Court reference needed.
3. Declared of unsound mind by a competent court
A direct ground, no Supreme Court reference needed.
4. Proved misbehaviour
Needs a Supreme Court inquiry and advice before removal.

points: LX p683-684: five direct grounds: insolvency, paid outside employment, infirmity of mind or body, unsound mind declared by a court, and conviction with imprisonment.
Misbehaviour and incapacity are questions of fact, so an impartial Supreme Court inquiry is required first.

POL-8.4.2-Q22.lead: Answer: option 3. For misbehaviour, the President must refer the matter to the Supreme Court; only if the Court upholds it and advises removal can the President remove the member.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Obtain the Governor's consent
The Governor appoints SHRC members, but removal is by the President only; the Governor's consent is not part of the removal procedure.
2. Get a resolution of the state Assembly
The Protection of Human Rights Act gives the state Assembly no role in removal, so no legislative resolution is needed (unlike judges, no address of the House is involved).
3. Refer the matter to the Supreme Court for inquiry
The required procedure for misbehaviour or incapacity.
4. Consult the NHRC Chairperson
The NHRC is a separate national body; the Act does not require the President to consult its Chairperson before removing an SHRC member.

points: LX p684: President refers the matter to the Supreme Court; if the Court upholds the cause and advises so, the President removes.

POL-8.4.2-Q23.lead: Answer: option 1 (State government). The salaries and service conditions of SHRC members are determined by the state government.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. State government
Fixes the salaries and service conditions of SHRC members.
2. Central government
The Central government fixes salaries and service conditions for the NHRC; for the state body, the SHRC, this is done by the state government.
3. Parliament by law
Parliament made the Act but does not fix these amounts.
4. NHRC
The NHRC has no power to fix the pay or service conditions of SHRC members; the two commissions are independent of each other.

points: LX p684: salaries, allowances and conditions of service are determined by the state government and cannot be varied to their disadvantage after appointment.
Hook: who pays decides: the state pays the SHRC, the Centre pays the NHRC (LX p679).

POL-8.4.2-Q24.lead: Answer: option 3 (State List and Concurrent List). An SHRC can inquire only into subjects in Lists II and III of the Seventh Schedule.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Union List only
Union subjects (like defence) are outside the SHRC.
2. State List only
Too narrow; the Concurrent List is also covered.
3. State List and Concurrent List
Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, the SHRC can inquire only into subjects in the State List (List II) and the Concurrent List (List III).
4. All three Lists
Describes the national body, the NHRC, not the SHRC.

points: LX p683: an SHRC can inquire into violations only in respect of subjects in the State List (List II) and the Concurrent List (List III).
Reason: a state body works in the area where the state has legislative power.

POL-8.4.2-Q25.lead: Answer: option 2. If the NHRC or any other statutory commission is already inquiring into a case, the SHRC does not inquire into it.

What it is / means
Correct?

Barred, to avoid two bodies giving conflicting findings.
2. SHRC will not inquire into that matter
The Act says the SHRC shall not inquire into a matter already being inquired into by the NHRC or any other statutory commission, so it will not take up this case.
3. SHRC will take over the case from NHRC
The SHRC has no power to take a case from the NHRC.
4. SHRC will refer it to the High Court
The Act gives the SHRC no procedure to refer a pending NHRC case to the High Court; it simply does not inquire into it.

points: LX p683: 'if any such case is already being inquired into by the NHRC or any other Statutory Commission, then the SHRC does not inquire into that case.'

POL-8.4.2-Q26.lead: Answer: option 3. Defence is a Union subject, so the SHRC has no jurisdiction; the NHRC has only a limited role over the armed forces.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong: armed forces fall under the Union List, outside the SHRC.
2. SHRC can seek a report from the Centre
Wrong: this is the NHRC's power regarding armed forces.
3. SHRC has no jurisdiction; only NHRC has a limited role
Correct: NHRC may seek a report from the Centre and make recommendations.
4. Neither NHRC nor SHRC has any role
Wrong: the NHRC does have a limited role.

points: LX p681: the NHRC may seek a report from the Central government on armed forces and recommend; the Centre informs it of action within three months.
LX p683: SHRC jurisdiction is limited to the State and Concurrent Lists.

POL-8.4.2-Q27.lead: 1 and 2 are true, 3 is false, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why

True

2. Delhi is dealt with by the NHRC
True

3. Introduced by the 2006 Amendment
False
This UT provision was added by the 2019 Amendment (LX p686).

points: Option 1 (2 and 3), option 3 (1 and 3) and option 4 (all three) include false statement 3.

POL-8.4.2-Q28.lead: All three are true, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Suo motu
True
The SHRC can start an inquiry on its own (LX p684).
2. On a petition by the victim
True
It can act on a petition presented to it (LX p684).
3. On the direction of a court
True
It can act on an order of a court (LX p684).

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out at least one valid route.
The inquiry covers a violation, or negligence in preventing a violation, by a public servant.

POL-8.4.2-Q29.lead: Answer: option 1. Visiting jails and detention places to study inmates' living conditions and recommending improvements is an SHRC function.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Visit jails and detention places
Visiting jails and detention places to study inmates' living conditions and recommend improvements is function 3 in the SHRC's list (LX p684).
2. Sentence a guilty police officer
The SHRC cannot punish; it can only recommend prosecution.
3. Ratify human rights treaties
Treaties are a Union matter; even the NHRC only studies them.
4. Dismiss a public servant
It can only recommend action, not dismiss.

points: LX p684: function 3 is visiting jails; LX p685: 'It has no power to punish the violators of human rights.'

POL-8.4.2-Q30.lead: Answer: option 4. Making laws is the job of the legislature; the SHRC can only review safeguards and recommend.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Spreading human rights literacy
Spreading human rights literacy and awareness of safeguards is function 7 of the SHRC, so it cannot be the 'NOT a function' answer.
2. Encouraging NGOs in human rights
Encouraging the efforts of NGOs working in human rights is function 8 of the SHRC, so it is a genuine function, not the answer.
3. Reviewing factors such as terrorism
A listed SHRC function: review factors, including terrorism, that inhibit human rights.
4. Framing human rights legislation
Not a function; legislation belongs to the state legislature.

points: LX p684: the nine SHRC functions include reviewing safeguards, reviewing terrorism-related factors, research, literacy and encouraging NGOs; none is law-making.

POL-8.4.2-Q31.lead: Answer: option 3 (Both NHRC and SHRC). Research in human rights appears in the function lists of both commissions.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. NHRC only
'NHRC only' is wrong because undertaking and promoting research in human rights is also listed among the SHRC's functions.
2. SHRC only
'SHRC only' is wrong because research in human rights is also an NHRC function, not something unique to the state body.
3. Both NHRC and SHRC
Research appears in both lists (NHRC function 7 and SHRC function 6), so the function belongs to both commissions.
4. Neither
'Neither' is wrong: both the NHRC and the SHRC have research in human rights as a listed function.

points: LX p680 (NHRC) and p684 (SHRC) both list 'to undertake and promote research in the field of human rights'.
The only NHRC function missing in the SHRC list is studying international treaties.

POL-8.4.2-Q32.lead: Answer: option 1. Studying treaties and international instruments is an NHRC function with no SHRC counterpart, because treaties are a Union matter.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Studying international treaties
NHRC only; foreign affairs and treaties are Union subjects.
2. Intervening in court proceedings
Intervening in court proceedings involving human rights violations is a function of both the NHRC and the SHRC, so it has an SHRC counterpart.
3. Visiting jails
Visiting jails and detention places to study inmates' conditions is listed for both the NHRC and the SHRC, so it has a counterpart.
4. Encouraging NGOs
Encouraging NGOs working in human rights is a function of both commissions, so it is not unique to the NHRC.

points: LX p679-680: NHRC has 10 functions; LX p684: SHRC has 9. The missing one is the treaty-study function.

POL-8.4.2-Q33.lead: All three are true, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Regulates its own procedure
True
The SHRC is vested with power to regulate its own procedure (LX p684).
2. Has all powers of a civil court
True
It has all the powers of a civil court, e.g. summoning witnesses and taking evidence (LX p684).
3. Proceedings have a judicial character
True
The Act gives its proceedings a judicial character (LX p684).

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out one true statement.

POL-8.4.2-Q34.lead: Answer: option 2. The SHRC may call for information or a report from the state government or any authority subordinate to it.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Only from the Central government
Wrong: calling for reports from the Centre (and on armed forces) is an NHRC power.
2. From the state government or any subordinate authority
Laxmikanth (p684): the SHRC may call for information or a report from the state government or any authority subordinate to it.
3. Only from the High Court
Courts are not its reporting authorities.
4. Only from the NHRC
The NHRC and SHRC are independent bodies; the NHRC does not report to the SHRC, so the SHRC cannot call for reports only from it.

points: LX p684: 'It may call for information or report from the state government or any other authority subordinate thereto.'
Contrast LX p680: the NHRC may call for reports from both Central and state governments.

POL-8.4.2-Q35.lead: Answer: option 2. The SHRC cannot inquire into a matter after one year from the date of the alleged violation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Inquire, as there is no time limit
Wrong: the SHRC cannot inquire into any matter after one year from the date of the alleged violation, so there is a time limit.
2. Not inquire, as more than one year has passed
Correct: 2023 to 2026 is beyond one year.
3. Inquire only with the Governor's permission
The Act has no route by which the Governor's permission can extend the one-year limit; the bar applies regardless.
4. Transfer it to the NHRC
The NHRC is bound by the same one-year limit.

points: LX p685: 'not empowered to inquire into any matter after the expiry of one year' from the alleged act; the same rule applies to the NHRC (LX p680).

POL-8.4.2-Q36.lead: All three are true, so the answer is option 4 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Recommend compensation to the victim
True
It may recommend payment of compensation or damages (LX p685).
2. Recommend prosecution of the guilty public servant
True
It may recommend proceedings for prosecution or other action (LX p685).
3. Approach the SC or HC for directions or writs
True
It may approach the Supreme Court or the state High Court (LX p685).

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each leave out a true statement.
It may also recommend immediate interim relief to the victim.

POL-8.4.2-Q37.lead: Answer: option 1 (both true, R explains A): Being recommendatory, it can only ask the government to pay.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
SHRC cannot itself pay or order monetary relief; it recommends it.
R
True
True. Like the NHRC, the SHRC can only recommend action, such as compensation, to the government; its functions are recommendatory.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. A body that can only recommend (R) cannot itself grant relief (A).
Option 2 fails: R is not just a separate true fact; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.

POL-8.4.2-Q38.lead: Only 2 is true, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
