Unitary States may also have written constitutions, e.g. France.
Number of Houses
Unitary States can be bicameral (Britain) or unicameral (China).

points: Laxmikanth opens the Federal System chapter with this definition.

POL-9.2.1-Q02.lead: Option 2: Switzerland is federal (cantons); France, China and Japan are unitary.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: France
Unitary: all power with the national government.
Switzerland
Federal: the Constitution shares power with cantons.
China
Unitary: regional units get power from the Centre.
Japan
Unitary: regional units get power from the Centre.

points: Unitary: regional units derive power from the Centre. Federal: the Constitution itself divides power.
Laxmikanth lists Britain, France, Japan, China as unitary; USA, Switzerland, Canada, Australia as federal.

POL-9.2.1-Q03.lead: Option 3: 'foedus' means treaty or agreement, so a federation is a new State formed by agreement between units.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Union
Joining into one whole, e.g. India as a 'Union of States'; not the meaning of foedus.
Sovereignty
Supreme power without outside control; not the meaning of foedus.
Treaty or agreement
Correct meaning of the Latin word foedus.
Division
Splitting into parts; not the meaning of foedus.

points: Units have different names: States (USA), cantons (Switzerland), provinces (Canada), republics (Russia).

POL-9.2.1-Q04.lead: Option 4 (1 only): a confederation is a voluntary league of sovereign States, and members can leave it.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Voluntary association, agreement between governments
True
Sovereign States join by a pact between their governments; the people are not direct parties.
2. Members cannot secede
False
Members keep their sovereignty, so they may withdraw; it is a federation whose units cannot secede.

points: Options 2 and 3 fail because statement 2 is false; option 1 fails because statement 1 is true.
The US Articles of Confederation (1781-89) later gave way to a federation.

POL-9.2.1-Q05.lead: Option 2: in a federation the central government acts directly on citizens and the units cannot secede.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Federation units keep full sovereignty, may leave
This describes a confederation, not a federation.
Federation: Centre acts directly on citizens, no secession
Correct: federal laws bind every citizen directly, and the union is permanent.
Confederation has single citizenship, integrated judiciary
Wrong: a confederation is a loose league; single citizenship and integrated judiciary are features of a strong State like India.
Confederation created by unamendable constitution
Wrong: a confederation is created by a treaty between governments, not by a constitution binding the people.

points: Confederation = league of sovereign States (can leave); federation = one State with two levels of government (cannot leave).

POL-9.2.1-Q06.lead: Correct option: 2 (A-3, B-1, C-2). Federations form either by states coming together or by a unitary state devolving.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Federation by integration
Independent States came together and gave up some power to form a Union (coming-together).
B. Federation by disintegration
1. Canada, 1867
A unitary set-up was divided into provinces with their own powers (holding-together) — India is of this type too.
C. Confederation
2. Articles of Confederation, USA
A loose league (1781–89) where member States kept sovereignty; it was replaced by the 1787 federation.

points: Canada model is closer to India: strong Centre, residuary powers with the Centre.
Option 1 is wrong: it gives A→1 (Canada, 1867); B→3 (USA, 1787).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives B→2 (Articles of Confederation, USA); C→1 (Canada, 1867).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A→2 (Articles of Confederation, USA); C→3 (USA, 1787).

POL-9.2.1-Q07.lead: Option 3 (both): the USA is the oldest federation (1787), with 13 States originally and 50 now.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Oldest federation, 1787
True
Laxmikanth: the US is the first and oldest federation, formed in 1787 after the American Revolution (1775-83).
2. 13 States then, 50 now
True
The American federation began with 13 States in 1787 and now has 50, so this statement is true.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each reject a true statement.
The US federation was formed by integration ('coming together').

POL-9.2.1-Q08.lead: Option 2: when a big unitary country grants autonomy to provinces, it is a 'holding together' federation (disintegration route), as in Canada and India.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Confederation
A loose league of sovereign States that can leave; not a federation at all.
Holding together federation
A unitary country divides power with provinces to keep the country united.
Coming together federation
Independent States join to form a strong union, e.g. USA (1787) - the integration route.
Bargaining federation
Morris Jones' term ('bargaining federalism') for how Indian federalism works through Centre-State bargaining; it is not a route of formation.

points: Laxmikanth calls these two routes 'integration' (USA) and 'disintegration' (Canada).
India resembles Canada in its formation by disintegration.

POL-9.2.1-Q09.lead: Option 1: from Canada India took a federation with a strong Centre and residuary powers with the Centre.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Strong Centre federation, residuary powers with Centre
Borrowed from Canada, along with appointment of Governors by the Centre.
Concurrent List and joint sitting
The Concurrent List and the joint sitting of the two Houses were borrowed from the Australian Constitution, not the Canadian.
Directive Principles
The Directive Principles of State Policy were borrowed from the Irish Constitution, not the Canadian.
Suspension of FRs during Emergency
Suspension of Fundamental Rights during an Emergency was borrowed from the Weimar Constitution of Germany, not Canada.

points: Hook: Canada = Centre strong; Australia = Concurrent; Ireland = DPSP; Weimar = Emergency.

POL-9.2.1-Q10.lead: Option 2 (1, 3, 2, 4): Mayo's resolution (1870), Simon Commission (1927-30), GoI Act (1935), Constituent Assembly (1946-49).

head: Event
Year
Why this place

Appointed 1927, report 1930, recommending a federal constitution before the 1935 Act.
2. GoI Act, All-India Federation
Built on the Simon report and Round Table Conferences.

Met only from December 1946 after Independence talks.

POL-9.2.1-Q11.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A. The federation needed the princely states; since they stayed out, it failed.

Correct?

POL-9.2.1-Q13.lead: Option 3 (2 only): Article 1 says 'Union of States', not 'Federation of States', and States cannot secede.

True/False

True/False

True

POL-9.2.1-Q15.lead: Option 3: residuary powers are with the Centre in India, so 'residuary powers in provinces' is not a resemblance to Canada.

What it is / means
Correct?

A resemblance: like Canada, India vests more power in the Centre.
Use of the term 'Union'

Not a resemblance: in India (Art 248) and Canada residuary powers lie with the Centre; States hold them in the USA.

A resemblance: both were formed by a unitary State granting autonomy.

points: Laxmikanth names exactly three resemblances: formation, the term 'Union', centralising tendency.

POL-9.2.1-Q16.lead: Option 2 (1 and 3 only): a written Constitution and bicameralism are federal; All-India Services and emergency provisions are unitary.

True/False

Federal

Unitary
During an emergency the Centre becomes all-powerful, turning the system unitary without an amendment.

points: Option 1 and option 3 include All-India Services; option 4 includes emergency provisions.

POL-9.2.1-Q17.lead: Option 4: dual polity means the Union at the Centre and States at the periphery, each sovereign in its own field.

What it is / means
Correct?

Only Indian citizenship, no State citizenship; a unitary feature.

One chain of courts for Central and State laws; a unitary feature.

Two Houses in the legislature; about Houses, not levels of government.

Two levels of government created by the Constitution, each with its own field (defence vs public order etc.).

POL-9.2.1-Q18.lead: Option 1: originally the Constitution had a Preamble, 395 Articles, 22 Parts and 8 Schedules.

What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong: the original text had 395 Articles, so 448 cannot be the original count.

POL-9.2.1-Q20.lead: Option 4 (1 only): on a Concurrent subject Central law prevails; residuary powers are with the Centre, not the States.

True/False
Why

2. Residuary powers with States as in USA
False
In India residuary powers lie with Parliament (Art 248); only in the USA do States hold them.

points: Options 1 and 3 fail because statement 2 is false; option 2 fails because statement 1 is true.

POL-9.2.1-Q21.lead: Option 4: judicial review is the power of courts to declare a law that violates the Constitution void.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

SC gives its opinion when the President asks (Art 143); it does not strike down laws.
Original jurisdiction
SC hears certain cases first-hand, e.g. Centre-State disputes (Art 131).
Curative petition
A last remedy to correct an SC final judgment after review fails (Rupa Hurra case, 2002).
Judicial review
Courts test laws against the Constitution and declare inconsistent ones invalid.

points: SC uses it via Arts 13 and 32, High Courts via Art 226; it protects the supremacy of the Constitution.

POL-9.2.1-Q22.lead: Option 4: federal provisions need a special majority of Parliament plus ratification by half of the State legislatures.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Consent of all State legislatures
Consent of all State legislatures is not required; Art 368 needs ratification by only half of them.
Approval of Inter-State Council
The Inter-State Council (Art 263) is advisory and has no role in amendments.
A referendum
India has no referendum procedure for amendments.
Ratification by half the State legislatures
Required under Art 368 for federal provisions.

points: This is why the Constitution is called rigid in its federal parts and flexible in others.

POL-9.2.1-Q23.lead: Option 1 (both): the Rajya Sabha represents the States and maintains federal equilibrium.

head: Statement
True/False
Why

True
Its members are elected by State legislatures, so it represents the States.
2. Maintains federal equilibrium
True
Laxmikanth: though less powerful, it protects State interests against undue interference of the Centre.

The Lok Sabha represents the people of India as a whole.

POL-9.2.1-Q24.lead: Option 1: integrated audit machinery (one CAG for Centre and States) is a unitary feature, so it is not federal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Integrated audit machinery
Not federal: the CAG audits both levels and is appointed and removed without consulting States.
Rigid Constitution
Federal: federal provisions need State ratification.
Bicameralism
Federal: the Rajya Sabha represents the States.
Independent judiciary
Federal: it settles Centre-State disputes.

points: The US Comptroller-General has no role in State accounts - a contrast Laxmikanth draws.

POL-9.2.1-Q25.lead: Option 1 (1 and 3 only): a unitary State may have an unwritten constitution; a federation needs a written one; a unitary State need not be unicameral.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Unitary may be unwritten
True
Britain is unitary with an unwritten constitution.
2. Unitary must be unicameral
False
Unitary Britain is bicameral; China is unicameral, so either is possible.
3. Federation needs written constitution
True
A written text is needed to fix the division of powers between levels.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 wrongly include statement 2.

POL-9.2.1-Q26.lead: Option 4: residuary powers are with the Centre (Art 248), not the States, so this statement cannot be a reason.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Centre overrides on Concurrent List
In a conflict on a Concurrent List subject, Central law prevails over state law, which is a real reason the Centre is strong.
Defence etc. in Union List
A real reason: the important subjects are with the Union.
Union List has more subjects
Laxmikanth notes the Union List has more subjects than the State List, which is a real reason the division favours the Centre.
Residuary powers with the States
Factually false: they are with the Centre, which is itself one more reason the Centre is strong.

points: Laxmikanth's four reasons: more subjects, more important subjects, overriding Concurrent power, residuary powers with Centre.

POL-9.2.1-Q27.lead: Option 3: India is 'an indestructible Union of destructible States'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Describes the USA, where States have territorial integrity.
Destructible Union of destructible States
Wrong: no State can secede, so the Union is indestructible.

India: the Union cannot break, but Parliament can change State areas, boundaries or names by simple majority.
Destructible Union of indestructible States
Wrong on both counts: Indian States can be reorganised by Parliament (so they are destructible), and no State can secede (so the Union is indestructible).

POL-9.2.1-Q28.lead: Option 4 (both): Indian Parliament can alter a State by simple majority, while US States have territorial integrity.

head: Statement
True/False
Why

True
Under Arts 3-4 a simple majority is enough, and such a law is not treated as an amendment under Art 368.
2. US Congress cannot change boundaries without consent
True
US States have territorial integrity - an 'indestructible Union of indestructible States'.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each reject a true statement.

POL-9.2.1-Q29.lead: Option 1 (1 only): India has a single Constitution; Jammu and Kashmir's separate constitution ended in 2019.

True/False
Why

True
The Constitution contains both Centre and State frameworks; States cannot frame their own.
2. J&K still has its own constitution
False

POL-9.2.1-Q30.lead: Option 2: only the Centre (Parliament) can initiate a constitutional amendment, a unitary feature.

What it is / means
Correct?

False: only federal provisions need ratification by half the States.

True: amendment bills start only in Parliament, showing central dominance.

False: the Indian Constitution has no referendum procedure; amendments are passed by Parliament under Article 368, with State ratification only for some federal provisions.

False in India; this is possible in the USA.

POL-9.2.1-Q31.lead: Option 4 (1 and 2 only): Rajya Sabha seats are based on population (UP 31, Sikkim 1), so States are not equal as in the US Senate.

True/False

True

True

POL-9.2.1-Q33.lead: Option 3: A true, R false. It happens automatically under the Constitution's emergency provisions; no amendment or State ratification is needed.

True/False
Why
rows: A
True
During an emergency the federal structure becomes unitary.

True/False

True

POL-9.2.1-Q35.lead: The answer is option 2, Integrated judiciary: one chain of courts in India enforces both Central and state laws.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Judicial federalism
A loose idea of courts divided along federal lines; India does not have separate courts for Centre and states.
Integrated judiciary
A single court system with the Supreme Court at the top and High Courts and subordinate courts below it, enforcing both Central and state laws.
Separation of powers
The division of functions among legislature, executive and judiciary; it says nothing about which laws a court applies.
Double system of courts

head: Statement
True/False
Why

False

True
Section 93 of the 1935 Act let the Governor take over a province when its government could not be carried on; Article 356 copies this idea for the States.

POL-9.2.2-Q34.lead: Article 365: if a State does not follow Union directions, the President may hold that its constitutional machinery has failed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 355
Duty of the Union to protect every State against external aggression and internal disturbance and to ensure it is governed as per the Constitution. It is the duty behind Art 356, not this ground.
Article 257
Empowers the Centre to give directions to the States in certain matters. It gives the direction, but does not say what happens when a State ignores it.
Article 360
Financial Emergency, when the financial stability or credit of India is threatened. It has nothing to do with defying Union directions.
Article 365
Says that when a State fails to comply with Union directions, the President may hold that its government cannot be carried on as per the Constitution.

points: President's Rule has two grounds: Article 356 itself (failure of machinery) and Article 365 (non-compliance with Union directions) (LX p251).
Chain to remember: 257 gives the direction, 365 is the consequence of ignoring it, 356 is the remedy.

POL-9.2.2-Q35.lead: Two months for approval and three years at most, so option 4 is correct.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Two months; one year
Two months is right, but one year is not the maximum. One year is only the point after which extra conditions (National Emergency + EC certificate) apply.
One month; no limit
This describes National Emergency: approval within one month and no maximum period. It is not President's Rule.
One month; three years
Three years is right, but one month is the approval period for National Emergency, not for President's Rule.
Two months; three years
A President's Rule proclamation must be approved by both Houses within two months, and with six-monthly approvals it can go on for at most three years.

points: Each approval keeps President's Rule alive for six months (LX p251).
Memory hook: National Emergency = 1 month, no limit; President's Rule = 2 months, 3 years; Financial Emergency = 2 months, no limit.

POL-9.2.2-Q36.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so the answer is option 4 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 42nd made each approval valid for one year; 44th restored six months
True
The 42nd Amendment (1976) raised the period of each approval from six months to one year, and the 44th Amendment (1978) brought it back to six months (LX footnote 6).
2. Beyond one year, either a National Emergency or an EC certificate is enough
False
The 44th Amendment requires BOTH conditions together: a National Emergency in operation AND an Election Commission certificate that assembly elections cannot be held.

points: Option 1 (2 only) and option 2 (both) fail because statement 2 uses 'either…or' where the Constitution needs both.
Option 3 (neither) fails because statement 1 is true.
Exam trap: the word 'either' turns a correct rule into a wrong statement.

POL-9.2.2-Q37.lead: The 68th Amendment Act, 1991 allowed Punjab's President's Rule (imposed May 1987) to continue for five years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 64th Amendment Act, 1990
Allowed Punjab's President's Rule to go on up to three years and six months. It was an earlier step, not the five-year extension.

Allowed Punjab's President's Rule up to three years and permitted National Emergency in Punjab on internal disturbance (later repealed by the 63rd).
73rd Amendment Act, 1992
Gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj institutions. It has nothing to do with President's Rule.
68th Amendment Act, 1991
Allowed Punjab's President's Rule to continue up to a total of five years, beyond the normal three-year ceiling.

points: The normal maximum is three years, so each longer Punjab spell needed a special amendment to Article 356.
Order to remember: 59th (3 yrs) → 64th (3½ yrs) → 67th (4 yrs) → 68th (5 yrs).

Correct?

This does not happen: the Constitution bars the President from taking High Court powers or suspending provisions about it.
✓ (NOT a consequence)

True/False
Why

True

2. Such laws lapse automatically when President's Rule ends
False
These laws continue even after President's Rule ends; they stay until the State legislature repeals, alters or re-enacts them.
3. President may authorise expenditure from the State's Consolidated Fund
True
When the Lok Sabha is not in session, the President can authorise such expenditure pending Parliament's sanction.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 all include statement 2, which is false.

What it is / means
Correct?

True: President's Rule does not touch Fundamental Rights, whereas National Emergency affects them.
✗ (true)
It affects only the State under Rule
True: only that State's relationship with the Centre changes, while National Emergency changes it for all States.
✗ (true)
Lok Sabha can force its revocation by a resolution
Not true: this power exists only for National Emergency (44th Amendment). President's Rule is revoked by the President on his own.
✓ (NOT true)

points: In a NOT question, three options are true facts and the odd one out is the answer.
Lok Sabha disapproval resolution = National Emergency only (LX p247, Table 17.1).

False
Under President's Rule only the State under Rule has a changed relationship with the Centre; it is National Emergency that affects all States.

Correct?

Kerala's E.M.S. Namboodiripad ministry was dismissed under Article 356 in 1959. It is a famous case but not the first.

The Patiala and East Punjab States Union came under President's Rule in 1953, after Punjab, so it was not the first.

Andhra State came under President's Rule in 1954, after the fall of the T. Prakasam ministry. This was later than Punjab.

Correct?

The rule after the 2016 change to the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968; a party keeps status in the next election even if it misses the criteria once.
Three consecutive general elections (once in fifteen years)
Wrong: no such rule exists; since 2016 status is reviewed after two consecutive general elections (once in ten years).
Only when another party files a complaint
Recognition is reviewed on the basis of poll performance, not on complaints.

points: Recognition is granted under the Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 on the basis of poll performance (LX p806, p809).
Purpose of the change: to give parties stability so that one bad election does not take away their reserved symbol.
This is why AAP gained, and NCP, CPI and TMC lost, national status only in April 2023, after two election cycles were reviewed.

POL-9.3.1-Q64.lead: Option 4 — in August 1995 the Election Commission recognised the faction led by N. Chandrababu Naidu, which had the support of most TDP legislators, as the real TDP.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Faction led by Lakshmi Parvathi
NTR's wife; after NTR's death (January 1996) she led a separate party, NTR TDP (LP); she did not get the TDP name or symbol.
Faction led by Nadendla Bhaskara Rao
He led the earlier August 1984 revolt against NTR, which failed within a month; not the 1995 split.
Faction led by N.T. Rama Rao
The founder's group, which lost the support of most MLAs in 1995 and therefore lost the party name and bicycle symbol.
Faction led by N. Chandrababu Naidu
The majority faction recognised as the real TDP; Naidu became Chief Minister in September 1995.

points: In a party split the Election Commission decides which group is the real party under Paragraph 15 of the Election Symbols Order, 1968, looking mainly at support in the legislature and organisation.
Lesson: the founder does not automatically keep the party — the majority test decides.

Correct?

True/False

True

2. Centralising tendency of the Congress
True
Over-centralised Congress rule ignored state leaders and state demands, so state-based parties grew.
3. Alienation of tribal people
True
Tribal groups who felt left out formed their own parties, such as in Jharkhand and the North-East.
4. Proportional representation for Lok Sabha
False
Lok Sabha members are elected by first-past-the-post in single-member constituencies; PR is used only for indirect elections like Rajya Sabha and President.

points: Option 1 leaves out the true statement 3.
Option 2 includes the false statement 4 and drops statement 1.

Correct?

A real positive role, but the case is about a Governor, not about breaking Congress dominance.

Free gifts that strain state finances; this is a dysfunction, not a positive role.
Causing jumbo ministries
Very large ministries are a demerit of coalition governments (LX p842), not a positive role.
Exposing partisan misuse of the Governor's office
The case fits: dismissing a CM and reserving bills for the President are areas where Governors are accused of acting for the Centre.

3. Basic purpose is to seize and retain power
True

POL-9.5.1-Q49.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true; 3 is false, so the answer is option 3 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 42nd Amendment froze at 1971 till 2000
True
The 42nd Amendment Act, 1976 froze seat allocation and constituencies at the 1971 level till 2000 (LX p329).
2. 84th Amendment extended till after 2026
True
The 84th Amendment Act, 2001 extended the freeze till the first census after 2026, to encourage population control (LX p329, p751).
3. 87th raised Lok Sabha seats on 2001 census
False
The 87th Amendment Act, 2003 allowed redrawing boundaries and re-fixing reserved seats on the 2001 census, without changing the number of seats (LX p329).

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 all include the false statement 3.
Key idea: seat NUMBERS still rest on 1971; seat BOUNDARIES rest on 2001.

POL-9.5.1-Q50.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A. The freeze was an incentive for population control: R is the reason.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
The 42nd Amendment froze seat allocation at the 1971 census.
R
True
States controlling population should not lose seats.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. The freeze was an incentive for population control: R is the reason.
Option 2 (both true but R does not explain A) fails: it says R does not explain A, but it does.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: it requires R to be false.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: it requires A to be false.

POL-9.5.1-Q51.lead: Correct option: 1 (A-1, B-2, C-2, D-3). Different censuses for different delimitation purposes.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. LS seats per State
1. 1971 census
Total LS seats per State stay frozen on the 1971 census (42nd and 84th Amendments) so that States that controlled population are not punished.
B. Constituency boundaries
2. 2001 census
The Fourth Delimitation Commission (Kuldip Singh, Delimitation Act 2002) redrew boundaries on the 2001 census (87th Amendment).
C. SC/ST seats
2. 2001 census
SC/ST reserved seats were recalculated on the 2001 census along with the boundaries.
D. J&K delimitation 2022
3. 2011 census
J&K (as a UT after 2019) was delimited in 2022 by the Ranjana Desai Commission on the 2011 census.

points: Option 2 is wrong: it gives A→2 (2001 census); B→1 (1971 census).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives D→2 (2001 census).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives C→1 (1971 census).

True/False
Why

True
Justice Kuldip Singh, a retired Supreme Court judge, chaired the Fourth (2002) Commission (LX p753).
2. Associate members could vote
False
The 10 associate members per state (5 MPs, 5 MLAs) had no right to vote or to sign any order (LX p753).
3. State Election Commissioner was ex-officio member
True
The three members were the chairperson, the CEC or his nominee EC, and the State Election Commissioner of the concerned state (LX p753).

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 all include the false statement 2.
Associate members were nominated by the Speakers of the Lok Sabha and the State Assemblies (LX p753).

POL-9.5.1-Q53.lead: The Commission's final order for Jharkhand was nullified, so it was not implemented there (option 1).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Meghalaya

Tripura

Mizoram
New constituencies were implemented here.

The 2009 Lok Sabha poll used new boundaries in 499 of 543 seats (LX p753).

POL-9.5.1-Q54.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true; 3 is false, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False

True

2. Sushil Chandra ex-officio member
True
Election Commissioner Sushil Chandra was an ex-officio member, along with the State Election Commissioner concerned (LX p754).
3. Completed NE states too
False
In March 2021 the four north-eastern states were removed from its purview, so it delimited only J&K (LX p754).

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 all include the false statement 3.
Its final J&K order came in May 2022 (LX p755).

POL-9.5.1-Q55.lead: 114 seats minus 24 seats kept vacant for PoJK leaves 90 seats filled by election (option 1).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 114 total minus 24 vacant PoJK seats; these 90 were delimited in May 2022.
This has no basis; it neither subtracts PoJK seats nor matches any old figure.
This was the elected strength of the old J&K State Assembly, which included 4 Ladakh seats.
This was the old figure excluding Ladakh, before 7 new seats were added.

points: Of the 90, 43 are in Jammu and 47 in Kashmir (LX p755).
The Lieutenant Governor may also nominate members, so the House is larger than 90 in practice.

POL-9.5.1-Q56.lead: Statements 2 and 3 are true; 1 is false, so the answer is option 4.

head: Statement
True/False

rows: 1. Jammu has more seats
False
Jammu region has 43 and Kashmir region 47 of the 90 Assembly constituencies (LX p755).
2. 9 ST seats, first time
True
9 seats were reserved for STs (6 Jammu, 3 Kashmir); the old J&K Constitution had no ST reservation in the Assembly (LX p755).
3. 18 ACs in each of 5 PCs
True
Treating J&K as one unit, all 5 Parliamentary constituencies got 18 Assembly constituencies each (LX p755).

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 all include the false statement 1.
Anantnag-Rajouri PC combines areas of both regions; 7 seats are reserved for SCs (LX p755).

POL-9.5.1-Q57.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true; 2 is false, so the answer is option 1.

head: Statement
True/False

True
The Commission recommended at least two members from the Kashmiri migrant community, one of them a woman (LX p756).
2. Part of binding May 2022 order
False
These were recommendations to the Central Government, made outside the binding delimitation order (LX p755-756).
3. Nomination for PoJK displaced persons
True
It recommended that the Centre consider representation for displaced persons from PoJK by nomination (LX p756).

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 all include the false statement 2.
Parliament later acted on these through the J&K Reorganisation (Amendment) Act, 2023.

POL-9.5.1-Q58.lead: The Bill was defeated: it got 298 votes for and 230 against, short of the two-thirds needed (option 2).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Passed by special majority
298 of 528 voting is about 56%, below two-thirds, so it did not pass.
Defeated, short of two-thirds
An amendment Bill needs a majority of total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting; it failed the second test.
Passed and sent to the states
It never passed the Lok Sabha, so ratification by states did not arise.
Referred to a Joint Committee
It was put to vote and defeated, not referred.

points: Article 368 special majority = majority of total membership plus two-thirds of members present and voting.
The companion Delimitation Bill was withdrawn by the Centre the same day.
So the freeze of seats till the first census after 2026 continues.
POL-9.5.1-Q58.also: Southern states, including Andhra Pradesh, feared losing seat share.

POL-9.5.2-Q01.lead: Article 171 fixes the maximum and minimum size of a Legislative Council (option 1).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 171
Composition of Legislative Councils: maximum one-third of the Assembly's strength, minimum 40.
Article 170
Composition of Legislative Assemblies (60 to 500 members).
Article 81
Wrong: Article 81 deals with the composition of the Lok Sabha, not the size of a State Legislative Council.
Article 168
Constitution of state legislatures (which states have one or two Houses).

points: Laxmikanth: Article 171 lays down the maximum and minimum number of Council seats (LX p820).

POL-9.5.2-Q02.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A. The Constitution left the details to law, so Parliament had to make the RPAs.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Parliament enacted the RPA 1950 and 1951.
R
True
Arts 81 and 170 give only maximum seats and broad principles.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. The Constitution left the details to law, so Parliament had to make the RPAs.
Option 2 (both true but R does not explain A) fails: it says R does not explain A, but it does.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: it requires R to be false.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: it requires A to be false.

POL-9.5.2-Q03.lead: Correct option: 1 (A-1, B-2, C-1, D-2). RPA 1950 = before the election; RPA 1951 = conduct of election.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Electoral rolls
RPA 1950 covers allocation of seats, delimitation and preparation of electoral rolls (the before-election work).
B. Corrupt practices
RPA 1951 covers the actual conduct of elections, including corrupt practices.
C. Delimitation
Delimitation of constituencies falls under RPA 1950 (along with Delimitation Acts).
D. Party registration
Registration of parties is Sec 29A of RPA 1951.

points: Option 2 is wrong: it gives B→1 (RPA 1950); C→2 (RPA 1951).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives C→2 (RPA 1951); D→1 (RPA 1950).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A→2 (RPA 1951); B→1 (RPA 1950).

POL-9.5.2-Q04.lead: Option 1: delimitation orders have the force of law and cannot be questioned in any court, because Article 329(a) bars courts from examining the validity of laws on delimitation.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Force of law; validity cannot be questioned in any court

Article 329(a) says the validity of any law on delimitation of constituencies, or allotment of seats, made under Article 327 or 328, cannot be questioned in any court; the Delimitation Act makes the Commission's published orders final in the same way.
Take effect only after state legislature approval
Wrong: the orders take effect on the date notified once they are published; no approval by any state legislature is needed.
Parliament may modify them when laid before it
Wrong: the orders are laid before the Lok Sabha and the Assemblies only for information; the House cannot change them.
Can be challenged by election petition in the High Court
Wrong: an election petition questions a particular election result, not the drawing of constituency boundaries; Article 329(a) keeps delimitation out of court.

points: Delimitation means redrawing constituency boundaries; Parliament has made Delimitation Commission Acts in 1952, 1962, 1972 and 2002 (LX).
The bar exists so that boundary disputes cannot hold up elections.
Memory hook: 329(a) = boundaries are final; 329(b) = election results only through election petition.

POL-9.5.2-Q05.lead: Option 4: settling election disputes by election petition is in the Representation of the People Act, 1951, not the 1950 Act.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Appointment of Chief Electoral Officer and Electoral Registration Officer
These election officers who prepare the rolls are provided for in RPA 1950, so this IS a matter of the 1950 Act.
Bar on jurisdiction of civil courts
RPA 1950 bars civil courts from deciding questions about entries in electoral rolls; RPA 1951 also has its own civil-court bar. So this IS in the 1950 Act.
Filling of Rajya Sabha seats allotted to Union Territories
RPA 1950 lays down the manner of filling the Council of States seats for representatives of Union Territories, so this IS in the 1950 Act.
Settlement of election disputes by election petition
Election petitions to the High Court, their trial and appeal to the Supreme Court are in RPA 1951, so this is NOT in the 1950 Act.

points: RPA 1950 = preparation stage: allocation of seats, delimitation, electoral rolls, voter qualifications.
RPA 1951 = conduct stage: candidate qualifications, nomination, poll, counting, corrupt practices, disputes.
Memory hook: 1950 makes the voter list; 1951 runs the election and settles fights about it.

POL-9.5.2-Q06.lead: Both statements are true, so the answer is option 3 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Qualifications for registration as an elector are in RPA 1950
True
True: RPA 1950 provides for registration of electors and the qualifications and disqualifications for such registration.
2. Qualifications for membership of Parliament and state legislatures are in RPA 1951
True
True: RPA 1951 contains the qualifications and disqualifications for membership of the Houses, building on Articles 84, 102, 173 and 191.

points: Option 1 and option 2 each leave out one true statement.
Option 4 is wrong because both statements are true.
Trap: voter-side rules (1950) and candidate-side rules (1951) are often swapped.

POL-9.5.2-Q07.lead: Option 4: the Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 created four qualifying dates — 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Three
Wrong: no law has ever fixed three qualifying dates; the 2021 Act jumped from one date to four.
One
Wrong now: before 2021 only 1 January of the year was the qualifying date, but the 2021 Act changed this.
Two
Wrong: two qualifying dates was never the rule under the RPA 1950.
Four
Right: the 2021 Act fixed 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October as qualifying dates for preparing or revising rolls.

points: A qualifying date is the date on which a person's age of 18 is counted for enrolment.
With four dates, a youth who turns 18 in, say, February can apply from 1 April instead of waiting till next January.
The same Act also enabled Aadhaar linking and replaced 'wife' with 'spouse' for service voters (LX).

POL-9.5.2-Q08.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Aadhaar linking permitted on a voluntary basis
True
True: the 2021 Act enabled linking electoral roll data with Aadhaar to curb multiple enrolment, and the Act says no application can be refused for inability to give Aadhaar.
2. 'Wife' replaced with 'spouse' for service voters
True
True: the word was changed to make the law gender-neutral, so the husband of a woman service voter can also vote as a service voter.
3. Aadhaar made compulsory for enrolment
False
False: linking is voluntary; a person cannot be denied enrolment for not furnishing Aadhaar.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 all include statement 3, which is false.
Remember: 2021 Act = Aadhaar (voluntary), four qualifying dates, 'spouse', and requisition of premises for counting/storage.

POL-9.5.2-Q09.lead: Option 4: a state's power under Article 328 to make election laws exists only so far as Parliament has not made provision on that matter under Article 327.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: State law prevails under Article 327
Wrong: Article 327 is Parliament's power to legislate on elections to Parliament and state legislatures, not the state's.
Both laws apply equally
Wrong: the Constitution expressly makes the state law subordinate on a matter Parliament has already covered.
Matter goes to the Election Commission
Wrong: the Election Commission conducts elections; it does not decide which law is valid — that is for courts.
State power under Article 328 exists only so far as Parliament has not legislated
Right: Article 328 opens with 'subject to the provisions of this Constitution and in so far as provision is not made by Parliament', so Parliament's law governs.

points: Article 327: Parliament may legislate on all matters of elections, including electoral rolls and delimitation.
Article 328: a state legislature may legislate on its own elections only where Parliament has not.
Electoral rolls today are governed by Parliament's RPA 1950, so there is little room left for state law.

POL-9.5.2-Q10.lead: Option 4: a defeated candidate forfeits the deposit if his votes do not exceed one-sixth of the total valid votes polled.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: One-third
Wrong: one-third is not the forfeiture limit in the RPA.
One-fourth
Wrong for the present law; 25% was only a reform proposal — the NCRWC suggested raising the limit from 16.67% to 25% (LX).
One-tenth
Wrong: one-tenth is too low; the law requires more than one-sixth of valid votes to save the deposit.
One-sixth
Right: under the RPA 1951 the deposit is returned only if the candidate polls more than one-sixth (about 16.67%) of the valid votes.

points: The security deposit is money paid at nomination to discourage non-serious candidates.
Deposits were raised in 2009 to ₹25,000 (Lok Sabha) and ₹10,000 (Assembly) for general candidates, half for SC/ST (LX).
A winner always gets the deposit back, even below one-sixth.

POL-9.5.2-Q11.lead: Option 4: a person elected from two seats must resign one of them within the prescribed time; the vacated seat is then filled by a bye-election.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The Speaker chooses which seat he keeps
Wrong: the choice is the member's own; the Speaker has no role in choosing the seat.
He may keep both seats
Wrong: one person cannot represent two constituencies at the same time, so he must give up all but one seat.
Both elections become void
Wrong: both elections are valid. Only if he fails to resign one seat within the prescribed time do the seats fall vacant — that is vacancy, not a void election.
He must resign one seat; a bye-election follows
Right: the RPA 1951 requires him to resign all but one seat, and the seat he gives up is filled by a bye-election.

points: Since the 1996 amendment a candidate cannot contest from more than two constituencies at a general election (LX p827).
Bye-elections must normally be held within six months of a vacancy (LX p827).

POL-9.5.2-Q13.lead: Correct option: 3 (A-1, B-2, C-1, D-2). Upper Houses need 30, lower Houses need 25.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Lok Sabha
1. 25 years
Under Art 84, a Lok Sabha member must be at least 25 years old.
B. Rajya Sabha
2. 30 years
Under Art 84, a Rajya Sabha member must be at least 30 years old.
C. Legislative Assembly
1. 25 years
Legislative Assembly: 25 years (Art 173).
D. Legislative Council
2. 30 years
Legislative Council: 30 years (Art 173).

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives B→1 (25 years); C→2 (30 years).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A→2 (30 years); B→1 (25 years); C→2 (30 years); D→1 (25 years).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives C→2 (30 years); D→1 (25 years).

POL-9.5.2-Q14.lead: Statement 1 is true and statement 2 is false, so the answer is option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Oath or affirmation before a person authorised by the Election Commission
True
True: Article 84(a) (and Article 173(a) for states) requires a candidate to make and subscribe an oath before a person authorised by the Election Commission, in the form in the Third Schedule.
2. A candidate for Parliament need not be an elector anywhere
False

False: the RPA 1951 requires a candidate for Parliament to be registered as an elector — for the Lok Sabha, of any parliamentary constituency; for the Rajya Sabha, of any parliamentary constituency since 2003.

points: Option 2 picks only the false statement.
Option 3 wrongly accepts statement 2, and option 4 wrongly rejects statement 1.
This candidate oath is different from the oath taken after election before taking the seat (Article 99).

POL-9.5.2-Q15.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are true and 3 is false, so the answer is option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. A Lok Sabha candidate may be an elector of any parliamentary constituency
True
True: the RPA 1951 lets a Lok Sabha candidate be an elector of any parliamentary constituency in India (a reserved seat additionally needs an SC/ST candidate).
2. Since 2003 a Rajya Sabha candidate need not reside in the state
True
True: the 2003 amendment removed the domicile requirement; being an elector in any parliamentary constituency in the country is enough (LX).
3. Kuldip Nayar (2006) struck down the 2003 change
False
False: in Kuldip Nayar v Union of India (2006) the Supreme Court upheld both the removal of domicile and the open ballot for Rajya Sabha elections.

points: Options 1, 3 and 4 all include statement 3, which is false.
The 2003 open ballot means a party MLA must show his marked ballot to his party's authorised agent, to curb cross-voting (LX).

POL-9.5.2-Q16.lead: Option 2: a candidate not set up by a recognised political party needs ten electors of the constituency as proposers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: One elector
Wrong for an independent: one proposer is enough only for a candidate of a recognised political party.
Ten electors
Right: since 1996 an independent (or unrecognised-party) candidate needs ten registered electors of the constituency as proposers.
Five electors
Wrong: five is not the number fixed by law for any Lok Sabha candidate.
Fifty electors
Wrong: fifty proposers is the rule for a Presidential candidate (since 1997), not for a Lok Sabha seat.

points: The rule was added in 1996 on the Dinesh Goswami Committee's suggestions to discourage non-serious candidates (LX).
Memory hook: party gives credibility, so 1 proposer; independent must show local support, so 10.

POL-9.5.2-Q17.lead: Option 2: Articles 102 (Parliament) and 191 (state legislature) list the disqualifications for membership and allow Parliament to add more by law.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Articles 101 and 190
These deal with vacation of seats (resignation, absence for 60 days, dual membership), not disqualifications.
Articles 102 and 191
These list disqualifications: office of profit, unsound mind, undischarged insolvent, non-citizen, any law of Parliament, and defection under the Tenth Schedule.
Articles 99 and 188
These deal with the oath or affirmation by members before taking their seats.
Articles 84 and 173
These lay down qualifications (citizenship, age, oath before an EC-authorised person), not disqualifications.

points: The 'law made by Parliament' under Article 102(1)(e) is mainly the RPA 1951, which adds grounds such as conviction and corrupt practices.
Under Article 103 the President decides disqualification questions (other than defection) on the Election Commission's opinion.

POL-9.5.2-Q18.lead: Option 3: under Section 8(3) a person sentenced to two years or more is disqualified from the date of conviction and for a further six years after release.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Only during imprisonment
Wrong: this ignores the further six-year bar after release.
For 6 years from conviction only
Wrong: six years from conviction is the Section 8(1) pattern when only a fine is imposed; with imprisonment the six years run from release.
From conviction and for 6 more years after release
Right: Section 8(3) covers any offence with a sentence of two years or more, so a 3-year sentence means about 3 + 6 = 9 years out of elections.
For 5 years after release
Wrong: five years is the period for a government servant dismissed for corruption or disloyalty (Section 9).

points: Since Lily Thomas (2013) the disqualification of a sitting MLA starts immediately on conviction (LX p831).
Detention under a preventive detention law is not a disqualification (LX).

POL-9.5.2-Q19.lead: Statement 1 is false and statement 2 is true, so the answer is option 2 (2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Section 8(2): dowry/food adulteration needs a sentence of at least 6 years
False
False: the threshold in Section 8(2) is imprisonment of not less than six months, not six years.
2. Section 8(1): offences like promoting enmity disqualify whatever the sentence
True
True: for Section 8(1) offences, conviction itself disqualifies — even if only a fine is imposed — because these offences strike at social harmony and free elections.

points: Option 1 picks the false statement; option 3 wrongly includes it.
Option 4 wrongly rejects statement 2.
Ladder: 8(1) any sentence → 8(2) six months → 8(3) two years for all other offences.

POL-9.5.2-Q20.lead: Option 2: in Lily Thomas v Union of India (2013) the Supreme Court struck down Section 8(4), so sitting legislators are disqualified immediately on conviction.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Anoop Baranwal (2023)
On appointment of the CEC and Election Commissioners; the Court ordered a committee of PM, Leader of Opposition and CJI until Parliament made a law.
Lily Thomas (2013)
Struck down Section 8(4), which had given sitting MPs/MLAs three months to appeal before disqualification took effect.
Kuldip Nayar (2006)
Upheld removal of the domicile rule and the open ballot for Rajya Sabha elections.
PUCL (2013)
Directed the NOTA option on ballot papers and EVMs.

points: Section 8(4) was seen as unequal: an ordinary convict was disqualified at once but a sitting member was not.
A 2013 bill to undo the judgment was withdrawn (LX).

POL-9.5.2-Q21.lead: Option 3: under Section 8A the President decides disqualification for corrupt practice, after obtaining the Election Commission's opinion.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: The High Court
The High Court only finds, in the election petition, that a corrupt practice was committed; it does not fix the disqualification under Section 8A.
The Speaker
The Speaker or Chairman decides defection cases under the Tenth Schedule, not corrupt-practice disqualification.
The President, on the Election Commission's opinion
Right: the case is sent to the President, who must act on the Commission's opinion; the period can be up to six years.
The Election Commission alone
Wrong: the Commission only gives its opinion; the formal decision is the President's.

points: A 2009 amendment fixed a three-month limit for the authority to send such a case to the President (LX).
Compare Article 103: the President, acting on EC opinion, decides other disqualification questions of sitting MPs.

POL-9.5.2-Q22.lead: Option 2: Section 9 disqualifies a government servant dismissed for corruption or disloyalty for five years from the date of dismissal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 3 years
Wrong: three years is the period for failing to lodge an election expense account (Section 10A).
5 years from dismissal
Right: dismissal for corruption or disloyalty to the State bars the person for five years from the date of dismissal.
10 years
Wrong: no RPA disqualification runs for ten years.
6 years
Wrong: six years is linked to conviction (Section 8) and the maximum for corrupt practice (Section 8A).

points: Memory hook: 3 (accounts) – 5 (dismissal) – 6 (conviction/corrupt practice).

POL-9.5.2-Q23.lead: Correct option: 4 (A-2, B-3, C-4, D-1). RPA 1951 fixes how long each disqualification lasts.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Dismissal for corruption
2. 5 years
Sec 9 RPA: dismissal for corruption or disloyalty disqualifies for five years from dismissal.
B. Failure to lodge expense account
3. 3 years from ECI order
Sec 10A: failing to lodge the election expense account disqualifies for three years from the ECI's order.
C. Corrupt practice
4. Up to 6 years by President on ECI opinion
Sec 8A: a person found guilty of a corrupt practice may be disqualified for up to six years; the President decides on the ECI's opinion.
D. Govt contract
1. While contract subsists
Sec 9A: a subsisting contract with the government disqualifies only so long as the contract lasts.

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives B→4 (Up to 6 years by President on ECI opinion); C→3 (3 years from ECI order).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A→3 (3 years from ECI order); B→2 (5 years).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives A→1 (While contract subsists); D→2 (5 years).

POL-9.5.2-Q24.lead: Option 3: Section 10A applies to every contesting candidate, winner or loser, and the Election Commission may disqualify him for three years.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Disqualified for life
Wrong: the disqualification under Section 10A is for three years, not for life.
Nothing, as he lost
Wrong: the duty to lodge accounts applies to every contesting candidate, so losing does not excuse him.
ECI may disqualify him for 3 years under Section 10A
Right: if the Commission is satisfied there is no good reason for the failure, it may declare him disqualified for three years.
The High Court fines him
Wrong: this is an order of the Election Commission, not a court fine.

points: Accounts must be lodged with the District Election Officer within 30 days of the declaration of result.
The rule enforces the expenditure ceiling — without accounts the ceiling cannot be checked.

POL-9.5.2-Q25.lead: Statements 1 and 3 are true and 2 is false, so the answer is option 3 (1 and 3 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Parties register with the Election Commission under Section 29A
True
True: Section 29A of the RPA 1951 provides for registration of political parties with the Commission.
