Exception 2: the Election Commission, in consultation with the Central Government, certifies that it is difficult to hold the by-election in six months.
Memory hook: 'Six months to fill, unless under a year or too difficult'.

POL-9.5.3-Q24.lead: Option 2: the ban on exit polls came in 2009 (effective 2010), not in 1996; the other three were 1996 reforms.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Withdrawal-to-poll gap reduced from 20 to 14 days
A 1996 reform: the minimum campaign gap between the last date of withdrawal and polling was cut from 20 to 14 days.
Ban on exit polls
Not a 1996 reform. A 2009 amendment bars conducting or publishing exit polls during the period notified by the Election Commission, so this is the answer.
Limit of two constituencies per candidate
A 1996 reform: a candidate cannot contest from more than two Parliamentary or assembly constituencies at a general election.
Paid holiday for employees on polling day
A 1996 reform: registered voters employed in any trade or business, even daily wagers, get a paid holiday on polling day.

points: The 1996 reforms came from the Dinesh Goswami Committee (1990) recommendations.
Other 1996 reforms: by-elections within six months, 48-hour liquor ban, no countermanding on a candidate's death, ban on arms near polling stations.

POL-9.5.3-Q26.lead: Option 3: the 1997 amendment raised the security deposit for both President and Vice-President elections from ₹2,500 to ₹15,000.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong. This was the old deposit before 1997.
Wrong. ₹10,000 is the deposit of a general candidate for a state assembly election after 2009.
Correct. The Presidential and Vice-Presidential Elections (Amendment) Act, 1997 fixed ₹15,000 for both offices to discourage frivolous candidates.
Wrong. ₹25,000 is the deposit of a general candidate for a Lok Sabha election after 2009.

points: The same 1997 Act raised proposers and seconders for the President from 10 to 50 each, and for the Vice-President from 5 to 20 each.
Purpose of both changes: keep non-serious candidates out.

POL-9.5.3-Q27.lead: Correct option: 3 (A-2, B-1). 1997 amendment raised proposer/seconder numbers.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. President
2. 50 proposers and 50 seconders
Since 1997 a Presidential nomination needs 50 electors as proposers and 50 as seconders (to stop non-serious candidates).
B. Vice-President
1. 20 proposers and 20 seconders
A Vice-Presidential nomination needs 20 proposers and 20 seconders.

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives B→3 (10 proposers and 10 seconders).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A→1 (20 proposers and 20 seconders); B→2 (50 proposers and 50 seconders).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A→3 (10 proposers and 10 seconders).

POL-9.5.3-Q28.lead: Correct option: 1 (A-2, B-3, C-1, D-4). Special voting facilities.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. Proxy voting
2. Service voters authorising another person
Proxy voting is for classified service voters (armed forces) who authorise a relative to vote for them.
B. Postal ballot
3. Notified classes like election-duty staff
Postal ballot is for notified classes like election-duty staff, service voters, senior citizens 85+ and PwD.
C. Tendered vote
1. Elector whose vote someone already cast
A tendered ballot is given to an elector who finds someone has already voted in his name.
D. NOTA
4. Voter rejecting all candidates
NOTA lets a voter reject all candidates (PUCL, 2013).

points: Option 2 is wrong: it gives A→3 (Notified classes like election-duty staff); B→2 (Service voters authorising another person).
Option 3 is wrong: it gives B→1 (Elector whose vote someone already cast); C→3 (Notified classes like election-duty staff).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A→1 (Elector whose vote someone already cast); C→2 (Service voters authorising another person).

POL-9.5.3-Q29.lead: Option 3: since 2003, service voters of the Armed Forces can appoint a proxy, such as a relative at home, to vote on their behalf.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: NOTA
Wrong. NOTA (2013) lets a voter reject all candidates; it does not let another person vote for him.
Tendered vote
Wrong. A tendered vote is given on a separate paper to a person who finds that someone has already voted in his name; it is not voting through another person.
Proxy voting
Correct. A 2003 provision lets Armed Forces service voters appoint a proxy in a prescribed format and inform the Returning Officer.
Open ballot
Wrong. Open ballot (2003) applies to Rajya Sabha elections, where party MLAs show their ballot to the party agent.

points: Proxy voting is available only to service voters (Armed Forces and forces under the Army Act), not to ordinary citizens.
The soldier in Ladakh is a classified service voter, so his relative can vote as his proxy.

POL-9.5.3-Q30.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct and 3 is wrong, so option 1 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Followed the SC's 2002 ADR ruling
True
The 2003 disclosure order followed the Supreme Court's 2002 judgment in Union of India v Association for Democratic Reforms, which held that voters have a right to know a candidate's background.
2. Spouse and dependants' assets disclosed
True
The affidavit covers movable and immovable assets and bank balances of the candidate, his or her spouse and dependants.
3. False affidavit only a civil wrong
False
Furnishing false information in the affidavit is an electoral offence, not just a civil wrong.

points: Option 2 wrongly includes statement 3; options 3 and 4 wrongly include 3 and also drop a true statement.
Five disclosure items: past criminal record, pending cases (offence of 2+ years with charges framed or cognizance taken), assets, liabilities, educational qualifications.

POL-9.5.3-Q31.lead: Option 3: caste and religion are not among the five items a candidate must disclose in the 2003 affidavit.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Liabilities to public financial institutions
Must be disclosed: liabilities, especially dues to public financial institutions or the government, are item 4.
Pending criminal cases
Must be disclosed: pending cases of offences punishable with two years or more, where charges were framed or cognizance taken, are item 2.
Caste and religion
Not a disclosure item. The aim of the affidavit is to reveal criminal record, wealth and education, not personal identity like caste or religion.
Educational qualifications
Must be disclosed: educational qualifications are item 5.

points: The five: past criminal record, pending cases, assets (own, spouse, dependants), liabilities, education.
Purpose: help voters make an informed choice; a false affidavit is an electoral offence.

POL-9.5.3-Q32.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A. R is the purpose of A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Since 2003, open ballot in Rajya Sabha elections.
R
True
It was introduced to curb cross-voting and money power.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. R is the purpose of A.
Option 2 (both true but R does not explain A) fails: it says R does not explain A, but it does.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: it requires R to be false.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: it requires A to be false.

POL-9.5.3-Q33.lead: Option 3: since 2003, a Rajya Sabha candidate needs only to be an elector in any parliamentary constituency in India; the domicile rule was removed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: An elector in Andhra Pradesh only
Wrong. This was the rule before 2003, when the candidate had to be an elector of the state he was to represent.
A resident of AP for five years
Wrong. No residence period has ever been prescribed; the 2003 change removed the residency link altogether.
An elector in any parliamentary constituency in India
Correct. The 2003 amendment to the RPA made it sufficient to be an elector anywhere in the country.
A member of the AP assembly
Wrong. MLAs are the electors who vote in a Rajya Sabha election; the candidate himself need not be an MLA.

points: The other 2003 Rajya Sabha change: open ballot instead of secret ballot, to curb cross-voting and money power.
Effect: a person from any state can be sent to the Rajya Sabha from AP.

POL-9.5.3-Q34.lead: Statements 1 and 2 are correct and 3 is wrong, so option 2 (1 and 2 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Party leaders' travel excluded from expenditure
True
A 2003 provision exempts the travel expenses of a party's campaigning leaders from the candidate's election expenses.
2. Media time by past performance
True
A 2003 provision asks the Election Commission to allot equitable time on electronic media, decided on the past performance of a recognised party.
3. Free rolls only to independents
False
Free copies of electoral rolls and other material go to candidates of recognised political parties, not to independents.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes 3; options 3 and 4 include the false statement 3 and drop a true one.
Statement 3 reverses the beneficiary: recognised-party candidates, not independents.

POL-9.5.3-Q36.lead: Correct order is 1-3-2: EPIC decision (1993), EVMs in all Lok Sabha seats (2004), NOTA (2013); so option 1.

head: Event / item
Year
Why / concept
rows: 1. EC decides to issue EPICs
The Election Commission decided in 1993 to issue photo identity cards to all electors to check bogus voting and impersonation.
3. EVMs in all Lok Sabha constituencies
The 2004 Lok Sabha general election was the first held with EVMs in every constituency.
2. NOTA on EVMs
NOTA came on Supreme Court directions and was used from the 2013 assembly elections and then in the 2014 Lok Sabha election.

points: Option 2 (1-2-3) puts NOTA before full EVM use; option 3 puts EVMs before EPIC; option 4 starts with NOTA, the latest event.
Memory hook: card (1993), machine (2004), 'none' button (2013).

POL-9.5.3-Q37.lead: Both statements are 2009 reforms, so option 4 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Exit-poll ban in notified period
True
The 2009 amendment (effective 2010) bars conducting or publishing any exit poll during the period notified by the Election Commission.
2. Corrupt-practice case to President in three months
True
The 2009 amendment fixed a three-month limit for the specified authority to send a corrupt-practice case to the President for deciding disqualification.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each reject at least one true statement.
2009 also brought all officials deputed by the EC within the corrupt practice of 'obtaining assistance', and raised security deposits.

POL-9.5.3-Q38.lead: Option 4: the 2009 amendment raised the Lok Sabha deposit for SC/ST candidates from ₹5,000 to ₹12,500.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Wrong. ₹10,000 is the new assembly deposit for a general candidate (and the old Lok Sabha general deposit).
Wrong. ₹25,000 is the Lok Sabha deposit for a general candidate.
Wrong. ₹5,000 was the old SC/ST Lok Sabha deposit; it is now the SC/ST assembly deposit.
Correct. SC/ST candidates pay half the general Lok Sabha deposit: half of ₹25,000 is ₹12,500.

points: Memory hook: SC/ST always pay half.

POL-9.5.3-Q39.lead: Option 1: since 2009, the first appeal against an Electoral Registration Officer's order lies with the District Magistrate (or ADM, Executive Magistrate, Collector or equivalent officer).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: District Magistrate or equivalent officer
Correct. The 2009 amendment created an appellate authority within the district so voters need not go far for the first appeal.
Chief Election Commissioner
Wrong. The CEC heads the Election Commission of India and is not an appellate forum for roll entries.
High Court
Wrong. A statutory appeal lies first with the officers named in the law, not with a court.
Chief Electoral Officer
Wrong as the first appeal. Before 2009 the appeal went to the state's Chief Electoral Officer; now he hears only the second appeal against the DM's order.

points: Ladder: ERO → District Magistrate (first appeal) → Chief Electoral Officer of the state (second appeal).
Reason for the reform: bring the appeal closer to the voter, within his district.

POL-9.5.3-Q40.lead: Both statements are correct, so option 1 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. NRI registration at passport address (2010)
True
The 2010 amendment lets an Indian citizen living abroad, who has not taken foreign citizenship and is not on any roll, register in the constituency of the residence shown in his passport.
2. Online enrolment by 2013 rules
True
The Registration of Electors (Amendment) Rules, 2013 allowed online filing of enrolment applications.

points: Options 2, 3 and 4 each reject a true statement.
An NRI who has acquired foreign citizenship loses Indian citizenship, so he cannot register.

POL-9.5.3-Q41.lead: Correct option: 3 (A-2, B-1, C-3). 2013 was a big year for electoral judgments.

head: List-I
Correct match (List-II)
Why / concept
rows: A. PUCL
2. NOTA
In PUCL v. Union of India (2013) the SC directed a NOTA option on EVMs and ballots.
B. Subramanian Swamy v ECI
1. VVPAT indispensable
Subramanian Swamy v. ECI (2013): VVPAT is indispensable for free and fair elections.
C. Lily Thomas
3. Sec 8(4) RPA struck down
Lily Thomas (2013): Sec 8(4) RPA struck down.

points: Option 1 is wrong: it gives B→3 (Sec 8(4) RPA struck down); C→1 (VVPAT indispensable).
Option 2 is wrong: it gives A→1 (VVPAT indispensable); B→2 (NOTA).
Option 4 is wrong: it gives A→3 (Sec 8(4) RPA struck down); C→2 (NOTA).

POL-9.5.3-Q42.lead: Option 4: the VVPAT slip stays visible through a transparent window for seven seconds, then is cut and falls into a sealed box.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 15 seconds
Wrong. The display time is seven seconds, not fifteen.
3 seconds
Wrong. Three seconds would be too short; the prescribed time is seven seconds.
10 seconds
Wrong. The display time is seven seconds, not ten.
7 seconds
Correct. The slip shows the serial number, name and symbol of the candidate for seven seconds.

points: VVPAT = Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail; it lets the voter check that his vote went to the intended candidate and allows paper counting in a dispute.
First used in the Noksen by-election, Nagaland, 2013; the SC called it an indispensable requirement of free and fair elections.

POL-9.5.3-Q43.lead: Option 2: both true but R does not explain A. R by itself would stop a jailed person contesting.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
True. A person in jail can contest today, because the 2013 amendment to the RPA made clear he does not lose that right.
R
True
Jan Chaukidar (2013) held a person in jail is not an 'elector'.

points: Does R explain A? No. R by itself would stop a jailed person contesting. A is true because Parliament's RP (Amendment and Validation) Act, 2013 overturned that effect.
Option 1 (both true and R explains A) fails: it requires R to explain A.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: it requires R to be false.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: it requires A to be false.

POL-9.5.3-Q44.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so option 3 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Struck down Sec 8(4) RPA
True
Lily Thomas (2013) struck down Section 8(4), which gave sitting MPs and MLAs three months to appeal; now they are disqualified immediately on conviction.
2. Nullified by the 2013 Act
False
The Representation of the People (Second Amendment and Validation) Bill, 2013 was introduced to nullify the ruling but was withdrawn, so it never became law.

points: Option 1 wrongly accepts 2; option 2 rejects the true statement 1; option 4 picks only the false statement.
Do not confuse: the separate 2013 Validation Act that did pass reversed the Jan Chaukidar ruling, so persons in jail can still contest.

POL-9.5.3-Q45.lead: Option 2: photographs of candidates were added from May 2015 to avoid voter confusion where candidates with the same or similar names contest in one constituency.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Replace party election symbols with photographs
Wrong. The photo is printed along with the name and party symbol; symbols were not replaced.
Avoid confusion among voters when candidates have the same or similar names
Correct. The EC found that suffixes to names were not enough to stop confusion caused by namesake candidates.
Help identify candidates with criminal cases
Wrong. Criminal records are disclosed through the nomination affidavit, not through photographs.
Enable voting by voters who do not have an EPIC
Wrong. The photo is of the candidate, not of the voter; it has nothing to do with voter identification.

points: Failure to give a photograph is not a ground for rejecting the nomination.
Concept: namesake ('dummy') candidates are sometimes put up to split a rival's votes.

POL-9.5.3-Q46.lead: Both statements are correct 2017 Budget changes, so option 4 (Both 1 and 2).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Cash donation limit ₹20,000 → ₹2,000
True
The 2017 Budget lowered the limit of anonymous cash donations from one person to a party from ₹20,000 to ₹2,000.
2. 7.5% corporate cap removed
True

The 2017 Budget removed the cap of 7.5% of average net profit of the past three years, so a company could give any amount; companies also no longer had to show such donations in their profit and loss account.

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each reject a true statement.
In ADR v Union of India (2024) the Supreme Court struck down the removal of the cap as manifestly arbitrary under Article 14.

POL-9.5.3-Q47.lead: All three statements describe the 2018 scheme correctly, so option 3 (1, 2 and 3).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Issued only by SBI
True
The State Bank of India was the only authorised bank to sell and encash electoral bonds.
2. Only parties with 1% votes
True
Only registered parties that secured at least 1% of the votes in the last Lok Sabha or state assembly election could receive bonds.
3. Unencashed bonds to PM's Relief Fund
True
A bond not encashed within its 15-day validity was deposited by the bank in the Prime Minister's National Relief Fund.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each drop one true statement.
Bonds were bearer instruments like a promissory note, carrying no name of buyer or payee; the scheme was struck down in February 2024.

POL-9.5.3-Q48.lead: Option 4 is NOT correct: electoral bonds were interest-free; no interest was paid to anyone.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: They were bearer instruments that did not carry the name of the donor
Correct statement. The bond was a bearer banking instrument like a promissory note with no name of buyer or payee.
They could be bought by a citizen of India or a body incorporated in India
Correct statement. Indian citizens and entities incorporated or established in India could buy them.
They had to be encashed by the party within 15 days
Correct statement. The bond was valid for 15 days and had to be encashed through the party's account with the authorised bank.
They carried interest, which was payable to the party on encashment
Incorrect statement, so this is the answer. Bonds were interest-free; they were only a channel for donations.

points: Donor anonymity was the main reason the Supreme Court struck down the scheme in 2024 (violating voters' right to information under Article 19(1)(a)).
Denominations: ₹1,000, ₹10,000, ₹1 lakh, ₹10 lakh, ₹1 crore.

POL-9.5.3-Q49.lead: Option 2: the Finance Acts of 2016 and 2018 amended the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010, changing the definition of 'foreign company' so that parties could take funds from Indian subsidiaries of foreign firms.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Companies Act, 2013
Wrong. Its Section 182 was amended in 2017 to remove the 7.5% cap on corporate donations, not to redefine 'foreign company'.
Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010
Correct. The FCRA was amended (with retrospective effect) to modify the definition of a foreign company, easing foreign corporate funding of parties.
RBI Act, 1934
Wrong. Its Section 31(3) was amended to allow electoral bonds as bearer instruments, a different change.
FEMA, 1999
Wrong. FEMA governs foreign exchange transactions; it was not the Act used to allow foreign funding of parties.

points: Laxmikanth: in the 2018 Budget, foreign funding of parties was allowed by amending the FCRA, 2010 and modifying the definition of foreign company.
Link: each of the 2016-18 funding changes amended a different Act (FCRA, Companies Act, RBI Act, RPA, Income Tax Act).

POL-9.5.3-Q50.lead: Option 1: the scheme was struck down mainly because anonymous bonds violated voters' right to information, which is part of freedom of speech and expression under Article 19(1)(a).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Article 19(1)(a)
Correct. Voters have a right to know who funds parties; hiding donors violated this right.
Article 32
Wrong. Article 32 is the right to move the Supreme Court for enforcement of fundamental rights; it was the remedy used, not the right violated.
Article 21
Wrong. Article 21 protects life and personal liberty; the Court based its main reasoning on the right to information under 19(1)(a).
Article 324
Wrong. Article 324 vests superintendence of elections in the Election Commission; it is not a fundamental right.

points: The removal of the cap on corporate donations was also struck down as manifestly arbitrary under Article 14.
SBI was ordered to give bond details to the Election Commission for publication.

POL-9.5.3-Q51.lead: Only statement 1 is correct, so option 1 (1 only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. 15 Feb 2024, five judges, CJI Chandrachud
True
The verdict in ADR v Union of India was delivered on 15 February 2024 by a five-judge Constitution Bench headed by CJI D.Y. Chandrachud.
2. 3:2 split
False
The decision was unanimous (5:0); Justice Sanjiv Khanna wrote a separate concurring opinion reaching the same result.

points: Option 2 picks only the false statement; option 3 accepts the false statement 2; option 4 rejects the true statement 1.
Other judges: Sanjiv Khanna, B.R. Gavai, J.B. Pardiwala, Manoj Misra.
A concurring opinion agrees with the result, so it is not a dissent.

POL-9.5.3-Q52.lead: Option 4: Section 8(4) of the RPA was struck down in Lily Thomas (2013), not in the electoral bonds judgment.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Section 31(3), RBI Act
Invalidated in 2024. Its amendment allowed bearer electoral bonds.
Section 29C proviso, RPA 1951
Invalidated in 2024. The proviso exempted bond donations from the party's duty to report donations above ₹20,000 to the Election Commission.
Section 182, Companies Act, 2013
Invalidated in 2024. The amendment removed the 7.5% cap and the duty to show party-wise donations; unlimited corporate funding was held manifestly arbitrary under Article 14.
Section 8(4), RPA 1951
Not part of the bonds case, so this is the answer. It was the three-month appeal protection for convicted legislators, struck down in Lily Thomas (2013).

points: The 2024 verdict also struck down the related amendment to Section 13A of the Income Tax Act.
Hook: bonds case = money provisions; Lily Thomas = conviction provision.

POL-9.5.3-Q53.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A. Striking down the amendment that removed the cap revived it.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
The 7.5% cap on corporate donations is back.
R
True
The Court struck down the 2017 amendment to Section 182 of the Companies Act.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. Striking down the amendment that removed the cap revived it.
Option 2 (both true but R does not explain A) fails: it says R does not explain A, but it does.
Option 3 (A true, R false) fails: it requires R to be false.
Option 4 (A false, R true) fails: it requires A to be false.

POL-9.5.3-Q54.lead: Option 1: the Election Laws (Amendment) Act, 2021 did not change the voting age, which remains 18; the other three were its changes.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Lowering the voting age to 17
Not a change. The voting age is 18 under Article 326 (since the 61st Amendment, 1988); changing it would need a constitutional amendment, not an ordinary Act.
Wider requisition of premises for counting and EVM storage
A 2021 change: premises can now be requisitioned for counting, storing voting machines and VVPATs, and housing security forces and polling staff.
Replacing 'wife' with 'spouse' for service voters
A 2021 change: it made the law gender-neutral so the husband of a woman service voter can also vote.
Linking electoral rolls with Aadhaar
A 2021 change: roll data can be linked with Aadhaar to curb multiple enrolment of the same person.

points: The Act also gave four qualifying dates a year: 1 January, 1 April, 1 July and 1 October.
Hook for 2021: Aadhaar, four dates, spouse, premises.

POL-9.5.3-Q55.lead: Option 1: electoral trusts are non-profit bodies that collect donations from companies and individuals and pass them on to parties, reporting donors and recipients.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Electoral trusts
Correct. They pool corporate donations and distribute them to parties, with disclosure to the Election Commission, so they became the main legal channel after bonds ended.
State funding
Wrong. India has no general scheme of state funding of elections; committees like Indrajit Gupta (1998) only recommended it.
Cash donations above ₹2,000
Wrong. Anonymous cash donations above ₹2,000 to a party are not allowed since 2017.
Foreign PACs
Wrong. Political Action Committees are a US funding device; foreign sources are restricted by law in India.

points: Electoral trusts must spend most of what they receive in donations to parties and file annual reports to the ECI.
Unlike bonds, the trust route reveals both who gave and which party got the money.

POL-9.5.3-Q56.lead: Option 3: BJP MP P.P. Chaudhary chairs the Joint Parliamentary Committee examining the Constitution (129th Amendment) Bill on simultaneous elections.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Ram Nath Kovind
Wrong. The former President chaired the 2023-24 High-Level Committee that recommended simultaneous elections, not the JPC.
Arjun Ram Meghwal
Wrong. As Union Law Minister he introduced the Bill in the Lok Sabha in December 2024.
P.P. Chaudhary
Correct. He heads the JPC on the 'One Nation, One Election' Bills, and still did so in 2026.
Om Birla
Wrong. He is the Speaker of the Lok Sabha; he does not chair the JPC.

points: Two different bodies: Kovind committee (government, report March 2024) and the JPC (Parliament, examining the Bill).
POL-9.5.3-Q56.also: The JPC chairman has signalled 2029 as a realistic rollout target.

POL-9.6.1-Q01.lead: Option 2: 'floor crossing' and 'carpet crossing' both mean defection, a legislator leaving his party for another.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Walk-out from the House
Wrong. A walk-out is a protest in which members leave the House for a while; they keep their party.
Defection of legislators
Correct. The terms come from a member physically crossing the floor to sit with the other side; the Tenth Schedule targets this.
Filibustering a bill
Wrong. Filibuster means delaying a bill by long speeches or tactics.
Cross-voting in Rajya Sabha polls
Wrong. Cross-voting is voting against the party line in one vote; the member does not change his party.

points: 'Party hopping' is another name for defection.
The 52nd Amendment (1985) added the Tenth Schedule to curb it.

POL-9.6.1-Q02.lead: Option 4: Haryana MLA Gaya Lal changed parties three times in 1967, giving rise to the phrase 'Aya Ram Gaya Ram'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Punjab
Wrong. Haryana had been carved out of Punjab in 1966; the episode happened in the new state of Haryana.
Uttar Pradesh
Wrong. UP also saw defections after 1967, but the phrase came from Gaya Lal of Haryana.
Bihar
Wrong. Bihar also saw defections in that period, but not the incident behind the phrase.
Haryana
Correct. Gaya Lal, an MLA of Haryana, switched parties three times in 1967.

points: The phrase came to mean any politician who keeps changing parties.
Such defections after the 1967 elections led to demands for an anti-defection law.

POL-9.6.1-Q03.lead: Option 2: Pendekanti Venkatasubbaiah moved the first resolution on defection in the 4th Lok Sabha in 1967.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Dinesh Goswami
Wrong. He headed the 1990 committee on electoral reforms.
Pendekanti Venkatasubbaiah
Correct. His 1967 resolution led to a committee on defections, the first step towards the law.
Rajiv Gandhi
Wrong. He was Prime Minister when the 52nd Amendment was passed in 1985, much later.
Rabi Ray
Wrong. He was a later Lok Sabha Speaker (1989-91), not the mover of the 1967 resolution.

points: Timeline: 1967 resolution → 52nd Amendment (1985).

POL-9.6.1-Q04.lead: Option 4: the anti-defection law (52nd Amendment, 1985) was passed when Rajiv Gandhi was Prime Minister.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Indira Gandhi
Wrong. Her terms ended in 1977 and 1984; the anti-defection law was not passed under her.
V.P. Singh
Wrong. He became PM in 1989, after the law; his government set up the Goswami Committee in 1990.
Morarji Desai
Wrong. He was PM in 1977-79; the law was not passed in his time.
Rajiv Gandhi
Correct. The 52nd Amendment Act of 1985 added the Tenth Schedule during his government.

POL-9.6.1-Q06.lead: Option 2: an independent member who joins any political party after his election is disqualified.

Correct?

is disqualified

is safe if he joins within one year
Wrong. There is no grace period for independents.

Wrong. The Schedule covers party members, independents and nominated members.

points: The six-month window exists only for nominated members.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Not disqualified, as he joined within six months

Wrong. The presiding officer has no power to condone; condonation is by the party for whip breaches.

Wrong. The law gives them six months to join one.
Not disqualified only if he was a party member earlier
Wrong. Earlier party membership is irrelevant; only the six-month time limit matters.

points: Critics call the different treatment of independents (no window) and nominated members (six months) illogical.

POL-9.6.1-Q08.lead: Option 4: defection cases are decided by the presiding officer of the member's own House; for a Legislative Council it is the Chairman.

Correct. The Tenth Schedule makes the presiding officer of the House the deciding authority.

After Kihoto Hollohan (1992), the decision is subject to judicial review.

POL-9.6.1-Q09.lead: Option 1: in Kihoto Hollohan v Zachillhu (1992), the Supreme Court struck down the 'finality' clause and held the presiding officer's decision open to judicial review.

head: Option

Correct?

Wrong. This 1973 case gave the basic structure doctrine.

points: Review is limited to grounds like mala fides and perversity.
The Court upheld giving the presiding officer the power to decide.

POL-9.6.1-Q10.lead: Option 3: Kihoto Hollohan held that the presiding officer acts as a tribunal while deciding defection cases, so his decision is open to judicial review.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Agent of the President
Wrong. The President has no role in defection cases.
Executive authority
Wrong. The decision is a quasi-judicial ruling, not an executive act.
Tribunal
Correct. Like any tribunal, he decides disputes, and his decision can be reviewed by courts.
Arm of the Election Commission
Wrong. The EC has no role in defection; it advises only on other disqualifications under Articles 103 and 192.

points: Link: tribunal → judicial review possible.
The Court rejected the argument that giving this power to the presiding officer is invalid for political bias.

POL-9.6.1-Q11.lead: Option 3: Ravi S. Naik (1994). The SC held that 'voluntarily giving up membership' can be inferred from a member's conduct; a formal resignation is not needed.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Kihoto Hollohan vs Zachillhu (1992)
Upheld the Tenth Schedule but held the presiding officer's decision open to judicial review.
Rajendra Singh Rana case (2007)
Held that the Speaker's failure to decide a petition, and acceptance of a 'split' without proper enquiry, can be examined by courts.
Ravi S. Naik vs Union of India (1994)
Held that conduct, such as going to the Governor with a rival group to withdraw support, can show a member has voluntarily given up party membership.
Ramesh Jarkiholi case (2019)
The Karnataka case of 17 MLAs; disqualification upheld but the members were allowed to contest by-elections.

points: The Tenth Schedule disqualifies a member who 'voluntarily gives up' membership of his party (LX p0830).

Memory hook: Naik = 'Not In words, but in Konduct'.

POL-9.6.1-Q12.lead: Option 1. In G. Viswanathan (1996) the SC held that an expelled member continues to belong to his original party for the Tenth Schedule; if he joins another party, he is deemed to have voluntarily given up membership.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Deemed to have voluntarily given up membership; can be disqualified
Correct: expulsion does not end his link with the party that set him up, so joining a new party counts as giving it up.
Protected because expulsion was by the party
Wrong: expulsion protects him only while he stays unattached; joining another party is his own voluntary act.
Becomes an independent and is safe
Wrong: an expelled member is not treated as an independent; even a real independent is disqualified if he joins a party (LX p0830).
Disqualified only by the Governor
Wrong: Tenth Schedule questions are decided by the presiding officer of the House, not the Governor (LX p0831).

points: The rule stops parties and members from using 'expulsion' as a back door to defect without penalty.
LX also notes, as a criticism, that the law does not provide for expulsion of a legislator for activities outside the legislature (LX p0832).

POL-9.6.1-Q13.lead: Option 3: Rajendra Singh Rana vs Swami Prasad Maurya (2007), arising from the UP Speaker accepting a claimed BSP 'split'. The SC held that the Speaker's failure to decide, or acceptance of a split/merger without proper enquiry, is open to judicial review.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Subhash Desai vs Principal Secretary
The 2023 Maharashtra (Shiv Sena) Constitution Bench case on the Governor's floor-test call and the party whip.
G. Viswanathan vs TN Speaker
The 1996 case holding that an expelled member who joins another party can be disqualified.
Rajendra Singh Rana vs Swami Prasad Maurya
The 2007 UP case on the Speaker's inaction and acceptance of a 'split'; held reviewable by courts.
Keisham Meghachandra Singh vs Manipur Speaker
The 2020 case saying Speakers should ordinarily decide petitions within three months and suggesting an independent tribunal.

points: Kihoto Hollohan (1992) had already said the presiding officer acts as a tribunal and is subject to judicial review (LX p0831).
Rana extended this logic to a Speaker's failure to act at all.

POL-9.6.1-Q14.lead: Option 2: Mizoram. Lalduhoma was the first Lok Sabha member disqualified under the anti-defection law (1988); he later led the ZPM and became Mizoram Chief Minister in December 2023.

Not his state; some guides wrongly print Nagaland, so be careful.

POL-9.6.1-Q15.lead: Option 1: Chairman M. Venkaiah Naidu. For a Rajya Sabha member, the Tenth Schedule question is decided by the Chairman of the Rajya Sabha (LX p0319).

What it is / means
Correct?

Lok Sabha Speaker Sumitra Mahajan
Wrong: the Speaker decides only for Lok Sabha members.

POL-9.6.1-Q16.lead: Option 4: Three months. In Keisham Meghachandra Singh (2020) the SC said the Speaker should ordinarily decide a petition within three months and suggested Parliament create an independent tribunal.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Three months

POL-9.6.1-Q17.lead: Option 3. In the 2019 Karnataka case the SC upheld the Speaker's disqualification of 17 MLAs but held he could not bar them from contesting till the end of the term, so they could contest by-elections.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Wrong: the Court upheld the disqualification itself.

Correct: disqualification ends membership of that House but does not by itself bar re-election.

Wrong: the Election Commission has no role in deciding Tenth Schedule questions; the presiding officer decides (LX p0831).

The Court also reviewed the Speaker's order, following Kihoto Hollohan (LX p0831).

POL-9.6.1-Q18.lead: Option 4. Failing to distinguish dissent from defection is a criticism of the law, not an advantage (LX p0832).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Reduces expense on by-elections
A listed advantage: it reduces non-developmental expenditure on irregular elections (LX p0832).

NOT an advantage: LX's first criticism is that the law does not differentiate dissent from defection and curbs freedom of conscience.

POL-9.6.1-Q19.lead: Option 1: Rajiv Gandhi, the then Prime Minister, described the anti-defection law as the 'first step towards cleaning-up public life' (LX p0831).

POL-9.6.1-Q25.lead: Option 1: Article 361B, inserted by the 91st Amendment, disqualifies a defection-disqualified member from holding any remunerative political post (LX p0985, p0833).

What it is / means
Correct?

POL-9.6.1-Q26.lead: Option 3: the 91st Amendment, 2003 deleted the exception for a 'split' by one-third of a legislature party (LX p0830).

Wrong: the presiding officer still decides (LX p0831).

POL-9.6.1-Q29.lead: Option 2. Under Art 75(1B), a member disqualified for defection cannot be appointed minister until his term ends or he is re-elected, whichever is earlier (LX p0833).

Correct: Article 75(1B) bars a member disqualified for defection from being a minister until his term ends or he is re-elected.

Wrong: Art 75(1B) covers MPs and Art 164(1B) covers state legislators (LX p0833).

True/False

Correct?

Ten years is wrong; the Act uses five years.

Correct: the 2019 Act limits SPG to the sitting PM and immediate family residing with them, and to a former PM and family at their official residence for five years after demitting office.

What it is / means

points: ST lists are notified by the President under Article 342 and changed only by a law of Parliament, which is why a Bill was needed.

head: Part
True/False
Why

True
True. Under the basic structure doctrine, courts can strike down amendments even if procedure was followed.
R
True
True. The doctrine treats the amending power as limited.

points: Does R explain A? Yes. A limited power means amendments beyond the limit are invalid even if passed correctly.
Option 2 (Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A) fails: R does explain A, so "does not explain" is wrong.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (A is false, but R is true) fails: A is true, not false.

POL-6.8.1-PG02.lead: Judicial activism is a way judges work, not a basic feature of the Constitution.

head: Option
Meaning
Fits?
rows: Judicial review
Courts can strike down laws and orders that break the Constitution (e.g. a law against Fundamental Rights is declared void).
No — it IS a basic feature (Indira Gandhi 1975, Minerva Mills 1980, L. Chandra Kumar 1997).
Judicial activism ✓
A style of working: judges take an active, bold role to protect rights and push the government to do its duty (e.g. PIL cases). Opposite of 'judicial restraint'.
Yes — it is only an approach of judges, never declared a basic feature.
Secularism
The State has no religion of its own and treats all religions equally.
No — it IS a basic feature (Kesavananda 1973; S.R. Bommai 1994).
Federalism / Federation
Power is shared between the Centre and the States, each with its own area.
No — it IS a basic feature (Kesavananda 1973; S.R. Bommai 1994).

points: Basic structure = core parts of the Constitution that even Parliament cannot destroy by amendment (Kesavananda Bharati, 1973).
Judicial review, secularism and federalism are parts of the Constitution itself; judicial activism is only how judges use their power.
Easy check: a basic feature is something IN the Constitution; activism is a behaviour OF the court.

Contains forms of oaths and affirmations.

Memory hook: 'First things first: First Schedule = the country's map'.

POL-6.9.1-PG09-04.lead: Option 4: under the former Article 370 arrangement, residuary powers for J&K lay with the State legislature, not with Parliament.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament
For other States residuary powers rest with Parliament (Article 248), but J&K was the exception under Article 370.
The President
The President applied Union provisions to J&K by orders under Article 370, but residuary legislative power was not his.
The Governor of J&K
The Governor (earlier Sadar-i-Riyasat) was the executive head; he did not hold residuary legislative power.
The State legislature of J&K
Residuary powers (except certain matters like terrorism) belonged to the J&K legislature, reflecting its special status.

points: Concept: 'residuary' means subjects not in any of the three Lists.
Article 370 provisions were made inoperative in August 2019; the Supreme Court upheld this in December 2023.

POL-6.9.1-PG09-05.lead: Option 3: the doctrine of paramountcy (Article 254) means a Union law prevails over a conflicting State law on a Concurrent List subject.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: State law prevails on State List subjects
This describes the State's own field, not paramountcy; paramountcy is about conflicts where both can legislate.
Courts decide which law is better
Courts only check repugnancy; they do not choose the 'better' law.
Union law prevails on a Concurrent subject
Article 254(1): in case of repugnancy on a Concurrent matter, the parliamentary law prevails and the State law is void to that extent.
President's ordinance prevails over all laws
An ordinance has only the force of an Act of Parliament; it cannot override the Constitution.

points: Exception, Article 254(2): a State law reserved for and assented to by the President prevails in that State.
Even then Parliament can later override it by a fresh law.

POL-6.9.1-PG09-06.lead: Option 1: under Article 239(2) a Governor who administers an adjoining UT acts independently of his State Council of Ministers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Independently of his State Council of Ministers
Correct; for the UT he is the President's Administrator, so his State ministry has no role.
On the advice of his State Council of Ministers
Wrong; that ministry is answerable to the State legislature, not for the UT.
On the advice of the State Chief Justice
Wrong; the judiciary does not advise on administration.
With the consent of the State legislature
Wrong; the State legislature has no power over a UT.

points: Example: the Governor of Punjab is the Administrator of Chandigarh.
He acts as the President's agent, as Article 239(1) makes the President the administrator of every UT.

POL-7.2.1-PG0403.lead: Option 3: a Legislative Council can only delay an ordinary bill (3 months + 1 month); the Assembly's will finally prevails.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. It can call a joint sitting
Wrong: there is no joint sitting in State legislatures; Article 108 joint sitting exists only for Parliament.
2. It can kill the bill permanently
Wrong: the Council cannot kill a bill; if the Assembly passes it again, it is deemed passed by both Houses.
3. It can only delay the bill
Correct: under Article 197 the Council can hold an ordinary bill for at most three months the first time and one month the second time, so its power is only delaying.

Wrong: the Governor does not decide disputes between the two Houses.

points: For a Money Bill the Council can delay only 14 days and can make only recommendations.
Compare: the Rajya Sabha has nearly equal power on ordinary bills, and a deadlock is solved by a joint sitting; the Council has no such equality.

The Constitution does not say the bill lapses. A bill lapses only on dissolution of Lok Sabha under Article 107(5); if the President has notified a joint sitting before dissolution, it does not lapse even then.

False
The proviso to Article 111 allows return only of non-money bills; a Money Bill can only be assented to or refused, because it is introduced with his prior recommendation.

Ending the life of Lok Sabha by the President (Article 85(2)); it works against the legislature, not for it.

Committees like the Public Accounts Committee and Estimates Committee examine spending; this is legislative control.

A motion to set aside normal business to discuss an urgent public matter; this is legislative control.

POL-7.3.1-PG03-01.lead: Option 2: Lord Morley described the Prime Minister as 'primus inter pares' and the 'key stone of the cabinet arch'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

Nominal head of State in India; acts on ministerial advice (Article 74), so he is not the central stone of the cabinet.

Head of the Council of Ministers; ministers are appointed on his advice and the ministry falls if he resigns. Morley's phrase describes this central position.
The Speaker
Presiding officer of the Lok Sabha; not a member of the cabinet at all.
The Chief Justice
Head of the judiciary; has no role in the cabinet.

points: A keystone is the top central stone of an arch; remove it and the whole arch collapses, as the ministry dissolves when the PM resigns or dies.

True

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Administration of Justice
True (Reserved)
Justice was a sensitive law-and-order subject, so the 1919 Act kept it with the Governor and his executive council, who were not answerable to the legislature.

False (Transferred)
Local self-government was a 'nation-building' subject handed to Indian ministers who were responsible to the provincial legislative council.

True (Reserved)
Land revenue and finance were the money base of the administration, so the British kept them Reserved under the Governor.
4. Police
True (Reserved)
Police, like justice and prisons, was a control subject that the British would not hand to elected ministers, so it was Reserved.

points: Concept: dyarchy (double rule) split provincial subjects into Reserved (Governor + executive council, not responsible to the legislature) and Transferred (Governor + ministers responsible to the legislature).

Memory hook: 'control' subjects (police, justice, prisons, land revenue, finance) were Reserved; 'welfare' subjects (education, health, local self-government, agriculture) were Transferred.

B. In a federal system it is about judiciary deciding ultra vires / intra vires
False (as framed)
Ambedkar said this power exists anyway in a federal Constitution; 'due process' would add a further power to judge whether a law is fair, so B does not describe due process.
C. It involves adjustment of the federal arrangement
True (official key)
Taken as true by the examiner: allowing due process would change the balance between legislature and courts in the federal set-up.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes B and drops A; option 2 wrongly includes B; option 3 includes B and drops C.
The Assembly adopted 'procedure established by law' (from Japan) in Article 21 instead of American 'due process'; Maneka Gandhi (1978) later read fairness into it (LX p148).

APPSC-G2-2017-P2-Q094.lead: Option 4: Article 43 asks the State to secure a living wage, a decent standard of life and full enjoyment of leisure and social and cultural opportunities for workers.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Article 39
Wrong: Article 39 covers livelihood, distribution of resources, equal pay and protection of workers and children, but not 'leisure and cultural opportunities'.
2. Article 40
Wrong: Article 40 is about organising village panchayats as units of self-government.
3. Article 42
Wrong: Article 42 is about just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief.
4. Article 43
Correct: these exact words come from Article 43, which also asks the State to promote cottage industries in rural areas.

points: A living wage is more than a minimum wage: it covers a decent life, not mere survival (LX p161).
Memory hook: 42 = work conditions + maternity; 43 = living wage + cottage industries; 43A = workers in management; 43B = co-operatives.

APPSC-G2-2025-C-101.lead: Statements A, B and D are true and C is false. So the answer is option 1 (A, B and D only).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
The 97th Amendment (2011) gave co-operative societies constitutional status and protection.
B
True
It added the words 'or co-operative societies' to Article 19(1)(c), making the right to form them a Fundamental Right.
C
False
It added Part IX-B (Articles 243ZH to 243ZT), not Part X-B; Part IX is Panchayats and IX-A is Municipalities.
D
True
It inserted Article 43B, which asks the State to promote voluntary formation, autonomous working, democratic control and professional management of co-operatives (LX p163).

points: Option 2 (A, B and C only) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement C, which is false; it leaves out true statement D.
Option 3 (A and B only) is wrong: it leaves out true statement D.
Option 4 (All of the above) is wrong: it wrongly includes statement C, which is false.
APPSC-G2-2025-C-101.also: In Rajendra Shah (Gujarat HC 2013; SC 2021) Part IX-B was struck down (SC: for State co-operatives) for want of State ratification, but the Art 19(1)(c) and 43B changes stand.

APPSC-G2-2025-C-102.lead: Option 2: Both A and R are true, but R does not explain A — Article 37 itself makes DPSPs non-justiciable; their role as a guide to law-making is a separate point.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
True. Article 37 says the Directive Principles 'shall not be enforceable by any court' (non-justiciable).
R
True
True. Article 37 also says they are fundamental in governance and the State must apply them in making laws, so they guide legislation.

points: Does R explain A? No (official key 2). Non-enforceability comes from the express words of Article 37, chosen for practical reasons (lack of resources, diversity). Guiding legislation is their role; it is not the reason they are unenforceable.
Option 1 (Both A and R are true, and R explains A) fails: R is true but is not the reason for A.
Option 3 (A is true, but R is false) fails: R is true, not false.
Option 4 (Both A and R are false) fails: both statements are true.

APPSC-G2-2025-C-112.lead: Option 2: both statements are present in the Constitution; A is Article 39(b) and B is Article 39(c).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Both Statements (A) and (B) are not there
Wrong: both statements are in Part IV, so saying neither is there is incorrect.
2. Both Statements (A) and (B) are present
Correct: Article 39(b) speaks of distributing ownership and control of material resources for the common good, and Article 39(c) of preventing concentration of wealth and means of production.
3. Only Statement (A) is there
Wrong: Statement B is also in the Constitution as Article 39(c).
4. Only Statement (B) is there
Wrong: Statement A is also in the Constitution as Article 39(b).

points: Both are Socialistic principles in the usual classification (LX p161).
Laws made to give effect to Article 39(b) and (c) get protection under Article 31C from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
APPSC-G2-2025-C-112.also: Property Owners Association (2024, 9 judges): not every private resource is a 'material resource of the community'.

APPSC-G2-2025-C-090.lead: Option 2: the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002 added the eleventh duty, Article 51A(k).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Correct amendment number but wrong year; the 86th Amendment was enacted in 2002.
The Act that inserted Article 21A, recast Article 45 and added duty 51A(k) on education of children aged 6–14.
There is no 96th Amendment of 2001; the 96th Amendment came only in 2011.
The 96th Amendment (2011) substituted 'Odia' for 'Oriya' in the Eighth Schedule and has nothing to do with duties.

points: Article 51A(k): a parent or guardian must provide opportunities for education to his child or ward between six and fourteen years.
The first ten duties came through the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (Part IVA); the eleventh came in 2002.
Memory hook: 86th Amendment = the 'education package' (21A right, 45 DPSP, 51A(k) duty).
APPSC-G2-2025-C-090.also: The 86th Amendment came into force on 1 April 2010.

APPSC-G2-2025-C-095.lead: Option 1: the Sardar Swaran Singh Committee (1976) recommended adding Fundamental Duties.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Swaran Singh Committee
Set up by the Congress Party in 1976 during the Emergency; recommended a separate chapter on Fundamental Duties.
Justice Verma Committee
The 1999 committee on Fundamental Duties of Citizens; it only listed existing laws that already enforce some duties, long after they were added.
Ram Nandan Committee
The Ram Nandan Prasad Committee (1993) identified the creamy layer among Other Backward Classes.
J. B. Kripalani Committee
Acharya J. B. Kripalani was a freedom fighter and Constituent Assembly member; no committee of his recommended Fundamental Duties.

points: The 42nd Amendment, 1976 added Part IVA with one Article, 51A, listing ten duties.
The Committee suggested eight duties, but Parliament added ten.
Do not confuse the 1976 Swaran Singh Committee (adding duties) with the 1999 Verma Committee (implementing duties).

APPSC-G2-2025-C-141.lead: Option 3: protecting the elderly, differently abled and children is not one of the eleven duties in Article 51A.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Safeguard public property and abjure violence
This is a real Fundamental Duty, Article 51A(i), so it is not the answer to 'not a duty'.
Value and preserve composite culture
This is a real Fundamental Duty, Article 51A(f), so it is not the answer to 'not a duty'.
Protect the elderly, differently abled and children
No clause of Article 51A says this; care of the aged and disabled belongs to Article 41 (a Directive Principle addressed to the State).
Promote harmony and common brotherhood
This is the duty in Article 51A(e), which also asks citizens to renounce practices against the dignity of women.

points: The question asks which is NOT a duty, so the one item missing from Article 51A is the answer.
The only child-related duty is 51A(k): parents or guardians must provide education to children aged 6–14.

APPSC-G2-2024-A-79.lead: Option 4: the Linguistic Provinces Commission was appointed in June 1948 under Justice S.K. Dhar, so it is called the Dhar Commission.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1948, Justice Fazal Ali
Fazl Ali chaired the States Reorganisation Commission appointed in December 1953, not the 1948 commission, so the name is wrong.
1949, Pattabhi Sitaramayya
Pattabhi Sitaramayya was one of the three members of the Congress JVP Committee (appointed December 1948), not chairman of a Constituent Assembly commission.
1950, Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
Patel too was only a member of the JVP Committee; the year 1950 and the role are both wrong.
1948, Justice S.K. Dhar
The Constituent Assembly President appointed the Linguistic Provinces Commission under S.K. Dhar in June 1948; it reported in December 1948.

points: The Dhar Commission recommended reorganisation on administrative convenience rather than language.
The JVP Committee (Jawaharlal Nehru, Vallabhbhai Patel, Pattabhi Sitaramayya) also rejected language as the basis in its April 1949 report.
Order to remember: Dhar (1948) → JVP (1948-49) → Andhra State (1953) → Fazl Ali SRC (1953-55).

APPSC-G2-2025-C-134.lead: Option 1: the Jammu and Kashmir Reorganisation Act, 2019 came into effect on 31 October 2019, its 'appointed day'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 31st October 2019
The appointed day fixed under the Act; on this day the State of J&K was replaced by two Union territories.
31st October 2018
Wrong year: in 2018 J&K was still a State (under Governor's/President's rule); the Act did not yet exist.
31st October 2017
Wrong year: no reorganisation law existed in 2017.
31st October 2020
Wrong year: by 2020 the two UTs had already existed for a year; in January 2020 the DNH and Daman-Diu merger took effect.

points: The Act received Presidential assent on 9 August 2019, days after Article 370 was made inoperative (5-6 August 2019).
It created the UT of Jammu and Kashmir (with a legislature) and the UT of Ladakh (without a legislature).
31 October is also Sardar Patel's birth anniversary (National Unity Day), a useful memory hook.

APPSC-G2-2025-C-62.lead: Option 1: Andhra State was formed on 1 October 1953, the first State created on a linguistic basis.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1st October 1953
The day the Telugu-speaking areas of Madras State became the separate Andhra State, with Kurnool as capital.
1st November 1953
Wrong month: 1 November is the date of the 1956 reorganisation, which students often mix up with 1953.
1st November 1956
This is the formation of Andhra Pradesh (Andhra State + Telangana region of Hyderabad) under the States Reorganisation Act, 1956, not of Andhra State.
26th January 1950
The day the Constitution came into force; Andhra was then still part of Madras State.

points: Andhra State followed Potti Sriramulu's death on 15 December 1952 after a 56-day fast.
Andhra State (1953) and Andhra Pradesh (1956) are different: first came the State, then the merger.

APPSC-G2-2025-C-63.lead: Option 2 (B, A, C, D): Dhar Commission (1948) → Visalandhra Mahasabha (1949) → Swami Sitaram's fast (1951) → States Reorganisation Commission (1953).

head: Event
Year
Why it comes here
rows: B. Dhar Commission
Appointed in June 1948 by the Constituent Assembly President; it is the earliest event.
A. Visalandhra Mahasabha
Formed to demand one State for all Telugu people (Andhra + Telangana areas); it comes after the Dhar report.
C. Swami Sitaram's fast
Swami Sitaram fasted for Andhra State in 1951 and gave it up on assurances; this was before Potti Sriramulu's 1952 fast.
D. States Reorganisation Commission
The Fazl Ali Commission was appointed in December 1953, after Andhra State was formed, so it is last.

points: Option 1 (A, B, C, D) wrongly puts the Mahasabha before the 1948 Dhar Commission.
Option 3 (C, A, B, D) wrongly starts with the 1951 fast.
Option 4 (D, C, A, B) puts the 1953 SRC first, which is the latest event.
Do not confuse Swami Sitaram's fast (1951) with Potti Sriramulu's fast (1952).

APPSC-G2-2024-A-080.lead: All three statements are false, so the answer is option 4 (None of the above).

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: I. Started in 1983
False. The Assam Movement led by AASU started in 1979, not 1983.
False
II. Safeguards for Bangladeshi migrants
False. It aimed to detect and expel illegal migrants and to give safeguards to the Assamese people (Clause 6), not to migrants.
False
III. Ended on 15 August 1989
False. The Assam Accord was signed on 15 August 1985, not 1989.
False

points: Options 1, 2 and 3 each accept at least one false statement.
Section 6A of the Citizenship Act (1985 amendment) gave legal effect to the Accord: cut-offs 1 January 1966 and 25 March 1971.

APPSC-G2-2025-A-130.lead: Option 1: a no-confidence motion, if passed in the Lok Sabha, forces the whole Council of Ministers to resign, so it is Parliament's strongest weapon.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. No Confidence Motion
A no-confidence motion says the Lok Sabha has lost faith in the Council of Ministers; if it is passed, the entire ministry must resign, so it is the ultimate check.
2. Zero Hour
Zero Hour is the informal time right after Question Hour (an Indian innovation of 1962) to raise urgent matters; it only draws attention and cannot remove a government.
3. Question Hour
Question Hour is the first hour of a sitting when members ask ministers questions; it exposes the government but has no power to remove it.
4. Election
Elections are the people's check on the government, not a device Parliament uses against the executive.

points: Article 75(3): the Council of Ministers is collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha; a no-confidence motion is the means of enforcing that responsibility.
It needs the support of 50 members to be admitted, can be moved only in the Lok Sabha, and need not state reasons.
Question Hour and Zero Hour are softer tools of accountability; only the no-confidence motion carries the penalty of removal.

APPSC-G2-2017-P2-Q148.lead: Option 3: dissolution of the House is not a legislative control over administration; it is an executive power over the legislature.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Questions
Questions are a legislative control: members ask ministers about administration during Question Hour and get answers on record.
2. Resolution
Resolutions are a legislative control: the House can discuss and express its view on policy and administration.
3. Dissolution of the House
Correct: dissolution is done by the President or Governor on the Cabinet's advice (Articles 85(2)(b) and 174(2)(b)); it is control by the executive over the House, not the reverse.
4. No confidence motion
The no-confidence motion is the strongest legislative control: if passed, the Council of Ministers must resign.

points: Legislative control devices let the House question, debate, censure or remove the government.
Dissolution works the other way, so it does not fit.

LX-PQ-132.lead: Option 2: both statements are true, but Statement II does not explain Statement I.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Under Article 113 only the Lok Sabha votes the demands for grants.
R
True
A Money Bill cannot be introduced in the Rajya Sabha (Article 109), nor can a taxing Finance Bill (Article 117).

points: Does R explain A? No: the power to vote demands is given by Article 113, while the rule on introduction of Bills comes from Articles 109 and 117, so R is a separate rule, not the reason.
Option 1 fails because R does not explain A.
Options 3 and 4 fail because both statements are true.

LX-PQ-187.lead: Statements 3, 4 and 5 are correct, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Parliament can increase a tax.
False
Parliament cannot increase a tax; under Article 117 only the government, on the President's recommendation, can propose new or higher taxes.
2. Parliament cannot reduce a tax.
False
This is wrong: Parliament is free to reduce a tax, since reducing a burden on the people needs no recommendation.
3. Parliament can abolish a tax.
True
Parliament can abolish a tax; Article 117 bars only proposals to impose or increase a tax without recommendation.
4. Parliament cannot increase a tax.
True
Parliament cannot increase a tax on its own; the proposal must come from the government with the President's recommendation.
5. Parliament can reduce a tax.
True
Parliament can reduce a proposed tax, because a motion to reduce a tax needs no President's recommendation.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes statement 1.
Option 3 wrongly includes statement 2.
Option 4 leaves out statement 5.

LX-UPSC-2013-Q06.lead: Only statement 2 is correct, so the answer is option 2.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. The Chairman and Deputy Chairman of the Rajya Sabha are not members.
False
The Chairman (Vice-President) is not a member, but the Deputy Chairman is elected from among its members.
2. Nominated members vote for the Vice-President but not the President.
True
Nominated members are part of the Vice-Presidential electoral college but not the Presidential one.

points: Option 1 wrongly includes statement 1.
Option 3 wrongly includes statement 1.
Option 4 fails because statement 2 is true.

APPSC-G2-2017-P2-Q138.lead: Option 3: under Article 169, the State Assembly passes a resolution by a special majority and then Parliament makes a law to create or abolish the Council.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: 1. Constitutional Amendment with simple majority
Wrong: no constitutional amendment is needed; Article 169(3) says such a law is not an amendment under Article 368.
2. Constitutional Amendment by 2/3 majority
Wrong: a two-thirds constitutional amendment is not required; Parliament passes an ordinary law by simple majority.
3. On the recommendation of State Legislature by passing a resolution with 2/3 majority, followed by an act of Parliament
Correct: the Assembly resolution needs a majority of its total membership and two-thirds of those present and voting; Parliament then acts by simple majority.
4. Parliament directly with simple majority
Wrong: Parliament cannot act on its own; the initiative must come from the State Assembly's resolution.

points: Parliament is not bound to act on the resolution; it 'may' make the law.
Example: Andhra Pradesh's Council was abolished in 1985 and revived in 2007.

LX-PQ-084.lead: Statements 1, 3 and 4 are true, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Statutory body
True
CAT was set up under the Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985, passed by Parliament under Article 323A (LX p525).
2. Members only from administrative background
False
Members are drawn from both judicial and administrative streams (LX p525).
3. Not bound by CPC
True
CAT is not bound by the Civil Procedure Code, 1908 and follows principles of natural justice.
4. Covers AIS, Central services and Central posts
True
Its jurisdiction extends to All-India Services, Central civil services, civil posts under the Centre and civilian defence employees.

points: Options 1 and 4 include the false statement 2.
Option 2 (1 and 4) leaves out the true statement 3.
Excluded from CAT: defence forces members, Supreme Court staff and Parliament secretariat staff.

LX-PQ-141.lead: Statements 3 and 4 are true, so the answer is option 3.

head: Statement
True/False
Why
rows: 1. Established under Article 312-A
False
CAT comes from Article 323A, added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976 (LX p525).
2. Set up by Presidential order
False
It was set up under a law of Parliament, not by an order of the President.
3. Set up in 1985
True
CAT was set up in 1985 with its principal bench at New Delhi.
4. Set up by an Act of Parliament
True
The Administrative Tribunals Act, 1985 created it.

points: Options 1, 2 and 4 each contain at least one false statement (1 or 2).
Article 323A only enables Parliament; the Act actually creates the tribunal.

PRAC-POL-01A436252B60.lead: Option 1: under Art 253 Parliament may legislate on any subject, including State List subjects, to implement international treaties.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: Parliament may legislate on any item in the State List for implementing international treaties
Correct: Art 253 overrides the division of Lists for implementing treaties, agreements and conventions.
✓ Correct
Parliament may legislate on any item irrespective of the lists but only with 2/3 majority
Wrong, because Art 253 needs only an ordinary law; no special majority is required.
✗ Wrong
The Union Government can implement international treaties without Parliament's intervention
Wrong where the treaty needs a change in law; such implementation needs a law of Parliament under Art 253.
✗ Wrong
International treaties require ratification by both Houses of Parliament
Wrong: the Constitution has no requirement that both Houses ratify treaties.
✗ Wrong

points: Making a treaty is an executive act; giving it force as law is Parliament's job under Art 253.
Art 253 needs no state's consent (unlike Art 252).

LX-PQ-018.lead: Option 3: Parliament regulates the recruitment and conditions of service of All-India Services; it did so through the All-India Services Act, 1951.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?
rows: President of India
Rules are made by the Central government, but only under the authority of the Act of Parliament, so the President is not the source.
✗ Wrong
Constitution of India
The Constitution does not itself lay down service conditions; it leaves them to Parliament's law.
✗ Wrong
Parliament of India
Correct: the AIS Act, 1951 is Parliament's law governing these services.
✓ Correct
Union Public Service Commission
UPSC conducts recruitment exams and advises; it does not decide service conditions.
✗ Wrong

points: Under the 1951 Act the Centre makes rules in consultation with the state governments.

LX-PQ-019.lead: Option 2: both true, but R does not explain A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
Civil servants are barred by conduct rules from joining parties, campaigning or contesting elections.
R
True
Like every adult citizen, civil servants have the right to vote (Art 326).

points: Does R explain A? No. The right to vote is a citizen's right; the restrictions come from the need for a neutral civil service. One does not cause the other.
Option 1 fails: both are true, but R does not give the reason for A.
Option 3 fails: R is true. Option 4 fails: A is true.

LX-PQ-020.lead: Option 1: both true and R explains A.

head: Part
True/False
Why
rows: A
True
An AIS officer working in a state can appeal against a State Government order to the President.
R
True
Art 311(1): no civil servant can be dismissed or removed by an authority subordinate to the one that appointed him.

Option 2 fails: R is not a separate fact here; it is the very reason for A.
Options 3 and 4 fail: both A and R are true.

LX-PQ-053.lead: Statements 2, 4 and 5 are correct, so book key option 3.

True/False
Why

False
LX: the Vice-Chairperson is appointed by the Prime Minister, who is the Chairperson.

LX-PQ-074.lead: Option 2: a new All-India Service is created only by an Act of Parliament, after a Rajya Sabha resolution (Art 312).

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

The Rajya Sabha resolution (two-thirds of members present and voting) is only a precondition; it does not itself create the service.
✗ Wrong
An act of Parliament
Correct: LX says a new All-India Service can be created only by an act of Parliament.
✓ Correct
An order of the President

✗ Wrong

LX-PQ-081.lead: Option 4: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, the chief protagonist of All-India Services in the Constituent Assembly, is called the 'Father of All-India Services'.

head: Option
What it is / means
Correct?

✗ Wrong

A Governor-General linked with organising the civil service in British India, not the post-1947 AIS.
✗ Wrong
B.R. Ambedkar

Member?

True/False
Why

True

LX-UPSC-2013-Q16.lead: None of the three is mentioned in the Constitution, so option 4.

In Constitution?
Why

No

2. Planning Commission
